The *Mahāvibhāṣā* explains that this is because, among all the realms of rebirth (*gati*), the realm of the gods is superior. Some say it comes from the heavens because humans hold them in high esteem.

Others say that when one comes from the heavens, there are miraculous transformations (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*), whereas such things do not occur when coming from the human realm. Furthermore, it is asked: for what reason does the Bodhisattva not [attain parinirvāṇa] immediately?
He attained Buddhahood in this heavenly realm and then came to the human world. The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* answers: "In accordance with the nature of all Buddhas' teachings.
That is to say, the World-Honored Buddhas, numbering more than the sands of the Ganges, all attain perfect enlightenment among humans.
Furthermore, the body of the celestial realm is not the basis for unsurpassed bodhi. Moreover, the faculties and natures of those in the human realm are sharp and intense in the majority.
One is able to receive the True Dharma of the Tathāgata; this is not the case for those in the celestial realms. Furthermore, there are two conditions for a Buddha to appear in the world:
first, the presence of a mind of renunciation (*saṃvega*); second, the presence of sharp and penetrating wisdom (*tīkṣṇaprajñā*). It should be known that these two exist only among the human realm.

Regarding the fifth stage, however, there are two types of paths for severing the afflictions (*kleśa*): first, the path with outflows (*sāsravamārga*); second, the path without outflows (*anāsravamārga*). As for the Bodhisattva...

Having gone forth in this final body, one immediately cultivates the path with outflows (*sāsrava-mārga*). Within the nine stages, one abandons the afflictions of seeing and cultivation belonging to the lower eight stages.

This path with outflows is able to sever the delusions only by taking delight in the higher [stages] and feeling aversion toward the lower; this applies to all except for the stage of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Since there is no higher stage to be sought after, the contaminated path (*sāsrava-mārga*) does not sever those afflictions (*kleśa*).

Nevertheless, at the time of severing the afflictions, there are likewise nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and nine paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*). This is because the afflictions to be severed are divided into nine grades (*navavidha*), and within each grade, both types of paths are present.

All paths of uninterrupted transition take the contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) of the immediately lower stage as their object, characterizing them by way of the three aspects: coarseness (*audārikatva*), suffering (*duḥkhatva*), and being an obstacle (*ādīnava*).
Regarding the aspects (*ākāra*): whichever aspect is taken, as for those aspects, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, chapter twenty-four, states:

"Because it is not tranquil, it is called 'coarse' (*audārika*); because it is not sublime, it is called 'suffering' (*duḥkha*); because it is not a renunciation, it is called an 'obstruction' (*āvaraṇa*).
One should understand that the three—tranquility, sublimity, and renunciation—are the opposites of these. At the sixth stage, beneath the Bodhi tree, [he practiced] for thirty...
Through the four applications of mindfulness, one realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. First, one abandons the afflictions of the path of seeing (*darśana-heya*).
At the time of abandoning the afflictions of the path of seeing, within the clear realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*), there are sixteen moments of mindfulness.

Immediately following the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*) roots of goodness, there arises a "receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena regarding suffering" (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*), which takes as its object the noble truth of suffering within the desire realm and is comprised of the untainted (*anāsrava*). This receptivity is called the "receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena regarding suffering. This receptivity...

When there is no longer a return to the objects of desire and suffering, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) arises; this is called the "knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering" (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna*). Question: What is meant by "knowledge of phenomena"? Answer:

It is so called because it is the first direct realization of the true reality (*tattva*) of all phenomena; therefore, it is named "knowledge of phenomena. Subsequently, taking the suffering within the two higher realms as its collective object, the "receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of suffering" (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*) arises;

this is called the "receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of suffering. Immediately following this receptivity, the "subsequent knowledge of suffering" (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) arises. Question: What is meant by [this]?

Subsequent Knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*). Answer: It is the knowledge of the subsequent objects, which is similar to the preceding [knowledge]. Furthermore, because the subsequent [knowledge] realizes its object by following the preceding one.

The old [translation] stating "inferential" (*anumāna*) is incorrect. The same applies to each of the four [knowledges] regarding the other three truths. Thus, these four sets of four constitute sixteen distinct modes of activity (*ākāra-viśeṣa*).

All of these are untainted (*anāsrava*) and have wisdom (*prajñā*) as their essence. Within the clear realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*), the sequence should be thus. However, regarding the Dharma-patience (*dharma-kṣānti*)...

Regarding wisdom (*jñāna*): one does not abandon the afflictions [of the lower stages], because those afflictions of the lower stages have already been completely abandoned. Only the subsequent patience (*anvaya-kṣānti*) and wisdom abandon the afflictions of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Next, one abandons the afflictions of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). There are eighteen moments of mind;

that is, for each of the nine grades of afflictions, there arises one uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) and one path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*). Adding these to the previous count, they total thirty-four. These thirty-four, the first three...
13. This is the mind of training of a bodhisattva; the thirty-fourth is the unawakened mind of a Buddha.

All bodhisattvas, having first definitely attained freedom from craving regarding the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), only then enter the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). Therefore, at the time of attaining Buddhahood, they do not sever the lower afflictions.
In Sanskrit, *dharma* (translated here as "Dharma"). There are two kinds of *dharma*: first, that which maintains its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); therefore, it is so named.

Regarding "dharma": the term *lakṣaṇa* (characteristic) refers to its *svabhāva* (intrinsic nature), meaning that its self-nature does not change; for example, dharmas such as form (*rūpa*) always maintain their own intrinsic natures, such as resistance (*sapratighatva*).

Second, it is called "dharma" because it serves as a guide to produce understanding in sentient beings; for example, dharmas such as impermanence (*anityatā*) produce in people the understanding of impermanence and so forth.

The Sanskrit word is *saṃgha* (translated here as "assembly"). The old translation of *saṃgha* as "harmony" (*hehé*) misses the correct meaning; however, its actual significance is as follows: [text continues].

The term *saṃgha* is translated as "community" (*zhòng*). "Harmony" (*héhé*) is the functional meaning of the *saṃgha*. This refers to four or more individuals performing legal acts (*dharmakarma*) to achieve harmony.
Therefore, the text states: "The *saṃgha* consists of four or more persons; 'harmony' means a single formal act (*karmavācanā*) and a single recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*)."
Regarding the common name "Reality" (satya): it is universally esteemed as a treasure of the age. *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, Chapter Two. Question:
For what reason are the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha called "Real"? Answer: There are six characteristics.

First is rarity, because sentient beings who lack roots of goodness cannot attain them even in hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas. Second is clarity and purity, because they are free from all...

1. It is with outflows (*sāsrava*), because it is a dharma characterized by outflows. 2. It possesses power, because it is endowed with the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) and inconceivable majestic virtue and mastery (*vaśitā*).
3. It is an adornment, because it is able to adorn the supramundane. 4. It is supreme, because it is a supramundane dharma. 5.
It is immutable, because having attained the untainted dharma (*anāsravadharma*), it cannot be moved by the eight worldly dharmas (*aṣṭalokadharma*).
Therefore, the second [section] establishes the essential nature (*svabhāva*). First, we explain that Buddha.

Regarding the Buddha’s essential nature, it is defined by excellence as the various dharmas of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) that constitute Buddhahood—namely, the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), and the knowledge of the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-samyagdṛṣṭi-jñāna*), together with their concomitants, consisting of the five untainted (*anāsrava*) aggregates.

This constitutes its essence. Nevertheless, when divided according to their meanings, they likewise possess the three types of Buddha: namely, the untainted fivefold Dharma-body (*pañcāṅga-dharmakāya*) is taken as the Dharma-Buddha;

those born in the royal palace and so forth are taken as the Reward-Buddha (*saṃbhoga-kāya*); and the manifested physical bodies that transform others throughout various realms are taken as the Transformation-Buddha (*nirmāṇa-kāya*).
Next, to clarify "Dharma": if it is named "Dharma" because it maintains its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), this then applies universally to...

All phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are now divided into four distinct categories according to their respective stages: namely, teaching (*śāsana*), principle (*nyāya*), practice (*caryā*), and fruit (*phala*). "Teaching" refers to the nature of sound, which consists of the twelvefold division of the scriptures (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*);
it is subsumed under the truths of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) and its origin (*samudaya-satya*). "Principle" refers to the principles of the Four Truths and the Sixteen Principles;

these principles of the truths are themselves subsumed within those very truths. Regarding "practice," generally speaking, there are two types: first, untainted practice (*anāsrava-caryā*); second, tainted [practice] (*sāsrava-caryā*).

Regarding the paths with outflows (*sāsrava*) and the paths without outflows (*anāsrava*): those that are exclusively paths without outflows are subsumed under the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*). Those that are paths with outflows pertain to both the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) and the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).

Herein, "path" refers specifically to the untainted [faculties], namely the two faculties of a Bodhisattva and the three faculties of a Pratyekabuddha. As for the "fruit," it refers to Nirvana as the fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*);

therefore, it is subsumed under the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). Next, regarding the essence of the Saṃgha: it refers to the Śrāvaka Saṃgha, consisting of the dharmas of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). (4)
The four fruits and the four paths constitute the essence of the Saṅgha Jewel; this explains the principle specifically, rather than relying on the harmony of formal ritual.

Regarding the third point, the intention of taking refuge, there are two types: general and specific. There are seven meanings to the general type. First, it reveals the subtle and profound nature of the Dharma to distinguish it from non-Buddhist paths;
for various heterodox practitioners hold to the views of existence or non-existence, and thus at the beginning of their teachings, they invariably place the two characters "A-yu" (the syllable *oṃ*).
Now, the Buddha-dharma is not like those other schools. When its disciples compose works, they must first pay homage to the Triple Gem.

They directly propagate the words of the Buddha by beginning with the phrase "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*). Therefore, the *Tattvasiddhi* states: "Because the Triple Gem is the most auspicious, I speak of it at the beginning of my treatise;
secondly, to manifest the faith and reverence of sentient beings. This is as transmitted by the various noble ones.

The purport of the Buddhist teachings is first to set forth the merits of the Triple Gem (*triratna*) and to exhort faith and refuge. This is especially so for ordinary, deluded beings who have not yet given rise to pure faith;
thus, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states that one should "awaken in sentient beings the mindfulness of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha" to reveal the true merits of these three equal gems.
Thirdly, it demonstrates the ultimate place of refuge in order to overturn the false attachments to erroneous doctrines held by sentient beings. Constantly...
People turn to celestial deities, groves, gardens, mountains, and *caityas* in order to seek blessings and protection. Therefore, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 34, states:
"This refuge is not supreme; this refuge is not honored. By means of this refuge, one cannot be liberated from all suffering.
Now, with a profound and pure mind, we take refuge in the Triple Gem to deliver sentient beings and open the eye of the True Dharma.
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* further states: "This refuge is the most excellent; this refuge is the most venerable. It is by means of this refuge that one can certainly be liberated from all suffering.

The fourth [point] reveals that there is reliance and the peace of mind derived from the transmitted teaching. If one does not take refuge, it is like a merchant without a companion or a kingdom without a sovereign;
the heart and mind are filled with terror and trembling, remaining in a state of unease. Thus, the second [chapter] of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* [states]:...
It says: "I am now without a master and without kin; I have no refuge and no destination. Fifth, this demonstrates the ritual procedures for monks and nuns to follow.

Now, the ultimate truth of the True Dharma is truly difficult to propagate and expound. Since one wishes to proclaim it, one must take refuge in the Triple Gem (as expressed in the various verses, etc.).
Sixth is the request for majestic protection. As one is about to transmit the holy teachings, there is concern regarding the existence of demonic adversaries;

it is essential to request their secret assistance before one can propagate the transformation [of beings]. It is the same for the various Bodhisattvas who transmit the teachings: they first request majestic protection and only thereafter proclaim them extensively.
Thus, the *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra* says: "Have pity on me and protect me, causing the seeds of the Dharma to increase. In this world and in future worlds, may the Buddha always [protect me]."
Accepting [the teaching]. Seventh is the offering of gratitude. The Three Jewels have bestowed profound kindness and great virtue upon living beings;

by hearing the Dharma and observing the precepts, one realizes the principle and forgets the trap [of the words]. Therefore, the subsequent text states that it is not robes or the other four requisites that can repay this debt, but rather the current transmission and propagation [of the teachings].

To ensure that the Dharma does not fall into decline, one employs this humble canopy to look upward and repay the profound kindness [of the Buddha]. Next, regarding the separate act of taking refuge: the Buddha is the Teacher;
since we now propagate his words, it is necessary to take refuge in him. The Precepts manifest the receiving and upholding of the Dharma, which is the teaching proclaimed by him;
its moisture is inexhaustible. If one does not first take refuge, there is concern that future transmission will lack benefit. The Saṃgha are those who transmit the teachings.
Regarding "cultivation, rectification, realization, and equality": if one does not take refuge with utmost sincerity, how can one manifest the reverence of one's practice?
Next, the three phrases are explained: *kai* (稽) means filiality; *shou* (首) means the head; *li* (禮) means respect. This refers to those who transmit the Dharma taking refuge in the Triple Gem;
by placing their heads upon the ground in a manner of filial devotion, they manifest the height of their respect. Therefore, it is called "prostrating with the head" (*kai-shou li*). It is also...

*Ke* (稽) means to bend. *Shou* (首) means the head. To bend one’s own honor and perform the ritual toward another’s inferiority is therefore called *keishu* (稽首). The *Dazhidu lun* (Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra), fascicle 12, states:
"Among the parts of the human body, the head is the most noble, for it is where the five sensory faculties reside and is situated at the highest point.

The feet are the most base, for they tread upon impurities and are situated at the lowest point. Therefore, one uses that which is to be honored [the head] to perform the ritual toward that which is to be honored."

[It is] base [to do otherwise], because one honors and makes offerings to what is precious. Furthermore, there are inferior, middling, and superior [forms]. The inferior is the bow; the middling is kneeling;
the superior is prostrating with the head and face touching the feet—this is the supreme offering. Moreover, the *Shatashasrika Prajnaparamita* (The Hundred Thousand Verse) states:
"There are three kinds of salutation: first, verbal salutation; second, bending the knee without the head touching the ground; third, the head touching the ground—this is the supreme salutation."
In a human body, the head is the highest part and the feet are the lowest. To prostrate with the head at the feet is the ultimate expression of reverence.

Although there are three types of prostration, this particular one clarifies the "superior" form. What is it that is being venerated? It refers to the Buddhas, because the transformative manifestations of the Buddhas across the three periods of time are not distinct;

thus, within the context of offering respect, the plural term "all" serves as a comprehensive inclusion. One may ask: on what basis is it known that this prostration extends throughout the three periods of time?

Answer: The *Śīla-sūtra* states: "As with the Buddhas of the past and those of the future, etc. If this is so, then since the principle of the Buddha’s transformation is uniform, reverence extends through the three periods of time;

thus, the teachings of the Buddhas of the past and future should both be received and upheld. Question: Based on what teaching is it known that the reception and upholding [of the Dharma] applies only to the past and present? Answer:

While the reception and upholding [of the Dharma] is indeed limited to the past and present, revering [the Buddhas] of the future provides benefit in advance; therefore, they are included among those to be revered. Question: By what means is it known that the reception and upholding [of the Dharma] applies only to the past and present?

Is it not the case that [the Buddhas] of the future are not included? The answer is that because the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* mentions Vipaśyin and the others, but does not mention the future Buddha Maitreya and so forth.
"Buddha" is explained as before, and furthermore, there are two meanings: first, the sense of mutual exclusion (*vyatireka*), and second, the sense of collective inclusion (*samuccaya*).
Here, the word "and" (*ca*) intends to signify collective inclusion. How is this known? It is known because the single act of prostration extends throughout the following two [sections].

Therefore, the meaning of the term "dharma" is as explained previously. Regarding the term *bhikṣu-saṃgha*: *bhikṣu* refers to the cause that brings about accomplishment, while *saṃgha* refers to the community that is accomplished.
Because the agent and the object are mentioned together, it is called the *bhikṣu-saṃgha*. As for *bhikṣu*, the phonetic transcription is not correct; the correct form is *bhi-kṣu*.
According to the fourth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, there are three correct meanings: first, the mendicant (*yācanaka*), so named because he maintains a pure livelihood.
The "Beggar" (bhikṣu). There are two meanings to "begging": first, to beg the Dharma from the Buddhas above in order to nourish the spirit;

second, to beg for food from laypeople below in order to sustain one's life. This, in turn, has two further meanings: first, to support the body so that the Path may be cultivated, as the *Teaching Left Behind* states:
"Hold the alms bowl and beg for your own livelihood. Second, to benefit the donors, as the following text says: "Out of compassion..."

Because he belongs to the family of white-robed householders, he must beg while remaining free from the four or five types of wrong livelihood. He dwells in right livelihood and is thus called a "beggar" (*bhikṣu*).
Regarding the "four wrong livelihoods," they are: downward-facing, upward-facing, square-facing, and crosswise-facing. Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 4, states:
"There are those among the renunciants who compound medicines, sow grain, plant trees, and so forth; such impure means of livelihood are called 'downward-facing food. There are..."
There are renunciants who observe the stars, constellations, sun, moon, wind, rain, thunder, lightning, and hail;

such impure means of livelihood are called "looking upward for food" (*ūrdhvamukha-bhikṣā*). There are renunciants who fawn upon the powerful and influential, acting as messengers to the four quarters, using clever speech to seek much;

such impure means of livelihood are called "looking toward the four directions for food" (*caturmukha-bhikṣā*). There are renunciants who study various incantations, arts, divination, and calculations.
Divination of fortune and misfortune through minor arts is improper. Such means of livelihood that are impure are called "food for the mouth. Regarding the five types of deceit (*śāṭhya*):
according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 22, first, one falsely manifests extraordinary and strange physical characteristics for the sake of gain and honor;
second, for the sake of gain and honor, one speaks of one's own merits; third, for the sake of gain and honor, one observes and interprets signs of fortune and misfortune.
Fourth, they preach the Dharma to others for the sake of gain and offerings; they raise their voices and manifest an air of authority to inspire awe and reverence in others.
Fifth, for the sake of gain and offerings, they proclaim the offerings they have received to move the hearts of people, thereby sustaining their lives through improper causes and conditions.
This is called "Ya-ming" (Wicked Life). Second is "Po-fan-nao" (Destroyer of Defilements): "Bi" means to destroy, and "Qiu" means defilement;
because one can destroy defilements, one is called a Bhikṣu. Third is "Bu-mo" (Terrifying Māra): "Bi" means to terrify, and "Qiu" means capability;

because one can terrify King Māra and his retinue, when one leaves the household life, shaves the head, dons the dyed kaṣāya robe, and receives the precepts, at that time Māra is terrified. Therefore, it is called [Bhikṣu]. First...

When [the Buddha] donned his dharma-robe, Pāpīyān trembled with fear; later, when he was exhorted to observe the precepts, he became even more terrified. Having concluded the section on the Śākya bhikṣu, the meaning of "Saṃgha" is as explained previously.

Next, the expression of respectful homage is presented. The main text is divided into three parts. The first consists of nine and a half verses, which praise the precepts and proclaim their benefits and virtues. First...
Regarding the second reason for establishing the King, there are thirty-six verses below that employ metaphors to explain its benefits and harms.

In the latter half of the third section, having finished the exposition, the author sighs in relief and pays homage. The preceding text consists of eight parts: first, one half-verse clarifies the long endurance of the Dharma;
second, one half-verse reveals the source of its transmission; third, one half-verse introduces the exhortation to listen. Fourth...

The first verse [shows] that precepts can benefit sentient beings. The five verses of the fifth [section] concern the merit and benefits of precepts. The two verses of the sixth [section] show that precepts can generate goodness.
The single verse of the seventh [section] shows that precepts can eliminate evil. The single verse of the eighth [section] shows that precepts discipline the three karmas.

First, I shall explain the initial passage. It is intended precisely to proclaim the rules and procedures for practice; therefore, it says, "I now expound. The meaning of *vinaya* has already been clarified as before.
However, the seventh fascicle of the *Mātṛkā-sūtra* states: "There are five meanings of *vinaya*: first, confession (*deśanā*); second, compliance (*anuvidhāna*);

third, cessation (*nirodha*); fourth, severance (*cheda*); and fifth, relinquishment (*prahāṇa*). Regarding confession: as in the case of the seven categories [of offenses], that which has been transgressed should...

Confession and the eradication through confession are called *vinaya*. "Conformity" means that the seven groups of followers accept and practice according to what the Tathāgata has prescribed and taught, without any opposition;
this is called *anuvartana-vinaya* (conforming *vinaya*). What is meant by "extinction"?

That which can extinguish the seven types of disputes is called *samatha-vinaya* (the *vinaya* of extinction). What is meant by "ability to sever"? It refers to that which brings about the cessation and elimination [of afflictions] in *nirvāṇa*.
Non-arising is called the *vinaya* of abandonment (*prahāṇa-vinaya*). What is meant by "abandoning"? There are two kinds of abandoning:
first, abandoning what has been done, which refers to the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses; this is accomplished by performing the formal motion (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) to relinquish the matter.

Second, abandoning views, as when the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa said, "I heard directly from the Buddha that engaging in sexual desire cannot obstruct the path. Because he abandoned this view, it is called [the *vinaya* of abandonment].

It is abandonment (*prahāṇa*). However, the textual accounts in the various teachings vary between being extensive and concise. This text contains eight [sections], as explained in the *Ekottarika-āgama*.

In the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, there are thirty-two; in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, there are five. First is the *Vinayakṣudraka* (the concise Vinaya), referring to the five categories of precepts (*pañca-pārājikādi*). Second is the extensive [Vinaya], referring to the two divisions of the Vinaya (*dvivarga-vinaya*).

There are three aspects: first, the five matters permitted for border regions, such as those for Śūrasena; second, the four firm [precepts], such as receiving the *kaṭhina* robe because of the abandonment of the five offenses;
third, that which accords with the Dharma, namely the *dharma-karman* and the *saṃgha-karman*. Regarding the *Vinayavibhāṣā*, there are nine categories:
first, the *vinaya* of bhikṣus, such as intentional emission of semen and so forth; second, the *vinaya* of bhikṣuṇīs, such as traveling alone and so forth; third...
1. The Vinaya of the Two Parts, such as the *pārājika* and so forth; 2. The Vinaya of the Four Offenses, which refers to those arising from the eight origins and their corresponding legal remedies;
3. The Vinaya of the Five Delusions, such as the nine knowledges of permanent abandonment regarding the five classes of delusions within the three realms; 4. The Vinaya of Vows.
This refers to the ten kinds of training rules, namely the ten precepts of a śrāmaṇera. These encompass all future matters in their entirety. As for why they are called "vows" (praṇidhāna):
if one does not receive these ten precepts, one cannot obtain the full precepts (upasaṃpadā).

Since these precepts serve as the means for attaining the full precepts and can encompass all future matters, they are called "vows. Seventh, the *apraṇihita-vinaya*: at the conclusion of the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*), forty-two thousand...
The training rules (*śikṣāpada*) arise simultaneously; there is no longer a single precept that does not arise, and for this reason it is called "wishless" (*apraṇihita*).

8. One-pointed Vinaya (*ekasthāna-vinaya*): This refers to matters such as receiving the precepts or bathing. "Place" (*sthāna*) has two meanings: first, a geographical location as a place, such as the exemptions granted in border regions;
second, a temporal period as a place, such as how one could formerly obtain the precepts through the Three Refuges, whereas today one cannot. Bathing serves as the middle [example].
"Regarding 'the country is hot, one should listen,' etc.: the nine *sarvatra-vinaya* (universal *vinaya*) refer to those training rules (*śikṣāpada*) that should be observed at all times.

As for these being called *vinaya-dharma*: *vinaya* itself is the *dharma*; thus it is named *vinaya-dharma*. This is an interpretation based on their common dependence. From the perspective of its meaning as a rule or standard, it is called *dharma*;
from the perspective of its meaning as the cessation of evil and the production of goodness, it is called *vinaya*. However, because this is proclaimed..."
This causes the Dharma to endure for a long time. As stated in the following passage, both the collective and individual practices established by the regulations yield ten benefits.
Furthermore, one who upholds the Vinaya attains five merits: first, the category of precepts becomes firm; second, they skillfully overcome all adversaries;

third, they possess fearlessness in making definitive judgments within the assembly; fourth, they are able to resolve doubts and regrets; and fifth, they skillfully maintain the Vinaya so that the True Dharma endures for a long time. This...
Because people do not establish [the Dharma] by themselves, it is accomplished through the provisional Dharma; because the Dharma does not propagate itself, it is manifested through people.
Therefore, it is said: "to cause the Dharma to abide for a long time. Furthermore, the sixth fascicle of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:

"The World-Honored One praised in various ways the recitation of the Vinaya, praised the upholding of the Vinaya, and praised the discourse of Upāli. There are five merits for a bhikṣu who upholds the Vinaya: first, he is firm in himself..."

1. Guarding the precepts; 2. being able to sever the doubts of those who possess a sense of shame and remorse; 3. abiding personally within the True Dharma; 4. being fearless regarding what is spoken within the Saṃgha;
and 5. subduing and eliminating adversaries. At that time, the bhikṣus had this thought: "The Buddha has made such a statement for our sake.
Why should we not diligently practice the recitation and inquiry of the Vinaya? Thereupon, they together began to recite and study it.
Day and night, one should not be indolent. Furthermore, in the *Ten Recitations Vinaya*, fascicle 47, Upāli asks: "How long will the Buddha-dharma of the past remain in the world? The Buddha replies:

"It is said that the Dharma remains in the world for as long as there are pure bhikṣus who do not corrupt the teaching when reciting the precepts. It is the same for the Buddhas of the future and the present.
Moreover, the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*, fascicle 16, states: "How does one cause the True Dharma to abide for a long time? First,"
One personally accords with the Dharma. Second, one enables others to attain the Dharma. Because they attain the Dharma, they maintain the Vinaya with a correct mind.
Because they maintain the Vinaya, they enter meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Because of meditative concentration, they immediately attain the fruits of the Path.

This is called the long endurance of the True Dharma. Furthermore, the Buddha said to Ānanda: "After my parinirvāṇa, there are five dharmas that will cause the Dharma to endure for a long time. First, the *Vibhaṅga*..."
"1. A *bhikṣuṇī* is your Great Teacher. 2. At the very least, five persons who uphold the Vinaya must exist in the world. 3.

If there are ten persons in a central region or five in a border region, one may receive the precepts according to the Dharma. 4. Even down to twenty persons, one may perform the ritual for the removal of offenses (*āpatti-vyutthāna*) according to the Dharma.
5. Because of the existence of Vinaya masters, the True Dharma is enabled to abide for a long time. These are called the five virtues of upholding the Vinaya. It is further said:

Because the *vinayadhara* masters uphold the *vinaya*, the Buddha-dharma shall remain in the world for five thousand years. For this reason, many bhikṣus approach the *vinaya* of Upāliputra. How does one study the *vinaya*?
Reciting it, reading it, and explaining its meaning—this is called studying the *vinaya*. Furthermore, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, chapter twenty-nine, states:
"The essence of the World-Honored One’s True Dharma (*saddharma*) is twofold: first, the teaching (*āgama*); second, the realization (*adhigama*). The teaching refers to the sūtras."
The Abhidharma of subduing [the afflictions] refers to the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) realized by the three vehicles.

When there are those capable of upholding and correctly expounding it, the Buddha’s True Teaching (śāsana) abides in the world. When there are those capable of practicing correctly in accordance with the teaching, the Buddha’s True Realization (adhigamadharma) [abides].

They thus remain in the world; therefore, one should know that the duration for which the True Dharma (saddharma) remains is equal to the lifespan of these three types of persons who abide in the world.
Next, to clarify those who have realized [the Dharma]: although we previously relied upon the same teaching together, none of us were able to practice and study it in its entirety.
Since capacities differ, what is seen and heard varies; thus, the sublime tracks are divided into stages and the profound words reach different depths.
Now that I wish to follow faith and practice accordingly, I fear there may be doubts regarding self-restraint; therefore, I cite my initial hearing [of the Dharma] as proof.
Nevertheless, what I have transmitted is truly not my own private error; it is that which was expounded by the Buddha and transmitted by Upāli.

The Buddha merely established the precepts, and on each occasion of their formulation, he assembled the community of monks. Because [Upāli] was the first to compile them based on specific causes, he is called the "Foremost" (Ādi).

Those who heard them together within the assembly were not limited to one person, hence they are referred to as "and others" (ca-anye). Alternatively, it may be said that Upāli was the first to collect the Dharma.
Therefore, he is called the "Foremost. When the various saints assemble together, it is termed "and the others.

Alternatively, since Upāli upheld the Vinaya, he may be designated as the "Foremost," while Kāśyapa and the rest transmitted [the teachings] and are thus called the "others" who were "body-witnesses" (kāyasākṣin). Question: Since Upāli himself expounded the Vinaya, why did he not transmit it himself?
In the transmissions, it is Kāśyapa and the other four who appear. An ancient commentary states: "Kāśyapa and the other four were both proficient in principle and practice."
Therefore, within the transmission of the Dharma, the succession was clearly established. As for Upāli, he merely clarified the practice of the teachings;

because his virtues were not fully complete, his name was omitted [from the lineage]. Now, the explanation is simply this: after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, Upāli lacked the karmic affinity with those to be born [into that lineage], and thus it was not entrusted to him.
This was not because he lacked the virtue required for transmission and propagation, for as great śrāvakas, they were all capable of transforming sentient beings. Kāśyapa...
These five [factors] have conditions for existence; therefore, the World-Honored One entrusted them to be transmitted. Question:
Why is it that Upāli is listed here, yet the Seven Buddhas are not manifested? When the precept-sūtra mentions the Seven Buddhas, it does not reveal Upāli. Answer: This listing of Upāli...

The transmission of the Manifestation [Sūtra] is trustworthy; as it was not received from other Buddhas, their names are not listed therein. The precepts arise from this [sūtra], and while it is logical that Upāli [received them] from others, he collectively manifested the precepts of the seven Buddhas for the sake of receiving those other teachings.
Furthermore, another interpretation holds that there is no difference in the monastic precepts themselves; rather, they are merely elegant expressions mutually elucidating one another.
This refers to the term "various" (zhū), which clarifies that [the precepts] encompass the seven categories; from this, the discipline (śīla) arises.

Having already mastered the general principles, Upāli next clarifies the exhortation to listen, expounding it without omission; this is termed "now" (jīn). To manifest what is set forth in the mouth, he thus engages in discourse.
The precepts are the root of virtue and are called the essential meaning. Therefore, the *Śāsanāntima-dharma-sūtra* says:

"If a person can maintain pure precepts, they will be able to possess wholesome dharmas; if there are no pure precepts, all wholesome merits and virtues cannot arise. For this reason, you should know."
Precepts are foremost. Furthermore, precepts can support the practice of renunciation; for anyone wishing to initiate cultivation, there is nothing that does not proceed from them.

Thus, they are called the essential meaning. To receive and practice them with harmony and uprightness is what is termed "virtuous. Because such virtuous ones are not singular, they are called "all" (*sarva*). It is my hope that all such virtuous ones [will uphold them].
I have aligned my will and examined the text in detail, fearing the error of misheard reports or the fault of erroneous transmission; thus, it is said that all shall listen together.

Next, I clarify how this benefits sentient beings: the precepts are the initial track for treading the path of the sages and the fundamental cause for initiating practice. Since they are the very basis of practice, [they must be upheld].
It is difficult to measure; therefore, it is called "profound. Thus, the text says: "The precepts are like the ocean, without limit.

Furthermore, the essence of the precepts is subtle and mysterious, and their boundaries are difficult to discern; hence, they are called "profound. The Buddha taught these precepts for two kinds of people:

first, those who maintain them through restraint (*saṃvara*), which is why it says "for those who delight in upholding the precepts"; second, those who maintain them through performance (*kriyā*), which is why it says "for those capable of reciting [the scriptures]."
Furthermore, by observing the precepts one cuts off evil; by reciting the scriptures one cultivates goodness. By relying on the teachings to practice accordingly, all receive benefit.
Since these benefits are not singular, they are called "various" (*zhū*). Generally speaking, the benefits are similar; yet according to their specific purposes, there are no differences.
That is to say, maintaining abstinence is termed "benefit" (*li*), while performing positive actions is termed "advantage" (*yì*). Moreover, cutting off evil is termed "benefit."

Cultivating virtue is called benefit. Furthermore, practicing it oneself is called profit, while transforming others is called benefit. Moreover, merit is called profit, while wisdom is called benefit.
Additionally, attaining present peace is called profit, while attaining freedom from the suffering of seeking is called benefit. Furthermore, attaining worldly goodness is called profit.
Attaining supramundane happiness is called "benefit" (*hita*). Furthermore, attaining conditioned merit is called "profit" (*lābha*), while manifesting unconditioned *nirvāṇa* is called "benefit.
Regarding the term "elder" (*sthavira*): it refers to one who possesses the conduct of an aged person. The first fascicle of the *Vyākhyāyukti* states:
"One who is called an elder does not necessarily have white hair, wrinkled skin, or missing teeth; what is esteemed is [wisdom]."
One who is able to cultivate merit, eliminate the evils of sentient beings, and purely practice the holy life (brahmacarya) is called an elder (*sthavira*).

Next, the text on the benefits of the precepts consists of three parts: first, half a verse that cites the number to manifest their excellence; second, two verses that reveal the nature of those benefits;
and finally, half a verse that concludes by establishing the intent of the regulation. Although the benefits of the precepts are boundless, this discussion shall limit itself to ten.
As for the phrase: that which manifests the meaning constitutes "virtue" (*guṇa*). The establishment of the benefits of these precepts belongs solely to the Buddha and none other;
therefore, it is called "the precept-dharma of all Buddhas. It may also be called the "prātimokṣa precepts," as they exist because of the Buddha.

When a Buddha does not appear in the world, this dharma does not exist; hence, it is called "the precept-dharma of all Buddhas. Furthermore, the realization of great *bodhi* is entirely dependent upon the precept-dharma. This is...
This is the method for attaining Buddhahood; therefore, it is called "the precept-dharma of all Buddhas.

Furthermore, since non-Buddhist teachers also possess their own systems of precepts, it is called "the precept-dharma of all Buddhas" in order to distinguish it from those of the non-Buddhists. This precept-dharma constitutes a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compound.
Next, the essence of the benefits is explained; there is a formal text below. For now, I shall briefly correlate these points, though they do not follow the original sequence.
The second and third benefits bring peace and permanence to the Saṃgha. The first benefit is to gather in the Saṃgha. The fourth benefit is to cause those who lack faith to believe.
The fifth benefit is to increase the growth of those who already believe. The sixth benefit is to sever those who do not maintain the precepts. [The seventh is] to lead those on false paths...
The eighth and ninth benefits are entering into the correct [path] and gaining profit; the seventh benefit is having a sense of shame and remorse;

the tenth benefit is the long endurance of the Buddha-dharma. Next, regarding the intent of establishing the retreat: nothing in the world is most excellent except for the Dharma of the precepts. Therefore, I now expound and disseminate it.
Therefore, it is said: "The World-Honored One is most supreme," and so forth.

Next, there are two sections on generating wholesome qualities. First, the initial verse presents a simile; next, the subsequent verse exhorts one to uphold [the teaching]. Within the former, the first half is the simile and the second half is the application.

In the simile, the various mountains and various streams generally represent the Three Piṭakas from the perspective of the teaching, and they generally represent the Three Trainings from the perspective of practice. However...

Mount Sumeru among mountains, and the great ocean among rivers—the latter is supreme among flowing waters; likewise, the practice of the precepts is supreme among all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).

Because it is comparable to those mountains and oceans, the *Śāsanānuśāsana-sūtra* (Teaching of the Last Instructions) states: "By relying on this precept, one attains the various dhyāna-concentrations as well as the wisdom that extinguishes suffering.

Since the teaching is established by means of this [precept], it is also called "supreme. However, in the text of the analogy, the comparison is presented through mutual implication and abbreviation; according to the teaching, it should be understood as follows:

It is said that the Vinaya is the foremost and supreme. In terms of practice, it should be described as encompassing hundreds of thousands of millions of deeds. Next, the most exalted [teaching] is explained to encourage its upholding.
Regarding "the foremost and supreme," this refers to the Buddha’s Bodhi; because there are those who joyfully aspire to it, it is called "seeking.

Those of the present age are precisely the monks and nuns of the current time; those of the future age are the monks and nuns of the future; and those of the past age are the monks and nuns of the past, who have personally received the Great [Teaching].
Regarding the teaching: since one has already received the Great Teaching, it is inappropriate to offer further exhortation. It is not that such exhortation is useless for one’s own sake;
rather, it is because one anticipates that others might harbor doubts, thinking that there are no precepts for future lives, and thus says, "One should uphold them," and so forth.
Next, the elimination of evil is explained. These are the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*): namely, attachment, aversion, pride, ignorance, views, grasping, doubt, stinginess, and envy.
Being bound by these fetters is called "obstruction. Although one removes these nine fetters through the power of wisdom, that wisdom arises from ethical discipline (*śīla*);

therefore, it is said that there is no obstruction. As for "bonds," there are three bonds: namely, greed, hatred, and delusion. That one attains liberation from these three bonds is likewise due to the merit of ethical discipline.
Therefore, it is said: "By means of this. Thus, the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra*, in its first fascicle, states: "Regarding the term 'liberation from bonds':

'bonds' refers to the three bonds—namely, the bonds of greed, hatred, and delusion. 'Liberation' refers to being free from these three bonds; this is what is meant by the term 'liberation from bonds. Furthermore, it is explained as follows:"

Bondage refers to delusion; that is to say, it is the root of creating karma. Since the precepts eliminate this root, karma cannot enchain one; therefore, it is said that there is no obstruction. The seventh [point] concerns those who are not bound:

what is called "bondage" is the act of binding, and what is called "attachment" is the arising of defilement. There is nothing that does not depend upon the precepts for the removal of these bonds and attachments; therefore, it is said that through them, one is liberated.
One clearly perceives and understands what is contrary and what is compliant, and examines in detail what is pure and what is defiled. Thus, one attains complete clarity.
Discrimination is like hanging a mirror in a high hall; beauty and ugliness are both revealed therein. Thus it is said, "By means of the precepts (*śīla*), etc.

Next, one regulates the three types of action (*trikarma*). When about to cultivate the practices of the two periods [of day and night], it is necessary to exert all three types of action simultaneously.

The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*, fascicle 4, states: "The Tathāgata, out of compassion for sentient beings whose three types of action are unwholesome, therefore taught the Vinaya-piṭaka to establish restraint."

Regarding the actions of body, speech, and mind: it is said that "one who desires [equanimity]," etc. To speak of lofty principles beforehand is difficult to rely upon; established rules are easy to emulate.

Rāhula, because he was afflicted by those three types of karma, he endured them without retaliating, instead feeling compassion for the other person. This was used as an illustration to encourage the cultivation of ritual procedures;
hence it is said, "One should contemplate," etc.

Next, the following section clarifies its benefits and harms. There are fourteen major topics. First, there are two verses providing a metaphor for the emergence of the teaching that expresses [the Dharma].

Second, one verse provides a metaphor for the characteristics of the transgressions expressed [by the Dharma]. Third, two verses provide a metaphor for the fear or lack thereof among the foolish and the wise.

Fourth, two verses provide a metaphor for distinguishing the correct from the incorrect. Fifth, two verses provide a metaphor for the precepts as feet. Sixth, two verses provide a metaphor for the precepts...
The simile of the life-preserving float is in the two verses of the seventh chapter. The simile of the steps of a staircase is in the two verses of the eighth chapter.

The simile of a craft or skill is in the two verses of the ninth chapter. The simile of the community of Dharma is in the twelfth verse. The simile of a compassionate mother is [in the twelfth verse].
The eleventh and twelfth verses provide the analogy of morality as a valiant general. The thirteenth and fourteenth verses provide the analogy of morality as a true birth.
The fifteenth and sixteenth verses provide the analogy of morality as a royal seal. The seventeenth and eighteenth verses provide the analogy of morality as an exhortation to practice.

First, I shall explain the initial analogy. Within this section, there are two parts: the first one and a half verses constitute the analogy, while the subsequent half-verse cites the Dharma to correspond with the analogy.
Within the analogy itself, there are two parts: the first verse explains the reason for the arising of the teaching, and the following half-verse explains the purpose for which the teaching arises.
This body of Vinaya teachings is noble and worthy of honor, revered by the monastic community of monks and nuns; it is likened to a king or a person of high status.

This is because it explains the origin of this teaching's emergence. Regarding the statement "the reason for establishing a king": if one follows the combined text, it says, "Just as a king governs according to the True Dharma.
Here, the focus is not on the reason for establishing a king, but rather on the reason for establishing the governing Dharma once a king has been established.
The text should have read: "The reason the king establishes the Dharma" refers to taking the Buddha as the king and the five offenses (*pañcāpatti*) and so forth as the governing Dharma.
If one takes the Vinaya as a king, one does not know by what means he should govern. Those who engage in worldly disputes are a metaphor for the bhikṣus who have committed offenses.
"The multitude raising [the matter]" is a metaphor for the bhikṣus reporting the transgressions to the Buddha.

"The constant law of antiquity" is a metaphor for all Buddhas, who invariably wait for an offense to be requested [to be addressed], assemble the community to reprimand [the offender], and establish the rules of training (śikṣāpada). This is the method.

It is not only now; it was so in the past and will be so in the future. Constant throughout all time, it is called the "Eternal Dharma" (*nityadharma*). Next, to explain the purpose for which this remedial method (*pratipakṣa-dharma*) was established:

it was originally intended for two types of persons. The first is one who, having committed an offense, is capable of repentance—meaning one who understands the medicine, the disease, and the ritual procedure for confession and purification.
Therefore, it is said that one who commits an offense knows the Dharma. Second, those who are single-mindedly diligent and do not transgress are called "teachers who uphold the instruction.

Because they exert themselves in cultivation and remain free from faults, it is said that those who accord with the Dharma achieve accomplishment. The meaning of the text may be understood accordingly.

Next, the characteristics of offenses are explained. This section contains two parts. First, there are two verses that provide a general analogy for the five types of transgressions. Second, there are eight verses that provide specific analogies for each of the five transgressions.
Within the general section, the analogy is presented first, followed by its application; the same pattern applies to all subsequent analogies.

In the initial analogy, the first line observes the illness, the second line establishes the framework, and the following two lines provide the explanation. The Vinaya clarifies the characteristics of the offenses with distinct clarity, as in the following example:
The King of Physicians observes the similarities among illnesses; therefore, he says they are "like" [one another]. Next, he establishes two gates: progress and cessation.

The four subsequent transgressions may all be removed through confession, and are thus termed "progress. The first offense is extremely grave and cannot be extinguished through repentance; it is termed "cessation."

This *śamatha* (calm abiding) possesses four meanings: first, it destroys the root; second, it obstructs the path through fixed impediments; third, it cannot be expiated; and fourth, it renders one unfit for the Saṃgha.

To reverse these four meanings is what is called *vipaśyanā* (insight). When this *vipaśyanā* and *śamatha* each accord with the proper ritual and the established methods are not deviated from, it is said that they have attained their proper place.
The explanation below is clear. Next is the text on the application of the metaphors: the first phrase corresponds to the first [phrase], and so forth.

The third [section] combines with the lower three; the four matters constitute one phrase. "Combining to attain cessation" means that what is impossible is abandoned. "That which can be saved," etc., constitutes two phrases;
"combining to attain progress" means that if it can be treated, one immediately administers medicine. Furthermore, according to another interpretation of the combination:

the first phrase combines with the first three characters; the four matters are thirteen. The remainder combines with the two characters "all diseases"; "that which cannot be treated" combines with "attaining cessation."

The Gate of Appropriate Action (*yathāsthāna-dvāra*). One may save those who can be saved, and need not save those who cannot. This constitutes the attainment of the gate of appropriate action. Next, the specific metaphors are explained.
The first two verses serve as metaphors for the first transgression; they expand upon the general principle stated above: one attains what is appropriate and abandons what is improper.
The next two verses are metaphors for the second transgression. The following two verses are metaphors for the third and fourth transgressions. The final two verses concern the fifth.

Regarding the analogies for transgressions: here, three analogies are used to elaborate upon the general summary above, so that one may advance to attain their respective states. If a transgression is curable, one advances by administering the medicine. Question:

Why are the remaining transgressions explained separately, while the third and fourth are discussed together? Answer: At the time of repentance for the five types of transgressions, the fifth—mental repentance (*manasikāra*)—does not involve facing an external object;
therefore, it is treated as a separate analogy. As for the other four transgressions, they are all removed by facing an external object. Among those involving an external object, the first...

The second offense is confessed before the Saṃgha; the third and fourth are confessed individually. However, although the first two offenses are alike in being confessed before the Saṃgha, they must be explained separately because their methods of confession and rehabilitation differ.
As for the third and fourth offenses, although one involves three [factors] and the other one, they are treated together because both are confessed individually.

If that is so, why are the four offenses explained separately within the section on "Fear of Offenses"? Answer: The fear of offenses is established to evoke dread and to manifest the nature of that dread.

"Separation from light. This passage is intended to encourage upholding [the precepts]. Because it encourages upholding, they are explained together. There is an interpretation: "taking fear" refers to the dread of transgression.

For those whose fear is slight, the name [of the offense] is submerged; for those whose fear is manifest and increased, four gates are presented. Therefore, three or four [gates] are separated. This metaphor does not manifest fear. Regarding the encouragement to uphold, there are similarities and differences.
Those that are the same are explained together as "light"; those that are different are explained separately. The first metaphor consists of four lines; the first line...

The first phrase is a metaphor for severing one's own continuity; the second phrase is a metaphor for severing the continuity of the various dharmas; the third phrase is a metaphor for discarding the performance of the ritual acts;

and the final phrase is a metaphor for purity that admits no impurity. If one commits a *pārājika* offense, it constitutes a permanent obstruction for the duration of this life, severing the life-force of wisdom;
this is called "death. Because one ultimately fails to function as a living bhikṣu, it is called a "corpse. As for the term "corpse," it possesses five meanings.

As the following text states: "There are five things that are undesirable about a dead person: first, impurity; second, a foul odor; third, being a source of fear; fourth, causing others to feel fear;
and fifth, providing an opportunity for malevolent spirits to take advantage, as well as being a dwelling place for evil beasts and non-human beings. These are the five.
A person who violates the precepts has faults and possesses impurities of body, speech, and mind, just like that corpse’s impurity; thus I speak."

This person is also like this. If there are impurities in their actions of body, speech, and mind, and an evil reputation spreads abroad—just as a foul odor emanates from that corpse—I say that this person is also like this.
Because their actions of body, speech, and mind are impure, the virtuous bhikṣus fear them; just as that corpse causes terror in people, I say that this person is likewise.
It is likewise so. If one possesses impurity of body, speech, and mind, it causes virtuous bhikṣus who see them to utter words of reproach:

"How is it that I have seen such an evil person? Just as a person seeing a corpse gives rise to fear and dread, allowing evil spirits to find an opportunity, I say that this person is also like this—one who possesses impurity of body, speech, and mind. With...
"To dwell together with unwholesome people is like dwelling among corpses where predatory beasts and non-humans reside; I say that such a person is exactly like this.
These are the five faults of one who violates the precepts, being like a corpse. Furthermore, it is said:
there are five disadvantages to breaking the precepts: one harms oneself, one is censured by the wise, an evil reputation spreads abroad, and at the time of death..."
One gives rise to regret while alive and falls into the evil realms after death; these are the five [faults]. To uphold the precepts is to possess five merits (the reverse of the above).
Furthermore, there are five matters: first, one is unable to obtain things previously sought; second, having obtained them, one does not protect them;
third, if one falls among a gathering—whether it be a group of kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, or bhikṣus—one feels shame and humiliation therein; fourth, [one lacks]... [no such thing].
Within a distance of several *yojanas*, śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas will proclaim his evil deeds; as a person who has broken the precepts, he will fall into the evil realms after death.
This is the fifth [fault]. There are five merits for upholding the precepts (the opposite of the above). Since his karma is so grave, the pure assembly will not accept him.
It is like the great ocean, which does not harbor corpses; therefore it is said that the great ocean does not tolerate them.

Having been excluded and expelled from the fourfold assembly, they have no means of remaining within the community. Like those tossed by a violent wind, they do not accord with the monastic discipline and are forever distinguished as being outside the assembly;
thus it is said they are "cast upon the shore. The *Upāsaka-śīla-lakṣaṇa-sūtra* states: The Buddha told the bhikṣus, "I have two bodies. One..."

First is the body of birth; second is the body of precepts. If a son of good family were to erect a stupa of the seven treasures for my body of birth reaching as high as the Brahma-heaven, yet someone were to damage it, that offense would still be light and there would be the possibility of repentance.

However, to damage my body of precepts constitutes an immeasurable offense that cannot be expiated through confession. Thus, the twenty-fifth verse of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "The Sangha is like the waters of the great ocean."
The establishment of the precepts serves as a boundary for exclusion. Should there be one who breaks the precepts, they shall never again be counted among the ranks of the Sangha.
It is like the waters of the great ocean, which do not cohabit with a corpse. Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle 33, states: "The great ocean does not harbor corpses.

'Corpses' refers to those who are icchantikas, those who have committed the four grave prohibitions, those who have committed the five crimes of immediate retribution, those who slander the Vaipulya sūtras, and those who propagate what is not the Dharma."
To preach the Dharma as non-Dharma; to accept and store the eight kinds of impure things; to use the property of the Buddha or the Sangha according to one's own will;
or to perform illegal acts toward bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs—these are called "corpses.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* is free from such things; therefore, it is called "not harboring corpses. Regarding the combinations: the first two [of the four] combine with the first phrase.

Third, the combined lower section [of the verse] provides four exhortations to uphold [the precepts]. Next, the second metaphor is explained. The first half of the verse is a metaphor for the benefit of upholding [the precepts], while the second half is a metaphor for their impairment.
By constantly dwelling in mindfulness and so forth, one restrains body and speech; thus, evil finds no opportunity, and it is therefore like guarding a gate.
When the practice of the antidote is perfected, it is ultimately pure and cannot be destroyed by conditions; this is called "firmness," as one has no fear of external [influences].
Because evil kalpas plunder the virtuous wealth of persons, it is said that one need not worry about losing material riches.

One should protect and maintain this practice so that all dharmas are accomplished, the structural framework is established, and its significance is like that of a constant wall. If one encounters conditions that lead to violation, it is termed "deficiency and ruin. Thus, one should be concerned about losing the wealth of the precepts.

Therefore, it is said: "sorrow and fear. This corresponds to the following passage in the text: the Buddha’s precepts correspond to wealth; being unimpaired corresponds to a gate that is firm and secure;
upholding them corresponds to guarding [the gate]; being without sorrow corresponds to not worrying about its loss; the prohibitive precepts correspond to possessing wealth;

not being firm and failing to observe them corresponds to the phrase "constantly having a breach in the wall"; and the ruin [of the precepts] corresponds to sorrow and fear. Next, the third metaphor: the first half-verse is a metaphor for destruction.

The latter half of the verse is a metaphor for maintaining [the precepts]. The three or four lines are subtle; they have not yet reached the fundamental root and are easily compromised by external conditions, being equivalent to an unbaked earthen vessel.
Once the earthen vessel is broken, the original practice is incomplete; this is termed "pierced and leaking. Those who act as monks or nuns are thus merely ordinary teachers.
Beholding one's own transgressions and fearing the evil realms is called "sorrowful anxiety.

When the three or four factors are established and not destroyed by conditions, and one is able to bring them to pure application, this is called "the vessel being complete. That which can accordingly provide support and reception is called "retinue.
The inner mind’s sense of jubilation is called "joy. The combined text is understandable. Regarding the sequence of the four similes: the first phrase presents the simile, and the second phrase...

This exhorts one to uphold [the precepts]. The second line distinguishes the impairment; the final line reveals the transgression. Although the offense may be minor, the injury it inflicts is not slight;
it is like a sudden spark of fire, and thus it is used as a metaphor. Though this offense is subtle, its nature is contrary to principle.

All roots of goodness will be incinerated and gradually exhausted; therefore, it is said: "Do not treat it lightly as small. A continuous wholesome mind is like grass and trees; do not [neglect] these.
They are not burned by fire; therefore it is said, "that which they traverse," and so forth. A single moment of subtle evil can open the gates of the five unwholesome paths.
Because these roots of goodness burn them away without remainder, it is said, "burning," and so forth. As for the "five unwholesome gates": first, they can burn away the roots of goodness;
second, they produce evil from evil; third, one is rebuked by the sages; fourth, one falls away from the fruits of the Path; fifth, [death].

One falls into the evil realms. The *Dazhidu lun* (Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom), fascicle 25, states: "The Buddha taught that although four things are small, they must not be treated lightly.
Although a prince is young, he shall become a king; thus he must not be treated lightly. Although a snake’s cub is small, its venom can kill a person."

One must not underestimate it either; though a small fire is minute, it can burn down mountains and forests. One must not underestimate it either; though a śrāmaṇera is young, he may attain noble supernatural powers.
Most of all, one must not underestimate it. Regarding the subsequent matching of the text: the phrases correspond individually;
alternatively, the first phrase may match the first [section], while the second phrase matches the following three. The final two phrases cite actual events to encourage its observance.

Next is the Parable of the Foolish and the Wise. In the first half of this parable, the analogy of the fool who knows no fear is presented. Having committed a grave transgression for the first time, one’s path to liberation is forever severed;
the evil reputation spreads abroad, and the dreadfulness is extreme—like the roar of a lion, which strikes terror into all who hear it.
Yet foolish monks and nuns, deluded and distracted, are called "drunkards"; regarding such ultimate sins, they do not fear sinking into the depths of suffering. Therefore, it says: "not afraid."
"Fearful. This is an instance of citing the heavy to illustrate the light; since one does not fear the heavy, it goes without saying regarding the light.

The latter half is a metaphor for those of wisdom who are capable of fear: even a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*) causes no ultimate harm, yet its ill repute spreads abroad, and thus they do not fail to fear it.

Just as the sound of small animals causes no fear upon being heard, so too wise *bhikṣus* and *bhikṣuṇīs* are not deluded or disturbed by such things; they are therefore called "Noble Ones" (*ārya*). Regarding...

This is a slight evil; fearing deeply that one might sink into the depths of saṃsāra, it is said, "hearing it, he fears. This wealth [of the teaching] uses the light to illustrate the heavy: if even the light is feared, then the heavy is already spoken of.
The first phrase of the parallel section corresponds to the "intoxicated person"; all evils correspond to the "lion’s roar"; "not fearing" corresponds to "not being terrified";
and the "wise person" corresponds to the "awakened person. Regarding "slight evil," it corresponds to the "small animal's sound": though the sound is faint, it is constant.
If one harbors even a single phrase that ought to be heard, one should feel dread.

Next, through the discernment of metaphors, one diligently cultivates the two types of observance (*dharani*) and is able to eliminate the seven transgressions. The mutual support of cessation (*śamatha*) and action (*pravṛtti*) is called "harmony."

The practices for removal are not singular; hence they are called "multitudinous. When these practices achieve the cessation of evil, they are termed "medicines. Among medicines there may be those that are ineffective;
logically, one must select and discard them, choosing only the efficacious ones to treat various ailments. Therefore, it is said: "Select and discard the ineffective.

Monks and nuns are constantly bound by the seven offenses and are thus called "the sick. By skillfully cultivating the two types of observance (*dharani*), when their practice achieves freedom from transgression, it is called...
Regarding this practice: there are seven instances where what ought not to arise does not arise. Once they have arisen, one confesses and eliminates them;

when this is called "elimination and recovery," the seven transgressions are severed, which is termed "physical health. Being no longer bound by external things is termed "peace and happiness. The combination of these phrases and their individual meanings correspond clearly and can be understood.

Next is the analogy of the feet. The first half [of the verse] is an analogy for "maintaining": seeking heavenly rewards while turning away from the path to Bodhi is called a "distant road," as the fruit remains far removed from the cause.
"Intending to set out" refers to the aspiration to proceed; though the mind intends to proceed, the feet of precepts must be complete.
If one’s *śīla* (ethical discipline) is deficient, there is no way to proceed; therefore it is said, "One should be equal to oneself. The second half of the verse serves as an analogy for refutation:

once the feet of discipline are impaired, one constantly sinks into the evil realms and cannot travel far; a favorable rebirth (*sugati*) is difficult to expect. In the first half of the combined explanation, the meaning corresponds directly;
in the second half, the act of maintaining discipline is raised as a counter-example to the refutation.
Next is the analogy of the life-preserving float. The seven non-precepts are like a deep and swift river; wishing to abandon what is non-virtuous is called "desiring to cross.

The essence of the precepts rises pure and upward, enabling one to transcend birth and death; it is likened to a life-preserving float. One should constantly practice the antidotes to eliminate faults and protect that which was originally received.
The meaning is the same as the function. It is not that although the river is deep, one does not fear being swept away or drowning; therefore it is said, "though deep, there is no worry of sinking.

Reaching the fruit of the two types of maintenance on the other shore, it is therefore said, "one is then able to level [the ground]. The first half of the middle section corresponds [to this], while the second half joins with a long vowel.
Furthermore, the first phrase may be joined as "like a person"; the practice is joined with the desire to cross and the use of the hand. The prohibition...
The precepts are like a life-preserving skin-bag; crossing the river of birth and death is like a river from which one never turns back. "And sinking" corresponds to the following two lines.
Next is the metaphor of the steps: the Dharma-hall of Bodhi forever cuts off perilous suffering, which is likened to the Hall of Śakra. By means of the thirty [stages]...

The seven factors of enlightenment adorn this hall; thus it is said to be "carved and decorated," and so forth. As one approaches this hall, one relies on the precepts as a lamp; therefore, they are like steps.
That which the sages and worthies traverse is called "the path traveled by devas and humans. [This] should be understood in detail according to the combined text.
This can be understood through reflection.

Next is the analogy of the arts (*śilpa*). Because one constantly practices the two types of retention (*dhāraṇī*) with skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), it is said to be "like one well-trained in worldly [matters].

One might also say "having reached" [mastery]; however, it should be stated as "well-trained in the world. "Art" (*śilpa*) refers to internal deliberation and resolution, while "craft" (*kalā*) refers to external perceptual capacity.
No. Furthermore, "skill" (*kī*) refers to ability, while "artistry" (*śilpa*) refers to craft. Since crafts and abilities are not limited to one kind, they are termed "all.

When one has perfected their artistry and craft and is thus recognized by the king, having received such excellent rewards, even though they may be poor and lowly, it is therefore said that they are "equal to the king."
It is not merely that their poverty and low status are severed; they also attain wealth and honor to delight themselves. Therefore it is said:
"By means of these," the first half of the middle section is distinguished by reaching [the goal], while the second half is distinguished by following [the path].

Next is the analogy of the assembly acting according to the Dharma. In the first verse, the assembly is made firm; in the subsequent verse, they are praised. Within the first verse, the first half is the analogy and the second half is the application (*yoga*).
The preservation of the Buddha-dharma relies upon the harmonious union of the assembly to fulfill the function of the Saṃgha, ensuring it is not corrupted by evil;

therefore, it is said that one must first make the assembly firm. Evil remaining outside of the good is referred to as "the enemy's army" (*parasenā*); being subdued and following the correct transformation is called...
This constitutes its destruction. The meaning of the combined text can be understood. The subsequent verse states that because the community is harmonious, the World-Honored One praises it;

since the Saṃgha is unified, the Buddha-Dharma will abide for a long time. Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa* says: "The harmony of the Saṃgha is blissful; practicing together with diligence is blissful. Furthermore, the thirteenth fascicle of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
"Moreover, by teaching and transforming sentient beings, they give rise to the bodhicitta; therefore, one is able to cause..."
The Jewel of the Buddha is not interrupted. By revealing and teaching the profound and wondrous treasury of all dharmas, he is thus able to ensure that the Jewel of the Dharma is not interrupted.
By being fully endowed with the precepts, dignified conduct, and the teachings of the Dharma, he is thus able to ensure that the Jewel of the Sangha is not interrupted.

Furthermore, he is able to praise all great vows, analyze and explain liberation through the twelve links of dependent origination, and practice the six points of harmonious respect. Moreover, below...
The seeds of the Buddha sprout as the shoots of perfect enlightenment within the field of sentient beings.
They protect and uphold the true Dharma without sparing their own bodies or lives, skillfully guiding the great assembly with minds free from anxiety or affliction.
By ensuring that the true Dharma taught by the Buddhas of the past, future, and present is not contravened, they are thus able to cause the Three Jewels to remain uninterrupted.

Next is the analogy of the compassionate mother. That which nourishes by suckling is called milk; that which gives birth to the body is called a mother. To extract suffering is termed "compassion" (*maitrī*);
to bestow happiness is named "love. To nurture means to cause growth; the precepts (*śīla*) can cause all sublime virtues to grow. To protect means to guard against harm;

the precepts can guard against all evils and unwholesome states. Just as a mother protects her child so that they possess the capacity for succession, the precepts protect the practitioner, whereby [they attain...]
Regarding the meaning of "attaining sainthood": all calamities of water and fire are matters that must be protected against.

The afflictions of the three miserable realms (*trāya*) are like water and fire; because the precepts protect the practitioner so that they do not encounter such calamities, it is said, "protecting them, etc.

In the verse of correspondence (*saṃgraha*), the first half corresponds to the first half [of the preceding verse], the subsequent phrase "never falling" corresponds to the fourth line, and "animals, etc. corresponds to the third line.

Next is the analogy of the valiant general. To have within a heart that discerns and guards the precepts is called "courageous. To perceive external non-virtues and prevent them from causing disturbance is termed "valiant.
To be able to defeat the army of transgressions is named a "general. To constantly cultivate the two types of observance is called "skillful practice."
To transgress what one has undertaken to uphold is equivalent in meaning to engaging in combat. In the *Ekottarika Āgama*, fascicle 25, the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"There are five types of heroic men capable of enduring combat who appear in the world.

What are these five? There is a person who, donning armor and grasping a staff, enters the army to fight; yet upon seeing dust and wind from afar, he immediately breaks down and becomes terrified. The second person, if he sees..."
The first person is not terrified by the wind and dust, but is terrified as soon as he sees the high banner.

The second person is not terrified by the wind, dust, or the high banner, but conceives terror upon seeing a flying arrow. The third person is not afraid of the wind, dust, the high banner, or the flying arrow;

however, when entering the fray, he is seized by others or has his life-force severed. The fourth person is not afraid of the dust, the high banner, or the flying arrow; yet, at the time of entering the battle, he is captured by others or has his life-force severed. As for the fifth person, if he sees...
