Amidst the dust and turmoil, if he sees a tall banner or flying arrows, or even if captured by others, he feels no fear until death;
he is able to destroy the enemy army, and though his domain has no external boundaries, he looks after the people. This is called the fifth type of warrior.
Now, among the bhikṣus there are likewise five types. The first, upon seeing a woman, immediately gives rise to lustful thoughts. [Excluding him...]

First, he discarded the three robes and returned the Buddha’s prohibitive precepts. Second, upon seeing a woman, he did not give rise to thoughts of desire; yet he engaged in flirtation and exchanged words with her.

Because of this flirtation, he then abandoned his dharma-robes. Third, upon seeing a woman, he did not give rise to thoughts of desire, and even when engaging in flirtation, he had no thoughts of desire;
however, as soon as he placed his hands together with that woman in a fist-clasp, thoughts of desire immediately arose, and he returned [the robes].
As a layperson, he saw women four times and did not give rise to thoughts of desire; even when conversing with them, he likewise had no thoughts of desire.
However, when those women touched him with their hands, he immediately gave rise to thoughts of desire, yet he did not discard his dharma robes. This was the fifth time he saw women.
He does not give rise to thoughts of desire. Even when joking or laughing together, or being touched and pinched, he still has no thoughts of desire.
At that time, the bhikṣu contemplates the thirty-six impure and foul substances within this body: "Who is it that clings to these? From what does desire arise? Where does this desire cease?
Does it come from the head, or does it emerge from the physical form? He contemplates these various things and realizes they are utterly non-existent.
From head to foot it is likewise so; this is explained at length. One thereby attains the four knowledges (*caturjñāna*).
What is here called the "Fierce General" is the fifth general. The two types of transgression—omission and commission—are contrary to the observance [of precepts] and are thus termed its "enemies.
Since observance can destroy these enemies of transgression, it is called "subjugation. Because at the time of subjugation one does not regret until death, it is said that one "dies without regard."
This "disregard for life" is as explained in the third chapter of the *Vyavahāra-śāstra* (The Treatise on Adornment), concerning the bhikṣu bound by grass to a wooden plank;

this corresponds to the first phrase of the verse. "The Son of the Buddha [is] well-awakened regarding the prohibitive precepts" corresponds to the second and third phrases. "When the five aggregates disintegrate" corresponds to the phrase "drowning in death.
"Ultimately [he does not]" corresponds to the preceding phrase "disregarding his life."

Next is the analogy of true birth. In the preceding verse there is "true birth," and in the subsequent verse there is "true death. Within the former, the first half presents the analogy, while the second half cites actual events to provide proof.
"Precepts" refers to the Buddha’s precepts; obtaining these is called "birth. Therefore, it says, "from the Buddha’s precepts," and so forth.

This contrasts with the aforementioned conventional birth, all of which is not truly real. The citation of proof is clear. Next, regarding "true death": having received the Buddha’s precepts, it is termed...

Zhen-sheng clearly understands that abandoning the precepts is equivalent to true death. Because he is unable to uphold them and has cast aside the practice of the Dharma, fearing it might be confused with an ordinary worldly death, he says, "Regarding the Buddha-dharma, etc.
The subsequent half-verse, which exhorts him to uphold [the precepts], is easy to understand.

Next is the analogy of the royal seal. The first half [of the verse] is an analogy for upholding [the precepts]: the Buddha’s precepts are difficult to encounter, the conditions for obtaining them are difficult to fulfill, and they are obtained only within what is difficult to obtain—just like a royal seal.
Once one has obtained the seal, one’s conduct becomes pure and elevated; one is no longer bound by evil fetters, which is called being "unimpeded."

The latter half of the verse is a metaphor for transgression. If one commits any of the four minor offenses (*pāyattika*), must one be interrogated and undergo confession? If one commits the first *pārājika*, one is certainly bound and cast into prison; this can be understood from the text. Question:
Since minor insults are not fixed [in their karmic result], why does the subsequent text state that slandering a pure person invariably leads to imprisonment?

Furthermore, why is it said that drinking alcohol or handling precious objects definitively disqualifies one from being a śramaṇa? Answer: These statements are intended to manifest the gravity of the faults; they are not literal descriptions of the underlying principle.
He asked again: "Since Mahākausthila has already entered the three evil realms, why did Nandika permit him to perform repentance? He replied: "This is spoken from the perspective of the majority.

Regarding those who do not repent, I shall next provide an analogy based on the Buddha's formulation of the precepts for two types of persons: first, those who are single-mindedly diligent and do not transgress; second, those who have already transgressed."

They are capable of repentance; since these two types of persons are not one and the same, it is said that "all" are included. However, these two types of persons are bound by deluded demons within the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*) and are unable to achieve liberation.
Out of great compassion, the Tathāgata established the Vinaya to teach the cultivation of counteractive measures for their removal, thereby causing them to eliminate their delusions and karma;
thus it is said, "subduing the demons. The term "immortal with the five supernatural powers" (*pañcābhijñā*) is a metaphor for the Buddha, who composed this incantation (*dhāraṇī*).

The analogy for the precepts: in the application (*yojanā*), "shame and dread" (*hrī-apatrāpya*) correspond to the first line; "restraining all that is devoid of shame and dread" corresponds to the second line;

"the Tathāgata" corresponds to the third; and "establishing the prohibitive precepts" corresponds to the fourth. Regarding the phrase "preaching every half-month," this indicates the time for exhortation and preaching;
it is not part of the text of the analogy itself. All practitioners must possess shame and dread. However, these two forms of shame and dread may at first appear similar, namely:

When people of the world see one who is without shame (*ahrī*), they call them "shameless" (*ahrīka*); when they see one who is without modesty (*anapatrāpya*), they call them "immodest" (*anapatrāpin*).

In reality, the distinction between these two is not the same; it is vast and boundless. Since this is discussed in detail in the *Dhātunirdeśa* (Chapter 1) and the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* (Chapter 2), the fourth chapter of the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states:
"Regarding all virtues and those who possess virtue, there is no respect, no veneration, no sense of dread or difficulty, and no compliance."
That which is censured and loathed by all virtuous persons is called "transgression. To see no fear in such transgressions is called "lack of shame" (*āhrīkya*).

Other masters say that regarding the transgressions one has committed, to feel no shame when observing oneself is called "lack of shame," while to feel no shame when observing others is called "lack of dread" (*anapatrāpya*). As for the distinction between shame and dread, it is the reverse of the former.
The commentary states: To have reverence, to have veneration, to have that which one avoids with dread, and to have that to which one is subjectively attached—this is called *hrī* (shame).

To perceive fear regarding transgressions—this is called *apatrāpya* (embarrassment). Reversing the latter explanation, it says: To feel shame upon self-examination regarding the transgressions one has committed is called *hrī*;
to feel shame upon considering others is called *apatrāpya*. Furthermore, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, fascicle 38, states: "There are two kinds of purity (*śukla*)."
The Dharma protects the world; it is through shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*) that this is so.

If these two pure dharmas did not protect the world, one would not distinguish between father, mother, brother, sister, son, daughter, or kinsmen, and the human dharma would be destroyed, becoming like cattle, sheep, chickens, dogs, jackals, birds, and wild beasts.
If these two pure dharmas—shame and dread of blame—exist within the world, then one distinguishes between father and mother.

Brothers, sisters, children, grandchildren, and kinsmen do not violate the laws of humanity; they are not like oxen, sheep, chickens, dogs, jackals, birds, or wild beasts that lack such shame and remorse (*hrī-apatrāpya*).
For one who possesses the pure dharmas (*śukla-dharma*), it is simply impossible for this [violation] to occur.

If the mind lacks the pure dharmas, there is only birth and death, and no liberation. If one possesses this shame and remorse, and the pure dharmas reside within the mind, one immediately attains purity, and thus [one does not...].

Birth and death; crossing to the shore beyond birth and death, one will no longer undergo further existence. Next, the exhortation is given in terms of time. A question is asked as to why the precepts must be recited every half-month.
The answer is: if they were recited daily, the recitations would be too frequent; being too frequent leads to weariness, and weariness leads to a lack of reverence.

If they were recited once a month, the recitations would be too infrequent; being too infrequent leads to negligence, and negligence leads to indolence. Therefore, it is now [recited] every half-month.
To eliminate the fault of excessive delay is precisely the Great Sage’s method for weighing urgency against slackness.

Thus, even if it takes half a month, it is still permissible on the remaining days. Why, then, must it specifically be at the end of the half-month? The answer is: according to secular reckoning, thirty days constitute a month;

this corresponds to the end of the half-month and the full moon. This is truly because at the midpoint of the month the moon is at its full height, while at the end of the month it is at its zenith; [the rule] is intended to prompt observation.
Regarding these signs: when the practitioner sees the moon at its full, they feel regret that their own goodness is insufficient; thus, there is no good they do not cultivate.

When they see it waning, they sigh that evil still abounds; thus, there is no evil they do not abandon. Being able to abandon evil and cultivate benefit, their practice of cessation and cultivation is perfected.
It is my hope that they may propagate the supreme teaching so that, at the time of their attainment, their noble legacy may be transmitted to distant generations. Furthermore, I desire—
Time is revealed as swift; every moment is impermanent. One who has committed an offense must diligently seek its purification through repentance before it can be rendered faultless.

For those who exert themselves in the practice of cultivation, they should fully rely on the teachings to establish both the "black" and "white" months. According to these two traditions, both conclude at the end of the month.

Regarding the third passage: mental phenomena are formless; thus, words are employed as a provisional means to manifest reverence. As the discussion of virtues is vast and extensive, I fear it might obstruct what is essential to be communicated.
Having completed the eulogy, I again prostrate myself. It is fitting that you conceal your own feelings, cease your sighs, and return to the act of worship.
Next, the introduction concerning the occasion of the composition is explained. However, some interpret the introductory text as being divided into two parts:

first, from the beginning of the verse up to "how should it be," which clarifies the Master of the Vinaya’s respectful praise and exhortation to believe and practice; second, from the words "Venerable Śāriputra" onwards, which clarifies the introduction concerning the occasion of the composition.
The preceding exhortation consists of two parts: first, clarifying how the Master of the Vinaya composed verses of praise to establish the thesis and encourage faithful practice;

second, from "At that time, the Buddha was traveling... onwards, citing specific instances to provide proof. Regarding these cited proofs, as explained in detail within the *Ātyayika-cīvara* (Urgent Robe) precept, there are six points which are identical to this text:
first, the donor is the same; second, the location is the same, namely Piṇḍavana; third, the placement...
After three months had passed, four groups of disciples were equal in number, and Ānanda was the fifth as attendant; yet none of them obtained alms-food.

Thus, one knows that this passage is a statement from that [text]. This [passage] (the nine characters concerning summer retreat) appears in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* within the precept on eating with non-Buddhists, and it also appears among the rules on medicinal substances (*bhaiṣajya*).
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* likewise contains this corroborating text. For what reason must it be cited? Because there are two meanings. First:

The proof of the teaching on maintaining and violating the precepts, and the resulting benefit or harm, is not false. Second, it is to manifest that one’s own transmission of exhortations is a distant inheritance of the Sage’s intent, rather than a matter of arbitrarily inflicting benefit or harm based on one's own whims.
Throughout the beginning and end of the preceding verse, it is stated that maintaining the precepts brings benefit while breaking them incurs harm.

The Master of the Vinaya feared that the assembly of his time might think his words were mere falsehoods or deceptive speech, and thus wonder why they should be cause for joy or aversion; therefore, he must cite the Buddha’s eating of barley.

The "personal matters" (or "intimate affairs") are established as trustworthy; this will be explained extensively in the text. Regarding those who transmit the teachings by following the intended meaning, as a verse says:

"Now I wish to speak of the profound precepts," and so forth, up to "for the benefit of the elders. The Master of the Vinaya, fearing that people of his time might claim he was acting arbitrarily and thus corrupting the original teaching of the Sage, cited the Buddha’s own sincere words:
"O you great men, it may be so for those who have attained supernormal powers (*ṛddhipāda*); however, in future ages..."
"How should a bhikṣu act? Thus one knows that it is necessary. Upon examining this explanation, it contradicts both principle and scripture.

What is the contradiction with principle? The text does not state that this [rule] arises from what follows below; rather, it means that one takes this [gift] because of an urgent offering, not that one takes an urgent offering for the sake of this [rule].
Why is this so? Because the text does not cite terms such as "the coastal regions" (*pāñcālaka*) to provide an occasion for giving, but instead directly takes the gift.
Regarding this matter, while the various conditions (*pratyaya*) herein are fully elucidated, the act of giving (*dāna*) is not clarified.

This is similar to the origination of taking up a dwelling by destroying what was produced, or the origination of conceiving great falsehoods upon actually attaining the Path; these cases are all alike. The root is broad while the branches are brief. As for those who contravene the teachings:
The *Jianlun* (Treatise on Views), fascicle four, states: "Venerable Śāriputra arose from samādhi and requested the Buddha to establish the precepts.
At that time, the Buddha was staying at Vairaṇyā. Furthermore, in the fifth [fascicle], it says: "When they were eating barley for their midday meal, Śāriputra made his request.

After the request was granted, he and Ānanda then went together to bid him farewell. For these reasons, it should be known that this is not a valid citation as evidence. The *Wufen lü* (Five-Part Vinaya) is likewise. Moreover—
There are those who judge this to be for the purpose of establishing the arising of the higher [realms] and the falling into the lower, or as medicinal remedies suited to specific capacities;

all such views are equally erroneous. Since the previous analysis was incorrect, I shall now set forth the correct meaning. This text is comprised within the *nidāna* (introductory) section. It consists of two parts:

first, up to the point where it says, "How should one request the establishment of the rules regarding the location"; second, from the passage beginning with Śāriputra, which describes the occasion for the request. The preceding text is further divided.
Five: 1. The place where the Great Sage traveled and transformed beings; 2. At Piḷaṇḍu, hearing of his virtue and meeting him with joy; 3.
At that time, at Piḷaṇḍu, generating faith and inviting the Buddha; 4. The World-Honored One, together with five hundred [monks], went to the invitation to eat barley; 5.
At that time, the Venerable [Ānanda] invited [the Buddha] to a meal provided spontaneously.
Regarding the opening phrase, "At that time" (*iti tadā*), it carries the sense of initiation; that is to say, it reveals the location of past conversion and the time of the teaching.
"To" (*yad*) signifies a contradiction in meaning. "Great" (*mahat*) is a title for a venerable elder. "Vairaṇyā" is the name of a town;
the king granted this town as a fief to this Brāhmaṇa. "Nalinī" is the name of a yakṣa spirit. "Bhin" means water.
As for "island" (*dvīpa*), it is a place where one may dwell; because it dwells upon the edge of the water, it is called a "coastal island.

As for *Mandāra*, it is the *nirmālya* tree. However, yakṣas and ghosts dwell in reliance upon this tree, which is the foremost among the lush forests and, moreover, is close to the city, making it convenient for coming and going.
For these reasons, the Tathāgata dwelt beneath this tree. Furthermore, dwelling beneath a tree was for the sake of all...
Disciples, in accordance with the dharma of renunciation, remove greed and desire. The *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle eight, states:
"The reason the Buddha and the great assembly dwelt in this grove was to accord with the four noble lineages (*catur-ārya-vaṃśa*) that were their original vow;
furthermore, it was to subdue the prideful minds of future disciples and to establish a model for them. Since the Buddha had accepted the location..."
In the mountains and marshes, his later disciples were willing to dwell out in the open air.

Furthermore, because he wished to preach the Dharma for the sake of devas, nāgas, and benevolent spirits—and since most devas and nāgas delight in quietude—the Tathāgata dwelt beneath the trees of the forest. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, fascicle 14, states:
"In that country, people believed in heterodoxy; previously there were no vihāras. To the north of the city was a grove of Śirīṣa trees, whose foliage was lush and beautiful."
The ground was exceedingly level and vast. The Buddha and the great assembly stayed within this forest. The second section has three parts:
first, hearing that the Tathāgata had traveled to his own country; second, from "this śramaṇa" downward, the virtuous name he heard;

third, from "Excellent! downward, the joy of having encountered him upon hearing it. Regarding the first part, the *brāhmaṇa* (here translated as "Pure Conduct") refers to the person at that location.
This is for the purpose of identifying the person. Next, the section on the titles of his virtues has two parts: first, the explanation of the ten epithets; second, the analysis of the three wheels.
Here, "this śramaṇa" and so forth provide a general reference, while "the Tathāgata" and below provide specific designations. "This one" refers to the individual.
"Śramaṇa" means one who inwardly harbors holy virtue. "Gautama" indicates his clan name. "Thus" is a term used to cite the Dharma, speaking generally of his virtues; therefore—

It is said: "Great Renown. Generally, in discourse, that which summons the essence is called a *ming* (name); that which expresses virtue is a *zi* (style). When name and reality correspond, it is called *cheng* (renown);
when the resonance spreads among humans and devas, it is a *hao* (title). Now, the titles of all Buddhas possess both general (*tong*) and specific (*bie*) aspects.

The specific reveals the birth-body (*janma-kāya*), distinguishing its manifested characteristics, such as Śākyamuni, Maitreya, and others. The general refers to actual virtues; because the Dharma-body is equal, it is termed "Tathāgata" and so forth.

Regarding the merit of the ten titles: furthermore, all Buddhas possess three similarities and six differences. As for the three similarities: first, because their accumulations (*saṃbhāra*) are equally perfected;
second, because their *dharmakāya* is equally accomplished; and third, because their benefit for others (*parārtha*) is equally consummated. As for the six differences:
first, the difference in lifespan, meaning that the lifespans of Buddhas vary in length; second, the difference in lineage (*gotra*).
First, the difference in caste, namely the Kṣatriya and Brāhmaṇa lineages. Second, the difference in clan, namely clans such as Gautama, Kāśyapa, and so forth.
Third, the difference in physical stature, namely that the Buddha’s body may be small or large. Fourth, the difference in the duration of the Dharma, namely seven hundred, two thousand, and so on.
Fifth, the difference in the *śarīra*, namely whether they are whole bodies or fragmented remains. Nevertheless, the measure of a Buddha’s virtues is in truth boundless; this is based on—
Virtues establish names; how could their number be limited? For now, based on the ritual of transformation (*nirmāṇa-vidhi*), we shall briefly set forth two sets of five.

Regarding the so-called "Tathāgata" and the others, we shall now explain the ten titles as clarified in the thirty-eighth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the eighteenth fascicle of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*. As for the term "Tathāgata":

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Because his words are without falsehood, he is called the Tathāgata. The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "As with all Buddhas of the past, what they have taught remains unchanging.
Why is it unchanging? Because the Buddhas of the past, in order to deliver sentient beings, preached the twelve divisions of the scriptures (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*)."

The Tathāgata is likewise; therefore, he is named the Tathāgata. Furthermore, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, come from the six pāramitās, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and the eleven kinds of emptiness, reaching up to Great Nirvāṇa. The Tathāgata is likewise; for this reason, the Buddha is titled the Tathāgata.

He is "unattached" because he has severed the two bonds. The two bonds refer to the bond of the object of cognition (*ālambana*) and the bond of association (*samprayoga*); alternatively, they are called...
He is "Arhat" (the Worthy One). The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Having attained all that is to be attained, he should be the unsurpassed field of merit for the world;
he should be the object of respect and offerings by all. For this reason, he is called 'Arhat. However, the term 'Arhat' alone encompasses the full meaning.
If one says 'Arhaṃt' (Worthy of Offerings), the scope of the meaning is not exhaustive. The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* says: "All worldly phenomena are termed enemies."
Because the Buddha is worthy of being honored (*arhat*), he is called "Worthy" (*Arhat*). Now, as for the four Māras, they are the enemies of Bodhisattvas.

When the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, were Bodhisattvas, they were able to destroy these four Māras through their wisdom; therefore, they are called "Worthy. Alternatively, regarding the name *Arhat*, the third fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"*Arhat* generally encompasses the stage of the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) across all three vehicles. All...

Because they have forever destroyed the thieves of the afflictions (*kleśa*), because they deserve to receive the sublime offerings of the world, and because they will never again undergo birth within the limits of the segmented realms of existence—possessing these three meanings, they are called *arhat*.
As for the term "Samyaksaṃbuddha," *samya* means equal or uniform.

This is precisely "right understanding. "Awakening" (jue) means to realize and awaken. Because the Buddha has equally realized and awakened to all phenomena, he is called the "Equally Rightly Awakened One" (Samyak-saṃbuddha).
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Because he awakens to all phenomena according to their ultimate reality (paramārtha), he is named the 'Rightly and Equally Awakened One'.

Nirvāṇa is termed "Right Universal Knowledge" (Samyak-saṃbodhi). "Right" means non-inverted; "universal knowledge" means there is nothing regarding the four inversions that he does not thoroughly penetrate. Furthermore,
"Furthermore, 'Right' (Sammā) means that which can be counted, measured, and weighed. 'Omniscient' (Vibhuññū) means that which cannot be counted, measured, or weighed;
for this reason, the Buddha is titled the 'Rightly Omniscient One' (Sam-māsambuddha). Moreover, 'Omniscient' (Vibhu) signifies equality, and 'Knowing' (Jñāna) signifies awakening;

thus, it carries the meaning of 'Equal and Right Awakening' (Samyaksambodhi). Regarding the 'One Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct' (Vidyācaraṇasampanna): the *Yogācārabhūmi* states that 'Knowledge' (Vidyā) refers to the three knowledges (*tisro vidyāḥ*), and 'Conduct' (Caraṇa) is as follows..."
The Sūtra states that the two categories of śamatha and vipaśyanā are perfectly fulfilled; therefore, it is called the perfection of knowledge and conduct (*vidyā-caryā-sampad*).
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "Knowledge" refers to attaining immeasurable virtuous fruits; "conduct" refers to the feet. "Virtuous fruits" refers to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
"feet" refers to ethical discipline (*śīla*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). By mounting the feet of wisdom and ethical discipline, one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. For this reason, it is so named.

Regarding "One Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct" (*vidyācaraṇasampanna*): The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle three, states: "Knowledge" (*vidyā*) refers to the three types of supernormal knowledge, such as the knowledge of past lives.

"Conduct" (*caraṇa*) refers to the actions of body and speech. Only the Buddha’s bodily and vocal actions are fully perfected; all others have defects. This is called being "perfected in knowledge and conduct.

Regarding "Well-Gone" (*sugata*): The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Because he has ascended to the ultimate limit and will never again fall back, he is called 'Well-Gone'. The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states: [and so forth].
The virtuous are called "exalted" (*unnata*); those who have passed away are not called "exalted. O son of good family, this is what is meant by worldly meaning.
"Exalted" refers to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; "not exalted" refers to the mind of the Tathāgata. Son of good family, if the mind were exalted, it would not be called the Tathāgata.
Therefore, the Tathāgata is named "Well-Gone" (*Sugata*). Regarding "Knower of the World" (*Lokavid*), the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that he is one who knows well.

Because he understands all categories of the world and the realm of sentient beings through their defiled and purified characteristics, he is called the Knower of the World (*lokavid*). The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"In the east, there are immeasurable asaṃkhyeya worlds that all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not know, see, or understand;
the Buddhas alone know them all, see them all, and understand them all. It is the same for the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir."

Thus it is. For this reason, the Buddha is titled the Knower of the World (*lokavid*). Regarding the title "Unsurpassed Man, Charioteer of Men" (*anuttaraḥ puruṣadamyasārathiḥ*), the *Yogācārabhūmi* states:
"In all the world, he is the one and only man who thoroughly knows the most excellent skillful means for taming the mind;

therefore, he is called the Unsurpassed Man, the Charioteer of Men. The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "The 'Superior Man' (*uttama-puruṣa*) is defined as one who has severed [all afflictions]; there is nothing further to be done..."
One who has severed [all defilements] is called the Unsurpassed One (*anuttara*). Since the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess no afflictions, there is nothing further to be severed;
for this reason, the Buddha is titled the Unsurpassed One. What is meant by "Tamer of Men" (*puruṣadamyasārathi*)? Having himself become a great man (*puruṣa*), he further tames other men.
"Good son, that which is called the Tathāgata is, in reality, neither a man nor not a man;
because he disciplines men, the Tathāgata is designated as a 'man. Good son, all men and women who possess four qualities are called 'men.
What are these four? First, having virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitra); second, being able to listen to the Dharma; third, reflecting upon its meaning; fourth, acting in accordance with it."
I shall speak of their practice. Good son, whether male or female, if one is endowed with four dharmas, they are called a "great man" (puruṣa).
Good son, if a man lacks these four dharmas, he cannot be called a great man. Why is this?

"Fold" (*aṅga*) means branch, category, or section; it refers to the fact that within the teaching there are twelve categories, branches, and segments, each distinct from the others, hence they are called "twelve.
Next is the "Gate of the Reasoning," which asks why it is necessary to clarify these twelve.
[Question on] the classification of teachings. Answer: Sentient beings awaken to the Way by relying on various conditions; because these conditions differ, twelve are taught among them.

Thus, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle one, states: "Although sentient beings possess the power of causes, if they lack the power of conditions to trigger awakening, they will ultimately be unable to cultivate superior and progressive practices.
Only upon encountering the power of conditions can they engage in cultivation. It is, for example, like a pond..."

Within [the pond], although there are various exquisite lotuses such as the *utpala* and others, if they are not touched by the light of the sun or moon, they will not open up to emit their various fragrances.
Only when touched by the light of the sun or moon can they, according to their kind, open up and emit fragrance.
Furthermore, it is like having various objects in the darkness; if there is no lamp to illuminate them, they can never be seen.
[The Buddha] saw that sentient beings were likewise so. Question: For what reason is the power of the conditions [of the twelve links] neither deficient nor excessive?
Answer: It is because those who hear the Dharma are fit to hear it; thus it is so. Furthermore, when the Wheel of Dharma was turned, the four noble truths were traversed through three cycles;

therefore, the teaching that elucidates them also consists of twelve factors, neither deficient nor excessive. The preceding extensive explanation of the transformative teaching is complete; hereafter, the abbreviated section on the prohibitions will follow.

Regarding "Extensive": next, as for why it is not explicitly stated [in the *Vinaya*], it is because those to be converted, upon hearing the extensive version, would find it cumbersome. For this reason, the Tathāgata did not state the two extensive versions.
Alternatively, the extensive version of the *deśanā-vinaya* (teaching for conversion) herein should not have been cited again;

its inclusion here is an error in the text. If one follows this interpretation, the *prātimokṣa-vinaya* (disciplinary rules) is not abbreviated. Next, regarding "the Dharma will not endure for long": this is because there is no extensive teaching upon which to rely for further cultivation; thus, it is abbreviated.
The Dharma is profound and subtle; furthermore, it is difficult to enter, which leads to weariness and causes the Dharma not to endure for long.

Next, the benefits manifest through concise exposition are clarified. This passage consists of five parts: first, presenting the essence of the concise [teaching]; second, the location of the discourse; third, the actual concise exposition;
fourth, demonstrating the manifest benefits; and fifth, identifying subsequent disadvantages. Regarding the first part, the *Sudarsana-vyākhyā* states: "Those who should practice mindfulness..."

To contemplate impermanence, suffering, impurity, and non-self when these are not objects for such contemplation—meaning, not to contemplate the impermanent as permanent, nor the impure as pure, and so forth—and to contemplate the three roots of goodness when they are objects for such contemplation, while not contemplating the three unwholesome roots when they are not objects for such contemplation;
next, the following pair summarizes the cultivation of equanimity (*upekṣā*): that which should be abandoned, namely...
The second set of four lines: "Do not think, do not contemplate; these must be severed and abandoned. This refers to those who should dwell in full accomplishment, meaning the first three lines.
One must think and contemplate; these are to be cultivated and advanced. This constitutes the *vyākaraṇa-saṃkṣepa* (abridged exposition), but there is no *niyama-saṃkṣepa* (abridged restraint).

As for the *niyama-saṃkṣepa*, it consists of the verses on "not slandering and not being envious," which is the Buddha’s abridgment according to karma. The verse on "do not let the mind be negligent" is the *go-gāthā* (ox-verse).

The *Anāgāmin-saṃkṣepa* is concluded. Next, the *Saṃkṣipta-sthāna* (Brief Exposition) is explained. By relying on this forest, one is led to develop weary detachment (*nirveda*). Once the mind has become weary, it is easy to enter the Path.
This can be understood from the subsequent formal exposition. Next, the immediate benefits are clarified;

for as long as the Sun of the Buddha has not set and the Śrāvakas remain in the world, even though the abbreviated teaching is transmitted, the Dharma will flourish and spread extensively. Next, the subsequent decline is clarified; there are three points within the text, namely: the Dharma...

The analogy and its application consist of four propositions within the Dharma: first, clarifying those who leave home from various backgrounds; second, from "For this reason" onwards, manifesting the rapid extinction of the Dharma;
third, "Why is this? expresses the sense of subtle extinction; fourth, from "Not... onwards, explaining the causes for such extinction.

Regarding the first section, "various names" refers to those such as Dharmagupta and others; "various lineages" refers to those such as Maudgalyāyana and others; "various [clans]"... [text fragment ends].

Regarding those who "plant the seeds of the family," this refers to the poor, the lowly, and so forth. These various classes all abandon worldly dust, shave their hair, dye their robes, and together enter the Buddha-dharma;
therefore, it is called "leaving home" (*pravrajyā*). Next, the extinction of the Dharma is revealed: because beings of diverse natures have entered the Dharma, it is extinguished. Why is this so?
It is simply because people are not of one kind and their lineages and clans are myriad and distinct; although they have joined the gateway of the Way, they are unable to attain awakening.
Briefly stated: because they do not awaken to the brief [teachings], they follow their own minds in making decisions and do not accept [the lineage] from one another;
thus, the Dharma quickly perishes. Next, to clarify the reason for this subtle extinction: these types of people have left the household life out of faith and ought to cause the Dharma to flourish.

Why, then, does it perish so quickly? Next, the reason is explained: because there is no extensive teaching, and the sutras are maintained like mere threads; the Dharma does not reside in the person, and for this reason, it quickly perishes. Next...

The metaphors are also four; they should be understood according to the Dharma. Question: What are the flower, the table, the wind, and the thread? Answer: The various characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) are the flower;
the Buddha-dharma is the table; the mental activities of sentient beings are the wind; and the extensive teachings are the thread. It is because there is no thread that it is so.

This is based on the *pariyatti* (transformative teaching). As for the *vinaya* (disciplinary teaching): the various names and surnames are the flower; the concise teaching is the table; and the Saṃgha...
The body and speech of the *bhikṣuṇī* are the wind; the extensive teachings are the thread. It is because there is no thread that it is so. The combined text may be understood [as follows].

Next, the response concerning the long endurance of the four Buddhas contains four parts: first, clarifying the extensiveness of the teachings of conversion and discipline (*vinaya*) spoken by the four Buddhas;

second, from "the disciples... onwards, clarifying that they further spoke the abbreviated [teachings]; third, from "in this way... onwards, clarifying their current dissemination; fourth, from "if those... onwards, clarifying the future.

[The Buddha] dwelt for a long time. However, when he taught the extensive texts, both the *vaipulya* (transformative) and the *vinaya* (disciplinary) were fully present; whereas within the concise teachings, there was the transformative but not the disciplinary.

Regarding those concise disciplinary rules, such as those found in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*—for example, "Patience is the supreme path"—I shall here explain the distinction between these two types of teaching through a fourfold analysis.
First, determining the extensive and concise teachings; second, explaining the names "extensive" and "concise"; third, clarifying...

Regarding their distinctions, the fourth section clarifies the differences between the *vinaya* (precepts) and other teachings. First, concerning the summary of the *śāsana* (teachings), there are briefly two types:

first, the summary of the *śikṣāpada* (training rules) for the gate of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and insight), such as "one should reflect upon such matters"; second, the summary of the gate of discipline for the *vinaya* (disciplinary code), such as "well-guarding one's speech.
Next, regarding the detailed exposition, there are likewise two: first, the detailed exposition of the *śikṣāpada*, such as the twelvefold division of the teachings (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*).

Second, the Vinaya teachings are extensive, such as the teachings of the *Prātimokṣa* and the *Vinaya*. Next, regarding the explanation of the name: it is called "extensive" because its textual expressions and meanings are vast and comprehensive;

this is a brief translation of that term. Furthermore, there are five meanings of "extensive": first, it possesses the *nidāna* (causal origin); second, it awaits transgressions; third, it relies upon requests.
Second, the manifestation of names and categories, such as "Yi" (夷) and "Can" (殘). Third, the clarification of distinctions in transgressions and practices, such as the "Extensive Explanations" (廣解).

Fourth, the description of karmic retributions, such as the text on "Maintaining and Breaking," which states that each falls into two paths; or as in the *Maudgalyāyana-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, regarding the transgression of a *pārājika* offense:
by human reckoning, one falls into the hells for nine hundred twenty-one billion and sixty thousand years.

The remaining offenses last for twenty-three billion four hundred million years; the *sthūlātyaya* offenses last for five billion six hundred million years; the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses last for two billion four hundred million years;
the *pāyattika* offenses last for three hundred million six hundred million years; and the *duṣkṛta* offenses last for nine hundred thousand years.
The methods for purifying and extinguishing these through the five types of confession are called "extensive" (*vistara*) by virtue of these five points. This is the summary (*samkṣepa*).
The absence of these five constitutes what is called "concise" (*saṃkṣipta*). As for the distinctions: first, there is the distinction between the root and the branches;

second, there is the distinction between those who are dull-witted and those who are sharp-witted—the teaching is extensive for the dull-witted and concise for the sharp-witted; third, there is the difference in the designation of offenses—names for offenses are established because the extensive teaching addresses transgressions, whereas this is not the case for the concise method, and thus it lacks the designation of "offense";
fourth, there is the sequence of exposition—the teachings for conversion are extensive or concise according to their chronological order.

It is indeterminate, for those to be converted require different teachings according to their suitability. Within the established instructions, one must first provide a brief summary and subsequently a detailed exposition.

The brief version is intended for those who are pure and may be presented immediately; the detailed version is for those who are defiled, which requires waiting for them to commit an offense before being requested. However, within this text:

According to the sequence of that explanation, in reality it is not the case that the broad comes first and the concise later, nor that the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* (the "Root of Precepts") is taken as the primary subject.
Thus, the five offenses come first and the seven verses are placed afterward. Regarding the differences in the subsequent regulations:

first, the concise version does not wait for an offense to arise before being applied to a lay attendant (*kappiya-kāraka*), whereas the broad version waits for an offense to occur before the transgression can even arise. Second, there is the difference between being requested and not being requested; the concise version...

This is the root; therefore, it may be stated directly. The extensive [version] is the branch, which necessarily requires a prior request. The remaining sequence of the text is the same as before, and the subsequent conclusion is evident.
Taking these abidings and cessations as the basis for the request, as in the *Pañcavargika* and the *Sudarsana-vinaya*, there are three abidings and three cessations.
In principle, they are all equal in terms of being extensive or abbreviated, as in the *Ekottarika-āgama*, which shall be fully analyzed below. Furthermore, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*...
The first [sūtra] says: When the Buddha was at the Jetavana, Śāriputra asked why the Dharma would not remain for long after his passing. The Buddha replied:

"Because I have not extensively expounded the ninefold scriptural teachings (navāṅga-dharma) to my disciples, nor have I established the precepts, nor have I instituted the recitation of the Prātimokṣa, the Dharma will not endure for long after my parinirvāṇa.
If, however, I had expounded the ninefold scriptural teachings and established their formal recitation, the Dharma would have endured for a long time. And so forth.
He did not specifically mention the names of the other two Buddhas. Śāriputra, on this account, immediately requested that the teaching be concluded.

Next, the fourth section below consists of the formal request, which has two parts: first the request, and then the response. Regarding the intent of the request: if the two Buddhas had not been extensive in their teachings, the Dharma would have quickly perished;

because the four Buddhas were extensive, it was able to endure for a long time. Thus, the request is identical in its aim to the benefit of the four Buddhas' long endurance, differing from the case of the two.

Because the Tathāgata would suffer the loss of its swift extinction, he said, "Now is precisely the right time. This means that now is precisely the time to establish the extensive [teachings]. "Only" (*kevalam*) has the sense of being exclusive or singular; thus it is said, "I only pray.
Regarding the formulation of the precepts (*śīla-saṃvara*) and so forth, the ancient commentary states: "The two sections of the *Prātimokṣa* are the formulation of the precepts;

the *Poṣadha-vastu* (Section on the Confession of Precepts) is the ritual procedure for reciting them; and the remaining sections, such as the ordination (*upasaṃpadā*), constitute the cultivation of the holy life (*brahmacarya*)."

Regarding the practice of the Dharma: it may also be that within each individual precept (*śīla*), one first establishes the rule (*prātimokṣa*) to correspond to this establishment, and subsequently recites the precepts, as well as the *Śikṣāpada-vastu*.

Furthermore, in response to this recitation, there are other matters such as receiving [the precepts], dwelling in peace, and so forth; these are specifically applicable to the method of practicing the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
How could one establish and recite [the rules] while departing from the mind of making such a request? As for the various other texts, they are not [applicable here].

The explanation of the *kamma* (formal act) follows. Furthermore, if the *saṃghādisesa* offenses and so forth were combined with their specific designations and remained so for a long duration, why would this not be the case?

Therefore, the current explanation of "binding and proclaiming" (*bandhana-saṃsāvana*) is as follows: "binding" refers to requesting the establishment of prohibitions and defenses; "proclaiming" refers to announcing them to the assembly. This is precisely what is meant by "binding and proclaiming."

This is the cultivation of the holy life (*brahmacarya*). Humans rely on the Dharma to be established; the Dharma depends on humans to be propagated. Because humans and the Dharma depend upon one another, they may endure for a long time. Furthermore, one may establish precepts and recite them.
Properly explaining and requesting prohibitions serves to guard against transgressions and to cause the cultivation of the holy life and so forth. This expresses the intent of the request. Question:

How is it known that these words regarding the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) refer to the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* itself, rather than the fortnightly recitation? Answer: As stated in the following text.
At that time, the fortnightly recitation of the precepts had not yet been established. The World-Honored One, reflecting in stillness, said:

"I have formulated the precepts for the bhikṣus and recited the Prātimokṣa within them, including [the requirements for] those with faith, and so forth," as explained at length. It is known from this.
The subsequent response consists of three parts: first, the establishment of two gates; second, the explanation of these two gates; and third, the conclusion of these two gates.

Regarding the establishment of the two gates, they are the gate of suppression (*niṣedha*) and the gate of permission (*anujñā*). "Cease for now" is the gate of suppression, while "knowing the proper time" is the gate of permission. This is not yet the conclusion.

It is termed "cessation" (*nirodha*). Since this cessation is not permanent, the word "provisionally" (*ca*) is further added. This is the "restraining gate" (*nigraha-mukha*); it awaits the commission of an offense before the formal rule is established, and is thus termed "knowledge.
It is for the purpose of instituting a regulation and is called "timely. This is the "permitting gate" (*anujñā-mukha*). Next, regarding the explanation of these two gates:
as for the phrases, there are six pairs, which allow for three interpretations. Only within the first, third, and fifth of these two sets of six is there an explanation.

The section on "Restriction" (*niyama*). Regarding the two sets of four *catuṣkoṭi* (fourfold alternatives) that explain the "Permission" (*anujñā*) gate: the first two lines may be taken as the direct explanation of both the Restriction and Permission gates.

The second pair of fourfold alternatives—beginning with "those who have not yet attained benefit"—closely explains the arising and non-arising of outflows (*āsrava*), while distantly explaining the phrases "let it be for now" (*tāvad astu*) and "knowing the proper time.
When Śāriputra says, "The Tathāgata has not yet laid down the precepts for the bhikṣus," this explains the phrase "let it be for now" mentioned above.

"Stop. As for the question "Why?", it seeks the reason for the prohibition. It explains the grounds for the prohibition by means of the passage from the *Bhikṣu-vinaya* (the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-bhikṣu-prakīrṇaka*).

If one were to prohibit [the practice] beforehand before any taints (*āsrava*) have arisen, as stated in the fifth chapter of the *Jñānaprasthāna*, there would be two faults: first, the incitement of slander;

second, the lack of reverence. Slander would consist in saying: "People like us, who have left the household life from noble families, have renounced wealth and sensual pleasure, and do not spare even our own bodies or lives."
Having no desire for worldly fame or profit, why would he instead bind them with the *prātimokṣa*?
Second, because they did not conceive a sense of reverence for what was prescribed and saw it as useless, he did not establish the rules beforehand.

If one were to commit a tainted offense (*sāsrava-dharma*) and only then establish the precepts, this explains the aforementioned "knowing the proper time" (*kāla-jña*). By reversing the two aforementioned harms, two benefits are achieved: first, praising the Tathāgata as being excellent.

First, because the physician skillfully cures our various diseases of outflows (*āsrava*). Second, so that they may give rise to a heart of reverence for the prohibitions and precepts I have established, causing the Dharma to endure for a long time.
The Buddha, knowing that at this time the formulation of precepts would be beneficial, immediately ordained them.

As for what is called "beneficial," it is for the sake of producing the merit of the ten advantages; thus the subsequent text says: "The Tathāgata appears in the world and perceives the faults of the multitude."
The precepts were established for the bhikṣus for a single purpose: namely, to encompass faith and the other [faculties].

Furthermore, if one were to establish the precepts only after first setting forth the detailed textual accounts of the faults arising from the commission of tainted dharmas (sāsrava-dharma), then one would likewise have to set forth the extensive textual accounts of all the various prohibitions.

Next, the explanation of the conditions for outflows (*āsrava*) is provided. Regarding the phrase "until one has not yet obtained gain and offerings": the proximate explanation is that outflows do not arise;

the remote explanation is set aside for now. As for the term "until" (*yāvat*): it skips over the intervening period, hence it is called "until. Regarding the phrase "if one obtains gain and offerings, etc.":

the proximate explanation is that outflows arise; the remote explanation is knowing the proper time. Regarding the phrase "one who does not yet have a reputation, etc.": the proximate explanation is that outflows do not arise.

Let us set aside the distant explanation for now. If one speaks of "name" (*nāman*) and so forth, the proximate explanation gives rise to outflows (*āsrava*), while the distant explanation refers to knowing the proper time.

This is what is meant by the speaker; thus one knows that he is widely recognized by others as being of great learning (*bahuśruta*). The two [explanations] may be understood together. In the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, chapter one, the Buddha replied:
"The Tathāgata does not establish precepts for his disciples or formulate the rules of the *pārājika* offenses based on causes and conditions that lack faults or dangers."
Regarding the *Prātimokṣa* Dharma: it is like a Wheel-Turning Sage King who does not establish punishments for Brahmins or householders unless they have committed an offense.

In the same way, Śāriputra, the Tathāgata likewise does not establish the *Prātimokṣa* Dharma by formulating precepts for his disciples except on account of causes and conditions involving transgressions. Thus far.
The text of the introductory section is concluded.
*Kai-zong-ji* on the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, Volume One, end;

*Kai-zong-ji* on the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, Volume Two (from the beginning of the main section until the conclusion of the explanation of the first offense, totaling thirty-seven thousand two hundred words).
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Huaisu of Xitaiyuan Temple, as the second part of the *Zhengzong* (Orthodox Tradition). Now, as for the origins of this tradition’s texts:

because monks and nuns are not of a single name or lineage, their karmic retributions differ, their minds vary, and their aspirations and inclinations are not the same; thus, tainted transgressions arise, largely due to fame and profit. Therefore, the teachings have been abridged.
It has been ruined; people lack its faithful observance. Alas, that the assembly of Śākyas has lost its reliance! The pearl of the precepts shines in secret, yet they vainly hope for liberation;

the jewel of the Vinaya conceals its light. Therefore, the Unsurpassed Dharma King, out of great compassion to universally save all, has entrusted this request to establish this text, desiring that what constitutes an offense and what does not be made brilliantly clear, and that what is grave and what is light be made manifest as if in a mirror.

This constitutes the five categories of offenses, the three realms of existence as a stationary wheel, the two types of observance for distinct lineages, and the cultivation and realization of the four fruits;
such is the intended meaning. Therefore, the "Principal Section" (Zhengzong) is initiated. The text of this Principal Section is divided into two parts:

the first two sections of the *Prātimokṣa* concern the characteristics of restraint (*saṃvara*) and observance (*dhāraṇa*), while from the second *Khandhaka* onwards, they concern the characteristics of performance (*karaṇa*) and observance. The preceding text is further divided into two: the first is for the Great Bhikṣus (*Mahāsāṃghika*).
The *śīla-dhāraṇa* (observance of restraint). Second, the *śīla-dhāraṇa* for the community of nuns. Explaining these two types of *śīla-dhāraṇa*, they are analyzed through two gates:
first, the distinction between the combination and separation of the *saṃgha* and nuns; second, the sequence of the *saṃgha* and nuns. Regarding "combination and separation": Question:

Since both the great *saṃgha* and the nuns equally aspire to renunciation (*nairyāṇika*), and both possess the full precepts (*upasampadā*) with no difference in their categories of offenses (*āpatti-skandha*), why are five specific offenses established separately for these two communities? Answer: The arising of transgressions depends on the person. [The fault lies in...]

Births are unequal; the precepts prevent these faults, and thus there are few or many. This constitutes the distinction between more or less, the difference in lightness or heaviness, the mutual absence or presence [of certain rules], and the fact that while the transgressions are the same, the conditions differ.
Because of these distinct characteristics, they cannot be treated as a single category. Question: Regarding the two assemblies who possess the full precepts, how many are there?
Why are the two classes of śrāmaṇeras fixed at ten? Answer: To ensure the fulfillment of the complete status and to provide protection...

Because transgressions were made to reach [the full extent of] the cycle, precepts were established in response to those transgressions; thus, there is variation in their number. The two groups of śrāmaṇeras should likewise not be equal.

Since they share the same expedient means, ten precepts were provisionally established for them. Furthermore, it is explained that the two groups of śrāmaṇeras are also the same as the two sets [of full ordination];

the number of precepts established varies according to the distinctions among transgressions. How is this known? Because at the conclusion of each individual precept, the offense is invariably defined. If this is so, what [is the reason]?

It does not explicitly list all five categories of offenses. The answer is that this is because the number is incomplete; in reality, only ten are prescribed. Since the meaning of their cultivation and advancement is identical, they all result in the same offense.

Therefore, beyond these ten items, the Upādhyāya should provide instruction. Since he has already provided such instruction, it is clear that they are equal in status. Regarding the sequence of priority:

if one asks why the characteristics of the full bhikṣu precepts are explained first, while the prohibitions for bhikṣuṇīs are clarified first [in this context] and then discussed later, the answer is as follows: [The text continues with the response: The answer is that... (as per the source).

teacher and disciple, and the sequence of ordination. For these reasons, it is so. Next, the explanation of the Bhikṣu’s *śīla* (precepts) consists of eight sections:
namely, from the four *pārājika* offenses down to the seven methods for settling disputes (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*). Within these eight, they are condensed into five classes of offenses, namely:

The two *nihsargika-pāyattikas* are combined with the *śaikṣa-dharmas*, and the seven *adhikaraṇa-śamathas* are combined with the *aniyata-dharmas*; thus, there are only five categories. To understand these five, one must employ two approaches:

However, for those who rely on the precepts at the outset, if they merely search through the text without completeness and simply listen to abstract discourse, they will be unable to achieve comprehension.

For the first gate, according to the *Vibhāṣā* (116), each and every unwholesome path of action is [analyzed] by means of three...
The roots serve as the preliminary application (*prayoga*). Regarding their completion (*niṣṭhā*): the two precepts of sexual misconduct and stealing are completed by greed (*lobha*);

taking life is completed by hatred (*dveṣa*); and false speech is completed by all three roots. Regarding the three ways in which sexual misconduct arises, the *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra*, fascicle six, states:
"If a person personally delights in practicing unchaste conduct, this is called [arising] from greed; engaging in sexual misconduct with the relatives of an enemy..."
This is called taking what is not given out of anger: when one commits unchaste acts with one’s own mother. This is called taking what is not given out of delusion:

when one simultaneously experiences pleasure in the object and the thought, and brings it to completion through greed. Regarding the three types of theft arising from greed: when one steals the wealth of others for the sake of oneself, one’s wife, children, or dependents, this is called theft arising from greed.
Stealing the property of an enemy is called theft arising from anger. Robbing those of lower status... [is called theft arising from delusion].
As for the [claim regarding] caste: this is called arising from delusion. Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa* states:

"It is said that kings and others, relying on worldly laws, seize the wealth of evil persons, claiming that such is the law and that there is no offense of theft. Furthermore, the Brahmins speak thus:
"At the beginning of the kalpa, all worldly wealth was bestowed upon the brahmins by Mahābrahmā; later, the power of the brahmins diminished."
"Inferior! They are of low birth and have their resources plundered by others.

Now, when these brahmins seize or steal the wealth of others in this world to provide for their clothing and food, they consider it all their own property and thus incur no guilt of theft. Such people have something to look toward; they are driven entirely by greed.
Regarding 'killing those who have arisen': if one takes life for the sake of greed, this is said to proceed from greed; if one kills an enemy..."
The family [is the object]. This is called arising from hatred (*dveṣa*). To kill one's aged parents is called arising from delusion (*moha*). Thus, the *Vibhāṣā* states:
"If tigers, leopards, jackals, wolves, centipedes, snakes, and the like harm humans, there is no sin in killing them.

If one is able to kill parents who are decrepit or afflicted by chronic illness, one will obtain immeasurable merit. Such disregard for moral considerations is entirely the culmination of hatred; it arises from the three [roots] through false conceptualization.

If one acts for the sake of wealth and profit, or to experience pleasure for oneself, this is called arising from greed. If it is for the purpose of destroying an enemy, this is called arising from hatred.

If it is out of fear of another’s death, this is called arising from delusion. Therefore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Those who [act] for the sake of their own or others' bodies, hardships, or lives..."

Regarding false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*), although one does not incur the offense of falsehood (*mṛṣā-āpatti*), it nevertheless constitutes a course of action (*karmapatha*). This is because it is also due to greed and the other [afflictions];

for when greed and the others are present, this karma is accomplished. Furthermore, the *Zengyi Ahan Jing* (Ekottarika Āgama) states: "There are three kinds of false speech that result in a *pārājika* offense:

those arising from greed, hatred, and delusion. It also says: "Hatred of body, hatred of speech, and hatred of both body and speech. The ancient commentaries explain that false speech arises from greed and delusion, thereby establishing the formal rule (*vidhi*) of false speech for the sake of profit.

Hatred is contrary to the heart’s desires; therefore, there is no state of mind characterized by hatred that initiates volition to constitute karma. This is merely the statement of a transmitter and does not rely on the Noble Teachings.
Since its meaning contradicts the text, there is no need for a separate refutation.

The second category consists of two parts: the states of body and speech. The first three [precepts] pertain exclusively to the body; the fourth pertains only to speech. Regarding the precept against sexual misconduct, physical intercourse is required, as it cannot be distinguished without the body.

Regarding killing and stealing, these are committed through the body; however, speech can also have the sense of performing an action, such as when instructing someone to enchant an object with incantations.
Regarding false speech, claiming to be an *arhat* cannot be proclaimed without words; yet the body can also have the sense of performing an action, such as when one writes a letter or displays signs.
In the third section concerning the stages of self and others regarding the precept against sexual misconduct, the gravity of the teaching is light while the gravity of the act itself is heavy.

Because one takes pleasure in causing another person to commit a transgression, the instructor incurs only a *duṣkṛta* (light offense). Regarding killing, stealing, and damaging property, whether committed by oneself or taught to another, there is no difference in the harm inflicted upon the object;
both parties commit the offense. Within these cases, there are only the two mental states of agent and object; they do not accord with the absence of expectation, as there is a discrepancy.

Regarding this, there are cases of transgression and non-transgression, which may be understood according to the text. If one lies and instructs another to claim for oneself the attainment of holiness (*ārya*), attributing the resulting fame and profit to oneself, then that which is the object of the act constitutes a *pārājika* offense, while that which is the agent constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*.

Conversely, if one generally instructs another such that the other person claims holiness for themselves, attributing the fame and profit to them, then that which is the agent constitutes a *pārājika* offense, while that which is the object constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*.

Based on this, we shall generally clarify the distinctions between self and other, agent and object, and the relative gravity of the offenses; this may be formulated as four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). First:

There are four categories regarding the gravity of the offense: first, when one’s own action is light while the teaching is grave; this refers to the initial precept against sexual misconduct. Second, when one’s own action is light while the teaching is grave;

this refers to violating the training rules concerning the emission of semen within the Saṃgha. Third, when both one’s own action and the teaching are grave; this refers to offenses such as killing or stealing, where both parties commit the same transgression. Fourth, when both one’s own action and the teaching are light;

this refers to cases such as instructing someone not to study, which constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (minor fault). Regarding whether an act constitutes an offense or not, there are likewise four permutations: first, when one commits the offense oneself but another does not; this refers, for example, to engaging in trade oneself.
Second, others commit an offense while one does not; for example, employing a nun to wash old clothes. Third, both oneself and others commit an offense; for example, killing or stealing.
Fourth, neither oneself nor others commits an offense; for example, instructing others to advance in their practice.

The fourth section concerns the relative breadth and narrowness of the two [offenses]. Sexual misconduct encompasses all four realms of existence (*gati*), and is therefore broad; the other three are restricted to human beings, and are therefore narrow.
This is because the nature of sexual desire flows with one's inclinations and finds internal release; as long as the proper path is followed, the resulting satisfaction is no different.

It does not distinguish between the beauty or ugliness of the object, nor does it inquire whether the partner is a human or a non-human (*amanuṣya*). Furthermore, this is because it is committed even with a corpse. It is not...
Since the object [of the offense] is impaired, how could one calculate the superiority or inferiority of that object such that there would be a gradation in the commission of the offense?

Furthermore, this applies even when the object is oneself, as in the case of those with weak backs. As for the other three precepts, they impair the preceding objects; because the destinies differ and the retributions vary, there is inequality in the degree of increase or decrease.
When a human commits a grave offense, it is light in other realms; this principle follows from the nature of the human object [of the offense]. Regarding the four precepts, all may incur offenses;
however, for a *pārājika* transgression, there is a distinction between humans and non-humans (*deva*). For animals, there are four grades: *pārājika*, *sthūlātyaya*, *pāyattika*, and *duṣkṛta*.

Fifth, regarding *niyata* (definite) and *aniyata* (indefinite): these four precepts share the same objective (*sabhāga-viṣaya*). When a commentator analyzes them, they are both *niyata* and *aniyata*, and in both cases one incurs the offense of *pārājika*.

Within this context, "same objective" means that the precept against sexual misconduct concerns the specific path (*mārga*), whereas the others are restricted to persons. Since sexual misconduct is defined by the path and not by the destination (*gati*), it cannot be treated as an analogy for the others.

Thus, the remaining three are alike in being both *niyata* and *aniyata*. If one were to apply this to other destinies (*gati*) and treat them as *niyata* or *aniyata*, the precept against sexual misconduct must be excluded.

Regarding the precepts, they are categorized according to the three lower realms. However, as with the "Great Universal" (mahā-sāmānya) precepts, the gravity of the offense is determined by the specific realm of the object;

if one focuses specifically on a particular case, one incurs an offense corresponding to that specific act. Alternatively, if there is a confusion or overlap between them, both constitute preparatory offenses (*prayoga*).

The sixth error concerns the precept against sexual misconduct. This category may be divided into three positions. First, regarding the precept against sexual misconduct, both types of error constitute a grave offense.

With respect to the path, it does not depend on the specific destination; rather, if one obtains the proper organ and the volition of the primary action is fulfilled, even if there is contact with the object, the gravity of the offense is established.
Thus the text states: "If there is doubt as to whether it is the proper path, yet one perceives it as such, it is a pārājika. Second...

Regarding the second point, concerning the three lower precepts: if one errs regarding the object in other realms of existence, there is no offense, because one originally had no intention toward a different object.

If, however, one errs regarding a human object, the error constitutes an offense; it is not non-offensive. This is because an error lacks duality, and thus one cannot claim that "there was no intention" or "it was an error.
Therefore, the text below states: if one perceives a woman as a man and steals her property, the Buddha declared this a *pārājika*.

The same applies to killing through deception. Because one acts erroneously while lacking the [intentional] mind, it does not constitute an offense—such as, for example, cases where the mother dies during an attempt to induce an abortion.
Question: If such accidental offenses are non-offenses due to error, why do people say that accidentally dropping a rafter, a beam, or the like is not an offense?
Answer: This is indeed a case of speaking with a mistaken sound. If that is so, how is it? The subsequent text speaks of harsh speech (*pāruṣya*);
one intended to speak of this, but mistakenly spoke of that. All *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses [arise] because this is indeed a case of speaking with a mistaken sound.
Furthermore, there is an interpretation regarding the two categories of "error" (*vibhram*) and "mistake" (*viparyāsa*), each of which applies to both offenses and non-offenses.

However, as long as one has the intention and the act is accomplished, it constitutes an offense regardless of whether it was an error or a mistake. Thus, the text states that if one perceives a male while stealing a female, the Buddha declared this a *pārājika* (this is an offense due to error).

In another passage, regarding the teaching on harsh speech, if one intends to speak to this person but mistakenly speaks to that person, it is entirely a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (this is an offense due to mistake). If...
When an action is accomplished unintentionally, both errors and mistakes do not constitute an offense. For example, if a wooden beam or rafter is mistakenly dropped, it is not an offense.

Furthermore, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Sengqi lü), fascicle 4, states: "If one intends to harm a person before, but by mistake harms another person in between, one incurs a *vyatikrama* (transgression).

Additionally, the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* (Shisong lü), fascicle 51, asks: "Is there a case where a bhikṣu falsely claims to possess noble dharmas (*āryadharma*) yet does not incur a *pārājika* offense? The answer is: [Yes].
There was a bhikṣu who, wishing to speak of the fruit of *srotāpanna*, mistakenly spoke of the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*;
even so, wishing to speak of the fruit of *anāgāmin*, he mistakenly spoke of the fruit of *arhat*. (This is from the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, chapter twenty-eight.

There was a bhikṣu who, wishing to kill that person, mistakenly killed this one. He gave rise to doubt and questioned the Buddha. The Buddha said: "He commits no offense; he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* [grave offense]. This mistake constitutes no offense. Below.

If one intends to give a woman an abortifacient but mistakenly gives her a drug that kills the mother, there is no offense if the mother dies. Likewise, if one intends to steal another's garment but mistakenly receives one's own, there is no offense.
If one intends to receive ghee but mistakenly receives oil, it is not accomplished [as the intended act]; such errors constitute no offense. Third, regarding errors in relation to lying:
concerning what is termed "dharma," the old translations state that in cases of error, there is no offense. For example, if one intends to call someone "holy" but mistakenly says "ordinary."

To claim that these are not objects of the offense—such as when one with overweening pride mistakes an ordinary person for a noble one, or when one acts out of a mistaken mind rather than skillfully—is an unreasonable interpretation that confuses the structure of the treatise.

How could it be that in the cases of killing and stealing, the gravity of the offense is determined solely by taking human beings as the heavy object, while disregarding insentient things or unowned property?
Yet, when it comes to the subject matter of false speech, the analysis instead proceeds according to ordinary worldly conventions.
It constitutes an object of error. If one follows the text of the school, both "error" (cuò) and "mistake" (wù) apply to a great many cases regarding the sublime Dharma;

if it is identical to the sublime Dharma, it is still a mistake-offense, because an error does not constitute an offense. The opening text of the *Mahāmṛṣāvāda-sūtra* says: "Desiring to speak this..."

It is stated erroneously that such a person does not commit an offense. Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, fascicle eight, asks: "If a bhikṣu intends to speak of the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*), but instead speaks of the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*) and so forth, what offense does he commit?
The answer is: "A *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense), or it is the same as the latter explanation—that it may be either an offense or not, depending on the circumstances."

Regarding the seventh point on establishing the intent: as stated in the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra*, fascicle thirty, the Buddha addressed Bimbisāra, saying, "Great King, according to the laws of your kingdom, what constitutes a grave offense?
The King replied, "World-Honored One, according to the laws of my kingdom, there are four grave offenses:
first, taking the life of another; second, stealing property worth five coins or more; third, committing adultery with the wife of another; fourth..."

This was for the sake of five coins; he intentionally spoke a falsehood in the presence of King Mahāsammata. Such a person who commits these four offenses cannot live [in the community]. The Buddha said:
"I now establish these four grave offenses (pārājika) for the sake of my future disciples. Furthermore, I establish the training in higher morality (adhiśīla-śikṣā) for the bhikṣus for two reasons:
first, because I wish to cause them to sever the three unwholesome roots. Ānanda answered Kōng... [text fragment ends].
Jueguan said: "The World-Honored One, wishing to subdue greed, hatred, and delusion so as to bring them to an end, established the training in higher morality for the bhikṣus.
The reason for doing so is that whenever a holy regulation is instituted, it is for the purpose of eliminating the root of affliction.

Although the roots of affliction are many, they are essentially the three poisons. Because these [afflictions], such as greed, can constantly lead one toward unwholesome karma, they must be regulated."

[The text says: "Severance. Question: Precepts can prevent wrongdoing, yet they do not sever the afflictions (*kleśa*). Why, then, is it said that precepts are established in opposition to them? Answer:

In truth, precepts only prevent wrongdoing and do not sever the afflictions. However, because meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) arise by means of the precepts, one attributes the merit to its source;

thus, it is said that they are established in opposition [to the afflictions]. Furthermore, another interpretation of the text states that "subduing greed and so forth" merely refers to restraining the phenomena [of the mind] so that they do not arise.
It is called "subduing" (*vinaya*), not because it intends to sever [the defilements], but because it is called "subduing. Second, it serves to generate ten kinds of meritorious benefits;
the textual evidence for this can be understood [from the scriptures].

Regarding the eighth sequence: since it is easy to commit violations, it is established at the beginning for clarification; this applies not only to this specific text but also to similar categories such as the *śeṣa* (residual) offenses.
Therefore, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "The first precept was committed on the twelfth day of the fifth half-month of the winter season in the fifth year after attaining enlightenment;
this corresponds to the twenty-seventh day of the tenth month. As for the remaining three precepts, they were all committed during the winter season of the sixth year after attaining enlightenment:

the second, the precept against stealing, on the tenth day of the second half-month (referring to the tenth day of the ninth month); and the third, the precept against killing, on the [fifteenth] day of the second half-month..."
The "ninth day of the month" refers to the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month. This is the fourth [offense] regarding false speech.
The "thirteenth day of the half-month" refers to the thirteenth day of the tenth month. By means of this textual evidence, the sequence is clearly established. Question:

Since these are offenses frequently committed, and the precept against sexual misconduct is placed first among the fifty [precepts], why is the precept against killing placed at the head? Answer: Among the many interpretations of the ancients, none were entirely appropriate. Now...

To clarify this correct principle, the wise should reflect: while the fifty precepts and others do not require a formal request for transgression, the full set of precepts—based on the fundamental paths of action beginning with killing—are extensive and must necessarily await a formal request for transgression;
furthermore, as previously explained, those who delight in transgressing place the precept against sexual misconduct at the very beginning.
