The ninth case, spontaneous transgression, is as follows: while still a śrāmaṇera, one instructs another to commit killing or theft and then claims for oneself that one has attained the state of an ārya;

having subsequently received full ordination (*upasampadā*), the prior act finally reaches completion. Because one was capable of spontaneously instructing others, one incurs the offense of a pārājika.
If one discusses acting for oneself, it is restricted solely to unwholesome [karma]. Now, taking the act of instructing others, it applies to all three natures.

If the instruction is completed before the receiving of the precepts is finished, this constitutes a person with the obstacle of a "limiting offense" (pārājika), and the category of the precepts does not arise. If the receiving of the precepts is completed [before the instruction is finished], [the obstacle does not apply].

One incurs both the offense and the transgression, because the wholesome cause is perfected while the evil karma is fulfilled. Therefore, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya), fascicle 51, states:

"If a person who has not yet received full ordination takes an object with the intent to steal, at the moment they have not yet received full ordination and the object is moved from its original place, they incur a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).

The next case: if a person who has not yet received full ordination takes [the object] and it is moved from its place at the time they receive full ordination, they incur a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense). The next case: a person who has not yet received full ordination..."

Regarding the taking of full ordination (*upasampadā*): if one departs from the place [where it was received], it is a *pārājika*. Next, regarding the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) at the time of receiving full ordination, there are two cases: one is a *sthūlātyaya* and the other is a *pārājika*.

Next, regarding the taking [of it] after the full ordination has been completed, there are again two cases: the first case is a *pārājika*, and the second case is the reception of the full precepts. Thus, for one who possesses the full precepts.

Taking one who does not possess full ordination constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense for one who has left the [monastic] residence; by this evidence, it is known that there is spontaneous (*anābhoga*) transgression. Since engaging in sexual intercourse through instruction incurs only a light offense, there is no spontaneous transgression in that case.
The tenth section, "Requital," concerns the majestic severity of the precepts, which open the spirit and benefit all beings. These are the rules for practice; how could one fail to cultivate them?

It is truly because many are deluded regarding the path of karma and do not fear sinking into the depths of suffering. Those who indulge such ignorant sentiments and commit transgressions—now, according to the holy teachings, we shall demonstrate the gravity or lightness of their offenses.
Those who preserve the principles and practice accordingly should especially revere this. Now, as for the full precepts (*upasampadā*), they are prohibitions...
Regarding the seven branches of diligence, these four meanings should be understood as applying universally. Within each branch, all three types of retribution are induced.
Thus, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 113, states: "If one practices, cultivates, or frequently cultivates sexual misconduct..."
Birth in the realms of hell-beings (*naraka*), animals (*tiryagyoni*), or hungry ghosts (*preta*) is the ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*).

When one passes away from those places and is reborn among humans, having a wife who is unchaste is the concordant fruit (*niṣyandaphala*). Due to that predominant influence (*adhipatiphala*), the external objects one experiences are frequently subject to hostility.

This is the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*). As for the remaining six courses of action (*karmapatha*), their maturation (*vipāka*) is identical, as they all lead to rebirth in the three evil realms where one undergoes various forms of theft (*adattādāna*).

When such a person is later born among humans, they suffer from a lack of wealth and treasures; this is the concordant fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*). This refers to the external objects experienced [as a result].
There are calamities and afflictions; frequent encounters with frost, hail, dust, filth, and other such hindrances constitute the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*).

Those who have taken the lives of others will, when reborn among humans, suffer from many illnesses and short lifespans—this is the concordant fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*). The external objects they experience will all lack luster.

That one does not remain for long is the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*). That those who have spoken falsehoods encounter much slander when reborn among humans is the concordant fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*).
That the external objects they experience are largely foul and impure is the dominant fruit. [This applies likewise to] all divisive speech.
When one is born among humans in a future life, being separated from friends and relatives is the fruit of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*).

That the external objects one encounters are mostly uneven and improper—consisting of hills, mounds, pits, ravines, precipices, and impassable barriers—is the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*). These are the results of various harsh and evil words when born among humans in a future life.

Constantly hearing various kinds of unpleasant sounds is the fruit of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*). The external objects experienced are coarse, inferior, and wretched, consisting of poisonous thorns and gravel;
even if gold and such are present, they are scarce, lack luster, and are unrefined and difficult to use—this is the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
Regarding various forms of frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*): when one is reborn among humans, one’s words lack majesty and authority; this is the *niṣyanda-phala* (concordant result).

As for the external objects experienced as a result, the seasons become irregular and aberrant, things perish rapidly, and they mostly fail to reach fruition; this is the *adhipati-phala* (dominant result).

The same applies to the *Upāsaka-sūtra*, though it cannot be cited in full here. The seven paths of wholesome action (*kuśala-karmapatha*) should be understood by reversing these [unwholesome results].
From here on follows the detailed explanation. Regarding the first precept, there are four sections: first, the intent of the formulation; second, the explanation of the name of the precept;
third, the fulfillment of conditions that constitutes an offense; and fourth, the meaning of the deficiency of conditions. These four points each have both general and specific aspects;
all subsequent precepts are the same in this regard.

Regarding the general intent [of the Vinaya], the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* (Dolun), fascicle two, sets forth four meanings: first, knowing that what was previously done is without fault allows one to eliminate sorrow and regret;
second, by means of this, the precepts are established to extinguish unrighteousness in the future;

third, by means of the Buddha’s establishment of the precepts, one knows the gravity of offenses—whether they are *sāvaśeṣa* (with remainder) or *anavaśeṣa* (without remainder), whether they are confessable or non-confessable—thereby resolving the web of doubts regarding the future; fourth, by means of this, the ten [types of] rebirth are brought about.

This is for the sake of beneficial merit. This should be understood through the intent established in the Vinaya; the textual evidence is clear. Regarding the specific intent of this regulation: the nature of sexual desire is inherently base and defiled.
When the fetter of craving entangles the mind, one becomes so deeply attached that it is difficult to relinquish. To indulge in it leads to sinking into the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*);
to refrain from it allows for liberation (*nirvāṇa*) to be anticipated. Therefore, through the skillful means of great compassion, the Tathāgata established this prohibition.

Precepts are the source for preventing transgressions. Second, regarding the explanation of their names, there are both general and specific aspects. The general sense refers to the practice of "precept" (*śīla*) which is capable of prevention;

the specific sense refers to "impure conduct," which is the transgression to be prevented. Since both the agent (the preventive practice) and the object (the transgression) are mentioned together, it is called the "precept against impure conduct."

The three knowledges (*vidyā*) possess specific conditions. There are three general conditions: first, being a *mahābhikṣu*, which excludes those not subject to the precepts, as the text states, "if [he is] a bhikṣu";
second, because after the extensive teachings were established, those who were practitioners at the outset were not yet included;
third, there must be no serious illness impairing the mind, since for those such as the insane, the Noble Ones have opened an exemption from offense. These three points encompass the foregoing.

Therefore, the *Vinayavibhāṣā* states: "If a person has already received the full bhikṣu precepts, and if the Tathāgata has already established this precept, and if that person does not fall into a state of delusion, then that person commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. The rest is explained in brief."

The same applies to the [other] marks (*nimitta*). There are four distinct conditions: first, the presence of a real object; second, the presence of a defiled mind; third, the arousal of preparatory effort;
and fourth, the conjunction with the object. Even when one is oppressed by an enemy, there are likewise four conditions: first, the presence of a real object; second, being oppressed by an enemy.
Third, contact with the object; fourth, the experience of pleasure. This precept is common to all three [stages] but distinct in its four [factors].

Seven conditions constitute an offense. Regarding the absence of conditions: if the common conditions are absent, there is no offense at all. Alternatively, if the first and third [of the specific conditions] are absent, there is an offense;

this refers to the "preparatory stage" (*prayoga*) where conditions are lacking. Next, regarding the absence of the specific conditions: if the first two are lacking, there is a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense); that is, [intercourse] not via the proper path.

Regarding the perception of what is the Path as not the Path, or doubt concerning the Path: if two or three of these conditions are missing, there is no offense. If the fourth condition is missing, there are two types of absences—light and heavy.
The absence of conditions due to being coerced by an enemy can be understood through these analogies. As for the preparatory acts (*prayoga*), there is one general absence and four specific absences;
combining the general and specific, there are five.
Next, regarding the explanation of the text: A verse in the *Vinayavibhāṣā-śāstra* states, "The precepts have five aspects; [the *Vinaya-vibhaṅga*] explains nine. The commentary on the *Vinaya* says:

"Regarding the precepts established by the various Buddhas, one should discern five aspects within each individual precept: first, the origin (*nidāna*); second, the person of the origin (*pudgala-nidāna*)."
Third, the establishment of the precepts; fourth, the differentiation of the established precepts; fifth, the determination of right and wrong.

Regarding these, the "originating cause" refers to the circumstance of famine as the causal condition. The "person who initiates the originating cause" is the bhikṣu Śāriputra, who established the precepts.
As for "if there are bhikṣus," this refers to those who differentiate the established precepts. Within this context, who are the "bhikṣus"?
Regarding the determination of right and wrong: herein, a bhikṣu commits a *pārājika* offense in three instances, up until the conclusion of the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*).
If a person can correctly discern the meaning of these five characteristics, that person will certainly be able to understand them.
Furthermore, according to the commentary on this treatise, there is also one approach; however, following the meaning here, it is divided separately into two parts. First, from the beginning until...

[The character] "Jù" (取) refers to the initial transgression of the precepts, wherein defilements arise and the brief rule is violated. That is to say, if one above has committed a tainted (*sāsrava*) dharma;

from the second phrase, "From this day forward," below, the extensive supplement to the brief rule is established. That is to say, the aforementioned [rule] is subsequently finalized as a formal precept (*śikṣāpada*). The preceding text is further divided into two parts:

first, up to the point of "having finished the reprimand," the arising of defilements is met with reprimand; second, from "He addressed the bhikṣus" below, the fault is manifested as a violation of the brief rule. The preceding text is further...
Two. The first section, up to the title "Seed," clarifies the characteristics of the offense, which are the outflows of transgression.

The second section, beginning with Sudinna, concerns the public exposure and reprimand. Within the former [section], there are four parts: first, identifying the site of the conversion; second, naming the offender;

third, clarifying the conditions for the offense; and fourth, correctly clarifying the offense itself. Having thus divided the text for this initial precept, the same method shall be applied throughout the subsequent precepts.

It is similar to that. Regarding the "first dwelling place," this indicates a method for manifesting transformation; it is the location where the prohibitions were transgressed. At that time, the World-Honored One had already finished explaining the above.
As for Vaiśālī—(the *Vinaya* states that in the Qin language it means "vast")—the name Vaiśālī is slightly corrupted; in its correct Sanskrit pronunciation, it is Vṛji (or Vaiśalī).

According to the first fascicle of the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, a question is raised regarding the *Sūtras* and the *Abhidharma*: they do not [begin] with "The Buddha was staying at... [but rather with the location].

First, regarding why the *Vinaya* alone places the Buddha at the beginning: the answer is that it is because he is supreme, because he is secret, and because the rules were uniquely ordained by the Buddha himself.
For example, in the *Sūtras*, when the disciples preach the Dharma, sometimes Śakra Devānām Indra speaks of himself, saying, "I consider generosity to be foremost.
Why? Because through generosity, I have become a Heavenly King and my wishes are fulfilled as I desire. The Buddha said, "It is so."
At times, he manifests as a transformation Buddha (*nirmāṇa-buddha*), and this transformation Buddha preaches the Dharma; the Vinaya is not like this.

All Buddhas preach [the Dharma], and for this reason, the Buddha is placed at the beginning. There are sūtras that provide decisions according to specific circumstances, but the Vinaya is not like this.

If there is a matter involving nuns, one may not settle it immediately; one must certainly go outside [the assembly]. If there is a matter with laypeople, it must be settled within the assembly. If...

If there is a matter within a village, it is also included among the assemblies. If there is a matter concerning the five groups [of monastics], it must necessarily be settled between the bhikṣus and the bhikṣuṇīs.

For this reason, the Buddha is mentioned first, followed by the transgressor. Regarding the village of Kalandaka, the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: [it was so called because] many... (text fragmentary).
It is named after a bird. Some say it is the name of a village headman; see the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, fascicle six. It is actually the name of a mountain rat.
At that time, the King of Vaiśālī, accompanied by various courtesans, entered the mountains for recreation. He fell asleep beneath a tree. Beneath the tree was a cave containing a venomous snake.
Sensing the scent of the king’s alcohol, the snake emerged, intending to bite him. A rat on the tree screeched and called out to wake the king. The king—
The king was awakened to the danger [of the plague] and, out of gratitude for the mouse's kindness, immediately granted this village to it and provided offerings.
Because the village was named after the mouse, it was called the Kalandaka Village. Within that village, there was a man who possessed forty billion gold coins;

the king conferred upon him the rank of *śreṣṭhin* (elder), and thus he took the name of the village as his own title, becoming known as the Elder Kalandaka. Now, regarding the son of Sūḍāna, the word order is inverted; it should be... [as follows].
He is called Sūdena, the son of Kalandaka. Accordingly, the subsequent text states: "At that time, [there was] the son of Kalandaka.
The *Śariputrābhidharma* (or *Shanjian*) says: "Sūdena is the son of the elder Kalandaka. The *Pañcavargika Vinaya* also says: "The son of Kalandaka is named Sūdena.
Regarding the name Sūdena, many say it means "one who has obtained through seeking," because he obtained [his wife] by petitioning the deities; thus its meaning is understood.

"Virtuous and generous" means that one who possesses abundant wealth has two kinds of assets according to the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*: first, animate wealth, such as male and female slaves, oxen, horses, and so forth;
second, inanimate wealth, such as gold, silver, and the seven treasures. Since these are all immeasurable, it is said that he "possesses abundant wealth and many treasures.

Having heard the Dharma, this person attained realization and understanding; weary of the clamor and dust of worldly life, he embraced faith and took refuge, his heart longing for the benefit of renunciation.
Therefore it is said: "Upholding faith, etc. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "Sudinna, having heard the Dharma with joy, immediately thought:
'As I understand what the Buddha has taught, those who live as householders are bound by affection and cannot practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*) extensively for the duration of their lives.
To leave the home life and be without attachment is like space. I should now, by means of the faith I have in my family, leave the home life to practice.'"
The *Dolun* (Treatise on Many Topics), fascicle two, states: "Now, those who have left the household life do so for the sake of extinguishing defilements and burdens.
Since the household is a causal condition for afflictions, one ought to distance oneself from it as much as possible."

Next, the section on the conditions for the offense has two parts: first, the remote conditions; second, the proximate conditions. This section has three parts: first, it cites the scarcity of grain as the cause that gives rise to the thought of begging;
second, from "Sudinna" onwards, it describes how he conceived the thought of returning home, intending to abandon both harms and pursue two benefits;

third, from "he had this thought" onwards, it describes his return to the village according to those thoughts. The section on the proximate conditions has two parts: first, it cites the exhortation regarding wealth; third...

There were three instances of exhortation and two of refusal. One instance is detailed at length; the other two are brief and easy to understand. Regarding the second: his mother sent her to abandon [the practice], using physical forms to urge him on, yet he did not refuse her.
When asked about this Śudinna, since his heart already delighted in the Way, for what reason did he answer his mother, saying, "I am able to do it"?
He replied: "As I contemplate the treatises, I think: 'If I do not bestow [the seed] upon her, she will never let me go,' day and night."
[They] harassed me. I gave them seeds for a short time to cause their minds to cease [their harassment] so that they would no longer disturb me.

Because of this, I was able to enter the gateway to the Way and cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*). It is because of this reflection that it is said, "I am capable. Question: Why did Sūti reject wealth but accept sensual forms? Answer:

Wealth encourages one for a long duration and turns one away from the Way; therefore, he rejected it. Sensual forms encourage one only for a short duration and are compatible with the Way; therefore, he accepted them.

Next, the actual explanation of the offense. This section contains two parts. First, regarding the actual offense: prior to the establishment of the precepts, one did not perceive the impurity of desire.
This principle applies universally to all precepts; before the extensive teachings were established, one who does not know how to practice desire is the same as a dead person.
He was expelled from the assembly. Although he had entered the gateway of the Way, his worldly attachments were not yet severed; because he hoped for gain, a transgression arose. Question:
Since it is said there are "three types of conduct," why is only the first mentioned? Answer: Because [the rules] had not yet been established. Thus, the third fascicle of the *Saṃgītiparyāya* says:

He committed numerous acts of sexual misconduct. The Buddha said, "At the time when the precepts had not yet been established, Sūdena committed an offense; at all such times, there was no transgression.

Next, within the garden, the following illustrates the faults of desire. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: At that time, a deva of great majesty from Tuṣita Heaven, having reached the end of his life, received a conception.
Then the Earth Deity addressed the Space Deity, saying: "The son of Kalandaka has performed an unprecedented deed."
Within the Saṃgha, he performed unprecedented deeds; word spread from one to another until it reached the Brahma Heaven.
Transcending the manifest marks of training, he was preeminent and peerless; therefore, he is called the Venerable Seed.
Next, the reprimand is explained. The text is divided into two parts: first, the reprimand by the bhikṣus; second, from "At that time, the World-Honored One...

onwards, the reprimand by the Tathāgata. The former section has three parts: first, up to "therefore he was grieved," which serves as the occasion for the reprimand, as he attained realization of the truth.
The second section, "Then the bhikṣus," etc., reveals the category [of the offense] by reporting the matter to the Venerable One. The preceding text consists of four parts: first, praising Sūdanī;
because he was previously well-versed and thoroughly practiced in ritual procedures, it says, "there was no matter he did not know";

because there was nothing he did not respectfully follow, it says, "he carried out every task"; and because he did not merely practice himself but was also able to guide others, it says, "he instructed and taught others. First...

2. "At that time" and below: [The youth] feels remorse for his transgression, and his inner mind is scorched with distress. 3. "His fellow students" and below: Seeing him sorrowful, they interrogate him.
First, they directly ask about his grief, saying, "Why are you so sorrowful and anxious? Next, they ask the cause of his grief:

"Since you are one whose understanding and practice are complete, you ought to be without worry; yet now you are instead filled with grief, which suggests you must have grown weary of the Path. 4. "Sudatta... [and so forth].
[The passage] below answers the reasons for his sorrow. First, he expresses his devotion to the Path, saying, "I am exceedingly fond of the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Next, as follows below, he expresses the reasons for his sorrow. The subsequent section on reproach consists of three parts. First, he generally states what is improper:
"Within the pure Dharma of the Tathāgata, you were capable of severing desire and the like; this was what you ought to do. Why, then, have you committed such evil?"

Regarding the second point, following the phrase "in the Tathāgata," there is a specific censure of what is inappropriate, which serves as a counter-illustration. "Desires" (*kāma*) refers to the five sensual desires;
because one does not give rise to longing or seeking for these five desires, it is called "desireless. "Defilements" (*mala*) refers to impurity and turbidity, as they can stain the pure mind;

hence they are named "defilements. There are six such [afflictions]: vexation, resentment, flattery, deception, and arrogance; because one can eternally eliminate these, it is said to be "without [them]."
Defilement. All sentient beings thirst for the five desires; this thirst arises from craving, and is therefore called "thirst-craving" (*tṛṣṇā*).

When a bhikṣu guards the precepts and right mindfulness is present before him, thirst-craving is naturally eliminated; this is called "being able to sever. Regarding the phrase "destroying the nest and den":

the ancient commentary states that birth-and-death among humans and devas above is metaphorically the "nest," while birth-and-death in the three miserable realms below is metaphorically the "den. Since the causes have accumulated...

When [the cause] perishes, the bitter fruit perishes along with it; therefore, it is said that the "nest and cave" are destroyed. In the *Śīlaskandhaka* (Chapter on Receiving Precepts) below, it says:
"The various devas above are like a nest, and humans dwelling below are called a cave. This interpretation follows mere sentiment and contradicts correct principle.
Our current explanation is not so: it means that any place of residence is termed a "nest and cave. Thus, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 52, states: [text follows].

It is said: Because it is contained within and hidden in the cave-dwelling of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), it is called "bound to the desire realm" (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*). It should be understood that the same applies to the form and formless realms (*rūpadhātu* and *ārūpyadhātu*).
"Bonds" (*saṃyojana*) refers to the nine bonds; "fetters" (*bandhana*) refers to the three fetters. Since these bonds and fetters are not singular, they are termed a "group" (*nikāya*).

By removing these bonds and fetters, one can attain the extinction of craving, which is *nirvāṇa*. Furthermore, "craving for the desirable" refers to craving for the three realms; "extinction" (*kṣaya*) means cessation. This is due to the three...
The exhaustion of craving for the realms (*dhātu-tṛṣṇā-kṣaya*) can manifest *nirvāṇa*; therefore, it is called "the extinction of craving is *nirvāṇa*.
This *nirvāṇa* is a Sanskrit term (here translated as "perfect stillness" [yuánjì]). The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 28, contains many interpretations.

It asks: For what reason is it named *nirvāṇa*? It answers: Because afflictions (*kleśa*) are exhausted, it is named *nirvāṇa*. Furthermore, because the three fires have subsided, it is named *nirvāṇa*. Furthermore...
Because the three marks are quiescent, it is called *nirvāṇa*. Furthermore, because it is free from foulness and impurity, it is called *nirvāṇa*.
Third, "How do you now... and so forth is the conclusion. It says "for two reasons" because it should not be done for long and because it is done correctly and appropriately;

thus it is said "for two. Next, regarding the address to the Buddha, the *Jianlun* (Treatise on Seeing), fascicle six, states: "The mind does not aspire to the Buddha, nor does it praise only oneself. Nor...

They caused the Buddha to feel slighted and dismissed Sūdanī. Furthermore, they did not seek to cause discord through such evil practices, but rather, relying on the true principle, they addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Now that this defiled practice has arisen, we pray that you will establish a precept for us, the śrāvaka disciples."

Next, regarding the Buddha’s reprimand, the text is divided into two parts. The first consists of the interrogation of his own words; the second, from "At that time" onwards, is the formal reprimand itself.
The former part has three sections: first, the assemblying of the Sangha; second, the clarification of the interrogation; third, the explanation of his own admission.
Regarding the first section, the phrase "for this reason" refers to the report submitted by the bhikṣu Sūti who had violated the precepts; therefore, it says "for this."

Regarding the "Causes and Conditions" (*nidāna*) for assembling the bhikṣus: according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (Duo lun), fascicle 2, there are five reasons for such an assembly. First, the Buddha does not act arbitrarily on his own initiative.

Second, he deliberates with the community before formulating a precept, thereby causing those who have committed an offense to submit their hearts. Third, [he acts] because the offense has been committed. Fourth, [he acts] because the offense has been concealed. Fifth, [he acts] because the offense has been repeated. It is for these reasons that he assembles [the community].

Third, although the Buddhas possess sovereign mastery, for the sake of upholding the Dharma, whenever there is a Dharma matter, they assemble the community to act in harmony so that the Dharma may endure for a long time.
Fourth, it is to discipline present and future disciples; regarding all monastic affairs, one must not distinguish between those who have power and those who do not.

One must consult the assembly for detailed deliberation and must not act alone or arbitrarily. This is the nature of all Buddhas; it is not unique to a single Buddha. Second, examining the text has two parts:
first, presenting the method for what should be asked; second, asking according to that method. Regarding the first, the method for what should be asked consists of three phrases.
"Knowing the question" means that because of the bhikṣu’s formal announcement, [the Buddha] knows the question. The Buddha, possessing all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñā*), always knows this.
No. Although it appears that he does not know, he poses a question. According to the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, there are four benefits: first, to conform to the eternal law of all Buddhas;
second, to conform to the method of self-confession and discipline (*pratideśanā*); third, to allow sentient beings to abide in peace and security, free from fear;

and fourth, to conform to the manner of great beings and noble sovereigns who do not speak of others based on their own knowledge and insight. Thus, the Tathāgata does not arbitrarily speak of others according to his own realization.
[The offense is] established. To testify that it is an offense, one must, by reversing the previous benefits, demonstrate four harms: first, it is not in accordance with the Buddha’s constant Dharma;

second, it violates the legal procedure of *pratijñā-karman* (governance by confession); third, it causes sentient beings to feel fear and insecurity; fourth, it involves speaking against another’s faults, which is not the conduct of a great man.

Although the substance [of the offense] is known through the formal announcement (*jñapti*) made by a bhikṣu, if it is not the proper time, one should neither question nor inquire about it. This is [the rule].
Next, regarding the inquiry at the proper time and the inquiry at the improper time: one should inquire at the proper time. There are three kinds of proper times:

first, the time for formal interrogation before the assembly; second, the time when the offender confesses of their own accord; and third, the time for the extensive formulation of the rule based on that incident. One should not inquire at an improper time.
There are also three [inappropriate] times: first, when it is not the time for formal interrogation before an assembly; second, when it is not the time for the offender to speak for themselves;

and third, when it is not the time for a broad exposition following the establishment of a rule. Furthermore, regarding "the proper time": this refers to questioning based on a monk’s request or inquiry, which constitutes the proper occasion.

At such a time, one does not question out of one's own initiative; thus it is said, "it is the proper time, yet one does not question. Although it may be timely, [if one fails to inquire, it is still an offense].

Regarding the reprimand and the establishment of the precepts: if one does not follow the meaning or satisfy the mind, nor raise inquiries about them, for this reason, it next clarifies whether the meaning is appropriate or inappropriate.
However, knowing this and inquiring at the proper time is called "inquiry that accords with the meaning"; knowing this and not inquiring when the time is right [is otherwise].
The name and its meaning do not coincide. Next, the correct inquiry may be understood. Regarding the "own words" [of the Buddha]:

it is asked, why did the Buddha, when questioned with a doubtful and unsettled mind, not refuse or evade, but instead submit? The answer is found in the first fascicle of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*: "It is the constant law of all Buddhas..."
There were five hundred Vajra deities attending him on his left and right. If the Buddha questioned him three times and he did not answer truthfully, his head would split into seven pieces;
fearing this consequence, he did not dare to refuse or conceal the truth.
Next, the reprimand of Maṇḍgalyāyana has three parts: first, a general introduction; second, a detailed enumeration; third, a summary conclusion. Regarding the general introduction:

the Sūtra compiler generally cites the World-Honored One’s reprimanding words, which are innumerable; these are precisely those that follow. Next, there are two distinct sections. The first reveals the necessity of [addressing] Śāriputra.

The conduct involved transgressions and omissions; the actions performed were improper. From the passage "He informed the bhikṣus" onwards, he raised these faults to show them to the Saṃgha, so that the community of the Dharma might collectively guard against them.
The preceding text is further divided into two parts: first, clarifying the presence of transgressions and omissions in his conduct; second, demonstrating that the tasks he undertook were improper.

Regarding the initial transgressions, they generally manifest his commission of non-virtuous acts; thus it says, "What you have done is not right," for it deviates from the established rules of practice and therefore does not constitute proper decorum (*īryāpatha*).
The nature of a śramaṇa is the untainted noble path. To commit evil is to oppose that; therefore, it is not the work of a śramaṇa. "Defilement" refers to non-pure conduct.
Since one's actions thus violate the teachings, they are not in accordance [with them]. Summarizing this as irrational, it is called "that which should not be done.
Next, "doing what should not be done" can be understood. Following this, the faults are cited to admonish the assembly; the text here consists of two parts. The first reveals...
The fault is particularly grave. Second, the section on the improper nature of performing such actions. This passage revealing the fault consists of three parts:

first, citing the harm and benefit within the matter to exhort [the practitioner] to abandon what is contrary and practice what is compliant; second, from "For what reason? onwards, explaining the intent behind the exhortation; third, from "For what reason? onwards...

To explain the reasons for falling [into the evil realms], first interpret the initial phrase. According to the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, there are seven meanings: First, one who is harmed by a venomous snake harms only this single body, whereas one who is harmed by a woman harms countless bodies.
Second, the harm caused by poison affects a body of neutral (*avyākṛta*) retribution, whereas the harm caused by a woman affects the body of wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*).

Third, the harm caused by poison affects the five consciousness-bodies (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*), whereas the harm caused by a woman affects the six consciousness-bodies (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna-kāya*). Fourth, the harm caused by poison results in the attainment of... [text truncated]

First, those harmed by poison may complete the required number for the Saṃgha, whereas those harmed by women do not count toward that number. Second, those harmed by poison may be reborn among gods or humans and encounter sages and saints; those harmed by women enter the three evil realms.

Third, those harmed by poison may attain the four fruits of the śramaṇa, whereas those harmed by women—even if the Eightfold Path were to fill the world like a great ocean—would find no benefit therein. Fourth... [Fifth]... those harmed by poison may be reborn in the heavens or among humans and meet with worthy sages; those harmed by women enter the three evil paths.

Sixth, those harmed by poison may attain the four fruits of the śramaṇa, whereas those harmed by women—even if the Eightfold Path were to fill the world like a great ocean—would find no benefit therein. Seventh...

One who harms others with poison should be regarded with compassion and protected; whereas one who harms others through women is collectively abandoned by all, finds no joy or pleasure in their heart, and is shunned by devas, nāgas, and benevolent spirits, as well as rebuked by all the sages and holy ones.

Because the principles governing these two types of harm differ, and the consequences of their respective gravity are distinct, I therefore urge you not to commit the offense of poison, but rather to refrain from the offense of women. Next, I shall explain the underlying intent of this exhortation.
Why is it that one statement accords with [the teaching] while two others incur blame? First, why is it recommended to violate a poisonous snake?

Although the poisonous snake brings temporary suffering in the present, it does not entail the calamity of long-term residence in hell; therefore, it is said that for this reason, one does not fall into the evil realms.
Second, why is it not permitted to violate a woman? Although violating a woman brings temporary pleasure in the present, it will inevitably bring about...
One comes to experience the calamities of long-term imprisonment in hell; therefore, it is said that "when the body perishes and life ends, one falls into the evil realms.

Next, the reasons for a woman’s transgression leading to her fall into hell are explained. This section contains two parts: first, the explicit revelation of the faults of desire; second, the use of analogies to manifest those faults.
First, regarding the manifestation of faults: this generally reveals the source of faults so that they may be forever eliminated;
hence it is called "teaching the dharma for severing desire. "Desire-thought" refers to the mind that contemplates women; "desire-remembrance" refers to the intention that pursues sensory objects;

"desire-fever" refers to being scorched by the fire of desire; and "knots of craving" clarifies the bondage of attachment. To not be submerged by these is termed "crossing over. Next, as for the illustration: desire burns.

Because of the virtuous mind, it is said that sensual desire is like fire wishing to burn the hand of one who holds it; it is like grasping a torch of straw, which further injures the body of precepts.
Sensual pleasure does not endure, like a borrowed object; sensual desire has no true flavor, like a dry bone; sensual desire accumulates manifold afflictions, like a piece of meat;
the pleasure of desire is unreal, like what is seen in a dream; and sensual desire wounds the feet of the precepts, like treading upon [a thorn].
Desire is like a sharp blade that seeks to destroy all wholesome virtues; it is like a new tile [easily broken], and its nature is to be feared like the head of a venomous serpent.
It seeks to annihilate goodness like a whirling sword, and it evokes perilous retribution as if standing upon a sharp spearhead. Its injury is as swift as being pierced by a keen halberd;
its affliction reaches the ultimate extreme, and is thus said to be utterly loathsome and evil. It is that which the Buddha rebuked, and here we conclude by taking refuge in the Teacher.
The subsequent administrative matters are as above; the third section, the summary, may be understood accordingly.
Next, the faults and violations are revealed. The brief address to the bhikṣus serves to manifest the fault, while the mention that Śuddhodana was aware of it serves to manifest the offense.
Regarding the phrase "addressing a deluded person": this refers to the *Dṛṣṭivāda*. When the Buddha saw Sudatta, he perceived that the man had already committed unwholesome deeds;

out of a heart of compassion, he addressed him as a "deluded person. It is like compassionate parents who, seeing their child commit evil, also scold and rebuke that child. Why [is he called] a "deluded person"? Because...
Having performed such an act, one asks: "The World-Honored One has already severed all afflictions (*kleśa*) and their latent tendencies (*anuśaya*);

why then do you call him a 'fool'? The answer is: Although the World-Honored One has exhausted both delusion and its tendencies, he speaks of things such as "affection" (*sneha*) for the sake of benefiting others;
therefore, he rebukes the fool. This is just as when a preceptor (*upādhyāya*) or a teacher (*ācārya*) has a resident disciple or one who relies upon them, and [the teacher] gives rise to...
Having censured [the monk] for his various faults, he said: "You are a foolish person. The World-Honored One did likewise.

When asked what the meaning of the Buddha’s reproach of a "foolish person" (mūḍha-puruṣa) was—whether one is called a foolish person because they have arisen from delusion (*moha*), or whether one is described as a foolish person because delusion is currently manifesting—[he replied:]
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 16, explains: "Because they arise from delusion (*moha*), they are called 'deluded persons' (*bāla*).

[Objection: But they also arise from greed, hatred, pride, views, and so forth; why does the World-Honored One speak only of "deluded persons"? [Response: Because delusion is all-pervasive (*sarvatraga*).
If the Buddha knew that rebuking Arhats and others as "deluded persons" would be beneficial for sentient beings, he would likewise rebuke them. This is because the Arhat...
The body, too, arises from delusion (*moha*). Furthermore, because one manifests active delusion, one is called a "deluded person" (*mūḍha-puruṣa*).
Even Arhats and others manifest active delusion; this is non-afflicted ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*), which has not yet been extinguished. Question: Other afflictions (*kleśa*) also manifest.
Why is it said that only the deluded person [is so described] and not others? The answer is: as previously stated, because delusion (*moha*) is universal.

Regarding the phrase "in many types of outflowing states" (*āsravasthāna*): this opens the gates of the outflows (*āsrava*), causing the source of the outflows to flourish. The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* says:
"Sudinna, since the beginning of the eon when male and female did not yet exist, he was the first person to engage in sexual desire; thus he committed evil."

The Dharma is the root. Now the Buddha-dharma is pure; there has been no non-Dharma until now. Yet Sūdanī was the first to commit an evil act, which will lead to future non-Dharma and mark the beginning of transgressions;

therefore, it is said that he opened the gates of the outflows (*āsrava*). This was the first violation of the precepts and the beginning of the contravention of the summary teaching (*saṃkṣipta-śikṣā*);
thus, the summary instruction was ruined.

Next follows the detailed formulation of the precept. This text consists of three parts: first, citing the fundamental principle to establish the regulation; second, collecting ten phrases to establish the merit of benefiting others;
third, stating "When about to recite the precepts" and below, correctly clarifying the establishment of the regulation.

Since this precept is thus, all other precepts are of a similar nature. The initial passage cites the time of the regulation; since it has been from that point onward, it says, "From this day forward. This is based on the cause.

The net of the teaching was once established so that it might universally benefit all; hence it is said, "together with the bhikṣus. Regarding the fixed gravity of offenses, their respective positions distinguish them for the prevention of wrongdoing, each having its own specific jurisdiction;

this is termed "establishing the precepts" (*śīla-saṃvara*). Question: Among all wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*), one does not speak of "establishing" (*saṃdhi*) them; why then is it said only to "establish the precepts"?
The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (*Duolun*) explains: "The precepts are the root of the myriad virtues. To establish the precepts is itself to establish everything."

Furthermore, the precepts may be established as a means to cease evil, while simultaneously establishing the designation of "offenses"; thus, when concluding the remaining wholesome [precepts], it is not so, and for this reason they are not called "concluded" (*saṃvara*).

To explain this meaning in contrast, there is a sixfold analysis: first, the expansion of what was restricted and the supplementation of what was abbreviated; second, the restriction for the purpose of removing obstacles to the Path.
Third, the distinction of the conditions for the establishment [of the precepts]. Fourth, the number of conditions for the establishment. Fifth, the meaning expressed by the teaching as established.
Sixth, the distinction between the intention and the aging.

Regarding the first gate: at the very beginning when the Buddha first attained enlightenment and initiated his transformation of beings, fearing that those entering the Dharma would have no place to entrust their minds, he first—
This brief exposition demonstrates the model for practice. Those of sharp faculties who respectfully cultivate it will remain free from any transgressions;

those of dull faculties, however, fail to realize it and, by violating this summary, give rise to non-virtue, thereby causing the teaching to be ruined—this is termed "deficiency in the teaching. Nevertheless, such violation of the teaching constitutes an offense, defiling what was originally received.

To allow the practice of impurity is called a deficiency in practice. Therefore, out of compassion and protective mindfulness, the Tathāgata established the extensive teachings to accord with the concise teachings;
now, these two sets of teachings shall be mutually consistent and complementary, so that the concise teachings may once again serve their purpose for those times.
The meaning is the same as "supplementary instruction. Having heard the detailed prohibitions, one reprimands oneself and recognizes the faults;

by maintaining awareness of these characteristics, one protects and upholds the precepts, thereby supporting their uninterrupted continuity so that they become even more pure than before—this is called "supplementary practice" (*pūraka-caryā*).

Furthermore, by repenting of what one has transgressed, one ensures it cannot serve as a cause for future bitter fruits, ultimately resulting in the complete non-experience of such suffering and restoring the purity of the precepts—this is also called "supplementary practice. Therefore, the aforementioned text says: "If there is..."
Regarding those who commit tainted dharmas (*sāsrava-dharma*), the World-Honored One subsequently established the precepts for the bhikṣus in order to sever those tainted dharmas.
In the second section, although the karmic activities that obstruct the Path are infinite, to summarize them, there are two kinds. What are they?

This refers to intrinsic evil (*prakṛti-duṣṭa*) and prohibited evil (*pratikṣepa-duṣṭa*). Regarding "intrinsic evil," such as killing, stealing, and so forth: regardless of whether they are forbidden by the sacred teachings, their harmfulness is profound;
to commit them is a transgression, and their very nature is unwholesome—thus they are called "intrinsic evil. Regarding "prohibited evil," such as the collapse of a dwelling and so forth:
their nature is not inherently unwholesome, but because the resulting disturbances can obstruct the cultivation of the path, prohibitions are established to prevent them.

This is called "prohibition" (*pratiṣedha*). These words refer to the prohibition of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), analyzed in terms of specific phenomena. If we discuss the category of offenses, they all consist of the prohibition of evil.
Prior to the establishment of the precepts, one could perform such acts without transgression; it is only after the Sage has established them that the offense is formally defined.
Furthermore, once a prohibition is in place, all instances of violating the teaching are equally categorized as evil, down to the most minor details. Moreover, greed, hatred, and delusion can—
It obstructs the Noble Path. The Buddha, in order to sever it, established the training in increased virtue (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*).

This may be understood from the text. The teaching in the third section does not arise in isolation; its arising must necessarily depend upon conditions (*pratyaya*). Although the objects of these conditions are manifold, they are essentially limited to the three natures:

namely, the wholesome (*kuśala*), the unwholesome (*akuśala*), and the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). When one relies on the wholesome to form a connection and give rise [to the teaching], it is as when, for instance, due to discussing the treatises, a woman preaches the Dharma or recites together [with others].

I have repeatedly instructed those who cover their heads and others of this sort: although such actions may be virtuous in nature, they nevertheless contravene the intention of the Sage and give rise to no small transgression.

For this reason, the Tathāgata established these teachings as a precaution against them. As for those things that arise based on unwholesome conditions, such as killing and stealing, [they are likewise forbidden].
The nature [of unwholesome states] is antagonistic and harmful; relying upon this, one is able to give rise to various unwholesome actions. Therefore, the teaching is established to prevent this.

As for those unwholesome acts that arise by relying on neutral (*avyākṛta*) conditions—such as digging the earth—although the act itself is neutral, the activity is agitated and distracting, creating many obstacles to the cultivation of the Path.

Thus, it is prohibited so that such agitation may be stilled, ultimately leading to the benefits of the Path. However, according to the *Karmavibhaṅga-śāstra*, initiating such an act constitutes an offense.

This mind also penetrates all three natures (*trisvabhāva*). Therefore, in the first chapter of the treatise, it asks: "Is there an offense committed with a wholesome mind (*kuśalacitta*), an unwholesome mind (*akuśalacitta*), or a neutral mind (*avyākṛtacitta*)?
The answer is: "Yes. How is there an offense committed with a wholesome mind?

For example, a newly ordained bhikṣu, not yet knowing the characteristics of the precepts, personally clears the ground and gathers flowers to weave a garland; this is an offense committed with a wholesome mind. How is there an offense committed with an unwholesome mind?
Regarding the transgression of the precepts: it is a transgression of the precepts established by the Buddha. How is there a transgression of the precepts with an indeterminate mind?

It is a transgression of the precepts established by the Buddha that is not committed intentionally. Question: According to this principle, transgressions pertain to all three natures (wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate). Why, then, does the subsequent text state that "transgressions and disputes are not wholesome"?

Answer: The subsequent text refers specifically to the transgression of the precepts. In reality, there is no such thing as a wholesome transgression. However, for the purpose of establishing the conditions for the teaching, it is permitted to pertain to all three natures.

Furthermore, regarding the following passage, one might think that a formal dispute (*adhikaraṇa*) cannot be "wholesome" (*kuśala*). However, with respect to the arising of the intention to dispute, it can indeed be wholesome.
Therefore, the text states: "A bhikṣu speaks with a wholesome mind regarding the matters of a dispute, such as [the performance of] ritual acts (*karma*)," and so forth.

The fourth section concerns the establishment of the precepts, which necessarily relies upon specific conditions. This matter depends on the commission of an offense through an invitation; it requires ten conditions for the Noble One to initiate the formal enactment.

First, there must be a prior request, as when Śāriputra had already granted permission and then outflows arose, necessitating the enactment. Second, the subject must be a bhikṣu, meaning one belonging to the great saṃgha, and not other assemblies.
Third, there must be the occurrence of an outflow offense, such as sexual misconduct and so forth, each according to its own category. Fourth, there must be a formal accusation. If...

1. Not to fail to bring it forth; otherwise, there would be no means by which it could be investigated and recovered. 2. Five Buddhas were seated [in the assembly]; as the matter pertains to the Teacher, it must be resolved by the Buddha himself. 3.

To assemble the Sangha and deliberate together with the multitude so that the Dharma may endure for a long time. 4. To interrogate before the assembly; for if one does not investigate and question, there may be false accusations or errors.
5. To obtain a confession; because when one obtains a confession, the mind submits to the guilt. 6. It is necessary to reprove [the offender]; if...

There is no censure, nor is there any explicit manifestation of what is incorrect. These ten [conditions] apply specifically to the initial [case], because the first person’s instruction has not yet been subsumed.

When these ten are fully present, the Noble One (the Buddha) then initiates the formal act of suspension (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*). If even one condition is deficient, he restrains himself and does not grant permission.
These ten conditions refer to the stage at which [the offense] arises. If there are any omissions, the meaning may be inferred accordingly.

The fifth section concerns how the principles and teachings arise through the convergence of conditions. Since the teaching is not established in vain, it must have that which it explicates. What is this that is explicated? It consists of four aspects:
first, transgression; second, non-transgression; third, light offenses; and fourth, grave offenses. These may be understood by referring to the text.

When one commits an error through the convergence of conditions, it defiles the essence of the vows received; this is termed "transgression. When wholesome conduct arises in accordance with the meaning, the essence of the vows is illuminated.

Hui says: This is called "non-offense. Expedient means are light; the final completion is heavy. Furthermore, one may compare the five types of offenses such that the preceding is heavy and the succeeding is light.
Within these four phrases, each gives rise to two modes of action. For example, when the five conditions are fully met, it is termed "committing an offense.
Regarding this commission of an offense, two modes of action arise: if, by relying on the five conditions, the act of killing is accomplished, it is then termed an offense.

"Practice" refers to the fulfillment of the transgressing dharma, which violates the intent of the Noble One’s regulations. If one recognizes the five conditions and ceases evil without committing it, this is called "practice of non-transgression," which is the fulfillment of the non-transgressing dharma and accords with the intent of the Noble One’s regulations.
By means of the non-transgressing dharma, there are what are known as the two types of observance: the observance of abstention and the observance of performance.
If one exerts oneself with diligence in practice, one achieves non-transgression; if one is indolent and fails to study, one incurs transgression. Question:
If one already possesses a transgressive dharma yet achieves non-transgression, why is it necessary to possess a non-transgressive dharma to achieve non-transgression?

Answer: Achieving non-transgression while possessing a transgressive dharma refers only to *saṃvara* (restraint through cessation); achieving non-transgression while possessing a non-transgressive dharma is itself *pravṛtti* (active observance). Furthermore, he asked:

Question: One who has not committed a transgression against the Dharma gives rise to an act of transgression; why then must one commit a transgression against the Dharma in order for an act of transgression to arise? Answer:

When an act of transgression arises from that which does not violate the Dharma, it is merely a "cessation-transgression" (zhi-fan). When an act of transgression arises from violating the Dharma, it is a "committed-transgression" (zuo-fan). Next, regarding the arising of heavy acts from heavy [conditions]:

this refers to cases such as when all three times are grave, or when one experiences pleasure while concealing [the offense], making it impossible to repent, and so forth. Regarding the arising of light [acts] from heavy [conditions]: [this is as previously explained].
Regarding "action": this refers to the seven lower types of action among the eight types of karma, as well as non-obscured (anivṛta) mind;

these can arise from conditions such as regret and so forth. Regarding "light [action] producing heavy results": this refers to actions involving heavy afflictions, such as striking a Buddha or an Arhat. Regarding "light [action] producing light results": [this refers to...]

As in the case of digging the earth with a frivolous mind and so forth, the sixth section concludes that the meanings are manifold and their principles are not uniform. To speak briefly, there are eight essential points:

first, profound prevention; second, delimiting the scope; third, censuring faults; fourth, infrequency; fifth, defining characteristics; sixth, demonstrating errors; seventh, the mental object; eighth, the mental state.

Regarding the eight internal and external [precepts]: "Deep prevention" refers to establishing heavy designations in advance when transgressions have reached their ultimate limit; it prohibits even the subtle and prevents attachment in order to protect the root.
This is like the prevention of the four solitary offenses, the two insects in food and drink, defiled clothing and food, and the seizing or releasing of stored items.

"Limiting the scope" refers to regulating conduct before it reaches its ultimate limit, maintaining the principle of proportionality according to one's capacity; if one lacks the strength to perform an act, even if it is committed, it is not considered grave. As for example...

Regarding the nun’s emission, the monk’s touching, and the concealment of a *pārājika* offense—wherein the objective conditions (*ālambana*) are deficient or absent—the term "reproach for faults" refers to the fact that the precepts can prevent what is non-virtuous and their essential nature is pure;
yet, in their observance and protection, one must remain free from suspicion.

This includes such matters as sitting with a woman in either a secluded or exposed place, staying overnight together, traveling or speaking [with her], and praising or pointing out food, and so forth. Regarding the term "frequency," although an offense relies upon an objective condition, the condition...
If there is a mind that finds ease in what is difficult, then arrogance and resentment will bind one in offenses as grave as those of stealing or killing a celestial being.

Regarding the two groups [of monks and nuns], there are coarse words, praising the body, building dwellings, destroying living beings, and digging the earth. As for the verbal expressions, they involve transgressions that damage the principle and violate the Way;

these bring shame upon both the clergy and the laity. Since the harm is so profound, it gives rise to karmic fetters based on specific matters. Although the manifestations are many, four are briefly cited here: regarding retribution, time, place, and the matter itself, a regulation is established.
They are not the same. Regarding the term "indicating the transgression": although the name of the offense exists, its actual substance has not yet been revealed;

first, the conditions for the transgression are signaled so that they may be heard and seen, such as proclaiming Devadatta’s great falsehood, groundless [accusations], drinking alcohol, possessing precious objects, and being no longer a śramaṇa. Regarding "mental object" (viṣaya): an offense does not arise in isolation;
it opens up the mind by relying on an object. Sometimes the prohibition follows from the mind, and sometimes the prohibition follows from the object, as in the case of sexual misconduct.
The Precept Against Alcohol: Restraining the mind according to its objects; for humans, non-humans, and so forth, restraining the objects according to the mind.

Regarding what is called "internal" and "external": an offense is not established in isolation; it is established through the convergence of conditions. Although causes and conditions vary in myriad ways, they are essentially comprised of only the internal and external.

For example, sexual intercourse is internal, while physical contact is external; food and medicine are internal, while robes and bowls are external. Next, the regulation of benefits is clarified: the first phrase provides a general heading, which is simply...
The mind has become dissolute and unruly, and the wild horse of the intellect is distracted and negligent toward the gateway of the True Teaching; thus, one is unable to maintain or protect it.

The Tathāgata, having long accumulated great compassion, did not abandon his vow regarding the four wisdoms. Consequently, he established precepts based on transgressions, all of which give rise to the merit of the ten benefits.
This means that the mind which commits transgressions is forever dispelled, while the intention to observe the precepts constantly arises; such arising is the very foundation for generating Bodhi.
To "dispatch" means to dispatch the very root of afflictions. Thus, practice does not establish itself independently; it is accomplished by relying upon the Teaching.

The Teaching is capable of giving birth to all manifold practices. As for the manifold practices thus produced, how could they be limited to these ten? This is merely a brief indication of the methods of transformation in one direction.
The two sets of five teachings that can express [the truth] manifest the four intended meanings; these constitute the subject matter (*artha*).

From this point downward, the text is divided into three parts for a detailed explanation: first, there are three benefits that can give rise to various practices; next, there are six benefits that can give rise to specific practices.

The latter benefit is that it enables the Dharma to endure. Because the two higher assemblies are established through their distinct practices, they are able to cause the True Dharma to abide for a long time without perishing.
As for the first three benefits: the precepts are able to prevent wrongdoing; that which violates them is not embraced, while that which accords with the teaching abandons what is improper.
This is called "gathering. Since body and speech are gathered, one's conduct accords with reverence and harmony, and all opposition and contention are severed; this is called "joy.

Being able to receive the teachings, one forever severs decline and peril, remaining at ease in both the present and the future; therefore, it is termed "peaceful bliss. Next follows the specific benefits.

The first two [stages] give rise to the wholesome; the next four eliminate the unwholesome. To cause those who have not yet attained faith to do so: the *Jianlun* (Treatise on Seeing), fascicle six, states:
"If a virtuous bhikṣu conforms to the Vinaya and is fully endowed with dignified deportment, those who have not yet attained faith will, upon seeing him, immediately give rise to faith and say:
'This son of the Śākya clan is diligent and energetic; he is able to perform what is difficult to perform, and his deeds are exceedingly weighty. Having seen this..."
Once this has been done, faith arises. If various non-Buddhists see this abbreviated Vinaya-piṭaka, they will say, "The Buddha’s words to the bhikṣus also include the Vedas;
they are no different from our own," and thus they will develop a heart of reverence. Those who already have faith will cause it to increase.

The Discourse on Views: If there is one who leaves the household life with faith and acts in accordance with what is taught in the prohibitions and precepts, people will see his conduct and treat him with great reverence.
Furthermore, they will say: "How is it that for as long as life lasts, he eats but one meal a day, practices the holy life, and guards and upholds the prohibitions and precepts?"
Having seen this, their faith increased. There were bhikṣus who violated the precepts and disturbed the Saṃgha; lacking shame within, they were called "the untamable.

The Buddha established the precepts for them and instructed the Saṃgha to impose penalties so that they might reform their evil ways and follow what is good; therefore, they are called "the tamed and compliant."
Due to the prohibition against shamelessness, one may not enter the assembly. A pure bhikṣu who practices the Dharma in peace and security, being free from affliction, is said to be "at ease.
One who harbors evil within and extensively commits various misdeeds, resulting in being beaten or killed by others, is said to have "outflows in the present life."
Because the Buddha established the precepts to instruct one in restraining body and speech so that present evils do not arise, this is called "abandonment.

Because creating the causes of evil in the present leads to falling into hell later and undergoing immeasurable suffering, this is called "future outflows. By means of the precepts established by the Buddha, the causes of evil are forever severed.

To not undergo future suffering is called "cessation. To abide in the lower dharmas by means of the extensive teachings that have been established, so that people may receive and practice them, internalizing the Dharma within themselves and ensuring it does not fall into ruin, is called "long endurance."
Next, the establishment of the regulations is explained. The text is divided into two parts. First, the ritual procedures for reciting the *Prātimokṣa* are explained; second, from "If a bhikṣu...

onwards, the four phrases of the *Prātimokṣa*, such as the offense (*āpatti*), are extensively interpreted. The first part has three sections: first, the brief formulation in response to specific circumstances;

second, citing the regulation to clarify its application; third, the completion of the *Prātimokṣa*. Regarding the first section, because the *Poṣadha* is about to be recited, [the author] first sets forth the heading.
To introduce the passage to be explained: what follows below is a brief establishment based on specific conditions, consisting of only four propositions.

Next, below that, it is clarified that the text is divided into two parts: first, it clarifies the differentiation of the *vadhaka-citta* (murderous intent) according to the formal act; second, it distinguishes the case within the forest.

The objects [of the precepts] vary according to their specific bindings. However, regarding those established according to circumstances (*anuprāpti*), the Great Sage formulated the root precepts (*mūla-śīla*) to provide a comprehensive defense against transgressions and omissions.

He intended to make the lifting of prohibitions explicit and to ensure that violations and observances were clearly determined. If the matters were already fully detailed, a single binding would suffice for determination.

But if the characteristics of the regulation were not yet complete, it was necessary to further clarify the rules according to circumstances. In this way, the teachings encompass all aspects of the path of practice, ensuring its firm stability from beginning to end and its continued circulation.

It is because they are fully endowed [with these factors]. Furthermore, according to the specific wording, there are instances of both offense and non-offense. Regarding offenses: when the prevention of transgressions is not yet complete, one must further apply the formal determination (*prajñapti*).
Such cases include this precept on improper speech, as well as [offenses regarding] before or after eating, reviling, digging the earth, and so forth. Regarding non-offenses: [the following apply].

The previous regulations contain implicit principles that must be further opened up according to circumstances. For example, in cases such as when one has an intense dream, or when bathing apart from the assembly due to various conditions, these are instances where the rules are relaxed. Regarding the seven phrases in the preceding text, although they concern the fault of arising with a different state of mind, the intention here is to clarify the principle of "following" (anuvartana). First, the previous regulation is restated: "However, if one delights in the Path, this may constitute an offense; but since I now delight in worldly life, there should be no violation. Second, regarding the passage beginning with "He forms the thought," it continues: [The text continues: ...Furthermore, [the Buddha] said: "If one knows that others have already bathed, one should not bathe again. If one bathes again, one commits an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). This was spoken by the Blessed One for the sake of those who delight in the Path. Now, I do not delight in the Path, but rather delight in worldly life. Therefore, I shall bathe again. There is no offense. Furthermore, there are other conditions for opening the rule, such as when one is ill, or when bathing together with the assembly, or when the water is cold, or when the body is covered in dust and filth, or when one has been traveling on a long road and is weary, or when one is about to perform a ritual, or when one is about to enter a village. If one bathes under such conditions, there is no offense. Furthermore, there are other conditions for opening the rule, such as when one is performing a *paritta* recitation, or when one is about to receive a gift, or when one is about to give a gift, or when one is about to offer incense or flowers, or when one is about to perform a *pūjā*, or when one is about to enter the presence of the King, or when one is about to meet with elders and teachers. If one bathes under such conditions, there is no offense. Furthermore, there are other conditions for opening the rule, such as when one is about to wash one's face, or when one is about to wash one's hands, or when one is about to wash one's feet, or when one is about to wash the private parts, or when one is about to wash the head, or when one is about to wash the body. If one bathes under such conditions, there is no offense. Furthermore, there are other conditions for opening the rule, such as when one is about to dye robes, or when one is about to sew robes, or when one is about to mend robes, or when one is about to wash robes, or when one is about to dry robes, or when one is about to store robes. If one bathes under such conditions, there is no offense. Furthermore, there are other conditions for opening the rule, such as when one is about to enter the fire hall, or when one is about to enter the refectory, or when one is about to enter the lecture hall, or when one is about to enter the meditation hall, or when one is about to enter the restroom, or when one is about to enter the latrine. If one bathes under such conditions, there is no offense. Furthermore, there are other conditions for opening the rule, such as when one is about to enter the forest, or when one is about to enter the cemetery, or when one is about to enter a dangerous place, or when one is about to cross a river, or when one is about to cross a mountain pass, or when one is about to cross a desert. If one bathes under such conditions, there is no offense. Furthermore, there are other conditions for opening the rule, such as when one is about to enter the presence of a deity, or when one is about to enter the presence of a *nāga*, or when one is about to enter the presence of a *yakṣa*, or when one is about to enter the presence of a *rākṣasa*, or when one is about to enter the presence of a *piśāca*, or when one is about to enter the presence of a *kumbhāṇḍa*. If one bathes under such conditions, there is no offense. Furthermore, there are other conditions for opening the rule, such as when one is about to enter the presence of a *bhūta*, or when one is about to enter the presence of a *preta*, or when one is about to enter the presence of an *asura*, or when one is about to enter the presence of a *garuḍa*, or when one is about to enter the presence of a *mahoraga*, or when one is about to enter the presence of a *kimnara*. If one bathes under such conditions, there is no offense. Furthermore, there are other conditions for opening the rule, such as when one is about to enter the presence of a *manuṣya*, or when one is about to enter the presence of a *strī*, or when one is about to enter the presence of a *puruṣa*, or when one is about to enter the presence of a *dāraka*, or when one is about to enter the presence of a *dārikā*. If one bathes under such conditions, there is no offense. Furthermore, there are other conditions for opening the rule, such as when one is about to enter the presence of a *brāhmaṇa*, or when one is about to enter the presence of a *kṣatriya*, or when one is about to enter the presence of a *vaiśya*, or when one is about to enter the presence of a *śūdra*. If one bathes under such conditions, there is no offense. Furthermore, there are other conditions for opening the rule, such as when one is about to enter the presence of a *gṛhapati*, or when one is about to enter the presence of a *śreṣṭhin*, or when one is about to enter the presence of a *sārthavāha*, or when one is about to enter the presence of a *rājāmātya*, or when one is about to enter the presence of a *rājaputra*. If one bathes under such conditions, there is no offense. Furthermore, there are other conditions for opening the rule, such as when one is about to enter the presence of a *rājamahāmātra*, or when one is about to enter the presence of a *rājapurohita*, or when one is about to enter the presence of a *rājaguru*, or when one is about to enter the presence of a *rājadūta*. If one bathes under such conditions, there is no offense. Furthermore, there are other conditions for opening the rule, such as when one is about to enter the presence of a *bhikṣu*, or when one is about to enter the presence of a *bhikṣuṇī*, or when one is about to enter the presence of a *śrāmaṇera*, or when one is about to enter the presence of a *śrāmaṇerī*, or when one is about to enter the presence of an *upāsaka*, or when one is about to enter the presence of an *upāsikā*. If one bathes under such conditions, there is no offense. Furthermore, there are other conditions for opening the rule, such as when one is about to enter the presence of a *tīrthika*, or when one is about to enter the presence of a *parivrājaka*, or when one is about to enter the presence of a *caraka*, or when one is about to enter the presence of a *maskarī*, or when one is about to enter the presence of a *saṃjayin*. If one bathes under such conditions, there is no offense. Furthermore, there are other conditions for opening the rule, such as when one is about to enter the presence of a *māṭhara*, or when one is about to enter the presence of a *kāśyapa*, or when one is about to enter the presence of a *gotama*, or when one is about to enter the presence of a *nirgrantha*, or when one is about to enter the presence of a *ājīvika*. If one bathes under such conditions, there is no offense. Furthermore, there are other conditions for opening the rule, such as when one is about to enter the presence of a *śrotriya*, or when one is about to enter the presence of a *vedapāṭhaka*, or when one is about to enter the presence of a *mantrajña*, or when one is about to enter the presence of a *yogin*, or when one is about to enter the presence of a *siddha*. If one bathes under such conditions, there is no offense. Furthermore, there are other conditions for opening the rule, such as when one is about to enter the presence of a *cakravartin*, or when one is about to enter the presence of a *balacakravartin*, or when one is about to enter the presence of a *koṭṭarāja*, or when one is about to enter the presence of a *maṇḍalika*. If one bathes

He gave rise to doubt: "Is it because I have grown weary of the Path and take delight in the mundane that I have lost my precepts without having actually transgressed them? Or is it that I have not lost them?

Regarding whether his possession of the precepts could be violated, he remained in a state of uncertainty as to whether he had committed an offense or not; thus, he said, "What shall I do? Thirdly, he immediately stepped down, set forth his doubts, and requested a definitive resolution.
Out of shame at facing the countenance of the Sage, he did not dare to petition him himself, but relied instead upon his fellow student to voice his own uncertainty.
1. [The Buddha] said, "The mind [is the culprit]. Because he did not heed the Buddha's instruction, it is said that one must "follow the teaching and practice accordingly.

2. From the passage "The four bhikṣus... onwards, this serves to clarify lingering doubts; since their doubts were identical, he did not reprimand them. Out of compassion for their state of mind, he cited the circumstances and made a full report.

3. From the passage "At that time, the World-Honored One... onwards, the Buddha judged this to be an offense. Although he had conceived a contrary intention, because his physical weakness prevented him from relinquishing it, he remained a bhikṣu by virtue of this.
These constitute transgressions of the limits. However, these bhikṣus both violate [the rules], though the details differ in their extent. Sūpananda violates only the abbreviated teaching;

as for the other six, they are permitted to renounce the precepts because they have become weary of the Path. Since the others are weak individuals who fall within the scope of transgression, they are permitted to renounce the precepts;
hence it is said, "If there are other persons," and so forth. Yet, if these bhikṣus, having renounced the precepts and returned to lay life, later wish to go forth...
