Now, these two [points] are subverted and explained erroneously, thus becoming false. According to the *Vinaya-vibhaṅga*, these too should have been cited together; the reason they were not cited is as follows:

If one considers what is appropriate and what is inappropriate, it is as explained in the *Dvayavardhana*. If one discusses the formal procedure (*karmavācanā*), it is clear from the *Tarjanīya* [Karma].

Now, in this discussion of admonition (*pratisaṃmodana*), why is there a need to cite the *Utkṣepaṇīya*? If that were the case, the same would apply to *Līḍha*; why then is there a citation for it? The answer is: because the matter depends upon the specific characteristics of the case.

Therefore, it is precisely the *ukkhepanīya-kamma* (act of suspension) that is brought forth. If that which is followed—the *ukkhepanīya*—is not brought forth, why would one incur this fault of following (*ānubandha*)?

Furthermore, since both following and opposing the admonition result in a fault, even if this were clarified, because following does not constitute a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (offense requiring formal meeting), it remains hidden;

thus, it is logically appropriate to treat it as a case of *ukkhepanīya*, and there is no need for this clarification. Alternatively, is it explained that the inversion [of the sequence] constitutes a fault? That which must logically be suspended refers to this.

If a person does not engage in divisive acts, there is no need to initiate formal proceedings against them. If they do engage in divisive acts, one should not initiate proceedings, as this would split the assembly and disrupt the orderly performance of Dharma activities;
such discord is not a state of unified harmony, so what need is there to wait for a formal charge? Furthermore, if one were to impose a formal charge, it would not serve as an effective remedy.
As for the latter two cases, they are not erroneous; why then would a formal charge be necessary? Therefore, in all four instances where advice is rejected, formal proceedings are unnecessary.

Next, following the specific explanation: there are three intentions for the prohibition. First, regarding the prohibition against causing a schism in the Saṃgha: the community of monks should be harmonious, peaceful, and possessed of the Dharma;
this is logically something that ought to be followed with meticulous care, like water and milk mixed together.

Now, conversely, some rely on the descriptions in the holy teachings and use deceptive speech to confuse the minds of the multitude, thereby destroying the Saṃgha and severing the Dharma until they fall into ruin. They commit evil without cause, and because of this, the damage becomes increasingly severe. Therefore, [it is prohibited].
The prohibition was established because it constitutes the meaning of "breaking the Saṃgha"; this will be explained in the relevant passage. Second, as for the purpose of the admonition:
since Devadatta established a counterfeit doctrine that obscured the true Dharma at a time when it was flourishing, the situation is truly pitiable;

thus, the Saṃgha must provide an admonition to reveal right from wrong, hoping that he might reform his errors to follow the correct path, abandon evil, and honor the good. Third, regarding the formal determination of the offense: the assembly of monks... [detailed the matter].
The mind may offer admonition, clearly proclaiming what is right and wrong and instructing one to renounce [the error];

yet if the person remains stubbornly attached to their own views and refuses to follow such exhortation, causing grave distress to the community, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense is established. Next, regarding the explanation of the name:

to alter the true Dharma with false teachings and to divide the assembly into divergent paths is called "breaking the Saṃgha" (*saṃghabheda*). To persist in evil intentions and disregard the commands of the community is called "defying admonition" (*anuvartana*).

There are five distinct conditions: first, the establishment of a false Triple Gem, which refers to the matter for which the admonition is intended; second, the timing of the transformative activity—if one does not engage in transformative activity, then admonition is unnecessary;
third, the formal delivery of the admonition according to the Dharma, distinguishing it from what is contrary to the Dharma; fourth, stubborn persistence and refusal to relinquish the position;
and fifth, the completion of the three *karmavācanās*.
Next is the deficiency of conditions. If the first condition is deficient, there is no offense whatsoever. If the second is deficient, the latter three are also deficient;
there is only a *duṣkṛta* (transgression) for the mere preparatory act toward the Three Jewels. If the third is deficient, there is no offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, *sthūlātyaya*, or *duṣkṛta*;
it may simply be a *duṣkṛta* for private admonition. If the Saṃgha performs the formal act (*dharmakarma*) but it is not valid—meaning it is not accomplished—then likewise [there is no offense].

If one does not comply with the admonition regarding offenses such as [denying] cause and effect, and if the *karmavācanā* falls into one of the seven improper forms while they harbor a mind of defiance toward what is lawful, they incur seven *thullaccaya* offenses.
If the fourth form is missing and they abandon the matter before the *ñatti* (motion) is completed, it is a *dukkaṭa*; once the *ñatti* is completed, it is one *thullaccaya*.
Up until the third [round of] admonition is not yet concluded, one incurs four *pācittika* offenses; the fifth condition is lacking. This may be understood by analogy with what precedes.

The explanations for the remaining rules regarding disobedience to admonitions are all the same as this. However, the conditions for the offense in these various rules of admonition differ slightly. In this text, there are two parts:
first, up to the phrase "not eating fish or meat," which establishes the cause for the breach and the matter to be admonished; second, from "a great number of bhikṣus" onwards, is the censure.
The Reprimand and the Exhortation to Remonstrate. The preceding text consists of five sections: First, the preliminary account identifying those capable of causing a schism in the Saṃgha;

Second, from "At that time the World-Honored One" onwards, the account of how the Prince was converted and subsequently conceived the intent to cause a schism; Third, from "Then Devadatta" onwards, the account of his usurpation of the superior position, his attempt to kill the Buddha, and his harm to the King;

Fourth, from "At that time Devadatta" onwards, the account of his acquisition of an evil reputation and the severance of his gains; Fifth, the account of his sympathizers separating [from the Saṃgha].
[The section on] Food. Fifth, Devadatta establishes a counterfeit Triple Gem below [the true one] and destroys the wheel of the Saṃgha.
The first part of the text has two sections: first, clarifying the conditions for his renunciation; second, from "At that time, the World-Honored One...

onwards, clarifying his renunciation and receiving of the precepts. Within the former section, there are six parts: first, witnessing an event as a condition; second, from "At that time... onwards, leading others by mutual agreement to seek ordination.

In the third section, from "Bhadrika descended" to "having finished with his distaste for worldly affairs," [the account ends]. In the fourth section, from "Aniruddha descended" to "all the Śākyas gathered like clouds," [the account continues].

In the fifth section, from "each having bathed themselves clean" to "proceeded forward to pay their respects," [the account proceeds]. In the sixth section, from "addressing the Buddha" to "formally requesting ordination," [the account concludes].
Regarding all the Śākyas who went forth in the initial passage, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 4, states: "When the Buddha first returned to his kingdom..."
The brothers Kāśyapa and their thousand bhikṣus had originally practiced the Brahmanical dharma, performing asceticism in the mountains until their appearances were haggard and emaciated.
When the King, their father, saw them, he felt that these bhikṣus were insufficient to adorn and glorify the world.

The World-Honored One then selected the sons of the noble Śākya clan—men who were both distinguished and in the prime of their youth—and sent one from every household, compelling them to leave the home life. Subsequently, they took turns bidding each other farewell as they departed.
The section on the father consists of two parts. First, the words of Nanda are clarified. Within the section on the father, there are four points: first, the entertainment of worldly customs;

second, mutual exhortation and yielding; third, the repeated refusal by Nanda; and fourth, because his affection for his son was so deep, he initially did not wish to part, hoping to spend the remainder of his life together, yet in the end he did not permit him to go.
Furthermore, death is not my concern; even if I wished to remain, I could not abandon this life, which is governed by my own karma.

How could one possibly permit such a separation? The four mothers offered their counsel to restrain [the Buddha’s] resolve. Next, regarding the section on Baddhi (Vāṣpa), there are five parts: first, the dialogue with Baddhi; second, the three exhortations and three refusals;
third, [the Buddha’s] insistence on his own practice; fourth, the inquiry into the reason for that insistence; fifth, the expression of his intent to exhort and take leave of his mother.
The ritual procedures are as before. Next, the honoring of the laity may be understood accordingly. Next, regarding those who gathered like clouds, he questioned Nanda and Baddhi.

The causal origins are fully set forth. Regarding the other six explanations: why did [the Buddha] suddenly come? According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, there were seven sons of the Śākyas who held one another in profound affection and esteem;
whatever they undertook, they vowed never to go against each other’s wishes. Thereupon, Aniruddha addressed King Bimbisāra, saying: "I now have a small request;
I pray that you will surely grant it. The King replied: "We originally made a pact that we would not go against one another. If we were to go against it..."
[If you do not comply], your head shall be split into seven pieces; however, I shall surely grant your wish. When Nanda first proposed this, Vimalakīrti did not consent;
but after raising the essential points and further exhorting him, they eventually did not disagree. Next, he informed the five [monks], who joyfully complied without opposition.

Then he proceeded to visit the four [kings]: first, leaving the city to approach them; second, renouncing their carriages and robes; third, abandoning their treasures to follow him; and fourth, all going together.

Homage. Next, the invitation is as in the text. Second, regarding leaving the household life and receiving the precepts, there are three parts within the text: first, leaving the household life and receiving the precepts;

second, cultivating the path and attaining realization; third, removing doubts and universally transforming others. When the Buddha delivered the five men, the other three had no affinity for him and were not delivered.
Furthermore, it was to stop slander that he did not deliver Devadatta and others. Question: Those delivered by the Buddha are all of the first fruit (*srotāpanna*). As [the text] says:
"How many times must this be done before one attains *adhipati*? The answer is: "The term *adhipati* refers to mastery (*abhijñā*). How could it be restricted to the first fruit alone?

Even when comparing the fourth [fruit] to the three preceding ones, all are *adhipati*. In the fivefold division, six types of persons exhaust their outflows and attain Arhatship; Ānanda served the Buddha."
Without having exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*), Devadatta alone was empty-handed and gained nothing. Having obtained nothing, his sense of shame deepened further.

He then went to where the Buddha was and requested that the Buddha teach him the methods for attaining supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*). The Buddha immediately taught them for him. Devadatta studied and mastered these powers during the retreat (*varṣā*).
He immediately attained supernatural powers (*abhijñā*).
Next, he transformed the Prince. Within this section, there are four parts: first, transforming him so that he conceived faith and gathered a following;

second, from "At that time" onwards, Maudgalyāyana reported Cāru’s words to the Buddha, and the Buddha revealed that those words were not true; third, from "At that time" onwards, [the transformation] was manifested once more.
Supernatural Powers (*ṛddhi*). Increasing Faith and Attaining Benefit. This section contains five parts: 1. Transforming the body and preaching the Dharma;

2. Increasing benefit, faith, and reverence; 3. Receiving beneficial offerings; 4. The bhikṣus address the Buddha; 5. The Buddha instructs them to collect their mindfulness. There are [sections on] the Dharma, the parable, and the application.
Regarding the four periods from Magadha down to the loss of powers at Tuḷi: seeking followers. This section contains four parts: 1. Envy toward the Buddha’s gravity...
[He] lost his supernatural powers (*abhijñā*). A "cauldron" (*bō*) is a name for a vessel; six *sheng* or four *sheng* is called a cauldron. First, he requested the assembly from the Buddha;

second, the Buddha rebuked him for not granting it; third, he gave rise to a mind of resentment; fourth, previously he had obtained external protection and increased his offerings, which was the height of his gratification;
now that he has lost his supernatural powers and is further rebuked, this is the extreme of his distress. For this reason...
He gave rise to a rebellious mind; therefore it is said that from the beginning he did not produce the mind of patience (*kṣānti*).
Next, regarding his plotting for a superior position, there are two parts in the text: first, the establishment of two chapters; second, the explanation according to those chapters.

Within the explanation, the killing of the Buddha is first addressed. This section contains three parts: first, the actual instigation of the harm; second, the disciples' desire to protect [the Buddha], as indicated by the passage "At that time, many..."; third, [the conclusion].

At that time, the World-Honored One told those below to assign a person to recount the events. The preceding section on "Harming by Words" has three parts: first, explaining the instigation of others;

second, from "Devadatta" onwards, correctly explaining the act of self-harm; third, from "At that time, the World-Honored One" onwards, responding to causes and reflecting on patience. The first part contains six sections: first, establishing the plot to kill the Buddha;
second, the Buddha’s recollection of past conditions, namely the matter of Māṇava Mātaṅga, as clarified in the text below; third...

Mindful of the harm, he did not go forward; setting aside his malice, he went to see him. The Four Noble Ones preached the Dharma of loving-kindness (*maitrī*). He obtained benefit and realized the Path.
In five stages, the lineage passed through thirty-two people, all of whom attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*). According to that text, these sixty-four also arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling.

Through the five teachings, they returned to their original path and refuted the previously established views. The six elders saw the original person, informed the Buddha, and he ordered them to be expelled. Next—
This clarifies self-harm; it was merely a wound to the toe. Among all other Buddha-kings, none have such a thing, yet I alone have this due to past karma involving the shedding of blood.
This deviates from the proper conduct of a Buddha, and therefore he declared it an unprecedented event (*abhūtapūrva*). Next, the thought of patience (*kṣānti*) accords with worldly law.
Next, regarding the four ways disciples protect the Dharma-texts: first, a bhikṣu protects the Buddha; second, the Buddha descends from his cave and engages in a dialogue concerning what...

1. By means of the three [points], the Buddha’s teaching below demonstrates superiority over all adversaries. 2. From "He addressed the bhikṣus" below, he enumerates the five things that must be protected;

the head does not need to be protected because it currently commits evil and subsequently undergoes the retribution of suffering; therefore, it is said: "Later, one shall know for oneself the precepts. This refers to the essence of what has been received.
Life is called "view," wisdom is called "understanding," and verbal expression is called "instruction. Because practice does not rely on instruction, there is the law and discipline (*vinaya*).

The five points of the lower section on the "external" [offenses] can be understood by reversing the explanation. Next, the four points regarding the text on "speaking of faults": first, being dispatched to speak of faults; second, presenting doubts for resolution;

third, receiving the command to manifest the fault, which—though not directed at the Buddha or the Sangha—also serves to manifest an evil reputation; this is the disciplinary punishment that, by being distantly applied, acts as a condition for liberation.
Fourth, clarifying the differences between what the great assembly endures and what they do not. Next is the explanation of the text on "killing. Text.
There are six points: first, receiving the instruction to harm the text; second, awakening to the realization of reality; third, a detailed evaluation and the imposition of punishment;

fourth, reporting the matter to the King to investigate the facts and issue a reprimand—although Devadatta had instructed the Prince to harm my Buddha-dharma, the treatment of such a person who proclaims evil is like a capital offense, yet no further penalty is added, hence it is said "it should not be done";
fifth, the command to pardon the transgression; sixth, the King’s dissatisfaction with the injustice.
Next, the section on separate eating consists of four parts: the transgression, the censure, the prohibition, and the subsequent performance of the schismatic act.

This latter section is divided into two: first, the arousal of the intent and the formulation of the plan; second, from "At that time Devadatta... onwards, the execution of the plan according to that intent. The former section contains five parts:

first, the inability to endure the prior prohibition and the arising of the thought to split the Saṃgha; second, from "At that time Devadatta... onwards, the exhortation and inducement through specific matters. I hope... [text ends].
They acted in concert. At the third stage, Devadatta’s subordinates feared that their undertaking would not succeed; they resisted and did not comply.
At the fourth stage, Devadatta’s subordinates established a true stratagem, hoping it would certainly be accomplished.

At the fifth stage, the three Śrutas and others manifested their heterodox capabilities and spoke words that were compliant and acceptable. The rest of the text is understandable. However, within the fourth section, it is divided into four parts.

1. Establishing the true nature of the conceptualization; 2. When speaking to those below, one should proclaim and reveal the plan; 3. Regarding the young ones below, what is broken, what is contrary, and what is compliant;
4. From this point downward, concluding the power of Māra. In the first section, the conceptualization is refuted as being like a phantom. To establish a self is the false Buddha;
the five aggregates are the false Dharma; and renunciation is the false Saṅgha. However, although the Buddha and Saṅgha have already recognized the false Dharma... [text continues]

Because it is known [as such]. Regarding the five things that emerge from below at the end of one's life, among these five "false" (*yā*) items, the first three are similar, while the latter two are false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*).
Therefore, the following text states: "The Saṃgha is split by two matters, namely, false speech and similar speech.

"Similar speech" refers to cases where the words agree but the meaning differs; "false speech" refers to acting according to one's own self-restraint. Alternatively, the first three may be understood as they appear in the text.
If one departs without having accepted the gift of a dwelling or other such things, departing without acceptance is likewise a false speech;

it is called "similar" because one departs from what was agreed upon. Regarding the latter two cases, if one departs from what has been accepted within the text, that too is "similar," because one departs from what was not accepted.

Therefore, it is called false speech. Salt and seasoning are combined into one category of "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*). Fish and meat involve the harming of living beings; thus, they are likewise grouped together as one.
As for the term "Elder" (*sthavira*), it refers to those who are aged and possess a thorough understanding of what is right and wrong. Thus, the *Abhidharmahṛdaya* (Third Chapter) states:

"Ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) are subject to regression, whereas noble ones (*ārya*) are not, because the latter possess the 'unbreakable purity' (*akopyaprasāda*) of the group of those fixed in rightness (*samyaktvaniyatarāśi*). Furthermore, it says that even ordinary persons who have attained "patience" (*kṣānti*) do not regress.
Having entered into certainty, the Noble Saṃgha is the World-Honored One’s indestructible retinue.
Next, the censure and admonition are clarified; first, the censure itself is distinguished. The text of the censure is divided into three parts: first, the bhikṣus address the Buddha;

second, from "The Buddha said" onwards, the correct teaching is explained while the erroneous is revealed; third, from "At that time, the World-Honored One" onwards, his own reproach is manifested. Question: [Regarding] the multitude...
"O Bhikṣu, why did you not rebuke him? He replied, "Because he was confused and deluded; since he did not understand, I saw no other way but to report it to the Buddha.
It may also be that he was apprehensive and did not dare to rebuke him rashly. The second section has three parts: first, a general statement of the desire to sever [the fault];
second, the presentation of the substance of what is to be severed; third, a summary of the desire to sever. The initial passage speaks of the five improper dharmas used for inducement.
Deceiving those who are newly trained, one causes them to practice what is false and extinguish what is right; this is precisely what is meant by "desiring to sever. Question:

Why are the five dharmas considered false and the four reliances considered right? Answer: The Buddha taught that because they possess four meanings, they are called "right": first, they are fundamental for the benefit of others.

What is spoken with a compassionate mind is not for the sake of seeking followers, fame, or profit. Second, by discerning the faculties and natures [of beings], one administers the medicine according to their capacity;

practicing in accordance with these instructions, they will surely attain the state of a sage. Third, by discerning the faculties and natures, one skillfully understands what is permitted and what is prohibited, enabling those of the three grades of persons to practice and progress in accordance with their respective faculties.
Fourth, by knowing the medicine for each faculty, one speaks in accordance with the Dharma, as stated in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*: "Four..."
The Noble Lineages (āryavaṃśa) enable one to attain the Eightfold Noble Path and realize the four fruits of śrāmaṇya. That which was taught by Devadatta is the opposite of these four meanings;

because it is not spoken according to reality, it is termed "false" (mithyā). First, it is governed by an evil mind, as he originally sought fame and profit, thus saying, "After our death, we shall obtain renown.

Second, he did not recognize the nature of the faculties (indriya), and thus there was no benefit for the long path. Third, he merely established prohibitions... [text ends]... without [further substance].
The benefits of opening [the path] are not complete. Fourth, they do not recognize the roots and medicines, and thus they speak erroneously and falsely.
Therefore, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* says: "The Eightfold Noble Path leads toward Nirvāṇa, yet it becomes slow and difficult; by practicing five dharmas to seek liberation, the path is very swift.

Next is the essence of what is to be abandoned. First there is the interrogation, followed by the explanation. Within the explanation, the first part relies on individual exposition, while the following three are clarified collectively. I—
"Those who should be regarded as equal" praises those of superior practice. Wearing rag-robes (*pāṃśukūla*), they have no further expectations regarding these garments;

therefore, it is said they "attain contentment. Next, those of middling and inferior capacity are addressed: when wearing robes given by donors (*dānapati*), they likewise eliminate attachment and stagnation;
therefore, it is said, "I also say," and so forth. The final three points may be understood by combining them for explanation. The conclusion follows the text. First.
Third, the reprimand. First, he asks for a confession; second, he formally reprimands him. Within the reprimand, there are three parts: namely, the introduction, the enumeration, and the conclusion.

Within the enumeration, there are three parts: first, the reprimand regarding the severance of conduct; second, from "For this reason" onwards, which demonstrates the certainty of the retribution; third, from "At that time, the World-Honored One... onwards.
The narrator of the sutra records this censure because it possesses some slight benefit. The initial passage consists of four points: First, the censure of their conduct; thus it says:

"Why do you teach the bhikṣus by means of five dharmas? as described above. Second, the censure of what they have abandoned; thus it says: "Do not abandon the four noble lineages," as described above.
Third, citing their previous conduct to demonstrate how it leads to the matter of schism; that is, it constitutes the abandonment of their previous conduct.
Therefore it is said: "Do not now employ means to cause a schism," and so forth. This fourth section cites what was previously abandoned and exhorts one not to abandon it;
that is, to practice what was previously abandoned. Hence it is said: "You should harmonize with the Sangha," and so forth. These constitute the first three phrases.

The two sets of four phrases following—criticizing the practice to bring about abandonment and criticizing the abandonment to bring about practice—are as follows. The remaining text may be understood accordingly. Next, the method of admonition is explained, divided into four parts.
1. The ritual procedure for a Buddhist bhikṣu to offer admonition. 2. The Saṃgha acts as the subordinate party; receiving the command, they perform the admonition. This should be explained in detail.
The rules for admonition are all set forth below in the section on defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), as it is convenient to clarify the meaning of the resulting offenses (*āpatti*) therein.
3. A bhikṣu informs the Buddha. 4. Consequently, the method of admonition is defined; it applies universally to all cases. However, Devadatta resisted the Saṃgha.

There ought to have been a formal reprimand; however, in order to establish the method of admonition, the *Śīlaskandha* (the core of the precepts) was formulated for the sake of comprehensive understanding. Consequently, neither the Buddha nor the Saṃgha issued a reprimand.
This applies not only to this particular rule, but also to other admonitions; even regarding violations of the summary [rules], there is no direct [reprimand] but rather a formal regulation.
By means of this extensive [explanation], one may understand that while the text may be violated, it is not overly complex in its interpretation.
Next, the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* (the root of the precepts) is explained. The *Prātimokṣa* consists of six sections: first, the person to whom the admonition is addressed;

second, from "desiring to cause schism" onwards, the matter for which the admonition is made; third, from "that bhikṣu" onwards, the method of private admonition; fourth, from "if that bhikṣu" onwards, the refusal of private admonition; fifth, from "that bhikṣu" onwards, the admonition by the Saṃgha;
sixth, from "if he does not relinquish [the position]" onwards, the determination of the offense. These six sections apply universally to all rules concerning admonition.
Next follows the detailed explanation. The text is divided into two parts: first, the explanation of the six phrases of the *Prātimokṣa* (Precept Text);

second, from "Having performed the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*" onwards, the clarification of the characteristics of light and heavy [offenses]. In the initial explanation, the first phrase is self-evident. Regarding the second point, the matters for which [the act] is performed, one first explains "the harmonious Saṃgha" (*saṃghasāmagra*).
This means that harmony is established through two factors: the assembly of four or more individuals, which explains the meaning of "Saṃgha," and the assembly being truly...
To translate *saṃgha* as "harmony" (*hehé*) is precisely the conventional usage within the monastic community; one must not universally use "harmonious assembly" (*héhé zhòng*) to translate *saṃgha*.
Next, the meaning of "breaking" (*huài*) is clarified. "Destruction" (*pò*) is a synonym for "breaking. There are four sections in the text: first, citing the number of breakings;

second, listing the names of the breakings; third, concluding the number of breakings; and fourth, assigning the matters of breaking. These eighteen dharmas all follow the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mātṛkā* (Duōlùn).
Third, the explanation. However, within the treatise, there are no [distinctions between] coarse and non-coarse;

rather, it establishes seven other pairs, fully clarifying dharma and non-dharma, and discipline (*vinaya*) and non-discipline, all based on the five factors and explained through the mutual relation of the eightfold path. Regarding what is called an offense but is not an offense:

if one does not shave the hair or clip the nails, the Buddha stated that one commits an offense; yet, regarding hair and nails, there is no offense when they possess life. Regarding what is called non-offense but is an offense: the *Vinaya*...
Regarding the precept on guarding speech while failing to restrain the mind: when the mind gives rise to the three poisons, this constitutes a violation of the precept.

An example of a light offense being treated as grave is that of the *Bhallaṭa* dragon; because he plucked a leaf from a tree, his sin was such that it could not be expiated. For this reason, it is said that killing plants and trees is entirely a grave offense.
Conversely, an example of a grave offense being treated as light is seen in the case of Sudarśana and others, whose prior actions did not constitute a grave offense.

He then said that acts such as sexual misconduct and theft are all minor offenses; those that entail a remainder (*sāvaśeṣa*)—namely, the four categories of precepts below [the *pārājika*]—are said to be without remainder when violated.

Furthermore, he claimed that those which are without remainder—the four grave offenses (*pārājika*)—are said to have a remainder when committed. This refers to what is called "coarse and evil" conduct.
Regarding the first two offenses and the two *ānantarya* (heinous) *sthūlātyaya*s, these are coarse and grave; yet they are described as not being coarse and grave.

As for those that are not coarse and grave—namely, the *pāyattika*s and other remaining *sthūlātyaya*s—they are described as being coarse and grave. Regarding "that which is always practiced" and "that which is not always practiced":

the eightfold *niyama* and the fivefold *dharma* are mutually explained as being established by rule (*prajñapti*). The five types of offenses proclaimed from the golden mouth [of the Buddha] are termed *niyama*. Thus it is said.
To claim that it is "not prescribed" means that these five matters were not uttered from the Golden Mouth; thus they are called "not prescribed.

To claim that what was not spoken is "prescribed" refers to the following: the four prohibitions are grave, while the remaining sections are light. This is the authentic teaching, and it is termed "that which was spoken."

To consider what is not the teaching as the teaching, or to explain the heavy and the light in reverse order—this is not the Buddha’s teaching; it is called "non-teaching," yet it is taken to be the teaching.

All subsequent passages concerning the eighteen factors are explained in this same manner and cannot be further clarified here. Next, regarding the third stage, the private admonition (*raho 'nuśāsanī*):

while the text mentions the fourfold assembly, in principle it should apply to all seven groups. Fourth, if one does not accept the advice, this constitutes a refusal of the private admonition. Question:

What offense does this incur? Answer: This violates the causes for the seven classes of practitioners and constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense). However, regarding the actual accomplishment of the act, there is a distinction between the preliminary offense (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and the completed offense (*niṣpanna-āpatti*).
The fifth [point], the monastic admonition, is as stated in the text. Regarding the sixth, if one does not relinquish [the position], the offense is established.

Taken together, these four *sthūlātyaya* offenses constitute a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. Within this, there are four major causal sequences, both superior and inferior: first, schism in the Saṃgha; second, violating the private admonition of a bhikṣu.

Third is to oppose the admonition of the great assembly, such as the *niḥsargika-pāyantikā* rules; fourth is to oppose the admonition of the *saṃgha*. These four causes correspond respectively to these four stages.
Regarding the attainment of the fruit, there are only two levels: the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* falls into the first category, while the remaining three belong to the second.
Thus, although the cause of the *pārājika* is posterior, its fruit is established first; whereas for the remaining three, although the cause is prior, the fruit is only realized later.
Next, the section on light and heavy [offenses] has two parts: first, regarding one's own actions; second, distinguishing those who instruct others. The former part further has two sections:

first, regarding the limits of the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual), clarifying the quantity of the karma; second, from "If all have not yet made the formal announcement" (*yadi sarveṣām na vijñaptam*) onwards, distinguishing the offenses of the preliminary preparations for the rite.

It varies according to the duration of time, up until before the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) has been performed; therefore, it is said that "all" [are included]. Next, there are three points regarding the instruction of others that should be understood:
one should maintain the perception of the Dharma (*dharmasaṃjñā*); as for those items not found in the text, they are omitted for brevity.

Next is the precept against assisting in the schism by refusing to heed admonition. Devadatta caused a schism in the Saṃgha; the assembly could not endure it. Since harmony had been lost, they united their minds to offer formal admonition.
While the Saṃgha was offering its formal admonition, his four companions assisted him like shadows. They subsequently offered their own admonitions as well, but he rejected them and would not comply;

hence, this is called the precept against assisting in a schism by refusing to heed admonition. It possesses six specific conditions: first, Devadatta adheres to false practices and proselytizes. Second...

The monks offer a formal admonition; thirdly, the Saṃgha offers a formal admonition, which assists in the accomplishment of a schism. Fourthly, the Saṃgha immediately admonishes him; fifthly, he refuses and does not comply;
sixthly, the three *karmavācanās* are completed. Regarding the deficiency of conditions, it is to be known through comparison with the two preceding texts.
The preceding text has three parts: first, citing Devadatta’s adherence to heterodox views and his breaking of the community; second, the monks’ admonition in accordance with the Dharma.

Exhortation. Third, the "Correct Shadow" (samyak-chāyā) assists as the object of the admonition. Next, the category of "Reproachful Admonition" is understood. The root of the precept consists of six phrases:
first, the enumeration of companions for the purpose of the admonition; second, clarifying the characteristics of the assisting companions regarding the matter for which the admonition is intended.

Within this section, there are two parts: first, a preliminary prohibition against the Saṃgha admonishing; second, from the words "This bhikṣu... onwards, the explanation of the intent behind the exhortation. The reason for this is...
"Exhortation" means acting in accordance with the Dharma for the sake of others; therefore, within these four phrases, the first two clarify the person.

For example, when Devadatta speaks, he does so according to a proper method, hence it is called "Dharma-speech. Furthermore, because he can eliminate evil and give rise to goodness, it is termed "Vinaya-speech. The subsequent two phrases concern the Dharma:
because this Dharma can harmonize us and we rejoice at hearing what we have encountered, it is called "joyful"; because it accords with principle, it is called "righteous."

To remain at ease and compliant is called "acceptance" (*kṣānti*). Next, the text for the private admonition consists of four parts: first, a general enumeration of the person and the dharma, which together preclude any external support;
second, from "Now, this bhikṣu... onwards, which specifically reveals the fault of the person, while the fault of the dharma is omitted as it is considered minor.
Below "The Three Great Virtuous Ones," his intent in offering the admonition is expressed. Below "The Four Great Virtuous Ones," the benefit of harmony is revealed.

The remaining phrases are understandable; a detailed explanation is provided in full. The first phrase consists of three parts: (1) regarding the meaning of "bhikṣu" as described above, this refers precisely to the person being admonished;
(2) "by means of compliance" explains the meaning of "companionship"; there are two kinds of compliance, both of which necessitate the offering of an admonition; (3) clarifying the companions.
When a faction of countless individuals collectively initiates a plot and devises a scheme, it is termed a "factional alliance" (*gaṇa-saṃghāta*).

When four or more persons are involved, it first constitutes a *saṃgha*. As for other groups, they are termed "auxiliary associates," referring to those ranging from a single individual up to a multitude;
even when there is no second faction, all must be admonished. The remaining text follows the previous [rules].
Next is the precept against slandering the Saṃgha and violating their admonitions; there are six distinct points. First, the meaning of "allowing [the monks] to rely on a village":

this means that for a bhikṣu to advance on the Path, he must rely on material support, and furthermore, it is appropriate for laypeople to cultivate meritorious deeds. Second, not allowing [the monks] to defile the household.

Listen with a mind free from malice. Based on the original matter concerning the village, [the monks] intended to benefit both themselves and others; yet now they have destroyed the public's faith and instead caused harm to both sides. Third, regarding the intention to expel them:

they have violated the teachings and corrupted their conduct, as evidenced by what has been seen and heard. If they are not expelled and disciplined, there will be no means for them to reform their past ways.

Fourth, regarding the intention to clear the charge of slandering the Saṃgha: among the six individuals who share the same fault, if the four were not disciplined, it would be said that the Saṃgha had accepted the hatred; therefore, they are expelled.

Regarding "I, two": the intent behind the five admonitions set forth is the same as for those with faults; thus, one merely disciplines two individuals. This appears to involve favoritism or aversion, and therefore requires the Saṃgha to issue the admonition.

The sixth point, concerning the formation of the offense, is as explained previously. Next, to explain the names: because one relies on power and wealth to damage the faith of the laity, it is called "defiling the family" (*kuladūṣaka*).
Because one's actions are defiled and turbid, capable of inducing foul retributions, they are termed "evil conduct" (*duścarita*). There are distinct conditions [for these offenses].

Seven [factors]: first, defiling the household; second, harboring an evil mind and failing to reform or repent; third, performing the act of banishment (*pravāsanīya-karman*); fourth, slanderously accusing the Saṃgha in an irrational manner;

fifth, the formal admonition being carried out according to the Dharma; sixth, refusing to comply; seventh, the completion of the three *karmavācanas*. If the middle and initial factors are entirely absent, there is no offense.

If only the second factor—defiling the household and so forth—is present, it is equivalent to the case where the third and fourth factors are absent (i.e., the offense is established). If the third and fourth factors are absent, it is the same as the case where the second factor is absent (i.e., no offense).

Regarding the omission of five [factors], it refers to the falling away from the seven [precepts] and the non-[performance of] the seven guest offenses (*pācittiya*). If six or seven factors are omitted, the meaning may be inferred accordingly.

Next, the text is explained: among the four matters regarding the object of admonition, the first is "engaging in evil conduct," while that which constitutes "defiling the family" is discussed within the section on defining the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

2. Explaining the reprimand. 3. From "He addressed Śāriputra" onwards, the formal act of banishment (*pravāsanīya-karman*). 4. At that time, from "Aśvajit... onwards, the irrational slander of the Saṃgha.
Within the section on banishment, there are two parts: first, establishing the method of banishment and entrusting it to Śāriputra;

second, from "Śāriputra... onwards, carrying out the punishment by imperial command. Within this [second part], there are six sections: 1. Leading his followers to the *Kālāma* village; 2. At that time, from "Aśvajit... onwards, seeking him out...

1. External protection. [The section] from "At the third period, the śarīra... onwards concerns the brief transformation through begging. 2. At the fourth period, from "Various [monks]... onwards, it concerns receiving the teaching and then slandering it. 3. At the fifth period, from "The śarīra...

onwards, it concerns subduing [the slanderer] so that faith arises. 4. At the sixth period, from "The Venerable... onwards, it concerns formal disciplinary action through banishment. Regarding the slander of the Saṃgha, it follows the text;
Śāriputra himself was slandered by another, yet there was no rebuke. One should simply report the matter of the slander in full to the World-Honored One. Next...
The reprimand and admonition are as stated in the text. The six phrases of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* are as before. Regarding the second [part], the object of the admonition, there are three points:
first, the arising of transgressions based on a specific situation, whereby both self and others are ruined; those who are close are "seen," while those who are distant are "heard.
Second, from the words "all bhikṣus" onwards, the transgression is cited and the offender is expelled. Third, from the words "those bhikṣus" onwards, it concerns groundless slander.
The Sangha: Because Dharmadinnā heard that Kālodayin was a member of the faction that refused to repent, yet they did not discipline him, he was called "one who has attachment.
Because Sundarika-Nandaka fled to the village of Rājagṛha out of fear that he would not be disciplined, he was called "one who has fear.
Only my two [disciples] were called "those who have anger. I observe that the Sangha is upholding this act of suspension (*pravāsanīya-karman*); it is not [otherwise].

This is because it is understood as being done by the mind; therefore, it is said that "there is delusion. The passage beginning with "In this way, they commit the same offense" and continuing down to "the bhikṣus" reveals the intent of the slander.
Next, the private admonition also consists of three parts: first, to exhort them not to listen to the slander of the Saṃgha, hence the words "Do not speak such words," and so forth;

second, from "But those bhikṣus... onwards, clarifying that the Saṃgha clears itself; and third, regarding those who repent before the assembly, since there is no offense to be punished, it is called "not being partial."

The fugitive does not appear; furthermore, it is not appropriate to treat him [as a fugitive]. This is called "not being afraid. You two, however, advance without confessing and retreat without fleeing.
Your faults are both manifest, which precisely warrants disciplinary action; therefore, it is said "not being angry. Nevertheless, the Sangha understands this well.
The method of formal exclusion (nissaya) is called "not insane. Regarding the phrase "the three great virtuous ones who defile families," the fault is attributed to them.

The remainder of the text is understandable. In the commentary, the first person may be known [from context]. Second, the text concerning the purpose has three parts: first, explaining the dwelling place upon which a bhikṣu relies.
Although the word "village" does not appear in the Prātimokṣa itself, cities and market towns are collectively designated as "villages. Second...

This clarifies the evil conduct that defiles a family. Herein, first the family is clarified, followed by the explanation of its defilement. Now, the text concerning the defilement of the family has four parts:
first, a general enumeration of the four; second, a listing of the four names; third, a detailed explanation of each one starting with "How so..."; and fourth, a summary starting with "By this...".
Next, the evil conduct can be understood. Third, from "If a bhikṣu... onwards, it clarifies the spreading of a foul reputation. Next is the private admonition.
The same as before.

Next is the precept concerning being of a bad character and defying admonition. The specific meaning is as follows: A foolish person of bad character acts according to his own whims and commits transgressions;

lacking respect for his teachers, he opposes everyone in every matter. When virtuous people attempt to enlighten him with the Dharma, he instead treats them with contempt and insults, refusing to accept their counsel.
The instructor said: "The Buddha is my family; the Buddha-dharma is my family dharma. I ought to instruct the Venerable Ones;
the Venerable Ones should not, in turn, instruct me. When he spoke these words, his partiality seemed justified. The Saṃgha must offer him admonition to clarify right from wrong.

Once right and wrong are distinguished, it is appropriate to follow the principle. If he remains obstinate and refuses to relinquish his position, he is to be charged with a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. [This case is] distinct.

The conditions are sixfold: first, impurity of body and speech through the repeated violation of the precepts; second, the admonition and exhortation by virtuous bhikṣus in accordance with the Dharma;

third, regarding those whom one regards as teachers, one does not accept their instruction; fourth, the Saṃgha offers admonition; fifth, one rejects it and does not comply; sixth, three factors are fulfilled.
Next, the explanation of the text regarding the matter for which the admonition is made has three parts: first, clarifying the refusal to accept words.
Second, the two analogies and their application; third, from "Therefore" onwards, the conclusion regarding the intent to reject counsel. In the first section concerning the observance of precepts:

to act in accordance with principle is called "good," while to violate the precepts and contravene principle is called "evil. Regarding these "good" and "evil," [the opponent] says, "Cease speaking to me; I shall instruct the various Venerable Ones.
This is an instance of relying on superior persons to bolster oneself and to treat others with contempt. As for the passage beginning "Why is this?", it explains the refusal to accept counsel.

[The] meaning. Next, regarding the two similes: water is a metaphor for the teaching (*śāsana*), and wind is a metaphor for practicing the teaching. [The teaching] has the benefit of moistening, just like water;

practicing [the teaching] has the capacity for far-reaching transformation, analogous to wind. The subsequent conclusion may be understood as before. The admonition through reproach is according to the text.
The six phrases of the *Prātimokṣa* are as previously stated. Within the section concerning the matter at hand, there are three parts: first, clarifying that one is of a bad character and does not...
1. Receiving the words of others. 2. Regarding the precepts and the Dharma: various virtuous bhikṣus admonish and exhort him in accordance with the Dharma.

3. Regarding himself: he rejects the admonition and does not comply. The text on private admonition has two parts: first, admonishing the person before them so that they may mutually receive the words; second, "In this way," and so forth.

This clarifies the benefit of admonishing. The remaining text may be understood accordingly; it is explained in detail in the full version of the scripture. When admonishing in private, each accepts the words of the other.
Because one advances toward the roots of the Path, it is called "augmentation" (*vṛddhi*). Training others with wholesome dharmas is termed "mutual instruction" (*saṃśikṣaṇa*).

Preventing future transgressions is referred to as "mutual admonition" (*saṃcodana*). Eradicating what has already arisen is thus called "repentance" (*pratideśanā*). Each acts for the sake of the other, and these are all termed "reciprocal" (*paryāya*). This occurs frequently.
Treatise IV. Question: The sūtras state that one should simply observe one’s own bodily conduct and clearly discern what is wholesome and unwholesome;

how is it that the present statement, which speaks of mutual instruction, does not contradict this? Answer: The Buddha established his teachings according to the specific circumstances of the time; thus, while the words may differ, their intent is consistent and they do not conflict.
Because people of former times possessed hearts of attachment and aversion, frequent speaking was detrimental; for this reason, he said, "One should simply observe oneself."

Regarding bodily conduct: if one possesses a compassionate mind and it would be beneficial, one should instruct others accordingly. Furthermore, it is explained that if one is of dull faculties and lacks wisdom, speaking will be of no benefit;
therefore, it is said that one should simply observe oneself. However, if one listens with wisdom and possesses sharp faculties, speaking will be beneficial;
thus, it says they should "instruct one another. The remainder of the text is understandable. The section on *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (Saṅghādisesa) is hereby concluded.

● Next, the indeterminate [offenses] are explained. First, a general summary is provided; second, they are analyzed through six gates. First, the definition of "indeterminate" is explained. Second, the substance of what is prevented is distinguished.
Third, the location where they are placed is established. Fourth, the determination of the offense is made regarding the first two [categories].
Fifth, the universality or restriction of persons and locations is discussed. Sixth, the presence or absence of these offenses for monks and nuns is examined.

Regarding the explanation of the name: although "credible" (*āpatti*) is mentioned, the specific name of the offense is not identified. Since the Saṃgha has not yet determined which [offense] it is, it is called "undetermined.
Furthermore, because the establishment of this precept serves as a general defense against various offenses rather than targeting one specifically, it is named "undetermined.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* (Ten Recitations), fascicle 4, asks: "What is meant by 'undetermined'?"

A trustworthy female lay follower (upāsikā) does not know whether an offense has been committed; she does not know whether it occurred in a secluded place or in public; she does not know the name of the offense.
She merely says, "I saw a woman coming and going from that place; I also saw a bhikṣu coming and going, sitting, or standing there, but I did not see him [doing anything].
Whether he engaged in sexual intercourse, committed theft, took a human life, or touched the body of a woman—if [she says this]...
Cutting down grass and trees, eating after midday, or drinking alcohol—in such matters, because [the offense] is not fixed, they are called "indeterminate" (aniyata).
This term "indeterminate" contains four meanings in its scope: first, the indeterminate offense.

Although it is fixed with respect to the actual act committed, it is called "indeterminate" because the specific category—such as *pārājika* and so forth—is not yet determined. Although two or three cases are cited in the text, the principle...

It applies to both the sixth and seventh [categories]. Second, the indefinite (aniyata) is raised; the noble woman does not recognize the name or the category, but simply reports the matter as it occurred to the Buddha.

Third, the indefinite by self-accusation, which refers to claims of being a *bhikṣuṇī* and so forth, or claims of non-offense. Fourth, the indefinite regarding the punishment, which refers to acts such as banishment (*pravāsanīya*) or concealment (*pārājika*).
If one remains entirely silent, the place of the offense is assigned. Furthermore, regarding the mention of "two," this refers to the private and the public. Although within this...

These encompass seven offenses, yet the number is insufficient; they merely include those precepts concerning defilement and the inciting of censure, such as the offense of a monk who persists despite being admonished.

Since these are not found among the *aniyata* (undetermined) rules, the *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā-śāstra* states: "These two undetermined cases resemble the original meaning of the Vinaya; because their number is small, they cannot be [included].
This is just like the original meaning of the *vibhaṅga* (sections of the Vinaya): this is concise while that is detailed. If one can lead the concise into the detailed...
"Extensive" means that one correlates offenses of the indeterminate category with the *pien-chu* (the formal categories of the Prātimokṣa), or includes the extensive within the concise;
or that one correlates offenses within the *pien-chu* with the indeterminate, thereby drawing the concise into the extensive and subsuming the extensive under the concise.
Such a person is then clear and proficient regarding the Vinaya.

Next, regarding the nature of what is to be prevented: the ancient commentary states that this refers to cases where a trustworthy woman brings a matter to the attention of the Saṃgha concerning two locations and four modes of deportment.

Once the Saṃgha has heard it, they must investigate thoroughly. Among the twenty-eight instances of concealment within the four modes of deportment—seven for each—and the twenty-four instances of exposure, if the truth has not yet been established, this constitutes the offense to be prevented;
there is no separate formal name for the transgression, as it is categorized under the "separation from defilement" (li-ran).
It is pure. It does not abide in two places; walking, standing, sitting, and staying—these are the practices that can counteract [defilements].

If this is so, are the three offenses and the two offenses not indeed called "offenses"? Answer: These are matters to be examined. If their reality has not yet been realized, they are subsumed under the indeterminate.

The *niyata* (definite) offenses correspond to the categories of the *śīla-skandha*; they are not included here. What is clarified now is the regulation requiring examination and scrutiny. Since these are called "indefinite" (*aniyata*), how could there be a fixed offense?
Although various masters of the past and present who valued the precepts were each sagely in their wisdom, they contemplated and attempted to explain what these rules prevent;

yet, because there was no actual case [to serve as a precedent], the underlying intent was difficult to perceive. Now, by recounting the ancient chapters, one interpretation will perhaps approach the truth.
The principle is as follows. Other commentaries are numerous; I cannot cite them all extensively. It may also be explained further: one simply takes what is credible.

Regarding the case where one does not recognize the names and categories of the Saṃgha, nor knows for certain which specific [offense] has been committed—this state, wherein one has not yet attained certainty regarding the matter in between, is called "uncertainty.
Yet this bhikṣu, with a mind intent on denial and concealment, does not cite the actual facts. This is the fault to be guarded against. Thus it is composed.

The "Heart of Truthful Speech" (*Satyavāda-hṛdaya*) states that inducing [confession] in accordance with the teachings is a practice capable of remedying transgressions. Furthermore, it explains that within this context, the purpose is merely to examine whether a bhikṣu recognizes his offense or not;

originally, there was no fault. This is like the case of receiving the precepts at an age less than required: after receiving them, doubt arises, and the rule is opened by counting from the time of conception and so forth to determine whether an offense was committed.
It is not the case that the offense is first established at the moment the rule is opened; this case is likewise. It is not...

Although there are many interpretations, once a bhikṣu has committed an offense, it is already established as a fact. Because the circumstances may be difficult to discern, the rule was established to require thorough investigation.

While the investigation has not yet reached the truth, the case is subsumed under the category of "indeterminate" (aniyata). Once the investigation confirms the facts, it is then categorized as "definite" (niyata). Why, then, is it necessary here to clarify the essential nature of what is being prohibited?
Next, regarding the clarification of the "locations" (*sthāna*): It is asked, "These two indeterminate [factors] are the causes of all offenses and are capable of giving rise to all offenses;

since they do not exceed the categories of 'secluded' or 'exposed,' this principle should have been explained at the beginning, or alternatively, they should be placed below the section on the determination of offenses. Answer: They are indeterminate.
If it were placed at the beginning, then even a minor offense of *tīkṣṇa* would rank above a grave offense of *pārājika*.

Alternatively, if it were placed below the determination of offenses, then a grave offense of *pārājika* would fall beneath a minor offense of *dukkaṭa*. In such cases, the logical sequence would be severed, and the gravity of the offenses could not be balanced.
Therefore, it cannot be placed either at the beginning or at the end; thus, we shall now discuss the five categories of offenses in their entirety.
They are capable of counteracting [faults] and all possess the quality of preventing what is non-virtuous; thus, they are collectively termed "precepts" (*śīla*).

Therefore, regarding the various precepts, it is said that the first violation of a precept—when based on the five categories of offenses—refers to the physical and verbal conduct and movements, all of which possess formal rules; these are collectively called "dignified deportment" (*īryāpatha*). Thus, regarding the various precepts, it is said that there are those such as "non-dignified deportment" (*anairyāpathika*) and so forth.

Now, for the time being, we shall divide them into two according to their stages: the former two involve coarse transgressions, and because they are capable of prevention, they are termed "precepts"; the latter three...
The offenses are subtle. Their practice is termed "dignified deportment" (*īryāpatha*). Placing them below the precepts (*śīla*) and above deportment serves to manifest their reliability.

Taking the seven groups of five [offenses] as a general category, those above are subsumed under the precepts, while those below are encompassed by deportment; thus, their meaning and scope are positioned in the middle.

For this reason, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* records that Upāli asked about the reliable [monks], citing the four lower categories of offenses which may fall within the indeterminate class (*aniyata*), and how they are to be disciplined. It is not the Buddha [who establishes this].

It is said that they have attained it. Next, the first two [categories] are clarified. The former interpretation was indeterminate; this refers to the second person. This is because the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* states:

"As with the *upāsikā*, the treatment is again indeterminate. There is no absence of the initial [precept]; having opened up the five [precepts], the indeterminate ones are excluded. They do not enter into the category of one who has committed a transgression against the *Prātimokṣa*. There is none.

Below the section on the "Methods for Punishing Offenses" (*Āpatti-vinaya*), there is the "Initial Opening of Quiescence. If so, what is the origin (*nidāna*)? There is the "Initial Transgression" (*ādi-prayoga*). The answer is: while the names are the same, the meanings differ;
the various chapters (*varga*) are concise in their violations, whereas here the offenses are detailed. Because the locations (*sthāna*) are distinct, each constitutes an initial transgression.

It is said that the five chapters (*pañca-varga*) were established extensively to supplement the concise [rules]. Thus, the initial [rules] here are not fixed; the general details supplement the five, and the specific details supplement the first five.

In this treatise, the rules are established separately according to specific matters; because it is difficult to address each matter individually, the rules are formulated concisely for general locations and extensively for specific ones, such that each individual case obtains its initial [classification].
However, my current interpretation is not so. If one were to establish the "initial" based on the three or two offenses being examined, how could that possibly be the second?
Since those offenses have all been defined from the beginning, it is clear that this attainment of the actual [offense] corresponds to the second [category].

If one examines this matter thoroughly, and the thorough examination has not yet resulted in a formal designation, then this very process of thorough examination constitutes the first stage for that person.
Because there had been no prior transgressions in contrast to this, the text states that it is the "first" transgression of the precepts; thus, these are the first two.

If one considers them among the transgressions, their essential natures are already different and they are categorically distinct. Question: This refers to a first-time offender; why is there no exemption? Answer:
This concerns a thorough investigation, which must result in the ascertainment of the facts. Since the facts have not yet been established, there is therefore no exemption.

Furthermore, another interpretation holds that there should be cases such as those in the *Sudarsana-vinaya*, where there is no offense for a first-time offender, as well as for those who are insane and so forth. The absence of such a passage here is merely an omission.

Next, regarding the scope and limitations of the human status (*pudgala-sthāna*): there are four categories of persons, namely the two classes of monastics (monks and nuns) and the two classes of laypeople (men and women). It is not yet known whether this is indeterminate;

it refers specifically to the laywoman (*upāsikā*). Does she also have access [to ordination]? Regarding the three positions of monks and so forth, one must understand the two positions of monks and nuns, as well as their essential nature, consciousness, names, and categories.
Furthermore, because they share the same path, there is no uncertainty. Moreover, when monks and nuns raise charges against others, this applies universally to both ordinary persons and sages;

however, it merely requires verification of the three roots, as the presence or absence [of these roots] is not explicitly revealed. This matter of investigation is entirely different from that of this secular woman.
For this reason, the case of monks and nuns does not hold. However, as for secular men, the principle likewise permits it; one may rely on the text, which allows only for the hearing of sages.

Regarding women: when brought forward by a layman, they are not subject to exhaustive investigation. Since the secular principle is the same, both women and men are permitted [to testify]. This is like the case of slandering someone:
even if one relies on Trapusa as the basis for the offense, those who do not understand monastic affairs still incur the offense of slander.

There are three locations [where this applies]: namely, the locations of the Saṃgha, nuns, and laypeople. If one adheres strictly to the literal text, it refers only to lay locations; however, if one applies the meaning broadly, it also encompasses [the other two].

There are two locations for monks and nuns. If one considers these locations, when both the noble and the secular are brought forward, how could it be that the residences of monks and nuns are not subject to thorough inspection?
If they must indeed be inspected, why would the principle not apply here as well? Furthermore, some have established an additional category that is not among the three mentioned above:

the "secluded place" (*praticchanna-sthāna*) apart from seeing and hearing. Yet this secluded place is not distinct from the preceding three; it cannot be found in the texts, and even if one were to speak of it separately, it would still be included within them.

The explanation is as in the text and need not be elaborated further. To speak again of the locations of obstruction: since the locations of obstruction should likewise be separated from the explanation of the obstructions themselves, and they are not distinct from the screened locations, why should they be explained separately with such prolixity?

Regarding the presence or absence of monks and nuns [in the act of accusing]: the traditional interpretation states that the Buddha established the rule for accusing of offenses such that the two assemblies, male and female, must mutually oversee one another and expose faults;
there must be no place where offenses are committed without being exposed. Thus, if a member of the great assembly (bhikṣu-saṃgha) commits an offense, others must likewise expose the fault together.

If a member of the female assembly sees it, she too must expose and report it. However, because a *śrāmaṇerī* disciple fears violating the respect due to her teacher, she is not permitted to expose the teacher. This is...

A trustworthy laywoman may raise a charge against a nun. This is because laywomen and noble women (āryikā) often find the truth easily, and since they do not know [the nuns'] names or lineages, discrepancies may arise;
thus, there are two *aniyata* rules for bhikṣus. If a nun commits an offense, both the male and female monastic communities may raise the charge.
Since the purpose of raising the charge is already fulfilled, why would a layman be required to replace the Sangha in raising a charge against a nun? There is no such *aniyata* rule.

Therefore, there is no uncertainty. This may indeed be so. Furthermore, there is another point: that for a nun, there is no case of "uncertainty" (aniyata), because she is prohibited from having a companion.

That is to say, if a monk who has been subject to formal suspension (*ukkhepaniya-kamma*) is permitted to have a companion or not—if one says he has no companion, he must first be dealt with for the offense committed alone.

Fearing that he might treat [the offense] alone, one should then bring along companions; since the companions provide stability, there may also be no offense. Thus, whether one advances or retreats, there is an impediment, and therefore there is no "indeterminate" case.
Furthermore, another interpretation is that this concerns monks and nuns whose presence or absence differs; as for the bhikṣu, it is because he has a specific reason [to be absent].

There are cases where a bhikṣuṇī acts without cause; therefore, no formal rule was established for her. She should not go out [to meet him], yet the Sage’s intention cannot be grasped by merely comparing matters through superficial analogies.
For instance, regarding the four subsequent admonitions for bhikṣuṇīs that result in *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses: why does a bhikṣu not incur an offense when performing the same act?

One should simply understand the presence or absence, and the lightness or gravity, of these matters, for such is the nature of the prohibitive rules of the Vinaya. There is no need for further elaborate analysis.
Next, the text is explained below. According to the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, it was established for four reasons: first, to stop slander; second, to eliminate strife and contention;
third, to increase the sublime Dharma; and fourth, because a bhikṣu who has left the household life follows a path distinct from the secular world and is thus revered by humans and devas.
To transform beings through the Way, yet to be in private with a woman involves private, crooked, and base conduct;

above, it violates the intent of the Sage, and below, it causes one to lose the faith, respect, and devotion of humans and devas. Fourth, it is for the sake of the sequential method for severing evil karma:

having first been in a private place, one gradually becomes entangled and obsessed until there is no improper act one does not commit; therefore, this is prohibited. The initial explanation of the name is as stated above. Regarding the specific conditions, there are...
Six conditions: first, a secluded place; second, a woman; third, no third person present; fourth, speaking what is not the truth regarding an actual fact;

fifth, reporting it to the Saṃgha as being credible; sixth, investigating but not yet having obtained the facts. When these six conditions are complete, it is subsumed under the *aniyata* (undetermined) offenses.

The same applies to the lower [offenses], with the sole difference that they occur in an open place. Deficient conditions may be inferred accordingly. The origin stories (*nidāna*) can be understood from this. The root text of the precepts consists of five phrases.

1. One person. 2. An indeterminate offense. 3. Regarding those who abide in faith and below, the raising [of the charge] is indeterminate. 4. Regarding those seated below, self-accusation is indeterminate. 5.
As with those abiding in faith and below, the adjudication of the offense is indeterminate; this is explained in detail within the full commentary on the second offense.

The text contains six phrases which are understandable. Regarding "faithful and joyful" and below, this explains the third phrase. In the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, one who is "trustworthy" is one who perceives the Four Truths.
Truthfully. Not for the sake of oneself, not for the sake of others, and not for the sake of profit, one utters false speech.

As for the phrase "if a bhikṣu," the fourth line is explained below. This self-assertion consists of five lines; ancient masters applied these to the five categories of offenses, stating that the first is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing), and so on, up to the fifth, which is a *pārājika* (defeat).
Furthermore, an old commentary states: "The destination toward which one’s own words are directed is the course of action (*caryā*)."

Regarding the deportments (*īryāpatha*): "arriving," "standing," "sitting," "sitting and lying," and "lying"—these constitute the seven types of secluded actions. When categorized according to the four deportments, there are twenty-eight offenses revealed;

however, excluding those involving *pārājika*, there are only twenty-four. Now, in explaining these seven offenses, although their meaning is comprehensive, it is not appropriate to restrict them to specific textual passages.
Furthermore, there is no need to fully manifest the details of the deportments here; logically, such an endeavor would be unnecessary. Thus, [the text] does not point them out.

The phrasing is appropriate. However, these five phrases explain only the three offenses based on the *Prātimokṣa* (Sūtra of Fundamental Precepts). The reason for this is known because the subsequent precepts do not include the *pārājika* (defeat);
thus, their specific actions are excluded here. This refers to what one intends to go toward, the place one approaches, and the place where one stays.

To sit there constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense), or it may also include the act of going toward that place, which likewise incurs a *sthūlātyaya*. To lie down there constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (offense requiring a formal meeting of the community). Thus it is performed.
"This is a *pārājika*. Next, from "If a bhikṣu... onwards, the fifth phrase explains that the punishment for an offense is not fixed.

Although within these five phrases there may be cases where the grounds for establishing the offense are cited or not cited, the location where the offense is established should indeed be fixed; however, regarding the actual administration of the punishment, it may be a *pārājika* or otherwise.

Since offenses such as *śaikṣa* and *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* are treated according to the circumstances, they are called "indeterminate" (*aniyata*). The same applies to the lower precepts; there is no need for a separate explanation. This concludes the section on the Indeterminate Offenses.
*The Record of the Opening of the Sects of the Four-Part Vinaya*, Fascicle Three, Part One.
*The Record of the Opening of the Sects of the Four-Part Vinaya*, Volume Three, Part Two.
Next, the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses are explained. These are analyzed by means of four topical gates. First, the explanation of the names of the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses.

Second is the sequence of priority; third is the comparative determination of the nine and ten [categories]; fourth is the formal exposition of the thirty. Regarding the first, the explanation of the names:
in Sanskrit it is called *niḥsargika* (translated here as "to be relinquished"). The ancient masters, relying on many interpretations, state that "relinquishment" (*śe*) has three meanings:

first, the relinquishing of material objects; second, the relinquishing of the continuous covetous mind; and third, the simultaneous relinquishing of both object and mind. Therefore, they follow this order.
Third, one is able to abandon the offense. Now, to explain: the treatise does not contain these three meanings. The main text relies on principle;

it is called "abandoning" (*prāyaścitta*) simply because one abandons the material object. If "abandoning" were defined by the abandonment of the mental offense, then a *pāyattika* (offense of simple transgression) would also have to be called "abandoning," since within a *pāyattika* one likewise abandons the mental offense.
That it is termed a "fall" (*pāyattika*) will be clarified below. Therefore, it is said:

Regarding the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* rules, as for their sequential order—namely, the thirty-ninth and the fortieth—their natures as offenses are equal; thus they are combined into a single transgression. This interpretation is reasonable.

First, the thirty [offenses] are explained, followed by the analysis of the ninety. The answer is that these thirty precepts originally arise from material wealth (*āmiṣa*). If one wishes to repent and eliminate them, one must first cut off the root;
therefore, it is necessary to face the proper object (*viṣaya*) and first relinquish the excessive wealth. Once the excessive wealth has been relinquished, the offense can then be repented.

Because of this requirement for relinquishment, the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*) is difficult. For the ninety [offenses], since there is no relinquishing of wealth, the ritual procedure is easy. If one desires...
This causes the monastics and nuns to first recognize what is difficult and later understand what is easy;

the sequence is thus. Next, regarding the resolution: ancient commentaries state that all who enter into renunciation (*naiḥsargika*) possess three characteristics: first, it must be property belonging to oneself;
second, the substance of the property must be currently present and its use constitutes an offense; third, once renounced, it must be returned to its owner for use.

There is no fault [in using it]. However, the present interpretation is not so; rather, it is because one has not relinquished [the object] that using wealth constitutes an offense. Once the ritual act of relinquishment (*prahāṇa*) is completed, there is no fault in using it.
For this reason, it enters into the category of "relinquishment" (*niḥsargika-pāyattika*), and the other two categories are not required.

Although among the ninety offenses below there are those arising from wealth, even if these are relinquished, using them still incurs an offense. Therefore, they remain within the ninety offenses and do not enter the thirty [offenses of wrong-doing].

Next, the thirty [rules] are explained. First, a general explanation of the tenfold classification: first, identifying those who can commit an offense; second, assigning [the offenses] to body and speech; third, acting on one’s own behalf or instructing others;
fourth, the distinction between prohibitive (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*) and natural (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) offenses; fifth, the procedures for maintaining and violating the precepts;
sixth, the intent behind the two questions; seventh, whether a repeated offense constitutes a grave offense; eighth, the ritual for relinquishing and repenting [the offense]. Ninth... [etc.]
9. The similarities and differences between the two sections. 10. The spontaneous application for the lower assembly.
