Regarding the reason why the first gate specifically identifies the person who commits the offense: because the subsequent text mentions three types of persons who commit *naiḥsargika* offenses, it is necessary here to establish this definitively.
Now, among these three positions, one person universally commits many offenses, some of which are offenses against the Saṃgha and some of which are not. For now...

Within the monastic community (*saṃgha*), there is the "present before the four directions" (*cāturdiśa-saṃmukha*). This *saṃgha* of the four directions is entirely non-offensive (*anāpatti*), because the objects belong to the assembly as a whole and no individual has a share.
Therefore, the subsequent text states: "When the robes of the assembly have passed ten days, the Buddha said there is no offense regarding what is present."

If those who occupy four or more positions and act collectively are designated as the *saṃgha*, then all the precepts would be simultaneously violated by them, because they each possess a share in the collective undertaking.
This would be like the case where a *saṃgha* acts as a matchmaker for marriage; or as when the entire *saṃgha* commits an offense together and cannot perform repentance;

or cases such as the *saṃgha* acting as the basis [for an accusation], the *saṃgha* performing the formal act of suspension (*ukṣepaṇīya-karman*), and so forth—wherein even those living together [within the same community] would be implicated.
Although four or more may be involved, they are merely co-residents (*sahavāsin*) and are not subsumed under the category of the Saṃgha.
Regarding those who commit many offenses, this refers to many people acting with a common intent. If "many" is defined according to this, then all are equally guilty of the offense.
If, however, "many" is defined in terms of how my own action causes others to become guilty, then only the co-residents are included; among them, there are those who do not share [the same intent].
Regarding the offenses, there are fifteen precepts. These refer to: (1) two cases of washing; (2) exceeding the limit for patching; (3) mixing black and white wool; (4) begging for six years;

(5) taking medicine during the rain-retreat; and (6) appropriating medicine. Although these medicines differ in length, logically they should constitute the same offense. However, because there is a specific rule that establishes a restriction, they are distinct from other cases of excess and therefore do not constitute the same offense.
Next is the gateway of body and speech. These thirty precepts comprise thirty-two when including the three types of abstention, or thirty-six when accounting for the two types of washing;
however, we shall follow the previous enumeration. Among these, the duty of carrying is restricted to the body, while the remainder apply to both body and speech.

Regarding those that pertain to the middle category, there are three types. First, there are five precepts where the verbal abstinence from action is shared with the bodily offense; these refer to the five [prohibitions against] long [hair, etc.].
Second, there are two precepts where the bodily and verbal performance of action is shared with the bodily offense; these refer to the two [prohibitions regarding] robes.

Third, there are the remaining twenty-three precepts where the verbal performance is shared with the bodily offense. This category is further divided into three: first, there are three precepts where one’s own speech relies on another’s body; these refer to...
Second, regarding washing and begging for thread; second, regarding the eight precepts (*aṣṭāṅga-śīla*). When one acts for oneself, the body is constrained.

If one looks toward instructing another, one's own speech relies on the body of another—namely, the five types of spreading [of robes], the two types of precious items, and the taking away of robes. Third, regarding the remaining twelve [offenses] involving the acceptance of precepts: when one's own speech relies on the body of another, an offense is committed.
Next, regarding "doing it oneself and teaching others": among these thirty [offenses], two—washing and begging for thread—are offenses committed solely through teaching others;

begging for thread oneself constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense). Washing it oneself carries no offense. As for the previous statement that one person commits all [the offenses]: [it refers to this].

This is because it involves both performing the act oneself and instructing another to do so. If one were to generally instruct another to perform these thirty acts without doing them for oneself, one would not commit a *thullaccaya* offense at all;
however, because one is instructing another to commit an evil deed, there is a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).

If, however, one instructs another to perform them for one's own sake, then only eleven [of the thirty] constitute an offense—namely, the two instances of washing and the begging for thread—as these involve offenses committed solely through instructing another. This is because even if a nun or someone who is not a relative [is instructed], [the offense still applies].

Weaving, as well as the five types of spreading, the two types of precious robes, and the forfeiture of robes—regarding all other precepts, it is not that they are not for one's own sake; however, because the benefit or loss is not exclusive [to oneself], one incurs only a *duṣkṛta* offense.

Furthermore, if one instructs another to engage in trade, to receive an urgent gift of rain-clothing beyond the limit, or to divert monastic property to oneself, since these acts are performed for one's own benefit and involve the fulfillment of personal desires, one should likewise incur the same offense. The fact that this is not mentioned in the text is due to abbreviation.

Next, regarding the prohibition of [inherent] nature (*svabhāva-pratiṣedha*): only returning the monastic robes constitutes a violation of nature; all others are prohibitions. Next, regarding observance and transgression:

among these eight precepts, two possess both types of observance and transgression. That is to say, the five [precepts] involve transgression through commission (*karma-samutthāna*), while the ten involve transgression through non-commission (*akarma-samutthāna*).

Although both [types] exist for six years, their characteristics can be understood through explanation. As for the precept against possessing precious objects, it generally possesses two types of observance; however, because one may not [possess them] oneself...

Because [the offenses involving] livestock are omitted and not discussed, the remaining precepts consist solely of "abstaining from what is maintained" (*zhi-chi*) and "committing what is transgressed" (*zuo-fan*).

Regarding the intent of the next two questions: for the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* rules, there is property that can be relinquished, yet the formal ritual (*dharmakarma*) cannot be performed in a separate assembly (*bhedasaṃgha*).

For the ninety *pāyattika* rules, there is no method for relinquishment; however, at the time of confession, it is permitted to perform them in a separate assembly. For this reason, they are divided into two questions. Thus, the preceding...

The distinction between admonishing and not admonishing in a group should likewise be divided into two. Answer: These are distinguished into two questions because the conditions for abandoning the offense differ.
In the former case, there is no separate group; therefore, they are combined into one. Furthermore, this [latter case] involves a separate group, whereas the former does not;

thus, they are distinguished into two questions. Although the former distinguishes between admonishing and not admonishing, it remains a single category because it concerns only the failure to listen to the admonition.

Next, regarding "repeated offenses": there are four precepts that constitute repeated offenses, namely: carrying, using, and the two instances of washing. However, the three *niḥsargika-pāyattikas* concerning washing, dyeing, and beating constitute a repeated offense of a different category;
they do not constitute a repeated offense of the same category as carrying and using, which refers to the number of times one carries wool exceeding the limit.
Regarding the number of times a rain-cloak may be used: Master Ji stated that the three *naiḥsargika* offenses—washing, dyeing, and beating—are incurred.

Since the offense is committed upon washing, it should be understood that the same applies by analogy to dyeing and beating; likewise, each act of washing constitutes a separate offense. My current interpretation is not so. Washing twice is considered the same as washing once; thus, a new garment does not incur a *naiḥsargika* offense.

However, according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra*, if one performs all three acts simultaneously, one incurs a single *pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture). If one merely washes it, one incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

The announcement regarding robes is auspicious. Since dyeing and beating are distinct acts, they do not constitute a repeated offense; how much less so for washing, which cannot incur a double transgression?
As for the remaining precepts, none may be committed repeatedly: namely, (1) confiscation; (2) although five or ten months [of storage], the bowl and medicine are urgent matters;

(3) exceeding six [units]; (4) making ten [units]; (5) miscellaneous matters; (6) two types of black and white wool; (7) the six types of weaving; (8) the four types of receiving robes. Regarding "receiving": this refers to taking from a *bhikṣuṇī*.
Regarding robes: begging for robes, exceeding the limit of sufficiency, accepting one or two [robes], and the two types of jewels belonging to householders or royal officials;

selling them; begging for bowls; encouraging the weaving [of robes]; the rainy-season robe; receiving [a robe] urgently; seeking and receiving [a robe] beyond the prescribed time; and diverting the property of the Saṃgha.

The reason it is necessary to clarify what is grave and what is not grave is precisely for the purpose of recognizing the magnitude of the karmic burden. Next, as for the confession through relinquishment (*pratyāpatti*), according to the texts there are four types, namely: confession through material goods (*dravya-pratyāpatti*).

Regarding the forfeiture of robes and the non-forfeiture [of others]: first, the forfeiture of material goods is clarified. There are four types of forfeiture of goods: first, the goods to be forfeited, namely robes, medicine, alms bowls, and precious objects;

for nuns, there are additionally sixteen items including milking vessels. This forfeiture is of two kinds: total destruction and partial deterioration; for example, a cotton mattress is forfeited upon its deterioration.

All others are complete [in their application]. Regarding the two types of objects they confront: some objects are resistant (*sapratigha*) and some are non-resistant (*apratigha*). A cotton mattress is the sole exception that is non-resistant; all others are resistant.

Among those that are resistant, there are distinctions between the laity and the ordained. For the laity, it applies only to the two jewels (the Buddha and the Dharma); for the ordained, it extends to all other precepts. Within the ordained, there are further distinctions: begging for a bowl is restricted to monks.

The remaining [procedures] apply to both the Saṃgha and individuals. Furthermore, regarding the two types of precious items—cotton and rugs—it is permitted for a separate group to perform the relinquishment (*pratyāśraya*), as these do not pertain to the Path;

for all other matters, everyone must assemble. Third, regarding the locations for relinquishing property: this refers to the *prakṛti-sthiti* (natural) and the *kṛta-karma* (formal ritual) procedures. For the begging of a bowl, it applies specifically to one case; for the rest, it applies to both categories.

Within the two types of formal rituals, there are further distinctions between "great" and "small": the bowl applies only to the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), while the rest apply to both great and small boundaries. Third, regarding dwellings and non-dwellings.

As for this [rule], the begging of a bowl is restricted to this specific residence because it involves leaving behind a superior item to enter the monastic storehouse. All other precepts apply universally to all locations.
Regarding the four methods of relinquishing property, within the category of "dharma" (procedural methods), there are two positions: verbal expression (*vāc*) and formal ritual (*karmavācanā*).

As for the single method of *karmavācanā*, it is absent from the relinquishing of property, because when one relinquishes one's own property, a formal ritual is not required. If we discuss the method of verbal expression, the cotton mattress (*tūlapaṭikā*) is excluded, because...

It does not apply to persons; how could it require an abundance of dharmas? The remainder applies universally. Within this, there are distinctions between the mundane and the supramundane, as well as specific categories for the Saṃgha;

these differences may be understood through analysis. Next, the forfeiture of offenses also consists of four types. First, regarding the offense to be forfeited, one must know the quantity of the material objects involved in the transgression.

Once the material wealth has been provided, the karmic burden must be extinguished. Regarding the necessity of knowing the conditions for offenses and their various categories, these categories shall be analyzed in the relevant passages.

Second, the relinquishing of the object of the offense: if one discusses the relinquishing of material wealth, there are distinctions between those that are perceptible (*sapratigha*) and those that are imperceptible (*apratigha*);

within the perceptible, there are further distinctions between the monastic and the lay. As for the relinquishing of the offense itself, it is entirely directed toward the Path (*mārga*) in order to eliminate past transgressions; the object must be of a similar category.

Regarding the begging for a bowl while on the road, this applies exclusively to the Saṃgha. The three precepts beginning with the *ratna* (jewel) apply specifically to individuals (*pudgala*). The remaining twenty-eight [offenses] pertain universally to all three objects.
This is explained in terms of whether the object addressed is a conventional designation (*prajñapti*) or not; however, as for the removal of the offense, it pertains solely to the individual.

Furthermore, regarding the three [categories] beginning with the *ratna* (jewel), the relinquishment and acquisition involve separate assemblies; when considering the time of confession, they likewise do not assemble together.

As for the three places where offenses are relinquished, the three precepts beginning with the *ratna* encompass all locations. Regarding the remaining twenty-nine, if one discusses the formal act performed by the *saṃgha*, the bowl (*pātra*) is restricted solely to the Great [Saṃgha].

The remaining [offenses] apply to both types of actions. If one excludes the bowl, the remaining twenty-eight [offenses] are treated in relation to the two lower categories of objects, similar to the case of the jewels and so forth.
Furthermore, they may also be applied interchangeably with the locations where property is relinquished; that is, one may relinquish property at this location while confessing the offense at another.

Regarding these distinctions of location, there are two positions: first, the begging of a bowl is restricted to the major category; second, excluding the three items beginning with jewels, the remainder [apply to both].

Twenty-eight [offenses] are relinquished before the Saṃgha; they are exclusively performed in two ways. Regarding the third category, the three precepts concerning precious objects and so forth, as well as the twenty-eight [other offenses], they are relinquished before the lower two classes of persons.

As for the location, it applies to all. Fourth, regarding the method for relinquishing offenses: the three precepts concerning precious objects and so forth are exclusively verbal procedures (*vāda-dharma*).

Excluding these three, the remaining twenty-nine are relinquished before the Saṃgha; where there is an acceptance of the confession and a formal announcement (*jñapti*), they possess both [characteristics].

Regarding the *dharmas*: excluding the bowl, there are twenty-eight remaining. When confronted with the two lower objects, these also consist merely of verbal *dharmas*. Next, regarding the returning of robes, there are likewise four [categories]:

first, the property to be returned. Within the returning of property, one must exclude cotton mattresses; since these do not involve confrontation with an object, they need not be discussed in terms of returning.

Among the remaining precepts concerning returning, the two types of precious items are excluded, making a total of four categories—namely, the five [offenses] such as "excess" (*atireka*) and so forth, which involve spending the night [with the item].

Just as he was returning, Li and twenty-three others were listening to the entrustment on that very seat. The reason for this was that because Chang and the others had stored the items for several days, their greedy minds continued to arise;

thus, they could not be entrusted immediately. It was necessary to let a night pass so that, once the matter was separated by time, the possessive mind of those returning would be severed, and only then would it become pure.
If there were a specific circumstance, it was permitted to transfer the entrustment. [Question: If the relinquishments are each distinct...
The method for returning [the robe] can be understood. Alternatively, if it is discarded together [with the offense], how is the return performed? Regarding the resolution:

if one, two, three, or more [robes] have been combined with the long [robe], the long robe itself must be returned after having passed one night; as for the others, there is no hindrance, and they should be returned immediately. Therefore, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (or *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-uttaragrantha*), fascicle 4, states:

"The robe has already been discarded, and the offense has already been confessed. Subsequently, the continuity of the mind is severed. At that point, it is said: 'If the robe previously sought should arrive...'"
When an unexpected robe arrives, it does not fall into the category of sequential [transgression], because the mind has already severed [the attachment].

This differs from the ancient commentators who claimed that when a robe exceeding the prescribed length or other dimensions is combined with another, it must be relinquished—except for the two cases of the "separation of two hairs" and the begging of a bowl; as for all other precepts, if they are relinquished, they are restored.

One may remain stained for a long duration; following this, one passes the night together [with the object]. Next, one returns to the territory where the property originated and removes the cotton bedding. This does not apply when facing an absent object (*avastuka*).

As for the remaining precepts, they apply to both the laity and the clergy, as well as to individual monks; in each case, one must relinquish the property and no confusion of these rules is permitted.

However, regarding the individual [confession], there may be instances of mutual interchangeability; whether one obtains it from a separate assembly can be understood by analogy with the principle. Next, regarding the place where the property is returned, this follows what was explained in the section on relinquishment (*pratyāśraya*).

Next, regarding the method of returning it, if we discuss the formal discourse (*vāda*), the principle is that its meaning is universal; yet when discussing the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*), [it must be specific].

There is no [procedure] for three or fewer people. If it is a *saṃgha* returning [the bowl], there must be a formal motion and announcement (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*). However, the procedure for the bowls differs, as fully recorded in the text.

It is simply because the relinquishing of property involves either separation or combination. If they are relinquished together, the return may be by two or one; if they are relinquished individually, [the return is likewise].

Only the first two cases involve confession. Next, regarding the "non-returner": a cotton mattress is not returned because it does not face an object; since other items do face objects, there is an offense for failing to return them. Second, regarding the "lay non-returner":
as the text states, one must pursue the return of the item, for one does not wish to render the faithful offering (śraddhā-deya) void, lest it be damaged. Thus it is.
If one does not return [to the precepts], it is reckoned as a grave offense.
Regarding the similarities and differences: eighteen precepts are identical and need not be explained in detail; twelve have variations that must be clarified separately.
Among these twelve [offenses], they are grouped into three categories. First, there are nine precepts with varying degrees of gravity:

namely, the five regarding bedding and requisites, taking [cloth for] washing, and the two regarding wool. Because these are performed by the Saṃgha, they constitute a *pāyattika*; because nuns perform them infrequently, they constitute a *duṣkṛta*. Next, there are two precepts.
The monks possess it while the nuns do not. Regarding the *varṣāśāṭī* (rain-bathing robe), the monks have specific restrictions and fixed limits for its use;

they fear that if they were permitted to seek it out with excessive zeal, it might lead to loss or seizure. Therefore, the six-night period was established as an allowance, which accounts for the case of exceeding those six nights. As for the nuns, this refers to their bathing robes.

The Noble One’s [permission] is for constant use; since there is no fixed limit, how could there be any transgression? Furthermore, as nuns are weak and do not practice in forest hermitages (*araṇya*), they are neither permitted to possess six bowls nor do they commit an offense by possessing more than six.
Regarding the three types of offenses where the precept is the same but the conditions differ, the "extra bowl" (*dīrgha-pātra*) is an example.

The fact that both monks and nuns commit the offense is termed "the same transgression" (*tong-ming*). The difference of ten days for a single night is termed "the difference in conditions" (*yuan-yi*).

Next, regarding those committed spontaneously (*ren-yun*): one commits thirteen precepts spontaneously. These are: the five offenses involving medicine (excluding the exception for medicinal substances), which are committed when the number of days reaches the limit;
and the two [offenses] of washing and begging for thread, the five [offenses] of spreading out [seats], and the taking of robes—these are all completed simply by the accomplishment of the act.
[The preceding] offenses are omitted; in all other cases, there is no spontaneous [violation].
Next, following the specific explanations: first, the interpretation of "extra robes" (*atireka-cīvara*). Regarding the intent behind the permissions and prohibitions:

it is truly because the faculties and natures of practitioners differ, their karmic retributions vary in strength, and their material requirements must consequently differ. Thus, the Great Sage established both permissions and prohibitions, providing remedies that ultimately serve as supplements, each according to [the individual's needs].
Regarding the suitability of the faculties, there are four distinctions, all of which provide the benefit of sustaining the body while cultivating the Path. As for the first type of person:

their karmic power and physical resources are strong; they are able to cultivate the Path by maintaining only the three robes. Therefore, the text below states: "In future ages, there will be good sons..."

One must not exceed the possession of these three robes. As for the second type of person, their karmic power is slightly inferior; if they were to keep as many as the first type, it would hinder their cultivation of the Path.

Therefore, it is permitted for them to possess the "one hundred and one" items that assist the body, provided they are clearly marked and maintained; there is no need to perform the ritual of *śuddhi* (purification). As for the third type of person, their karmic power is even more inferior;
although they possess the "one hundred and one" items, they still lack the capacity for diligent progress. For them, it is further permitted to accept offerings and perform the ritual of *śuddhi*.

One keeps [these items] purely, desiring that others may obtain the merit of giving; these are the conditions for supporting the path. As for the fourth type of person, their power of retribution is most inferior;

although they keep light requisites, they still do not advance on the path. Therefore, it is further permitted for them to possess heavy items such as bedding and mats, whereby they can sustain their bodies and progress in their practice with benefit.
Next, regarding the regulations, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (or *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*), fascicle four, states: "If one regards worldly gain as a benefit, then the Path..."
The benefit is not achieved; furthermore, it causes one to lose the faith, respect, and pure mind of the *dānapati*.

The bhikṣu becomes insatiable and no different from a layperson, thereby violating the Buddha’s teachings and the four noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*). Since this [practice] was permitted by the Noble One as a concession, to extensively accumulate and possess goods in excess is contrary to the practice of moderation and contentment.

Therefore, the "purification" (*pariśuddhi*) procedure is not applied, and the rule of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*) is established. This refers to the prohibition of the two lower [categories].
Regarding the person:
second, as for the explanation of the names, that which is stored for one’s own use is called "possessions" (*chù*); that which exceeds the allotted portion is termed "surplus" (*zhǎng*).
Because it exceeds the fixed period, it is said to be "more than ten days."
Regarding the third point, the conditions for possession, there are six distinct factors. First, it must be one’s own surplus property;

the three robes are excluded, as these are the robes appropriate to the Dharma for the Buddhas of the three periods, and by their very nature they do not constitute an excess. Therefore, they must be set aside. If the three robes are accepted [as part of the requisites], [they are not considered surplus].

This clarifies that there is no offense regarding "excess" (atireka). Even if one does not formally accept [the robe], there is likewise no fault of excess; therefore, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* states:

"If a bhikṣu does not formally accept his three robes and they exceed ten days, there is no offense of 'excess robe' (atireka-cīvara), nor is there an offense of 'staying overnight apart from the robe' (cīvara-vippavāsa); however, there is the offense of violating the established ritual."

There is the offense of possessing deficient clothing. Even if it is one's own clothing, there is no offense if one has forgotten [its ownership]. Therefore, the second requirement is that one must know the item belongs to oneself.

Although the item may belong to oneself, the wealth must be within the prescribed measure; if it is not within the measure, there is no offense in possessing it beyond that limit. Therefore, the third requirement is that the item must be of a measured quantity.

Although the item may be of a measured quantity, there is no fault only if the *śuddhi* (purification) has been performed. Thus, the fourth requirement is that the method of non-purification (*a-śuddhi-dharma*) must not be applied.

Even if one has not performed the formal purification (*pāriśuddhi*), there is no offense if, for a period of one month or five months, one is subject to the four types of perceptions, or if there are circumstances involving suspension or obstacles.

Therefore, the fifth requirement is that there be no such cause. Even if there is no such cause, if one keeps [the robe] beyond the limit, it constitutes an offense; however, if the limit has not yet been exceeded, there is no offense.
Nor does one incur an offense [before that time]. Therefore, the offense is incurred at the appearance of the dawn on the sixty-first day; this is according to the *Jianlun* (Treatise on Seeing).

In Sanskrit, it is called *aruṇa* (translated here as "appearance of light"). The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (*Duolun*) states: "The appearance of light has various synonyms and possesses three kinds of colors.
When the sun shines upon the Jambū tree, it appears black; when it shines upon the leaves of the tree, it appears blue; and when it passes beyond..."
When the trees illuminate the realm of Jambudvīpa, they appear white; among the three colors, white is considered the primary one.
The four absences of conditions can be understood [as follows].
Regarding the three seasonal robes within those conditions, this is likely because their thickness varies according to the time of year. In the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, the bhikṣus saw...
He asked, "The World-Honored One has not permitted the keeping of extra robes. Have you not heard this? He replied, "I have indeed heard it.

However, as for these robes of mine, some were obtained from the Sangha, some were obtained through the request of householders, and some were *pāṃśukūla* (rag-robes). Because they wished me to wear them, they gave them to me;
originally, they did not intend for me to keep them as 'property of the five families'."
The main text of the precepts has three sections; the supplementary explanations have five. First, raising a doubt regarding a regulation:

[The questioner] asks whether Ānanda’s giving of his robe to Kāśyapa was a definitive act of mind. The answer in the text states that since he "wished" to give it, it is clear that it was not a definitive act.
If it had been given definitively, it would no longer have been his own property; because it was not given definitively, he must state his doubt and request a decision. Second.

This clearly explains the request. Third, the inquiry regarding the time of return; fourth, the response concerning the time limit; fifth, the allowance of ten days. According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*:
"The Buddha, knowing the nature of dharmas—neither lax nor urgent, neither adding nor subtracting—properly established the limit of ten days."

This completes the *Śīlaskandha-vibhaṅga* (Sāntika-śīla). It is divided into three sections: first, the determination of the textual phrasing; second, the determination of the presence or absence of conditions;

and third, the determination of the similarities and differences regarding benefits. In the first section, the *Śīlaskandha* consists of six phrases: first, the offender; second, one for whom the robe-making is finished.
1. "Excessive" does not refer to the nature of the robe itself; because the robe is not finished, it is not termed "excessive. 2.

"When the three *kaṭhina* robes have been removed" indicates the time when an offense occurs; as long as the *kaṭhina* robes have not been removed, it is not termed the time of an offense. 3. "One who keeps an excessive robe."

Regarding the nature of the wealth one possesses, the five noble ones have opened a period of ten days. Sixth, if one exceeds this limit, it violates the teaching and constitutes an offense. Next, as for determining the conditions:

taking this precept alone, there is a circumstance regarding the ten-day period; however, it is not yet known whether the *kaṭhina* [robe] or the five rules concerning "excess" (*atireka*) and so forth come first or later.
If the *kaṭhina* were opened prior, then one could not say that the *kaṭhina* was received for the sake of opening the five rules concerning excess.
Regarding the *kaṭhina* robe: if the rules concerning excess [of cloth] and so forth were established first, and the *kaṭhina* was subsequently permitted, there would be no basis for it;

thus it is said that it has already been excluded. Answer: The rules concerning excess and so forth were established first, and the *kaṭhina* was permitted later. Therefore, the *Vinaya* below states:

"For the sake of the five types of excess and so forth, the acceptance of the *kaṭhina* robe is permitted. However, this statement regarding the lack of basis is merely an omission. Thus, in the initial *Prātimokṣa* of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*:

The Buddha said: "To keep an extra robe for more than one night constitutes an offense. Furthermore, when Nanda’s robe was damaged and he feared it would not be finished in a single day, he feared committing a *naiḥsargika* offense and did not dare to take up the robe from the Saṃgha.
Moreover, there were other bhikṣus who, having completed their summer retreat on the sixteenth day, proceeded to the place where the Buddha was.
The path was muddy and filled with water, and their three robes were coarse and heavy; they were utterly exhausted. They then reported the matter concerning Nanda."
The Buddha said, "I permit the acceptance of the *kaṭhina* robe; one shall not commit an offense regarding five matters. The second section of the *Śīla-mūla* states:
"If a bhikṣu has finished preparing his three robes and has already relinquished the *kaṭhina*, if he keeps an extra robe for more than one night, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

Furthermore, because Ānanda obtained two pieces of *karpāsa* cotton cloth and wished to give them to Śāriputra, fearing he might commit an offense, he informed the Buddha. The Buddha granted him a ten-day period. The second...
The *Tri-saṃvara-vibhaṅga* states: "If a bhikṣu has finished preparing his three robes and has relinquished the *kaṭhina* cloth, he may keep extra robes for up to ten days;
if he exceeds this, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. Regarding the similarities and differences between this rule and the other remaining precepts and benefits:

Question: The benefit of the time-period is opened to one month or five months; why is this applicable across all three precepts? Answer: Originally, for the sake of the five matters, the acceptance of the *kaṭhina* was opened.

Regarding robes: now, the first three cases constitute "excess" (*atireka*), while the second constitutes "separation" (*vippavāsa*). By means of these five advantages (*pañca-lābha*), one attains the application of all three precepts.
Question: Why is this exemption (*kappa*) not applicable to other precepts? Answer:

If other precepts were to be exempted by these five advantages, they would necessarily require specific exceptions (*paccaya*), such as the "robes given in haste" (*āpadā-cīvara*) or the "separate from the back" (*paṭibāhita*) precept. However, if [a precept] is not related to these five advantages, then...

There is no opening [for this]. A questioner asks: "Why are the permissions for urgent giving and so forth different from this? The answer is: "The permissions differ according to the differences in the matters at hand;
thus, the wording of the permissions also differs. Although the wording differs, the timing and benefit are no different. There are further interpretations, but all of them encounter difficulties.
For now, I shall provide this explanation to resolve the textual contradiction.

Next follows the extensive explanation of the text, which has two parts: first, the commentary on the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*; second, the ritual procedures for relinquishing and confessing [transgressions]. Regarding the commentary, the first sentence is clear.

As for the second sentence, "the robe is finished," the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "finished means washed, dyed, and sewn. The third sentence, "the *kaṭhina* robe has been removed (*uddhṛta*)," means it has been relinquished (*pratyuddhṛta*).
It is called "removal" because it depends on the eight ways of relinquishing the *kaṭhina*, whether extended or abbreviated. This concludes the commentary on the following two rules.
The conclusion is the same as this. Regarding the phrase "as for robes" (*cīvara*) and below, this explains the fourth line. Within this section, there are two parts:

first, distinguishing the substance of the ten kinds of robes to explain the meaning of "superior robes. As for "silk" (*kauśeya*), it is made from *kośa* (silkworms). As for "cotton cloth" (*kārpāsa*), it is made from flowers.
As for *kambala*, it is made from wool. As for *śāṇa*, it is made from ramie. As for *kṣauma*, it is made from wild hemp. As for "hemp" (*māṇava*), it is made from cultivated hemp.
*Maśāna* is made from the wool of white sheep; *kaiyira* is made from bird feathers; *kauyira* is dyed red wool;
*caṇḍāvaṇīya* cloth is variegated wool. Regarding the measurement and limits of the two types of robes: this explains the meaning of "length.
This explanation of the meaning of length is analyzed through three gates: first, the measurement and limits; second, that which should... [text continues].

Regarding the measure of the offense: the third section concerns the mutual application of the rules. First, as for the measure: according to this text, it is one chi, six cun, eight fen, and five mu.

With the exception of the three long robes (*tricīvara*), if any other garment—even down to a hand-towel—exceeds ten days [without being processed], it constitutes a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).

The *Saṃghāṭī*. Regarding "extra robes" (*atireka-cīvara*): these are robes other than those that have been formally accepted and maintained. Furthermore, they must be one cubit wide and two cubits long. Second Section. Question:

Does the offense occur at the very moment the robe reaches the prescribed measurement, or does it wait until it exceeds it? Answer: One must purify [the robe] immediately; for if it is not purified, one commits an offense.
As for what is called an "extra robe," if it is as long as eight finger-breadths of the Tathāgata, and so forth. Third Section. Question: Regarding the robe...

If the measurements are mutually reduced, is it necessary to perform the ritual purification (*parikarma*)? Answer: If the measurements are mutually reduced, it is not necessary to perform the purification.

If that is so, the same applies to rooms. Why must they be demarcated? Answer: Regarding rooms, there is the fear of obstruction or difficulty; therefore, even if they are mutually [adjoining], they must be demarcated.

Clothing does not face this difficulty; thus, if the measurements are mutually reduced, it is not necessary. Next, the two lines concerning "five" and "six" shall be explained together. Within this, there are two parts. First:

There is the offense of keeping [the robe] beyond the limit; second, the offense of trading with one who is defiled or ignorant. The first section consists of eight chapters, beginning from "obtaining" and "not obtaining," and ending with "forgetting" and "not forgetting.
The first chapter, concerning "obtaining" and "not obtaining," comprises ten days, with each day constituting one chapter, thus totaling ten chapters.

Regarding the initial day of obtaining the robe, there are cases where it is obtained in large quantities and cases where it is obtained in small quantities, which intermingle with one another to form a total of forty-six phrases. First:

Regarding the rule that one acquires the offense on the eleventh day after having obtained robes on the tenth day: because the substance [of the robe] has exceeded the limit on the first day, an offense is committed;

as for the subsequent nine days, because the robes from the first day have been stained and thus become associated with them, all are declared *niḥsargika* (relinquishable). According to the *Jianlun* (Treatise on Observations), section 14:
"If many robes are tied together in one place and exceed ten days, one incurs a single offense. If the robes are scattered and not tied together, [the offenses are counted individually]."
The number of offenses incurred corresponds to the quantity of robes. The *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*, fascicle seven, asks: "How does one obtain an extra robe (*atireka-cīvara*)? It means:

if it has entered the hand, or if one forms the thought over it on the knees or the shoulder, "This is my property. Next, the second chapter contains nine propositions; there is one established rule and eight descending variations.
That is to say, turning from the empty day downward, one obtains the day upward. The third chapter contains two [sections].
Regarding the section on "not obtaining robes," there are eight phrases. There is one established rule (*vidhi*), and seven descending variations (*paryāya*).

Thus it continues down to the second phrase of the ninth chapter; for each established rule and descending variation, there is one phrase. Upon examining the textual flow and the underlying meaning within this chapter, they do not accord with one another.
Furthermore, there are sub-commentaries regarding these descending variations; however, where such [redundant] text exists, it is logically an error. If it were not an error...
How can one repeat the previous phrases? Someone, based on this, has constructed seven inverted phrases.
Continuing this process upward, until reaching the third chapter, there is one [phrase]; thus, twenty-eight phrases are formed. Now, because the text is disordered, it need not be elaborated further.
The first phrase of the tenth chapter is obtained in one day; the second chapter is obtained in nine days.
Attainment: [The cases of] two relative to one make thirteen; nine relative to one make twenty-four; eight make thirty-five; seven make forty.
In the sixth chapter, attainment over five days constitutes five phrases; in the first chapter, attainment over ten days constitutes one phrase.
Thus, there are six phrases in total, which together form forty-six phrases. Next is the section on Pure Giving (*śuddha-dāna*); the first chapter is omitted here.
Since ten days are all impure, there are only nine [remaining]. This should likewise apply by analogy to the lower gate (*adhaḥ-mukha*).

If one sends [the cloth] to another person to replace a previous pure gift (*śuddha-dāna*), or on the day the cloth cannot be obtained—this mentions only one side—it should also be stated that "one does not send it to another.
Thus, as for what is ruined: it is ruined because it was made by a messenger to be of improper measure or not a garment (*a-cīvara*), such as making a leather sandal bag, or through forgetfulness.

As for this, if one forgets the substance of the property and considers it to have been nonexistent from the start, even though many days have passed, opening [the storehouse] does not constitute an offense.
Next, regarding the offense of defilement: this refers to having someone else purchase it, or purchasing it oneself from among the five groups of monastics; these do not constitute an offense.

As for "selling," because it constitutes a prior act of prolonged defilement, it is called "one *niḥsargika-pāyattika*. Furthermore, this robe subject to forfeiture (*naiḥsargika*) ought, according to principle, to be forfeited and then traded [for something else].

If one trades [an item] without it being appropriate or without relinquishing it, one further incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense. This does not accord with the former interpretation which states that this is the offense of wearing impure clothing;
for if one calculates it thus, it would not fit the discussion regarding the fault of using [such items]. If this were the intended clarification, the sequence of the meaning would be incorrect.

Next, the procedure for relinquishing and repenting is explained. The text is divided into four parts: first, the relinquishment of material objects and the Dharma; second, the method for relinquishing the *kaṭhina* robe following the section "When he has finished relinquishing that robe";

third, the method for returning the material objects following the section "If the Saṃgha is numerous"; and fourth, the offense incurred when not returning them following the section "If it is a bhikṣu.
The reason the sequence of these four sections is as it is is that this transgression originally arises from material objects; if one wishes to repent and eliminate it, it is essential...
First, one must strike at the root. Therefore, one first renounces wealth that is accompanied by fault. Although such faulty wealth has been renounced, the karmic burden has not yet been eliminated;

as long as the transgression remains present, one does not become compliant with the Dharma. Consequently, one next performs the confession of sins. Once the material goods have been relinquished and the offenses have been repented and removed, one’s conduct is free from violation and is capable of receiving the benefits of offerings.
Thus, one next returns the robes. When the holy teaching is proclaimed, it is only right to comply with its principles. If...

If one acts contrary to this, there will inevitably be transgression. Therefore, the offenses of those who do not return [to the precepts] are next defined. These four texts constitute the great protocol for ritual practice;

since they apply universally to all precepts, those who raise them should understand this. Although there are three categories of objects for these confessions, they are here explained primarily with reference to the Sangha.
The initial text consists of four parts: first, the forfeiture of accumulated wealth; second, the objects of the confession, beginning with "to the Saṃgha";
third, the formal procedure for forfeiture, beginning with "having forfeited"; and fourth, the actual words of forfeiture, beginning with "one should act as follows.

Regarding the first point, the statement "this *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* robe must be forfeited" refers to the forfeiture of accumulated wealth. This necessitates the removal of debts; that which has not yet entered one's possession [is not subject to this rule].
As for shared items and those of an undivided nature, one must exclude the material goods themselves and instead apply the ritual of *pariśuddhi* (purification).

If one does not perform this purification, why would it be necessary to place them in the category of relinquishment (*utsarga*)? Furthermore, regarding items entrusted to others, one must also reclaim them; if they are not fully assembled, they return to their original owner and remain subject to defilement.

Question: Regarding the relinquishment of property that was not entirely given away, one mistakenly thought it was nonexistent. Only after the relinquishment did one see that there was remaining property. It is not known whether the prior relinquishment was valid. Answer:
If the object relinquished remained with the Sangha and had not yet been returned, the prior relinquishment is valid; one may continue to relinquish what was forgotten.

If the object has been returned to its owner and the *śuddhi* (purification) has already been performed, the validity is as stated before, and one may continue to relinquish what was forgotten. If the object has been returned to its owner but the *śuddhi* has not yet been performed...

Once it is seen, mutual defilement occurs; both must further relinquish [the offense]. Next, regarding the object to be relinquished, since the assembly must observe it in full detail, everyone must gather.

This is intended to cause the offender to feel profound shame before the assembly, to give rise to a sense of self-reproach within, and to cease transgressions hereafter. Next, one relinquishes their deportment and apologizes for the fault before the assembly;
in principle, one must be humble and submissive. If one is not lowly and respectful, it will be difficult to eliminate the karma. However, provided that...

When facing the Saṃgha, one must uniformly possess five factors. When facing an individual, the matter is divided into two categories: the minor case involves only four factors, lacking the prostration at the feet;

the major case is the same as that for the Saṃgha, also possessing five factors. Next, regarding the formula for relinquishment: since one is personally relinquishing an object, it is logically necessary to express one's intention.

If one does not state these words, the relinquishment will likely fail to be accomplished. As for the phrase "so many" (*etāvantaḥ*) in the text, this is the formal expression of the rule; it is excellent.
The *Jian* (Observations) states in section fourteen: "If there is one robe, one says 'one'; if there are two, three, or many, one likewise says 'two,' 'three,' or 'many.
This is called a discrepancy, whereby the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*) is not accomplished. According to the Vinaya, it requires only a single recitation; it is unnecessary to go up to three."

Next, the confession of offenses (*pāpadeśanā*) is explained. This section is divided into six parts: first, requesting confession from the Saṃgha; second, separately inviting a presiding master of confession (*deśakācārya*); third, the presiding master harmonizing with the Saṃgha;

fourth, the formal presentation of the method of confession; fifth, the reprimand and disciplinary treatment; sixth, receiving [the instruction] and establishing the essential vows. The text states: "When he has finished relinquishing the robe, he should confess.

One should understand that this meaning implicitly includes the act of requesting. This is in accordance with the *Pratideśanīya* (Confession by Personal Declaration) rules found below. Regarding the... [text ends].

Among the various forms of confession (*poṣadha*), there is the act of requesting; this [confession] likewise ought to include it. That the text does not mention it is for the sake of brevity. The wording for the request for confession should be understood as being analogous to the formal relinquishment (*pratyāśraya*).
Having made the request, one must further invite the presiding master of confession (*pratideśanā-adhipati*).

This presiding master must have already perfected the conditions for arising [of the path], be pure, and possess the qualities detailed below. Once the presiding master has accepted the invitation, he may not grant permission immediately; rather, after performing the formal announcement (*jñapti*) to harmonize the assembly, he shall then grant his consent.
Next is the formal removal of offenses. When one is about to perform the repentance, one first distinguishes the quantity of the offenses and their distinct stages from beginning to end;

there are twelve positions in total, comprising three types of offenses. These refer to the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offenses involving forfeiture), as well as the two kinds of concealment: the fundamental and the successive.

These combine to form one set of three, continuing up to the twelfth. Regarding the three *niḥsargika-pāyattika* robes, within these twelve categories, with the exception of the original *naiḥsargika*, the remaining thirty-five are indefinite as to whether they exist or not.
Nevertheless, one wishes to establish a mind for repentance and the removal of past karma.
Each and every one must be examined for completeness or deficiency. According to the correct interpretation of the text, the confession (*pratideśanā*) opens up three stages:
first, one first confesses the twenty-four offenses of concealment (*paryavasthāna*), as these belong to the same category of concealment and are thus collectively reduced by one.

Second, one confesses the seven types of offenses of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*), such as those involving improper speech; as these do not belong to the category of concealment, they are likewise collectively reduced by one. Third, one confesses the *dharmas* of excess.
The wording for the confession and relinquishment of the five categories of *pāyattika* offenses will be explained in the following section.

If the article subject to forfeiture has been used up and one simply confesses the offense, the number of items involved should be understood according to the above principles. Next, the procedure for returning the robe is clarified. Having fulfilled the ten methods mentioned above, one’s transgression is purified;
however, the Path relies on material requisites for its accomplishment and is established by depending upon conditions. If these are not compassionately provided, [the practice] is deficient.
One must return the robe because one is practicing renunciation. Regarding the method for returning the robe: first, the conditions are set forth; second, the ritual procedure is performed.

If there are no such conditions, it must necessarily be returned after having been kept overnight. However, because it is difficult for the great assembly to gather and because that person is traveling far away, it is permitted to transfer the robe through a *karmavācanā* to a relative or friend.
Once the relative or friend has received it, they must return it after keeping it overnight. [From] the *Saṃghāṭī-vinaya*: The Vinaya Master asked, "This assembly..."
"Among these, who is your acquaintance? [The respondent] answers, "So-and-so. He then performs the ritual and hands it over. This is the procedure for the immediate transfer of goods on the spot;

there is no requirement for overnight storage, nor is there a formal *karmavācanā* (ritual motion) for its direct return. Next, regarding those who do not return [the object]: this text provisionally concludes that [non-return] constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.

However, if the non-return is final, one incurs an offense based on the value [of the object]. Therefore, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*, fascicle five, states: "In terms of the offense, it is..."

Regarding the fundamental relinquishment (*mūla-tyāga*): in terms of the Dharma, this constitutes a temporary relinquishment. This is relinquished before the Saṃgha; from beginning to end, it involves twelve formal acts (*dharmas*).
If there are many people, there are eleven formal acts—meaning that if one person is excluded from the request, there are only ten—and this excludes the questioning of those at the periphery.
As for the meaning of the thirty-two explanations, there are five distinct stages. Excluding the two precious items (wool and mattresses), there are twenty-nine remaining.

Regarding the twelve *dharmas* for the Saṃgha: furthermore, excluding the begging of a bowl, there are eleven *dharmas* for a multitude, ten *dharmas* for a single person, and nine *dharmas* for two persons.

For cotton mattresses, there are only six; as for the upper and lower [robes], they are subsumed within these five. Thus, the distinctions between their characteristics are determined according to the number of *dharmas* possessed.
If categorized by the type of object, the procedures for relinquishing and returning them differ; these stages likewise constitute five categories, including the miscellaneous and the wild.

1. Regarding the one precept on the destruction and abandonment [of a bowl]: it is abandoned without being returned. 2. Regarding the two precepts concerning precious objects (*ratna*) in relation to laypeople: they are completely abandoned and their substance is transformed, yet they must be fully returned. 3. Regarding the precept on begging for a bowl:

it is abandoned by entering the Saṃgha and returning it to its owner. 4. Regarding the seven-day medicine: it is abandoned by entering the Saṃgha or entering among laypeople and returning it to its owner.

5. Regarding the remaining twenty-seven precepts: they are abandoned solely by returning them to their owners. The four preceding sections have concluded the exposition regarding the Saṃgha. For the remaining cases involving many individuals or a single person, the principle is applied accordingly.
This should be understood from the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-vaibhāṣikā* (Shaluolun), fascicle four. A śrāmaṇera should possess two upper and lower garments:
first, the *antarvāsa*, which is his constant undergarment; second, the *uttarāsaṅga*, which he should wear when entering the community of monks or when traveling.
He may also keep one *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī*, one *kaṭicīvara*, and one *pūrvaka*. Regarding these items worn on the body, it is permitted for him to keep only one of each. From himself...

All external things are entirely considered surplus property. Regarding what constitutes non-offense: within ten days, if one performs acts such as *pariṣkāra-dāna* (the ritual of giving for use), there is no offense;
however, once ten days have passed, it is already an offense, and no further circumstances can provide an exemption.
Next is the precept regarding staying overnight separated from one's robe (*cīvara*). The specific intent is as follows: the robe is the garment appropriate for the Dharma;
it perfects dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*) and is something not found among other paths. Therefore, there must be no deficiency. Thus, the text below states:

"Wherever a bhikṣu goes, his robe and bowl follow him like the two wings of a bird; feathers and body are inseparable. Now, however, he has left his robe here while his person dwells in another realm—how can he endure the cold?
The summer heat arises suddenly; it is urgent and difficult to obtain [replacements]. Furthermore, lacking protection, one may suffer loss or theft, which ruins the resources for sustaining the body.

Such a matter is not a minor affliction. Therefore, the Sage established this rule. Regarding the explanation of the name: when a person's robe is in a different location, it is called "separated" (*niḥsargika*).

To remain overnight is called "staying" (*śayana*). If this lasts long, the matter becomes lax; if it is too brief, it leads to distress. The time limit is set at one night; if one exceeds this, one commits an offense. Hence, it is called "separation."

The *Cīvara-vastu* (Chapter on Robes). Next, there are six specific conditions: first, the three robes; second, the addition of the formal undertaking (*dhāraṇa-dharma*); third, the person and the robe being in different boundaries (*sīmā*);

fourth, not relinquishing [the robes] during an assembly; fifth, the absence of a valid cause or condition; and sixth, the appearance of the dawn light (*aruṇodaya*). Next, the explanation of the text:

the core of the precept (*śikṣāpada*) consists of three phrases, while the explanatory expansion (*anuvartana*) consists of five. First, the circumstance for clearing [the offense] when one is ill and the robes are heavy. Second, from "He himself reflects" (*svayam samanvāharati*) onwards...

The first section, "Raising the Restriction," gives rise to doubt. The third section, "Then He Spoke to Those Below," presents the doubt for reliance and entrustment. The fourth section, "At That Time, Those Below," serves to explain the intent of the doubt.
The fifth section, "The World-Honored One Below," opens the method for the *akalaka-cīvara* (the non-separation of robes). Regarding the phrase in the text, "the method for the *akalaka-cīvara*":

it means that having obtained this method, one receives the benefit of non-separation and incurs no fault of being apart from the robes; therefore, it is called the "method of the non-separation of robes. If...
Regarding the formulation of the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), only the first phrase—“the robe of a person who is ill”—is established;

the remaining three phrases are not established. This differs from the category of full ordination in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (or *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*). Regarding the long robe (*atireka-cīvara*) as well, there are three gates;

here, however, only the textual phrases are definitively established, while the other two are to be inferred by analogy. The subsequent rules are likewise. The root text of the precepts consists of seven phrases: first, the person who commits the offense; second, the distinguishing of the robe.
1. The substance (*dravya*). 2. The three occasions of transgression. 3. This occasion of non-transgression. This refers to an opening based solely on time, namely one month or five months.

As for the old interpretation that this also includes openings based on non-time (*akāla*), that is not correct. 4. Regarding the four types of robes: this enumerates the names of the robes from which one must be separated. 5.

Being separated from each of these, even down to a single person’s robe, while being in a different boundary (*sīmā*). 6. Excluding those cases where there is a formal monastic authorization (*saṃgha-karman*): this is an opening based on non-time. There are two kinds of *karman*.
First, obtaining the dharma and being separated from one's lodgings; second, establishing the *acchinna-cīvara* (non-forfeiture of robes) boundary.

Regarding the seven *niḥsargika-pāyattika* rules, the following provides a detailed explanation. Of these, the first four and the sixth can be understood through their individual explanations. From "non-forfeiture of robes" onwards, the fifth and seventh phrases are explained together.

Within this section, there are two parts: first, clarifying separation with respect to the ten boundaries; second, from "non-forfeiture of robes" onwards, treating the case of the *araṇya* (wilderness).

Clarifying the Separation. The preceding text consists of five parts: first, listing the names of the ten realms; second, explaining the essence of the ten realms, beginning with "monastery" (saṃghārāma);
third, the distinctions among the ten realms, beginning with "monastery"; fourth, the jurisdictional boundaries (sīmā) of the ten realms, beginning with "monastery";
and fifth, the offense incurred by staying overnight [in a place], beginning with "monastery. First, we explain the initial section. This is divided into two parts: the first relies upon this...

Commentary on the Text. Second, the clarification of the similarities and differences among the various schools. First, regarding the definition of "a single boundary" (*ekasīma*) based on this interpretation:
it refers to a single monastery (*ārāma*) where monks reside together, and throughout the monastery there are no divisions; this is called a single boundary.

If laymen or women come into the boundary and dwell intermingled with them, a village boundary arises, which is termed "multiple boundaries. Therefore, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (or *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-uttaragrantha*), fascicle four, states: "As..."

When a king enters within the boundaries of a monastery, he sets up a tent and resides there; the areas for preparing food and drink near the king’s left and right, as well as the places for his defecation and urination, are all not part of the robe-boundary (*cīvara-sīmā*).
This is because they are not where the king comes to reside, and it is also according to royal law.

Furthermore, another interpretation holds that if a monastery has the characteristics of four surrounding enclosures, then although the individual rooms are distinct, they are all subsumed under the monastery and designated as a single boundary. However, if the characteristics of the monastery's enclosure are not complete...
When separate rooms do not encompass one another, they are called "several boundaries" (*nānā-sīmā*).

Furthermore, it is explained that even within the same boundary, if there are obstructions such that one cannot move about freely, these are all called "several boundaries. Thus, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, fascicle four, states:

"If they are different, the Saṃgha does not perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) to establish a 'boundary for not losing robes. Even if such a boundary is established, within it [one may not move] at will."
Regarding the coming and going, although this principle exists, we shall for now rely on the previous explanation. The explanations for the lower realms are all the same as this.
As for those points that are identical, they cannot be described in detail. However, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations), fascicle five, states:
"A tree may have one boundary (*sīmā*) or distinct boundaries. Regarding the non-contiguous tree-boundary therein: if it is at midday, it is the area shaded by its shadow. If a bhikṣu is in..."
If one is under a tree while one's robe is under another tree, one should have the robe brought to oneself. If one goes to the place where the robe is, or receives another robe;
or if one does not have the robe brought, nor go to the place where it is, nor receive another robe, then at the conclusion of the time [of the formal act], it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Regarding the "interconnected tree-boundary": if the branches and leaves of these trees are interconnected for even as far as one *krośa*, within that space, according to...
Regarding the robes one wears: when they reach the ground, there is no offense. Furthermore, as for the village boundary (*grāma-sīman*):
when a bhikṣu arrives at a village and stays in one place, the extent of that residence is called a single boundary (*ekasīman*), provided there is no distinction within its limits.

If a different boundary arises within these limits, it is called a "multiple boundary" (*nānāsīman*). Question: Why is this not the same as the *Saṃghāṭi*? Answer: Because the brothers share a common heart, they may go wherever they please.

Regarding the rule that "one who comes shall not lose their robe," the answer is that this is restricted by ordinary worldly circumstances; this case is not the same as that. It is simply because there is much public censure and defilement in a village that it is improper to leave one's robe there.
The subsequent text excludes the village, clarifying that it is not a robe-boundary (*cīvara-sīmā*).

Even if one’s own family members are present and there is no emotional obstruction, if a bhikṣu is staying in a separate room while his robe is in the dwelling of men or women, and he needs the robe at night, he might fear taking it [if it were otherwise].
If one is pressed by contact [with others], such that one cannot go there, this is called a "difficulty" (*durga*). A "difficulty" signifies that the robe is not being given;

how then could one leave the robe in this room and stay overnight in another room? Some ancient masters have established the obstacle of "staining" (*rañjana*), which is logically consistent and easy to understand;
however, as there is no formal scriptural authority for it, we do not establish it here.
Next, regarding the similarities and differences among the various schools: In the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, chapter eight, there is the "Boundary of the Path of Practice.

A teacher was traveling together with his companions, proceeding while engaging in doctrinal discussion. His disciple followed behind carrying the robes and bowl, but could not catch up with the teacher.

When the sun set, the teacher, fearing that he would be separated from his robes overnight, went outside the path to wait for the disciple. The disciple, carrying the robes, passed straight through without seeing the teacher. Upon arriving...
They wait for dawn. If the teacher waits at the place where the robe is kept, and it is within twenty-five cubits (*hasta*) of the path and in contact with the robe, there is no offense;

if it is beyond that, there is an offense. If the disciple carries the robe ahead, the same applies to the exchange of questions and answers. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra*, it is forty-nine fathoms (*vyāma*).
Furthermore, according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, there is also the "empty space" (*ākāśa-dhātu*), which refers to the case where the robe is on the ground and the bhikṣu is in the air.
Alternatively, if the robe is in the air and the bhikṣu is on the ground, he commits an offense when the dawn light appears. This is because the air constitutes a space outside the boundary;

thus, according to the *Jianlun* (Treatise on Seeing), there is such a thing as a "forest boundary. If the robe is within the inner part of a forest, it is not lost for fourteen cubits [from the body].

The same applies to islands in the sea. If people come and go through this forest, there is no fourteen-cubit boundary; the robe should remain with one's person. If it does not remain with one, [the rule is violated].

Losing one's robe. Furthermore, there is the water-element boundary. A bhikṣu staying in an araṇya (wilderness) sits in meditation throughout the night. As dawn approaches, he suffers from drowsiness and his eyes close.

He takes off his robe and places it on the bank, then enters the pool to bathe. Before his bathing is finished, the first light of dawn appears; this constitutes an offense of forfeiture (*niḥsargika-pāyattika*) regarding the robe.

According to the *Vinayavibhāṣā-śāstra*, the methods for resolving such cases are naturally clear. There are six ways in which one does not lose the "robe-boundary" (*acchinna-cīvara*). The verse of the treatise says: "Virtuous..."
"Regarding the three robes and the six acts of compassion. The commentary states:

In the Vinaya, the Buddha permitted six instances where one may be separated from the three robes for the benefit of the Saṃgha, provided there is a collective agreement (*saṃmata*) for the performance of formal ritual acts (*karmavācanā*). There are two types of these: first, those pertaining to the *kaṭhina* robe.
1. That which is performed by a harmonious Saṃgha. 2. That which is performed for travelers and for those who are ill;

these are performed by a harmonious Saṃgha. 3. That which is performed based on a location, as explained in the training rules (*śikṣāpada*) concerning the Poṣadha ceremony, such as at the Vaijayanta pavilion or beneath the Jambu tree.
4. That which is performed within an enclosure, namely, within a monastery (*saṃghārāma*).

5. Regarding what is done in an open space: as when a bhikṣu is traveling on a road, at a distance of forty-nine bow-lengths from one another, they cover the ground, stand with bodies straight and arms extended, each holding a corner of their robe;
if they reach one another [in this manner], it is permitted that they are not separated from their robes. 6. Regarding what is done in a residence during the months of the season: at...
This should be understood as explained in detail within the *Varṣā-śikṣāpada* (Precepts on the Rainy Season Retreat).

Furthermore, regarding matters such as being pressed by the need for urination and so forth, which are difficult to perform due to the intervention of others, this is called "the three robes and the six considerations" (*trīṇi cīvarāṇi ṣaṭ-anukampāḥ*). According to the *Mahāsāṃghika*, if [one must attend to] the large or small [calls of nature] during the night...
Regarding the practice: if one remains within twenty-five cubits of the robe, being in physical contact with it, there is no offense.
Next, the essence of the ten realms is as stated in the text. Next, regarding the distinctions among the ten realms—meaning "this" is not "that"—there are one hundred permutations.
There are thirty [cases] in total; the remaining ones are easy to categorize. Next, regarding the "sphere of influence" (*pradeśa*), the *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, fascicle 8, states:
"Neither robust nor infirm. "Throws" means throwing with all one's might. One takes the location where the stone lands, not the location where it rolls from its sphere of influence.
Next, regarding the enumeration of the offenses (*āpatti*), there are in total one hundred phrases; however, because they are abbreviated, there are only twenty.

Furthermore, these twenty are established according to the stages (*avasthā*), yet based on the text, there are only eighteen. This is because the phrase "leaving the robe here in this monastery while going to stay overnight in that monastery" is missing;
thus, there are nine cases for each of the two positions. The first group consists of five textual items: (1) a single person with a different robe; (2) a different boundary (*sīmā*); [and so forth].

Second, regarding "the boundary markers have not yet appeared," this teaches the method for avoiding offenses. Looking at the sequence of permissions, one should first state that the robe is being cast by hand;

next, it reaches the point where a stone is thrown; only then does one need to state that it is relinquished (*utsarga*). The current text follows the order of explanation, and thus states "relinquish" first.
As for "casting by hand," this refers to various boundaries; it must be cast by hand, reaching as far as the place where a stone can be thrown.

This refers to being within the sphere of influence (*iśvabhāga*) of a single boundary (*dhātu*), whereby one’s robes are considered to be in assembly. As for "leaving" (*utsarga*), it means not reaching the assembly;

rather than being deficient in robes and thus committing an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*), one must not be separated from one's robes and thereby incur an offense of transgression (*sthūlātyaya*). Thus, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Sengqi lü), fascicle eight, states:
"A bhikṣu, wearing his upper and lower robes, entered a village. The host, wishing to make merit by making offerings to an image, earnestly invited him to stay overnight."
If the bhikṣus at that residence have extra robes, they should temporarily borrow them for use.
If there are none, they should borrow from whichever nearby residence has bhikṣus. If there are none there, they should go to a residence where bhikṣuṇīs reside.

One may also borrow from them. If there are none, and there is a layperson at that place who possesses robes and bedding, one should borrow them, perform the ritual of *viśuddhi-dāna* (pure giving), and have them sewn;

only then should one accept and maintain them. If such things are unavailable, when the city gates open during the latter part of the night, one should return quickly to the monastery and not go out by leaping over the walls.
Upon reaching the gate of the vihāra, if it has not yet opened, one should ask for it to be opened. If [the gatekeeper] does not...
Regarding "attaining [entry]": even if there is no opening for hands or feet to enter, one may scale over walls and enter.
One should make signs so that those inside recognize [the visitor], ensuring they do not suspect a thief and become alarmed. If entry cannot be gained, one should quickly discard the robe;

it is better to be without the robe and incur a *vyatikrama* offense than to risk the grave [crime of theft], because the light is preferred over the heavy. (3) If one does not discard the robe below, one does not proceed to discard it.

[This is] a summary. Regarding "When the four marks of dawn appear" (*caturvidha-rātry-anta-nimitta*), although [leaving] the three robes constitutes a *pāyattika* offense, regarding "Except for the three robes" (*trai-cīvara-varja*), leaving other robes incurs a *duṣkṛta*.

This refers to those that assist the body. As for the method of receiving the *pariṣaṇḍa* (the hundred-plus), the remaining text is clear. Next, the text concerning the *araṇya* (forest hermitage) has five parts.

First, to clarify the substance of the realm: there are eight trees with seven intervals between them. Each interval is seven *dhanus* (bows) long; one *dhanus* is four *hasta* (cubits), and each *hasta* is eighteen *angula* (finger-breadths).
These eighteen *angula* refer to the old small measure; compared to the current large measure, they are only fifteen *angula*. Thus, one *dhanus* consists of four *hasta*.
The total length is six chi. Calculated at seven *dhanus*, it is forty-two chi. Each of the remaining six intervals is likewise; thus, the total is two hundred and ninety-four chi.
With five chi making one *bu* (step), this amounts to fifty-eight *bu* and four chi, plus a fifth part. Regarding those within the same boundary on open ground:
[one may] sit in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka-bandha*) at a distance of seven chi from the face of the body. Regarding those in different boundaries: [it is] beyond seven chi.

This is the boundary of the araṇya (forest hermitage). Second, the boundaries for robes differ between two persons. Third, one does not go to relinquish or assemble [the robes]. Fourth, being separated from the three robes constitutes a grave offense;
fifth, being separated from other robes constitutes a light offense. Regarding whether or not one should subsequently relinquish and repent, all is as clarified above.

Next is the precept on the one-month robe. When the three robes are worn out and tattered, unable to sustain the body, and one lacks the means to acquire new ones, the Buddha permitted [the use of] a full set even if it exceeds the standard length.

Because the group of six monks (Ṣaḍvargika) used insufficient robes and, in order to obtain sufficient ones, committed an offense by entrusting them to others, the Buddha established this rule with a maximum limit of one month.
Even if one lacks the resources, exceeding this period constitutes an offense. There are six specific conditions; the first is the three...

1. The robes are worn out and tattered. 2. One obtains new ones but lacks sufficient [old ones to replace them]. 3. One intends to make three robes (tricīvara) to substitute for those that are old; if one makes other types of robes instead, this is subsumed under the first precept. 4.

One does not perform the prescribed methods of opening [the robe], such as the *pariśuddhi* (purification/declaration of purity). 5. Excluding circumstances where there is no offense. 6. Determining the offense according to the transgression.

The textual analysis of the characteristics of the offense has two parts: first, the opening of the full [rule]; second, the section beginning with "At that time, the group of six," which provides the occasion for the opening.
Regarding the arising of an offense: those who possess *pāṃśukūla* (rag-robes) refer to those received without an owner; other types of robes refer to those bestowed as gifts by donors (*dānapati*).

"If the robes are not of the same kind" means that these two types of robes are of different categories. "If they are insufficient, one should take from among them" means that if the two types of robes mentioned above are insufficient, one should take the *pāṃśukūla* robe, prepare it, and perform the purification (*parikarma*).
The root text of the precept consists of seven phrases: first, the person who commits the offense; second, excluding what is not "extra"; third...
This clarifies the time of the offense. 4. From "If a bhikṣu... onwards, it clarifies the improper time and the robe. 5. From "Having received it, quickly...
onwards, because the robe is already sufficient, no exception is granted. 6. From "If it is insufficient... onwards, when the robe is insufficient, an exception is granted for a limit of one month.
