7. From "If it exceeds... onwards, the offense is incurred according to the transgression; this is explained in detail in the *Vibhaṅga*. The first four phrases are explained individually. From "If ten days... onwards, they are combined.
The remaining phrases are explained. This section is divided into two parts. First, up until the twenty-ninth day, there is the distinction between what constitutes an offense and what does not.
Second, from the thirtieth day onward, all [cases] constitute an offense. Regarding the first part, it initially takes ten days as the standard rule;

within these ten days, one who maintains the regular practice incurs no offense. Within these ten days, the period is further divided into two sections. First, it clarifies the case of "sharing [a robe]."
Regarding robes: if they are sufficient and do not require alteration, teaching their construction does not constitute an offense; this explains the fifth phrase.

Second, "if one does not cut or trim" refers to violating the rule and thus committing an offense; this explains the seventh phrase. In this manner, eleven [phrases] correspond to twelve, and twelve correspond to thirteen;
the meaning of permitting an offense is the same. Therefore it is said: "up to the twenty-ninth day, it is likewise. This applies to all such stages.
In the middle [of the period], if the requisite robes (*sabhāga-cīvara*) are insufficient, this constitutes the meaning of the sixth case.

Regarding the second [period] of thirty days or more, one incurs an offense regardless of whether the requisite robes are sufficient or not. Now, "requisite robes" refers to those of the same category within the ten types of robes;

"not requisite" means they are of different categories and thus not the same. Furthermore, "requisite robes" may also refer to the materials for the three robes (*tricīvara*), while "not requisite" refers to the remainder.
The *dīrghacīvara* (extra robe).
Next, taking up the precept regarding robes from a nun who is not a relative (*apratisaṃbandhinī*). The reason this was established is due to three meanings:
first, because in general, when those below show reverence to those above, their devotion is so earnest that they do not begrudge any of their possessions; however, the Great Saṅgha [is not so].

First, if one lacks skillful deliberation and accepts [offerings] upon being given an opportunity, it will cause the donor to fall into poverty. Second, as the forms of male and female are distinct, there is no principle for them to intermingle;

yet once wealth and goods have been exchanged, the bonds of affection become biased and intimate. From this, defilement arises, which may cause the destruction of the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*). Such a perilous situation is extremely fearsome.
Third, the circumstances involve public censure and suspicion, making it difficult to distinguish between purity and impurity; should one be slandered, there would be no [defense].

This is for the sake of self-clarification. Because of these various transgressions, they are prohibited. There are five specific conditions: first, [the recipient] must be a *bhikṣuṇī*, excluding the two lower assemblies; second, she must not be a relative;
third, it must be one’s own five robes of proper measure, excluding other items (according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*, even a bowl of proper measure constitutes an offense);
fourth, it must be intended as a gift, excluding cases of trade; fifth, the offense is incurred upon receiving it. According to the fifth section of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*, if...

Regarding many bhikṣus taking a single robe from a bhikṣuṇī: if many people take it, there is an offense for all; if one bhikṣu takes a single robe from many bhikṣuṇīs, the offense is calculated according to the number of bhikṣuṇīs.

(From the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Chapter Six. If she gives it because she was previously invited, or because he is staying in her private room, or because she gives it for the purpose of preaching the Dharma to him, there is no offense.
In the section on "Rebukes": When a bhikṣuṇī wearing tattered robes went to the Buddha’s presence, this served as the occasion for his awakening. The Buddha... [text ends].
Regarding the statement, "One should not speak to a nun in such a manner," etc.: the five robes are originally intended to sustain the body for the sake of cultivating the Path.
To now give them away to others at will is to lack the full set of robes; to practice giving while violating the precepts is contrary to the Dharma. Therefore, it is said that one "should not.

The Buddha permitted other robes—meaning those outside the five—to be given to others as one pleases. This completes the five phrases of the precept: first, the person who commits the offense; second, [the object] which is not...

Regarding relatives (*ñāti*): there are three ways of taking robes, four exceptions regarding trade, and five points concerning the commission of an offense; these are explained in detail [in the *Vinaya-vibhaṅga*].
Now, as for "relatives," this refers to parents and so forth, up to blood relations within seven generations. According to the *Vinaya-uttaragrantha*, there are four types of relative associations:
first, association through the mother’s mother; second, association through the mother’s father; third, association through the father’s mother; and fourth, association through the father’s father.
Regarding the section on relatives: these four types of relatives exhaustively encompass all categories of kinship. All subsequent textual explanations of relatives are identical to this. Question:

Why does a nun who takes a robe from the Saṃgha incur only a *duṣkṛta* (light) offense? Answer: The Great Saṃgha consists of those of high status and seniority; they do not interact frequently with nuns.

Since the occasion for a nun to receive [robes] from them is rare, she incurs only a *duṣkṛta*. Question: If the giving by the Saṃgha is so rare, why would it constitute a *sthūlātyaya* (grave) offense? Answer: Regarding the giving by the Saṃgha... [text continues].

Regarding the *ni* (nun’s) robe: the prohibition against criticizing [a nun] for taking [robes] after midday is established because the underlying fault is profound. Therefore, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.

Those who offer this interpretation distinguish between the two cases based on whether there is criticism or not. As for the two types of taking, the frequency differs; thus, for the *bhikṣu* (monk), both the act of taking and the criticism incur a *pāyattika* offense.
For the *bhikṣuṇī* (nun), however, the act is rare and there is no criticism; both the taking and the giving incur only a *duṣkṛta* offense.

Next is the precept against having a nun who is not a relative wash one’s old clothes. The reason this was established is that the Saṃgha consists of those who are superior and venerable, while [the laity] occupy a subordinate position;

nuns likewise occupy a lower rank, and it is difficult for them to perform tasks intended for superiors. Thus, without due consideration, one might suddenly command their labor, which leads to the arising of defilement and transgression, the neglect of one's duties, and the inciting of public reproach.
There are five specific conditions: first, she must be a *bhikṣuṇī*; this excludes the two lower assemblies (śrāmaṇerīs and śikṣamāṇās). Second...
1. Not a relative; 2. It is an old garment; 3. Except for specific causes (as stated below in the text, which opens with the exceptions of illness and borrowing, which do not constitute an offense);
4. Having finished washing, dyeing, and beating it; 5. The full formulation of the precept consists of five clauses: first, a person; second, a nun who is not a relative;

third, an old garment; fourth, causing her to wash, dye, or beat it; fifth, the incurrence of the offense. Question: Why are the three precepts regarding washing, dyeing, and beating combined into one regulation? Answer: Because of three reasons.
Combined: (1) the location of the nun is the same; (2) the old garment is no different; (3) the characteristics of the offense: because it has become soiled, it must be washed;
because the color has faded, it must be dyed; because it is shrunken, it must be beaten. In the commentary, the first three are explained individually, while the latter two are explained together.

According to these eight actions, there should be eight cases, yet here there are only five: the first case consists of three *thullaccaya* offenses; the next three cases consist of two *thullaccaya* offenses each.

One *kṣema* (auspicious). Next, there are three further phrases: one *uddiṣṭa* (instructed) and two *kṣema*. These are omitted in the text. Next, one phrase consists of three *kṣema* with no *uddiṣṭa*.

According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*: if one instructs to dye and then washes; if one instructs to dye and then beats [the cloth]; if one instructs to beat and then washes; if one does not perform what was instructed to be done;
or if one performs what was not instructed to be done—these constitute offenses against the *vinaya*.

Next is the precept against begging for robes from a householder who is not a relative. The reason it was established is that, according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*, there are four benefits:
first, to cause the Buddha-dharma to flourish; second, to bring an end to disputes and litigation; third, to extinguish the unwholesome minds of others;
and fourth, to inspire faith and joy in sentient beings toward the True Dharma. There are six specific conditions [for its violation], the first of which is...
1. Possessing the three robes in full; 2. lacking two of the four causes and conditions; 3. from a non-relative householder;

4. for one's own sake; 5. of proper measure; 6. having come into one's possession. These are the five phrases that complete the precept: 1. a person; 2. a non-relative householder and his wife; 3. begging for a robe.

Fourth, the exclusion of causes and conditions; fifth, the offense incurred immediately upon acceptance. Regarding "other times," the following lists the conditions for non-offense; however, only the four propositions are explained, while the opening conditions are not.

Next is the precept against receiving robes beyond one's needs. Should one suddenly encounter the four calamities and lose or have the three robes stolen, a person of pure faith may hear of this and exhaust their poverty to give as an offering.

In such a case, it is not improper to receive more than the usual limit without moderation; however, to exceed the limit when not in such circumstances fosters greed and distresses others, which is utterly inappropriate.

There are six distinct conditions: first, the loss or theft of the three robes; second, a householder who is not a relative; third, giving because of such a loss—if it is not for the sake of a loss, one may accept whatever is given;
fourth, knowing that the gift was given for the sake of a loss; fifth, exceeding the prescribed measure; sixth, receiving and taking possession of the item.
Among these conditions, regarding the taking of a householder’s robe to give to the group of six bhikṣus or to others: this refers to...
It is also an offense for another. According to this text, provided that one accepts [the gift] improperly, it constitutes an offense regardless of whether the person is oneself or another.

Thus, according to the three ancient interpretations, an offense occurs regarding property belonging to another; in the case of one's own property, it is a violation of the precept. The six phrases of the root text are: first, the offender;
second, encountering the four conditions; third, a non-relative householder; fourth, being invited at one’s own discretion and below, for the sake of a husband.

[The text] explains that giving is [the first point]. "Five are for bhikṣus" and below teaches receiving with contentment. "Sixth, if exceeding" and below concerns the offense incurred by receiving in excess.

Next, it explains the phrase "except for the second," wherein the others are fully clarified. Regarding "if one loses one robe" and below, this explains the fifth clause, which teaches the characteristics of what should be received.
Within this section there are four parts: first, clarifying whether or not one should take [a robe], meaning that if one loses one or two, one should not receive [another].
If one loses these three, one should accept with contentment. Regarding the second type of contentment, there are two lower categories that explain the distinctions of contentment.
When a layperson gives robes because a bhikṣu has lost his robes, and the recipient accepts them merely in accordance with the donor’s original intention, this is called "contentment.
However, since this contentment accords with the dharma of householders, it is called "the contentment of householders. As for renunciants...
Contentment refers to the three robes. That is to say, if one originally loses these three, it is called "lack of contentment.

Now, to receive these three again is contentment. Furthermore, this contentment accords with the dharma of those who have gone forth; therefore, it is called "the contentment of those who have gone forth.

If a layperson makes an unrestricted invitation (*pavāraṇā*), it is permitted to accept such an unrestricted invitation. Regarding robes that are fine or thin, accepting more than the standard amount does not constitute an offense. If there is... [text ends]

"Any remainder below [the limit]" does not constitute a transgression; one may accept and receive according to what is offered. This explains the fourth phrase. "If a bhikṣu... and so forth explains the sixth phrase:
"accepting beyond [the limit] constitutes an offense. This refers to losing one acceptance for two, and so on, up to losing three acceptances for four.
All such cases constitute accepting beyond the point of sufficiency.

Next is the precept against encouraging a layperson to increase the price [of a robe]. The reason it was established is as follows: although a gift may be offered with pure faith, the donor’s intention is limited.

Yet, if one now finds this insufficient and demands more, it violates the donor’s feelings and causes them distress. This offense is complete when six conditions are met: (1) a non-relative layperson has provided the funds for a robe;
(2) the donor’s intention is limited; (3) one knows the gift is limited; (4) one finds it insufficient and encourages an increase; (5) the other [party]...

Increasing the price of the thread; sixth, the offense is incurred upon acceptance. There are six phrases for the full precept: first, the offender; second, the donor is not a relative; third, the price of the robe is fixed;
fourth, being a bhikṣu who has not accepted an invitation to choose [the material]; fifth, arriving at the house of a layperson; sixth, [the act of] taking.
If one finds it insufficient, one should encourage an increase. Sixth, if one obtains a robe, the offense is incurred upon acceptance; this is explained in detail in the *Vistara*.
Regarding the phrase "the seeker" and those that follow, this explains the fifth clause. Although the word "seeker" does not appear in the root text (*mūla*), the sense of seeking is present;

therefore, it is cited and explained in the *Vistara*. Herein, "increase" must refer to an increase upon the primary substance itself; if it were a different substance, it would fall under the preceding category of "begging for robes."

Question: Why is it that adding even a single thread constitutes an offense, whereas begging for [a robe] requires one full set? Answer: Begging was not his original intention; he left it to their deliberation.

Since the sense of causing distress was minimal, an offense occurred only with one full set. However, having first encouraged [the donor] and fixed a specific deadline, if he now violates the donor’s intention, an offense occurs immediately upon a single thread.
This concludes the explanation of the four and six lines of the second section, beginning with "This bhikṣu... and so forth.

Next, the exhortation to the two householders: the remaining meaning is as before; the only distinction is that they are exhorted to act together. Question: If one exhorts them to act together, whether there is an increase [in the number of participants] or not, what offense is committed?
Answer: Although one commits an offense if there is an increase, one does not commit an offense if there is no increase.

Since it is still the case that two people are acting together, it belongs to this precept. According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, the offense is incurred precisely when one exhorts a husband and wife to act together.
Next is the precept concerning the solicitation of robes beyond the limit. The reason it was established is that the price for robes is a precious commodity, and the locus of excessive greed is deep.

A bhikṣu who advances in practice must renounce such things; since he does not keep them himself, he has them entrusted to laypeople. Later, if he requires a robe, he should solicit it with due consideration and patience.
Now, however, he urges and hastens the matter, causing distress to the person before him. Therefore, a time limit was set, and exceeding it is prohibited.

[This constitutes] an offense. This precept follows the precept concerning the possession of precious objects; therefore, such expedients are employed. There are four constituent conditions: first, the sending of the price for a robe;

second, the entrustment to a *kappiyakāraka* (a person authorized to handle pure items) to purchase clothing; third, the demand for it after the time limit has passed; fourth, the acquisition of the robe, which immediately constitutes the offense.

This precept is established solely because the mind of a king or minister is moved [by greed], leading them to demand with haste and urgency, thereby causing harm to the *kappiyakāraka* and resulting in the binding of the offense.
This consists of ten phrases: 1. The offender. 2. "If a king," etc.: the donor sends a messenger to deliver precious goods as the price for robes.
3. "That messenger," etc.: having received the command, he delivers them. 4. "That bhikṣu," etc.: fearing the offense of possessing precious goods, he does not dare to accept them himself.
5. "That messenger says," etc.: the messenger asks for a *viśuddhika* (pure) agent. 6. "The bhikṣu who requires robes," etc.: [the offender] indicates the location of the *viśuddhika* agent.
7. At that time, the messenger returns with the report after having delivered [the message]. 8. From "The bhikṣu who requires robes" onwards, the method for seeking [robes] is explained. 9.
From "If he does not obtain them" onwards, the offense incurred by seeking beyond the limit is explained. 10. From "If he does not obtain them" onwards, whether or not one proceeds is discussed.

Regarding the explanation of these ten points, only the first two, as well as the eighth, ninth, and tenth, are explained; the remainder are not explained at all. The text for the explanation of the eighth sentence consists of three parts, the first of which has three sub-sections.
[The section on] Speech. Second, six [instances of] silence. Third, speech and silence mutually canceling each other. First, regarding "speech," it is as the text states.

Next, regarding "silence": not knowing when the time for silence has arrived. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Sengqi lü), fascicle nine, says: "It is like a person entering a storehouse to take goods and placing them upon a shop counter;

or like wrapping up goods in a bundle—one must depart immediately. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Jianlun), fascicle fifteen, asks: "What is meant by 'silence'? It means not speaking with the mouth.
One should stand and not sit. If one is called to sit, one must not sit; if food or drink is offered, it must likewise not be accepted.

If invited to preach the Dharma or offer prayers of blessing (*dhāraṇī-praṇidhāna*), one must not do so in any case. If a donor asks, "For what reason have you come here? one should reply, "The householder should know for himself.
Next, the manner of speech and silence that mutually refute [the opponent] is as described in the text. The remaining signs are understandable.
Next is the precept concerning the making of bedding from mixed wild silk cotton (*tūla*). According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*, volume five, it was established for four reasons:
first, to prevent slander; second, to increase faith and respect; third, to ensure peace and comfort while practicing the Path; and fourth, to avoid harming living beings.

The separate conditions consist of five factors: (1) going to a silkworm house; (2) [it being] *koseyya* (silk); (3) seeking it for one's own sake; (4) making it into bedding; and (5) its completion constitutes an offense.
The three phrases in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* can be understood accordingly. The term "various wild silkworms" used here indicates its general name.
The other text’s use of the term *koseyya* is a designation for cotton-wool. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "*Koseyya* refers to insects..."
Regarding "cotton" (*karpāsa*) and bedding: "bedding" refers to mattresses and cushions. The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (Wǎndùn lù), fascicle 5, states: "Kauśeya is the name for cotton.
In this country, silkworms are raised according to the custom of the land of Qin; when the worms have matured and the cotton is obtained, it is called kauśeya.

In this country, they make garments from cotton, which are of two kinds: first, by carding the cotton and weaving it, according to the method used for making felt; second, by spinning the cotton into thread."
Weaving them to make garments—when these two types of clothing are made, they are called "reclining requisites" (*śayanāsana*). "Reclining requisites" is a name for clothing.

Because these [first two] involve harming living beings, one must relinquish them and have them cut to pieces. As for the others, which do not harm living beings, it is permitted to relinquish them in their entirety. There is only the relinquishing of the material object;
the confession of the offense is omitted because there is no object before one to face, and thus there is no returning of the item.

Next is the precept concerning black-furred bedding. Regarding various bedding materials, they may confuse people; some say they are the three robes (*tricīvara*), while others say they are bedding (*śayanāsana*).
Now, examining the intent behind the regulation, one can briefly discern its purpose.

However, as for the preceding precept, because it involves the destruction of living beings, any act of making robes, bedding, or other such items constitutes an offense. The remaining precepts are not like this, as they do not involve the destruction of living beings.

Because they were obtained in accordance with the Dharma, he made them into robes and wore them; because this invited criticism, it was prohibited. However, if one makes them into bedding or mats for lying down, there is no fault.
If [the prohibition] applied to bedding and mats for lying down, then all the bhikṣus currently using black or white woolen blankets for their beds would be committing an offense.
Yet, since they do not commit an offense, why should one be confused by this matter? Although the instruction speaks of "bedding and mats," when putting them to use, one need not hesitate.
"Black and white. Is this not a case where successive transmitters have become confused regarding the text, thereby causing practitioners to fall short of the intended meaning of the teaching?
Furthermore, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "There are also two methods for making robes from black wool: first, by carding and weaving black wool to produce fine felt;
second, by spinning it into thread and weaving it into cloth. Both of these types of robes are termed 'reclining requisites' (*niṣīdana*). As for 'reclining requisites':"

This is a name for clothing. Furthermore, it is said that this woolen garment may be used as one of the three robes (tricīvara) and may be maintained throughout the entire period [of the rainy season retreat].

If so, how is it that this text refers to it as a "reclining mat" (śayanāsana)? Answer: A "reclining mat" is a general term for clothing; alternatively, it may be so called because it is used for covering while reclining, rather than for spreading out.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Sengqi lü), fascicle nine, states: "A bhikṣu makes a felt [blanket] for his three robes and his *niṣīdana* (sitting mat), with the sole exception of..."
The water-strainer and the net-bag are all made of felt. Before the Buddha had prescribed the rules, the bhikṣus wore felt garments;

while staying in the open air, they lived securely as if in a tent. After the precepts were established, they no longer wore felt garments; consequently, they suffered much illness and did not live in security.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha permitted them to make them by mixing materials—namely, black, white, and the three lower grades. It was for this reason.
It is known that this is not for spreading as bedding. Furthermore, the opening passage mentions "wool mats for lying down," which serves as clear evidence.

Moreover, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "It should be relinquished to the Saṃgha, and the Saṃgha shall spread it on the ground; if it is spread upon a rope bed or a wooden bed, [it is permissible].

As for why pure black wool is not permitted: it is because this hair is precious, and its use increases greed; furthermore, it would be confused with the worldly practice of sexual desire. This is established through specific conditions.
Four [factors]: first, pure black wool; second, making it into bedding; third, for one's own sake; fourth, the offense is incurred upon completion.

According to the *Jianlun* (Treatise on Seeing), "pure" means not mixed with other types of wool. The tenth fascicle of the *Shisonglü* (Ten Recitation Vinaya) states that there are four kinds of black wool from black sheep:
naturally black, dyed blue-black, dyed black with mud, and dyed black with tree bark. The commentary explains: "making it into a mat, a pillow, or a small square seat."
Regarding bedding such as woolen mats, there is no offense if one does not wear [the prescribed colors].
Next is the precept concerning white bedding: white is an improper garment, and black likewise incurs fault; only by mixing them may it be appropriate.

Since pure white already gives rise to transgression, the rule was established to require that they be made mixed. If one relies on the case of pure white, the specific conditions for the offense are complete.

The four [points] are as before. The *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* consists of four sections: first, the person who commits the offense; second, the making of bedding; third, the instruction to participate in the construction; and fourth, from the words "If a bhikṣu...
onwards, the non-participation and the determination of the offense. This text does not clarify this point. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "The second part is black;
the third part is white; the fourth part is below. A *pātra* is four *liang*."
Next is the precept against discarding bedding and furniture before six years have passed. Although these items are old, they are still capable of serving as requisites for the body;

yet, by now discarding them to create new ones, one constantly engages in such construction, thereby perpetuating one’s own bonds of greed, wasting the offerings of the faithful, and inviting no small censure.

Therefore, the Noble One established this rule. It possesses five specific conditions: first, the bedding and furniture previously possessed are old and have not yet reached six years; second, [one must not...]
The Monastic Law (*Saṃghadharma*): 1. Discarding the old to create the new; 2. For one’s own sake; 3. Completing the construction constitutes an offense. In the text, does this accord with the law?

It is as clarified above regarding "staying overnight separated from one's robe. There are six clauses for the full precept: 1. The offender; 2. Making a new bedding; 3. The restriction of six years; 4.
Creating another before the period is complete; 5. Excluding cases where there is a permitted exception; 6. The prescribed offense.
Next is the precept against not attaching a sitting cloth (*niṣīdana*). The sitting cloth is for the support of the body; it matters not whether it is new or old.

To discard the old and create a new one increases greed and wastes material resources. The Buddha, in order to quell greed and prevent the waste of the faithful’s offerings, prescribed that one must attach the old cloth.

To fail to attach it constitutes an offense. There are five specific conditions [for this rule]: first, possessing an old sitting cloth; second, further creating a new one; third, doing so for one's own sake; fourth, not using the old cloth [to patch the new].

The *tiē* (patch). Regarding the five points for composing the section on the offense of commissioning [a new sitting mat]: In the text, first is the original regulation that one must patch the old when making a new one; second, the six groups of monks failed to apply the patches, which gave rise to the transgression.

The preceding passage has three parts: first, observing the disorderly state of the sitting mats (*niṣīdana*); second, the arising of the intention to establish the regulation regarding patches; third, informing the assembly so they may know. The three phrases of the *Prātimokṣa* [text] are as follows;
the remaining text is self-evident. According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*: "If a bhikṣu makes a *niṣīdana*..."
Regarding the bedding and sitting mats used for practical purposes, they must be bordered by a span (*vitasti*) on all sides to ensure they are of a discolored hue (*kāsāya*).
Next is the precept concerning carrying wool over three *yojanas*: when one who has left the household life carries wool, it is as improper as carrying broken tiles;

since this violates the rules of decorum, it is inconsistent with the protocols of the Path. Furthermore, because this conditioned physical form relies upon material sustenance to exist, three exceptions are permitted beyond that limit.

The offense of carrying [wool] has four specific conditions: first, it must be noble wool; second, for one's own sake; third, carrying it oneself; fourth, exceeding three *yojana*s, which constitutes the offense.

The root text of the precept consists of three phrases: first, the person who commits the offense; second, the allowance to carry it up to three *yojana*s; third, the transgression beyond that limit, which constitutes the offense.
In the detailed commentary, the first two [phrases] are self-evident. The phrase "If someone carries... explains the third phrase. Within this section, there are three parts: first...
One must not assist in holding [the wool]. Second, one must not employ other members of the community. Third, one must not carry other lowly items.
Next is the precept concerning employing a nun who is not a relative to wash, dye, or card wool. According to the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, this was established for three reasons:
to increase the superior Dharma; because if the community of nuns engages in manual labor such as washing and dyeing, they will neglect their own proper duties and consequently lack majestic virtue.

This is to refute superior dharmas; furthermore, it is for the sake of establishing the sequential causes and conditions for ceasing unwholesome dharmas; and furthermore, it is so that both communities may each possess purity.
The remaining meanings are the same as before. In this case, both new and old [offenses] constitute a transgression; it was prescribed solely because it diminishes spiritual merit. Question:

Why is it that nuns are permitted to card wool but prohibited from carrying wool? Answer: Because carrying wool is a rare occurrence while carding it is frequent, there is a distinction between light and heavy offenses.

Next is the precept against possessing precious objects. The substance of such treasures is of great value and weight; they foster greed and obstruct the Path. According to the *Mahā-saṃghika-vinaya-śāstra*, the establishment of this precept provides three benefits:

to stop slander, to extinguish strife and contention, and to establish the various practices of the noble ones, such as alms-seeking. The specific conditions for its violation consist of four factors:
first, it must be money or treasure—referring to gold, silver, or the currency used in a country; second, one must know it to be money or treasure; third...
For oneself. Regarding the four types of taking and receiving, within the text: from "At that time, the King" downward, it clarifies whether [the action] was appropriate or not.
Within this section, there are four parts: first, a minister speaks of the impropriety to the Buddha; second, from "The Buddha said" downward, it clarifies the fault and its inappropriateness;
"one is certainly not a śramaṇa or a son of the Śākya" is the statement clarifying the fault; third, from "I have... downward... [text continues].

It was opened to construct a dwelling for the purpose of supporting the essentials of the Path. Regarding the passage from the fourth minister downward that cites the metaphor of the four afflictions (*upakleśa*)—the sun and moon—the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Póshā zhèngwén) should divide these into five;
it enumerates them as five obscurations (*pañca-āvaraṇa*). That the present text speaks of only four is because they are intended to correspond to the four afflictions of the śramaṇas.
Since those four have been cited, by implication smoke and clouds are included. The reason for this is: [The remainder of the text follows...]
Because they are identical. Alternatively, that which can produce smoke is the smoke of the asuras. Regarding the afflictions of the śramaṇa:
alcohol is the root of negligence; lust is the source of birth and death; gold and silver give rise to heavy afflictions; and wrong livelihood destroys the roots of goodness.
Next, the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* (the root text of the precepts) will be explained through seven sections: first, the wording of the precept; second, the nature of the objects to be grasped;

third, the action of the one who grasps; fourth, the exceptions where grasping does not constitute an offense; fifth, the permission to employ a "pure person" (*śucika-puruṣa*) as an assistant; sixth, the method for performing the ritual of purification (*pariśuddhi*); and seventh, whether a *śrāmaṇera* should or should not [grasp such objects].

In the first section, the root text of the precept consists of five phrases: first, the person who commits the offense; second, the act of grasping by oneself; third, the object to be grasped; [fourth, the intention; and fifth, the completion of the act].

Treasure. Fourth, the karma of instructing others; fifth, the determination of the offense. Regarding the essence (*tattva*) next: according to this text, there are three based on the essence, which, when divided, become seven.

The remainder constitutes "treasure. To possess it constitutes a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*). However, as for money, it is said that if it bears inscriptions or images upon it—presumably because it is what is used in a particular country—it is not established as [the full object of the rule].

Among the four phrases in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, there are cases where, although it is used in a certain country, the characteristics are not fully met; such instances constitute a *vyatikrama* (transgression).
For a bhikṣuṇī: if it is not for use in the country, and she grasps it despite its being complete in its characteristics, she commits a *vyatikrama* (transgression).

If it is for use in the country and she grasps it while it is complete in its characteristics, she commits a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture). If it is not for use in the country and it is not complete in its characteristics, there is no offense even if she grasps it made of copper or iron.
The fifth section of the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*. "Precious things" refers to the seven types of precious substances: gold, silver, mani-jewels, pearls, coral, carnelian, and agate.

If one accepts or keeps such treasures, it constitutes an offense of expiation with forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*). This also applies to various forms of currency resembling precious things, such as crystal, amber, and quartz.
Various kinds of beads—such as brass, ancient copper, iron, white wax, lead, and tin—are called "counterfeit jewels. If one keeps money or counterfeit jewels, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one makes vessels from counterfeit jewels, they are included within the category of the "one hundred and one items" (*ekādaśa-vastu*) and do not require the ritual of purification (*viśuddhi*).
If they are not included among the one hundred and one items, then all vessels, whether they are [specific] utensils or not, must be declared pure (*viśodhayitavya*). Next...
Regarding "one who seizes": the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Sengqi lü), chapter ten, states: "With one's own hand" means either the body itself, a part of the body, or a continuity of the body.
"The body" refers to the entire body. "A part of the body" refers to the hands, feet, elbows, or knees. "A continuity of the body" refers to...
If one fastens various robes such as the three dharma-robes, or places items such as a bowl, a small bowl, or a needle-case [kancani], this is called "continuity with the body.
Whenever a bhikṣu obtains money or the value of an *anvāraka* robe, he must not take it with his own hand; he should have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person) handle it.
If there is no *kappiya-kāraka*, he should point toward a border region and say, "The people there know how to do this. Once it has been placed on the ground, he may then use it himself.

One should cast grass, leaves, bricks, tiles, or similar objects from afar onto it to cover it, waiting for a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to handle requisites) to arrive so that they may be informed.
If the *kappiya-kāraka* arrives and, having learned of it, takes it away, one should instruct them to walk in front [of the object] so that they know to place it in a certain spot.

If the *kappiya-kāraka* is trustworthy, one may allow them to take it according to their own judgment and inform them to place it in a certain spot. Next, regarding those who may handle it: the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, chapter nineteen, states:
The Dragon King Anavatapta invited the bhikṣus to observe the rains retreat (varṣā). He offered gold and silver to them, but the bhikṣus did not dare to accept it.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said: "That gold and silver are like these stones and earth; you may use them as you please. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* also states the same.
Furthermore, when non-humans or devas invite bhikṣus, it is also like this. Moreover, regarding objects belonging to humans, it is as prescribed in the ninety rules of training (*navati-śikṣāpada*).
Regarding the picking up of items dropped in a dye-vat or treasures left at a lodging, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"If there is gold, silver, or money within a bundle or upon a wooden peg, one must not pick it up oneself; rather, one should have a pure person (*śuci*) take charge of it.
If the pure person is too small [to carry it], one may lift it up and have them take charge of it. When lifting it, one should say: 'I am lifting the pure person.'"

I shall describe the case of the *kappiya-kāraka* (the one who makes things permissible). Once he has received the inferior items, he should be made to untie them. If he does not know how to untie them, one may take him by the hand and teach him how to untie them.
Once they are untied, he should be taught how to count them. If he does not know how to count them, one may take the *kappiya-kāraka*’s hand and count with him.

Once counted, as for the remainder, he should be taught to place them back into the bag. If he does not know how to place them, one may take his hand and teach him to place them in the bag. Having placed them...
The bag has already been tied by a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to handle what is not permitted).

If it is not known to have been tied, the *kappiya-kāraka* should hold the bottom of the bag while the bhikṣu may tie it himself. Having tied it, he should place it back upon the ground. If the *kappiya-kāraka* is too short to reach it, he may lift it up.
If a box, a basket, or similar items are on a shelf, when setting them aside, taking them, lifting them, or covering them, it is likewise. If...
When walking along the road, if an attendant (*karmadāna*) is carrying gold or silver, and if the attendant is small in stature, one may take the hand and lead them away.
When crossing water, one may carry them across; one should say: "I am ferrying the attendant; I am ferrying the attendant.

If the attendant is small and cannot board the boat, one may carry them aboard; one should say: "I am lifting the attendant; I am lifting the attendant. The same applies when disembarking from the boat.

It is thus. Furthermore, on the eighth day of the fourth month, during the time of the great assembly and offerings, a bhikṣu must not take with his own hands any golden or silver stūpas, images of bodhisattvas, banners, flags, or offering implements that are plated with gold or silver;

he should have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person) hold them. If they should fall to the ground, he should grasp them where there is no gold or silver. If they are entirely coated [with precious metals], he should use a cloth [to hold them].

One should grasp objects such as flowers while wrapping one's hands with them. If there is nothing to wrap the hands with, one may grasp the image at any spot where it has not yet been smeared [with ointment].

When bathing images made of gold or silver, one should have a *kappiyakāraka* (a person authorized to handle pure items) wash them. During a great assembly, if there are images of gold or silver, one should have the *kappiyakāraka* carry them out;
a monk may assist him, but he must not grasp any part containing gold or silver. A monk must not go before [the image].

"Having seized them, release them. Next, regarding the ritual for purification (*viśuddhi-dharma*), the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (Daolun), fascicle 4, states: "As for the ritual of pure giving (*viśuddhi-pradāna-dharma*):

regarding money and all precious objects, one should first seek out a lay attendant (*upāsaka*) who understands the Dharma and whose meaning can be communicated. One should say: 'According to the dharma of us bhikṣus, we do not store money or treasures.
I now appoint you, the donor (*dānapati*), as the master of purity (*viśuddhi-adhipati*). Hereafter, whatever money or treasures I obtain, I shall give them all to you.'"
[If] the one who acts as the purifier dies or departs for a distant foreign land, one should seek another purifier. However, there are two ways of declaring [an object] pure (*pariśuddha*).
If a layperson brings money or precious objects and gives them to a bhikṣu, the bhikṣu should simply say: "This is an impure thing; I should not possess it. If it is pure, I shall accept it.
This is the method of purification (*pariśuddhi-dharma*). If a layperson says, "I give these precious objects to the bhikṣu," and the bhikṣu...
He said, "I should not keep this. The attendant said, "Keep it after purifying the object; that itself constitutes the act of purification (*śodhana*).

If a layperson does not say to keep it after purifying the object, and the bhikṣu himself does not declare it purified, but simply sets it aside on the ground—if there is another bhikṣu, one should follow him in declaring it purified, and may keep it for as long as is necessary.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, fascicle 54, also says: "This is an impure object. If..."
The *śuddha* (pure person) shall receive it. Next, the *śrāmaṇera* should not be known [as the recipient]. Next follows the detailed explanation of the method of relinquishing (*utsarga*).

Since this does not face the Path, there is no confession of transgressions (*pāpadeśanā*). This treasure the Buddha did not permit to be kept; therefore, one relinquishes it by saying, "This is not for me to possess.

In the section on returning, there are two parts. First, regarding the matter of relinquishment: if the pure master returns the treasure, one should receive it for that person's sake and cause the pure attendant (*śuddhakarmakara*) to [handle it].
Appreciate this. Accept it after exchanging it for pure items. Next, regarding the method for purifying the owner: immediately transfer the pure items to them. Next, do not pursue or reclaim them.
If one proceeds contrary to the text, it is improper.
Next is the precept against trading for jewels. Because the substance of these jewels is of great value and profit, and because they foster deep-seated greed, their trade incurs public censure;

thus, it is likewise prohibited. Furthermore, since the possession [of jewels] does not require trade, and trade does not require possession, these two precepts—possession and trade—are established separately.
Moreover, this differs in nature from the subsequent precept against buying and selling; therefore, two distinct precepts for trading are established. These have five specific conditions.
First, it is a treasure; second, mutual exchange; third, fixing the price; fourth, for one’s own sake; fifth, receiving. These are the three phrases of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.
In the detailed explanation, gold and silver each have three [categories], and with money added, there are seven. Each of these is mutually exchanged, forming forty-nine phrases (seven times seven).
Regarding "gold and so forth," the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "finished vessels, unfinished vessels, and so on. "Finished vessels" refers to rings, bracelets, tongs, chains, and the like.
The rest may be understood by analogy.

Next is the precept concerning buying and selling (*mūlyavikraya-śīla*). According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*, fascicle five: it was established because there are four benefits, and for the sake of the flourishing of the Buddha-dharma.
It is for the purpose of ceasing strife and contention; for the purpose of establishing the noble lineages; and for the purpose of increasing faith and reverence.
Among all the *pāyattika* offenses, this act of trafficking is the most grave. It would be better to be a butcher than to engage in trafficking. Why?
Because a butcher merely harms animals, whereas a trafficker deceives and harms everyone—whether layperson or monastic, wise or foolish, and whether they observe the precepts or not.
They violate the precepts; there is nowhere they do not practice deception. Furthermore, they constantly harbor evil intentions.

If they deal in grain, their minds always hope for the world to suffer famine and hunger, or for frost, hail, and pestilence to strike. If they store salt or other goods, their thoughts are always fixed on the chaos and rebellion of distant regions, and the obstruction of royal highways.
Such are the evils of those who engage in trade. As for these traded goods—should [they be sold]...
If food is prepared for the community of monks, the monks should not eat it. If a dwelling for the Saṃgha of the four directions is built, one must not reside within it.
If a stūpa or an image is made, one should not pay homage toward it; rather, as it is said, one should simply pay homage with the intention directed toward the Buddha.
Any bhikṣu who maintains the precepts should not make use of these items. If such a bhikṣu dies, the community of monks should perform a *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) to divide these items.

Regarding the explanation of terms: there are five types of commercial transactions, which are collectively termed "various kinds. When one settles a price by lowering what is high, it is called "buying and selling" (*kraya-vikraya*).
This text stipulates that if one engages in buying and selling, one commits an offense. Even if not for the sake of profit, taking [goods] directly also constitutes an offense.

Furthermore, pure speech (*viśuddha-vāk*) is not permitted here; this differs from other texts. Regarding pure speech in other texts, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations), fascicle seven, states: "If it is truly necessary..."

Regarding the object: one should deliberate carefully and say, "I shall purchase this with such-and-such an amount of goods. If the other does not give it, one should speak a second time. If they still do not give it, one should speak a third time.
If, after three requests, they still do not give it, and the bhikṣu has an urgent need for that object, he should seek out a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person) and have them purchase the object.
If the *kappiya-kāraka* does not know how to bargain in the market, the bhikṣu should first instruct them with these words: "With such-and-such an amount..."
When purchasing an item, one should be instructed as to how much that item costs. Regarding the phrase "you should consider it well":

according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, tenth [chapter], when clothing already has a fixed price in a shop and a bhikṣu comes with the payment to buy it, at the moment he places the money on the ground, he should say to the owner, "I understand this price for this garment.
If he does not speak and instead takes it away in silence, he commits an offense. This applies equally when purchasing other items.
Thus it is. The distinct conditions consist of five: first, being a householder or one from the assembly (which also includes non-Buddhists);

second, engaging in mutual trade; third, for one's own sake; fourth, fixing the price oneself; and fifth, receiving [the goods]. In the text, the five assemblies are distinguished because they share the same path;

since their discourse is straightforward, it says "one should fix the price oneself," etc. One must not engage in trade with the two types of laypeople or non-Buddhists; therefore, it says "not... [prohibiting it].
One may trade with others, but since one may not trade for oneself, one should have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person) conduct the exchange.

The fundamental nature of the monastic discipline requires that one follow the sentiments of the objects [involved]; therefore, if there are those who regret [the transaction], they are all sent back [to their original state]. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, the limit is within seven days. Regarding the property of the Saṃgha, it is generally said:
"If the price for a robe of the Saṃgha has not been increased after the three proclamations, it may be increased; once the three proclamations have been made, it should not be increased."
The Saṃgha should also not give the robe, as it has already been assigned to another. When a bhikṣu has received the robe after three proclamations, he should not regret it;
even if he regrets it, the Saṃgha must not return it. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If an item is sold among the members of the Saṃgha, there is no offense in taking the highest price offered.
If the upādhyāya or ācārya wishes to take [the item], they may not preempt it. If a bhikṣu returns [an item] to another bhikṣu, they may trade with him."
Regarding buying and bartering: if one engages in impure speech while buying, the buyer incurs no offense.
This applies even when engaging in impure speech with any of the ninety-six types of renunciants; the buyer incurs no offense. The root precept consists of three phrases.

Within the section on the Śākyas, these are applied to five objects, each serving as a heading, thus forming five sets of five phrases. As for buying and selling, we shall first explain the act of selling; there are three textual sections.

First, there is the general statement of "up and down. Next is the increased sale; next is the further increased sale—this constitutes the higher price. In the purchase, there are likewise three stages:
first, the direct payment of five *kārsāpaṇas*; then repeatedly going up and down; next, giving three *kārsāpaṇas* is called "reduced purchase";
next, giving one *kārsāpaṇa* is called "further reduced. The purchase follows the pattern of the sale; therefore it is said that "the purchase is also like this."

Next is the Precept on the Alms Bowl. The alms bowl is a vessel for receiving offerings; it serves first to sustain the body. Now, to store and accumulate them without satiety invites censure and harms the Path.
Furthermore, because material objects are subject to constant change, the Buddha permitted their acceptance through donation, setting a limit of ten days;

should this period be exceeded, an offense is incurred. There are five specific conditions [for this rule]: first, one already possesses a bowl that has been formally accepted and maintained; second, one further obtains another bowl that conforms to the Dharma—namely:

Regarding the substance, measurement, and color—these three are as previously stated. Three points are not mentioned as pure: fourth, the absence of a formal cause; fifth, the offense incurred after ten days have passed. These constitute the four phrases of the full precept:
first, the offender; second, the extra bowl; third, the allowance for ten days; fourth, the formal conclusion of the offense.

In the commentary, the section beginning with "As for the bowl" explains the second phrase. This passage contains four parts: first, a general enumeration of the six types of bowls, comprehensively clarifying their substance, location, and color. Second...

The essential points are as follows: first, the distinction that the substance [of the bowl] consists of only two types; second, the determination of its dimensions and limits; third, the prescription for receiving and maintaining it, as well as performing the ritual of purification (*śuddhi*), based on its possession of the three characteristics of conformity;
and fourth, the specific rules for its acceptance. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations), chapter 21, regarding the acceptance of the bowl, states:

"I, [Name], accept this *pātra* bowl, which is of the proper measure, for the purpose of long-term use" (recited three times). The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, chapter 23, states: "This is my *pātra* bowl, which is of the proper measure."

One should accept and maintain a begging bowl of appropriate size. Now, [the formula for] acceptance is recited three times. From the words "If a bhikṣu... onwards, the fourth and third phrases are explained together.

There are eight sections regarding the characteristics of an offense, and the rules for relinquishing and returning [the bowl] follow the same procedure as those for extra robes (*atireka-cīvara*), with the exception that the bowl is the specific object concerned.
Next is the precept on begging for a bowl: One bowl with five patches is sufficient to support one's body;

yet if it is still not worn out and does not leak, to beg for another again is to increase one's own greed and cause no small amount of damage and disgrace to the Saṃgha. Therefore, the Sage established this regulation. There are six specific conditions [for this offense]:

first, one already possesses a bowl that is being used; second, it has fewer than five patches and does not leak; third, one further seeks it from someone who is not a relative and resides outside the monastery.

A layperson begs [for it]. Fourth, for oneself. Fifth, obtaining a bowl in accordance with the Dharma. Sixth, upon receiving it, one commits an offense. The root text of the precept consists of two phrases;
the first section has three parts: first, the person who commits the offense; second, the old bowl not yet having reached its full lifespan; third, seeking another and the resulting formal offense.

Second, from the passage beginning "That bhikṣu," because this is distinct from other precepts, the procedure for reciting the relinquishment and returning the object is set forth. Within this, there are again two parts: first, the recitation of the relinquishment of the bowl; second, [the procedure for returning it].
Proceeding downward, one recites the text for returning [the precepts] in its entirety. Regarding the phrase "this is the time," it means using the old [precepts] while holding the new ones.

Furthermore, the four lines of text concerning the return below should all be recited in this manner; there is no difference between the confession and the non-return, so they are not recited separately.

The characteristics of the *Śīlaskandha* (Precept Text) can be understood through this explanation. Next is the method for relinquishing the confession (*pratyāpatti-dharma*). There are four parts as usual. However, regarding the wording for relinquishing, "this residence" refers to...

This means that the *sīmā* (boundary) of the precept-platform (*śīla-maṇḍala*), the minor boundary (*kṣudra-sīmā*), and the natural boundary (*prakṛti-sīmā*) are excluded, as these three are not places where one dwells.

Furthermore, a "non-dwelling place" is excluded because there is no monastic storehouse (*saṃgha-koṣṭhaka*) there. The phrase "among the Saṃgha" distinguishes this from groups of three or fewer. Next, the confession is performed according to the text. Next, regarding the four procedures for returning the bowl:
first, if a person of high status seizes and retains it, one returns the bowl of lower value directly. Second, when that bhikṣu lowers [the bowl], yet still considers it...
"Victory. Second, taking down the bowl. Third, if one takes down the bowl of this bhikṣu, he is penalized by being made to hold a new one while using his old bowl to take it down.
Fourth, when a bhikṣu guards this bowl because he fears breaking it, he is restricted by being made to guard the old bowl taken down.
These four passages all concern taking down the bowl and making [the bhikṣu] hold it. The first passage is divided into two parts: first, the assignment and retention.

Returning. Regarding the procedure for returning [the bowl] below: The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Sengqi), fascicle ten, states: "If the bowl is of great value, one should sell it and take the proceeds of ten bowls;
nine portions of the proceeds are placed in the Sangha’s pure kitchen, and one portion is returned to the owner. In this manner, it is done according to whatever amount is obtained."

All [the bowls] are limited to one being returned to their owners; the remainder shall all enter the Sangha. Next, regarding the procedure for taking down the bowls in succession, there are also two parts:

first, the formal announcement (*jñapti*); second, the distribution of the bowls. According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, a monk who knows the ritual rules is appointed by *karmavācanā* to distribute them within the assembly.

That monk should then announce: "Let each of you monks come forth holding your own bowls. Only after this does he take the bowl that has been relinquished and proceed to the seat of the senior elder (*sthavira*).
First, one should ask whether a bowl is required. If it is said that one is required, one should take the bowl of the senior monk (upādhyāya) to inspect it.
If there is no bowl, or if it is too large, too small, cracked, broken, or crooked, it should not be given. If these five defects are absent, it should be given.

Once it has been given, one takes the senior monk’s bowl and distributes it, starting from the second senior monk down to the newly ordained person; the distribution of the bowls is conducted in this same manner.

This is the Dharma. It should be determined according to the measure of the Sangha; it may be appropriate to take a new one, which is why it says to take the bowl of the senior monk (upādhyāya) and give it to the next seat.
Alternatively, if the senior monk assigns it, it is also permissible to return that bhikṣu’s bowl to him;

hence it says, "If it is given to that bhikṣu, that bhikṣu should follow the instruction of the senior monk and take this bowl. He should not fail to take it out of regard for the feelings of the other monks, nor...
One should take away what is good and give it to the wicked due to the causes and conditions of hatred. One receives and holds the lower bowl, and so on until the lower seat;

the same applies in successive order. Next, regarding the punishment for holding new items for use, there are two sections below. First, the previous two "lower" [cases] are cited because they are indeterminate.

Second, the performance of the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) to cause him to maintain [the bowls]. Regarding the scriptural statement, "to cause this bhikṣu to receive and maintain [them]," this does not mean that they are called "received and maintained" because they are received through the addition of a ritual (*adhikāra*).
It simply means that he is punished and ordered to accept and practice [this rule], namely, to maintain these two bowls; therefore, it is called "receiving and maintaining.

As for the phrase "until broken," it means that he must constantly maintain them even when the old bowls have broken; hence, it says "until broken. The majority of [commentators] say: "If, at the time of eating..."
One should carry two alms bowls, doing so for the rest of one's life. This is to demonstrate the fault of excessive desire and to sever the causal conditions for future unwholesome states.
Next, protect the bowl as prescribed in the text; the remaining passages may be understood accordingly.
Next is the precept against begging for thread oneself and having a householder who is not a relative weave a robe.

When the three robes are fully provided for, one’s resources for the Path are not deficient; yet now, by begging for thread and relying upon one's influence, one compels a weaver to weave the three robes.

This leads to the increase of greed and invites public censure; therefore, the Sage established this regulation. There are four specific conditions: first, begging for the thread oneself; second, the weaver being a non-relative.

Third, relying on one's influence, one does not pay the proper price; fourth, one commits the offense as soon as the weaving is completed. The four phrases of the root text (*śikṣāpada*) may be understood accordingly;

the detailed explanation follows the text. Regarding the explanation of the third phrase, "one who is not a relative": herein, among weavers, there are those who are relatives, those who are not relatives, and those who are both relatives and non-relatives combined.

It is the same for the one who provides the thread. By cross-referencing these factors with one another, nine permutations should be established; however, [the case] where both are relatives is not [included here].

Because there are eight permutations regarding the offense, this precept primarily constitutes a *thullaccaya* (grave offense) for the weaver, while for the owner of the thread it is merely a *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing).
Since a single phrase serves to encompass both positions, it is therefore stated simply that "one who is not a relative commits [the offense]."
Next is the precept against secretly encouraging a weaver to increase the thread when weaving a robe. A layperson originally had a robe woven for a bhikṣu;

it was right that [the bhikṣu] should acknowledge this kindness and accept it as a gift. Yet, [the bhikṣu] now secretly encourages the weaver and personally provides the payment, thereby undermining the benefactor’s merit.
For this reason, the rule was established. There are six constituent conditions: first, a layperson prepares the thread and dispatches a weaver; second, there is a deliberate intention.
It is limited. Third, knowing it is limited. Fourth, encouraging an increase in the price. Fifth, that person increases the weaving.

Sixth, accepting and committing the offense. Question: What is the difference between this and the previous precept regarding the weaver? Answer: There are four points of distinction. First, in the former case, the weaver is harmed.

1. In the former case, the owner of the yarn is not harmed; here, the owner of the yarn is harmed. In the former case, the weaver is not harmed; in both cases, the offense was incurred by harming the weaver. In the former case, one commits an offense for failing to pay the wage;

here, one incurs the offense by taking the wage after having harmed the owner of the yarn. 2. In the former case, harming the weaver, it was permitted for relatives and thus there was no offense; here, [harming the owner of the yarn], it is not permitted even for relatives and constitutes an offense. 3. In the former case, harming the weaver, it was permitted for relatives and thus there was no offense.

Regarding this offense of damaging the owner of the yarn: it constitutes an offense whether the owner is a relative or a non-relative. There are four preliminary conditions for the full offense: first, the person who commits the act;

second, the owner of the yarn dispatches a weaver to weave on their behalf; third, that bhikṣu encourages and praises the weaver and personally provides the payment; fourth, upon obtaining [the robe], the offense is finalized. These constitute the four clauses of the full precept. First, the offender.

Second, the owner of the yarn sends a weaver to weave for them. Third, that bhikṣu [and so forth] encourages and praises the weaver and personally provides the price. Fourth, "if he obtains" and so forth, which concludes the offense.
The explanation of the characteristics [of this precept] may be understood.

Next is the precept against forcibly seizing back a robe previously given to another. If one first gives a robe to another person with the intention of traveling together as companions, and that person subsequently refuses to go, one must request it back with gentleness and courtesy.
To suddenly seize it back by force out of a mind of anger is particularly inappropriate; because it involves deep-seated affliction and distress, it is forbidden.
Therefore, the regulation is established. There are five distinct conditions: first, it is a bhikṣu (excluding a śrāmaṇera); second, there is a mutual agreement to provide and receive a robe;

third, the provision is not yet fixed for the recipient, yet the recipient has already made a definitive decision to take it; fourth, within this situation, four permutations should be formulated: the first is when there is a definitive provision and a definitive taking.
Second, taking what is given with certainty but not with certainty; these two cases involve a grave offense, yet one does not violate this precept.

If one takes what is given neither with certainty nor with certainty, one commits a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*). If one takes what is given neither with certainty nor with certainty, a dispute arises in all instances; therefore, it constitutes an offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).

Fourth, taking by force through intense anger. Fifth, obtaining the object and incorporating it into one’s own possession. Regarding the phrase "not knowing how to recite the precepts" and so forth mentioned previously: [End of excerpt]
The two phrases of the fixed rule prevent the arising of transgressions. The first phrase concerns failing to recognize one’s own conduct;

the second phrase concerns not knowing the communal rules. The latter two phrases exclude offenses already committed: the first phrase concerns the method for repenting one’s own conduct, and the second phrase concerns the ritual for repentance before the community.

Regarding the four phrases of the *Prātimokṣa*: first, the offender; second, having previously given a robe to another; third, forcibly seizing it out of anger; fourth, the formal conclusion of the offense. Explanation.
Regarding "seizing and concealing": this refers to what is present before one's eyes. Subsequently, seizing items on trees and so forth refers to seizing what is not present before one's eyes.

The distinction in the resulting offense depends solely on whether the seizure occurred in the presence [of the victim] or not; it does not mean that there are these two different categories based on repeated offenses.

Next, regarding seven-day medicines: when the four great elements are in disharmony, various illnesses arise in competition; when the six viscera are out of order, all manner of medicines are required.

Because the Sage, in order to eliminate ailments, permitted their storage and consumption, they were subsequently accumulated. To prevent this, a regulation was established. There are four specific conditions: first, it must be a seven-day medicine;
second, it must be received by mouth. [Question: Why is it known that the essential addition of the "receiving by mouth" method is necessary? [Answer: It is because most...

The sixth fascicle of the *Śāstra* states: "If a sick bhikṣu requires medicine for seven days, and he has no attendant (*kappiyakāraka*) of his own such that it is difficult to find one to hire, he should receive it directly from the hands of a pure person (*kappiyakāraka*).
Having received it from the mouth of a bhikṣu, he should keep it in one place and take it himself to eat within the seven-day period.
Even if an attendant touches it after it has been received, it must be received again. If the medicine has already been received for two or three [days]..."
If medicine is placed inside [the bowl] on the first day, it should be formally accepted once again, starting the count anew from that first day. This continues through the seventh day;

by the time this medicine reaches the seventh day, it must be purified (*pariṣkāra*) before being given to others or consumed. If it is not purified, one must neither give it to others nor consume it oneself.

When the eighth day arrives at the end of the watch, there is an offense of expiation (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*). Furthermore, according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, the formal acceptance is performed by raising both hands and engaging in a question-and-answer exchange.

The *Pañcavargika-prātimokṣa-sūtra* states: "From one day up to seven days. In the section on the rules for medicinal substances (*bhaiṣajya*), it says in all cases that one may take them for seven days.

If there is no formal ritual (*vāk-karma*), how can one keep them by hand for seven days? Furthermore, regarding three types of medicine, one does not perform the rite of "purifying through declaration" (*viśuddhi-uddeśana*).

Fourth, there is the keeping of medicine beyond the limit. Question: Why is the keeping of seven-day medicine considered heavy, while the other three types of medicine are light? Answer: Seven-day medicine provides strong sustenance and its use extends to both internal and external [medicinal purposes]; thus, its storage and accumulation are significant.
The sentiment is earnest; transgressing the limit constitutes a grave offense, whereas the other three cases are not so, and thus their offenses are light.

Next, the text is explained. Regarding the section on the characteristics of the offense, there are two parts: first, the allowance for taking medicine; second, from "At that time, the World-Honored One" onwards, the arising of transgressions due to that allowance. The preceding text further contains two sections.
The first section formally opens the allowance for medicines. The second section addresses various points to resolve doubts. The preceding text is further divided into two parts:

first, the opening of the allowance in response to illness; second, from "At that time, the World-Honored One... onwards, the permission to take them even when not ill. The former part consists of three sections: first, the opening of the five medicines; second, from "At that time, the bhikṣus...

onwards, the explanation of the *śeṣa-bhakṣa* (leftover food) rule; third, from "Śāriputra... onwards, the permission to consume the five types of fat. The former of these [three] sections is further divided into three parts: first...

The Tathāgata, dwelling in stillness, gave rise to a thought. Second, descending from his secluded place, he set forth the thought he had kept hidden and announced it to the assembly for their acceptance.

Third, regarding the passage beginning with "At that time, the bhikṣus," this concludes the previous discussion on erroneous attachments concerning the timing of clothing. The preceding text has four parts:

first, the person for whom the thought was intended, whose body suffered two ailments, namely wind-disease and sores; second, the passage beginning with "I now," which reflects upon the efficacy of the medicine.
Because it possesses the capacity to sustain the body, it is called "proper food" (*yogya-āhāra*); because it has the efficacy to eliminate illness, it is termed "proper medicine" (*yogya-auṣadha*).

Since it is free from the reproach of being taken at an improper time, it is said that "one does not allow the coarse [nature] to manifest. Third, the passage beginning with "Furthermore, one should... sets forth the names and substances of the medicines.

Fourth, the section beginning with "Listen, O bhikṣus... establishes the permission for their consumption. Next, the recitation is presented according to the text; taking illness as the basis, they are treated as if they were livestock.
This is the causal condition for the medicine; hence it is said: "The cause of the illness, its conditions, and its time. Next, the four sections of the instructional text:

first, a mistaken interpretation of the holy teaching, whereby the illness is not swiftly removed; second, confusion regarding the previous statement of time, namely that it was not after noon; third, the World-Honored One’s inquiry; fourth, Ānanda’s response.

The fourth is the explanation according to the explicit teaching (*nītārtha*). Regarding the previous mention of "time," this refers to the time of illness; since the substance of this medicine is permitted for times other than those [restricted by the rules], it is said that it may be taken at both "proper" and "improper" times.

Next, regarding the textual passage on other methods, there are two parts: first, the remnants of food from one who is ill need not undergo formal ritual procedures (*karmavācanā*), as they might otherwise damage the offerings of the faithful;

thus, the consumption of food by a caregiver for the sick is permitted. Second, regarding the formal procedures for the remnants of food when one is not ill, there are two types: first, the food of the Saṃgha; second, the food of individuals.

[The text] notes below: "This is the food of a *dānapati*. Is it appropriate to perform the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*)? This shall be clarified in the subsequent section. Next, the five types of fat are permitted;

since these fats belong to the category of oils, they are included among the seven-day medicines (*saptāhika-bhaiṣajya*). However, they are mentioned separately because they are prescribed specifically for certain illnesses. Regarding the statement that there is no fixed time for receiving [the medicine] within the substance of the medicine itself:
this refers to cases where a pure attendant (*śuddha-puruṣa*) is difficult to find and there is no one to prepare it, so one has a pure attendant briefly boil it on one's behalf.
It transforms the raw into the cooked; one receives it from that [source] and cooks it oneself on pure ground. Because it was raw when transformed, there is no fault of cooking for oneself;
because it is on pure ground, there is no transgression of overnight storage; and because it is done at the proper time, the rules for receiving it are not lost.

Once cooked, it is clarified until the water droplets separate from the dregs and juices, whereby it may be used in accordance with the Dharma. If, however, one cooks and strains it at an improper time...

If time passes and the formal acceptance (*parigraha*) is lost, the fault of improper contact arises; by consuming it, one incurs an offense. Therefore, it is said that one must treat it according to the Dharma.

As for the case where there is a guest laborer acting as a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person who makes things permissible), there is no distinction between the proper time (*kāla*) and the improper time (*akāla*). Thus, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, chapter twenty-two, states:
"If one cooks during the proper time, strains it during the preceding [proper] time, and accepts it, one may consume it for seven days. If one accepts it at an improper time, one may not."
Take it after having stayed overnight. Next, it is also permitted for a healthy bhikṣu to take medicine according to the occasion.
In the text, the instruction to cause [the practitioner] to practice giving toward the two fields of compassion and reverence is intended to ensure that the donor’s field of merit is fulfilled.

This residual rock honey that undergoes transformation is the Buddha’s supernatural power; no one else is capable of fashioning it. Therefore, it is said that none among the devas and others can digest it, with the sole exception of...
The Tathāgata. Next, the resolution of doubts follows the text.

The remainder can be understood through the explanation of the *Śīla-mūla* (Root Precepts), which is analyzed by way of two gates: first, the definitive analysis of the textual phrases; second, the resolution of difficulties through question and answer. Regarding the first gate, the *Śīla-mūla* consists of five sections:

first, the person who commits the offense; second, the circumstances for a sick person to store medicine; third, the section on "residual medicine" (*śeṣa-bhaiṣajya*) and below, concerning what is stored.

The substance of the medicine. Fourth, the opening of the seven-day period; fifth, the offense incurred upon transgression. Next, regarding the question and answer: Why is this called "residual" (*śeṣa*)?
Regarding the "ten-day robe," it is called "extra" (*atireka*). The answer is: the three robes are not "extra," so they receive the name "extra" in contrast to what is not extra.

Since there is nothing that is not "extra" to contrast with in the case of medicine, and because it is the remainder of food, it is called "residual. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that the meanings of "residual" and "extra" are as follows: [text continues].
They are similar; to cite them against one another would be redundant and unnecessary. Regarding why seven days are specifically permitted, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

"One knows [the duration] based on the potency of the medicine; it is only after seven days that this becomes clear. It further states: "Seven days" refers to the numerical limit being exactly seven days. The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* (or *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*) also says: [The same].
It arises from the formal ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*), while also following the power of the medicine. Regarding "following the power of the medicine":
