for example, if on the first day it is permissible, and one touches it on the second or third day, being permitted to receive it again for seven days—this is what arises from the formal procedure. Question: The root text of the precepts (*śīla-sūtra*) should say "to store" (*dhāraṇa*), yet why does it say "excessive use" (*atisevana*)? Answer:

This is because those who "store" for the sake of use may incur the fault of keeping [medicine] beyond the permitted time (*dīrgha-āpatti*). Thus, this term serves to distinguish it from external use, wherein such excessive storage does not exist.
[This constitutes] an offense. For this reason, although the text says "wearing," in principle it actually refers to the commission of the offense; it does not depend on the act of wearing at all.
Alternatively, the word order in the text may be inverted; it should rather say "if the wearing exceeds [the limit]."

Next, the explanation of the three types of *atireka* (excess) above is clarified by combining the fourth and fifth [sections]. Within this combined explanation, there are eight sections regarding the limits of application, all of which are identical to those for long robes (*atireka-cīvara*), with only a few phrases differing.
First, the initial section is explained through a twofold classification: first, whether one incurs an offense regarding excess or not;

second, the degree of offense incurred when consuming medicinal substances that have become excessive. Regarding the first category: if one obtains medicine on the first day and continues to obtain it until the seventh day, but obtains it again on the eighth day—
When the dawn appears, both the act of receiving and the state of being stained constitute an offense; therefore, it is said that "the *niḥsargika* [offense] is complete. Question:

Regarding the six-day medicinal substances, if they are stained and thus become subject to the offense of *atireka* (excess), one wonders whether the formal act of receiving (*parigraha*) is thereby lost or not. Answer: When medicinal substances are obtained for seven days, if they are collectively not given away as pure gifts (*viśuddha-dāna*), their status as *atireka* is identical.

Both [the receiving and the excess] constitute offenses together. While the act of receiving prevents the fault of overnight storage (*rātri-sparśana*), it does not prevent the fault of excess. Since the objects of prevention differ, [the receiving does not remove the offense of excess].

If it were possible for the formal acceptance (*paribhoga*) to be lost, that would mean the first day; [in that case], when the limit for the formal acceptance has expired, and six days have already passed from the beginning, the formal acceptance would not yet have lapsed.
Therefore, the text states: "On the seventh day, give the medicine to the bhikṣus to eat.

If the acceptance were indeed lost, then faults such as "overnight contact" (*sāmiṣa-sparśana*) would arise. Why, then, would it permit the bhikṣus to eat? Thus, since the acceptance has not [lapsed]...

[The robe] was lost. Upon returning, he reached the time for his meal; this is why he was ordered to apply [oil] and light a lamp. The answer was that because the [robe] had been received, it was not lost.

Since he had already committed the offense of hoarding, he was therefore sent to apply oil to his feet and light a lamp as a punishment for the fault of possessing [the robe], being penalized by being forbidden from wearing it.

The second case involves one who has consumed the seven-day medicine while it was still raw. A single swallow incurs six offenses: three *tissa* for eating at an improper time, for eating what has not been formally accepted, and for eating what has been stored overnight;

and three *duṣkṛta* for internal storage, for impure contact, and for eating medicine that should have been relinquished. These offenses differ in their objective bases (*ālambana*) and do not depend upon one another.
If one considers the eight offenses regarding drinking, adding two for boiling, then to clarify the number of remaining offenses concerning medicinal substances:
taking [medicine] at an improper time constitutes five offenses; if it is boiled, there are seven. A single swallow of a timely medicine (*kālabhojana*) likewise logically entails seven.

One should understand accordingly that for any deficiency, the count is adjusted. For lifetime-long medicines (*yāvajjīvika*), there is no limit, as the formal acceptance (*parigraha*) does not lapse. If there is no occasion of illness, however—only...
One incurs the offense of *pāyattika*. If one does not apply the oral formula to the dharma-robes, there is only the absence of the "improper time" [restriction];

all other aspects are identical to those that possess it. Other phrases are to be understood by analogy. In total, there are twenty-two [cases]. The stages for relinquishing and confessing are the same. Regarding the text on returning medicine, there are four parts; the first corresponds to the statement of relinquishment and the act of returning.

2. Regarding the phrase "that bhikṣu" and below: as for the formal assignment (*adhikāra*), whether it should be performed or not, and all matters concerning the period exceeding seven days, these three types of formal assignments are all calculated based on the day of relinquishment (*pratyākhyāna*) and explained in relation to that.
Alternatively, if the three [conditions] are not fully met, the meaning may be understood by analogy. 3. Regarding the phrase "one should perform the formal announcement (*jñapti*)" and below:
The ritual procedure is entrusted to him. From "This bhikṣu... onwards, the method of application is shown.

Next is the precept concerning the rain-bathing robe (*varṣāśāṭī*). This refers to requesting it before the [proper] time and using it before the [proper] time; these two rules are established together.

The reason for this establishment is that the rain-bathing robe is for the support of the body and is not an absolute necessity. Therefore, the Sage permitted begging for and using it during the [proper] season. At present, [the time has not yet...]

To request [a robe] in advance for prior use is a violation of the precepts due to excessive greed; therefore, it is prohibited to seek one before the designated time. There are five specific conditions [for this offense]:
first, it is a rain-bath robe (*varṣāśāṭī*); second, it is sought before the designated time; third, it is for oneself; fourth, the other party gives it; and fifth, one accepts it.

Regarding the offense of using it before the designated time, there are four specific conditions: first, it is one’s own rain-bath robe; second, it is obtained before the designated time; third, it is before the designated time; [and fourth, one uses it].

Regarding the formal acceptance (*dhāraṇa*): according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra*, one must necessarily accept it by adding the formal ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*). To use it before the four [specified] occasions constitutes an offense.

There are two parts to the textual description of the characteristics of this offense: first, the allowance for the rain-bath robe; second, the transgression of the group of six monks (*ṣaḍvargika*) arising from their conduct during the rainy season retreat. The first part contains three sections: first, the formulation of the eight vows.

The Circumstances of Bestowing Bathing Robes. 1. From "At that time, the Buddha spoke" onwards, [the section on] praising and requesting permission to hear and accept [the precepts]. 2. From "Briefly setting aside what has been heard" onwards, [the section on] practicing the eight vows.
The preceding text contains five parts: (i) Making a vow due to an offering; (ii) The Buddha suppressing and not permitting it;

(iii) Declaring one's own purity; (iv) The Buddha subsequently granting permission; (v) The formal enumeration of the eight vows. Of these, the first six concern internal requisites, while the latter two concern external requisites.

Regarding these eight vows, since the field of the Master and the Sangha provides such broad benefit, they were subsequently praised by the Buddha. The subsequent praise and exposition consists of three parts:

first, from "The Tathāgata asked about his wishes" down to "I have made my vow and prayer," where the Tathāgata questions the Master regarding his aspirations, and the Master responds by praying for his own vows; second, from "World-Honored One" downwards...
The Buddha praised this as exquisite. [The passage] from "At that time" onwards consists of his addressing the Sangha to receive [the request], followed by the eight preceding vows.

The preceding text has two parts: first the question, then the answer. Within the answer, the question and answer are clarified through a reverse exposition. This section contains three parts: first, asking about the fruit toward which the eight persons are tending;

second, asking whether these eight persons have come to this land; third, regarding the phrase "If I hear they have previously come," it indicates knowledge obtained through retrocognition (*pratyutpanna-jñāna*).
One will certainly receive offerings for the eight vows. By providing these as sustenance for the field of the Sangha, the mind becomes joyful.

Seeing this benefit, I have thus given rise to these vows. Next, the praise and exposition has two parts: first, describing that it is not in vain, hence saying "this matter is according to reality," and so forth;
second, the verses of praise, which cause the mind to rejoice. Within the verses, there are three sections; the first line of verse is the praise.
The cause is profound and superior. Since the cause is thus superior, the resulting fruit is exquisite and refined; therefore, the next verse concerns the excellence of the future fruit.
Although the fruit is transcendent, there may be a fear that it will not be constant; hence, the third verse reveals that the fruit is inexhaustible.

In the first verse, the first half cites the six internal requisites, while the second half cites the two external requisites. "Joyful" refers to a mind free from the stain of stinginess, pure throughout all three times.
One rejoices in what one has done; hence it is called "joyful. This praises the purity of the mind. Regarding the giving of food and drink: these are things that accord with the Dharma.
When given to the Sangha for their use, they are distinguished from other items not in accordance with the Dharma, which yield meager merit. This constitutes the purity of the material gift.

If one gives to non-Buddhists or to disciples who have broken the precepts, the field of merit is shallow and the planting of merit is not great; therefore, it is said that one must uphold the precepts.
Disciple, this is the purification of the field of objects. Since these three factors are thus superior, how could they not be exquisite?
By offering external requisites such as robes to the assembly of monks, it is said that "one gives to the multitude. This may also extend to robes and food;
by offering these to the great assembly, it is called "giving, etc. Although such giving cannot ultimately sever the fetters, it can nonetheless temporarily suppress their active manifestation.

Because of a greedy mind, it is said that one must "subdue" it and so forth. Next, regarding the verse on the ripening of results: the first half concerns the excellence of the ripened result, while the second half pertains to the specific location.
Because a pleasant result is achieved through a pleasant cause, it is said to be "based on pleasure. This clarifies the medicine of the cause.

Regarding those who receive pleasant retribution: they proximately obtain the retribution of pleasure among humans and devas; "permanently obtaining" refers to the distant attainment of the fruit of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*).
This should be understood accordingly. Next, the verse reveals that the fruits are inexhaustible: the first half-verse reveals the untainted fruit, while the second half clarifies the tainted fruit.
Within the former, the first phrase cites the excellence of the preceding cause, and the second phrase reveals the inexhaustibility of the fruit—namely, the attainment of...

The supramundane fruit of further advancement brings spiritual satisfaction; therefore, it is called "bliss. This bliss can only be known through direct realization and cannot be illustrated by worldly affairs;
hence, it is said to be "incomparable. Next, the mundane fruit with outflows may be understood.

The root precepts consist of three phrases: first, the offender; second, the time of seeking and using [the object]; and third, the offense incurred by seeking and using it beyond that time. A detailed explanation may be found elsewhere.
[The *Mahāsāṃghika Vinaya*, Chapter Eleven: This is the rain-bathing robe (*varṣāśāṭī*). It may be used for four and a half months;

on the fifteenth day of the eighth month, it must be relinquished. As for the method of relinquishment: one bhikṣu should make this proclamation in the midst of the assembly: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

Today the Saṃgha relinquishes the rain-bathing robe" (this is to be said three times). If it is relinquished after the sixteenth day, there is an offense of *vinayātikrama*. For bhikṣuṇīs, there is none.
Regarding the previous [offense] and the current *duṣkṛta*: because it involves seeking much while providing little benefit, it is light.

Next is the precept on robes for urgent needs (*ātyayika-cīvara*): when one's labor and toil are not yet complete, it is improper to accept a gift; however, in the presence of an urgent cause, the Buddha opened the allowance for acceptance.

Because of this opening for urgent cases, people began to accept even when there was no urgency. Since a transgression had arisen, the Noble One (the Buddha) established the regulation. These two [cases]—
Regarding the "conjunction with the precept" (*śīla-saṃyoga*): because it arises from the same single garment, it exceeds the five conditions for receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*).

These are: first, it is an urgent gift; second, one knows it to be such; third, it is received more than ten days prior; fourth, there is no underlying cause or condition; and fifth, upon taking possession, one immediately commits an offense. Regarding the six conditions for keeping [the robe] after the period has passed:

first, it is an urgent gift; second, one knows it to be such; third, it was obtained within thirty days; fourth, one does not perform the ritual of purification (*viśuddhi*); and fifth, there is no...

The causes and conditions: regarding the transgression of exceeding the limit for the six types of livestock, there are three textual sections concerning the characteristics of the offense. First, the allowance for receiving summer robes. Second, the section beginning with "the group of six," wherein the transgression arose due to that allowance;
the Buddha immediately rebuked them and established the regulation. Third, the section beginning with "at that time," which allows for the acceptance of urgent offerings;

since accepting within ten days was permitted, there should have been a transgression for accepting prior to that period, but it is omitted from the text. The *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* consists of five phrases: first, the person who commits the offense; second, the acceptance...

1. The time limit for wearing the robe. 2. From "The three bhikṣus" downwards: this refers to receiving [the robe] when there is an urgent need; it is not permitted when there is no urgency. 3. From "Receiving the robe" downwards:
it is permitted to keep it during that period without fault. 4. If one exceeds [the limit], the offense is established. Furthermore, within the preceding circumstances, both offenses are absent.

The root of the precept (śīla-mūla) only establishes the offense for keeping it after the period has passed. It is only in the detailed explanation and the exceptions that both [offenses] are fully present. Within the detailed explanation, the first and the fifth are distinct.
In the commentary, three points are combined for explanation. Within these three combined explanations: first, the third phrase, "the robe given in haste," is explained;

second, below the section on "the time for robes," the fourth phrase, "the time for robes," is explained; and third, with "ten days after the *pravāraṇā*" mentioned below, all three phrases are summarized together.
Combining these points for a broad explanation: since it is stated that ten days remain until the *pravāraṇā*, it is clear that this refers to the second phrase of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.

Question: From that point on, one commits an offense if an extra robe (*atireka-cīvara*) exceeds ten days; why then is this "cloth offered as a gift" (*akālacīvara*) received on the sixth day of the seventh month?

When the dawn of the sixteenth day appears, if one further says that [the robe] may be kept for one month or five months, and if this long-term robe does not connect with the period of the previous allowance, there is only the former opening;
therefore, one incurs an offense immediately. This emergency gift-robe (*ātyayika-cīvara*), however, connects both openings;

therefore, one does not incur an offense. Thus, if one goes outside the boundary on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, it does not constitute a breach of separation, because one has entered [the new period].
The sixteenth day is the limit by which one must depart. The answer is that regarding summer robes (*varṣāśāṭī*), there is only a subsequent opening period, but no prior opening period.
Because on the night of the fifteenth day, one must still observe the rains retreat (*vassa*) to obtain the robe, this case is not analogous; to depart [at that time] would constitute an offense.
Next, the second phrase opens a one-month period to encompass ten days, and a five-month period to encompass one month. Why is it that here, during the *kārttika*...
Regarding the *guṇavastra* (robe of merit) and the month: it does not include the ten days, yet it is said that after one month or five months have passed, an additional day is added.

Answer: As for the inclusion of the ten days within the month, first, both are "out-of-season" (*akāla*); second, both serve to prevent excess. Since their functional capacity is equal, the longer period subsumes the shorter.
As for the *guṇavastra* subsuming the *kārttika* month, both share the same temporal position and both possess the five benefits; thus, their functional capacity is likewise [equal].

The *śīta* (winter robe) compensates for the short by means of the long. Now, regarding the *kaṭhina* robe and the *deyavastra*, they do not include the ten-day period because their timing and non-timing are distinct;
the twenty-day period is unique, and while the five types of benefits—such as the *deyavastra* and so forth—possess varying degrees of scope, they therefore do not include one another.
Because they do not include one another, an additional day is added. The remaining phrases are of a similar nature and cannot be explained exhaustively here; one should simply return the robe.

Regarding the phrase "before the [stipulated] time has passed" and "after the [stipulated] time has passed": these are terms used for the formal relinquishment (*naiḥsargika*) of the object. In actual principle, if it is before the time has passed, one must return it to the owner on that very seat;

if it is after the time has passed, it becomes a long-term possession, and one should return it after one night has elapsed. Within the section on non-offenses, there is first a general statement and then a specific analysis. In the specific analysis, the allowance for returning it before the time has passed is presented first, followed by the explanation of returning it after the time has passed.
Next is the precept concerning staying apart from one's robes for six nights in an araṇya. The similarities and differences of this precept are as previously explained;

however, while the previous precept was violated by staying overnight in a village, this precept regarding a fearful place in an araṇya is violated after exceeding six nights. Furthermore, while the previous precept was violated by those who dwell there permanently, this one applies to others.
Regarding the allowance for the *kaṭhina* robe: this superior practitioner does not accept the *kaṭhina* robe; however, because of specific difficulties, it is permitted for six nights.
If that is so, since he is a superior practitioner and there is no allowance for the *kaṭhina* robe, how can there be the removal [of the *kaṭhina*] during the month of Kārttika?

Answer: The month of Kārttika is not a formal ritual act (*dharma-kriyā*); therefore, it is permitted. There are seven distinct conditions: first, the possession of the three robes; second, the winter season...
1. It is not the proper time. 2. A place where there is doubt or fear. 3. Placing the robe in a village. 4. Not relinquishing the assembly.

5. Having no cause or condition. 6. On the seventh day, at the appearance of dawn. Within this text, there are two parts: first, the allowance for placing [the robe] inside a house due to the danger of thieves;

second, from "At that time, the group of six" onwards, the arising of transgressions based on that allowance. Since it originated with the group of six, wrong practices arose by following their teachings. Even if one stays in an ārāma...

If [the offense occurs], it is likewise limited to six nights. The five phrases of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* are as follows: first, the person; second, the explicit indication of the time of the offense;

third, the conditions for exemption from the difficulty [of the rule] below the section on the *araṇya*; fourth, the allowance for a single meeting during the six nights below the section on the *bhikṣu*;

and fifth, the formal conclusion regarding the offense below the phrase "if one exceeds. In the commentary, the second phrase is not explained, while the others are fully explained. Below the section on the *araṇya*, the third phrase is explained. [The section on] the *śālā*.
"Internally below" explains the fourth phrase. "If a bhikṣu... and so forth explains the fifth phrase. According to the *Jian lun* (Treatise on Seeing):

"If in a forest hermitage (*araṇya*) there are many monks and the dwellings are secure and well-sealed, it is not necessary to entrust one's robes to a village. Furthermore, this is also exempted by a formal monastic act (*saṃgha-karman*).
Although there is no explicit textual authority for this, there is no fault in applying the meaning broadly."

Next is the precept against misappropriating the property of the Saṃgha. Regarding the intent behind its formulation: the benefits of the Saṃgha are not insignificant; to arbitrarily divert them into one’s own possession causes distress to the community and fosters greed.

Therefore, a prohibition by the Sage was necessary. The specific conditions consist of four factors: first, it must be the property of the Saṃgha; second, one must have the perception that it is such property; third, one must divert it into one’s own possession; and fourth, one must accept it.
The four permutations of the full offense can be understood accordingly. In the commentary, the second and fourth factors are explained together, while the first three are treated separately.

Commentary: Regarding the section "Regarding the property of the Saṃgha," this explains the third phrase. The gravity of the offense regarding these three types of objects varies. For the first object, its misappropriation constitutes an offense involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).
For the second object, there is no offense in diverting it, as it has not yet been permitted [for such use]; however, if one perceives it as permitted when it is not, it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).

Thus, we know that it is not permitted; if one perceives what is not permitted as permitted, there is no offense. As for the third object, it is definitively the property of the Saṃgha; to divert it for other purposes constitutes a grave offense (*pārājika* or *saṃghāvaśeṣa*). These three objects are contrasted with one another.

Therefore, it is raised [for discussion]. When items that are fixed as belonging to a specific individual are diverted out of sequence or across categories, the specific ownership is impaired; calculating their value constitutes a grave offense (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*). Furthermore, another interpretation holds:
regarding the object in the second case, which is precisely the basis for the arising of the offense, diverting it constitutes an offense involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*);

the other two cases both involve items fixed as belonging to the Saṃgha, and diverting them results in a grave offense. Moreover, another interpretation holds: these three types of objects all constitute the offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*), because diverting them from their original owners does not constitute theft.
Because of this mental state, one does not commit a grave offense. Regarding the passage "If a bhikṣu... and below, the explanation of the second and fourth lines consists of three parts:

first, the formal explanation of diverting property into one's own possession; second, the section beginning with "If the object... which addresses the four pairs of eight lines concerning cases where the object is not diverted into one's own possession, but a minor transgression is still committed;

third, the comparison between the stūpa and the Saṃgha; fourth, the comparison between the present community of the four directions and the two assemblies of monks and nuns; and fifth, the detailed analysis of the similarities among the aforementioned three.

Regarding "similar" (*sabhāga*): when the same category is transferred from this to that, it is said that they are "admitted as being in different locations" (*visabhāga*). There are four permutations regarding the three objects and perceptions.
The thirty *niḥsargika-pāyattika* rules concluded above.
*The Record of the Opening of the Sects of the Four-Part Vinaya*, Scroll Three, End;

*The Record of the Opening of the Sects of the Four-Part Vinaya*, Scroll Four (from the beginning of the ninety rules to the conclusion of the seven rules for settling disputes, totaling thirty-seven thousand two hundred words).
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Huaisu of the Western Taiyuan Monastery.
● Next, the ninety *pāyattika* offenses are explained. First, they are generally interpreted through a sevenfold classification:

first, their assignment to body or speech; second, whether committed by oneself or by instructing another; third, the distinction between prohibitive and natural offenses; fourth, the procedures for maintaining and violating the precepts.
Fifth, there is a difference regarding violations of prohibitions. Second, there are distinctions among the six classes [of offenses]. Seventh, the lower assembly acts spontaneously.
In the first gate, the stages of body and speech are divided into three: first, thirty-one precepts where the offense is completed through bodily action;

second, twenty precepts where the transgression is incurred through vocal action; and third, thirty-nine precepts where the offense is committed through both body and speech combined. First, the three [bodily actions]:

Eleventh: [The ten offenses of] two nights, strong arms, covering, making a screen, giving separately, three non-nights, not inviting outside, three seats, three armies, water, wine, striking, half-white, two following, beating, palace. Next, the twenty [offenses of] speech:
lying, slander, two same-speech, obtaining, woman, dislike, sudden mockery, daily, hope, doubt, arousing desire, encouraging, slandering, regretting, same-blame. Next, body.

Regarding the combination of speech: this is further divided into three parts. First, there are two cases where the karma of the body and speech—consisting of both the act of stopping and the act of performing—is shared with the body.

This refers to the two types of bedding, the private and the exposed. If one spreads the bedding oneself, it is an act performed by the body; if one instructs another to spread it, it is an act performed by speech.

Upon departing, if one does not personally lift [the bedding], it is the cessation of bodily action; if one does not instruct another to lift it, it is the cessation of vocal action. Since the offense is incurred upon crossing the boundary of the monastery, is this not so?

Regarding the offenses of the body: there are seven precepts. Those belonging to the category of speech that are shared with the body consist of the concealment of a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*) and the two instances of entering a village while wearing [the robe] improperly or without having received consent (*chanda*).
For example, the concealment of a grave offense—refraining from disclosing it—is called a verbal action of restraint (*vāk-karman-saṃvara*).

Since the Sūtra clarifies that the offense is incurred through the conjunction [of speech and body], how could this not be a shared offense with the body? The others are all similar; they cannot be detailed exhaustively here. Third, there are three...

Regarding the ten precepts, verbal actions are classified as offenses involving the body. Within this category, there are four positions. First, there are nineteen precepts where the verbal action is performed by oneself, yet the offense is committed through the agency of another’s body.

If one were to discuss only those actions performed by oneself, they would be restricted solely to bodily offenses; however, for now, we shall explain them according to the principle of instructing another.

This refers to digging, destroying, pulling, using, encouraging, burning, hiding, killing, driving away, drinking, giving a robe to a nun, and throwing [an object] under a high bed—there are seven such cases.
For example, regarding the instruction to dig the earth: although one says, "Son, you are not to dig," the instructor has not yet committed an offense;

it is only by relying on the instructed person's actual digging that the offense of instruction is established. Therefore, this is called "committing an offense through one's own words while relying on another's body. The remaining cases are all analogous.
I cannot describe them all in detail. The second category consists of four precepts that constitute an offense through the use of another’s words by oneself.

These are: praising food, concealing one’s age, not remaining secluded, and eavesdropping. Since a nun does not praise food, there is no fault in the act of eating itself; it is only because of the false praise that the eating becomes an offense.
Since this first case is thus, the others are likewise. The third category consists of five precepts: they involve one’s own body and speech, with the offense committed through another’s body.
An example is the four-month period of seeking fine food. The fourth category consists of two precepts: they involve one’s own body and speech, with the offense committed through another’s speech.

These are: speaking heterodoxly to annoy others and not accepting admonition. Regarding "speaking heterodoxly," it refers to falsely performing the formal motion (*jñapti*) on behalf of the Sangha, as well as the necessity of summoning and questioning during an admonition—the very act being admonished.
This matter applies to all seven types of offenses. That is to say, there are those committed by one's own speech, those committed by false speech, and those committed by the speech of another.
The second section is divided into four parts: first, there is one precept that is committed solely by instructing another, namely, encouraging another to eat to fullness;

second, there are eleven precepts that are committed by both oneself and others, namely: digging, destroying, pulling [insects], two rules regarding insects, frightening, fire, hiding, killing, slandering, seizing, and [the rule on] holding.
The Jewel [Chapter], Number Eleven. Third, there are ten precepts concerning instructing others; these are categorized as either "identical" or "non-identical.

That is to say, regarding the two types of bedding (in private or in public), the wearing of robes, and the high bed—these seven involve instructing others to benefit oneself and are thus "non-identical" offenses.

To simply instruct [others] without personal benefit results only in a minor transgression (*dukkaṭa*). These twenty-one precepts are "exhortatory," meaning they apply solely to instructing others; the remaining [precepts] apply to both oneself and others.

In the fourth category, among the remaining sixty-eight precepts, sixty-seven involve heavy offenses for oneself and light offenses for the teaching; the single precept on eating after the proper time involves only the act committed by oneself.

In the third section, thirty are *prakṛti-sāvadya* (intrinsic offenses): namely, lying, slandering, the two types of harsh speech, divisive speech, malicious speech, forceful dragging, using [another's] belongings, reviling, and driving away.

Fearing death, drinking, doubt, concealment, causing [a fault] to arise, speaking [of another's fault], suspension (pravāsanīya), refusal, reviling, sharing the same desire, repentance, listening, striking, fighting, and slandering—these and the remaining sixty precepts are all prohibitions (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*).

The fourth section is divided into four parts. First, there are ten precepts that possess both observance and violation; these refer to speaking of coarse [faults] and teaching [others] without authorization.
Turning one's back on the assembly and entering a village to perform the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta* (the ritual for leftover food) does not constitute an offense regarding overeating (*pūrṇa-bhojana*).

Likewise, there is no offense of acting arbitrarily (*svayaṃ-kṛta*) when one has informed the host, requested that the food be made pure, and given consent (*chanda*) for the monastic affairs. These two types of offenses differ in name but are identical in substance.

Regarding the two stages of the two types of observance (*dhāraṇī*), they should be understood according to the above; I shall not elaborate further here. Next, there are two precepts: abstaining from food kept overnight and abstaining from food received [after the proper time].

These refer to the seven-day and lifelong observances. Once the ritual for the oral undertaking is completed, one does not commit an offense. Furthermore, these two offenses do not exist at improper times.

The *kālika-bhaiṣajya* (medicines taken at specific times) are not included; they consist solely of active performance (*kriyā*). Because their meaning differs from the others, they must be explained separately.

Third, there is one precept that consists solely of observance through action (*kriyā-dhāraṇa*) and violation through non-action (*akriyā-āpatti*), namely the precept against listening while eavesdropping. Fourth, the remaining seventy-six precepts consist of observance through non-action (*akriyā-dhāraṇa*) and violation through action (*kriyā-āpatti*).
It may also be said that the precept against eavesdropping consists solely of observance through action and violation through non-action, as do the aforementioned thirteen minor rules.
There are also cases where the meanings of "abstaining and maintaining" (zhichi) and "acting and transgressing" (zuofan) apply.

Furthermore, regarding the remaining seventy-six precepts and a portion of the thirteen [Śaikṣa rules], from the perspective of their distinct individual natures, they likewise possess the meanings of abstaining and maintaining as well as acting and transgressing.
The fifth section. Generally speaking, all of these contravene the Buddha’s regulations. However, regarding the establishment of offenses, they are divided into two categories.
In cases where the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) must necessarily be performed by the Saṃgha, if the Saṃgha does not perform the ritual, one may contravene it without incurring an offense;

this refers to the four rules concerning speaking otherwise, communicating one's consent (*chanda*), and the two types of following. Thus, these four precepts constitute offenses for contravening the Saṃgha’s regulations. All remaining precepts constitute offenses for contravening the Buddha’s regulations.

The sixth section contains twenty-one precepts. There are three instances where the status [of these rules] differs from those within this [section]. First, there are three precepts that exist for monks but not for nuns;
these are known to be so because they concern teaching at sunset and disparaging instruction. Second, there are thirteen precepts where the gravity of the offense differs; these are:

eating [alone], the three robes, the five [rules on] sitting, the one [rule on] walking, and the three [rules on] mutual [use of] needle-cases and tubes. These are considered grave offenses for the great assembly of monks (bhikṣu-saṃgha) due to their frequency.
The nun [offense] is light because it is rare. Regarding the "three types of food": this refers to praising, encouraging, and soliciting for fine food. Regarding the "five types of robes":

this refers to giving a robe to a nun, making a robe [for her], and the three cases of exceeding the prescribed measurements. The remainder may be understood [by the context]. Regarding the three sets of five precepts (*pañca-śīla*), the offenses are the same while the conditions (*pratyaya*) differ.

For instance, regarding the precept against eating after the invitation has been accepted (*pavāraṇā*) or eating when already satisfied (*pūrṇa-bhaktika*), the permitted conditions (*anujñā-pratyaya*) are not the same; or perhaps they differ in how they are categorized as distinct or combined. This applies to the precept regarding giving food to non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). With... [text ends].
The conditions differ. Receiving ordination at an age below the required limit—the conditions for receiving it differ. Using an oversized bathing robe—the purpose for its use differs.
Or perhaps the names differ; in all these cases, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense. If the offense were identical, yet because the conditions differ, the *Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya* establishes a separate rule.
The specific meaning of these distinct conditions will be explained further below. The remaining sixty-nine [rules] are the same as those in the *Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya*; they are simply...
The *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* is listed here according to their sequential positions; however, upon detailed analysis, there are also discrepancies.

For instance, there are cases where the concealment of offenses differs between monks and nuns, or where the objective circumstances are reversed, such as when the two-night limit for criticizing [another] is exceeded by five or six words. These distinctions follow the specific nuances of the meaning.
One may reflect upon this.
Regarding the seventh section: among the four stages of offenses previously taught for instructing others, we take the second and third stages to instruct people.

Of the twenty-one precepts, excluding the two concerning the private and public spreading of mats, the remaining nineteen precepts possess the sense of "spontaneous occurrence" (*anuvartana*). There is nothing further to be said regarding the remainder.
Knowing this, the precept against false speech was established. The reason for its enactment is that those who cherish the Way must ensure their words accord with reality.

Now, to the contrary, they act in opposition to their own perceptions and intentions, deceiving those before them and causing others to hold false understandings. Thus, they lose the benefits of the holy path for themselves; this is among the most grievous of transgressions.

Therefore, it is thus prescribed. To explain the definition of the terms: to clearly realize that the mind is not real is called "knowing" (*jñā*); to seek out an offense without falsehood is termed "intentionally" (*saṃcintya*).

That which does not accord with reality is called "false" (*mṛṣā*); to manifest this through the mouth is called "speech" (*vāda*). This is what is meant by "intentional false speech" (*saṃcintya-mṛṣāvāda*).

There are six conditions for a separate offense: first, a person; second, the perception that it is a person; third, speaking with a contrary perception; fourth, knowing one is speaking with a contrary perception;

fifth, the words being clearly articulated; sixth, the listener understanding them. If these conditions are deficient, the offense is determined by comparison. When all seven preparatory factors are complete, the characteristics of the offense are evident.

Regarding the three phrases of the root precept, they are explained in detail in the full text. The first phrase is self-evident. The second, "knowing yet speaking falsely," and so forth, follows accordingly.

The explanation of the second and third phrases consists of two parts within the text: first, the method for speaking falsehoods; second, the clarification of the characteristics of lightness and gravity regarding the assembly.
The preceding section further divides into two: first, up to the point where it says "against external matters," explaining the violation in relation to external objects;

second, from "what is seen differently" onwards, defining falsehood with respect to internal mental states. The former section contains four parts: first, listing the eight types of impure speech contexts.

Second, the explanation of the eightfold distinctions of combination and separation. Third, if one does not see [the object], it constitutes the meaning of deceiving others; this is the offense. Fourth, regarding the passage beginning with "The original text states: 'He forms this thought...

and so forth, which concerns the preliminary and subsequent preparatory stages (*pūrvāpara-prayoga*). In the preceding text, first the four cases beginning with "not seeing" are listed, followed by the four cases beginning with "seeing."

Next, I shall explain the latter four [faculties] previously mentioned: seeing, hearing, touching, and cognizing. Regarding "seeing": it is called seeing because five conditions are fulfilled: first, the visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) is unimpaired;
second, there is a visible object (*rūpa-viṣaya*); third, there is space; fourth, there is light; and fifth, there is the mental application that initiates consciousness.

Hearing has four conditions: first, the auditory faculty (*śrotra-indriya*) is pure; second, there is a sound-object (*śabda-viṣaya*); third, there is space; and fourth, there is the mental application that initiates consciousness.
The mental faculty (*manas*) possesses three conditions for contact: first, the three faculties are unimpaired; second, there is a tangible object that reaches the faculty;

and third, there is the mental activity that gives rise to consciousness. The mind knows all things without depending on the full assembly of conditions. Question: Why are the six faculties categorized as three being "combined" and three being "separate"? Answer: The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle six, states:
"The natures of the three [faculties] are sharp, and their functional power is predominant; thus each is designated by its own name. The natures of the other three faculties are dull..."

Their functional capacity is limited; collectively, they are termed "cognition" (*vijñāna*). Furthermore, three faculties apprehend their objects from a distance and are thus designated individually as "names" (*nāman*);

the other three faculties apprehend their objects in close proximity, and are therefore combined and termed "name. Next, to resolve the previous [section on] the four [terms] beginning with "not seeing":

regarding the statement "not seeing excludes visual consciousness," "excluding" (*chü*) means "absence. That is to say, the absence of visual consciousness is called "not seeing. Since it has been stated...
The other five consciousnesses are likewise [instances of] this. It is clearly understood that deceiving others by means of what is apprehended by the five consciousnesses is also "not seeing.

The explanations for the three lower categories follow this principle and should be understood accordingly. When one understands it in this way, the four [categories] beginning with "not seeing" take the non-existent as their object.

Because the scope of the objects contradicted [by these categories] is broad, it is like simply not seeing; this is termed "not seeing. That which is apprehended by the other five consciousnesses is also "not seeing."

The scope of what they refer to is narrow. That is to say, they claim to see what they have not seen; yet seeing is exclusively visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*). Therefore, their claim is narrow.

Since this one case is thus, the same applies to the following three. As for the four lower [faculties], such as seeing and so forth, they take conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) as their objects; thus, the objects they contradict are narrow.

This refers solely to visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*). The scope of what is designated here is broad, referring to "not seeing" and so forth. Next, false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*) is explained. First, the six mental states of "not seeing" and so forth are interpreted;

these are fully elucidated according to their meaning, which would result in twenty-four permutations. However, as this is now stated according to their respective positions, they are summarized into six.
There are two methods for analyzing these six mental states: first, defining the names of the mental states; second, the section on questions and answers.

Different. Regarding the mind of the first dhyāna, there are four states: first, the mind without ideation; second, the mind with ideation; third, the mind with doubt; and fourth, the mind without doubt.

Now, when six are mentioned, the "mind without ideation" refers exclusively to the state of simultaneous contradiction (*ubhaya-vipakṣa*). The "mind with ideation" refers to the state of simple contradiction (*eka-vipakṣa*).

Within the categories of "with doubt" and "without doubt," each gives rise to a state of simple contradiction. Thus, the first, third, and fifth are states of simultaneous contradiction, while the second, fourth, and sixth are [states of simple contradiction].

The first is the single contradiction. Second Gate: Question—Why is it that within the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-citta*) there is only the phrase of "simultaneous contradiction," whereas within the state of perception (*saṃjñi-citta*) there is only the phrase of "single contradiction"?
This is unlike the cases of having doubt (*savicikitsā*) and being without doubt (*nirvicikitsā*), where each has both the phrases of "single contradiction" and "simultaneous contradiction.
Answer: Perception (*saṃjñā*) is thorough and cannot be equated with doubt. The reason for this is that perception unilaterally knows [the object] as non-existent.

One must not say that [the object] exists. To say it exists is the first alternative; this contradicts both the mind and the object. If the perception (*saṃjñā*) were truly existent, then speaking of it as real would not constitute an offense.

It is only when one speaks in contradiction to this perception that it is called an offense. This constitutes a contradiction with the mind; in relation to the object, however, it is concordant. Thus, this is the second case:
the object is concordant while the mind is contradictory. For this reason, where there is no perception, there is only a contradiction with both; a contradiction with only one cannot occur.
The phrase: "Because it contradicts the mind alone, it is the second [category]. There is perception that contradicts alone;

there cannot be a category where both contradict, for if both were to contradict, that would be the first category. Doubt involves two conditions and thus can possess concealment; therefore, within doubt, both the single and the combined [contradictions] are present.
Question: Why is this lack of a false mind different from one who slanders? Answer: Slander involves grasping at a false mind.
It must necessarily be false. If it were not false, how could the mind be real? This grasping contradicts the mind; it cannot possibly be false.
If it were indeed false, how could the mind be real? Next, the text is explained according to its phrasing. Regarding the first phrase, "truly not seeing," etc., the answer is "seeing," etc.;
this is a phrase in which both subject and object are contradictory within a state of non-perception. Regarding the second, "truly not seeing," etc., it means:

First, when one actually sees and so forth, yet deceives others by saying "I did not see" and so forth, this is the case of a mind with perception (*saṃjñin*) where the object is agreeable to the mind but the verbal expression is contrary.
Third, when one has actually not seen and so forth, and internally gives rise to doubt—being uncertain whether one saw or did not see—yet deceives others by saying "I have no doubt;

I saw," this is the case of a mind with doubt (*sāṃśayika*) where both [the object and the expression] are contrary. Fourth, when one has actually not seen and so forth... [gives rise to... (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.)
The doubt is the same as before. To deceive another without doubt, saying "I do not see," and so forth, is a single instance of contradicting one's own mind while in a state of doubt.

Fifth, when one has truly not seen and so forth, and there is no doubt in one's mind, yet one says "I have doubt" and "I have seen," and so forth, this is a case of contradicting both [the facts and one's mind] while in a state of no doubt.
Sixth, when one has truly not seen and so forth, and likewise has no doubt in one's mind, yet one says "I have doubt."
"I do not see" and so forth constitute the single contrary mental phrase within the state of being free from doubt. Regarding what "should be explained in detail":

this refers to the four subsequent [phrases]—seeing, hearing, touching, and knowing—their ritual procedures being the same as those previously described; they cannot be recounted here again. Next, regarding the preliminary and subsequent preparatory practices (*pūrvāpara-prayoga*):

In total, there should be eight [possibilities], yet for the purpose of establishing the *thullaccaya* offense, there are only four permutations. The first permutation involves having a mind during all three periods;

the next two permutations involve having a mind during two periods and lacking a mind during one period; and the final permutation involves having a mind at the root moment while lacking a mind before and after.
There are four remaining permutations that do not constitute a *thullaccaya*: namely, those where there is no mind at the root moment but a mind exists before and after.

In the first case, there is mental engagement (*citta*) at the beginning and none at the two subsequent moments; in the last case, there is mental engagement at the end and none at the two preceding moments.
These three instances constitute *duṣkṛta* offenses. In the third instance, there is no mental engagement during all three times; thus, there is no offense. Next, regarding the internal mind:

while the mind is occupied with the thought of seeing tigers and wolves, one says with the mouth that one sees a Buddha image, answering the other differently from what was actually seen; hence it is said, "the seen is different. While the mind is occupied with enduring suffering, one deceives another and gains [something].

Delight. Within the mind that acts, there is a longing for wealth, beauty, fame, and desire. When answering another who wishes to hear the Dharma, one experiences a sensation of coolness but says one feels heat;

one actually harbors thoughts of enmity but says one has thoughts of kinship. The mind acts by taking this as its object, yet answers that it takes that as its object. Next, regarding the two texts on light and heavy offenses:

first, the formal conclusion of a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation) according to our own school; second, the conclusion of a *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing) for silent falsehood. According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*: "If previously..."
Speaking falsehoods unintentionally, or speaking out of confusion or error, constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense) in all such cases.

When preaching the Dharma, engaging in discussion, or transmitting the words of others, or when discussing any matter of right and wrong, do not claim for yourself that you are correct; always ensure that your assertions are based on a source, and then there will be no fault.

Next, the four [cases] beginning with "not seeing" (*adṛṣṭa*) are clarified as exceptions; among the preceding six [cases], these are the first three and the fifth, namely the four [cases] beginning with "seeing" (*dṛṣṭa*).

Regarding the opening of the latter six [categories], the first three and the fifth [of the former] involve intention accompanied by both seeing and perception; thus, one speaks of opening the first six.

The second phrase logically implies there should further be intention accompanied by perception but lacking seeing; thus, one speaks of opening the second phrase among the latter six. Furthermore, there should be doubt;
thus, one speaks of opening the fourth phrases of each of the preceding two sets of six. Finally, one should further state that there is intention without [either seeing or perception].

Doubt arises; thus, it is explained that the first two sets of six [cases] each refer to the sixth phrase. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that the four [cases] beginning with "not seeing" (adṛṣṭa) correspond to the first six, while the four beginning with "seeing" (dṛṣṭa) correspond to the latter six.
As for the intention regarding "one who has the perception of having seen," this corresponds to the "difference from what was seen" (dṛṣṭāntara) and so forth.
Next is disparaging the precepts. It is the principle of those who have left the household life that they should mutually praise one another to bring joy to each other and not neglect right practice.
Now, to wound others with vile speech exceeds the pain of being cut by a sword; the state of affliction is no light matter. Therefore, this rule was established.
The specific conditions for its violation consist of six factors: first, a *bhikṣu*; second, speaking words of disparagement; third, knowing it is disparagement; fourth, intending to humiliate.

The mind. The five words clarify [the meaning] completely. Sixth, it is for others to know and hear. Regarding the three phrases of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, the first is explained individually, while the following two are explained together.
There are two parts to this combined explanation: first, the disparagement of unwholesome dharmas; second, from "If one speaks...

onwards, the disparagement of wholesome dharmas. The preceding section has three parts: first, listing the seven kinds of unwholesome dharmas; first, the headings are listed, followed by their explanation.
Explanation: Second, regarding the method for a bhikṣu to revile by means of inferior conduct, there are likewise first the headings and then the explanation.

Third, regarding the bhikṣu’s conclusion on the offense, there are three parts: first, the enumeration; second, the explanation; and third, the conclusion. The remaining text may be understood accordingly.

Next is the precept against divisive speech (*paiśunya*). It is the principle that those who have left the household life should be of one mind and in harmony. Now, by whispering words in private, one destroys the relationship between others;

thus, disputes that do not yet exist are caused to arise, and those already present are not extinguished. This affliction and ruin are no small matter. Therefore, the Sage established this rule. There are six specific conditions:
first, it must be a *mahābhikṣu*, excluding those who assist in causing a schism in the Saṃgha; second, the matter spoken of must be base and evil; third, [it must be] transmitted to...

[The factors are: (1) both parties; (2) the intention to cause separation; (3) the words being clear and distinct; (4) the object being known and heard by the other party. According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (or *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*), there are four permutations.

There may be double-tongued speech (*paiśunya*) that is neither false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*) nor harsh speech (*pāruṣya*). Because one transmits a message and speaks what is true, it is not false speech. Because one speaks with gentle words, it is not harsh speech.
Because one acts with a mind intent on division, it is called double-tongued speech. Alternatively, there may be double-tongued speech that is...
False speech is not necessarily harsh speech. Because it creates a mind of separation, it is divisive speech (*paiśunya*); because it is spoken falsely, it is false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*);
and because it is spoken with gentle words, it is not harsh speech (*pāruṣya*). Alternatively, there may be divisive speech that is harsh speech but not false speech:
because it creates a mind of separation, it is divisive speech; and because it is spoken with coarse words, it is harsh speech; yet, because it speaks what is true, it is not false speech.

It is not false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*). There may be divisive speech (*paiśunya*); this is false speech and it is harsh speech (*pāruṣya*). Because it creates a mind of separation, it is divisive speech;
because it is spoken falsely, it is false speech; because it is spoken with evil sounds, it is harsh speech. The four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) of false speech and harsh speech are likewise.
The three phrases in the root text [of the *Prātimokṣa*] are explained in detail therein. Regarding divisive speech, the second [phrase] is explained below.
[This section consists of] phrases. Within this, there are two parts. First, the enumeration of the objects of contention and discord. There are ten groups of such objects;

five belonging to the monastic community and five to the lay community. By taking each as a primary subject in turn, they collectively form one hundred phrases. Second, from "Next, [regarding] contention and discord" onwards, the words transmitted are set forth. From "If a bhikṣu... onwards, the third phrase concerning the establishment of the offense is explained.
Although ten groups are listed as the objects of this contention and discord, when discussing what constitutes a *thullaccaya* (grave offense), it is restricted to the great *bhikṣu*.

The Buddha asked why he disparaged the existence of wholesome dharmas, asking, "What is it that does not exist here? He replied, "In this case, wholesome dharmas are transmitted in private without causing affliction;
whereas previously, they were conducted face-to-face, which is why there was a minor offense."
Next is the precept regarding sleeping in the same room with a woman. Since the physical forms of men and women differ, it is logically necessary that they reside in separate places.
As for lodging, one must avoid giving rise to suspicion or scandal; now, to lightly share a room with them allows for the possibility of impure defilement, which is no small affliction.

Therefore, the Sage established this rule, and the underlying intent of the subsequent rules concerning defilement is the same as this. There are five specific conditions: first, the person must be a woman; second, she must be a human being... [and so forth].

Regarding women: first, they do not distinguish between monastics and laypeople or between kin and strangers; second, they are distinguished from men by their separate realms of rebirth; third, they achieve the completion of the two chambers;
fourth, they cohabit in the same room; fifth, they know of this cohabitation; sixth, they turn over while lying together. Among these conditions, it appears as an offense.

This precept was established based on these circumstantial factors, for those whose craving has been exhausted have no such intent and thus do not transgress. Within the text there are three parts; the first concerns the appearance of an offense based on circumstantial factors.

[The first part] concerns the offense. Second, from "That courtesan... downwards, it clarifies that there was in fact no transgression. Third, from "The courtesan saw... downwards, it concerns the benefits obtained through repentance.
Regarding the old interpretation—that because an Arhat possesses both types of liberation (vimukti), one may say they are "without delusion" (*amoha*)—this explanation is incorrect.

As clarified above, even an Arhat can be said to possess delusion. Furthermore, within the section on the common precepts (*sādhāraṇa-śīla*), there are many instances of speech involving outflows (*āsrava*). Moreover, [it is] sufficient...
Within the precepts on eating and the precepts on untimely food, there is no mention of "ignorance" (*moha*). How could a person who violates these two precepts be an Arhat?

Furthermore, in the sections of the Bhikṣuṇī-prātimokṣa where such matters are censured, there is likewise no mention of "ignorance. This can be understood from the four-line root text and its extensive commentary.
*Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, Chapter Eight: If there is one woman in a room, it constitutes one *pārājika*; if there are ten women, it constitutes ten *pārājikas*.

This precept is established as an offense through bodily action (*kāya-karman*), and it is also established as an offense with respect to the person. One instance of lying down constitutes one *pārājika*; ten instances of lying down constitute ten *pārājikas*. This is called "establishment of the offense through bodily action.

If one lies down with one woman, it constitutes one *pārājika*; if one lies down with ten women, it constitutes ten *pārājikas*. This is called [establishment of the offense] with respect to the person.

Regarding the offense for the superior [grade]: The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that there is no offense if one shares a cover but has a different partition; or if it is a large assembly preaching the Dharma; or if a mother, sister, or close relative is ill;
or if one is accompanied by a knowledgeable man and does not lie down. This permissive text excludes cases where one is personally ill, in which case there is no offense.
The same applies to the lower precepts.
Next is the precept regarding staying overnight with one who has not yet received full ordination for more than three nights. According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*, fascicle eight:
The reason the precepts were established for the bhikṣus was out of respect for the Buddha-dharma and to prevent slander.

As for why staying for two nights was permitted, it was because if no [overnight stay] were allowed at all, there might be circumstances where one’s life is endangered, as well as various other causes for distress. Therefore, [staying for two nights] was permitted.
Out of compassion, it is permitted to stay together for two nights; however, to protect the Buddha-dharma, staying for three nights is not allowed. There are five specific conditions:

first, the person must be a male who has not yet received full ordination (this excludes women, as for women, even two nights are not permitted, so how could there be an offense for exceeding three?);

second, the room's characteristics must be fulfilled; third, they sleep in the same room together; fourth, they know they are sleeping in the same room together; fifth, exceeding three nights constitutes an offense. [Question: Regarding these...
The bhikṣu Vairaṭīputra departed, acting in full accordance with the Buddha’s teachings. How then can he be rebuked as a "foolish man lacking compassion"? Answer:

As for the law of a disciple, one must consult [the teacher] on every matter. Now, to have summarily driven him away—is this not a failure of decorum? The Buddha established rules based on specific circumstances and permitted exceptions based on specific circumstances.
It is for this reason that he was rebuked as being "foolish and lacking compassion. This constitutes a violation of the fourfold formulation of the full precepts (pātimokkha). One offense.
1. A person who has received full ordination; 2. A person who has not yet received full ordination; 3. Sleeping together; 4. Exceeding three nights and incurring an offense.
However, in the previous allowance, if one falls into sleeping for three nights, one should rise and depart before the dawn appears.

Upon reaching the fourth night, whether one departs oneself or sends a person who has not received full ordination to leave, should the third and fourth nights then constitute a violation? The *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* directly concludes that exceeding three nights constitutes an offense.

Regarding the offense, the detailed explanation discusses only the transgression of the fourth night. Since it states that one commits the offense by following [the monk] as far as his side, it is clear that this refers to the person who avoids the appearance of light on the third night;
the definition of the characteristics can be understood from this explanation.
Next, one may recite the precepts together with those who have not yet received full ordination. According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*, this was established for four reasons:

first, to distinguish [the Buddhist community] from non-Buddhists; second, to differentiate between teacher and disciple; third, to facilitate clear verbal expression so that the meaning is understood;

and fourth, because the true meaning is relied upon rather than the mere sound of the words. There are five specific conditions [for this exception]: the first is that it is spoken by the Buddha himself.
The Dharma. Second, the words, phrases, and meanings. Second, those who have not yet received full ordination. Fourth, reciting together in unison. Fifth, the speech being clearly articulated.

The four lines of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* can be understood [as follows]. In the commentary, the first two lines provide a specific explanation of the meaning of the phrases, while the following part explains the third line.

The text here consists of two parts: first, the explanation of *jù-yì* (reciting together); second, the exposition of the essential nature of the dharma. Within the first part, there are again two sections: first, the enumeration; second, the explanation.
Regarding the meaning of the term *jù-yì* in the explanation: when two people chant the words and meanings in unison, it signifies that the practice of the principle is complete;

thus it is called *jù-yì*. As for what is not *jù-yì*: when the preceding speaker has not yet finished, the person behind copies and recites; this signifies that the practice is incomplete, and is therefore called "not *jù-yì*."

Regarding the meaning: this also incurs a *pāyattika* offense. This is because it would cause the teaching and its meaning to fail to circulate universally; for what reason would it not be an offense?
The explanations of the characteristics of the following two cases should be understood by analogy. As for the term *arapacanā*, it is intended to reveal that the name expresses a universal essence;
this is the meaning of the word. Regarding "Dharma," the *Jian lun* (Treatise on Seeing) states: "If, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, Kāśyapa serves as the Elder, [and] the five..."
The Tripiṭaka compiled by the hundred Arhats was recited together as this Dharma; [if one recites it otherwise,] one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.

By this standard, Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas of the final age who compose various treatises do not incur an offense when they recite them. Regarding the phrase "the Śrāvakas and others here speak," it means that because they have received the Buddha’s seal of approval, their words are established as Sūtra.
Next, from "If a bhikṣu... onwards, the fourth sentence concerning the determination of the offense is explained. First, the recitation.

"Those" refers to the meaning of the preceding phrase; "second utterance" refers to the phrasing (*vyañjana*); "third utterance" refers to the meaning of the syllables (*akṣara*). Alternatively, within the recitation of phrases, phrasings, and syllables, there may be one, two, or three [instances];
if these are clearly discerned, all constitute an offense. For now, the number three is cited as the rule; the others are to be understood by analogy.
If it is transmitted orally, one recites what has been abridged; if it is transmitted in writing, one copies what has been truncated. The remaining characteristics can be understood.

Next, the precepts concerning grave offenses (*sthūlātyaya*) are explained. According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*, fascicle six: The reason for establishing the precepts with regard to bhikṣus is to provide great protection for the Buddha-dharma.
If one were to speak of the faults and evils of a bhikṣu to a layperson (*avadātavasana*), that person would have no faith in the Buddha-dharma.
With a respectful mind, one would rather destroy a stūpa or damage an image than speak of the faults or transgressions of a bhikṣu to one who has not received full ordination (*upasampadā*).

If one speaks of such offenses, one destroys the Dharma-body. There are seven specific conditions [for this offense]: first, the person is a bhikṣu; second, he has committed a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*); third, one knows he has committed a grave offense;

fourth, one speaks of it to one who has not received full ordination; fifth, there is no valid reason—excluding those who have been specifically appointed; sixth, the words are explicit; [seventh, the listener understands].
Clearly understood. Seven points for others to hear and know. Five phrases regarding the full precept: first, the offender; second, knowing it is a gross offense (*sthūlātyaya*);
third, speaking to one who has not yet received full ordination; fourth, excluding cases where the offense is waived or not committed; fifth, the formal determination of the offense (*āpatti*).

In the commentary, the third point is explained first, followed by the second, which differs [from other rules]. This definitively concerns gross offenses. However, in the text regarding the initial two offenses, the phrase "except for those [cases] involving a formal act of the Saṃgha (*saṃghakamma*)" is excluded.
While it is based on the case of Devadatta as the illustrative condition, in principle the actual offenses are established only for the first two cases; thus, the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:

"If one speaks of shedding the blood of a Buddha or destroying the wheel of the Saṃgha, it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense) requiring confession before another person; if one speaks of the four pārājika offenses or the thirteen saṃghāvaśeṣa offenses, [it is likewise]."
In all cases of *sthūlātyaya*, one incurs a *duṣkṛta*. This explains the fifth phrase, which is expanded into four parts:

first, speaking of another; within this, there are two sub-categories. Second, speaking of oneself. Question: Why is it that when one speaks of oneself, the grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*) is considered light? Answer: Because [speaking of] others occurs frequently while [speaking of] oneself is rare.

Furthermore, speaking of another’s faults excessively leads to three harms: first, self-destruction; second, vexing others; and third, corrupting the laity. Speaking of oneself lacks these [consequences].
This causes distress to others; therefore, it is merely inauspicious. Third, the remaining groups. Fourth, the perception of the object.

Next, regarding the teaching of the precepts to one who has actually attained the Path but has not yet received full ordination (*upasampadā*): the reasons for establishing this rule are given in two points according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*.
First, it is for the sake of the way of the great man (*mahāpuruṣa*). To conceal one's faults while praising one's own virtuous conduct is the way of the petty man (*kṣudrapuruṣa*).

Second, it is for the sake of the way of equality. If one were to claim one's own saintly virtues, then the wise and the foolish would become distinct, and the person in question would lack a mind of impartiality toward the Saṃgha.
There are five conditions for this [claim]: first, possessing actual virtue within while dispelling arrogance; second, personally declaring that one has realized [the truth].
Third, speaking to one who has not yet received full ordination; fourth, the words being clearly articulated; fifth, the object being known or heard by the listener.

Since there are no other contributing conditions, this refers to those who speak actual falsehoods among the great lies (*mahāvadya*). The ancient commentary states: "Once this was established as a prohibition for the Noble Ones (*ārya*), they would never again commit such an offense."
To say that this rule restricts the noble ones while excluding ordinary persons is incorrect. For instance, a person in training (śaikṣa) may still commit intentional transgressions;

these are not inherent precepts (prakṛti-śīla). How could there be any contradiction in this? Reflecting on this principle, it remains a restriction for the noble ones. When an ordinary person attains [false] meditations such as the contemplation of impurity (aśubha-bhāvanā), they likewise incur an offense.

The original text of the precept consists of five points: first, the person; second, the object toward whom the confession is made; third, the claim of having attained superhuman states (uttara-manuṣya-dharma); fourth, oneself...

He speaks of his own realization. Regarding the five offenses involving formal confession (*pācittiya*), the commentary provides a detailed explanation. If one follows the fifth phrase of the lower section, the four textual points are clear.

Next is the precept concerning teaching the Dharma to women for more than five or six sentences. Teaching the Dharma gives rise to [the opportunity for] spiritual growth; by principle, one must not force it upon others.
To engage in such matters at an improper time only serves to increase one's luxury and arrogance; yet, even though these are defiled objects, they must still be used as a means of guidance.

If one were not permitted to do so at all, the path of escape would be forever cut off. Therefore, it was further permitted to speak five or six words; to exceed this limit incurs public censure, and thus the rule was established as a prohibition.

The separate conditions consist of six: first, it is a woman; second, one knows her to be such; third, she has not requested [instruction]; fourth, there is no layman present; fifth, the words are completed;
sixth, exceeding five or six sentences constitutes an offense. If she requests [instruction], one may speak accordingly; even if the limit is exceeded, there is no offense.

The full precept can be understood through its five clauses, which are clearly explained in the commentary. Regarding "a man who understands," the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* states: "This refers to one who understands human sentiments, speech, and meaning."
This may serve as proof. If the categories differ, it is not permitted in any case. A man must be a layperson (*avadātavasana*);
no ordained person is permitted [to preach]. Because their status is identical, even when the assembly of monks is gathered, one must not preach for them.
However, preaching for a *bhikṣuṇī* is permitted, because she is subject to formal instruction. According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, a *bhikṣu* may preach for a woman.
Having finished speaking five or six words, she says, "Sisters, the Dharma is correctly established up to this point," and rises from her seat and departs.

On another occasion, having returned to sit again due to further circumstances, she speaks for them regarding what constitutes non-offense. If, after finishing five or six words, another woman arrives, she speaks for that later woman;
thus, through such successive causes, she may speak for countless women, and in all cases it is non-offense. If she recites it herself...
Sūtra: If a woman comes to listen, and if she asks about the meaning [of the Dharma], one must ensure she understands it; there is no offense in exceeding five or six words.
Next, the precept against digging the earth. *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*: Regarding this precept and the precept against destroying living beings, their establishment has three benefits:

first, to avoid causing affliction to sentient beings; second, to stop slander; and third, to provide great protection for the Buddha-dharma. If these were not established, [the following would occur].
All kings shall cause bhikṣus to perform various types of labor; because they possess this precept, emperors, kings, and all rulers of nations will have their minds stilled.
There are five specific conditions: first, it is native soil; second, one perceives it as native soil; third, one digs it oneself.
Fourth, when employing others to dig, one does not utter the words of "purification. Fifth, the offense is established according to the injury incurred.

There are three points for establishing the precept: first, it is formulated briefly regarding digging oneself; second, because the characteristics of the prohibition were not yet complete when instructing others to dig without uttering the words of purification, the subsequent offense is further clarified;
third, the full completion of the rule. This completion consists of five factors: first, the offender; second, the act performed by oneself; third, the ground that is injured.
Fourth, the instruction on the karma of others; fifth, the formal confession of the *pāyattika* offense. Regarding the commentary, the first three [sections] are explained individually.

If one uses a hoe to dig, it would be appropriate to explain the second, fourth, fifth, and third phrases together. However, within the explanation of "earth," there is first a general division into two:

that which has not yet been dug constitutes one fixed category, while that which has already been dug is further divided into two. Thus, through the opening and closing of the categories of earth, there are three. This does not depend on whether it is covered.

"Exposed. Those who destroy it all fall [into hell]. *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, fascicle 19: "There are two kinds of earth: namely, natural (*jāti*) and constructed (*kṛta*). 'Natural' refers to the great earth. 'Constructed' has two types:

first, the foundation; second, the superstructure. Regarding the construction of a foundation, this refers to walls on open ground. Regarding the construction of a superstructure, this refers to covering the ground above a multi-storied building.
If one destroys the substance of such grounds, it is all a *pārājika* offense. The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: 'There are two kinds of earth...'"
