There are two kinds of ground. First is true ground, which contains no sand, stones, or rubble, but is pure soil.

Second is non-true ground; one should take a small amount of soil and wash it with water to examine it. If three-quarters is stone and one-quarter is soil, it may be excavated. If it is true ground, one may dig.

The offense of *khārodaka* (digging/digging up). Next, the combined explanation of the text contains five parts. First, the offense regarding the damaging of the earth. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"With one's own hand" refers to either the body itself or bodily expedients. Regarding "the body": it means jumping, leaping, running, coming, or going with the whole body.
Regarding "parts of the body": it means the hands, feet, knees, elbows, or pointing with the fingers. Regarding "bodily expedients": if...
If one uses a spade, a hoe, an axe, or a chisel to dig the earth with one's own hand, or throws something from afar with the intent to cause damage, it is a *pāyattika*.
Furthermore, it is said: if a bhikṣu wishes to level the ground and employs a means such as sweeping it, it is an offense of *vyatikrama-vinaya* (transgression of discipline).

If [the ground] is injured even by as much as a mosquito’s leg, it is a *pāyattika*. If no means were employed, there is no offense. If one employs a means such as dragging wood or driving oxen and horses [over the ground], [it is likewise].

The same applies to other such cases. If one steps on a hole by a riverbank with one's foot, it is a *yati* offense for each step taken. If earth collapses from the edge of a pond or a bank while walking there, there is no offense.

If a clod of earth is so large that one person cannot lift it, breaking it constitutes a *yati* offense; if it is heavy enough that more than one person is required to move it, there is no offense in breaking it.
If the earth is saturated with rain, one may not take it oneself; one must have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person) take it, provided the rain has ceased.
Once the area has been moistened, only then may the bhikṣu draw water for himself without fault. If it is after a fresh rain, a bhikṣu must not draw from a well by himself;

he should have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a lay attendant) draw it. If the *kappiya-kāraka* is too small or incapable, he should first cause the *kappiya-kāraka* to stir up the water until it becomes turbid, and only then may he draw it himself.
If it is pond water or floodwater after a fresh rain, a bhikṣu must not draw it by himself. [The same applies] if it is the water of oxen or horses...
First, regarding crossing [water]: one may draw water for oneself. However, if there are objects such as jars or pots on the open ground after rain, a bhikṣu must not take them himself;

he should have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a lay attendant) know of it. Second, regarding driving a stake into the ground: the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that if one strikes a stake into the ground, it is a *vinayātikrama* (transgression of discipline);
if it harms [the ground] even as much as a mosquito's leg, it is a *pācittiya*. The same applies to pulling out a stake. Third, regarding lighting a fire upon the ground: this damages the earth.

Therefore, according to the *Jianlun* (Treatise on Observations): if one holds fire and burns one's hand, throwing it to the ground does not constitute an offense. The fourth point, regarding the perception of the object (*viṣaya-saṃjñā*), may be understood accordingly.
Fifth, regarding the offense of losing the Dharma (*dharmaparihāṇi-āpatti*): according to the *Jianlun*, there are fifteen cases.

If a bhikṣu says to a lay attendant (*upāsaka*), "Dig the earth and chop wood for the sake of the Saṃgha," there is no offense. However, if he points out and instructs, "Dig this" or "Chop this," it is a *thullaccaya* (grave offense). Now, based on this text, it is simply...

One does not speak pure speech; if one does not inquire whether [the ground] is prepared or not, it is all an offense of expiation (*pāyattika*). For those of lower status, digging for no purpose is a fault (*dukkaṭa*).

However, if it is for the benefit of the Triple Gem, there is no offense in excavating. Therefore, in the *Kṣudraka-vastu* (The Book on Minor Rules), it says: "If the Saṃgha acquires a fruit orchard and does not know who should manage it, the Buddha said:
'Whether it be a monastery attendant or a śrāmaṇera, the principle regarding the destruction of living beings is the same. This is the opening text.
It is simply permitted to clear away the soil, but one must not damage the ground. The *Jianlun* (Treatise on Seeing), fascicle 11, states:

"If someone sets fire that approaches a monastery, for the sake of protecting the dwelling place, a bhikṣu may dig up grass and excavate earth to cut off the fire; this does not constitute an offense.

In the passage below, when fire burning outside the Jetavana Monastery spreads over the mats and approaches, the bhikṣus did not know what to do. The Buddha said: "I permit you to go against it [and extinguish it]."

One should remove the intermediate grass. Whether one cuts it by making a trench or pit, or extinguishes it with earth, or burns it against the grain—although the text does not explicitly state that a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to perform such acts) should be employed, if such measures are taken, they are likewise permitted and free from fault.

Next is the precept against destroying living things. The regulation of the mind and the requisite conditions are the same as above; there is no distinct characteristic of transgression. This is the causal context for the precept regarding dwellings.

The root text of the precept consists of four phrases: first, the person who commits the offense; second, the act of destruction; third, the object damaged; and fourth, the formal determination of the offense.
Regarding the commentary, the first phrase is self-evident. Next, the third phrase is briefly explained: all grasses and trees are the abodes of non-human beings. (10)
Recite: Regarding the "tenth village," this refers to the dwelling places of sentient beings consisting of grasses and trees.

As for "sentient beings," these include tree deities (*vṛkṣadeva*) and so forth, up to the deities of the great highways; as well as mosquitoes, gadflies, dung beetles, butterflies, and so forth, down to ants.

These sentient beings take grass and water as their dwellings, and likewise regard them as villages, hamlets, cities, and towns. If one cuts or chops [the plants], it explains the second phrase. If...

If one leaf is destroyed, many lives are destroyed along with it, and one incurs much demerit. Therefore, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If a bhikṣu burns five types of seeds at once, he commits five *pāyattika* offenses simultaneously;
if he burns them one by one, he commits one *pāyattika* for each. Regarding the term "village" (*grāma*), there are five kinds of villages, as explained extensively in the third [section] below.

This passage consists of three parts: first, the introduction; second, the enumeration; and third, the explanation. Within the enumeration, there are five items, which correspond to the following meanings.

There are three [types], namely: root, branch, and seed. As for the fivefold division of the text: among the roots, those that do not depend on joints to grow are given the name "root-seed" (*mūla-bīja*);
those that depend on joints to grow are termed "covered-seed" (*kanda-bīja*). Branch-seeds are divided into two; their meaning is likewise.

Within seed-seeds, they are one in their essential substance, but when differentiated by their beginning and end, they become five types. This corresponds to the fourteen [categories] of the *Mahāsāṃghika*.
These five types clarify the methods for purifying seeds. Regarding the two types, root and stem: if they are purified by slicing with a knife, they are "knife-purified.
If they are joint-seeds, they are purified by slicing and then splitting. If they are scale-seeds, such as coriander, *śāliñca*, or *nīla*, they are purified by crushing them flat.
As for seed-seeds, the seventeen types of grain are purified by removing the husks. Fire-purification applies to all five types. Furthermore, it is said that if...
When distributing beans, sesame, sugarcane, and so forth among the Sangha, the Elder should ask whether they have been purified (*kappiya*).
If it is said they have not been purified, he should have them purified. If it is said they have already been purified, they may be eaten.

If there are many fruits within a single vessel, if one fruit is purified at its location, the others are also collectively considered purified. If they are in separate vessels, each must be purified individually.

Regarding the ritual for a single vessel: if sugarcane has leaves, each stalk must be purified individually. If it is without leaves, it may be bound together as a bundle and purified as a whole, like fruit.

Furthermore, when Māmakī had grain in a granary that had not yet been purified, fearing that young bhikṣus would not know the Dharma, she had a *kappiya-kāraka* (purifier) perform the fire-purification.
When the grain in the granary was exhausted, the bhikṣus were always permitted to say, "Grind [it]."

There is no offense in departing. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Sengqi lü), fascicle 31, states: "If one wishes to eat the kernel of a fruit, it is permitted to eat it after it has been purified by fire.
If it is purified by peeling the skin but not by fire, and one eats the kernel, it is a *pāyattika*. If it is purified by fire but not by peeling the skin, both the skin and the kernel may be eaten."
If one eats food that has not been purified by fire or purified by peeling, there is one *pācittiya* offense and one *duṣkṛta* offense. If both methods are performed, there is no offense.

Now, as for performing the purification, it is not intended to prevent [the seeds] from ever sprouting again; rather, it is done to quell the slander of non-Buddhists (tīrthikas). Therefore, it is called the "purifying dharma of the śramaṇas."
The following section provides a word-for-word reversal and explanation, all of which may be found in the fifteenth fascicle of the *Śāstra*. *Harīta* refers to yellow ginger;
both the Chinese and Sanskrit terms are clearly indicated in the text. *Uśīra* is sweet flag (*cēngqián*). *Mūlaka-ṭha* is *nakha-gandha* (stag’s nail incense).
*Rōhaṇa* is *hùlián* (coptis). *Dhava* is the name of a foreign herb. *Vata* is easily understood [as the banyan tree]. *Salmali* is the Bodhi tree. *Bhallātaka*...
The *tāla* and *pippala* trees (these two types of trees are found only in Jiǎo and Guǎng; they are not seen in other regions). The *sumanā* flower:
its fragrance is similar to that of the *mallikā* (this flowering vine grows in Jiǎngzhōu). The *surabha* (the name of this grass is not [widely] known).

The *puṣkara* (a foreign name for a grass). Other characteristics can be understood. If one explains the fourth phrase according to the commentary below, it also constitutes a text concerning the gravity of karmic results.

The text contains seven points. The first concerns the perception regarding the object (*ālambana-saṃjñā*). Based on the destruction of seeds that can grow, this refers to the four types of offenses for one act (*ekāpatti-catur-guṇa*).
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If one throws five types of seeds into a pond, or into a well, or into excrement or urine, or onto refuse heaps, one incurs a *vinayātikrama*.
If the seeds have rotted and perished, it is a *pāyattika*. If a bhikṣu wishes to prevent grass from growing..."
While walking during the midday period, if one steps upon grass and injures it even to the extent of a mosquito's leg, one incurs a *pāyattika*.
The same applies when standing, sitting, or lying down. If one cuts a fresh, green, tender leaf, it is a *pāyattika*. If one cuts a long, stalked, hard leaf, it is a *pāyattika*.
If the leaves have already withered and turned yellow, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing). If the wind blows these three kinds of leaves [and they fall], there is no offense.

If it falls, there is no offense in taking and using it. If one plucks a fresh flower, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense; if it is half-ripe, it is a *vinayātikrama*; if it is fully ripe, there is no offense.
Regarding the second point concerning plants and trees, this clarifies the destruction based on their state of growth. The remainder of the text is understandable.

As for "pure speech" (*viśuddha-vāk*), according to the sixth fascicle of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, when a bhikṣu requires anything, he says to a lay attendant (*kappiya-kāraka*), "You know this. If they do not understand, he speaks again.
"You look at this. If he does not understand, speak again, saying, "I need this. If he still does not understand, speak again, saying, "Give this to me. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"If one serves as an administrator for the Saṃgha, one must never use impure speech. One should say, 'Cut this,' 'Break this,' 'Crush this,' 'Burn this,' or 'Strip this';
in all such cases, one should say, 'Know this' or 'This is pure,' and there is no offense. The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (Duo-lun) says:

The three groups [of novices] are *kappiya-kārakas* (purifiers); therefore, there is no offense. In all these allowances, there is no intention to cause damage. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*:

if one is staying in the mountains and the mud and rain make the ground slippery such that one is about to fall, and one grasps a blade of grass which breaks, or grasps it again after it has broken—in such cases, there is no offense.
If one is being swept away by water and grasps a blade of grass which breaks as one follows along, there is likewise no offense even though it breaks.
Next is the precept on vexing the Saṃgha with discordant speech. One who has left the household life ought, as a matter of principle, to maintain a pure mind and guard the Way.

Whatever one says must accord with proper decorum. Now, however, one abandons the truth and harbors the false, employing deceitful words and flowery rhetoric. Although the karma may seem slight, it causes extreme vexation to the Saṃgha. Therefore, the assembly of monks establishes a rule to rebuke and restrain such behavior;
because it violates the Dharma and is committed with gravity, one incurs the offense of *thullaccaya* (grave transgression). The specific conditions for this are fully detailed.
Five [factors]: 1. Mutual frivolity of body and speech; 2. Repeatedly acting without ceasing; 3. The disciplinary rules established by the Saṃgha; 4.

Being summoned and questioned according to the Dharma; 5. Committing an offense through repeated action. If one violates [the rule] before the Saṃgha has performed the formal act (karman), it is a light offense (duṣkṛta);

once the formal act has been performed, one incurs a *thullaccaya* offense. Frivolity of verbal karma is termed "speaking differently" (*visabhāga-vāda*); frivolity of bodily karma is termed "touching."

This is the designation for "annoyance. Here, these two *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses are combined into a single precept because there is no difference in the manner of annoying the Saṃgha regardless of whether one answers or does not answer when questioned.

As for the subsequent precepts, since the administrative duties involved are identical, the two offenses are likewise combined. Therefore, among the ninety [offenses], only these two are combined into a single rule.
First: frivolous speech—four parts: (1) the arising of the fault; (2) the reprimand; (3) the formal procedure (*karmavācanā*); and (4) the establishment of the precept. Next...
The four ways of adorning the body are as previously stated. Regarding the three phrases in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, the first is explained individually, while the latter two are explained together.

In the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, there is no answering according to the question; rather, every question results in a *pārājika* offense. This statement that "all are *pārājika*" is identical to that [text’s] treatment of each individual question.
As for whether one should respond when summoned by an elder, the *Pañcavargika* provides a general clarification: if one mistakenly takes up another's words...
Answer: Furthermore, because he previously harbored resentment and did not speak with him, he did not answer;

thus, there is no offense. Next is the precept against disparaging and reviling. Generally, monastic affairs are extensive and difficult to manage. Therefore, one should select virtuous persons to handle them according to the Dharma.

It is only right that one recognize their toil and praise their virtue; yet, instead, one acts out of personal bias to disparage and revile them. Since this matter is not trivial, it must be addressed.
The Sacred Regulation. Regarding the explanation of the names: in a place where one sees but does not hear, it is called "finding fault" (*āghāta*) when there is attachment and so forth;

in a place where one hears but does not see, it is called "reviling. These two preceding and succeeding formulations are combined into a single precept. There are six distinct conditions: first, one who knows the person performing the *karmavācanā* for monastic affairs;
second, knowing that it is such a person; third, [knowing] that they have performed their duties according to the Dharma without attachment and so forth; fourth, speaking...
Regarding abusive speech: it consists of five-word phrases that are clearly articulated. Sixth, there is the case where another person sees it but does not hear it, or hears it but does not see it;

this constitutes an offense of *pācittiya*. The disciplinary text has three parts: first, the occurrence of the transgression; second, the reprimand; and third, the establishment of the precept. This is likewise the same for verbal abuse.
The three phrases of the *Prātimokṣa* [Sūtra] can be understood through their explanation of the characteristics.
Next is the precept concerning the spreading of monastic bedding in an exposed place. According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*, it was established for three reasons:

first, to ensure the peace and comfort of those practicing the Path; second, to nurture faith and reverence; and third, to cause the roots of merit of the donors (*dānapati*) to reach fulfillment. Thus, in the *Mātṛkā-sūtra*, Chapter... [number].
Fourth: The reason for instructing the bhikṣus to protect their bedding and mats is that five kinds of faults are observed: first, not letting them be blown by the wind;
second, not letting them be scorched by the sun; third, not letting them be rained upon; fourth, not letting dust and soil settle upon them;
and fifth, not letting insects or birds deposit impurities upon the bedding and mats. There are seven distinct conditions [for this], the first of which is the Saṃgha.

[The offense concerning] the bedding and requisites of the Saṃgha: 1. Knowing it belongs to the Saṃgha; 2. It is an item belonging to the Saṃgha; 3. It is in an open place; 4. One uses it for one’s own enjoyment; 5. One spreads it oneself or instructs another to spread it; 6.

Upon departing, one neither puts it away oneself nor instructs another to put it away; 7. The offense is incurred as soon as one passes through the door. The four phrases of the root precept are: 1. The person who commits the offense;
2. The property belonging to the Saṃgha; 3. In an open place, spreading it for one's own use; 4. Departing and abandoning it, which constitutes the formal incurrence of the offense.

This provides a detailed explanation of the characteristics [of the offense]. The first phrase is self-evident. Regarding the second phrase, which explains the "locations," it lists three types of monastic property (*saṃghika-vastu*).

This is the same as the previous precept concerning the misappropriation of monastic property; although the wording is identical, the meaning of "misappropriating" and "receiving back" differs. Therefore, one must examine the textual intent within these three cases:

in the first two, one incurs a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation); in the second, a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*). Alternatively, these three may all equally be considered monastic property, and thus [the offenses] are uniform.
[This constitutes] an offense of *thullaccaya*. According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*: There were certain bhikṣus who saw monastic bedding (*śayanāsana*) spread out in the open air;
yet, because they did not spread it themselves nor cause others to spread it, and neither sat upon it nor lay down upon it, they failed to gather it up and put it away. The Buddha said:

"If one sees monastic bedding spread out in the open air and does not gather it up, it is a *pāyattika* offense. There were also certain laypeople who came into the monastery and sought [the use of] the monastic [bedding].
Regarding bedding and seats: if one spreads them out in the open air, the Buddha said that if they are not picked up when the time for departure approaches, it is a *pāyattika*.
Furthermore, if a layperson invites the monks and borrows monastic bedding to spread in their home, and the monks sit there and depart without picking it up, it is a *pāyattika*.
If a monk goes to a nuns' quarters and spreads out the nuns' bedding in the open air, thinking it is not monastic bedding...

If one does not perform the formal act of suspension (*ukkhepana*), it is also a *pāyattika* offense. The commentary below the third sentence explains the procedure for suspension and demonstrates the conditions under which there is no offense;
the commentary below the fourth sentence concerns the formal establishment of the offense for violating the rule.
These two sections each contain four points, which may be understood accordingly.
Next is the precept concerning the spreading of monastic bedding in a secluded place. The intent of the prohibition and the full set of conditions are as previously stated.

The core text of the precept consists of four phrases: first, the person who commits the offense; second, the act of spreading bedding in a secluded place; third, the condition that one does so for one’s own use;

and fourth, the conclusion regarding the offense upon departure. Of these, the first three can be understood from the commentary. As for the fourth phrase, "if one departs," this is explained as follows: [The text continues with the detailed explanation of the fourth phrase.]

Chinese Text II. First, the explanation of permanent departure; this section has two parts, as can be understood. Second, the discussion of temporary travel also has two parts, as above. Within the opening [of the discussion], there are also two parts:
first, the opening regarding permanent departure; second, from "If at some time he returns" onwards, the opening regarding the temporary.
Next is the precept against forcibly spreading bedding: First, one exerts effort oneself to seek a place to stay; subsequently, it is only proper to deliberate upon whether to enter or not.

To now act with forceful compulsion is contrary to both the facts and human sentiment; the nature of this transgression is no small matter, and thus it was necessary for the Noble One to establish this rule.

There are five constituent conditions: first, the place is already occupied and settled; second, one knows it is already occupied and settled; third, one forcibly spreads the bedding out of malice; fourth, there is no [justification].
The causal conditions (*nidāna*) refer to two difficulties: the absence of a supportive friend and illness. There are five offenses regarding reclining.

The full precept consists of four clauses: first, the person who commits the offense; second, knowing that the dwelling was already occupied; third, arriving later and forcibly spreading one's bedding to cause distress;

fourth, performing such an act, which constitutes the formal completion of the offense. The phrase "by means of such causal conditions" refers specifically to the causal conditions for causing distress, and not to any other.

It is not the case that others do not incur an offense; [this applies] except in circumstances such as illness. Regarding "not being in a state of proper deportment" (*iriyāpatha*), this indicates the fault and constitutes an offense.
In the commentary, the first three lines are explained individually, while the section beginning with "If a bhikṣu... explains them collectively in two sets of four phrases.
Next is the precept against forcibly ejecting another from a dwelling. Monastic quarters belong to the community as a whole; they are not restricted to any single individual.
To suddenly expel a former resident out of anger is a grave offense. Since the prior occupant’s residence was already established, to be driven out by a newcomer causes excessive distress.

According to the *Mahāsaṃghika-vinaya*, the reason for establishing this precept is to prevent the suffering of sentient beings and to extinguish strife and contention. There are six specific conditions for its transgression.
1. A monk’s quarters during spring or winter; 2. Previously already designated as a fixed residence; 3. Intending to cause annoyance to the resident; 4. Being dragged out by a mind of anger; 5.

Lacking a valid cause or condition, such as being subject to formal censure (*ukkhepanīya-kamma*) and so forth; 6. The offense occurs upon exiting the door. Question: In the previous case regarding the quarters, it was stated that one does not distinguish between relatives and non-relatives, nor between pure and impure.

Why is this case restricted to the "pure" while excluding relatives? Answer: The former refers to a private location where one does not differentiate between pure and impure, as it belongs to [the individual].
Regarding those who borrow first: if they are relatives, there is no fault. This is a monastic dwelling; one who is pure may stay. One must not allow a relative to enter;
if one drives out an impure person, there is no offense. The four lines of the root precept can be understood through this explanation.

According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*: if one drags [an item] from a back room to a front room; or if one drags it out of a front room to the outdoors; or if one drags it from the outdoors to the courtyard; or if one drags it from the courtyard...

If one drags them out beyond the threshold, it is a *pāyattika* offense in all such cases. However, there is no offense if one drags out a person who is shameless or if one drags out a disciple in order to subdue them.
Next is the precept concerning sitting on a bed with removable legs atop a multi-storied building. When a bhikṣu performs a task, he ought to be careful and deliberate;

in dangerous places, one must especially act with composure. Now, if one recklessly uses a bed with removable legs atop a multi-storied building with a thin roof-covering, one may fall and injure others.
This rule was established because it causes distress to others. The remaining details can be understood from the context.
Next is the precept concerning water containing insects. It is the principle of the ordained life that one should treat all beings with a compassionate heart;

how could it befit a person of mercy to cause injury to living beings? There are four specific conditions for this offense: first, water containing insects; second, knowing [it contains insects]; third, not employing a straining method;

and fourth, using the water as intended, which constitutes the full offense. The full precept consists of five factors: first, the person; second, knowing there are insects; third, personally washing mud or grass; and fourth, employing another person [to do so].

Regarding the five offenses of the *pañca-saṃghāvaśeṣa* (five *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules): in the commentary, the first is explained individually, while the following four are clarified collectively. Within the collective explanation, there are three matters:

first, water containing insects; second, fermented gruel containing insects; third, the perception regarding the object. The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (or *Shan-chi-pu lü piposha*), fascicle six, states:

"This precept against taking life consists of four distinct rules. This [first] rule was established earliest. Since one may not use water containing insects to sprinkle grass or mix with clay, one must instead take [water] that is free of insects..."
Regarding drinking water: since one must not use any water containing living beings, one would thereby intentionally deprive those creatures of their lives.

Since it was prohibited to deprive animals of life, one would then deprive human beings of their lives. Generally, there are four established precepts concerning the taking of life, as the circumstances differ;
all are designated as "previously committed" (*pūrva-kṛta*). If a bhikṣu takes water containing living beings and pours it upon grass or mixes it with mud, according to however much he uses—

Having used the *pāyattika* [confession], if one wishes to establish a dwelling, one should first examine the water. Using a fine cloth of one cubit (*hasta*), one should make a water-strainer (*parisrāvaṇa*).
One who is scrupulous and observant of the precepts should filter the water, place it in a vessel, and examine it carefully toward the light of the sun.
If there are still insects present, one should make a triple-layered strainer. If there are still insects present even then, one should not dwell in that place. The rest is as [previously stated].

This is clarified in the *Vinaya-ksudraka-vastu*. Regarding the *Śaila-vinaya*: if one pours water oneself while following the breath, one incurs a *pāyattika* for each instance. If one instructs another to pour it, one incurs a *pāyattika* for every word spoken.
Next is the precept concerning the inspection of roof repairs exceeding three layers: if, out of greed, one causes a heavy roof to collapse, resulting in damage and loss, [one incurs an offense].

[This constitutes] an offense. It was established because it invites censure. The specific conditions (*pratyaya*) consist of four factors: (1) building a house for oneself; (2) having another person thatch it;
(3) not departing from the range of sight or hearing while the three stages are not yet completed; and (4) committing the offense immediately upon the completion of the third stage.

The remaining characteristics are easily understood. This precept is rarely encountered, so I shall not explain it at length. However, the characteristics of the three stages are difficult to discern, as explained in the context of the conditions: using three [layers of] grass...
Because it is covered in layers, it is called "three sections" (trikhaṇḍa). Regarding the five parts:
if one reaches the fourth layer, whether it be covered with grass, tiles, or boards, each individual blade of grass, tile, or board constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.

Next, regarding the unauthorized teaching of the *bhikṣuṇī* precepts by one who has not been appointed by the Saṃgha: there are three points to this. First, the intention behind the *bhikṣuṇī*s' request for instruction.
Since women have left the household life fundamentally to revere and honor the Dharma, now that they have entered the Path, it is only logical that they should reverently uphold and practice it.

If they do not request instruction on the rules of conduct every half-month, they will remain ignorant of their proper deportment in all circumstances; how then could they progress in their cultivation? Second, the necessity... [text truncated]
The Master’s intention is as follows: For a woman on the road, it is not possible to remain at ease; in principle, she must advance in her practice to achieve the benefit of liberation.
While she desires only to cultivate progress, she lacks the opportunity for travel abroad; therefore, she relies upon the Great Monks (Mahāsaṃgha) to demonstrate the rules of practice.

Thirdly, regarding the necessity of appointing a qualified person: the task of instruction is difficult and requires one endowed with virtuous conduct. For this reason, the assembly is entrusted with the responsibility to deliberate and dispatch a person of merit. Since [she] has not yet received...
Regarding "dispatching": to go and proclaim [the teachings] on one's own initiative—how could such a dispatch of instruction benefit sentient beings?
There are five conditions for this specific case: first, not being dispatched by the Saṃgha; second, going to the place of the nuns; third, assembling the assembly of nuns;

fourth, preaching the Eight Respectful Precepts and the Dharma; fifth, the completion of the speech as it is being delivered. Regarding the characteristics of the offense, there are two parts: first, the permission to teach; second, the consequence of listening.
The section on the arising of transgressions has three parts: first, the nuns’ request for instruction; second, from "At that time" onwards, the appointment based on the request;
third, at that time, the Venerable One, not following the appointment, proceeded [to the nuns]. The first part has five sections: first, listing the community upon which the nuns rely.

The first section lists twelve individuals; the term "etc. includes five hundred others. Because they required consultation to resolve their doubts and obstructions, they relied upon the great monks (*bhikṣu*).
Second, the second section lists fifteen capable nuns; the term "etc. here also includes five hundred others. Third, Mahāprajāpatī requests the monks for instruction. Question:
Why does she not request the Buddha, but rather the monks? Answer: It is because she follows the protocol of showing respect to the teaching; therefore, she does not [request the Buddha].

[The nun] requested the Buddha. Since she had already made her request half a month earlier out of respect for the teaching, why did she not come directly to ask the Saṃgha, but instead informed the Buddha again?

Answer: Although there was such a request in her respectful communication, the bhikṣus had not yet received it. The Buddha dispatched Mahāprajāpatī [to inform them], knowing beforehand that they would not comply.
Therefore, she informed the Buddha once more. "To instruct and preach the Dharma" refers to the methods of principle and practice. (The four [sections] below follow the Buddha’s instruction.)
Please grant your permission. The *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle seven, states: "The reason for instructing and admonishing the bhikṣuṇīs through the disciples is that there are four meanings:
first, to demonstrate that one has no stinginess regarding the Dharma; second, because the teacher and disciple share the same knowledge and vision;
third, to manifest the merit, virtue, and wisdom of the bhikṣu Panthaka; and fourth, so that the bhikṣus may each [have their own] [regard for] the community of bhikṣuṇīs."

Because the conditions for their transformation were ripe, the five [disciples], having had their request granted, paid their respects and withdrew. Next follows the section on the dispatching of messengers, which has three parts:
first, the command to dispatch; second, the execution of the command; third, the prior expression of derision.

This is intended to clarify that the position of an instructor is difficult to fulfill and requires one who possesses the requisite rank. Furthermore, it serves as an introduction to the two subsequent types of instruction: preaching the Dharma to those with faith and providing formal teaching.

Transformation. For those who revile and disparage him, he employs the miraculous power of spiritual transformation (*ṛddhi*) to teach them. Next, in proceeding to the instruction contained within the text, there are two parts: first, the skillful means of preaching the Dharma;
second, from the passage beginning "At that time, Āmrapālī... onwards, the actual exposition of the Dharma. Within the former section, there are four parts: first, leading his retinue forward;
second, the community of nuns coming out to meet him; third, the Venerable One taking his seat; fourth, the nuns rising and gathering around. [If they do not come...]

In such cases, one must grant the *chanda* (consent). Thus, the Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya states: "Regarding matters of serving the Three Jewels or attending to the sick, it is permitted for these to be entrusted to the instructor (*śāstṛ*).
Toward the bhikṣuṇīs, he should regard them as daughters; the bhikṣuṇīs, toward the instructor, should regard him as the Buddha. Next, he correctly expounds the Dharma:
first for those with faith, then for those without faith. The preceding section has three parts: namely, the three requests and the three expositions, each of which contains four sub-points.

First, the invitation by Mahāprajāpatī; second, the actual teaching; third, entering meditative absorption after the teaching; fourth, the nuns’ expressions of praise and veneration. Only the second section is missing.
Regarding the verses spoken during the main teaching in the fourth section, these are the verses by which Panthaka attained the Path.
These verses are divided into three parts: the first two lines establish the Dharma; the next four lines provide an analogy; and the final two lines reveal [the realization].

Victorious! The preceding passage establishes the attainment of the untainted (*anāsrava*). Because the realization of principle is clear and distinct, it is said that one "enters tranquility and attains peace and bliss.

Next, the metaphor consists of two pairs; examples of worldly pleasure are brought forward for comparison, all of which are explained by the subsequent lines. Among these, the former is supreme. Furthermore, to manifest this excellence:

it is not merely that pride is eliminated, but other afflictions are also exhausted. When these afflictions are exhausted, one realizes cessation (*nirodha*); thus it is called the "foremost" (*agra*) as well.
"Agreed. The preceding four lines refer to contaminated (*sāsrava*) bliss; the two lines below refer to uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) bliss.

Uncontaminated bliss surpasses the contaminated; there is nothing superior to it, hence it is called 'foremost. Next, the entry into dhyāna and the expressions of praise and respect are as in the text.

However, because his thirst for the Dharma was so earnest and he delighted in hearing it without weariness, he requested the teaching again and again, repeatedly and with increasing fervor. Subsequently, [the Buddha spoke] for the sake of those without faith."

Through the transformation of supernatural powers (*ṛddhipāda*), as recorded in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (T. 1435) and the *Ekottarika-āgama* (T. 125), having manifested various miraculous powers, he returned to his original seat.
When the bhikṣuṇīs saw this, their thoughts of contempt were completely extinguished; they gave rise to faith and reverence, a heart of respectful purity, and subdued their arrogance.
He then expounded the Dharma according to what the bhikṣuṇīs delighted in and what they required for their understanding.
Among the assembly, some attained the fruit of srotāpanna up to the fruit of arhat; some planted the causal conditions for the path of the śrāvaka;
some planted the causal conditions for the path of the pratyekabuddha; and some gave rise to the causal conditions for the unsurpassed path. At that time, within the assembly—

Because such various great benefits are obtained, the subsequent procedure for rectifying transgressions follows. The text is divided into two parts: first, the rectification through formal motion (*jñapti*) within the assembly;

second, the self-rectification outside the boundary (*sīmā*). Each of these two sections contains three sub-parts: the occurrence of the transgression, the censure and prohibition, and the prior transgression. Within the section on the prior transgression, there are two parts:

first, informing the community of nuns so they may know the matter and inquire whether it is appropriate; second, proceeding to the instructor (*śikṣamāṇā*). This latter part also contains two sub-sections.

Advancing toward the assembly of nuns is itself the skillful means for preaching the Dharma. Second, the actual exposition of the Dharma is clarified. The text for this exposition consists of four parts: 1.
Clarifying what the group of six (ṣaḍvargika) monks did not preach; three categories are cited here as examples, and other cases are to be understood by analogy. 2.

Simply stating what was preached below, which is the "emergence of the preached Dharma" that contrasts with the aforementioned improper teachings. 3. From "Or laughing... onwards, [this concerns] non-Dharmic deportment (*īryāpatha*), contrasting with the aforementioned spiritual demeanor.

[The section on] the *pācittiya* offense for a nun who reviles a monk is complete. The fourfold explanation of the nuns’ assembly’s silent admiration and their subsequent reversal of their previous derision and respect follows.

Next is the reprimand and the establishment of the rule as in the text. Regarding the three transgressions, the first section has four parts: (1) appointing [a messenger] oneself outside the boundary; (2) sending a nun to inform the assembly; (3) the monks intervening with a reprimand;

and (4) the nun making the announcement to the assembly. Next, the two assemblies report this to the Buddha, who reprimands them. Finally, the method for establishing the rule is set forth, which requires ten essential factors.

Virtue. Only one who is thus qualified may undertake instruction. This section contains three parts: first, the heading; second, the enumeration; and third, the conclusion. Regarding "one who is fully endowed with the precepts":

they uphold the practice of the precepts without the slightest deficiency, guarding the disciplinary codes with a mind free from retreat or discouragement. Regarding "one who is widely learned": they have extensively investigated the sūtras and śāstras, such that there is no question they cannot answer;
they have gathered and examined various teachings, enabling them to resolve all matters. Regarding "one who recites the precepts": [they do so before] the two assemblies...
Regarding *mokṣa* (liberation): one who upholds it well without forgetting and possesses decisive certainty does not merely recite the text, but is also able to discern its meaning.

One who is skillful can provide guidance in accordance with the Dharma, never deviating from principle. One of noble lineage is born into a high-ranking family, possessing a reputation for excellence.
One whose appearance is such has a countenance that is upright and majestic, inspiring reverence in those who behold them. One who is capable is able to expound the Dharma and provide instruction...

[The teaching] is born; it accords with the capacity [of the listener] and satisfies their desires. Question: What is the difference between this and the previously mentioned "skillful ability to preach the Dharma"? Answer:

The previous explanation accorded with the Dharma and was free from the fault of error, yet it did not necessarily enable one to respond to the capacity and satisfy the desires [of the listener]. This [present case] is what is meant by "accordance with capacity," and thus it differs from the former.
"Those who do not act for the sake of the Buddha" refers to those who have left the household life with heterodox views; therefore, it says "not for the sake of the Buddha.

Although they have left the household life and donned the dharma robes, they commit a grave offense (*pārājika*). By analogy, one should say that those who leave the household life for the sake of the Buddha and don the dharma robes, yet do not commit a grave offense, are capable of instructing *bhikṣuṇīs*.
Question: What constitutes a grave offense? Answer: According to the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*, it is as follows:
Regarding the three groups of *śikṣamāṇās* and the two types of *sthūlātyaya* involving physical contact: these are considered "heavy dharmas" (*gurudharma*).

Because one has committed such acts, even if they have subsequently repented and become pure, nuns still treat them with contempt and do not permit them to receive instruction. Furthermore, it is explained that committing any of the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses is termed a "heavy dharma.

Even after repenting, they are likewise not permitted to receive instruction. By analogy, one should understand that for [offenses] such as the *pāyattika*, once the confession is completed, one immediately receives instruction. [Question: What about this?

How does this differ from the first virtue? Answer: When one has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and finished repenting, one possesses the first [virtue] but lacks the other nine. When one has committed other offenses but has not yet repented, one possesses the nine but lacks the first.
If the remaining offenses have been repented, both the nine and the first are possessed. If the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense has not been repented, both the nine and the first are lacking.

Regarding those who have reached twenty years of age, it is said that they uphold the Dharma with firm resolve and rarely suffer decline; whereas those who are young and impulsive are easily led to fall away.
[This] is a defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). Question: It is not yet known whether the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of appointing a person who lacks merit is valid. Answer:

All masters of the past and present have unanimously stated that as few as five [qualities] must be possessed for the appointment to be successfully accomplished. This is in order to distinguish such a person from one who is entirely devoid of merit, for whom there can never be the principle of providing instruction, and so forth.
Although these points cannot be fully set forth here, the commentators fail to understand that the conditions and phenomena are as they are; thus, I shall now explain how it is obtained.

Regarding the reason why [the formal act] is established: it is because the requisite qualities (*guṇa*) are not explicitly listed within the *karmavācanā*, as is the case with other procedures such as the *pravāraṇā*.

Even when appointing a person for a task, their requisite qualities are required; yet in this case, they lack those qualities, and thus its validity is beyond doubt. This is the same as the previous case; why then do you laboriously cause confusion?

It is the same for those who, lacking the requisite qualities, attempt to ordain others. If that is so, why are the person and the robe mutually incompatible? There is no basis for receiving the day [of the ceremony], as it would obstruct [the procedure].
Regarding the "difficult location" (durbhikṣa) and the "room" (vāsaka): if one receives [the robes] at the boundary of a village or the robe-zone (cīvarasīmā), etc., it is entirely not accomplished.

Answer: Previously, based on the circumstances, one entered the formal ritual procedure (karmavācanā). Because the matter was improper, the ritual was not accomplished; this is analogous to all other formal rituals.

Regarding the mention of the matter (*vastu*) within the *karmavācanā* text: if the matter is mentioned, the procedure is not invalid. However, if the matter is not mentioned in the text, the procedure may still be accomplished even if it is contrary to the Dharma.
How is this so? The subsequent text states: "At the very least, one who possesses the five virtues should instruct the nuns.

In the answer, the text merely says that one who possesses the five [virtues] should instruct; it does not say that the five are required for the appointment to be valid. Furthermore, it asks: "As for..."

When establishing a great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), the road is not formally recited [as a marker] if it is separated by a river. If the road is distant and separated by a river, the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*) should be performed accordingly.
Although the text does not formally recite the road as a boundary marker, it is included within the *karmavācanā* because the road is distant and separated by a river.

The formal proclamation (āśvāsana) is not established. Since the proclamation is invalid, how can the ritual action (karmavācanā) be accomplished? Furthermore, the text specifies that it must be recited by those "dwelling together" (samānavāsin).
If such an obstacle exists, the recitation for dwelling together is not established.

The *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* consists of three sections: first, the person; second, not being appointed; and third, the instruction and the concluding determination of the offense. In the commentary, the first section is self-evident.

The following two sections—numbers two and three—are explained together. Within this, there are two parts: first, the explanation of the ritual procedure for the person who has been appointed to instruct;

second, the explanation of the determination of the offense for not being appointed, beginning with the words "If the Saṃgha... The former part further divides into two: the first explains the appointment by the Saṃgha, which is self-evident.
Second, the explanation of the ritual for instruction (*avavāda-vidhi*). This section further consists of two parts: first, explaining the nature of the dharma taught in the instruction;

second, explaining the ritual for instruction following the recitation of the precepts (*śīla*). Regarding the first, the nature of the dharma taught, this refers to the eight dharmas that must not be transgressed.

The text contains three elements: the heading, the inquiry, and the enumeration. The meaning will be explained below. Next, the text on the ritual has four parts: first, the time of requesting [instruction] from the Saṃgha.
Second, the time for the two assemblies to select [the candidate]; third, the time for fixing the date and going; fourth, the time for welcoming, making offerings, and receiving instruction.
Although the fixed text is thus, the explanation of the meaning consists of four sections: first, regarding time; second, regarding place; third, regarding persons; and fourth, regarding the Dharma.

First, regarding time: there are six periods in total. First, the time when the Bhikṣuṇī assembly selects and requests the person; second, the time for the entrustment to the Bhikṣu. This concludes the above...

Second, during the two seasonal periods within the nuns' legal framework; third, when the nuns request [instruction] from the Saṃgha; fourth, when the assembly appoints [an instructor]; fifth, when the time for a scheduled visit has been fixed;
and sixth, when receiving offerings and instruction. These four times are explained according to the text.

However, regarding the time of instruction, during both the waxing and waning phases of the moon, one must exclude the first three [periods] as well as the latter two. Thus, the Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya states: "The white..."
From the first day to the third day of the month is called "the time not yet arrived. From the fourteenth to the fifteenth day is called "the time already passed.
During the ten days in between, one may choose any single day; however, one must go at a time that corresponds to these periods in order to avoid the offense of violating the proper date.

Regarding the second point: as for the location, it must be a place where ritual procedures (*dharmakarma*) are performed; among such places, it must be a Great Boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) and not a Small Boundary (*khuḍḍaka-sīmā*). This Great...

It is not for those of minor status; it applies throughout the six periods of the day. Regarding the third person [the messenger]: both the monastic community of monks and nuns must consist of at least five members.
Although the number is five, they are categorized as a "four-member assembly" (caturvarga-saṃgha). However, the nun who acts as the messenger must clearly understand the Dharma;
one who is ignorant or dull-witted is unfit to serve as a messenger. The same principle applies to a monk who is under formal assignment. *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, Chapter 27.
It is said: From this day forward, bhikṣuṇīs should receive the *chanda* (consent). With the exception of five persons: first, the senior elder (*sthavira*);
second, the person who instructs the bhikṣuṇīs; third, the person who recites the *Prātimokṣa*. These three should each declare their own situation and should not receive [the consent].
Fourth, the person who guards the dwelling; fifth, the sick person. These two should say, "I will not go," and the Saṃgha should further grant it to another person. If one says, "I..."

These are: begging for alms, dwelling in the forest (āraṇyaka), and wearing rag-robes (pāṃśukūlika). If the Venerable One does not accept these, he commits an offense of transgression against the community.

Once the assembly is complete and in harmony, it is appropriate—provided there is no underlying illness—to dispatch him. Furthermore, the one so dispatched must possess the aforementioned qualities. Regarding the fourth rule:

it is performed by a formal motion and a second proclamation (jñapti-dvitīya-karman), and not otherwise. This same procedure for dispatching applies equally to both the sending and receiving communities. Moreover, there should further be the rite of formal entrustment and the public invitation.

Regarding the *Dharmas*: this text contains only the detailed rules (*vistara-dharma*) and lacks the abbreviated rules (*saṃkṣepa-dharma*). However, in the twenty-ninth section of the *Pañcavargika*, there are abbreviated rules which state:

"There were certain bhikṣuṇīs who performed the *poṣadha* together with the bhikṣus. When they saw a bhikṣu commit an offense, they wished to censure him. They reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
'Bhikṣuṇīs must not perform the *poṣadha* together with bhikṣus; it should be held every half-month.'"

[The nuns] requested that a single bhikṣu be sent from the community of bhikṣus to ask for an instructor. The bhikṣus were unwilling to go and ask. The Buddha said, "I allow the nuns to provide offerings [to him]:
an alms-bowl bag, a water-strainer, a waist-band, fragrant oil, food before and after the meal, or whether the *poṣadha* has not yet been performed, they should announce it;
or if the *poṣadha* has already been performed, they should announce it. They then announced this to the Buddha, saying, "This should not be done. It should be proclaimed as follows:"
[The nuns] do not come. When the bhikṣus announce the desire for purity (*pārisuddhi*), [a nun] rises from her seat, stands before the Saṃgha, and says:

"Venerable Saṃgha, listen. This vihāra is in harmony; the community of bhikṣuṇīs bows its head in homage to the harmony and requests the community of bhikṣus at their feet for an instructor (*anuśāsaka*).
(This is said once, not three times). If there is no instructor, the Elder should reply: "There is no instructor here."
He admonishes the people: "Furthermore, there is no one capable of preaching the Dharma. You all must not be negligent.
When the nuns arrive tomorrow, you bhikṣus should transmit the words of the Elder in this manner. The explanation of the text is self-evident.

Next, the explanation of the offense for not appointing [a preacher] is divided into two parts: first, the offense of not appointing on a specific day; second, clarifying the calculation of the offense when not inquiring.

First, the initial section is explained. The ancient commentators state: "If the Saṃgha does not appoint someone to preach the Eightfold Respectful Precepts (Aṣṭa-guru-dharma), there is an offense of *duṣkṛta*.

Because the text of the Eightfold Respectful Precepts is fixed and its meaning is subtle, it gives rise to affliction; therefore, failing to preach them constitutes a minor offense. If one preaches the Dharma with laxity and negligence, it is difficult to distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox, and such preaching may lead to error."
The *yāvad-dharmika* (Ya-fa) [monks] corrupt the mind and conduct of the *bhikṣuṇīs*. Because they give rise to many causes for affliction, they commit a *thullaccaya* offense.

If it is not the day for the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*, both commit a *duṣkṛta* offense. Since it is not the designated day and instruction (*śikṣā*) is not permitted, and there is no other fault, they are equally guilty of a minor offense.
This applies generally to those appointed [as instructors]. There may be four permutations. If one is not appointed and it is not the designated day, then there are four cases.
Regarding offenses: on the third *guṇa* (virtuous) day, there is one *tissa* (offense) and two *guṇas*. On this [specific] day, there are two offenses: one *tissa* and one *guṇa*.

If one who has been appointed goes on a day that is not [the designated] offense-day, there are two *dukkaṭas* (wrongdoings). If one goes on this day, there is no offense regardless of whether the gravity [of the act] is light or heavy.

If the Saṃgha has not appointed [the person], or if one recites the Eight Respectful Rules (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*) on a day that is not for instruction, there are two [offenses]: first, the *dukkaṭa* of reciting the rules of respect when not appointed; second, the *dukkaṭa* of the day [itself] being non-[designated]. Both are [thus classified].

Two types of offenses are incurred; therefore, they are tied together as a pair. It is permissible to go on that day. Thus it is said: "Alternatively, on the following morning, one may preach the Dharma without error. Question:
Why, when preaching the Dharma, do you only mention the absence of error and not cite the specific date? Answer:

In the previous explanation of the Eight Respectful Rules, both the absence of error regarding the date and the non-observance of the date were stated to incur the same offense of *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). Since a single name for the offense subsumes two categories of offenses, it is necessary to treat them together.

[The opponent] cites [the rule]: "In this context, if one preaches the Dharma without being appointed, it is a heavy offense; on an improper day, it is light. [They argue that] not only are the categories of offenses distinct, but their names are also different and thus do not overlap;
therefore, they do not cite the case of "improper days. They claim that preaching the Dharma is not auspicious on improper days. Now, our explanation is not so.

Even for preaching the Eight Respectful Rules (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*), one incurs a *pāyattika* offense. As for the statement that it is auspicious to go and preach the Eight Respectful Rules if one has been appointed by the Saṃgha or if it is not a day of instruction—this is merely an illustration.

The formal act (*jñapti*) regarding the *aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ* (Eight Rules of Reverence) does not constitute an offense. It is not that the recitation of the Eight Rules of Reverence is itself a transgression; rather, by reciting "Reverence," one incurs a *pāyattika*.

Once the formal act has been performed according to the *Prātimokṣa*, as stated in the *Prātimokṣa* text: "If one instructs [a nun], it is a *pāyattika*. Regarding the term "instructor" (*anuśāsaka*) in the commentary, it refers to the Eight Rules of Irrevocable Law.
Furthermore, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "The instructor speaks the Eight Rules of Reverence. If one who has not been appointed as an instructor speaks to a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika*."

The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya-śāstra*, fascicle two, states: "What is the instruction for bhikṣuṇīs? It answers: "To expound the eight *gurudharma*s is called 'instruction. Therefore, these two precepts are combined in their formulation;

thus, [the offenses of] speaking with disparagement, reviling, and requiring respect are all *pāyattika* (提). In the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, it is concluded that speaking of the Dharma [inappropriately] incurs a *pāyattika*.
This is clarified in the *Vibhaṅga* (Broad Explanation). Furthermore, explaining respect and the Dharma together incurs one *pāyattika*. If one speaks of respect..."

Second, being appointed by the Saṃgha; third, the offense incurred through instruction. Regarding the commentary, the first two points can be understood.

"Not deaf. This opens the previous phrase "blind but not deaf. "Neither deaf nor blind" opens the previous phrase "deaf but not blind";

This invites public censure and damages the Path; furthermore, it praises those without virtue and surely brings ruin upon the worthy and good. Because the fault lies in the act of praising, not in the eating itself. If one eats without praising, there is no violation. Therefore, the rule applies to all cases except when one is ill and merely accepts out of necessity. Thus, the prohibition is solely directed at the act of praising. One must grant permission for praise only when it is for the sake of treating an illness. If, while granting such permission for the patient, one still disparages those who are virtuous and excellent, this is not permitted.

The conditions: there are six offenses. Among these six, with the exception of the fifth which allows for certain circumstances (*kappiyavatthu*), the remaining phrases are not explained here; however, the first, second, and fourth are fully clarified.

The formulation [of the rule] consists of five distinct conditions: first, the gift is limited to a single meal; second, one knows the gift is limited to a single meal;

"Eating" refers to the proper measure for eating. If one exceeds the five limits, it constitutes an offense (*pācittiya*). The analysis of these characteristics is fully explained in the text, though not in sequential order.

next, from "one who is ill" downward, the conditions for exemption are explained in sequence; finally, from "if one is not ill" downward, the fifth phrase is explained. The two sections of the text are easily understood.

However, because food is an essential necessity and because one delights in transgressing [the rules regarding it], this offense is grave; other offenses are not so frequent, and for that reason they are light.

having completed the act of giving, if one then immediately violates the agreement, not only are the six flavors offered in vain, but it also causes both parties to lose benefit.

Having already accepted a prior invitation, to then accept a subsequent invitation and thus turn one's back on the former while facing the latter is termed "successive invitations" (*krama*). The specific conditions for this offense consist of five factors:

One offense; it encompasses both the back-biting and the foot-stirring. Therefore, it is said that one must be dealt with according to the Dharma. Next, regarding the offense of eating the five types of staple foods after having accepted an invitation for a meal:

Dividing the benefits. Furthermore, any other time than this is an improper time (*akāla*). Regarding the fifth phrase of the current section, there are two parts:

"When the Saṃgha is about to eat alms-food, four signs should be made: first, striking the *gandī*; second, blowing the conch; third, beating the drum;
and fourth, shouting a command so that those within the boundary may hear and know it. These four kinds of signs must be present; they are never permitted to be omitted."

At times they strike the ghaṇṭā, or again they beat the drum, or again they strike the *karaṇḍaka*; thus the proceedings become disordered and lack fixed rules, so that the monastic law (*saṃghadharma*) is not established.
If one eats the food offered to the Saṃgha (*saṃghabhakta*) without performing the four formalities, it is impure;
this is called "stealing the Saṃgha's food. If there is an obstruction [to the assembly], even if the ghaṇṭā is struck, it is impure; this is called "stealing the Saṃgha's food."

Furthermore, the treatise states: "If there are four or more persons within the boundary (*sīmā*), even though they each have their own food, it is not an offense to eat together [if they do so] collectively.
Because of this, there must be a separate donor (*dānapati*). As for this donor, they may be either a monastic or a layperson.
Therefore, the treatise says: "If among four persons, one brings forth food while three have no food, and they eat together in one place, it is a *pāyattika* [offense]."

"Ti. This text further states: "As for those śramaṇas who eat," this refers to those renunciants outside of these Śākya-sons (the Buddhist monastics), as well as those who have gone forth from among the non-Buddhist paths (tīrthikas).
Therefore, it is known that even the śramaṇas of our own school (the Buddhists) incur the offense of exceeding the limit.

As for the previous statement regarding showing compassion toward the families of laypeople, that was spoken merely in reference to the specific circumstances. Next, regarding the second condition: one must be within the proper time. If [one is]...

During non-appropriate times, there is no sense of "common flavor" (samānarasa); therefore, there is no fault in making separate [invitations]. Thus, a specific time is required. Furthermore, regarding the third condition:

although a donor may exist, if the invitation is made according to the sequence of the Saṃgha, there is likewise no fault in making separate [invitations]. Therefore, one must specifically invite and specifically beg.
Therefore, the *Śāstra* states: "There are two kinds of eating apart from the community (*gaṇabhojana*): first, by invitation; second, by begging. How is it that an invitation is fulfilled?
Suppose there is one lay follower (*upāsaka*) who goes to where four bhikṣus are and invites them to a formal meal, saying:
'Venerable sirs, please accept this. This is called the fulfillment of an invitation. How does one incur an offense through begging apart from the community? There are four types of beggars."
Monks, whether sitting or standing, they see the upāsaka speaking and say: "Give food to us four," or they beg one by one, saying:
"Give me food," and it is likewise for each. They may depart together or depart separately, receiving their food at the same time.

This is called "incurring an offense through begging. Regarding the phrase "this person begs": Devadatta separately took four others with him, making five in total, and went from house to house to beg for food.

It was because of this incident that the Buddha established the prohibition. There are two types of separate invitations (*pratyekapraṇidhāna*): first, when names are specifically mentioned and designated, it constitutes a separate invitation by principle;
second, when one takes people based on their dharma (status or role), it likewise constitutes a separate invitation—for example, as when saying, "If the Meditation Master... or...
“Gan” refers to the Vinaya Master Jian; others are similar. This clarifies that it is not [a case of] being invited according to the monastic order (*saṃghakrama*).
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: “If, within the assembly, four or more individuals are specially invited, this is called ‘separately inviting a group for a meal.

Even if there is a separate invitation, if there is someone following the monastic order, there is no offense. This is because the person following the order disrupts their collective plan and intent. Its...

There are two types of monastic order (*saṃgha*). First is the direct designation of "the saṃgha. Second is the designation by name. Furthermore, a sequence of several individuals starting from the *sthavira* (senior monk) also constitutes a monastic order.
However, if a donor (*dānapati*) invites [monks] who are outside the boundary (*sīmā*), it does not constitute an offense regardless of which monastic order is used.
If they are within the boundary, one must invite the monks of that specific boundary at the place of the *poṣadha*; only then will one be exempt from fault.
Because it constitutes a separate assembly. The *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:

"If there is a donor who invites four or more persons within the boundary of the Sangha's *poṣadha*, and food is to be distributed at the site of the meal, one person from the invited Sangha must be sent [to receive the food].

If one person is not invited and one portion of food is not sent, it is a *pāyattika*. This applies likewise if there are two or three locations. If [the invitations] reach each location individually..."
At the place of the *poṣadha*, one person shall be selected from among the Saṃgha. If one portion of food is sent [to him], he shall remain pure in his own place;

there is no need for a succession of people to be sent to deliver the food. Even if one person has been appointed to send one portion of food, if another bhikṣu comes from outside and [the resident] obstructs him—refusing to give even a single portion of food—it is a *pāyattika* offense. If the Saṃgha has finished eating and there are guests...
When a bhikṣu arrives, there is no offense if the donor provides food for four or more people. Regarding the five conditions:
as for "proper food," if it were not proper food, its utility for sustaining the body would be minimal; therefore, one must consume proper food to fill the body, which constitutes an offense.
Thus the text states: "Food refers to rice, parched grain, and so forth. Regarding the fifth condition: although it may be proper food, it must be pure in substance; [if] it is impure food...
There is no sense of "common flavor" (samāna-rasa). An old question-and-answer states: "If that were so, then an illegal *karmavācanā* (formal act) would not be fit for collective adherence;

consequently, one should not incur the offense of a separate assembly (*pṛthaggaṇa*). The answer is: Although it is an illegal gathering, it is possible to reverse the 'illegal' into 'legal' (like). Therefore, the rule establishes the existence of a separate assembly. Once the meal has been taken, it is impure;
even if one goes [to the assembly], one cannot turn it back to make it pure. Since going would be of no benefit, there is thus no offense. Hence [the rule].
The text below states: "An illegal separate assembly. This objection and its resolution are both unreasonable.

However, that which is detailed as "illegal" yet followed [as if it were] legal is called "legal," yet the food remains impure; thus, it may serve as a subject for inquiry and response. Even if they follow it together, it does not constitute a legal assembly.
What need is there to pair this with the "responding to food" (āhāra-prativacana) to resolve objections? Furthermore, regarding this illegal *karmavācanā*:

although it was originally intended to be valid (*yathādharma*), by the time it is actually performed, it falls into the category of the non-valid (*adharmika*) and fails to be accomplished. Therefore, it is called an "illegal separate assembly" (*adharmika-bhinna-saṃgha*). Next, regarding the sixth condition, it must necessarily be fulfilled.
Because food was insufficient and there was a lack of provisions for sustaining the body, the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:

"If, in a separate room (*paryaṅka*, here translated as 'large'), a donor provides small meals for four or more persons, it does not constitute a full meal; therefore, there is no offense. Next is the seventh condition:

the place where the separate meal is taken must form a formal assembly (*saṃgha*). Thus the text says: "If there are four or more, they shall be divided into two groups and [the meal] shared between them."
Regarding eating: the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states that if they eat separately, the meal is not considered a communal meal (*gaṇa-bhojana*), and thus there is no offense.
It further states that three bhikṣus and one bhikṣuṇī, three bhikṣuṇīs and one bhikṣu, and so forth, down to three bhikṣus and one śrāmaṇerikā, do not constitute an offense.
Furthermore, if three bhikṣus are outside the boundary (*sīmā*) and one bhikṣu is inside the boundary, or if three bhikṣus are... [text ends]

If one is within the boundary and one is outside the boundary; or if three bhikṣus are on the ground and one is in the air, or if three are in the air and one is on the ground—in each case, there is no offense.
The same applies if the fourth person is one who is insane, mentally deranged, mentally impaired, or one who has been expelled (nirghāta).
Next is the eighth condition: if the boundary within the village is not exhausted, even down to a single person, the offense is not fully incurred. Therefore, the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:

"If four or more companions are within the village boundary and receive food from a single donor, even if there was no previously established Saṃgha, if they know that at least one bhikṣu is present and do not invite him to eat together, it is a *pāyattika*. If doubt arises..."

Regarding the mind: if one does not inquire whether food is present or not, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. If one wishes to act in accordance with the Dharma, one should properly conceal oneself within the village;

if there are monks or no monks, and one eats without giving rise to doubt, there is no fault. If this is not done, one should strike the *gandī* (wooden gong), whereby one becomes pure and in accordance with the Dharma.
The ninety-two conditions will be explained in the relevant passages. Next, the following section explains the transgressions of the text.
The similarities may be understood as before.

Next, regarding the five phrases of the *pūrṇa-śīla* (full precepts), they are the same as the preceding *anuparivartaka-bhojana-śīla* (the rule against eating in succession). In contrast to this, the phrases concerning the opening of the conditions (*kṣaṇa*) are explained through a fivefold classification:

first, determining the number of conditions; second, determining whether it is the proper time or improper time; third, determining whether the conditions are shared or individual. Fourth... [text continues].
Fourth, the relative strength and weakness of the inclusion [of cases]; fifth, the commonalities and differences regarding what is permitted or obstructed.

First, regarding the determination of the conditions (*pratyaya*): according to this opening of the conditions, there are only seven; however, if one takes the benefit of the *kaṭhina* robe as included, there are eight.

This constitutes a case of no condition (*apratyaya*), and the meaning of not being excluded has been explained as before. Regarding the time for making robes: it was originally permitted because robes were made during the month of Kārttika. Question: This...
Regarding the question of how one may separately receive food during the month of Kārttika, why is it said that this is permitted for the purpose of making robes? The answer is:
with the expectation that during the original month of Kārttika there was no *kaṭhina* robe, one must act upon that condition; only then is it permitted.

If one does not act, and subsequently there is a *kaṭhina* robe, even if one does not make a robe, during the month of Kārttika, the separate reception of food is permitted based on this principle. It should be so.
Regarding the time for making robes: the phrase "the time for making robes" is used here to designate the initial specific occasion in contrast to the subsequent general conditions;
that is, it refers to the "robe-season. Therefore, within the detailed explanation, both conditions are made manifest.

Thus, when speaking of "the time for making robes," it refers to the period from the conclusion of the *pravāraṇā* ceremony until the end of the month [of the robe season], which—when there is no *kaṭhina* cloth—is five months, and so on, up to the point where one makes a "horse-tooth" mark upon the robe.
[The Buddha] said: "If one sews, then at the time of making the robe, since one has already obtained it oneself, there is no need to separately make another robe for someone else.
This is why it is said that one should make a 'horse-tooth' stitch upon the robe. Answer: This passage is intended to illustrate the recipient of the benefit;

it does not serve as proof that one must necessarily make a separate robe. Furthermore, [another] interpretation holds: if, later on, the person who was to receive it is no longer present, one is not permitted to accept the benefit. This refers to the month of Kārttika.
In the middle [of the rainy season], one must also make robes. This refers to making robes on borrowed materials; only then is it permitted not to make them.

It is not allowed for these two [types of persons] to make robes together. Therefore, outside of that time, there is the allowance for making robes. Furthermore, according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, there are also eight conditions.

In that precept, first the condition of illness is permitted, followed by the conditions of the time for robes and the time for the gift of robes, as explained in the section on the precept regarding frequent eating.
Regarding the precept on frequent eating, it says: "The World-Honored One permitted the bhikṣus to accept the kaṭhina robe and not violate five matters.
When the bhikṣus think, 'It is for the sake of making robes,' they do not violate [the rule]. Even when the robe-making is finished, they do not violate [the rule]. Thus spoke the Buddha.
There is no offense during the robe season; there is an offense once the robe season has passed. Regarding the circumstances of the subsequent gift of robes:

there were some laypeople who, knowing that bhikṣus may not eat more than once a day, thought, "I shall employ a skillful means for the sake of the bhikṣus so that they may receive robes and also receive offerings.
They then had robes made and invited the bhikṣus. The bhikṣus said, "We [do not...]"
[They said,] "We will give you food, but only if you give us our robes. The white-clad laypeople said, "Venerable sirs, if you accept our food, then you must give us the robes.
The bhikṣus thought to themselves, "World-Honored One, if you permit us to eat repeatedly for the sake of receiving robes, we might fail to obtain them.

They reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha permitted eating repeatedly; subsequently, he made a specific exception, stating that there is no offense in making robes. The text says: "There is..."

The bhikṣus wished to make robes for the sake of begging for food, but because their old robes had not yet been finished, it hindered and interrupted their practice of the Path. They thought to themselves:
"If the Buddha would permit us to accept special invitations to communal meals while making robes, then the robes would be completed quickly and our practice of the Path would not be interrupted.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha granted his permission. Next, it is explained that the practice of the Path and so forth consists of eight conditions in total; by means of those—

To realize this, there are eight conditions. Next, regarding the determination of what constitutes the proper time (*kāla*) and the improper time (*akāla*): only the period of the *kaṭhina* robe is the proper time;

the remaining seven are allowances for the improper time. Although the other seven conditions may exist during the month of the *guṇa-kaṭhina*, they are permitted specifically because the period of the *kaṭhina* is the proper time.
