It is not permitted on account of other conditions; therefore, one who does not accept the *guṇavastra* (robe of merit) is not included even if other conditions exist within the designated time period.
That is to say, with respect to a person receiving a benefit, it is determined that they do not obtain it because it is restricted by the temporal limit.

One must distinguish between the proper time (*kāla*) and the improper time (*akāla*). Even if it falls within another's designated period or month of benefit, if it does not accord with one's own [expectations], it is considered "improper time.

Next, regarding what is common and what is distinct: the time for the distribution of robes, the time when the Great Assembly gathers, and the time for the distribution of food to śramaṇas—these three are common.

This is because the distribution of robes and the śramaṇas themselves do not belong exclusively to any individual; since they are opened up as objects for the preceding [conditions], they are shared by all. The Great Assembly...

"Accumulation" (saṃnipāta) means mutual dependence for the sake of functioning. A single [condition] does not achieve [the result]; it is also subsumed under common conditions. Therefore, these three [conditions] are opened up as being necessarily common.
All other conditions are exclusively distinct. Alternatively, there may be those that individually carry distinct conditions yet are termed "common."
This distinction between the common and the specific is not the same as in the preceding stages. Next, regarding the relative strength of their mutual inclusion:

if one considers the person receiving the benefit, during the month of the timely benefit (*kālalābha*), no further conditions may arise to open [the opportunity]; even if such conditions exist, they are subsumed solely within the timely benefit and are thus termed "strong.
If, however, these conditions are considered in relation to one another, there are only the three aforementioned common conditions, which constitute the common conditions (*sāmānyapratyaya*).

This summarizes the root [text]. It is opened because of shared conditions (*sādhāraṇa-pratyaya*), and not permitted because of other conditions; for in the absence of other conditions, it is established as distinct in itself.

Even if other conditions are mixed, each is subsumed under its own respective condition. Next, regarding similarities and differences: while the "Traveling by Boat" rule applies specifically to the *śramaṇa*, this precept on walking on the road is common to both the bathing precept and others.
There are slight similarities and differences, the meaning of which can be understood by analogy. This applies to the rules concerning robes, time, and so forth.

The opening [of the door] and the passage [through it] occur in succession; furthermore, regarding the precepts for before and after meals, the allowances for those with illness are somewhat more relaxed. Nevertheless, there are distinctions, which differ from the meaning of [the term] "opening and closing" (kai-tō).
These should be understood according to their respective applications.

Next, the characteristics are explained below. The first three [points] are easily understood. From the words "the sick person" onwards, the phrase regarding the opening of the conditions (*pratyaya*) is interpreted:

because the sick person is collectively troubled, it is permitted for them to receive food from a separate assembly (*pṛthaggaṇa*). Furthermore, there is no intention to cause a schism in the Saṃgha; this is seen in the *Śāstra*. Regarding "the sick person’s foot is broken":
because sand and dust have entered the wound and he is unable to walk, he is permitted to receive food from a separate assembly. Regarding "when making robes," this refers to one...

In the fifth month, for the purpose of making robes, one seeks food to make the robes; fearing that the task might not be accomplished, the rule for eating in a group apart from the community (*pṛthag-bhakta*) is permitted.
If this text were opened as two distinct conditions, the characteristics would likewise be evident, as clarified by the meaning above.

However, it is simply because at the time of making robes there is one opening, whereas the time for receiving benefits is fixed; for making robes is precisely outside the scope of "time" and "benefits. Later, regarding persons such as Ānanda, at [the time of] Kāśyapa...
Regarding the opening [of the rules] for making robes during the *cīvarakāla* (robe season): this is also included within the "non-season" (*akāla*).

As for the time when robes are offered, although the benefit of the robe is significant, it is permitted for two reasons: first, to benefit the donor; second, to benefit the bhikṣu. However, according to this text, the offering of robes applies to both times.

During the [proper] season, one may obtain [robes] from a separate group (*pṛthaggaṇa*) without depending on the offering of robes. But that which is opened specifically by the offering of robes refers to the non-season, because...

The remainder refers to those outside the designated time-periods. Regarding the next point, the "traveler": this must refer to one who travels on that very day; it is permitted for one who comes or goes even as far as half a *yojana*.

The *Daśabhāṇavāra* states: "If one ate today after traveling yesterday, or if one intends to travel tomorrow and eats today, it is all a *pāyattika*, because the time has passed or has not yet arrived.
The same applies to traveling by boat. Next is the "gathering of the great assembly."
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: It is the constant law of all Buddhas to hold two great assemblies each year, at the end of the spring and summer months.
Monks from all directions come to pay their respects; because they are so numerous, invitations for meals are very infrequent and alms-food is difficult to obtain. The monks then reflect:
"If the Blessed One would allow us to accept separate invitations for communal meals during the Great Assembly, we would not suffer such hardship.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha then permitted the acceptance of separate invitations for communal meals. Regarding the circumstances of this allowance:
at that time, many bhikṣus were traveling through the kingdom of Kosala and arrived at a small village. The local laypeople thought to themselves, "The community of monks is numerous..."
"The village is small; how can we provide food for the community of monks? Let us not cause the monks to suffer from exhaustion.

Thinking thus, they came to invite the monks. The Buddha then granted his permission. Having considered this thoroughly, [he realized] that it would be difficult for a large assembly to provide offerings. Out of compassion for the bhikṣus, the Buddha [spoke].

Regarding the opening of the rule on eating in a separate group (*pṛthaggaṇabhojana*): as for the statement that "four persons constitute a full meal, with one additional person being a cause for offense," the ancient interpretation says this refers to the one additional person among the four, not someone outside the group of four.
It does not mean that if there were one additional person beyond the four, or even up to a hundred, it would be considered an offense;

rather, it should be said that adding ninety-seven people constitutes an offense. This is simply because they share the same name, and the meaning of the term "additional" (*atireka*) is identical in both cases.

It is said that for one person it is auspicious. The commentary explains: regarding the gathering of the great assembly, this is permitted because food exists only in this place and is absent elsewhere.
As for the statement "if four people have one extra person as a cause for distress," since food is easily obtained, this constitutes a transgression due to such distress;

however, if food is difficult to obtain, the distress is permitted and there is no offense. Even down to having one extra person as a cause for distress, much more need not be said—this extends even to a hundred.
It is the same for a person who is one *man* (a tall man) in height. Now, to explain:

the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states that whether due to Dharma matters or other circumstances, when the assembly of monks gathers in its smallest possible number—four old bhikṣus and room for four more bhikṣus—it is termed a "great assembly.

Even if food is not difficult to obtain when such a great assembly has gathered, the separate assembly (*pṛthag-saṃgha*) is not permitted; it is only allowed as an exception in cases of difficulty. Based on this, it is established.

When food is difficult to obtain, even if there is a distinction of one [person], it is not called a transgression. If food is easily obtained, a distinction of even one person can immediately constitute a *pācittiya* offense;

this is called a "transgression. This passage cites the transgression to clarify what does not constitute a transgression. This applies even up to a group of one hundred people where only one is extra;
"transgression" here refers to the offense of a separate assembly (*pṛthaggaṇa*). Next, regarding "food given by a śramaṇa," many say this refers to outsiders.

Regarding the term "śramaṇa": with the exception of the fivefold assembly of the Buddha, all those who have left the household life among the various non-Buddhist paths (tīrthikas) are called śramaṇas.
However, because these followers of external paths hold divergent views, they may occasionally give rise to faith and invite bhikṣus; for their benefit, [the Buddha] permitted it. As the text states:
"In this regard, those other than the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākya, who have left the household life—namely, the 'old śramaṇas' and those who have gone forth from external paths [are included]."
This concerns those who first wish to leave the household life. Next is the explanation of the section on the offense for breaking the rule.

This section is divided into two parts: first, the instruction on the proper procedure for a bhikṣu regarding food; second, from "If a bhikṣu... onwards, the formulation of the offense for violating the rule. The first part consists of four sentences.

The first sentence, "If there is no reason, one must inform [the assembly] before going out," explains away doubts held outside the community; thus, it implies that while everyone possesses "leftover food" (*vighasa*), the specific circumstances (*pratyaya*) are not all the same.

"Monks! Next, [if] it cannot benefit me—this refers to having a connection or lacking a connection. Because these are mixed together in one place, I, being without a connection, announce my departure.
As for the others who lack a connection, do not enter during the subsequent phrase. The assembly shall listen and eat at will.

During the subsequent phrase, when the multitude is divided into two groups and after they have eaten, those with a connection who must announce their entry do so to remove doubts within the assembly; this is for the sake of clarification."

"I am not [qualified]. If one is unable to benefit others due to the order of the Saṃgha, or if there are others who lack the necessary conditions, it is logically required that one announce one's departure. Next, the determination of the offense may be understood.

Next is the precept concerning taking more than three bowlfuls of food from a woman returning home or the provisions for a merchant on a journey. Regarding the woman returning home and the merchant: within their hearts...
Out of faith, one may carry provisions to offer to the Saṃgha; however, these must be received with careful consideration, for if one exceeds this limit, they will be exhausted.

Therefore, a restriction is established, and to transgress it constitutes an offense. There are five specific conditions [for this rule]: first, being a guest arriving from afar; second, possessing provisions; third, knowing them to be such;

fourth, having no other reason for taking more than three bowls except in the case of illness, in which case there is no offense; fifth, the offense is incurred the moment one steps outside the door. Regarding the text, there are two parts.
The conditions are fully manifest. Gañjana is translated here as "blind. Thus, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "I shall no longer use you, blind woman. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"This woman is so beautiful that I fear the King will forcibly take her. I shall give her an inauspicious name.
Later, when the King indeed desired to take her, because of the inauspicious name, she was instead given to another man. This completes the three phrases of the precept. Number [ ].
First, if bhikṣus are invited to receive two meals; second, if bhikṣus are permitted to accept and eat them;
third, regarding the offense for bhikṣus who are not ill: the offense of *thullaccaya* is established because they accepted [the food] improperly, not because it was not distributed.
In the text, this is mentioned incidentally, hence the statement: "if one does not distribute it by giving food to other bhikṣus. Each of these three passages has its own specific context.

Two parts: first, citing the person; second, clarifying the ritual procedure. Below this follows the detailed explanation. Regarding the explanation of the *bhikṣu*: the meaning applies to all three stages.

First, the person is explained; next, the householder's home; next, the exception for the cause of illness; next, from "If a bhikṣu... onwards is the detailed explanation. Second, the opening for receiving and eating. Next, from "If a bhikṣu...
onwards is the establishment of the offense for one who is not ill. The text contains five phrases: first, the summary; fourth, the [detailed] exposition.

"An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). This fourth bowl constitutes an offense. According to the treatise, the meaning is that when one takes more than the lower limit of bowls and goes out the door, one incurs a *pācittiya*;
however, if one does not divide it to eat alone, there is only a *dukkaṭa*. Thus, we know that within the body of the precept, the words are spoken based on faith."
*The Record Opening the Sectarian Tenets of the Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, Fascicle Four, Part One;
*The Record Opening the Sectarian Tenets of the Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, Fascicle Four, Part Two.

Next is the Precept on Sufficient Food (*paryāpta-bhojana*). Generally, food sustains the body so that one may cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*). If it is too little, the Way is impaired; if it is too much, [it leads to excess].

Because of greed for food, the Buddha established four methods of supplementation according to the faculties of his disciples, ranging from the practice of a single morsel to the formal rite of leaving a remainder (*atirikta-dharma*).
Now, this fourth person does not perform the rite of leaving a remainder; because his greedy mind is heavy and he eats further, he violates the teaching and incurs an offense.
The separate conditions consist of five factors: first, having finished eating; second, the perception that one has finished eating; third, abandoning the formal posture (*īryāpatha*);
fourth, being without a valid cause—meaning, except in cases of illness or performing a ritual act; and fifth, eating again, which constitutes an offense of *thullaccaya*.
Next, the explanation of the text follows. There are five sections regarding the characteristics of offenses: first, the exposition of the one-meal practice for those of superior capacity;

second, the allowance for the sick to have no limit on food, beginning with "At that time, various sick bhikṣus..."; third, the allowance for the sick to consume leftovers, beginning with "At that time, various sick bhikṣus...";

fourth, the regulation prohibiting leftovers, beginning with "At that time, the bhikṣus..."; and fifth, the arising of transgressions due to violating the rule, beginning with "At that time, in the kingdom of Śrāvastī..."

The initial passage consists of three parts: first, the exposition of the practice of eating one meal a day; second, from "At that time" onwards, the conclusion of the preceding regulation regarding the single meal;

third, from "The bhikṣus" onwards, the conclusion of the preceding statement on being fully satiated. The first part addresses those who are practitioners of the higher path (ūrdhvaga), and thus it expounds the practice of eating one meal a day.
However, since practicing this single meal necessarily enables one to economize on conditions and cultivate the Path, it is said to be a praise of the practice of eating one meal a day. Second...

Section Two: Four Passages. First, a mistaken interpretation of the sacred teachings led him to practice the Dharma while wearing inferior robes; lacking the sustenance of food, his body became emaciated.

Second, the Buddha compassionately inquired after him. Third, Ānanda gave a detailed response. Fourth, he understood that although one observes the practice of eating only once a day, one must still eat until fully satiated.

The next three passages likewise each contain four sections as before: the second concerns the allowance for those who are ill, and the third concerns the removal of leftovers. Each is as described above.

The four [points] are as before; they cannot be fully detailed here. Regarding the fourth [point], the remaining rules consist of two sections. The first concerns the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta* (the ritual for leftover food) in relation to the Sangha’s meal.

This section has four parts, identical to those before. However, the performance of the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta* requires ten conditions: first, the bhikṣu must have had sufficient food, excluding those who have not yet had enough;
second, it must be within the proper time, not during a famine or after midday; third, it must be a *kālabhojana* (meal at the proper time), excluding meals taken outside the proper time; fourth...
One must physically remove impurities, such as food touched overnight, remnants of illness, and so forth. Thus, the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle seven, states:

"If one receives impure food or impure meat, it is called the 'receiving of leftover food' (*saṃkhaḍika-bhakta-dharma*). Impure food refers to that which is leftover from the previous night, that which was poorly handled, or that which has been kept overnight.
Impure meat refers to dog meat, the meat of evil birds, and the like. [This applies when] the fifth hand receives [the food], or when it is held exposed.
1. Stretching out the hand; 2. The sixth verbal expression, namely saying, "I have had enough," and so forth; 3. The seventh, regarding a monk who has not yet finished eating;
4. The eighth, taking food for oneself; 5. The ninth, saying, "Stop; you may take the food."
The tenth [section], "Returning to the Original Food Master," can be understood according to the text. However, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Sengqi lü), fascicle 16, states:

"There are five kinds of non-dharmic [acts] that do not constitute the practice of *vighasa* (leftover food). What are the five? Departing from the place; departing from the food; departing from the boundary; departing from the reach of the hand; and departing from speech."

First, regarding "separation from place": if one prepares *kṛtapiṇḍa* (leftover food) for a bhikṣu while he is walking, and gives him the food to eat while he is standing, sitting, or lying down, this is not called "preparing [the food].
The same applies when the other three postures are mutually exchanged. Second, regarding "separation from food":

1. Not making it "leftover" by eating together: one should speak immediately after eating; if one gives [food] away, it is not called "leftover. 2. Separation from the object: one makes it leftover by placing it on the ground;
it is not leftover while still in the hand. 3. Separation from the reach of the hand: one makes it leftover outside the reach of the hand, not within the reach of the hand. 4. Separation from speech:
as when one does not say, "The food in my hand, in my bowl—I do not need any of this now; it is leftover."

If one gives food to an elder, these five [cases] are non-dharmic and do not constitute [the offense]. Conversely, the five instances of being separated from [the requirements] are the opposite; that is, the five instances of not being separated from them constitute its accomplishment.
One should understand that the five instances of not being separated from them are the reverse of the above. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, chapter eight, states:

The Buddha said, "One should perform the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (leftover-food) rite in the presence of a monk whose meal is not yet finished. If there is no such person, one should perform it in the presence of a monk who has not yet eaten. If...
If there is no bhikṣu among the assembly who has not yet eaten, one should go to a nearby place;

if none is found in a nearby place, one should grant the full ordination (upasaṃpadā) to the śrāmaṇera and quickly confer the precepts upon him. Then, in the presence of that person, [the others] act as the bhikṣus.
Not knowing how to perform the ritual for leftover food (vighasa-vidhi), they inform the Buddha. The Buddha said: "Place the food in a bowl, hold it up with your hands, and bare your right shoulder."
With the right shoulder bared and the right knee touching the ground, one should say: "Venerable sir, please attend to me with a focused mind. I, [Name], have finished eating my fill;
please perform for me the ritual of the leftover food (*kṛtapiṇḍaka-vidhi*). That bhikṣu shall take the bowl and ask: "Is this food to be given to me?
If the answer is "Yes," he shall eat it; if there is a small remainder, he shall return it. If he has not eaten at all, he shall simply take it and return it.
Regarding the terminology: "This is my leavings; I give them to you as well, so they are called 'leftover food' (*vighasa*). The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (Duolun) further states:
"If a donor offers the five kinds of food while a bhikṣu is performing the ritual of rinsing his mouth, the bhikṣu should eat it, provided he performs the rite for receiving leftover food."

One should not remain standing, sitting, or lying down [while eating]. If one remains standing, sitting, or lying down, it should be known that this violates the rules of decorum (*airyāpathika*) and does not constitute formal acceptance (*paribhoga*).
If one considers such conduct to be formal acceptance, it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense; the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* is likewise. Question:

It is not yet known whether, once the ritual for leftover food (*atiriktakalpa*) has been completed, other monks may eat it without understanding the procedure. However, according to the Sūtra, once the ritual is performed and concluded, the remaining people may eat it without fault. Therefore...
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Sengqi lü), fascicle 16, states: "From now on, it is permitted for one person to perform the *śeṣa-bhakta* (leftover food) rite;

all other people may then eat. If this is so, how is it to be understood? The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-vaibhāṣikā* (Duolun), fascicle 7, states: "If one person performs the *śeṣa-bhakta* rite, the eating by others does not constitute a valid completion [of the rite].

The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-vaibhāṣikā* holds that the rite is restricted to the individual; since others lack the rite, they may not eat. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, however, simply bases itself on the successful completion of the *śeṣa-bhakta*.

Therefore, one may obtain food through other means. Next, regarding the donor’s meal, it is the same as before. Fifth, concerning the transgression of rising [from the seat]: not knowing that the formal meal (*bhojana*) has been completed renders it invalid;

if it is not completed, it is not valid. Hence, it is said that one does not know when the meal is finished. Furthermore, regarding the insufficient meal, one does not know how many conditions must be fulfilled for the ritual procedure (*vidhi*) to be effective, nor how many are lacking for it to be invalid.
Thus, it is said that one does not know what constitutes "leftover food" (*atirikta-bhojana*) and what does not.
The Prātimokṣa Sūtra consists of three phrases: first, the person; second, "having finished eating," which indicates that one’s own needs have been satisfied;

third, "or at times," and so forth, which refers to taking food from a donor while violating the rule, thereby constituting an offense. Next, the explanation of the text has two parts: first, the interpretation of the three phrases of the Prātimokṣa Sūtra; second, from "At that time, the Venerable...

onwards, the inquiry and resolution regarding the conditions for sufficiency. The preceding text explaining the first phrase is easily understood. Next, from "as for 'eating,'" the second phrase is explained.
There are two phrases. Within these, there are further two parts: first, the explanation of food; second, the conclusion thereof. Regarding the five types of food:

rice and meat each have two varieties, while parched grain (*maṃsa*) alone constitutes one. Based on this combination and separation, there are thus five. However, in terms of their actual substance, there are only three:
namely, rice, parched grain, and meat—just as with the five types of living seeds. Next is the conclusion thereof; within the text, there are two sections, the first of which...

This explains satiety (*tṛpti*). Next, the conditions for satiety are clarified. There are two types of satiety: namely, satiety through self-contentment (*svacchanda*) and satiety through the object (*viṣaya*). Regarding satiety through self-contentment, one must be fully satiated.

Regarding satiety through the object, it refers to receiving a large amount of food; in relation to the object, it constitutes satiety. Even if one consumes but a single mouthful, once it has left the mouth, it constitutes satiety.

Therefore, the introductory text of the *Pratideśanīya* (Offenses to be Confessed) states: "If one does not perform the *kṛta-śeṣa-bhikṣā-dharma* (the ritual of leaving food remaining), one shall not rise..."

There is no offense. Thus we know that it is called "sufficient" because the objects [of the meal] are many. If it were otherwise, why would the Buddha need to grant this permission for one to eat as soon as the thought arises?
Next, there are five conditions for satiety (*pāripūri*): first, knowing it is rice; that is, knowing that rice constitutes a proper meal that brings satiety. Second, knowing it has been brought;

that is, understanding that another has brought it while forming the perception that it is one's own meal. Third, knowing the limit; that is, knowing that the quantity is sufficient to satisfy and precludes further eating.

Fourth, knowing the deportment; that is, being aware of the four modes of conduct, such as walking and so forth. Fifth, knowing the relinquishing of deportment; that is, having ceased [the previous mode].
Regarding walking, standing, and so forth: as it is with rice, so it is with the other four types of food. Thus, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"In each of these five types of food, there are five factors that constitute 'having finished eating' (*paryāpta-bhakta*): first, there is the food; second, it is offered;
third, it is handed over for consumption; fourth, one does not receive further benefit; and fifth, having finished eating, the body must leave its original position. This has been explained.

The third phrase states: "Having finished eating and abandoned the formal deportment" (*pārivāsika*) indicates that the matter of satiety is concluded. "Not performing [the ritual]" (*akṛta-ādi*) refers to violating the permission and incurring an offense.

Next, the text concerning the inquiry and resolution has two parts: first, the actual explanation of the question and answer; second, the explanation of whether the ritual action is accomplished or not.

The preceding text consists of two parts. The first concerns the five types of *bhojana* (solid food) as the basis for full offenses; the second concerns *khādanīya* (hard food) and below as the basis for incomplete offenses.

The first part further consists of two sections: the first provides an extensive analysis based on the deportment of walking; the second treats the remaining three categories with ease. The first section contains five elements:

first, the question; second, the answer; third, the inquiry; fourth, the explanation; and fifth, the conclusion. Within the fourth element, the explanation, there are five textual passages concerning the five types of food.
Regarding the first meal, there are two phrases: first, concerning the offense regarding the completion of eating rice; second, concerning the offense regarding miscellaneous foods.

Since rice constitutes the primary category with these two [offenses], the remaining four types of food are likewise treated. This thus forms five pairs of ten phrases. As it is for this practice, so it is for the other three categories.
These forty phrases are sufficient when calculated according to principle. Next, we consider the nine kinds of *khādaniya* (solid) foods.
This serves to clarify the characteristics of the offense. "Fine powder" refers to that which is not a primary food; it is an improper powder.

This *khādanīya* (solid food) does not constitute a sufficient condition for satiety if one has not yet eaten the five types of primary foods (*paṃca bhojanāni*). Eating it at such a time incurs no fault.

However, if one has eaten the five primary foods and then, having abandoned the formal deportment (*īryāpatha*), eats improper food again, it constitutes an offense. Furthermore, regarding the offense involving oil and honey, this refers to their being mixed with food taken at the improper time.
If one eats alone, there is no offense. As in the "Ten Unlawful Acts," it is established that [eating] mixed food is permissible. A question was asked: "What is meant by 'mixed'? The answer was:
"Having finished eating and abandoned the formal deportment, if one mixes curd with ghee, honey, and so forth, may it be eaten in one place?
Upāli replied: "It is not permitted. He asked: "Where was this prohibited? The answer was: "In Śrāvastī, regarding the rule on not performing the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta* (the ritual of leftover food)."
The Vinaya rules establish this as proof: that which constitutes a transgression is [the act of] mixing. If it were not mixed, the reason for pointing to these same rules would be untenable.

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* also states: "Mixing butter and the like with curd. This is followed by an explanation of the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*) regarding whether the act is accomplished or not, consisting of four pairs of eight propositions.

The first two pairs contrast ignorance and darkness; the next two, respect and pride; the next two, the monastic and the lay; and the final two, stinginess and greed. Regarding the sixth phrase herein:

performing the ritual act in the presence of a *kappiya-kāraka* (a "pure person") succeeds [in its formal validity], yet it constitutes an offense. This is because it is performed in response to a *bhikṣu*;
however, one should not lose the efficacy of the rite by being in the presence of a *kappiya-kāraka*, nor should one incur an offense thereby. As for the remaining seven phrases, they do not succeed.

Because one incurs an offense and loses the Dharma, it is auspicious [to avoid it]; because it is not accomplished, it is a *pāyattika* (offense). Next, regarding the perception of the object (*viṣaya-saṃjñā*), there are only four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
The first two permutations concern the primary meal (*bhojana*). In the first permutation, if the mind perceives the food as being beyond the proper measure, it is a *pāyattika*.

In the second permutation, if one eats thick gruel at dawn while harboring a doubtful mind—eating due to such doubt—the mind is light and one incurs only an *aniyata* (indefinite) offense. Question: Why is there no third permutation?

Regarding the phrase "having finished eating while perceiving it as not finished": the answer is that there is no offense if one’s mind is deluded, as this falls under the category of the provision for exceptions. Thus, the text on exceptions states: "If one eats while perceiving it as not food, there is no offense.

Furthermore, another interpretation holds that a change in perception may still entail an offense; the absence of such a statement in the text is merely an abbreviation. As for the following two phrases, they do not refer to the primary meal.
In the first case, one sees thin gruel that has been standing for a long time and perceives it as thick, thinking it is the primary meal; thus, one incurs no offense.
It is precisely *an-āpatti* (no offense). The second phrase raises a doubt regarding a difference. As for *ni-gi-la*, it is the same as in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra*.

That treatise states: "This precept is not shared [with the other three assemblies]; they do not commit an offense. Furthermore, according to another interpretation based on the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, it says:

"For nuns, it is also like this," clarifying that they commit the offense together with the monks. Why is this? Because this text concludes it as a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). The answer is: it is to demonstrate the differences in their combinations and separations. For now...
This constitutes a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*). Next, the text opens with: "Regarding the perception of food as non-food," and so forth.
Although it is indeed food, because one consistently perceives it as non-food, one does not undergo the ritual of *parivāsa* (probation) or other formal procedures. Next, regarding "non-food":

because its substance is not food, if one performs the procedure oneself without [the mediation of] others, this opens the fifth clause concerning the use of a *śuddhaka-purūṣa* (pure person). Furthermore, if one does not place it on the ground, this is permitted.

Regarding the preliminary stage (*pūrvakāla*): it is neither placed on the ground, but should be held in the hand or kept within reach. If one opens it for another, one first takes hold of it oneself;
if one opens it for oneself, one takes it all away from the front. Of the eight phrases, four are briefly reversed; the remaining cases of opening may be understood accordingly.

Next is the precept against encouraging another to eat to fullness. The specific intent is as follows: One who has left the household life and maintains their practice ought to benefit both themselves and others.

Now, if one’s vigilance is incomplete and they encourage another toward evil, since the person has already accepted the encouragement, both self and other are harmed, and there is no benefit for either party;

therefore, this rule was established. Question: Why are "eating to fullness" and "refraining from encouraging others" treated as two separate precepts? Answer: Because the conditions differ—namely, encouraging oneself versus encouraging another. Furthermore, it should be...

The commentary explains: There are many differing meanings regarding how a single action gives rise to different karmas. That is to say, when one has already finished eating, if greed arises, it constitutes the karma of "encouraging another to eat";

if anger arises, it constitutes two karmas. These possess distinct characteristics relative to the act of eating: the verbal restraint of the mouth coincides with the physical transgression of the body. Encouraging another to eat is the verbal karma of restraint.

1. Offenses committed by proxy through another’s body. 2. The specific allowance for *paryāpta-bhakṣa* (sufficient food) under three exceptional circumstances; there is no allowance for encouraging *paryāpta-bhakṣa* under the circumstance of illness.

3. The distinction between eating and not eating regarding *paryāpta-bhakṣa*: one commits an offense if they eat it, while one commits an offense if they encourage another to eat it even though they themselves do not eat it.

Because these distinct characteristics exist, they cannot be combined. Next, there are four conditions: first, knowing that the other has finished eating; second, not performing the *atirikta-dharma* (the rite of leaving food remaining); third, encouraging with malicious intent.
Regarding those four offenses committed by eating before the meal: the full precept consists of three factors: (1) a person; (2) knowing that another has finished eating;

and (3) if one has accepted an invitation, violating it results in the formal charge of an offense. In the commentary, the first factor is explained individually, while the remaining two are clarified together. Within the combined explanation, the substance of the food is first presented, followed by the formal clarification of the offense.
Among the eight factors, the first carries the weightiest intention; the second is a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation), and the following seven are likewise [pāyattikas].

Because the conditions differ, both are auspicious. Since the case of a nun is rare, it is merely classified as a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing). The remaining phrases within the opening section are all reversed;
only the preceding phrase concerning illness is omitted and not reversed.

Next is the precept against eating at improper times. One’s resolve and sustenance should be timely, so as to increase one’s spiritual practice. To eat past the proper time brings affliction and obstructs the gateway to the Path.
Since it is contrary to the Dharma, it harms the Path and invites reproach; as this fault is not slight, it was strictly regulated by the Sage. Next, regarding the definition of "time":
from dawn until midday, eating produces no offense, and thus it is called "time. Once the sun has passed the meridian, eating...
This gives rise to sinful burdens; therefore, it is called "untimely. For this reason, various sutras state that there are five divine blessings in not eating after midday:
first, little lust; second, little sleep; third, attainment of one-pointedness of mind; fourth, freedom from flatulence;
and fifth, physical stability and the absence of illness. Therefore, śramaṇas and practitioners of the Way, knowing these blessings, do not eat [after midday].
This results in five transgressions; therefore, it is not the proper time. There are four specific conditions: first, it is not the proper time;
second, one perceives it as not being the proper time; third, it is food to be eaten at the proper time; fourth, by eating it, one commits an offense.

Among these conditions, Nanda and Upananda, having watched a musical performance, ate at an improper time and did not return until near dusk. Kāḷodāyin, while patrolling the gates at night, startled and terrified the householders. Thus...

This damages the life-force of the embryo. The four phrases of the root precept are: first, a person; second, at an improper time; third, food; and fourth, the formal conclusion (*saṃvara*). These are explained in detail in the commentary. The first three are easily understood.

Regarding the explanation of the fourth phrase on the formal conclusion of the offense, there are four types: first, eating at the proper time; second, regarding the improper time; third, for seven days; and fourth, for as long as one lives.
However, since there is no loss of the limit for receiving [the medicine] that lasts for the duration of one’s life, it is therefore established in relation to those who are not ill.
[This concerns] the understanding of "improper time. Next, regarding the five propositions on the perception of the object (*ālambana-saṃjñā*), the opening of the text states:

"As for barley, provided the husks are not broken, it is permitted because it is a clear liquid and lacks coarse characteristics. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, chapter eight, says: There was a bhikṣu who had taken emetic and purgative medicine;
before the mealtime had passed, his stomach became empty and distressed. The other bhikṣus did not know what to do, so they informed the Buddha. The Buddha said: [He should take it].
He smeared his body with ghee, yet it was still not cured. The Buddha said, "Smeared his body with parched flour (maṇḍa)," yet it was still not cured.
The Buddha said, "Smeared his body with ghee mixed with parched flour," yet it was still not cured. The Buddha said, "Washed him with warm water," yet it was still not cured.
The Buddha said, "Gave him warm water to drink," yet it was still not cured. The Buddha said, "Place him in a basin filled with melted fat."

By means of such [examples], it is sufficient to understand that one must not eat at an improper time until dawn. Only belching during midday is considered to lack the characteristic of coarseness and is thus not an offense.
According to the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*: if food has been vomited but has not yet passed the throat, swallowing it again is not an offense;
if it has passed the throat and entered the mouth, swallowing it again constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.

Next is the precept concerning leftover food from the previous night (*pūrvāhṇa-śeṣa-bhakṣaṇa-virati*). Food and drink increase greed and cause one to lack moderation. To say that one seeks only to sustain life is what defines a *śramaṇa*.

Yet now, one intentionally stores food intended for a later meal; such conduct is defiled. This rule was established to prevent it. Regarding the definition of the terms: that which is eaten now is the remainder of what was prepared;
because it is a remainder, it is called "leftover" (*śeṣa*). Because it has remained overnight, it is called "stayed" (*vāsita*). Within this [precept], there are four [categories].

There are four cases: First, that which is residual but not stored overnight (*śeṣa-anāstika*). This refers to food remaining from a meal that is set aside to supplement a later meal. Because it was stored overnight but not in the same boundary (*sīmā*), one incurs only a *duṣkṛta* offense.

Second, that which is stored overnight but not residual (*anāstika-aśeṣa*). This refers to food stored overnight that is not a remnant of a previous meal. One incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense for storing within the boundary (*antar-āstika*). Third, that which is both residual and stored overnight (*śeṣa-anāstika*).

This entails both a *pāyattika* and a *duṣkṛta* offense. It is a *pāyattika* because it is residual and stored overnight; it is a *duṣkṛta* because of the internal storage within the boundary. Fourth, that which is neither residual nor [stored overnight]...

"Overnight" (sukhita) refers to pure food. There are three specific conditions: first, it is leftover overnight food; second, one knows it to be such; third, eating it constitutes an offense. The four phrases of the root precept are:
first, the person; second, the leftover overnight food; third, the act of eating; fourth, the formal conclusion (*niḥsargika-pāyattika*). The explanation is as follows.

Within the conclusion there are also four points, similar to the aforementioned "leftover food": if one has permanently discarded it with no intention to eat it again, and subsequently encounters it and obtains it, it is not termed "leftover. Five.
The twenty-second section states: There was a resident bhikṣu who ate mangoes until he was full and gave the remainder to a lay attendant (kappiyakāraka).
The next day, the attendant prepared a soup with them and gave it to the bhikṣu. The bhikṣu did not dare to eat it and reported the matter to the Buddha.
If one did not originally intend to return for food, it is permitted to eat it all without offense. Furthermore, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

If leftover food from yesterday was discarded upon a stone or upon grass leaves, and on the following day one enters a village to beg for food but obtains nothing at all, returning with an empty bowl, and without intending to return for food, comes back by the same path and sees that the mass of rice remains as it was on the original stone—if [one eats this]...
If there is a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to handle food), one should have that *kappiya-kāraka* hand it over; having received it, one may eat.

If there is no *kappiya-kāraka*, and there is a place where crows or birds have eaten, one should wash it clean and then take the food oneself. Furthermore, it is said: when a bhikṣu rises in the morning, he should wash his hands clean.
He must not merely roughly wash the tips of his five fingers, nor should he wash up to the armpits; he should ensure they are clean from the wrist upward. Not...
One may become coarse; one must not scrub so as to cause blood to flow. One should instead use *śamī* grass or the ashes of *umbara* wood.
If using ashes or earth, wash thoroughly and rub the hands until they make a sound. Once the hands have been washed clean, if one rubs them against each other again, it is called impure.
It should be washed again. If the bowl has been washed, it should be polished again while it is still wet; wiping it [dry] is called "impurity," so it should be set aside to dry.

When a bhikṣu is about to eat, he must keep his hands clean. If he polishes his head, or takes up his *nirvāṇa-saṅghāṭī* (undergarment), grass sandals, or a bag for holding ghee or oil, he must wash them again as before. This also applies if he takes up his *saṃghāṭī* or other robes.
It should be washed again. *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, chapter 56: A bhikṣu newly lacquered a bowl and placed it in his alms-bowl;

after washing it two or three times, the oily odor remained impure. He then informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said: "If one washes it three times with single-minded attention, this bowl is called pure."

Next is the precept against eating food not formally received. As for the reason it was established, the eighth fascicle of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: Before the World-Honored One had established this rule, monks would accept food and eat;
they would go to the homes of their personal acquaintances and eat there without having formally received the food. Laypeople criticized them, saying: [text continues]
We do not delight in seeing this evil person’s body wearing robes that have been cut and dyed a discolored hue; we do not accept food from such a person.

To eat [from them] constitutes taking what is not given (*adattādāna*). Furthermore, in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 8, it states that there are five reasons for this: first, to sever the causes and conditions for theft;
second, to serve as a witness—receiving food from a non-human being may constitute receiving food, but it does not constitute valid testimony.
Explanation: The reason for permitting the acceptance of food from non-human beings is that it is permitted in desolate wilderness areas because no humans are present.
However, if one is among people, it is not permitted to accept food from non-humans, animals, or ignorant children, for three reasons: to prevent slander.
Fourth, it is for the sake of having few desires and being content; fifth, it is for the sake of engendering a mind of faith and respect in others.
Because one accepts the four types of medicine by means of robes, vessels, and so forth, it is called "receiving" (pratigraha).
The distinct conditions consist of four: first, it must be edible food; second, it has not been formally accepted (*pratigṛhīta*); third, one knows that it has not been accepted;

fourth, the act of eating constitutes an offense. This fulfills the five phrases of the precept: first, the person; second, the lack of formal acceptance; third, the substance of the food; fourth, the exclusion of permissible exceptions; and fifth, the formal determination of the offense.
The commentary provides a detailed explanation. Regarding the second sentence, there are two parts: first, the clarification of non-reception;

second, the clarification of the method of reception. To explain the meaning in contrast to this, there is a threefold analysis: first, the explanation of manual reception; second, the explanation of oral reception; third, the distinction between these two types of reception.
Within the first section, there are four points: first, the object of the food received; second, the substance of the food received; third, the action of the recipient.
Mind. Fourth, has it been lost after being received? Regarding the objects of the first gate, there are generally four types.
Thus, the eighth fascicle of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: Śāriputra suffered from a wind ailment. Maudgalyāyana took lotus roots from a nāga and gave them to Śāriputra.
Śāriputra did not dare to eat them. The Buddha said, "I permit you to accept food from a nāga. He also permitted accepting food from a monkey. Furthermore, Śakra manifested as a poor man...

A woman offered food to Kāśyapa; Kāśyapa, observing and knowing [the circumstances], did not dare to eat it. He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said: "From now on, I permit the bhikṣus to receive food from devas.
Furthermore, because of an invitation by a spirit, the Buddha and the Saṃgha personally served the food with their own hands;

the bhikṣus did not dare to eat it. The Buddha said: "I permit you to receive food from spirits. Moreover, in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya), chapter fifty-eight, the Buddha said: "From now on..."
Regarding the practice of receiving food from non-humans and eating it daily: as for the substance of the food, whatever is fit to be eaten must be received.
Thus, the text states that "food" refers to *khādaniya* (solid foods) and so forth. Furthermore, the *Vyākhyāyukti* says: "There are five kinds of substances: first, those measured by time;
second, those measured by the watch of the night; third, those measured by seven days; fourth, those measured by a lifetime; and fifth, those measured by a great [period]."
The measure is established. These five encompass all things: namely, those that are edible and do not give rise to reproach, and those that are not naturally obstructive.
Thus, one is permitted to accept food [containing] these. Therefore, in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, chapter fifty-seven, the Buddha said:

"From this day forward, I permit [the presence of] five types of dust within food that should not otherwise be accepted: rice dust, grain dust, water dust, cloth dust, and wind dust. If that is so, how should one proceed?
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If wind blows dust, grass, leaves, or food [onto one's person], one must receive it all again.

The answer to this is that this rule exists because it is easy to find a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to handle food); therefore, one must receive it again. However, in places where a *kappiya-kāraka* is difficult to find, not receiving it is permitted.
The reason for knowing this is stated in the seventeenth fascicle of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*: "When a bhikṣu wishes to eat, he should receive [the food] from a *kappiya-kāraka*. If..."
If there is no *kappiya-kāraka* (one who makes things permissible), one should wash one's hands to make them clean and then take the food oneself. The same applies to ice and hail.

Furthermore, the *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra* (Jianlun), fascicle 16, states: "If the dust particles are large, they may be removed; eating [the food] then does not constitute an offense. If the dust particles are fine and cannot be removed, [one may eat it]."

One should have another person carry [the provisions] across. However, due to the cause of a sudden illness, or for the purpose of using urine, excrement, ash, or earth, one may take them oneself and consume them.

Furthermore, in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, chapter fifty-six, the Buddha said: "From this day forward, I permit you to carry food and hide it so that others do not see it. When eating, you should go out onto the path and take a handful;
you may eat it without having formally received it (parigṛhīta), because you are passing through a vast wilderness. Next, regarding the mind of action (*karmacitta*), it is essential...
One must fully observe the ritual procedures. Holding the vessel, lift it above the ground; with mind and object in accord, receive it with clean hands held upward.

As for the statement in the subsequent text that "receiving erroneously does not constitute [the rite]," this is because there is no [proper] mental intention. However, the mind may still be subject to error regarding the specific or general objects, such as the medicinal substances and so forth.

This can be understood through reflection. Furthermore, within this text, there are ten types of formal acceptance (*pratigraha*) regarding food. The first nine are based on prohibitions, while the last one concerns permissions. Regarding acceptance accomplished by a single thought:
as the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states, "There were elder bhikṣus whose vision was failing. The Buddha said: 'They should accept grass or leaves and spread them out;
pressing the edge with their hands, they should place the food upon them. This is also called acceptance. There is also the "white [announcement]" (*śukla-uddeśa*).
A certain person despised a bhikṣu and was unwilling to hand the food to him directly; instead, he placed the food on the ground before the bhikṣu and told him to take it himself.

The Buddha said, "It is also permitted to accept food by taking it according to that person's instruction. In the eighth fascicle of the *Mātṛkā-sūtra*, there is an account of a man in a certain country who held ascetics in contempt;
he placed food on the ground rather than passing it through his hands. A bhikṣu reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "Although it was not received by hand, [it is still valid]."
"The intention to give has already been completed; you may take this food. (Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya 56). There was a horse-keeper who had faith in the Buddha-Dharma.
He prepared various kinds of food and drink and placed them before the Saṃgha. This man heard that a fire had broken out in the stable. He said, "Venerable sirs, please eat yourselves.
We have an urgent matter. Having left the food behind, he departed. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha. The Buddha said, "If one has faith in the Buddha..."
If the donor gives with a single-minded intention and then departs, one should eat. Furthermore, the *Vinayavibhaṅga* states that there are three ways for food to reach [the recipient]:
first, reaching the side of the body (*kāyapārśva*), which refers to placing the food into the hand of a bhikṣu; this is called reaching the side of the body.

Second, reaching the side of the object (*vastupārśva*), which refers to the gift being placed within the grasp of the food, or being carried such that the bhikṣu takes it himself; when the bhikṣu’s hand reaches the side of the food, he takes the food himself.

"Reaching the edge of the food" refers to three cases: reaching the edge of the vessel, the vessel being used to hold the food and presented to the bhikṣu, and the bhikṣu’s hand not reaching the edge of the food but merely grasping the vessel—this is called "reaching the edge of the vessel.
(Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya, Chapter 16). This clarifies the rules for receiving [food]. First, the headings are listed:
namely, receiving from atop a tree, from atop a well, from atop a house, from a clean kitchen, from a vessel, from what is not a vessel, and from a bed, boat, or vehicle.
Mental reflection: Receiving provisions for the journey. Next, the explanation according to the chapters. Regarding "on food":
if, while a bhikṣu is eating, wind blows dust that settles on the grass beneath the bowl but does not settle on the food, he may eat; the grass and leaves must be received [as a formal act].
If it settles on the grass and leaves as well as the food, everything must be received again. If dust settles [from] a galloping ox or the like, it is the same. If an animal shakes its body...
When dust comes, if one perceives it with intention, it is called "receiving. This applies to dust from birds, or when a woman walks by and her trailing garment drags up dust from the ground;
it is the same for dust from the earth. When a pure person walks through grass or leaves, one should tell them to set them aside; the same applies to other things as well.
If a fruit being carried falls onto the grass and moves away immediately, it is not considered "received. If it stops for even a brief moment, it is considered "received.
During a great assembly when a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person) is difficult to find, a bhikṣu may go to the edge of the vegetable heap and receive salt, flour, or rice;

this is likewise the case. If the *kappiya-kāraka* lifts [the food] but does not let it leave the ground, it is considered "received," though it is not in accordance with proper decorum (*airyāpathika*) for a bhikṣu.
One should say to the *kappiya-kāraka*: "Lift it off the ground and give it to me. If the *kappiya-kāraka* is too small to lift it, one should say:

"Divide it into portions and give them to me one by one. The same applies when receiving soup, cakes, and so forth. When receiving a jar of clarified butter (*sarpis*), if the rope is touching the ground, one should say:
"Lift it up by this rope. If the *kappiya-kāraka* is too small to lift it, one should instruct him to gradually reduce the weight.
"Grant me all such things as these. If one cannot receive [food] from a hot cauldron or pot, one should place two pieces of wood crosswise on the ground;
the bhikṣu should step upon them and say, 'I accept. This is called receiving food from above. Regarding 'from a tree':
if a lay attendant (*kappiya-kāraka*) eats fruit while on a tree, the bhikṣu says, 'Give me fruit. The lay attendant then shakes the tree so that the fruit falls onto the bhikṣu."
That which is placed into the *pātra* of the *bhikṣu* is termed "received," though it does not constitute proper decorum (*airyāpathika*).
If, when placing fruit with the hands or feet, the fruit touches the branches or leaves, the *bhikṣu* should again form the thought, "I receive, I receive"; this is termed "received.

When a lay attendant (*kappiyakāraka*) is eating parched grain or beans and the *bhikṣu* wishes to have some, he should immediately ask for it, saying: "Give me the parched grain and beans," [to which] the lay attendant...

He does not give it. The bhikṣu instructs the attendant (kappiyakāraka) to write [the name] with his hand and place it inside his robe-sack; when he says, "I have received, I have received," it is called "received.
However, this is not proper decorum. This is what is meant by "from a tree. Regarding "from a well":

if a bhikṣu stays at a residence where the well water is full and there is no attendant, and the bhikṣu himself draws water from the well wishing to eat food from within the well, the attendant should take the food and drink and place it in one [vessel].
Within the vessel, tie it at the bottom with a cord. At the time of eating, the bhikṣu at the bottom of the well should say to the attendant (kappiya-kāraka):

"Lower the cord; grasp it with your hand. If there are living plants or grass growing along the sides of the well, he should instruct [the attendant] to avoid them. Once it has reached the bottom of the well—
A bhikṣu should pull the rope with one hand and hold it with the other, saying, "I receive, I receive.

This is called receiving. If the well water is clear, he may take it for himself to drink. If it is turbid, he should speak to a *kappiyakāraka* (a lay attendant), saying: "Take a new, clean jar, tie a rope to it, and lower it into the water," as described above.
This refers to [water from] a well. Regarding [water] on a roof: if there is no *kappiyakāraka*, the bhikṣu should... [admonish].

Regarding receiving food from one’s own roof: if it is difficult to descend, one who is eating on the roof should place the food into a vessel, have a monk above lower down a long pole with a hook (*ku*), and instruct a lay attendant (*kappiyakāraka*) to place it upon that hook, saying, "I receive; I receive. This is called "receiving from below.

The same applies to using a rope. This is called "receiving from atop a roof. Other instances should be understood by analogy; they cannot be detailed exhaustively here. Next is "loss of the formal act of receiving" (*parihāra*).

If not, there are three ways in which the formal acceptance (*paribhoga*) is lost: first, loss by natural course (*svarasena*), which refers to when the time for receiving food has passed after midday, whereby the remainder is naturally lost;

second, transgression of the limit (*sīmātikrama*), as in the case of medicines to be taken for life, which, although they have no fixed limit, are nonetheless restricted by the condition of being free from illness.

First, it is lost because the formal undertaking (*samādāna*) is not maintained. Second, it is lost through contact with conditions (*pratyaya*), such as when, after having accepted food, a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person who makes things allowable) touches it; thus, the method of acceptance (*paribhoga-dharma*) is immediately lost.
According to the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*, even for one who does not abide in their own nature (*svabhāva*), contact-food (*sparśāhāra*) is still established.

One who does not abide in their own nature refers to those subject to the thirteen *antarāyika-dharmas* (obstructive factors), those who have been suspended (*ukkhittaka*), those who have been expelled (*pabbājita*), those who should be expelled, and those who are undergoing penance (*parivāsika*). Third, it is lost through the transformation of raw into cooked.
This can be understood.
Next, the oral transmission (*mukhāgama*) is explained. There is no textual record for this section, but it must exist according to the underlying principle.

Since medicines such as those taken at improper times (*akāla-bhaiṣajya*) are permitted to be consumed over a period of time, how could they be maintained for long if they were not prepared according to the Dharma? Thus, in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, fascicle 26, when Upāli questioned the Buddha:
Regarding the three types of medicine—divided medicine, seven-day medicine, and lifetime medicine—is it permissible to keep them overnight, to hold them with the hand, or to receive them orally?

The Buddha said: "It is not permissible. Is it permissible to receive these three types of medicine with the hand or to receive them orally when one is not ill? The Buddha said: "It is not permissible."

"If one is ill, may one take [the medicine]? The Buddha said, "One may. By this it is proven that for the sake of performing the *khou-fa* (oral authorization), one must inquire about purity and illness.

If one were to receive [medicine] directly with the hands, would one not inquire about illness? Furthermore, the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states regarding the seven-day medicinal precept that it is also received orally;
the text is cited above. Since the meaning of the text is thus established, we know there is oral authorization (*khou-shou*). To explain this oral authorization, there are four [points].
The Analysis of the Gates. First, the object of the precept being received; second, the substance of the medicine received; third, the mental action of the receiver;

fourth, whether it is lost after having been received. Regarding the first gate, the object: one should understand that this refers to the path of the monastic and not the worldly path, and includes distinctions such as those who possess the requisite [robes] and those who do not, as well as the physical retribution [of gender].
Next, to clarify the medicine: although there are four types of medicine, regarding the oral dharma, it is restricted to the lower three.

Regarding medicine: once the three types of medicine have been administered, the ritual of "adding the mouth" (*mukha-dhāraṇa*) is performed. The substance of the medicine must be pure and free from faults;
that is to say, it must not involve the two internal faults of self-cooking or improper contact, nor must there be the fault of having been kept for even a brief moment after receiving it.

Furthermore, if the substance has undergone transformation, the reception is not valid. Question: Why is the ritual of adding the mouth not applied to *kālika-bhaiṣajya* (medicines to be taken at specific times)? Answer: Because *kālika-bhaiṣajya* is permitted only during the designated time.
When taking medicine during the proper time (*kāla*), it is "near" and thus not lost; since receiving it with the hand is already not lost, there is no need to guard against it with the mouth.

However, because medicines such as those taken outside the proper time (*vikāla*) are permitted for long durations, one adds the verbal reception (*vāc-ādāna*) to prolong the hand-reception (*hasta-ādāna*). Next, the mental action (*manas-karman*) is explained.

There are instances of intentional deviation and error. Regarding intentional deviation (*vyatikrama*): this refers to the designation of a name for a ritual procedure; it must be performed intentionally for it to be accomplished.
Within the category of similar substances, deviation is also generally permissible. As for error (*viparyāsa*), this refers to mistakenly forming a different substance rather than the intended one;

one should understand this according to its underlying meaning. Regarding the "action" (*karma*): the application of mantras to the substances varies according to their specific distinctions. The requisite conditions are as follows...

No; it can be understood through reflection. Regarding the subsequent point on "losing the formal acceptance" (*pratigraha*): if one is touched by a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to handle requisites), the formal acceptance is immediately lost.

Therefore, the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Once touched, one must accept [the object] again. Thus, we know that the acceptance is lost. Question: Since the acceptance is already lost by the touch, what is the purpose of using the mouth?

Answer: The mouth-guard prevents what occurs spontaneously (*svarasa*), but it does not prevent what arises from encountering conditions (*pratyaya*). Because the force of encountering conditions is strong, it does not prevent them.

Furthermore, since there is no spontaneous occurrence regarding food taken at the proper time (*kālabhojana*), the ritual of the mouth-guard (*mukha-bandhana*) is not applied; this clearly shows that the guard prevents the spontaneous, but does not prevent what arises from conditions.
Moreover, it is explained that encountering conditions involves no fault, and thus the ritual of the mouth-guard does not prevent them.

Next, the distinctions are clarified through a fivefold analysis: namely, the object (*viṣaya*), the medicine (*bhaiṣajya*), prevention (*pratiṣedha*), arising (*utpāda*), and strength (*balābala*). Regarding the "object":

the hand belongs to a different category (*vijātīya*) and does not apply to its own kind (*sajātīya*), because within its own kind, factors such as prior contact and conditions are present. The mouth, however, applies only to its own kind.

It does not apply to different categories (*vijātīya*), because it is governed by the Dharma; thus, a different category is not established. Furthermore, the mouth possesses two objects—namely, the same category and the different category—whereas the hand has only one object, which is exclusively the different category.

Next, regarding the medicinal substance (*bhaiṣajya*): medicines may be pure or impure; receiving them with the hand is always valid, whereas receiving them orally for the purpose of keeping them is permitted only when they are pure.
Thus, it is restricted solely to the pure, just as in the case of the *kaṭhina* robe, which must be brought on that very day to be in accordance with the Dharma.

Furthermore, regarding the single category of *kālika-bhaiṣajya* (medicines for the day), it may be received only by the hand and not by the mouth; the remaining three types of medicine may be received by both hand and mouth. Next, concerning the prevention [of transgressions]:

the hand prevents only two—namely, receiving what is impure (*asat-sparśa*) and losing [the substance] immediately thereafter—but it does not prevent the two-night storage or taking at an improper time (*akāla*).

As for the two types of boiling (*dvipākya*), these are likewise not countered by this [method], because receiving with the hand applies only to those two cases and is thus limited; whereas the rule for the mouth applies universally.

Regarding the three lower medicinal substances: as for the statement "in contrast to the three," they also prevent two offenses regarding the improper time (*akāla*), namely, the offense of not having received [the substance] and the offense of improper contact (*duṣṭa-sparśana*).
This prevention occurs spontaneously; it is not like the prevention regarding manual receipt, which involves first not receiving [the substance] and then improper contact.

This principle applies to the two lower medicinal substances, but because they last only until the appearance of dawn, there is no offense of "two nights" (*dvi-rātra*). Furthermore, boiling [the substances] is also not a case of "contrasting exclusion," and therefore it does not prevent [these offenses].
Likewise, for seven days one guards against four [offenses]. Because it involves an overnight stay, two additional nights are added;

throughout one’s life, the principle is the same, as one also guards against four offenses, or guards against two "boiling" offenses, as will be clarified below. Next, regarding those produced [by formal acceptance]: for *kālika* (timely) medicine, it is received solely by hand;

when the hand is correctly applied, the meaning of "residual" (*vighasa*) also includes "defiled contact" (*duṣṭa-sparśa*). This is because the formal acceptance (*paribhoga-vidhi*) is lost automatically, thereby resulting in defiled contact. This exceeds the three [categories] produced below.
Regarding medicines: those produced from the mouth are indeed auspicious when taken at improper times (*akāla*), for long durations, or without a specific cause.

Thus it is said that taking them at an improper time is a transgression of the improper time; taking them after seven days is a transgression of the seven-day limit; and taking them for the duration of one's life is likewise [regulated]. Without a cause, there is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

This also implicitly clarifies the faults of [medicines] that have passed the night, leftovers, and those touched by impurity. Although these are offenses even after the appearance of the dawn light (*aruṇodaya*), there are further remaining offenses beyond that; however, none of these arise from the mouth.

It arises from the Dharma. Next, regarding the relative strength [of the faculties]: because it possesses two meanings, the hand is stronger than the mouth. First, if one does not receive with the hand, it is not appropriate to apply the mouth;
second, receiving with the hand is the fundamental basis. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that receiving with the mouth also possesses two meanings.

It is called "strong" because, first, if there is no formal verbal procedure (*karmavācanā*), it is received by extending the hand; if the time passes, it is lost, and it cannot be maintained for a long duration.
Second, receiving [the precepts] verbally is established to prevent excess. Thus, these two modes of reception are mutually strong or weak. The subsequent explanation of the text will clarify this.
In the summary verse, the four lines are the same as before.
Next, the precept against soliciting delicious food: It is the principle of renunciation that one should abandon all exquisite delicacies.

To crave fine food disturbs the mind and increases greed. This offense is established through four conditions: first, it must be a delicious food; second, it must be for oneself; third, there must be no valid cause or condition; and fourth, the act of eating constitutes the offense.
The four phrases of this full precept are: first, the four kinds of delicious foods; second, the person who commits the offense; third, "in this manner," and so forth.

"Being without illness. Fourth, regarding seeking for oneself and the resulting offense: the commentary on the text is clear. Since the meaning of a *bhikṣuṇī* begging [for food] is rare, the offense is censurable.
This *duṣkṛta* constitutes an offense of preliminary preparation (*prayoga*). The eighth fascicle of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"If one seeks for a sick *bhikṣu*, or seeks from the home of a relative, or seeks from the home of an acquaintance, there is no offense."

Next is the precept regarding giving food to non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Those of heterodox learning are coarse and negligent; they do not recognize the debt of gratitude [for what they receive]. Even when they obtain food and drink, they instead give rise to slander.
Furthermore, these perverse people would unhesitatingly offer food themselves, claiming that [the recipient] is a superior field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) while the bhikṣu is inferior.
Thus, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states regarding laypeople: "If even the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, still provide offerings to non-Buddhists, why should we not do so?"
Regarding service [to others], there are six distinct conditions. First is the householder non-Buddhist (*tīrthika*). An ancient commentary states that this refers to the renunciant non-Buddhist;

this excludes the householder non-Buddhist layperson because their offense is minor. The reason for this is that while the name "renunciant" is the same for both, it is difficult to distinguish between the genuine and the false, which may give rise to delusion and inversion;
therefore, the rule is established as a grave offense. As for the householder layperson, they occupy the status of both the secular and the monastic.

[The opponent says: "This is distinct; it does not give rise to confusion among people, and therefore the offense is minor. This explanation is incorrect. Examining the meaning of the text, it refers exclusively to laypeople; thus it says:
"At that time, among the crowd of beggars, there was a naked ascetic (nirgrantha), and the daughter of the householder was of upright countenance."
Furthermore, regarding the subsequent passage concerning the "cloud" (or "assembly"): at that time, there was a brahmin within that assembly.

Since he was among a gathering of beggars, he certainly could not have been an ordained monastic. For this reason, the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* states: "male non-Buddhists (*tīrthika-puruṣa*) and female non-Buddhists (*tīrthikī-strī*).
From this, it is known that he was exclusively a layperson. However, the *Vibhaṅga* (Extensive Commentary) states: "The *pāśupata-ājīvaka* was in this assembly."
Regarding the phrase "those who have gone forth" (pravrajita): by this standard, it would generally include both monastics and non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*).

However, since this specific term is used as a heading, and neither in the *Nidāna* (Explanatory Introduction) nor in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* (Fundamental Code of Precepts) is there any instance where it does not refer to this [monastic] sense, it is proven that this refers specifically to those who have gone forth.

If one applies this principle to distinguish the case of nuns (*bhikṣuṇī*), this refers exclusively to lay nuns; whereas for the *saṃgha*, it includes both those who have gone forth and lay white-robed followers (*avadātavasana*).
The *Jì* (祇) [Vinaya] in thirty-eight fascicles also states this. It says that it applies to lay householders as well as non-Buddhist renunciants (*tīrthika*).

Furthermore, according to another interpretation based on the text of the *Guǎngshì* (廣解), it also extends to Buddhist renunciants. Thus, the eighth fascicle of the *Shanmùlùpíduólúnfǎshìyìchāo* (善見律毘婆沙) states:

"If one gives with one's own hand, it is a *pāyattika* offense for all ninety-five kinds of followers of heterodox views to eat; regardless of whether they are householders or renunciants, whether they are naked or clothed, it is all a *pāyattika*."
According to this principle, all non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) commit an offense, regardless of whether they are lay or ordained nuns.
If one relies on the literal text, however, it refers only to ordained non-Buddhists and laypeople; for this reason, the conditions differ.

It may also be interpreted more broadly to include lay non-Buddhists, as they likewise commit an offense with laypeople; thus, the conditions differ in two respects. Third, regarding those who are not kin: this excludes parents.

The fourth [condition] is that food is given while clothing is excluded; giving clothing constitutes a minor offense (*dukkaṭa*). The fifth is giving with one's own hand, excluding the case of placing it on the ground and sending someone else to take it.

The sixth is that the act of receiving constitutes an immediate offense. Regarding the fact that there was no censure during the circumstances [of the rule], it was because there was no fault in the inanimate object.

In the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, the Buddha likewise censured [the donor] in various ways. The four phrases of the full precept are: first, the person; second, male or female non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*); third, giving food with one's own hand; and fourth, the formal determination of the offense (*sāpattika*).
The explanation is as follows. For a *bhikṣuṇī*, the offense is the same, though the conditions differ.

First, regarding the precept against visiting other households before or after a meal once an invitation has been accepted: having accepted another’s invitation, one must arrive at the appointed time.

To go elsewhere on one’s own initiative and fail to attend punctually is a violation. Furthermore, if the assembly of monks is not yet complete, food must not be served; to cause such delay is a fault.
O Great Assembly: eating until full is not permitted, for it causes distress to others and is not a minor matter. Therefore, the Sage established this rule. There are five specific conditions:

first, having previously accepted an invitation; second, not being under the supervision of a donor; third, going to the home of a layperson; fourth, except when there is a special cause; and fifth, the offense is committed upon entering the gate.
The *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* has three parts. First, the brief summary of the preceding meal. Second, the detailed explanation of the two categories:

that which is restricted (*niyama*) and that which is permitted (*anujñā*). Regarding the permitted, there are four: first, permission for the assignment of robes; second, permission during times of illness; third, [permission regarding] making robes.

Fourth, the giving of robes. Alternatively, one may add the time for giving robes to make five; this is established by opening and closing [the categories] as clarified in the section on separate groups (*pṛthaggaṇa*).
Regarding the three full precepts, there are five phrases: first, a bhikṣu has previously accepted an invitation from another; second, he visits other households before or after the meal.
