Third, that which does not pertain to formal authorization (*anujñā*). Fourth, excluding the occasions for exemption. Fifth, the determination of the offense. Regarding "at other times," [the text] recites the fourth phrase from above.

In the commentary, the section beginning with "as for the other bhikṣus" fully explains the third point. As for the phrase "pertaining to authorization," one who requires authorization must do so within the boundary (*sīmā*), with those who have accepted the invitation together;
it is not permitted otherwise or at improper times. They must inform one another in succession. Thus, the *Mātṛkā-sūtra*, fascicle seven, states:
If there is no donor, one may enter a village to beg for alms without informing the monk sitting beside one; there is no fault in this.

Second, one cannot give [an article] to others in order to cultivate a good reputation. *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, chapter eight: Upāli asks regarding long-term extra robes (*atireka-cīvara*):

"To what kind of person should one perform the ritual of purification (*śuddhi*)? The Buddha says: "One should perform the ritual of purification before the five groups of practitioners, beginning with the bhikṣus. He asks again:

"What is the distance for being separated [from the robe], such that one may perform the ritual of purification from afar? The Buddha says: "Up to three *yojanas*, provided that one knows whether they are alive or dead. He asks again regarding śrāmaṇeras: [The same applies].

[Question: Regarding the purification (*viśuddhi*) performed at the boundary: how does a *śrāmaṇera* undergo full ordination (*upasampadā*)? [The Buddha] said: "One should perform the purification by calling upon the name of a monk who has no [remaining] year [of seniority].

Again, [the questioner] asked: "What if he dies? [The Buddha] said: "He may remain [in that state] for ten days; one should then perform the purification before another person of knowledge. [The questioner] asked:

"In this context, the 'purification master' (*viśuddhi-pradhāna*) lists the five groups of practitioners (*pañca-nikāya*). I do not yet know whether these five groups may act as proxies for one another. [The answer: To discuss their mutual application...
[The object] is transferred; it is not handed over to another person, so as not to give rise to censure or fault. Both parties thus obtain [the merit].

Although this principle exists, when considering the great underlying truth, it is not as good as having two or three people present in the assembly who act for themselves as a true purification. It is necessary that those of the same class hand over the object; it is not like a successive transfer.
Furthermore, there is no reciprocal formal procedure between monks and nuns. Such being the case, this is the truth.
Regarding the "actual pure precepts" (*bhūta-śīla-viśuddhi*), how are their five groups enumerated? For this reason, it is known that the two types of purity apply to all five.
This explanation indicates that the common precepts (*sādhāraṇa-śīla*) are raised collectively for the five groups. According to the principle of reality, they must necessarily be of the same class.

Furthermore, the following two purities are explained to manifest the presence of the *kappiya-kāraka* (one who makes things allowable). As for the root text’s general mention of the five groups, these two are those capable of acting as the *kappiya-kāraka*, namely the *bhikkhu*.

Because the group of five, including the Buddha, is subsumed under the internal teaching [of the monastic community], there are three types of persons who act as the "makers of purification" (kāraka):

first, if it is a "successive purification" (paramparā-pariśuddhi), each person acts in relation to their own kind; second, if it is a "true purification" (bhūta-pariśuddhi), one acts in relation to the donor;

third, regarding the objects, this refers to robes, medicine, bowls, and the sixteen types of utensils used by nuns, as well as precious items—these are all suitable for a "purifier" (pariśuddhi-pradhāna), and not for the group of five. Therefore, they are excluded from the definition here.

This is explained separately. However, ancient masters have said that for all heavy items, such as fine silks, damasks, brocades, and the like, it is unnecessary to perform the ritual of "purifying" (śuddhi).
This interpretation is incorrect. Having examined various texts, I find no provision for such an exception.

If one were to claim that heavy objects do not require purification, then consider the sixteen types of medicinal herbs used by the herders—would these be considered light? Regarding their measurement, it should not differ from what has been clarified above. Next, concerning...
Regarding the Dharma: first is the method for requesting a donor. For a major [offering], one must maintain dignified decorum (*īryāpatha*) before formally stating the request;

for a minor [offering], one may request directly without such decorum. As for the discourse on the method of purifying through transfer (*viśuddhi*), it should be understood as usual regarding the objects and the recipients.
However, when performing the method of mutual purification, one must not face the donor directly. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Sects 19) states: "One must not face them directly."
Regarding the declaration of pure giving (*śuddhaka-dāna*): one should declare the pure gift in the presence of another person. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, chapter sixteen, states:

"There was a bhikṣu who performed a formal declaration of purity in the presence [of others], gave a robe to another, and then refused to take it back. A dispute immediately arose. This matter was reported to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:"
One should not give it in their presence. Furthermore, if a bhikṣu has accepted another’s robe and then refuses to return it, the Buddha said:
"This gift is not called true; it was given for the sake of pure causes and conditions. At that time, the bhikṣu should immediately go back and demand it.
If he obtains it, that is well. If he does not obtain it, he should take it by force. He should be instructed to perform a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense) confession.

This is the *pratideśanīya-dharma* (the method of confession before another). Other texts also contain the *manasikāra-dharma* (the method of mental recollection). Thus, the ninth fascicle of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:

"There were certain bhikṣus who, being alone in their quarters, possessed an extra robe (*atireka-cīvara*) but did not know how to perform the ritual of *viśuddhi-dāna* (purification by gift). They reported this matter to the Buddha."

The Buddha said: "One should perform the ritual of 'purification by distant indication. One should bare the right shoulder, remove one's leather sandals, kneel with the right knee on the ground, hold up the robe, and with both mind and speech declare:
'I hereby purify this long robe as a gift; may so-and-so receive and use it. This shall continue until the eleventh day."

Furthermore, one should follow the procedure as previously described. Next, regarding whether the *śuddhi-dharma* (the rite of purification) is lost: according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, it is lost simply by being three *yojanas* away;
thus, one loses the ten [purifications]. The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states: "If one leaves the country, abandons the path, is expelled, or dies, one completely loses the *śuddhi-dharma*.

Below this is the commentary on the text, which contains four parts: first, the introduction; second, the enumeration of items, namely the entrustment of taking and giving; third, the necessity of inquiry; and fourth, the naming.

The true method of transference involves not handing over the object to the recipient; this is called "successive transference" (*kṣepa-kṣepa*). All such acts are forms of giving that sever greed and are termed "pure giving.

This constitutes the third distinction in interpretation. The fourth is the detailed analysis of the middle and lower grades. Next, the passage beginning with "If a bhikṣu... explains the two phrases concerning the third and fourth [grades].
Next is the precept concerning white three-robed garments. Generally, robes should be dyed with a dull color (kāsāya) and worn as monastic attire;

furthermore, this can internally dispel greedy sentiments and externally increase faith and respect. Now, to wear white robes destroys both the internal and external [virtues], and the fault is not slight.

Therefore, the Sage established this regulation. The specific conditions consist of four factors: first, it must be the three robes; second, they must be one's own property; third, they must be white; fourth, they must be worn.
[This constitutes] an offense. The *Śīla-mūla* (Precept Text) has three points: first, the person; second, the ritual procedure for dyeing [the robe] to change its color; third, from "If a bhikṣu...

onwards, it explains that because the color was not changed, one incurs an offense for violating the teaching. This is explained in detail in the commentary. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, chapter nine, states:

"If one obtains a new robe, one should mark it with three kinds of colors. If one does not mark it, then for every wearing of it, there is a *pāyattika* offense; if one does not wear it, then for every night it remains overnight, there is a *pāyattika* offense. [This is a minor offense.]
Regarding "heavy robes not having been purified": this refers to the method of *tīṭhaka-pariśuddhi* (spot-purification). According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, section eighteen:
if one obtains a new *saṃghāṭī* robe that is blue, black, or madder-colored, or even a *niṣīdana* (sitting mat) for covering sores, and does not perform the purification, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
When performing the purification, it must be neither too large nor too small; the maximum size is four finger-widths, and the minimum is like a pea. If...
Take *harītakī*, *bibhītaka*, and *āmalaka*. Grind them on an iron surface and extract the juice to make an application (*añjana*). This purification must not be performed simultaneously;
one may perform it once, three times, five times, seven times, or nine times, but not more. Perform the purification in the shape of a flower.

If mud falls upon a dyed woolen cloth, or if a crow or a bird with muddy feet steps upon it, it is then considered purified. If one obtains many small fragments [of these fruits], [they may also be used].

Regarding items that are to be patched in one place: if they are patched in a single location, perform the purification (*parikamma*) once for that spot. If they are patched individually in separate places, perform the purification for each one.
For all robes, even down to new patches or seams, the folding (*saṃvidhāna*) must also be purified.
Next is the precept against intentionally killing animals. According to the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, it was established for three reasons:

first, out of compassion; second, to sever sinful evil; and third, to foster respectful faith. It possesses five specific conditions, which should be understood by analogy with what precedes. Regarding the four clauses that complete this precept: first, the person;
second, intentional killing—encompassing both one's own and others' actions; third, the object killed; and fourth, the formal determination of the offense. [This concludes the] explanation.

In the middle [section], the first three are explained individually, while the second and fourth are explained together. Within the combined section, first nineteen chapters are listed; next, from "acts in this manner" onwards, the offenses are defined.

Next is the precept regarding drinking water containing insects. The intent for its establishment and the requisite conditions are all identical to those above; whereas the previous [precept] was based on external application, this one concerns—
For internal use. This may be understood through the *Pūrṇa-śīla* and the *Śāstra*. In the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, chapter eighteen, it states:
"Once a bhikṣu has received full ordination (*upasampadā*), he must possess a water-strainer (*parisrāvaṇa*). When performing ritual ablutions or traveling, he should carry a water-strainer.

If he does not have one, he should at least hold onto a corner of his upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*) while examining the water. When observing the water, he must not use the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), nor [should he rely on other such means]."
One should have a person with impaired vision examine it, down to the point where they can see the fine lines on the palm of the hand; such a person may be employed to inspect the water.
When examining it, one must not be weary or dismissive, but should look with a sincere mind. It should not be too fast, nor should it be too long;

it should take about the time for a large elephant to turn around, or the time for a bamboo cart to complete a circuit. If there are no insects, it may be used; if there are insects, it should be strained.

Regarding the use of water: according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*, fascicle eight, there was an infinite and immeasurable amount of millet in a vessel. Having seen this, [the monks] ceased eating for two or three days.
The Buddha commanded them to eat it. Generally, the regulation concerning water containing insects refers only to what is visible to the naked eye and what is caught by a water-strainer.

Next is the precept against intentionally vexing other bhikṣus. Now, one who has left the household life should protect the feelings of others; yet, by means of the six matters such as one's age and so forth, one may vex another bhikṣu.
This is not merely a matter of physical provocation; how deep is the gravity of the offense? It prevents one from honoring the Path.

An offense is established through five conditions: first, the person must be a *mahābhikṣu*; second, one must harbor the intention to cause vexation; third, one must engage in any of the six matters; fourth, the matter must be made manifest; and fifth, the other person must understand it.

[The Buddha] showed: fourth, the words must be clearly understood; fifth, the object before one must be known or heard. If one merely causes it to be heard or known, one commits the offense; it does not depend on whether it causes distress or not.
The root text of the precept says, "even for a short time, [if they] are unhappy. This refers to the intention of the one who causes distress;

it does not mean that the offense is committed only when the person before one actually becomes unhappy. The root text has three points: first, the person; second, intentionally causing distress to another; third, the formal conclusion of the offense. [This is the] explanation.

The second section of the middle commentary has two parts: first, a listing of the six chapters, including the year of birth and so forth; second, a sequential citation of these chapters followed by their explanation.
Next, from "If a bhikṣu... onwards, the section explaining the formulation of the offense (*āpatti*) opens up the six matters within it, sequentially clarifying the preceding five.
"All say that the matter is indeed so" means that the person before one actually has this [fault], yet one forms a sincere mind with the intention of benefiting them;
however, there may still be no opening [to the teaching]. The sixth sentence states:

"If that person is by nature coarse and does not understand speech," meaning that when the questioner speaks such words as "you have troubled me," it is made clear that "it is not as you say; I have not caused you distress," or it is said in jest.
Regarding "smiling" and so forth: this generally opens up the preceding six [precepts].
Next is the precept against concealing gross offenses. It is the principle of those who have left the household life that they should mutually confess their faults;

yet now, by concealing another’s offense, one causes the mind to become impure and further allows the other person’s commission of sin to spread and proliferate. Since this is of no benefit to either party, it was therefore strictly prohibited by the Noble One. This is a distinct [offense].

The conditions are sevenfold: first, being a *mahābhikṣu*; second, having committed a gross offense, namely a *pārājika* or a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; third, knowing that it is a gross offense; fourth, forming the intention to conceal it; fifth, not confessing it;

sixth, the absence of a cause or condition—referring to the passage below stating there is no person toward whom one may speak, as well as the presence of the two difficulties of life or *brahmacarya*;
and seventh, the appearance of the dawn. The three phrases for the completion of the offense can be understood accordingly. Regarding the explanation, the first two points are as stated in the text.
That bhikṣu explains the third phrase below. There are four parts in the text: first, the offense incurred by concealing a major bhikṣu;

second, the two specific cases of self-concealment, where seven offenses are all *duṣkṛta*; third, concealing other members of the assembly; fourth, the four permutations regarding the perception of the object.
Regarding the perception of a grave offense as not grave: this refers to being deluded toward what is not an offense, and thus it is included in the exemption.

Next is the reduction of the age for receiving full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*). When one has reached twenty years of age, their will and physical capacity are established; they are capable of maintaining the precepts and enduring various hardships.

To grant ordination to one who has not yet reached this age causes harm to the Path and is not a minor matter; it lacks the conditions for spiritual progress. Therefore, the Noble One’s regulation was established.

There are five specific conditions [for such a case]: first, the year is not yet complete; second, one knows the year is not yet complete; third, one grants the full ordination; fourth, one acts as the preceptor (*upādhyāya*); fifth, [the candidate]...
The *karmavācanā* concludes. There are four sections in the text: first, the ordination of one whose age was not yet full; second, when the young boys went down to seek food and were discovered;
third, the Tathāgata’s inquiry; and fourth, the prohibition against ordaining them. Within this precept, there is no mention of a formal censure (*ākrośa*).

This is because prior to this point, the limit on years had not been established, and thus there was no fault of the mind; for this reason, there is no censure. This constitutes the third section of the complete precept.

The phrases are as follows: first, the period of years for which one should receive [ordination] and the limits thereof; second, the person who commits the offense; third, from "knowing the age" onwards, it clarifies the formation of the offense through transgression.
Question: Why is it said that this is "reprehensible and invalid"? Answer: Since one knows the age is not yet fulfilled, it is improper to undergo [ordination].

To laboriously perform the ritual for the Saṃgha while teaching such ignorance is extremely grave; therefore, it is called "reprehensible and invalid. In the commentary, the first phrase is abbreviated and not [further explained].
Explanation: The second offender may be understood. Regarding the phrase "the person receiving the precepts," the following explains the sentence concerning the determination of the offense.

This section contains two parts: first, determining whether an offense is committed based on the four mental states; second, from "That bhikṣu... onwards, clarifying the boundaries of light and heavy offenses.

In the preceding text there are sixteen phrases; however, regarding the preceptor, there are only four mental states: "knowing" refers to being doubtful or not knowing, while "knowing" means having full awareness. Not...

Regarding "one who is full [of years]": although one has not yet reached the required age, one perceives the physical signs and forms the notion that they are full. Regarding "one who doubts": this refers to being indecisive and uncertain. Regarding "one who knows nothing": this refers to having no knowledge at all.
The Saṃgha, regarding that object, likewise possesses four types of minds.

Now, taking each of the four minds of the Upādhyāya and applying them sequentially to each of the four minds of the Saṃgha—since there are four sets of four, this results in sixteen. Within these four sets of four, the first three pairs of fours [are as follows]: the Upādhyāya...

The first offense constitutes a *thullaccaya* (grave offense). In both the second and fourth cases, there are four [offenses]. For the *upajjhāya* (preceptor), there is no offense. Regarding the four sets of four [cases] for the *saṃgha* (monastic community):

in each, the first three constitute a *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing), while the second and fourth are non-offenses. This is because the *upajjhāya* is the principal authority; if he knows or suspects [the facts], he incurs a *thullaccaya*.

The *saṃgha*, however, is not the principal authority; if they know or suspect, they incur a *dukkaṭa*. Other mental states (*saññā*) may be understood accordingly. Regarding the non-offenses where it is permitted to count the gestational period, intercalary months, and so forth: this refers to the original calculation of the [conception].
At that time, when the secular age was calculated to be complete, doubts arose because the subsequent calculation of days and months was insufficient; therefore, an exception was established.

However, if one’s original reception [of the precepts] occurred when the secular age was also short, this means it was known that the age was not yet full, and thus there is no basis for an exception. Therefore, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*, fascicle nine, states:

A year is reckoned as being fulfilled only when the number of days is complete. As for those who receive the precepts before the period is full, it is because the time spent in the mother’s womb is included.
According to this principle, suppose a person were born on the first day of the twelfth month and received the precepts on the first day of the first month of their twentieth year;
calculating by actual days, they would have been eighteen years old plus two days short, totaling seven hundred and eighteen days.

Day. Not yet twenty years of age. However, regarding the opening of the womb: there are nine months within the womb. Calculating the days of these nine months of gestation, one must reach full completion;
this includes four small months, which amount to a deficiency of four days. By adding those four days, it becomes nine months and four days of actual days, totaling only two hundred and seventy.
Next, regarding the opening of the intercalary month: according to the secular calendar system, nineteen years constitute [one cycle].
One chapter. A chapter contains seven intercalary months. Now, in eighteen years, the intercalary months do not total seven; one obtains only six months and a remainder of nineteen days.
Among these, there are three small months, lacking three days; thus, the actual number of days is one hundred and ninety-six.
Next, regarding the opening of the fourteen-day *poṣadha*: one year is reduced by eighteen days. Calculated over eighteen years, this totals three hundred and twenty-four days.
These three positions have not yet accounted for the double subtraction of intercalary months (*kṣudramāsa*) nor the opening of the fourteen-day *poṣadha*.
Having already obtained seven hundred and ninety days, if one subtracts the count of intercalary months from within that total, there remain seven hundred and sixty.
[If] one has already reached twenty years of age, there remain eighty-four days until the end of the year.

If these days are further extended forward, then the secular age would be incomplete, and the precepts could not be received. Alternatively, at the time of receiving them, the secular age may indeed be incomplete;

however, observing only the outward appearance, one is deluded into the thought that it is complete, and thus seeks to take those preceding days and extend them forward [to satisfy the requirement]. Furthermore...
One should calculate it again. Within the previous seven hundred and ninety days, fourteen days—consisting of small months and intercalary periods—are excluded when reciting the *Poṣadha*.
Venerable sirs, although various reckonings differ, this text is concise yet comprehensive in meaning; do not exceed this.

Next, the precept against instigating disputes: Whenever a dispute has already been settled by the Saṃgha through a process that accords with the Dharma, to willfully instigate it again so as to cause it to flare up further constitutes an offense.

This is because such an act involves harboring malice toward the Saṃgha; therefore, the Noble One established this prohibition. It possesses five specific conditions: first, it concerns one of the four types of disputes;

second, the Saṃgha’s legal procedure has already extinguished it; third, one knows it was extinguished in accordance with the Dharma; fourth, one willfully instigates it; and fifth, there is the verbal expression [of the dispute].

This explains the origin [of the dispute]. The text states: "Those who do not observe well" means that the Saṃgha does not recognize [the truth]; because this is the root cause from which the dispute arises, it is called "not observing well.
"Observing" (觀) refers to investigation (*vipaśyanā*). If one forms such an observation, it does not constitute right observation (*samyag-darśana*). "Not understanding well" means...

It is said that the Sangha does not recognize the right and wrong of the seven medicines; therefore, it is called "not skillfully understanding. "Understanding" (*vijñā*) means to resolve and comprehend.

If one understands in such a manner, it does not constitute correct understanding. Regarding "not skillfully extinguishing," it means the Sangha does not recognize the ritual procedures for eliminating [afflictions] by applying medicine to the illness;
therefore, it is called "not skillfully extinguishing. "Extinguishing" (*nirvāṇa*) means to eradicate and eliminate. If one extinguishes in such a manner, it does not constitute [correct] extinction.
It is being extinguished; therefore, it is said that extinction is not established. These three phrases initiate all [the cases] and complete the four phrases of the precept:
first, the person; second, knowing these four types of disputes; third, having extinguished them according to the Dharma; and fourth, initiating the formal charge of the offense.

This is explained in detail within the commentary. However, the second and third phrases are out of order; the section beginning with "That bhikṣu" explains the fourth phrase. Within this passage, there are five parts.

1. Initiating the four types of disputes constitutes a *pāyattika* offense. 2. Initiating other disputes. *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, Chapter Six: If one initiates a formal proceeding by means of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* when the Saṃgha has not been informed, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one initiates private matters, it is a *duṣkṛta*. 3. Disputes arising from oneself. 4. Other assemblies. 5. Perception regarding the object (*viṣaya-saṃjñā*).
Regarding this perception of the object, if it is applied to the seven medicines and the correspondence between medicine and illness, each should be combined accordingly.
There are four propositions. The phrase "no other two" means that [the latter] is omitted.
Next is the precept regarding traveling with thieves. Thieves injure people and are prohibited by the royal law; to willfully travel with them is to take on the same appearance as a thief.
In this case, one's purity becomes difficult to distinguish, bringing disgrace upon the Buddha-dharma; the resulting ruin is not slight. Therefore, the Sage—

The regulation: The complete set of conditions consists of seven factors: first, it is a thief; second, one knows it is such; third, there is a mutual agreement; fourth, they travel along the same path;

fifth, they do not remain within range of sight or hearing; sixth, there is no valid cause or condition; seventh, upon crossing the boundary, the offense is committed. The full precept has five clauses: first, the person.
1. Knowing it to be a thief; 2. Making a formal agreement; 3. Traveling on the same path; 4. Establishing the offense. The explanation of these points is clear.
Next is the precept concerning the refusal to heed admonitions regarding evil views: Desire is the source of birth and death and the root of obstacles to the Path.

One should not claim that such things are not dharmas that obstruct the Path. However, this bhikṣu, with a perverted mind, speaks erroneously, relying on ambiguous precedents; therefore, the Saṃgha must intervene.
[The Buddha] rebuked him. Thus it is stated in the eighth fascicle of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*. The bhikṣus asked again: "How do you interpret this? He replied:
"I have heard that there were two elders, Viśākha and Sudatta, as well as many upāsakas, all of whom were consumed by the five desires and burned by desire;
yet they have now attained the paths of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, and anāgāmin. Furthermore...
There are those among the various non-Buddhists who, without abandoning their original views, nonetheless go forth into the True Dharma and attain the four fruits of the śramaṇa.
For this reason, I have formed this understanding: that which acts in contradiction to principle is called "evil"; a mind of heterodoxy that penetrates deeply is termed a "view" (*dṛṣṭi*);

and stubbornly adhering to one's position while rejecting the Saṃgha is termed "defiance of admonition. There are four conditions for this [admonition]: first, a mind of heterodoxy regarding what is correctly taught; second, the Saṃgha...

He was admonished in accordance with the Dharma three times, yet he refused and did not comply. After the third *karmavācanā* was completed, the formal disciplinary procedure (*karman*) was carried out as previously described;
there is no need to recount it again. However, Ariṣṭa, with a deceitful mind, spoke falsely in hopes that people would place their trust in him, saying: "This alone is the truth;
all else is false."

Next, regarding the precepts for a monk who has been subject to formal censure (*ukkhepanīya-kamma*) due to adherence to wrong views: there are two points concerning the regulation of the mind. First, as for the necessity of censuring the mind:

since lustful desire contradicts the principle [of the Path] and acts as a calamity to the Way, if one now speaks with a deviant mind claiming that it does not constitute an obstruction, this will result in self-destruction and harm to others, increasing birth and death.
Within the True Dharma, such a person serves no purpose; therefore, the Sangha must formally censure and expel them.
Outside the assembly, he orders the messenger to cause [the offender] to reflect on his transgression and reform his ways to follow the Way. Next, regarding those who do not comply with this intent:

since these bhikṣus have given rise to false slanders against the Buddha and the Saṃgha, the original proclamation states that they must be excluded from transformative guidance. In principle, they should be treated as one with the [excluded] monks; do not associate with them.
Now, if one were to arbitrarily comply with them, it would cause those evil monks to further ruin their own conduct and be unable to cultivate the Path. Such an emotional transgression is grave.

Because it is a minor offense, a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation) is prescribed. There are four distinct conditions for its completion: first, a person who has been censured for holding wrong views;

second, knowing that this is the case; third, being without a valid reason or basis; and fourth, acting in conformity with that person’s conduct. Each of these constitutes an offense. The textual description of the characteristics of the violation consists of four parts:

first, the monk who holds the wrong view whom one follows; second, the admonition to abandon such views; third, the application of legal procedures to the censure; and fourth, the arising of conformity [with the offender].

The transgression consists of five phrases regarding the full precept: first, the person; second, knowing that the person has been formally charged with holding an evil view; third, that no formal act has been performed, meaning the charge has not yet been lifted;
fourth, as indicated by the phrase "in this manner," it refers to following and acting in concert with the person who holds the evil view;

fifth, the conclusion of the offense. Regarding the commentary, the first three [phrases] are understandable. The fourth phrase contains four parts: first, explaining the evil view; second, clarifying its non-abandonment; third, providing support...

[Grant]. There are four cases of "dwelling. Herein, the four phrases manifest the characteristics of a completed dwelling (*sālā-lakṣaṇa*). The nine phrases [following] the opening do not constitute the characteristics of a dwelling. Other precepts regarding dwellings do not equal this one.
Regarding the phrase "if a bhikṣu," etc., the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* explains the fifth phrase: if they converse for a long or short duration, for every word spoken, it is a *pāyattika*;
if they sit together, for every act of sitting, it is a *pāyattika*; if they stay overnight together, for every night spent, it is a *pāyattika*; and if they perform work together...
Item by item, it is raised.
Next is the precept on following the formal act of banishment for a *śrāmaṇera*. The intent behind the regulation and the full set of conditions are identical to the preceding precepts.
Question: Why is the name "banishment" applied to a *śrāmaṇera*? Answer: One who wishes to enter the Path must necessarily possess faith; yet now, because of false speech, he harbors [doubt].
Regarding his faith: if it were not reinforced by further measures, there would be no way to expel him; yet, to cause him to fear and follow the Path, he must be made to practice impurity.
His transgression was not slight. However, practicing impurity here refers to the emission of semen and not sexual intercourse. If it were sexual intercourse, [the offense would be far more grave].

They must be permanently expelled. How could there be any need for admonition? If they do not listen, how can they follow [the rule]? Furthermore, the second volume of the *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra* states: "If they repent, they should be readmitted.

There are four textual sections regarding the characteristics of offenses: first, refusing to desist despite being admonished; second, rebuking what should not be rebuked; third, applying legal procedures for expulsion;
and fourth, following along and giving rise to transgressions. The first section further contains four parts: first, declaring one's desire and that it does not constitute an obstruction.

Regarding the matter for which one is being admonished: (1) the reprimand; (2) the formal admonition; (3) the refusal of the admonition; and (4) the completion of the five clauses of the *pārājika* offense. (1) The offender.

(2) Clarifying that the śrāmaṇera’s statement of desire does not obstruct the ritual procedure for refusing the admonition. (3) That bhikṣu should speak as follows, correctly governing the words of the formal act of banishment (*pravāsanīya-karman*):
"Three nights" means that on the third night, the dawn light has not yet appeared. There is no further second or third [clause].
Regarding the incident of staying overnight together: [the Buddha] said, "There is no such thing; you must leave," and so forth, thereby formalizing the act of *pravāsanīya* (banishment).

Fourth, from the passage beginning "If a bhikṣu... onwards, it concerns the arising of faults through compliance. Fifth, the formalization of the offense (*āpatti*). In the commentary (*vibhaṅga*), with the exception of the second phrase, the remainder is fully explained.
Next, Refusing Exhortations to Study and Precepts: Whenever one wishes to initiate practice, one cannot achieve it alone; one must rely upon virtuous conditions before one can advance in the work.
Now that such virtuous conditions have exhorted you to progress, it is only right that you comply. Yet, wishing to act contrary to what is right, you refuse and do not accept their counsel.
Therefore, this statement was made: "I will not now train in this precept; I shall instead consult other wise bhikṣus who uphold the Vinaya.

This constitutes a slighting and disparaging of superior persons, a lack of intent to advance in goodness, and is of no benefit to the Path; thus, it must be prohibited by the Noble One. There are five factors that constitute the specific conditions: first, the intention not to train;
second, the person before one exhorting one to train in accordance with the Dharma; third, the intention not to accept [the advice]; fourth, the absence of... [text truncated]
The causal conditions: five phrases clarify the offense. The four lines of the *Prātimokṣa* are as follows: first, the person; second, the other person’s proper exhortation to train;
third, the offense of not accepting such words; fourth, the exemption from the offense. If one acts for the sake of knowledge or training, one should instead pose counter-questions.
Furthermore, the subsequent exemption states: "That bhikṣu was deluded and did not understand," and also: "The fact is indeed so. As for "the fact" (*vastu*):
The previous exhortation was improper; one must further consult those of superior virtue. In the commentary, the opening phrases were not explained, though the first three were fully elucidated.
Next, regarding the disparagement of the Vinaya precepts: the precepts are the source for extinguishing evil and the foundation of all virtues; they ought to be praised accordingly.
It was intended to cause the Dharma to flourish and manifest; yet now, on the contrary, people revile it, causing others to abandon its recitation and study, thereby inflicting no small damage.
For this reason, the Sage established these precepts. Thus, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (Duo-lun), fascicle six, states:

"The reason for establishing the precepts for the bhikṣus is to show respect for the Prātimokṣa, to nurture the precepts, and to extinguish unwholesome dharmas. There are five specific conditions [for an offense]: first, it must be a matter of the Vinaya.
1. When the person before one is reciting, one removes [the text] before it has been recited; 2. after it has been finished; 3. with the intention of causing the dharma to cease;

4. speaking words of contemptuous reproach; 5. the offense is committed as soon as the words are finished. The *Śīla-mūla* (Root of the Precepts) consists of three phrases: first, the person; second, the time when the person before one is reciting;

third, from the phrase "speaking these words" downward, which raises the intent of the reproach and establishes the offense. The reason one must reproach is that when this precept is being taught, it causes...

It causes people distress, it causes people shame, and it causes people to harbor doubts. This will be explained clearly below. However, since the teaching distinguishes between self and others, the recitation should likewise do so;
yet the text, referring to the whole, simply says "at the time of recitation. Question: Why is the offense for violating the precepts heavier than those of the other two [categories]? Answer:

According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*, there are five reasons why the offense for a single precept is heavy: first, this precept is the level ground of the Buddha-dharma, the foundation for all myriad virtues.
1. It is from this that [all virtues] arise. 2. All disciples of the Buddhas rely upon it for their abiding; were there no precepts, they would have nothing to rely upon.
3. All sentient beings exist by virtue of the precepts. 4. They are the initial gateway into the Buddha-dharma;
were there no precepts, there would be no means of entering the city of Nirvana. 5. The precepts are the jeweled necklace of the Buddha-dharma, serving as its adornment.
The Buddha-Dharma. For this reason, the offense is grave.

Next is the precept against failing to lend an ear to listen. Now, regarding the matter of understanding: it cannot arise spontaneously; it requires the hearing of the teaching before one can attain awakening.
Yet now, with a deluded mind, you are negligent toward the Dharma and refuse to listen and receive it. Not knowing what is erroneous and what is correct, how could you possibly comprehend this?

If one is like someone facing a blank wall regarding the subject matter, there will be no way to advance on the Path; the loss of benefit is profound. Therefore, the Sage established a rule: a specific condition consists of four factors. First, it is the time when the precepts are being recited in detail.
Second, one’s body is seated within the assembly. Third, one forms the intention not to listen. Fourth, as soon as the recitation is finished, one commits an offense.

For each individual precept not listened to during that interval, there is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). Regarding the four phrases of the root of the precepts, the first is: [The text continues with the first phrase of the *Prātimokṣa*: *Pāṇātipātā veramaṇī sikkhāpadaṃ samādiyāmi.* (I undertake the training rule of abstaining from taking life.)
1. A person. 2. When about to recite the *Prātimokṣa*, he says of himself, "I only now know. 3. Other bhikṣus testify below that he has known it for a long time.

If he actually knew it for a long time but says he only now knows, he commits the offense of lying (*mṛṣāvāda*), which is a *pāyattika*. If he actually had no knowledge or understanding from the beginning, there is no offense of lying;
however, there is the fault of not listening to the Dharma. 4. From "That bhikṣu" below, the offense is established. It pertains to him because...

Because they did not listen, they did not recognize the characteristics of the precepts; therefore, it is said that they were "without knowledge and without understanding. Although they lacked knowledge and understanding, because they recognized the matter at hand, they committed a fundamental offense by acting accordingly;
thus it is said: "If one commits an offense, one should be dealt with according to the Dharma. (The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:

"If a bhikṣu confers the full ordination upon another bhikṣu, he should immediately instruct him to recite the extensive exposition [of the precepts] two or three times while sitting within the assembly for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*)."

Whether one knows or does not know, if one speaks these words, it is a *pāyattika*. Because one fails to understand the underlying cause of the fundamental offense (*mūlāpatti*), there is furthermore the fault of ignorance;
thus it is said that the fault of ignorance is "further increased. The phrase "speaking" below reveals the transgression of not listening. To explain the characteristics fully:
in addition to the fundamental offense and the fault of ignorance, there is further the fault of not attending with the ears; therefore, it is so called.
"Important. Whether [the instruction] is given or not, it is auspicious. This refers to those who preside over the assembly of bhikṣus;
they may also be termed "ignorant for listening to the Dharma without a focused mind," which constitutes a pāyattika offense.

Next is the precept against later regretting and slandering the Saṃgha after having participated in a formal act (*karmavācanā*) for the distribution of goods. The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-vaibhāṣikā* states:

"The reason for establishing this precept for the bhikṣus is to extinguish strife and contention, to extinguish suffering and affliction, and to attain peace and happiness so that the Path may be practiced."

The separate conditions consist of four factors: first, it must be property belonging to the Saṃgha; this refers to items acquired as offerings by the Saṃgha, not to permanent endowments (*sthavira-vastu*).

Regarding permanent endowments, it is improper to reward the administrative officers (*vaiyāvṛtyakara*); thus the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "Saṃgha property refers to the saṃghāṭī robe and so forth—all such items that ought to be distributed.

Second, the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) must have been performed collectively to reward the administrative officer. Third, one must subsequently slander the Saṃgha. Fourth, there must be the verbal expression [of the slander].
This is clear. Regarding the three phrases of the *Prātimokṣa* Sūtra: first, the individual; second, performing the *karmavācanā* together with the community administrators (*saṃgha-karmadāna*);

and third, the subsequent statement "thus speaking" which constitutes the offense of slandering the Saṃgha. In the commentary (*vibhāṣā*), the second phrase is not explained. Within the explanation of the third phrase, there are three sections:
first, friends and relatives; second, the property of the Saṃgha; and third, the determination of the offense.

Next is the precept against departing without desire [to remain]: When a matter concerning the Saṃgha is conducted according to the Dharma, it ought to be followed with careful deliberation. To now depart abruptly without giving notice is improper; the resulting disturbance to the assembly is not slight.
Therefore, the Noble One established the rule that five specific conditions must be met: first, a matter concerning the Saṃgha that is in accordance with the Dharma.

1. To reject what is contrary to the Dharma (*adharma*). 2. To know [the matter] as being in accordance with the Dharma (*dharma*). 3. To not grant one’s consent (*chanda*). 4. To rise and depart abruptly. 5.

To swing one’s feet as one exits the door. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, Chapter Eight, states: Regarding those who adjudicate matters for the Saṃgha—namely, the *jñapti-karman*, the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*, and the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*—if one steps out during a formal act (*karman*) performed indoors, each instance of such departure constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If it is a formal act performed outdoors, [one commits an offense] for every step taken outside the face-length of the area.
Upon investigation, it is a *pāyattika*. If one who possesses supernormal powers departs, [the offense] is incurred upon leaving the ground by the distance of four fingers.

If one leaves after the Saṃgha has not performed the formal act (*karmavācanā*) regarding the settlement of a matter, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one leaves after coming to a private room for the settlement of a matter, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

There are three phrases concerning the full offense: first, the individual; second, the formal procedure of the Saṃgha; third, departing without having granted one's consent (*chanda*). The explanation of these characteristics can be understood accordingly.
Next is the offense of regretting a formal consent (*chanda*) after having already granted it. One first understands the affairs of the Saṃgha and grants consent in accordance with the Dharma;

yet afterwards, out of partiality and personal bias, one suddenly regrets and reverses that decision. Associating with such evil companions, they increase the cycle of birth and death, and their harassment of the assembly is not slight.

Therefore, the Sage’s regulations distinguish four conditions for this offense: first, it must be a monastic matter conducted according to the Dharma; second, one has already granted consent (*chanda*);

third, one subsequently regrets and reverses that decision; and fourth, the verbal expression is complete. The root text consists of three phrases: first, the person; second, having granted consent according to the Dharma;
and third, the subsequent regret that constitutes the offense. These are fully explained in the commentary.
Next, the precept on secretly eavesdropping on the four types of disputes: Whenever there is secret talk, it mostly follows from lustful desires and is intended for inciting strife.
To go and secretly eavesdrop upon such matters is a grave transgression; therefore, the Sage established this rule. It is complete when five specific conditions are met:

first, the matter of one of the four disputes has already arisen; second, the parties involved are deliberating; third, one harbors the intent to incite strife; fourth, one goes and secretly eavesdrops; and fifth, one does not inform the other party.

[The Buddha] said: "It is an offense upon hearing. Question: Regarding the establishment of the offense for eavesdropping, since it occurs at the time of hearing, why does the root precept state, "Hearing these words, one speaks them to another"?

Answer: This refers to the listener’s original intention, which was to speak them to another; in reality, the offense is incurred at the moment of hearing, without waiting for the other person to speak.
If one actually speaks them to that person, it is then subsumed under the precept against divisive speech (*paiśunya*). Furthermore, [the questioner] asked: Why?
Regarding this precept, one commits an offense at the very moment of listening. In the previous case concerning divisive speech (*paiśunya*), one must first speak to the other party;
thus, there was no prior dispute, and one does not commit an offense while listening because the dispute has not yet been definitively established.

In this present precept, however, one commits an offense as soon as one goes to listen to an existing dispute, because the dispute is certain to arise at the time of listening. The three clauses of the root text and their commentary should be understood accordingly.

Next is the precept against striking a bhikṣu with a mind of anger. It is the principle of renunciation that one should practice patience equally, dwell in harmony with others, and not neglect the right practice.
Now, because one strikes another who possesses full ordination with a mind of anger, the resulting affliction is profound; therefore, the Sage established this prohibition.

The separate conditions consist of four factors: first, being a bhikṣu; second, giving rise to anger; third, forming the intent to strike; and fourth, committing the offense through the persistence of fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Question: If striking a bhikṣu incurs the offense of *sthūlātyaya*, how is it that the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states, "Striking or reviling those who have left the household life"?

[The offense] exceeds that of shedding the blood of ten trillion Buddhas. The answer is: the Sūtra is grave because it contradicts reason; the Vinaya is light because it concerns a violation of the formal teaching.

Furthermore, another interpretation holds that the Vinaya establishes the name based on the prohibition against striking those of the same class, whereas the Sūtra concerns striking a supreme being in the secular sense, which is why the offense is grave.
It is just as striking an ordinary person is light, while striking a superior is grave; this case is likewise. [Thus the rule is] concluded.
Because the intention differs, the remaining characteristics are easy to understand.

Next, regarding the *pāṭa* (hand-span) of a *bhikṣu*: it was established as a preliminary restriction within the preceding precept; thus, the offense is incurred from the very beginning of wearing [the garment].

This precept was strictly formulated to prevent [excessive size], so that even the mere proposal of obtaining [an oversized garment] incurs a transgression. The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, fascicle 18, states: "The six groups of *bhikṣus* used the side of their palms as a knife."
Suspecting the group of sixteen, he spoke these words: "I shall strike your face with my palm-blade and cut it off. Because of his terror, the other immediately wailed loudly;
the meaning of the text is easily understood.
Next is the precept against groundless accusation of *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. The intent of the prohibition and so forth are the same as the previous precept on major accusations.

The core text (*sūtra*) consists of five phrases: first, a person; second, a mind of anger; third, being groundless; fourth, raising an accusation of *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; and fifth, the conclusion of the offense.

Within the analysis of its characteristics, the second phrase is briefly not explained, while the others are fully elucidated. That is to say, the first three are explained individually, while the fourth and fifth are explained together; this should likewise be fully understood.
The six types of mental states for guarding against craftiness and writing, as well as hand gestures, are all identical to the preceding cases regarding the offense based on a false pretext;
these are omitted in the text.
Next is the precept concerning entering the royal palace by force: A king possesses sovereign power and holds marriage banquets at no fixed time; [if one] enters the palace together with them...
To press and reproach one another out of mutual shame is most inappropriate; such an emotional excess is not slight. Therefore, the Sage established a rule, as will be explained below.
There are five specific conditions: first, it must be a Kṣatriya king; second, the king and his consort must be in the same place; third, the jewels have not yet been removed or concealed;
fourth, there must be no extenuating circumstances—meaning there is no formal petition, invitation, or difficulty; and fifth, [the fifth condition].

Entering within the palace gates constitutes an offense according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*. If both feet pass through, it is a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense). For every step taken, whether far or near, there is a *sthūlātyaya*.

There are four textual descriptions of the nature of the offense: first, because she offered food to the Buddha, she obtained an immediate reward by becoming a queen; second, while on a high tower, she descended to repay his kindness and pay her respects;
third, returning to the base of the palace, she transformed the king so that he conceived faith; fourth, she permitted the bhikṣus to enter and exit the palace.
In the middle [section], the fourth period adds the supplementary explanation, clearly elucidating the transgression. In the second section, the passage on paying respect, there are three parts.

First, having paid respect, she immediately asks about the four points of doubt regarding cause and effect. Second, from "At that time, the World-Honored One" onwards, he provides a detailed explanation so that she may now give rise to faith and joy.
Third, from "Thus, Mallikā," each point is individually concluded and demonstrated. Third, at that time...
Mallikā, having heard the Dharma below, attained realization, received the Way, and gained benefit;

even those who took refuge in the Triple Gem two or three times merely increased their wholesome minds, yet the precepts were not formally conferred again. The rest of the text may be understood accordingly.

The root of the precepts consists of four sections: first, the Kṣatriya king Janaka; second, the three kings together with their consorts in one place; third, [the section on] entering; fourth, the conclusion.
An offense. This is explained in detail within the *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra*. The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*, fascicle nine, states:

"At the time of approaching [the woman], the precious garments she wears are light, bright, and translucent, such that her inner body is revealed externally, thereby inciting lustful intent. As long as these garments have not yet been removed, it is called 'not having hidden the treasure' (*asaṃvṛta-ratna*).

Furthermore, the woman herself is the 'man's treasure. As long as the lady has not covered her body with other clothes, this is also called 'not having hidden the treasure. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* says: "Treasure..."

The objects held in high esteem by such persons, as well as various women, are all termed "treasures. "Those not yet brought out" refers to women who remain within the palace and have not been brought forth;
"those not yet hidden away" refers to women who are in this palace and have not been made to conceal themselves.

Next is the rule regarding the seizing of precious objects. Among the previous thirty rules, one was for the purpose of keeping [an item]; this case involves seizing it directly rather than for the purpose of keeping, and thus constitutes an offense.
The underlying intent of the regulation is the same as before. However, as for items that have been lost or dropped, it is difficult to discern whether they are valuable or not.

Even if one intends to return them to the owner, one will ultimately incur censure and slander. Furthermore, taking such an object may give rise to the thought of theft. To prohibit even minor infractions and prevent attachment, the Noble One established this regulation; its specific conditions are complete.
Three points: first, precious objects; second, excluding those within a monastery or at a lodging; third, taking hold of them constitutes an offense.

The ancient masters all said that if one takes hold of something that was not dropped or left behind, one commits a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*). However, they do not know upon what principle or teaching this statement is based.
In reality, this precept temporarily takes "dropped or left behind" as its condition; once the prohibition is established, all such precious objects are forbidden.

However, this is not an omission; rather, it is precisely because those who seize [an object] are permitted that, in response to specific cases, monasteries (*ārāma*) and so forth are separately exempted.

By this analogy, other instances are likewise subject to the same prohibitions and restrictions. Furthermore, in other passages, the primary condition is "another's property" (*paradravya*). Moreover, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle eight, states:
If the Sangha’s wall is outside [the boundary], and it is not the dwelling place of a layperson (avadātavasana), one should not take [the items]. Furthermore, the fifth [section] states:

"If one takes another's treasure and claims it to be 'purified' (pariśuddha) treasure, one incurs a *pāyattika*. Regarding all money—whether it be another's money or money that has been declared purified—if one takes it, one incurs a *duṣkṛta*.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, chapter fifteen, states: "In this regard, the offense is as follows: if a bhikṣu takes up or lifts another's..."
[To handle] money, gold, silver, carnelian, agate, lapis lazuli, or pearls constitutes a *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu possesses objects resembling jewels—such as ornaments for men, ornaments for women, weapons, or implements of war—and takes them up or holds them, [it is an offense].
*Pāyattika*. To grasp it [thinking it] is a jewel is a *duṣkṛta*. In that text, if it is not another’s property, it is subsumed under the thirtieth precept.

In the preceding precept, obtaining gold or silver constitutes a *pāyattika*, whereas for money, one incurs only a *duṣkṛta*. This precept consists of five sections: first, the person; second, the substance of the treasure grasped; third, the act of grasping by oneself or another;
fourth, the exceptions where there is no offense; and fifth, the formal conclusion of the offense. Next, if one recites the preceding [text] from the *Vinaya*...

Regarding the phrase "offense" (*āpatti-pada*): when such conditions are met, it refers to an occasion of permission (*anujñāta-pratyaya*). It is not otherwise; that is to say, one does not commit an offense only within the monastery grounds (*ārāma*) or at one's own lodging.
In all other cases, there is an offense. Therefore, it says "not otherwise. In the commentary (*vyākhyā*), the two phrases concerning the three and five [categories] are not explained;

the rest is fully clarified. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Sengqi lü), fascicle 18, states: "If one sees treasure within the precincts of a stūpa garden, one may take it oneself if it is pure; if it is impure..."
One should have someone pick it up. One should form the thought: "If there is an owner who comes seeking it, it should be given.

Forming such a thought is no different from when the Buddha was born and others forgot their ornaments and various articles at the great assembly. When a bhikṣu sees them, he should take them and should make a proclamation asking:
"To whom does this belong? If there is an owner, it should be given to them. If there is no one who recognizes it, it should be hung upon a pillar.
It should be displayed in a prominent location so that people may see it. If someone says, "This is my property," one should ask, "Where did you lose it?
If the answer corresponds [to the facts], it should be given to them. If no one recognizes it, it should be kept for three years.
If it is found within the grounds of a stūpa, it shall be used for the stūpa. If it is found within the grounds of the Saṃgha, it shall be made for the Saṃgha of the four directions.
Regarding the use of objects: if they are valuable items, such as precious necklaces, gold, or silver, one must not leave them exposed or announce that treasure has been found.
A bhikṣu should carefully examine them to ascertain their characteristics before picking them up. If anyone asks about them, [he should explain].
"I have forgotten my belongings. Has anyone seen them? The bhikṣu should ask: "Where did you forget your belongings? What are their characteristics?
If the description does not correspond, he should say: "This monastery is vast; you may search for them extensively.
If it corresponds, he should produce the belongings and show them, saying: "Long-lived one, are these your things or not? If he says, "Yes," [he should not take them].
If there is only one person present, one should assemble many people and instruct them, saying: "Take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
If the World-Honored One had not established the precepts, you would not even be able to see [the object], and so forth, as explained at length.
If no one comes, then for up to three years, one should use it within the boundary according to where it was obtained, as described above.

Next is the precept against entering a village at an improper time. The proper time is for the purpose of sustaining the body; to travel back and forth at an improper time for idle wandering obstructs and ruins right practice. This would incur no small censure, and therefore it was strictly regulated by the Noble One. The specific conditions [for an offense] consist of five factors: first, it is an improper time; second, one goes to a layperson’s village; third, there is no legitimate cause—meaning there is no formal announcement, invitation, summons, or difficulty; fourth, one enters the village; and fifth, one has not informed a fellow monk. If these conditions are met, it constitutes an offense. If there is a legitimate cause, there is no offense. Furthermore, even if there is no legitimate cause, if one enters a monastery or a dwelling place, or if one enters a village where there is a danger of being harmed by wild animals or robbers, there is no offense. If one enters a village during the proper time, there is no offense. If one enters a village at an improper time with a legitimate cause, there is no offense. If one enters a village at an improper time without a legitimate cause, it is an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*). If one enters a village at an improper time without a legitimate cause, but does so with the intention of returning before the sun sets, there is no offense. If one enters a village at an improper time without a legitimate cause, but does so with the intention of returning before the sun sets, yet returns after sunset, it is an offense of wrong-doing.
