It is not necessary for both parties to have a heavy (intense) state of mind; the offense is incurred as soon as the ten types of contact occur. The following explanations of the text regarding the characteristics of the offense can be understood accordingly.

The eight clauses of the core precept (*śikṣāpada*) are: first, the person; second, clarifying that the nun possesses a defiled mind; third, clarifying that the object touched also possesses a defiled mind.

4. The body parts emerging from beneath the armpits; 5. The section on Caṇḍa, clarifying the nature of the tactile act; 6. The section on bhikṣuṇīs, concerning the commission of offenses for violating the precepts;
7. Expulsion and disciplinary measures for those who do not live in common; 8. The designation of the name for those whose bodies come into physical contact.

Regarding physical contact with members of the Sangha, there are four distinctions: First, when a *bhikṣu* touches a woman without fear of sexual assault, he commits an offense regardless of whether the woman was previously alive or dead;
for a *bhikṣuṇī*, however, she must take one who is capable of sexual assault, excluding those who are deceased, and only then does she commit an offense.

Second, when a *bhikṣu* touches a woman without fear of sexual assault, he commits an offense immediately upon contact, regardless of the woman’s age—whether large or small. For a *bhikṣuṇī*, this is not the case; she must touch one who is large and capable, not one who is small. Third, regarding a *bhikṣu*... [text continues]
When a *bhikṣu* touches a woman, both must be defiled by passion. A *bhikṣuṇī*, fearing sexual assault, likewise requires the prior presence of passion.

Regarding the four cases where a *bhikṣu* touches a woman, the gravity of the object is not distinguished; therefore, the text states: "Whether grasping the hand or grasping the hair. For a *bhikṣuṇī*, fearing sexual assault, it must be a grave case;
if it were a light case, it would fall under the eight categories of offenses. Next, the characteristics are clarified; the seven [cases] are omitted here without explanation.

The eight items consist of two phrases each; the remainder is fully explained. The same applies to the three subsequent precepts. Question: Regarding the demarcation of the body parts for the offenses of *pārājika* and *saṃghāvaśeṣa*:

if one grasps below the armpits, it is a *pārājika*; it is clearly understood that above the knees, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. Why, among the eight items, is grasping the hand up to the wrist a *sthūlātyaya*?

Answer: The preceding explanation clarifies the demarcation within the body itself; therefore, [the limit] must be below the armpits and above the knees. Grasping the hand, however, is determined by the demarcation of the limb. This is so.

"From the wrist forward and from the elbow backward is *nirgaṇḍa*. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, fascicle eleven, states: "Below the hairline, above the knees, and behind the elbows—the text is explicit.
In the *Śramaṇera-śikṣāpada*, first the chapters are listed, then they are explained. Regarding the phrase "for a male," it explains the sentence concerning the offense of *pārājika*.
Within this, there are three parts; the first two both concern *nirgaṇḍa* when one is unclothed. The second [part] begins with: "If it is a male and one perceives him as a male... and so forth.
If the mutual intent is subtle, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense. If three men, perceiving each other as men, engage in the act together, it is even more subtle; they merely incur a *duṣkṛta*.

The distinctions within these cases—whether they are abandoned or not, and the variations in their frequency—are identical to those for a bhikṣu and may be understood by reference to the preceding explanation.

Next, regarding the five texts on gravity and lightness: first, concerning what is about to arise; second, clarifying different destinies; third, if with a woman, the lower parts... [the retribution].
Discourse: Fourth, whether or not there is a mind directed toward a lower object when [the offender] is a male; fifth, the five propositions regarding the perception of the object.
Next, the eight matters that constitute a grave offense (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*). In the previous precept, one encounters a grave object, and the arising of defilement is not slight;

it is deeply guarded against and regulated by the intermediate rule, such that a single touch constitutes a grave offense. This precept, although also committed with a defiled mind, is because the object is light, and the harm produced is not [as severe].
This is grave. To rely on these eight matters as requisites is even more excessive; as defiled passions deepen, one incurs the offense of *pārājika*. The specific conditions consist of ten factors:

first, a male person; second, the perception of him as a male; third, the object before one has defilement; fourth, knowing that the object before one has defilement; fifth, having a defiled mind oneself;
sixth, having committed the preceding seven matters without repentance; seventh, performing them up to the eighth, at which point the offense is incurred; or [the eighth], a single...
A man commits eight [offenses], or eight men commit eight, or one commits eight at once, or one commits eight over eight years; provided they total eight, all constitute a *pārājika* offense.
If one grasps the hand eight times, although eight *thullaccaya* offenses are committed, because the matter is one and the same, the *pārājika* offense is not incurred.
The root of the precept has seven phrases: first, a person; second, having a defiled mind within; third, the object of the offense is also defiled; fourth...

There are eight matters to be performed: the five *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses, the sixth *pravāsanīya*, and the seventh designation of names; these can be understood from the commentary. However, within the explanation of the offenses for breaking the precepts (*pārājika*), there are three points:

first, regarding the "approach" (*abhisamaya*). When examining this text, it appears that the *pārājika* offenses collectively lead to the formation of the *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense), and once the fruit [of the offense] is established, even if seven days have passed without confession, it is not stated that one must repent again once the *pārājika* has been incurred.
Second, regarding the "different approach. Third, regarding the "physical retribution. Within the section on non-offenses (*anāpatti*)...

The eight matters are separately explained. Question: In the text below, it is stated that entering a secluded place constitutes a *thullaccaya* offense. Why, then, is this [present case] opened as non-offensive? Answer:
If, in the case below, there is no basis for suspicion of censure, it is a *thullaccaya*; however, because this is for the sake of a meritorious cause, it is opened as non-offensive.
Next is the precept on concealing a bhikṣuṇī’s grave offense. The intent of the regulation is the same as for a bhikṣu;

however, because one knowingly conceals another’s commission of a grave offense, the resulting transgression becomes more severe. It corrupts oneself and defiles the Saṃgha; therefore, it is strictly prohibited. Consequently, it differs from the *pārājika* offenses in that it requires six specific conditions:
first, the person must be a full bhikṣuṇī (excluding the two lower groups); second, she must have committed a grave offense (excluding the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* and other lesser categories).

Third, knowing one has committed a grave offense; this excludes cases where the offense was committed unknowingly. Fourth, harboring a mind of concealment; this excludes those who enter a state of protective restraint (*ārakṣa-citta*) and thus do not commit the offense.
Therefore, the explanatory text states: "If one says there is a danger to life or a danger to the holy life (*brahmacarya*), it is not an offense.

Fifth, failing to confess; this specifically excludes those who have already performed the formal confession (*saṃvara*). If one does confess, it must be done before someone who does not yet know of the offense. If that person already knows, both parties share the fault, as [stated] in the *Vinaya-vibhaṅga*.

Regarding those who have committed an offense, it is not appropriate to perform confession face-to-face. Generally, one who discloses an offense must obtain the name of the offender as well as the specific category and nature of the offense;
if this is not done, the disclosure is not valid. Since the disclosure is not valid, the concealment is likewise not established.
If the recipient of the disclosure does not need to disclose it further, there would be the fault of infinite regress. This is like the case of a nun who violates a formal admonition by the Sangha.
All know this. If one acts with a concealing intent, it constitutes concealment (*paticchādana*); if there is no concealing intent, concealment does not constitute concealment.

If that person who committed the offense has already confessed, further concealment does not constitute concealment, because the original basis no longer exists. Six: the offense occurs when the dawn appears; this fulfills the seven points of the precept: first, the person;
second, knowing another has committed a grave offense; third, not confessing—“not confessing” means not confessing by oneself.
1. Addressing one person rather than addressing a group, which refers to two or three people; 2. Not before the great assembly, which means not confessing before the Saṃgha;
3. At another time, [the offense] is brought forward by one's own admission; 4. Concealment; 5. Formal conclusion; 6. Banishment; 7. Establishing the name.
In this commentary, the first phrase may be understood as it stands. "The knower" (*jñātṛ*) below explains the second phrase. "The Saṃgha" below explains the third phrase;
however, the term *saṃgha* is incomplete within the text of the *Prātimokṣa*, whereas "the great assembly" (*mahājana*) is the complete version found in the text of the *Prātimokṣa*.

"One who has abandoned the path" (*tyaktamārga*) below explains the fourth phrase. These five phrases herein are a systematic restatement of the explanations for the first two sections of the *Prātimokṣa*.
Explanation: This may be understood by examining it. In that section of the *Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya* concerning the offense of concealing [another's] transgressions (*pācittiya*), there are three parts.

First, concealing the offenses of others; since the offenses of others vary in gravity, the text is divided into two levels. Second, concealing one’s own offenses; regarding the concealment of offenses committed by monks or nuns themselves...

Regarding the gravity or lightness [of the offense]: it is because there are different distinctions in the limits of deep prevention; that is why it is so. Third, as for the remaining groups, they are briefly without the perception of the object.

Next, concerning the rule against a monk who has been subject to suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*) violating the three-fold admonition of the *bhikṣuṇī* Saṃgha: there are two intentions for its establishment. First, he is not permitted [to do so].

Regarding "compliance": if a bhikṣu is seen to have fallen into ruin and is no longer fit for the Path, and the Great Saṃgha has performed the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of suspending him and casting him out from the community, once the Saṃgha has suspended him, a bhikṣuṇī must cease all acts of reverence;
yet if she nonetheless complies with him, her offense against the community is not slight. Furthermore, if she grants permission for compliance, it constitutes a *thullaccaya* (grave offense).
That person holds wrong views and never reforms their faults or repents to follow the good; thus, they ruin themselves and harm others, and such behavior must be restrained and not permitted.
Second, regarding the necessity of admonishing the intent: this bhikṣuṇī relies upon her close teacher, saying in words, "This is my elder brother;
if he does not receive offerings now, when will he? Furthermore, because the Buddha has sent her to show respect to the great assembly of monks, she acts in this manner.

Regarding the matter of improper conduct: the Saṃgha must offer a formal admonition. As for the statement that the Buddha permitted [reverence] toward relatives and those who show respect—this refers to a bhikṣu of right view and pure conduct who possesses the qualities to benefit nuns;
therefore, he ought to be reverently served. However, this bhikṣu has achieved a mind of wickedness; although he is a relative, he is unworthy of reverence.
Now, the Saṃgha intends to make him recognize what is right and what is wrong; thus, it is necessary to offer this admonition.

Xiao said this. He asked: "Since monks and nuns follow [the rules] equally, why is there a distinction between those who receive admonition and those who do not? He replied: "It is because of the presence or absence of support and reliance;

therefore, there is a distinction regarding admonition. He asked again: "Why is it that when a nun follows the two assemblies [of monks and laypeople], her offenses are categorized as *pārājika* or *sthūlātyaya*?"

The answer regarding nuns is of the same category as the question. The determination of the offense is the same as for monks. In the third case, one may take hold [of her]; in the first two cases, one commits a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).

Since a monk and a nun are not of the same class, one commits a *duṣkṛta* in accordance with each of the three types of formal accusation (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*). The intent behind the determination of the three offenses is as explained previously.

There are six specific conditions: first, there is the monk who has been subjected to the formal accusation; second, one knows that he has been so accused by the Saṃgha and that the Saṃgha has not yet lifted the suspension; third, one follows...
1. Compliance. 2. The four bhikṣuṇīs offer their admonition. 3. She rejects it and does not comply. 4. The threefold *karmavācanā* is completed.

The textual characteristics are as before. The *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* has eight phrases: 1. The person being admonished; 2. The matter for which she is admonished—herein, according to the extensive commentary, there are five phrases:
1. The Saṃgha’s formal act is in accordance with the Dharma; 2. She does not comply; 3. She does not repent; 4. The Saṃgha has not yet acted [for her].
Explanation: Regarding "the five [cases] which are followed and obeyed," these refer precisely to the matters to which one accords with the admonitions:

(3) private admonition, (4) refusal of admonition, (5) monastic admonition, (6) incurring guilt by disobeying the Sangha, (7) not living together [with the Sangha], and (8) the designation of the name. The explanation of their characteristics can be understood.
● Next, the seventeen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses are explained. First, they are summarized and analyzed through seven categories: 1. Body and speech; 2. Personal performance and instructing others;
3. Prohibitive and natural offenses; 4. Observance and violation; 5. Distinction between admonishment and non-admonishment; 6. Similarities and differences between the two divisions [of the Vinaya].
The seven minor categories [of offenses] arise spontaneously. In the first gate, there are three positions regarding body and speech: first, the single precept that is exclusively a physical act;

second, the nine precepts that are exclusively vocal acts, among which the one precept concerning encouraging others to receive [the precepts] constitutes an offense through the completion of the vocal action; third, there are six precepts that encompass both types of acts, among which there are four positions.

Regarding the ordination [precept]: [Note: The provided text fragment appears to be a technical commentary on the Vinaya classification of offenses, specifically concerning the *pācittiya* rules, categorized by their nature as physical (*kāyakamma*), vocal (*vācākamma*), or both.]

The first precept regarding thieves: an offense committed through speech by oneself while relying on another; that is, once the legal procedure (*dharmakarma*) has been completed, the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) is the first to be defiled. Next, the precept regarding the suspension of one [monk]:
if the one who performs the legal procedure commits it solely through speech, the rest of the Saṃgha is equally guilty for having ordained a "thief-woman.

Next, the two precepts regarding slander: these are offenses committed through both speech and body. Next, the two precepts regarding matchmaking: these are offenses committed through both body and speech. Next, the precept regarding performing [the act] oneself or instructing others...

Regarding persons, the categories are approximately fourfold. First, the exhortation to receive a single precept pertains exclusively to the karma of teaching others. Next, regarding the two precepts on slander, both parties commit the offense equally.

Following that, concerning the two precepts on matchmaking, committing the act oneself constitutes the primary offense; as for teaching others, there are cases where the offense is shared and cases where it is not. Finally, there are the remaining twelve.

Regarding the gravity of the precepts: the secondary prohibitions (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*) are light, while the primary transgressions of nature (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) are grave. Next, concerning the prohibition of nature: only the act of acting as a matchmaker is a prohibition;

all others are of the nature of transgression. Next, regarding observance and violation: ordaining a female thief who has been exposed constitutes both observance and violation. That is to say, not ordaining a royal official is an observance by abstention (*virati-āpatti*);

ordaining her and conferring the precepts upon her is a violation by action (*kriyā-āpatti*). Though the substance is one, the names differ. If, when ordaining her, she informs the king and great ministers, it is an observance by action (*kriyā-śīla*). Conferring [the precepts]...
When observing the precepts, there is no transgression; conversely, to transgress them is to violate them. Is this not "abstention and observance" (*śīla*)?

These two also share the same essence but differ in name. Regarding their distinct essences as two types of observance: first, not crossing [the boundary] is abstention and observance; second, crossing it by informing the king and great ministers is active observance (*kriyā-śīla*). One should understand other cases by analogy.
As for the remaining fifteen precepts, they involve only abstention and observance and active transgression. This may also apply here.

Regarding the two precepts: from the perspective of their distinct natures, they consist of the commission of offenses (*āpatti*) and the observance of prohibitions (*dhāraṇa*). These apply generally to seventeen precepts. Next, concerning those who do not offer admonition:
while the first nine [precepts] are free from confusion, the latter eight involve confusion; for this reason, there is a distinction between those who must be admonished and those who need not.

This act of offering admonition constitutes an offense of violating the regulations of the Saṃgha, whereas the other cases where one does not offer admonition constitute an offense of violating the regulations of the Buddha. Next, regarding their similarities and differences:

Among these, there are seven offenses that are identical in their transgression: namely, the two regarding matchmaking and the two regarding slander, as well as the four regarding the violation of admonitions. However, the first three precepts are entirely equal;
whereas the fourth precept concerning the violation of admonitions differs in the person who administers them, because each individual violates the admonition of their respective assembly.

As for the remaining ten precepts, they differ in terms of presence or absence, or perhaps in terms of gravity, such as in the case of the precept on associating with those who have committed offenses.

Regarding the precepts: it is said that for a bhikṣu, depending on the offense committed—specifically regarding the concealment of an offense—the remaining nine precepts all result in a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
This is because their meaning is rarely encountered, and furthermore, because the censure for such transgressions is not grave. Next, concerning those that arise spontaneously (*anābhoga*):

among the five aforementioned offenses of instructing others, with the exception of the one involving "encouraging [another] to accept," the remaining four precepts may involve the sense of instructing another to act on one's own behalf.

Therefore, there is spontaneous transgression (*anābhoga*). Regarding the exhortation to undertake a single precept, it refers exclusively to what one has done oneself; since it is stated that the offense is completed upon full awareness, there is no spontaneous transgression.

Next, following the text for explanation: among the nine initial offenses, the first three are identical to the precepts as briefly set forth in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, while the latter six are different.
Each point shall be explained separately.

Regarding the prohibition against [informing] others: first, because those who have left the household life must constantly provide relief to sentient beings, to now abruptly inform others would be a profound violation of the Dharma.
Second, because women are naturally reserved and not accustomed to intervening in external affairs or speaking on behalf of others.
This brings disgrace upon the Buddha’s Dharma. The specific conditions [for this offense] consist of four factors: first, going before a judicial official; second, addressing a lay householder;
third, pointing out the details of the case; and fourth, reaching a final judgment. Regarding the three points in the root text and the five points in the exceptions:
first, for the sake of another, the Buddha permitted speaking in accordance with the facts; second, at that time, the nun spoke falsely regarding the matter; third, the various judicial officials...
4. At that time, the bhikṣus [acted as] holy judges to determine right from wrong. Previously, she had bestowed [a gift] upon a nun;
once the matter was finalized, she later took back that object which definitely belonged to the recipient and transferred it to another person. This, therefore, was not a valid bestowal. 5.
At that time, the King, upholding the Buddha’s regulations, punished the judicial officers for having brought such ruin through their ignorance and incompetence. Full [of retribution].
The precept consists of five phrases: first, the person; second, going to the authorities and speaking; third, the scope of what was said by the laywoman;
fourth, the time at which the words were spoken, starting from "if [the matter] is exhausted"; and fifth, the formal determination of the offense, starting from "if she is a bhikṣuṇī.

Because women have little wisdom, these must be explained separately; therefore it says, "having committed the first rule, it should be relinquished. In the commentary, the first three are explained individually, while the latter two are clarified together. (From the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*).
Eleventh: If a bhikṣuṇī is insulted or oppressed by others, she should inform her parents;
if she has no parents, she should inform her relatives; if she has no relatives, she should inform the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās.
If there are bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs who have the authority to intervene but do not provide protection, it is a duṣkṛta offense. When informing them, one should act as follows:

It is said: "If one says, 'He insulted me,' or 'I rebuked and admonished him,' such words should not be spoken. If one goes to an official to speak against another person, for each round-trip journey, there is one *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense."
Next, the Ordination of Female Thieves: Generally, those who are supreme fields of merit ought to be pure and manifest, so as to inspire faith in others and demonstrate the height of reverence.

Yet this woman committed theft unto death, yet she was nonetheless ordained and entered the monastic order, thereby bringing disgrace upon the community of nuns. There are six specific conditions [for this offense]:
first, she is a female thief whose crime merits death; second, one knows her to be such; third, one does not inform the king or his ministers.

1. Four times conferring full ordination (*upasampadā*); 2. acting as a preceptor (*upādhyāya*); 3. completing the *karmavācanā*; 4. the five factors for the perfection of the precepts; 5. a single person; 6. knowing her to be a female thief;
7. known by many people; 8. not having asked the king or his ministers; 9. the formal determination of the offense. These are fully explained in the commentary (*vibhāṣā*).

Because the preceptor is the principal [agent], it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense; because the others are not the principals, they are *sthūlātyaya*. The text states "after three *karmavācanās*," which refers to this case.
The *karmavācanā* of Kūṭa was not according to the original rule; all precepts for ordaining others should be explained according to this interpretation.
It is auspicious because bhikṣus rarely perform ordinations, or perhaps it is auspicious precisely because he ordained a woman.

Next is the lifting of the suspension outside the boundary. That nun has corrupted her views and is unfit to remain within the community. If she were not disciplined and suspended, there would be no means to bring peace.
Now that she has already been suspended, she refuses to comply; she has not received the command of the Saṃgha, yet she has privately and arbitrarily lifted the suspension herself.

This constitutes siding with an evil person and showing contempt for the Saṃgha; her transgression is no light matter, and therefore the offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* is prescribed. Thus says the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*.
It is said: Once that bhikṣuṇī had been released from the suspension, she became even more arrogant and showed no respect toward the Saṃgha.

There are six conditions for this: first, the former bhikṣuṇī had undergone the formal act of *tri-ud-dhāna* (threefold censure) by the Saṃgha; second, she did not comply with or subsequently repent; third, she did not inform the Saṃgha;

fourth, there was no valid reason—this reason is as explained in the opening [text]; fifth, she proceeded to release [the other] on her own authority; sixth, the three *karmavācanās* were completed. This is from the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.
Five phrases: 1. A person; 2. Knowing her to be a nun who has been formally charged by the Saṃgha. Within this, there are four points: 1. The Saṃgha’s formal charge was in accordance with the Dharma;
2. She did not comply; 3. She has not yet repented; 4. She has not yet been released from the charge. Third, for the sake of receiving [the offense], she does not inform the Saṃgha below.

Fourth, she goes outside the boundary to be released. Fifth, the determination of the offense. These are fully explained in the commentary (*śāstra*); here, it is simply that all those who participate in the *karmavācanā* [are included].

[Fragment]. Because the names [of the individuals] were not recorded, there was no distinction made; this differs from the case of ordaining a female thief, where because the name was recorded, there was a specific offense and the penalty was accordingly reduced.

Next, the four individual precepts: Women have weak resolve and fear being subjected to harassment or oppression; they must rely on the support of companions before they can depart [from worldly life].
[This constitutes] an offense. Therefore, whether in a village lodging, in water, or on a road, one must never be alone.

To cross a river alone, four conditions must be met: first, it must be a river; second, one must cross alone; third, if the preceding nun enters the water quickly and does not wait for her companion, she incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense;

fourth, when both feet have emerged and she has stepped onto the bank, she incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. If the subsequent nun enters alone, she incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense. Upon [reaching the bank], [she incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*].

When reaching the opposite shore, if she has a nun as a companion, there is no offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. If both enter together and both exit together, or if they travel by carriage or on animals where there is no ritual propriety (*īryāpatha*) for crossing water, there is no offense.

Third, regarding the absence of causes and conditions: if it is due to the two hardships of life or celibacy (*brahmacarya*), or if her companion dies, or if she is taken away by bandits, there is no offense.
Fourth, if she exits at the opposite shore and enters a village alone; there are likewise four distinct conditions [for this].
First, regarding a village of laypeople: regardless of whether one is within the boundary or inside a monastery, entering alone constitutes an offense.
Second, entering alone without a valid reason—except in cases such as the two types of difficulties mentioned previously. Third, the offense is incurred upon crossing the boundary;

if one reaches the village and enters the village gate, the offense is committed once both feet have entered the village, provided one does not wait for a companion. Fourth, if there are already nuns present in the village, there is no offense. This is because...
Because a former nun was her companion, it is the same when entering a city gate. If she encounters [the boundary] directly, she commits an offense by crossing the boundary.
Regarding the three conditions for staying alone overnight ten *li* from a village: first, it must be outside the reach of one's outstretched hand;

if there is no gate within the village or monastery, and they share the same grove but have separate beds, one does not commit an offense as long as they remain within the reach of one's outstretched hand. Once one goes outside, one commits an offense. If they were originally close together, but become distant due to sleeping, [the rule applies].

There is no offense in three cases: first, when there is no underlying cause, namely during two types of difficult circumstances (*dvangasa*) or when accompanying others in defecating or urinating, or when engaged in activities that require quietude;
second, when turning over from side to side [while sleeping]; and third, for each instance of a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense committed while traveling alone, which involves three conditions:

first, traveling on a road; second, being without a supporting cause, such as the two types of difficulties mentioned above; and third, being separated from one's companions within the range of sight or hearing. Regarding the three rules in the root text, this constitutes one offense.
Two sections in four parts; third, the determination of the offense. Regarding the commentary, the first phrase is self-evident. The following two phrases are explained together.

Having explained the four cases of "crossing alone," the text is further divided into four. Regarding "crossing alone through water," it first teaches the rules for non-offense. In the text, "water" refers to river water.
If one cannot cross alone, regardless of whether it is wide or narrow, deep or shallow, within the boundary of a village, it suffices that one's feet are removed [from the water].

Lifting one’s robes differs from the etiquette for walking on land; both constitute offenses. This does not differ from the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, which states that if the water is wide by more than ten cubits and deep enough to reach half the body, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.

Next, the rules regarding offenses are clarified. First, the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses are explained. Regarding the passage in the text stating that one enters the water such that companions cannot keep up and incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*:
this refers to proceeding directly without waiting for one's companions. As for the act of entering [the water], it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense), not a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. Next...
This clarifies the *sthūlātyaya*. Regarding this *sthūlātyaya*, there are offenses and non-offenses on both this shore and the other shore, as can be understood from the text.

Because it does not constitute a full transgression, it is classified as a *sthūlātyaya*. Next, regarding entering a village alone: first, the instruction on non-offense; next, the clarification of its offense.

Within the section on the offense, there are three parts—*saṃghāvaśeṣa*, *sthūlātyaya*, and *duṣkṛta*—each with two phrases that may be understood from the text. As for "the sound of one drum," it is as explained above regarding traveling together.
In a place where there is no village, it extends for ten *li*. The *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle five, states: "Generally speaking, the distance reached by the sound of a drum is one *krośa*.

The Vinaya Master says: "This is the definitive definition. Next, regarding staying alone: it is non-offensive when within a monastery (*ārāma*), but offensive otherwise. Next, regarding being in a village:

it is non-offensive when not within [the defined area], but offensive otherwise. Next, regarding traveling alone: it is likewise non-offensive or offensive as can be understood. Among the non-offenses, four exceptions are fully set forth.
However, there are five textual sections. The first two are understandable. Third, "if two nuns stay together" and below, this permits staying overnight within the monastery grounds (*ārāma*).
Fourth, "with two nuns" and below, this permits traveling alone. Fifth, "if one nun" and below, this permits staying overnight within a village.

Next is the precept against receiving food from a man with a lustful mind. Women are prone to passion; they must constantly distance themselves from such conditions. Now, failing to distance oneself from these conditions, one accepts food out of indulgence.
Because of this acceptance, one is subjected to humiliation; it is difficult to maintain one's integrity, and the resulting ruin is no small matter.

Therefore, the Noble One established this prohibition. There are six constituent factors: first, the person is a man; second, one perceives him as a man; third, he offers food or clothing with a lustful mind.

Fourth, knowing that she has a defiled mind and giving; fifth, one’s own mind also becoming defiled; sixth, receiving and taking possession constitutes the offense. There are five phrases for the fullness of the precept:
first, the person; second, the nun has a defiled mind; third, the object before her has a defiled mind; fourth, receiving food and so forth from her while she is in a state of inferiority;

fifth, the formal conclusion of the offense. These are explained in detail within the commentary. Regarding the explanation of the fifth phrase by the Bhikṣuṇī, there are four internal points therein: first...

First, one must weigh the gravity or lightness of the offense. Second, the two deva sons descend to a different realm of existence. Third, a woman with a defiled mind receives a lower physical retribution. Fourth, the four propositions regarding the perception of the object are clarified.

Next, the precept concerning the prohibition against accepting food or clothing from a man with a defiled mind is established; there are three points in its formulation. First, it is not permitted to encourage such an act.

Previously, this was already considered a serious offense; the World-Honored One prohibited it. Now, to intentionally strike one another and encourage the acceptance of tainted food causes others to incur guilt and brings transgression upon oneself as well.
Since both self and others are harmed, it was therefore prohibited. Regarding the second point concerning the shared intent of the offense:

it involves encouraging others with a knowledge of their defiled and evil intentions, and further using speech to slander the Buddha and fail to follow the holy teachings; thus, the gravity of the mental transgression is not slight.

Therefore, they are made to be offenses of the same category. Regarding the three instances where the two precepts differ in intent: the former is an offense of the body, while this is an offense of speech;

furthermore, the former results in obtaining food and clothing, whereas this prevents their acquisition; additionally, there is a distinction between slandering the Buddha and slandering others. For these reasons, the two precepts are divided. Each has five distinct conditions for its completion.
First, there is a man. Second, one gives food and clothing with a defiled mind. Third, one knows that he has given them with a defiled mind. Fourth, one speaks words to encourage him to accept them.

Fifth, when the words are clearly articulated, the offense is committed. Regarding the three phrases in the root text of the precept: first, the person; second, encouraging another; third, the formal conclusion of the offense.
In the commentary, the first is explained individually, while the latter two are clarified together.

Next, the eight precepts concerning admonition. The first four are the same as those previously mentioned; the *śikṣāpada* texts for these are listed directly. As for the remaining points where they differ, each will be explained individually.

First, the precept regarding the offense of associating with a layperson after being admonished by the Saṃgha three times. There are three reasons for the establishment of this rule: first, not to permit such association.

Regarding "dwelling together": for women, whose resolve is difficult to stabilize, the Buddha established the requirement of having a companion as support, so that they might guard against transgressions.

Now, you have instead contrived a private intimacy, dwelling together with defiled minds and concealing each other's faults; since your hearts do not reform or repent, this is a source of disgrace and ruin.

The afflictions arising within the Buddha-dharma are not insignificant; therefore, one must exercise restraint and prevention so that practice may be established. Second, regarding the necessity of admonishing the mind:
relying upon the holy teachings, one establishes two [precepts] as companions. How can it be right for the Saṃgha to send me away to live separately? This would be a violation of the teachings.

The intention behind the prohibition is not understood; it is necessary for the Saṃgha to provide admonition and clarify right from wrong. The meaning of the threefold formal act of accusation (*karmavācanā*) is as previously stated.

The specific conditions consist of six factors: first, dwelling in close association with a defiled mind; second, the community of nuns exhorting her to live separately; third, relying on [the other] and refusing to comply;
fourth, the Saṃgha offering admonition in accordance with the Dharma; fifth, rejecting it and failing to follow; sixth, the completion of the three *karmavācanās*. The textual details are as before.
The six clauses of the *Prātimokṣa* are likewise [structured]. However, within the text regarding the matter at hand, there are four clauses, which are fully explained in the commentary.
Next is the precept concerning reviling the Saṃgha, encouraging [others] to dwell in proximity [to them], and violating the Saṃgha’s three-fold admonition. There are four reasons for its enactment:

first, regarding those who do not heed advice; because they dwell together with defiled minds and conceal each other’s offenses, the Saṃgha sees no benefit [in their association] and thus admonishes them to dwell separately.
This impure nun incited others to slander the Saṃgha; her transgression was not slight, and thus it was necessary for the Noble One to establish this rule. Next, as for the purpose of the admonition:
since worldly affairs are intermingled and their characteristics difficult to distinguish, when one's conduct involves attachment or aversion, it leads to the incitement of verbal slander.

Therefore, the community of monks must offer an admonition according to the Dharma to demonstrate that they themselves harbor no internal malice, intending only to cause the other to depart from her offense. Finally, the offense is defined.
The underlying intention involves three kinds of faults: first, inciting others to commit evil; second, unreasonably slandering the Saṃgha; and third, stubbornly refusing counsel.
Because these faults are profound, they are established as offenses of equal gravity. Regarding the intent behind the two subsequent precepts:

the former precept admonishes against personally associating with those who live near [evil], while this precept admonishes against slandering the Saṃgha and encouraging such association. Furthermore, because the wording of the admonitions differs, they are established as two distinct precepts.

The separate dwelling has six conditions: first, the nun previously practiced living in close association; second, the community of nuns exhorted her to live separately; third, she slandered the community while encouraging continued close association;
fourth, the community of nuns offered formal exhortation according to the Dharma; fifth, she refused and did not comply; sixth, the threefold *karmavācanā* was completed.
The remaining characteristics can be understood; they cannot be stated in full detail.
Next is the precept against abandoning the Triple Gem out of anger despite being exhorted to desist. There are three points for restraining the mind. First, regarding not permitting the abandonment:
one originally took refuge in the Triple Gem for the purpose of leaving the household life. Now, out of anger, one suddenly discards it;

this is to abandon the True Dharma and cast oneself into heterodox teachings, which would lead to a profound fall from the right path, and is therefore not permitted. Second, regarding the necessity of exhortation: it is simply because of [the influence of] women...

Seeing only what is near, they are unable to perceive the distant. Hearing that the name "renunciant" is the same [as that of householders], they claim that their holy life (*brahmacarya*) is likewise equal.

Their deluded minds thus turn toward [the wrong path]; this is most pitiable. The Saṃgha must provide admonition so that they may recognize what is correct and what is false. Next, the determination of the offense is concluded as above. The specific conditions consist of six factors:
first, giving rise to anger due to a particular matter; second, uttering words of renunciation; third, turning one's back on this and heading toward that; fourth, the Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha...

They offer admonition in accordance with the Dharma. Fifth, they refuse and do not comply. Sixth, the threefold *karmavācanā* is completed; the textual characteristics of these points are easily understood.

Next is the precept concerning the instigation of the four types of disputes, slandering the Saṃgha, and defying admonition. The intent behind its formulation is also threefold: first, not permitting the instigation of disputes that slander the Saṃgha.

Generally, when disputes deviate from principle, they cause the community to be discordant; once the Saṃgha has already adjudicated and eliminated them in accordance with the Dharma, [to reopen them is forbidden].
However, this woman’s vision does not reach far; she falsely draws analogies to incite slander against the Saṃgha. This fault and damage are no small matter, which is why the rule was established.

As for the purpose of the subsequent admonition: she herself is unable to manage the matters of dispute, yet she claims that the Saṃgha has decided them in violation of the Dharma, such that their conduct appears confused and as if influenced by favoritism or hatred. Therefore, it is necessary for the Saṃgha itself [to intervene].

One should reason with and admonish them. Next, the intent regarding the formal determination of the offense is as previously stated. There are six specific conditions: first, a dispute has already arisen;

second, the Saṃgha has settled it in accordance with the Dharma; third, one slanders the Saṃgha by instigating [the dispute]; fourth, the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha has formally offered admonition; and fifth, one rejects it and does not comply.
Six: The third *karmavācanā* is concluded; the remaining characteristics may be understood [from the previous].
● Next, the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses are explained. Following the above procedure within the Saṃgha, one must first perform a general analysis according to the four gates.

However, since the meaning of the first two gates is no different from before, we shall now respond directly by addressing them through the gate of the *pāyattika* (single-offense) rules. For now, however—

Speaking in terms of the manifest characteristics, there are thirty-eight precepts; these must be definitively established because they are otherwise confused. Within this, they are divided into two categories: internal requisites and external ones.

There are eleven internal requisites and ten common precepts, namely: (1) concealing a transgression, (2) individual offenses, (3) *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses, (4) not accepting medicine, (5) [using water] containing insects, and (6) [using] water [for other purposes].
There is one uncommon [precept], which is eating *vighasa*. These constitute offenses through the consumption of food; once the food has been eaten, there is nothing further that can be relinquished.

Therefore, these are included in the *Śaikṣa* (Training) rules and do not fall within the *Naiḥsargika* (Forfeiture) category. Next, regarding external requisites (*bāhyadravya*), there are twenty-seven items:

seven common precepts (*samāna-śīla*)—namely, [the rules concerning] sandals, looking at [nakedness], covering [the body], true purity (*viśuddha-dakṣiṇā*), the three white robes (*tricīvara*), high beds, and *tūla* (cotton) bathing cloths;
and twenty non-common precepts (*asamāna-śīla*)—namely, [rules concerning] water, fans, raw grain, shared beds, shared blankets, making robes, exceeding five days, and exceeding five days [again].
Wearing the *saṃghāṭī* improperly; wearing another’s robe; spinning yarn; taking robes [without permission]; not receiving [offerings] for storage; crossing over a robe—these ten;

keeping a woman’s ornaments; wearing them; not wearing the *saṃkakṣikā*; and applying the seven types of ointments—these twenty acts of commission invite public censure and are therefore all offenses.
However, as they lack utility, they do not constitute the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offenses involving forfeiture).
Next, the thirty [rules] are correctly expounded, organized into ten sections: first, identifying the person who commits the offense; second, assigning them to body or speech;

third, distinguishing between acting on one's own behalf and instructing others; fourth, differentiating between prohibitive and natural offenses; fifth, the procedures for maintaining and violating the precepts; sixth, the intent behind the two questions;
seventh, whether a repeated offense constitutes a grave transgression; eighth, the ritual for relinquishing and repenting; ninth, the two... [the text continues].

The categories of similarity and difference. The tenth [section], the spontaneous [offense] for the lower assembly. Regarding the first gate, there are three positions of persons: namely, the single individual, the plurality, and the Saṃgha.
If one discusses the single individual, it refers to one who universally opposes [the rule] without doubt. As for the "plurality," this refers to many people acting together with a common intent.
If one considers them as a plurality based on this, all are equally guilty of the offense. If, however, one looks at it from the perspective that the offense is incurred because of my own action...
He incurs an offense. Regarding "for many," this refers only to those living together. Among these, seven precepts are not shared offenses:

namely, [the rules on] being separated from one's robes, receiving more than allowed, begging for a bowl, the two types of confiscation, the seven-day medicine, and the medicinal robe. All others are offenses incurred in common. Within the ranks of the Saṃgha...

The Saṃgha of the four directions does not incur an offense [in this regard]. As for the *pratyutpanna-saṃgha* (the local community), if four or more persons act together, then all members of that group commit the same offense according to all the precepts, as clarified above.
Alternatively, it may be that only the medicinal robe (*glānapraticchādana-cīvara*) is excluded.

These are distinct entities. Next, regarding the two states of body and speech, there are five [offenses] that constitute bodily transgressions: namely, the four instances of mutual use and the robe for the ill.

The remaining [offenses] pertain to both body and speech. Within these, they are divided into three groups. First, there is one precept—the "staying overnight apart from one's robe"—wherein the cessation of activity through body and speech constitutes a bodily transgression.

Second, there are seven precepts: namely, the six cases where one takes out-of-season items during the permitted season, which involve the cessation of speech and are common to both [body and speech].
The third category consists of eighteen remaining precepts that involve both bodily and verbal offenses. This means there are two precepts concerning the "urgent robe" (*ātyayika-cīvara*).

Thus, there are eighteen. Among these, there are three further sub-divisions; the first is the single precept regarding begging for thread, which exclusively constitutes an offense through the agency of another's body.
Second, regarding the two offenses of receiving jewels and the two types of seizure: if one acts on one’s own, it is an offense of bodily action (*kāyakarman*);

if one instructs another to speak for oneself, it is an offense by means of another’s body. Third, there are three differences in the reception of the precepts; there are eleven commonalities, namely:
requesting from a non-relative, requesting clothing, exceeding the limit of sufficiency, and receiving clothing from a householder. (The first [of these eleven] is as follows: One.

The two cases of a householder or king’s minister sending precious goods for trade to beg for a bowl; the exhortation to weave; receiving more than the prescribed amount; accepting urgent offerings of robes (*ātyayika-cīvara*);

and returning property belonging to the Saṃgha—all these constitute offenses through one's own physical or vocal actions. If one employs the physical action of another, one commits an offense. Next, regarding "acting oneself or instructing others":
if one generally instructs another to act for someone else and not for oneself, it provides no benefit to oneself, and one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). If...
He also teaches others to act on his own behalf. There are four precepts for which one incurs an offense equally; these are called the three shared precepts:
namely, receiving precious objects, taking away robes, and begging for thread to have a weaver weave a robe. There is one that is not shared: namely, trading for a robe and then taking it back.

The others do not exist [as such]. However, regarding the classification by stage (*avasthā*), the single precept on begging for thread is committed solely through causing another to act; the two precepts on receiving precious objects and the two on seizing are applicable to both stages.

All remaining [offenses] are committed through one's own action and result in forfeiture (*naiḥsargika*). Next, concerning the distinction between prohibitory (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*) and natural (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) offenses:

four cases of mutual exchange involving the Saṃgha constitute natural offenses; all others are prohibitory. Next, regarding observance and violation: among these, there are seven precepts that possess both modes of observance.

Regarding transgressions (*āpatti*): these refer to the six offenses as well as the separation from one's robes. As for the precepts concerning these six offenses, if one does not perform the ritual of "purification by declaration" (*viśuddhi-uddeśa*), it is termed a "transgression of abstention" (*virati-āpatti*).

However, to possess [an item] beyond the permitted limit constitutes a "transgression of action" (*kriyā-āpatti*). These two types of transgression are identical in essence (*tattva*) though distinct in name;

they cannot be said to have separate names and essences. Regarding the two types of observance (*dhāraṇa*), they fully encompass both meanings: if one possesses [an item] and performs the purification by declaration, it is termed an "observance of action."

Regarding "observance" (dhāraṇa): by performing this practice, one does not commit an offense even when exceeding the limit; conversely, to do otherwise would constitute an offense—is this not "observance through restraint" (virati-dhāraṇa)?

This is likewise an offense. Their essential nature is one, though their names differ. If one strictly refrains from keeping [the robe], it is called "observance through restraint"; if one keeps it but performs the ritual of "purification" (viśuddhi), it is called "observance through performance" (kriyā-dhāraṇa).
These two types of observance differ both in name and essence. Their meaning regarding being separated from the robe is the same, so I shall not describe them at length here. From [this point]...
The remaining precepts consist of both abstinence-and-maintenance (*saṃvara*) and performance-and-transgression (*kriyā-āpatti*).

Alternatively, these seven precepts may be understood from the perspective of their distinct natures as being performance-and-transgression while abstinence-and-maintenance applies generally to all thirty-one precepts. The meaning of the subsequent two questions has already been clarified above.

Regarding subsequent transgressions (*punar-āpatti*): among these various precepts, there are none that constitute a "double offense" (*punar-āpatti*). There are four such cases: first, one instance of separation; second, one instance of begging for thread;
third, one instance of violating the rule regarding the inclusion of out-of-season items during the permitted season; and fourth, one instance of violating the requirement for a robe for the sick.

Second, there is no "double forfeiture" (*punar-nissaggiya*). Fourth, there is no "double mutual exchange" (*punar-parivattanā*). Sixth, there is no "double transgression" (*punar-atikrama*). Fifteenth, there is no "double acceptance" (*punar-samādāna*).

Regarding the reception [of the precepts]: among the preceding fourteen [rules], they are further like the "receiving of jewels. Herein, three precepts differ; the remainder are identical. Next, regarding the relinquishment and confession:
since there are no cotton mattresses, their relinquishment is entirely performed in the presence of the object and must ensure they are not destroyed.

The remaining meanings are largely the same and cannot be described in full detail. Next, regarding similarities and differences: there are eighteen precepts that both assemblies (monks and nuns) may commit equally; the remaining twelve precepts differ.

These are grouped into three categories. Regarding the precept on robes for the ill, there is a difference in whether it exists or not. Regarding the long bowl, the offense is the same but the conditions differ.

Among the remaining ten precepts, those for nuns are more serious while those for monks are lighter. Next, regarding those offenses committed spontaneously (*anupāta*): among the six types of transgressions, excluding those involving medicine, there are five;
and including the four cases of instructing others, there are nine precepts in total that may involve the possibility of spontaneous offense. For all other precepts, this does not apply.

Next, we shall separately explain the eighteen rules of common training (*sādhāraṇa-śikṣāpada*). This is the direct exposition of the *Śikṣāpada-mūla*; those points that differ from others will be explained individually one by one.
First, we shall analyze the rule concerning begging for ghee and oil. All material things that sustain the body must be used with moderation;

once obtained, they should be set aside, yet to seek further different items causes one's character to lack constancy, fosters greed and afflictive conditions, and invites irreproachable censure. Therefore, this rule was established.

Regarding the offense: there are six constituent conditions. First, it is a householder who is not a relative. Second, the request is made for one's own sake. Third, the clarified butter has already been requested and obtained.
Fourth, one does not use it but returns it to the owner. Fifth, one further seeks another object. Sixth, the offense is incurred when the object is received into one's hand.
The three phrases of the precept text can be understood through their explanation.
Next, the mutual use of the *śīla-śālā* (precept hall) and the *śīla-dhara* (precept keeper). Below this are four rules concerning mutual use; their explanations are all identical.
When a donor relinquishes property, their intention is already fixed, and according to principle, it must follow the intent of the gift and not be diverted or exchanged.

Now, to use it for other purposes deviates from the original intent of the donation, incurs public censure, and fosters greed; therefore, a sacred regulation was established. There are four specific conditions [for this offense]: first, the gift is for the *saṃgha* present before one's eyes.

Regarding the funds for the Poṣadha hall: first, excluding the funds for the hall of the Saṃgha of the four directions; second, knowing these are funds for that specific hall; third, receiving them and making them one’s own property;

fourth, diverting them for other uses constitutes an offense. The *Prātimokṣa* text has three phrases: first, the person; second, knowing the donor’s gift is distinct; third, diverting its use to incur the offense.
In the commentary, the first phrase is self-evident. The second and third are explained together. Within this combined section, there are three parts: first, clarifying the mutual [exchange].

Regarding the characteristics: originally, a hall was constructed, but it was diverted for use as clothing and entered into the relinquishment (*pratyāśraya*). If its original purpose was to provide clothing, yet it was diverted to build a hall, it would not be permissible to enter it into the relinquishment.
This text cites the principle of mutual exchange; therefore, they must be listed side by side. Next, the property of the Saṃgha is explained.

There are three phrases regarding Saṃgha property; this is the third, which definitively belongs to the Saṃgha present before one. It is different from the previous case of diverting Saṃgha property into one’s own possession. One should take [this meaning].

Regarding items not specifically assigned to the Saṃgha, these three types of objects may likewise be diverted and included in the forfeiture (*niḥsargika*). Next, the determination of the offense can be understood from this.

Furthermore, although the original request for food was designated as being for "peace and security," it may still be intended for providing to the assembly; or perhaps it was originally the intention of the donor to give it as an offering.
All [the merit] is redirected into equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Next is the private room; next is the communal hall for the Saṃgha. It is incorrect to refer to this as a "hall" (*táng*); examining the text, the character for "hall" does not appear.
It simply states that one may request permission to build a "house" (*wū*). Thus, although "hall" and "house" differ in name, they are identical in meaning.
Next is the precept on keeping an extra alms bowl (*atireka-pātra*). The intent of its formulation is the same as before. It possesses five distinct conditions:

first, one already possesses a bowl that is being used; second, one further obtains another bowl in accordance with the Dharma; third, it has not been declared pure (*avisuddha*); fourth, there is no valid reason [for keeping it]; and fifth, the offense is incurred after keeping it for more than one night. Question:
Why is it that nuns are permitted to keep an extra bowl for ten days, whereas monks are not? Answer: An ancient commentary states: First, because a nun...
This is a minor benefit. Once you have obtained a single bowl, you should immediately accept and maintain it, as well as perform the ritual of *śuddhi* (purity).

Why is it necessary to permit ten? A donor requires two; since there is already a companion, the rite of *śuddhi* can be performed. Why is it necessary to permit [the practice] for a day while seeking someone to perform the rite?

The great Saṃgha has many benefits, and a ten-day period is opened for them. This is because they require two people to deliberate upon the distribution of alms, and furthermore, there is no restriction regarding having a companion;

they delight in practicing the path alone. For these reasons, the ten-day period is not opened for them to seek companions for the *śuddhi-vyavahāra* (declaration of purity). Therefore, the cases are not the same.

If that is so, why is it that although there are two reasons why the ten-day period is not opened for Bhikṣuṇīs—namely, their possession of extra robes (*atireka-cīvara*)—there are also two reasons [for the case of the monks]? Why is this?
The ten-day period is granted for those who share [the robe] with the Saṃgha. The answer is that this bowl is for single use; logically, there should be no accumulation of many.

While there is no fault before it is completed, once it is completed, although its possession is prohibited, because one has a companion, one may immediately perform the *śuddhika-vyavahāra* (declaration of purity).

Therefore, the ten-day period is not granted for that case. As for a bhikṣu who lacks a companion, the ten-day period is granted. Regarding long robes and the use of requisites, even while they are not yet completed, there is indeed the fault of "excess" (*atireka*).
When mending a hairpin or a seam, it cannot be completed immediately. For this reason, a ten-day period is equally granted for both [the nun and the monk].

If one asks whether it is permissible to first declare the cloth as pure (*śuddha*) and only then begin making the robe, there is no doctrinal impediment to this. Why, then, must the ten-day period be granted simultaneously? Answer:

When the initial allowance was established, it was in response to a single nun who had not declared the cloth as pure; therefore, the ten-day period was granted so that she might wait for the robe to be finished. Once that initial allowance was made, [it applied to all].
In general, this applies to all three categories [of robes], and thus the ten-day limit is established for them. Furthermore, there is another point:

since nuns often live together, their "extra" robes (*atireka-cīvara*) are considered "co-owned," and they cannot perform the ritual of *śuddhika* (purification by declaration) because the items are used collectively. Therefore, it is necessary to find someone [to act as a witness], and the ten-day period is opened for them.

Although a bowl is also "co-owned," one may still perform the *śuddhika* ritual; because it has a companion [in the form of the ritual itself], it must be done on that very day, as there is no collective enjoyment of it. Now...

This is not the case. It is not necessarily the case that one obtains the "purification by direction" (*śuddhi*) through simultaneous birth; rather, it would cause an offense to be incurred on that very day.
However, because women have much greed for vessels and delight in hoarding them, the ten [rules] were not opened [for them] in order to subdue that greedy mind.

Furthermore, there is another interpretation: "Opening" means not opening again. Since the permission for sixteen vessels has already been granted, one is not permitted to keep more than that number of bowls;

if one were to keep them, one would incur an offense immediately upon the lapse of one night. Since the Sangha has not granted permission for sixteen vessels, if the limit were set at one night, it would be difficult to apply this to cases of urgent necessity or constant practice.

Another interpretation holds that the *niḥsīvana-bhikṣu* (extra bowl) was first prohibited for the community of nuns; one cannot, on account of the nuns, establish a rule for the monks. Subsequently, [the bowl] was entrusted...
The opening [of the rule] due to a specific occasion does not apply to the *bhikṣuṇī* precepts. If that is so, why is the long robe (*atireka-cīvara*) likewise permitted for ten days?

Answer: The circumstances regarding the long robe are identical; the lifting of the prohibition is uniform. However, the bowl constitutes a different circumstance, and thus the permission and the regulation differ.

This may be understood from the three phrases of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* and its commentary. According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, the possession of seven kinds of coarse bowls is permitted: first, for holding leftover drinks; second, for holding incense.
Third, for holding medicine; fourth, for holding leftover food; fifth, for removing saliva; sixth, for removing refuse;
seventh, for removing urine.
Beyond these, one may not keep more than sixteen vessels. Women have inferior resolve, and the practice of the Path is difficult; if these are not provided for, [the practice] cannot be sustained.
Because of the arising of such conduct, it was further permitted [to possess] sixteen additional items beyond the standard set of requisites for a worthy vessel (*pātra*).

Once these were sufficient according to the circumstances, one ought to advance in practice; however, because possessing more than this hinders the Path, it was prohibited. There are four conditions for this specific offense:

first, one already possesses the sixteen vessels; second, one further acquires a vessel; third, one does not perform the ritual of *viśuddhi* (purification); and fourth, one keeps it overnight, thereby committing the offense.

The three phrases of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* explain the characteristics [of these items], which may be understood accordingly. Regarding the "sixteen items": the two cauldrons refer to the large and small;
the two jars refer to the water jar and the washing jar; the four lids refer to one for each of the two cauldrons and two jars; the four basins consist of two large and two small;

and the four ladles likewise consist of two large and two small. These are permitted by the Buddha's allowance; all others must be given as pure gifts (*śuddha-dāna*). The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
Regarding "utensils," these refer to articles for sustaining life. It is permitted to keep only one jar each for storing ghee, oil, honey, incense, medicinal herbs, sauce, and vinegar.

Furthermore, it is permitted to keep one cauldron, one spit, and one hook, as well as a small bowl for storing cooked rice. Should one possess more than this, it constitutes an offense requiring forfeiture (niḥsargika-pāyattika).

Next, regarding the initial promise of a robe for the sick and the subsequent violation of the precept: Generally, the body is full of impurities; for women, these are redoubled, with monthly discharges that defile both the body and clothing.
If one does not provide protection, there will be no way to advance in spiritual cultivation. Having previously promised to provide one to another, it is only right that one should assist them;

yet now, by failing to keep one's word, one causes the other to suffer distress. Since this deviates from the Dharma and the rules, this regulation was established to prevent such conduct. This is the specific circumstance.
It possesses five factors: first, it is a robe for illness, distinguished from other articles of use; second, it was previously promised to another; third, the other person comes forward to take it;

fourth, there is no *an-antara-ya* (justification), namely, being subject to the two difficulties of being suspended for breaking the precepts and so forth; fifth, one commits an offense by not giving it to the other. These are the three phrases of the root text of the precept.
In the commentary, the relative weight of these and other garments is explained together for clarity.

Next, regarding the precept on accepting untimely gifts: although there are many types of giving, they may be categorized into two for the time being; since the objects are limited, [the scope is thus defined].

The distribution must accord with the proper ritual. If there is anything to be craved, one does not follow the holy teachings; to take what is an "out-of-season" object and receive it as if it were an "in-season" dharma-offering is a grave increase of evil.
Therefore, the holy regulations were established. This gift was originally intended for the proper season, yet the time period has already passed.

If one treats what belongs to the improper time (*akāla*) as being included within the rules for the proper time (*kāla*), yet during the improper time treats it as being included within the rules for the proper time, and thereby acquires this object, it constitutes an offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).
If one does not do so, it harms the Sangha regarding the improper time; when calculated, it constitutes a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*).
How could this not constitute a *pāyattika*? The *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, fascicle 12, states:

"If various bhikṣuṇīs accept out-of-season robes (*akālacīvara*) as in-season robes (*kālacīvara*), then visiting bhikṣuṇīs will be unable to obtain robes. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* divides this into two precepts:

[one for] accepting an out-of-season robe and treating it as an in-season robe, and [the other for] when the resident nun accepts an out-of-season robe and treats it as an out-of-season robe while the visiting nun commits the offense. The distinct conditions consist of four factors.

First, the items offered during the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat); second, entering the non-seasonal period; third, the method of distribution during the [appropriate] time; fourth, the offense incurred once the formal act of distribution is completed.
These can be understood through the three phrases of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* and their commentary.

Next is the precept against forcibly seizing after having completed a trade of robes. Regarding the trading of any goods, once the transaction has been finalized and concluded, to harbor anger and forcibly seize the item is contrary to the monastic code.
This constitutes a public disturbance that increases strife; as the transgression of intent is not slight, it was therefore necessary for the Sage to establish this prohibition.
There are six constituent conditions: first, there is a mutual trade; second, the price has already been fixed; third, there is a mind of anger.
1. Robbing by force. 2. Doing it oneself. 3. Instructing another to do it. 4. Without cause or condition—meaning there is no basis such as borrowing, entrusting, or lifting.

5. The offense is incurred when it enters one's hand. The three phrases of the *Prātimokṣa* Sūtra itself are: first, the person; second, the act of exchanging or trading; third, subsequently, out of anger, taking it back down from them, which constitutes the full offense. Explanation:
The allowance for trading is for the sake of those who share the same Dharma, so that they may avoid reproach and be free from the pursuit of gain.
This causes vexation because it deprives others of what is currently present or not yet present. In the text, the offense is concluded with two distinct phrases;

the remaining characteristics are easily understood. Next is the precept against begging for heavy robes: It is the principle of renunciation that one should direct the mind toward transcending worldly burdens. Yet, even regarding the acceptance of material requisites, one must conform to proper ritual decorum.
How could one fail to guard the Path and instead indulge extensively in greedy desires, rashly soliciting heavy robes? This brings harm to both oneself and others.

Because of these faults, a regulation was established to prevent them. Question: What is the difference between this and the previous precept regarding begging for robes from those who are not relatives?
Answer: There are three points of distinction. First, in the previous precept, one commits an offense by simply begging; there is no offense when invited according to one's own wish (*svacchandena*).

In this case, one commits an offense by seeking more than what is permitted within the context of being invited according to one’s own wish. Second, in the previous precept, one commits an offense upon obtaining a single strip of cloth; here, it is an offense upon obtaining sixteen strips or more.

Regarding the offense: while the three preceding precepts exclude relatives, this precept applies whether the recipient is a relative or not; thus there are these three distinctions, and for this reason two separate precepts are established.

The specific conditions comprise five factors: first, a layperson makes a voluntary invitation; second, one requests heavy robes; third, one requests an excessive amount, namely sixteen strips or more; fourth, it is for one's own sake;

and fifth, the robes have come into one's possession—this constitutes the offense. The textual account of the commission of the offense has two parts: first, when the recipient is not a relative; second, when the recipient is a relative.
Each may request as they wish; however, to seek more than one's share constitutes an offense. Regarding the three phrases in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, the commentary states:
"The sixteen strips" refers to the fact that four layers are spread out, each consisting of four strips, thus totaling sixteen. The remaining characteristics can be understood accordingly.

Next is the precept on begging for light clothing. The intent behind its formulation and the requisite conditions are identical to the preceding precepts; the only difference is that it concerns light clothing.
A detailed description would be too prolix.

● Next, we clarify the one hundred and seventy-eight *pāyattika* offenses of individual application (*ekottarika*). First, a general summary is provided, followed by an analysis according to five categories.
First, performing [an act] oneself and instructing others; second, the distinction between prohibitions and natures; third, the procedures for maintaining and violating [the precepts];

fourth, the similarities and differences between the two divisions [of the Vinaya]; and fifth, the spontaneous [application] for the lower assemblies. Regarding the first gate—performing oneself and instructing others—the stages are divided into four.
First, there are two types of precepts that consist solely of the karma of instructing others: namely, instruction and incantations (*mantra*), as well as worldly arts and crafts.
The first [section] concerns seizing white-robed persons. The second contains eleven precepts; whether committed by oneself or taught to others, both parties incur the offense. These are:
digging, destroying, pulling [beings], the two types of insects, fearing, large stores, killing, slandering, seizing, and treasure—this is the eleventh. The third contains eleven precepts.

Regarding the actual commission of an offense, there are five cases where it is identical to the precept: the two concerning private and public places, the spreading of bedding, the high-legged bed, and the cotton-wool mattress exceeding the prescribed measure, as well as the bathing robe.
There are six cases where it is not identical: the five concerning the application of ointments to the body, and during the *varṣā* retreat, the act of forcibly ejecting another from a room.
If one instructs another to perform an act that brings benefit to oneself, then the offense is identical; it is no different from committing it oneself. If...

If one teaches others without personal benefit, one incurs only a *duṣkṛta* (吉羅); thus, these cases differ from those involving actual transgression. Consequently, these two categories together comprise twenty-two precepts that share the sense of being transgressions [when teaching others].
In the fourth category, there are one hundred and fifty-four remaining; for these, committing them oneself constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* (提), whereas teaching others results only in a *duṣkṛta*.

Next, regarding the distinction between prohibitive (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*) and essential (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) offenses: there are thirty-six precepts that are essentially evil, such as those concerning the Saṃgha.

There are thirty precepts that constitute the nature [of the offenses]. These are: lying, slander, the two types of coarse speech, causing dissension, malicious enticement, using derisive speech, driving away, admonishing, threatening to kill, leading, doubting, exposing, initiating, speaking in accordance with [the offense], following [the instruction], expelling, rejecting, slandering, acting in concert, desiring, regretting, listening, striking, gambling, and slandering.

Among these, excluding the precept regarding the improper instruction of a teacher, there are twenty-nine remaining. Of these, seven do not correspond [to the standard categories], namely: excessive washing and cleansing, and the barbarian... [text fragment].

Adhesive. Striking one another. During the summer, leading others out of the room. The householder’s son Śikṣānanda violating the Sangha’s three admonitions. Reviling bhikṣus and reviling the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs.

All other such precepts are likewise subsumed under the category of prohibitions (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*). Next, regarding the stages of observance and violation, they may be divided into three positions.
First, there are twenty-three precepts that possess both aspects of observance and violation; among these, there are ten shared precepts, namely, those concerning speaking...

There are twelve distinct grave offenses (*sthūlātyaya*): taking food before or after the [proper] time, taking a pure cloth (*kappiyabhaṇḍa*) at will, storing [food] in the open air, and entering a village at an improper time during monastic affairs while having granted one's consent (*chanda*). There are eleven instances of "taking at will," which are grouped into five pairs:
first, sitting at will in a layperson's house and [the offense of] *jīvitavipatti*; second, staying overnight at will and departing; third... [and so forth].
The pair concerning opening the *nīla-dvāra* (blue gate) at sunset and after the sun has set; the pair concerning wearing another’s robe and lancing an abscess;
the pair concerning entering a monastery by force and inquiring into the meaning [of the Dharma]; the single item concerning entering a village at night;
