furthermore, the three items concerning wandering during the three periods of the day, taking only a small portion [of food], and keeping a retinue during the summer retreat—these twenty-three precepts are all designated as *dharmas of cessation*, meaning they must not be performed.

To cease transgression is called "observance" (*samvara*); when there is a violation in the performance of an action, it is called "transgression" (*āpatti*). These two terms refer to the same essence but differ in name.

When discussing the two types of observance, they fully encompass both meanings, which is why this can be understood. Second, there are nineteen precepts that consist solely of observance through action and cessation of transgression.

One is a common precept, namely not listening in on others' private conversations. The remaining eighteen are uncommon precepts; with respect to their reception, there are five [categories], namely: taking...
1. Not conferring full ordination upon one who has not yet been provided with robes; 2. Not granting two years of training in the precepts; 3. Not reciting the names of the six rules; 4.

Not conferring full ordination upon one who has already completed the *śikṣamāṇā* training; 5. Having performed the formal ritual (*dharmakarma*) and stayed overnight, then proceeding to the assembly of monks (*bhikṣusaṃgha*).

There are five violations of the eight rules that must not be transgressed: namely, not requesting [permission], not listening [to instructions], not being left to one's own will, and not relying on the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*).
Not paying homage; furthermore, there are eight [faults] regarding other matters: not remaining with one's preceptor for two years; not participating in another's *posadha*;
not observing the rains retreat (*varṣā*); not departing when expelled; not receiving disciples through the two methods of instruction;

not tending to the illness of a fellow resident nun; not departing after the conclusion of the rains retreat; and not escorting a courtesan more than five or six *yojanas* away. These are the rules of conduct.

This constitutes observance; for by merely abstaining, one avoids transgression. Regarding the remaining one hundred and thirty-six precepts of the third category, abstention constitutes observance, whereas action constitutes transgression.
Next, concerning their similarities and differences, they are likewise divided into three stages. First, there are three precepts where the presence or absence [of the offense] differs.
This refers to: excessive washing; animal glue; receiving the precepts among the great *saṃgha* after having stayed overnight;

the two cases where there are four precepts [for monks] but [only] two for nuns, where the offense is the same but the conditions differ—namely, the precept on food from non-Buddhists, lay clothing, accepting invitations while turning one's back, and a girl under age receiving the precepts.

Regarding all other precepts, those heavy for nuns are light for monks. This is stated by way of classification; for example, although the act of shaving body hair is the same, the names of the offenses differ.

They differ. Furthermore, regarding concealment, its breadth or narrowness, disparagement, and double-tongued speech, as well as staying overnight with a man or sitting in a secluded place—these involve a reversal of the objective sphere (*viṣaya*).
Such categories can be understood through reflection. Next, concerning those that occur spontaneously (*svarasa-vāhin*):

among the aforementioned twenty-four precepts involving teaching others to commit offenses, one specifically selects eleven precepts, such as digging the earth and destroying [vegetation], which are exclusively [of this nature].

Regarding those offenses committed simultaneously: [the rules concerning] high beds, cotton-wool (tūla), oversized bathing robes, and evicting another from their room during the *varṣā* retreat—these constitute fifteen precepts that possess the sense of "spontaneous" (*anuparivartin*) application.

Excluding the two regarding sorcery, the two regarding private and public bedding, and the five regarding anointing the body—these nine lack spontaneous application because they involve direct confrontation with the object of the act, even though one may cause another to perform them;
thus, while there is the sense of an offense being incurred, there is no spontaneous application.

Next, below, there are sixty-nine rules of common precepts (*samāna-śīla*). The root texts (*mūla*) of these precepts are listed directly; those that differ from the others will be explained in sequence.
First, we clarify the seventieth rule: the precept against eating garlic (*lasuna*). Garlic is not fragrant or pure; it defiles the gateway to the Path for those who advance in cultivation.

For a human being, it is logically appropriate to permanently sever [these attachments]. Yet now, out of greed for delicious flavors, one consumes these pungent spices; this harms the Path and invites reproach, and thus it was necessary for the Sage to establish this prohibition.

There are three specific conditions [for this offense]: first, the exclusion of all other pungent substances; second, the absence of a medical necessity; and third, the commission of the offense upon eating them.
The conditions for the offense may be understood [from the preceding]. In the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, three phrases are given;

in the commentary, those that are raw, cooked, or mixed, etc., are all declared *pāyattika*. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Sengqi lü), fascicle 38, states: "As for *nala*, it refers to *nala*-grass, *nala*-mountain *nala*, and so forth—none of these types of *nala* are permitted to be eaten. Regarding the more serious cases of cooked or raw [meat], even if burned to ashes, they are not permitted.
However, if there is a sore on the body, it is permitted to apply [the ash]; having applied it, one should remain in a secluded place. [Regarding] the sore...
After they had been thoroughly washed, they were permitted to enter the assembly. (From the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, Chapter 12).
Various bhikṣuṇīs consumed raw and cooked bamboo shoots before, during, and after the midday meal; whether eating them alone or mixed with other food, the dwellings became foul-smelling.
The laypeople criticized and disparaged this, so a regulation was immediately established: eating raw bamboo shoots is a *pāyattika* offense; eating cooked bamboo shoots is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

Next, one should shave the hair of the three places. Next, the four minor precepts are set forth; the transgressions and damages incurred therein are identical. All of these grow from the source of desire and equally violate the Noble Path.
However, for those who have turned their backs on worldly life and aspire to renunciation, it is logically necessary to sever thoughts of desire and forever cut off the heart of attachment.

Furthermore, regarding the hair of the three places, there are three specific conditions that must be met: first, it must be the hair of the three places; second, it must not be for the sake of curing illness or for the sake of physical strength.

[The section on] "Holding" (grasping). Third, the determination of the offense according to one's capacity; the textual characteristics are easily understood. A bhikṣu directly incurs a *sthūlātyaya* based on the obstruction of the Path.

Next, the precept concerning excessive cleansing: there are four conditions. First, cleansing with water. Second, having a defiled mind—that is, performing this act for the sake of satisfying sensual desire.
Third, lacking a valid cause—that is, it is not an offense if one has an illness or removes parasites. Fourth, excessiveness.
Regarding the limit of washing: the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Sengqi), fascicle 40, states: "As for the method of washing, it may extend no further than one finger-joint; it must not exceed this.

If one washes beyond this limit in order to quench lustful thoughts, it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense. This is called the method of washing. The *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra* (Jialun), fascicle 6, states:

If a bhikṣu has not declared that he will void urine or excrement, he must not perform prostrations, nor may he sit or lie upon the bedding and seats belonging to the Saṃgha, except in places where water is unavailable.
This also applies when he is being rebuked by non-humans, when he is being rebuked by the water deities, or when he is taking medicine.

Next, regarding the training rule concerning the use of gum-arabic to create a male form: there are four specific conditions. First, the materials—gum-arabic, beeswax, and other substances such as rice or parched grain flour;
second, the creation of a male form; third, the absence of illness; and fourth, the internal emission of semen. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Sengqi lü), fascicle 40, states:
Regarding "figures made of lacquer": each [figure] is made of lacquer, or each is made of copper, lead, tin, or white wax; or each is made of lacquer and honey.
To create such things as these for the purpose of satisfying lustful desires constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense. This is called "figures made of lacquer. (*Pañcavargika-vinaya*)
If a bhikṣuṇī inserts the male organ into the female organ, it is a pāyattika. If she inserts it within, it is a pāyattika;
if impurity is emitted, it is a sthūlātyaya.
Next, regarding the precept on slapping: according to the *Pañcavargika*, if one slaps with the hand, it is a pāyattika for the act of slapping; if impurity is emitted, it is a sthūlātyaya.
*Rāca*. Next is the precept on providing water and fans to healthy bhikṣus. Although the monastic robes are identical, the forms of monks and nuns differ.

In their conduct and deportment when coming and going, they must avoid censure and reproach. Now, to suddenly provide water and fans for the great assembly of monks is a source of no small disgrace; therefore—

This must be established by the Noble One. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, section thirty-eight: If a bhikṣuṇī carries a water vessel but does not carry a fan, she commits a *duṣkṛta* offense;
if she carries a fan but does not carry a vessel, she also commits a *duṣkṛta* offense; if she carries both, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense; if she carries neither, there is no offense.
This offense applies to one bhikṣu and one bhikṣuṇī; if many bhikṣus [are involved], there is no offense. If among the multitude there are parents...
[Regarding] this: there is no offense for [receiving] *śaṇa* fiber.
Next is the precept against begging for raw grain and so forth. Those who have left the household life should practice the alms-round well;

yet now they beg for raw grain and such things, which invite ridicule and disgrace, causing agitation and hindering spiritual cultivation. Therefore, the Noble One’s regulation was necessary. Whether begging from relatives or...
There is no offense for a renunciant who begs, whether for another’s sake, on behalf of oneself, or obtains it without begging. The distinct conditions consist of four factors:
first, the house of one who is not a relative; second, raw grain, wheat, and so forth; third, for one's own sake; and fourth, the offense is incurred according to the act of begging.
Next, regarding defecating or urinating upon living grass: all plants and trees are relied upon by both humans and non-humans for their common use.
To now void excrement or urine upon them invites deep censure; therefore, the Noble One established this prohibition. This rule is contingent upon four specific conditions:
first, it must be living grass; second, it must be a place where many people gather; third, one must not be ill or otherwise exempted; and fourth, [the act must be done] intentionally.
If one lives upon [the plants] growing on top of the four [types of trees], one commits an offense. Question: This regulation already exists within the *Śaikṣa* rules;
I do not know how this differs from that. An ancient interpretation states: "Within the *Śaikṣa* rules, this one precept should be excluded. My current interpretation is not so.
Here, it refers to living upon *śālu* grass and *kālānusārī* grass; because it must be a place where many people gather, one incurs a *thullaccaya* offense. Regarding the *Śaikṣa*...
The training rules for this category are largely the same as those preceding it;
however, they conclude with the precept on "not discarding impurities outside the wall while looking. In all activities one undertakes, one must act with careful deliberation.

To speak of discarding excrement or urine without first observing whether anyone is present, and thereby recklessly causing defilement and pollution to others, is a transgression of no small gravity; therefore, this is required.

The Noble Regulation: An offense is established through three conditions: first, the act of defecation; second, not looking outward; and third, the act of discarding [the waste] constitutes the offense.

Next is the precept regarding watching performances and music: those who have left the household life ought to maintain quiet contemplation for the sake of salvation, binding their minds to guard the Path.
This is precisely in accord with the proper regulations. Now, observing performances and music obstructs and ruins correct cultivation and invites not insignificant censure;

therefore, the Noble One established a prohibition. There are four specific conditions: first, various forms of playful amusement; second, going intentionally to observe them; third, having no other compelling circumstances;

and fourth, seeing them upon arrival constitutes an offense. According to the *Jianlun* (Treatise on Seeing), there are sixteen cases; even down to watching monkeys and peacocks playing together, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense for going to see them.
*Nyati*. If one goes to watch a performance within a monastery, there is no offense.

Other instances may be understood by analogy. Next is the eighty-first precept: regarding entering a secluded place with a man and conversing. Since men and women are distinct, it is logically improper for them to associate.
To enter a secluded place recklessly allows for the arising of defilement and impurity. The remaining principles are as stated above. The specific conditions consist of five factors: first, a person.

The term "man" (puruṣa) applies to both monastics and laypeople. In the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, regarding the precepts concerning entering secluded places, entering exposed places, and whispering to a companion, three rules are established for monks, and another three are established for laypeople and non-Buddhists;
thus, the total number of rules in this category is six. From this, it is known that these apply to both monastics and laity.
Other rules concerning secluded places and the like are all explained in the same manner. Second, [the distinction between] secluded places where one is out of sight and hearing.
Third, there is no third person present. Fourth, there is no causal condition. One does not commit an offense in cases of two difficulties, such as illness or lack of physical strength.

Fifth, speaking directly constitutes an offense; because this involves speaking directly with a mind free from defilement, it is a *thullaccaya*. If there is a defiled mind, it falls under the previous eight matters. If one stands upright without speaking, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
Regarding the *dukkaṭa* for a bhikkhu, it is incurred simply by provoking derision. If there is another bhikkhu who commits the offense [of deriding], he likewise incurs a *dukkaṭa*.
The explanations for all [the following] are the same as this.
Next is the precept regarding entering a secluded place with a man. Question: What is the difference between this and the preceding precept? Answer:

In the preceding precept, one commits the offense only by means of speech when the screen is out of sight or hearing; in this case, it is committed even without speech when there is a covering or enclosure. This is the distinction.

The same applies here; therefore, two precepts are established. There are five conditions that constitute an offense: first, a male person; second, a concealed place; third, the absence of a third person;

fourth, the absence of circumstances such as serious illness or the two kinds of difficulties; and fifth, the act of entering constitutes the offense. Regarding the establishment of positions, it is auspicious not to walk [into the space];
however, if one sits, it constitutes an offense immediately. Sitting together [in such a place] is a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation).
Next, the precept concerning whispering in a secluded place while sending a companion away from a man: this also involves being secluded from sight and hearing;
it differs only in that one sends a companion away to a distance and whispers. Five conditions constitute an offense: first, a male person; second, being secluded from sight and hearing;
third, sending a companion away to a distance, meaning departing from the companion’s range of sight and hearing; fourth, the absence of any mitigating circumstances such as an emergency.
This includes [the offenses of] "raising" and "expelling" a companion, as well as the fifth: the precept against sitting and whispering in the ear, which constitutes an offense immediately.
Next is the precept against departing from a layperson’s house without taking leave after having sat there. Those who have left the household life are guests from beyond the mundane world;

when coming and going on their travels, their conduct must accord with the Dharma. Now, to sit in another's home and depart without bidding farewell is to act in a manner identical to [worldly] secular people.

The conduct of a thief: how could this constitute the etiquette of a guest? Because of this, the host’s seat is damaged; the trouble caused by such an act is not slight. Therefore, the Sage established a rule.

There are five conditions that constitute an offense: first, it must be the house of a layperson (*avadātavasana*); second, one tells the host to sit on a fine seat; third, one departs without taking leave;
fourth, there is no valid reason [for the departure]; and fifth, the offense is committed the moment one steps out the door.
Next is the precept against sitting on another’s bed without permission. Since a bed has an owner, one must consult them before sitting; to sit without asking is entirely improper.
There are five conditions for its transgression: first, it is in the house of a layperson; second, it is a fine bed; third, one does not inform the owner;
fourth, there is no valid reason; and fifth, one sits down, thereby committing the offense.

Next, the precept against staying overnight at the house of a layperson without asking: to stay overnight in another's dwelling without informing the host is considered behavior identical to that of a thief;

therefore, it is not permitted. An offense is established through five conditions: first, it must be the house of a layperson; second, one does not inform the host; third, bedding and seating are prepared;
fourth, there is no valid reason [for staying]; and fifth, the act is completed by remaining there.
Next is the precept against entering a dark room with a man. The aforementioned "screened place" is a location that is enclosed but possesses light;
therefore, there is no offense if a third person is present. This, however, is a "dark room," which is utterly devoid of light; thus, even if it is daytime, [the offense applies].
The offense arises from a deep-seated transgression. Even if there are many people present, it is still an offense for him. Other characteristics are the same; this is what distinguishes it.
An offense is established through four conditions: first, a male person; second, a dark room without windows or light; third, the absence of a valid cause or reason.
The fourth entry constitutes an immediate offense.

Next is the precept on not receiving the teacher’s words with careful scrutiny: Whenever one receives the teacher’s instructions, one must necessarily examine them with precision, clearly memorize and retain them, and carry out the commands exactly as spoken.
How could one mistakenly receive the teacher’s words and transmit them erroneously with a negligent mind? Such a transgression is unforgivable; therefore—

It must be established by the Noble One. There are four specific conditions: first, the teacher instructs according to the Dharma; second, the recipient does not examine or verify with clarity; third, one transmits words to dispatch a thief;
fourth, the verbal expression is distinct and clear.

Next is the precept against cursing with a mind of anger. Those who have left the household life should give rise to virtuous vows, seeking to deliver themselves and others so that both self and others may benefit.
Now, to instead curse them into the three evil realms and cause them to abandon the Buddha-dharma creates deep defilements and obstructions;

therefore, this rule is established. An offense is completed through three conditions: first, the presence of a mind of anger; second, the act of cursing; third, the words reaching the ear [of the victim]. This is what is taught in the commentary.
"Namo Buddhāya" means invoking the Buddha as a witness. The Buddha possesses great compassion and the knowledge of others' minds.
If I were to deceive you, I would be the same as deceiving the Buddha. If this matter is not false, may he know my intent.
Next, due to a particular incident, he beat his breast and wept out of anger. One who has left the household life ought, by principle, to advance toward the Path with an empty mind;

even if encountering vexing circumstances, one must regulate them with the Dharma. Now, unable to endure the matter, he weeps and beats his breast—this violates the protocols of the Path and therefore requires a sacred regulation.
There are four constituent conditions: first, there is a contentious matter that was not properly managed; second, there is anger; third, there is no [other] cause.

The conditions: according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*, fascicle four, the four assemblies are not permitted to weep even when a member of their own group dies, let alone when parents pass away;
this is prohibited in all cases. For the four assemblies, [violating this] constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing); for a nun (*bhikṣuṇī*), it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense).

Next is the Ninetieth Precept: Lying on the Same Bed with One Who is Unclothed. If two people lie on the same bed, there is the potential for the arising of defiled habits, which will ruin one’s own mental conduct and obstruct the practice of the Path.
An offense is established through four conditions: first, they are on the same bed; second, they are naked;
third, there is no valid cause or condition—excluding cases of illness or emergencies; and fourth, the offense is committed as soon as one lies down.
Next is the precept concerning sharing a bedding. Sharing a bedding together causes defilement and habituation to increase, which harms the Path and invites censure;
therefore, this must also be regulated.

Next is the precept concerning verbal actions that distress others. It is the principle of those who have left the household life that they should be like water and milk—harmonious and in accord with one another. Not...

This disturbs the natural harmony of human feelings. When public officials provoke one another, both sides neglect their cultivation; therefore, a sacred regulation is required. There are four specific conditions for this offense:
first, knowing that the bhikṣuṇī arrived after oneself; second, having the intentional purpose of causing annoyance;
third, reciting the sūtras or inquiring about their meaning while standing before her; and fourth, the words being clearly articulated.

Next is the precept against neglecting the illness of a co-resident nun. When a patient is suffering together with others, she must be attended to; if one fails to provide such care, her illness will worsen.
Furthermore, since the bond of living together is significant, one might still lack compassion; yet, if one were to recite mantras for another person, they would be able to give rise to mercy.
The offense is established through three conditions: first, the person is a co-resident nun; second, there is no valid reason—namely, being ill oneself or facing the two types of hardship.
[And so forth. These three constitute an offense if one does not look [before acting].

Next is the precept concerning evicting another from their room during the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat). Once it has been agreed that one is to remain in a room for the retreat and the period is fixed, it is improper to move them during the summer months.
This bhikṣuṇī disregards others and treats the Dharma with contempt; even if driven by anger, she expels them, causing grave distress.

The Vinaya rules state that there are five factors for this specific offense: first, it must be a monastic dwelling that has been assigned to oneself; second, one has previously permitted another to stay there; third, one expels them out of a mind of anger;

fourth, there is no valid reason—meaning the person is not one who has broken the precepts or has been subject to formal censure or suspension; fifth, the offense is committed the moment they pass through the door. Question:

In the previous rule concerning the expulsion of a monk during the spring or winter, the infraction was a *thullaccaya* (grave offense). Why is it only a *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing) in this case? Answer: Because in the former case, it was during the spring or winter...

Regarding the *śayanāsana* (lodging): it carries the sense of being used in common. To drive someone out causes heavy affliction; thus, for both monks and nuns, this constitutes a *thullaccaya* (grave offense).

If the lodging belongs to oneself, the other person has no share in it; because the affliction is slight, it is a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing). This differs from the case of [driving out] a nun. If that is so, the principle for nuns is the same.

Why then is the gravity [of the offense] biased toward one side? An old commentary states: Monks have two aspects: first, they have no fixed allotment of rooms; second, they do not incur the offense of staying alone. Because the affliction is slight, it is light. As for nuns, however—

There are cases where one may commit the offense of *pṛthag-vāsa* (living alone), leading to distress and the return to lay life; thus, one incurs a *thullaccaya* offense. However, the current interpretation is not so. It is not because of residing alone that one is expelled and the offense is grave.
In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it merely states that by causing distress, the person returns to lay life; it does not say that expulsion constitutes the commission of the *pṛthag-vāsa* offense.
This is because during the rainy season retreat (*vassa*), bhikṣus who know the Dharma rarely expel others; therefore, one only incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense. For bhikṣuṇīs, however, it is frequent.
Deluded regarding the Dharma, they take pleasure in giving rise to jealousy and cast out those who possess the correct principles;

therefore, they incur a *thullaccaya* offense. Next is the precept against wandering about without purpose during the three periods [of the day]. For one who advances on the Path, it is logical to cease from worldly affairs;

to wander about aimlessly and dissipate oneself hinders and ruins right practice. Furthermore, it involves taking life, wasting one's own resources, and inviting irreproachable censure; thus, this must be strictly observed by the Noble Ones.
The regulation: The separate conditions consist of three factors. First, wandering during the three seasons of spring, summer, and winter.

Second, being without a valid reason—except for cases such as acting on behalf of the Three Jewels, attending to a sick nun, or facing difficulties regarding the observance day, which do not constitute an offense. Third, crossing a boundary.

Next is the precept against departing after having accepted an invitation for the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat). Originally, one was invited to provide offerings with the expectation that [the retreat] would take place during the summer months.

Now, because the time limit has long passed and one does not depart, it not only increases greed and craving, but also constitutes extreme shamelessness. The distress caused to others is no small matter;
therefore, the Sage’s regulation is necessary. There are four constituent conditions: first, having accepted the invitation for the *varṣā*; second, following [the schedule] either before or after...

The period of the *varṣā* retreat has concluded. There are three circumstances under which one is exempt from the offense: namely, illness, lack of a companion, or the two types of difficulties (*dvi-kaṣṭa*). Fourth, not remaining away for even a single night;
the principle of the "sage's clear signs" (*ārya-prakāśa-liṅga*) serves as the boundary, though this is omitted in the text.
Next is the precept regarding wandering in places of fear at the borders. Border regions are rugged and treacherous, serving as the haunts of bandits.

If a *bhikṣuṇī* wanders about there recklessly, she may suffer defilement or harm; therefore, wandering in such places is strictly prohibited. To now willfully violate this rule constitutes an offense of *thullaccaya*.

The specific conditions for this offense consist of three factors: first, it is a place of fear and danger on the border; second, there is no invitation or other such valid reason; and third, she travels beyond [the permitted limits].
Regarding the offense of the realm:
receiving the precept for wandering within a territory where there is fear; the formulation of the rule is the same as before.

Next is the training concerning the precept against associating with a householder’s son despite the Sangha’s three admonitions; there are three points regarding the intent of the formulation. First, it is not permitted to associate.
Recently, as the forms of men and women differ, it is logically impossible for them to intermingle. To associate closely with one another is feared to cause great harm.

Next, regarding those whose intentions must be admonished: since the Buddha permitted the keeping [of such items] through pure giving (*śuddha-dāna*) to lay donors (*dānapati*), some may see this as a pretext for worldly people and, being comforted by such pleasant words, refuse to live separately because they cling to these things.
Fearing that through this they might give rise to defiled attachment (*rāga*), the Sangha must provide admonition and open [the path of correction].

This demonstrates what is right and what is wrong, intending to cause one to recognize the right and cultivate it, and to know the wrong and abandon it. The intent behind the subsequent summary of the offense can be understood accordingly. Question:

Previously, for approaching a woman in a familiar manner, the offense for violating a formal admonition was grave; why is this offense for approaching a man in a similar manner reversed and considered light?
Answer: The former case involves those who are defiled and of the same class, whereas this case involves those who are undefiled and of a different class;

therefore, it is rare. Because they act with such rarity and their conduct is dissimilar, the gravity of the offense is also unequal. There are six specific conditions for this: first, dwelling in close association with the son of a householder;

second, being admonished by a bhikṣuṇī acting in accordance with the Dharma to live separately; third, remaining dependent on him and not relinquishing that association; fourth, [being addressed by] the Saṃgha acting in accordance with the Dharma... [and so forth].

[He] offered admonitions. Five times [the king] refused and would not comply. Sixth, the intent of the triple *karmavācanā* was concluded. The explanation of the text may be understood as above. Next, the hundredth precept:
Regarding the viewing of royal palaces, gardens, groves, and bathing pools. Royal palaces are magnificent, their affairs equaling those of the devas.

To go there to view them now would cause one to neglect the cultivation of right practice; furthermore, there is the fear of becoming defiled by worldly matters, thereby ruining one’s own mental conduct and causing harm.

This led to public censure. To prevent it, the Buddha prohibited it. There are four specific conditions for this offense: first, it must be a bathing pool within a royal palace; second, one must go there with the intention of looking at it;
third, there must be no other valid reason; and fourth, the offense is committed as soon as one sees it.
Next is the precept against bathing with the body exposed in river water. A woman’s form is base; it must be shielded and concealed.
Now, to intentionally expose the body invites censure and harms the Way. An offense is established through four conditions: first, river water; second, bathing with the body exposed;
third, having no valid reason; and fourth, washing the entire body.

Next is the precept concerning an oversized bathing robe (*snāna-śāṭikā*); the commentary is the same as the preceding one, with the sole difference being that it is called a "bathing robe. Furthermore, there is no limit to its use.
Next is the precept concerning sewing a *saṃghāṭī* during the proper time for more than five days: when making a robe for another, it ought to be finished early.
If one is motivated by a desire for gain and offerings, it will not be accomplished either quickly or over a long period; furthermore, it will deplete clothing and wealth, causing distress to others.

Since such a mental transgression is not minor, the Noble One established this prohibition. There are five specific conditions: first, making a robe for another; second, doing so during the proper season;

third, it is a *saṃghāṭī*; fourth, there is no valid reason; and fifth, exceeding five days. Logically, the "appearance of light" (*āloka*) should be taken as the limit for the completion of the act. This is sought in the text.
The *saṃghāṭī* is the robe of the nun who owns it. Regarding the "arising of the six difficulties," this refers to the nun who makes the robe.
As for the six difficulties, the Mother [Mahāprajāpatī] said: first, parents; second, brothers and sisters; third, the six types of relatives; fourth, kings and ministers;
fifth, thieves; and sixth, wild beasts.

Next, there is the precept against failing to inspect the saṃghāṭī for five days. Although all three robes may serve as monastic attire, the great robe (saṃghāṭī) is of high value and requires considerable effort to procure.
If it is not inspected and maintained for a long time, it may suffer damage; thus, its utility for sustaining the body would be lost.

Therefore, the noble regulations must be observed. An offense is established through three conditions: first, it must be the *saṃghāṭī* (outer robe), excluding all others; second, the place where it is left is not secure;

and third, more than five days pass without looking after it. Regarding the determination of the time limit for this rule, it is likewise reckoned by the appearance of dawn. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, failing to look after the five robes for five nights constitutes a *pāyattika*.

The Precept on Obstructing the Distribution of Robes to the Sangha: When practicing the Way and establishing one’s conduct, it is logically necessary to benefit others and diminish one's own attachments.
Upon seeing another person giving, one ought to assist and praise them. Now, however, [the monk] instead acts with stinginess regarding the property of others, causing them not to give to the Sangha;

thus both parties are harmed. Therefore, the Sage established this prohibition. The specific conditions for its violation consist of four factors: first, the donor intends to give; second, one knows that the donor intends to give; third, one encourages [the donor] not to give; [fourth, the gift is withheld].
Regarding the precept on accepting gifts: if one accepts the encouragement to cease [other activities] based on the four reliances (*catur-apāśraya*), one commits an offense.
Next is the precept on wearing another's robe without permission. To wear another's robe without authorization is identical in appearance to the marks of a thief;

it invites slander from others and fails to distinguish between the pure and the defiled. Furthermore, it causes the owner to feel distress, thinking they have lost their property. Because the emotional transgression is so grave, the Sage established this separate rule.
The conditions for this [offense] consist of three factors: first, it is another’s robe; second, one does not ask the owner; third, upon wearing it, one commits the offense.
Next is the precept regarding giving robes to laypeople or non-Buddhists; the intent of the prohibition is the same as before. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Sengqi lü), fascicle 38, states:

"To give a robe with one's own hand to a layperson, a non-Buddhist, or a śramaṇa constitutes a pāyattika offense. The specific conditions for this consist of four factors: first, it is someone who is not a relative.
First, a layperson or an outsider; second, a robe belonging to a śramaṇa; third, holding it and handing it to them; fourth, upon their receiving it, one commits an offense. Question:

Why is it not permitted to place the robe on the ground and give it? Answer: Because the robes of a śramaṇa are distinct [from those of others]. Even if one were permitted to place it on the ground and send someone else to deliver it, it would still incur censure and damage [to the Sangha's reputation].
Therefore, it is not permitted. This is unlike the case of food, which is not subject to such restrictions because there is no difference in its nature; thus, it is permitted and allowed.
A person has placed [the robes] on the ground.
Next, regarding the rule against obstructing the Sangha from distributing the robes according to the Dharma:

when the Sangha is in harmony and intends to distribute the donated robes, it is proper that they follow the principles in detail and allow for no discord or division. Now, as a disciple, you are obstructing the Sangha’s distribution of robes, thereby causing distress to the assembly.

Because it is a minor offense, it must be regulated by the rules of the Noble Ones (*ārya*). There are five specific conditions [for this offense]: first, the Sangha has obtained an object of offering; second, there is a desire to share and take possession of it; third, the assembly is gathered in harmony;

fourth, there is a fear that the disciples will not receive their share, leading to a prohibition against dividing it; fifth, failing to divide it constitutes an offense. Regarding the phrase "dividing at an improper time" in the section on permissions:
it refers to a time when the community of nuns has not yet assembled, such as when a *śrāmaṇerī* is present.

Next is the precept against obstructing the Saṃgha from distributing the *kaṭhina* robe. When the community of monks is in harmony and proceeds to distribute the *kaṭhina* robe, it is proper that they follow the principles in detail and perform the ritual together.
Now, out of greed for the five benefits, one obstructs them so that the robe is not distributed; because this causes deep distress to the assembly, the Noble One has established this regulation.
There are four specific conditions: first, the *kaṭhina* robe has already been accepted; second, the ritual is being performed during the prescribed time; third, it is for the sake of the benefits.

Therefore, it is prohibited. Regarding the four [cases] where departing [with the robe] constitutes an offense, the opening statement mentions "improper time," which refers to exceeding five months. While calculating the departure of the robe based on the *jñapti* (formal motion), there are only three improper points;

that five are mentioned here in the text is merely a sequential listing. Furthermore, one might argue that the departure is based on a false perception, and even if there were five improper points, they would not constitute an obstacle.
Next, the one hundred and tenth precept: Prohibiting the Saṃgha from bringing forth the *kaṭhina* robe. The explanation of the meaning is the same as before;

however, while the previous precept involves an offense arising when the act is currently being prohibited, the wording here states: "The community of monks brings forth the robe in accordance with the Dharma.

Furthermore, regarding the determination of the offense, it is not established by looking at the formal procedure (*dharma*), nor is there an offense if the Saṃgha does not bring it forth. This precept involves an offense arising precisely because it is being prohibited; the wording states: "At that time..."
The community of bhikṣuṇīs wishes to cast out the kaṭhina robe; furthermore, within the determination of offenses, they take the act of "making it clear" (*vyakta*) as the boundary.

However, there is an interpretation stating: "Because this is an obstruction through verbal action (*vākkarman*), one commits an offense when it is made clear. If this were indeed an obstruction, why would there be five types of non-offenses?

In the previous case, the obstruction pertained to the body (*kāya*), meaning that because the body was outside the reach of the hand, it was not said to be "made clear. This [current] interpretation is not [correct].

However, if one were to claim that these constitute verbal action simply because they prevent the occurrence of the five non-virtues, then since the preceding [category of] precepts constitutes bodily action, how could there be five non-virtues when the body is extended beyond the reach of the hands?
Since this reasoning holds whether one proceeds or retreats, the former interpretation is correct.
Next is the precept against failing to resolve a dispute for another.

When one possesses the wisdom and capability to extinguish a dispute, yet the disputant comes seeking its resolution and one ultimately refuses to settle it, causing the dispute to flare up, leading to distress, the return to lay life, and irreparable ruin, the Noble One’s regulation is therefore necessary.

This distinct condition consists of five factors: first, there is a matter involving one of the four types of disputes; second, the disputing parties request its resolution; third, [the mediator] possesses virtue...

Capable of being terminated. Fourth, there are four conditions where there is no offense: namely, when the person previously has been subject to formal suspension (*ukkhepanīya-kamma*) or is beset by the two kinds of hardships, and so forth.
Fifth, not for the sake of extinction. As the text opens: "If it is said that one does not practice," this means not practicing my verbal instructions.
Next is the precept against giving food to laypeople or non-Buddhists. The explanation is the same as for the monks. This is a precept where the offense is identical but the conditions differ.
If one gives [food] to a layperson, one likewise commits a *thullaccaya* (grave) offense.
Next is the precept against acting as a messenger for laypeople. It is the principle of one who has left the household life that the mind should dwell beyond worldly things.

Now, to act as a messenger for laypeople is particularly contrary to the meaning of practicing the Way. Furthermore, it causes laypeople to treat the monastic community with contempt; the harm incurred is not slight.

Therefore, the Sage established the regulations: the specific conditions for an offense consist of four factors. First, one is a layperson (*avadātavasana*). Second, one performs work that is contrary to the Dharma.

Third, there is no valid cause or condition—namely, the illness of one's parents or of those who are faithful and devoted, or being constrained by force and the like. In such cases, it does not constitute an offense.

Next is the precept against spinning and weaving: Spinning and weaving are laborious tasks performed by those of low station; for one who has left the household life to engage in them is particularly detrimental to the reputation of the Path.
This offense is complete when four conditions are met: first, the material, such as the ten kinds of cloth or thread; second, the act of spinning or weaving oneself;
third, the absence of a valid cause—meaning one does not seek thread out of necessity or is coerced by force; and fourth, the commission of the offense upon the movement of the hand.
Next is the precept against wearing lay clothing and sitting or lying upon another’s bed: A person who advances in the practice should always maintain purity;
they must constantly sever the mind toward objects of attachment. To suddenly don the finery of a woman and lie down in a place where one normally resides is a violation.

The faults incurred are not slight; therefore, the Sage established this rule. Five conditions constitute an offense: first, it must be the dwelling of a layperson; second, one must be wearing women's ornaments;
third, it must be a bed where a husband and wife habitually reside; fourth, there must be no valid reason—excluding cases of illness or the two kinds of danger;
and fifth, one must sit or lie down accordingly.

Next is the precept against departing without taking leave of one's host after staying overnight. Previously, it was stated that one does not take leave during the day; here, it concerns departing without taking leave after having stayed overnight.
The explanation of the meaning is the same as before.
Next is the precept against privately reciting incantations and arts. One who advances on the Path ought to uphold the True Dharma; now, to abandon it willfully—this is what is meant.

The practice of various incantations and arts increases the cycle of birth and death, brings affliction to the gateway of the Path, and its faults and damage are not slight; therefore, the Sage’s prohibition was necessary.
This specific case possesses three conditions: first, it is a worldly incantation or art; second, it lacks causal basis; and third, the words and phrases are complete.

Next is the instruction for others to recite the precepts. The explanation of the meaning is the same as before; however, because the karmic actions of oneself and others differ, the two sets of precepts are distinguished.

Furthermore, among the four matters permitted not to be transgressed during one's own recitation—namely, (1) treating illness, (2) learning scripts, (3) subduing non-Buddhists, and (4) protecting oneself—none of these exemptions apply at all when instructing others to recite.

Next, the precept concerning the ordination of women who are pregnant. It is only right that the community of ordained nuns remain pure and distinguished, forever eliminating grounds for reproach and fostering the growth of faith and reverence.
Now, it is known that some ordain women who are pregnant and grant them full admission (*upasampadā*); subsequently, they give birth to children, which brings about disgrace and entanglement.

Therefore, the Noble One established a specific regulation requiring five conditions: first, being pregnant; second, knowing [the condition]; third, intending to grant full admission; fourth, acting as the preceptor (*upādhyāyī*); and fifth, [the presence of] the three... [conditions].
The *karmavācanā* is concluded. The remainder is not a fundamental offense; one merely incurs a minor transgression.

Next is the one hundred and twentieth precept concerning the ordination of women nursing infants. The remaining meanings are the same as before; the only difference is the matter of nursing an infant.
In the twenty-ninth fascicle of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, it is recorded that there was a bhikṣuṇī who gave birth to a son. Not knowing what to do...

[The nuns] asked the Buddha. The Buddha said, "I permit you to appoint one nun as a companion through a formal motion consisting of two proclamations (jñapti-dvitīya-karman). At that time, the two nuns took charge of the child and became doubtful; the Buddha said, "There is no offense.
If the two nuns sleep together with the child, there is likewise no offense. If [the child] is removed from their embrace, they should give him to a bhikṣu to ordain.
If they do not wish to have him ordained, they should give him to a relative to raise until he reaches adulthood.
Next is the ordination of a girl who has reached the age of reduction [the two-year training period].

The explanation of its meaning is the same as that for the full monks (*bhikṣu*), with the sole difference that the girl undergoes two years of training in the precepts. The text consists of three parts: first, the arising of the fault; second, the reprimand;

and third, from "He addressed the bhikṣus" onwards, the explanation of the method for receiving the precepts. Within this, there are again three sections: first, the method for ordaining a *śrāmaṇerī*; second, from "From now on... onwards...
The method for conferring the *śikṣamāṇā* training precepts: Third, those who have been [in training] for two years and whose age has reached the requirement receive full ordination (*upasampadā*).
The text of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* and its commentary are clear in their meaning and can be understood. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, one should ask: "When were you born?

If they do not know, one should consult the birth register. If there is no such record, one should ask the parents or relatives. If they still do not know, one should ask during which king's reign it was, or during a time of great abundance.
During times of great famine, if one is further unable to discern [the signs], they cannot be compared by physical appearance.
If it is the daughter of a wealthy family who is young in years but large in stature, one should examine her hands, feet, bones, and joints.

Next, regarding the *karmavācanā* for the two-year training in the precepts (*śikṣamāṇā-śikṣā*): if one does not grant this training in the precepts, the individual will become confused about the characteristics of the precepts (*śīla-lakṣaṇa*).

Consequently, various faults will extensively arise, and their conduct will have no basis for establishment. Since this would both fail the teacher’s work of instruction and fail to achieve the path of mutual benefit, such a violation of the teaching is not a minor matter;
therefore, the Noble One (the Buddha) established this regulation. There are six specific conditions [for this]: first, she must be a girl aged eighteen or older; second...

The *karmavācanā* for training in the precepts (*śikṣamāṇā*) is not granted. When three years have passed and one is twenty-four, one receives full ordination (*upasampadā*). Five [conditions] constitute the *upādhyāya*;

six [steps] complete the three *karmavācanās*. The text states that those who are "not eighteen" refers to those under eighteen as well as those over [eighteen], to whom the training in the precepts is not granted, yet they immediately receive full ordination for the sake of purifying the body.
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* prescribes two years of training in the precepts.
16. Question: Within the *bhikṣuṇī* dharma, why is there a two-year period of training in the precepts (*śikṣamāṇā*)? Answer:

During the time when the Buddha was in the world, there was the wife of an elder who, without having trained in pregnancy, left the household life and received the precepts. When she later manifested a great transformation in her subsequent existence, the various elders reviled and disparaged her.
Consequently, this regulation of a two-year period of training in the precepts was established.

Next, regarding the failure to recite the names of the six dharmas: if one does not currently indicate the names and thus fails to recognize their characteristics, it constitutes a violation of conduct and a transgression of the teachings, no different from the cases mentioned previously.

The distinct conditions consist of seven factors: first, the person is an eighteen-year-old girl; second, she has received the *karmavācanā* for training in the precepts (*śikṣamāṇā*); third, the six dharmas have not been recited; fourth, she is twenty years of age;
fifth, she is to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*); sixth, [the candidate] acts as the preceptor (*upādhyāya*); and seventh, [the candidate] acts as the instructor (*ācārya*).

The three *karmavācanā* are concluded. Regarding the three phrases of the *Śīla-sūtra*: first, the person; second, not being granted the six rules (*ṣaḍ-dharma*); third, the full year and below, concluding with the offense. To explain the second phrase:
these "six rules" refer to the four preliminary preparations (*upāya*) and the two fundamental [offenses]. These are the rules to be studied (*śikṣitavya-dharma*).

The four preliminary preparations and the fundamental offenses must result in expulsion (*pravāsanīya-karman*) for violation; they are not merely rules to be studied. Furthermore, regarding the study of these six rules...

One must complete the period for as long as one lives. When approaching the time to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*), the minimum requirement is two years. If one commits any of these six offenses before the two years are completed, the training rules (*śikṣāpada*) are deficient;
one must be granted another two-year period. If one commits an offense outside of these six, it is merely a deficiency in conduct and does not constitute a deficiency in the training rules;
no further period need be granted. Even if the two years are completed, if one has not received the precepts and there is a deficiency in the training, one must likewise undergo [another period].

If one has been granted [the probationary period] for two years due to an offense involving a deficiency in training, it is not permissible to receive the full ordination. If that were the case, once the *parivāsa* (period of concealment) is completed, the offense would constitute a "corrupted dharma.
Answer: The treatment follows the number of days; it is not for life. Therefore, it is said that when the period is fulfilled, the previous dharma is not corrupted.
Regarding the dharma of training (*śikṣamāṇā*), it is for life; an offense therein immediately corrupts the dharma, and thus it must be granted anew.
Next is the ordination of girls who possess obstructing conditions (*antarāyika-dharma*). The monastic community must assemble with superior persons.

First, one should manifest the benefits of the Buddha’s Dharma for the world. Now, this woman lacks the complete sense faculties; were she to be ordained and enter the homeless life by force, she would bring disgrace upon the assembly of *bhikṣuṇīs*, and the resulting blemish would not be slight.
Therefore, this rule was established. There are five specific conditions [for such a case]: first, the lack of complete sense faculties; second, knowing that she lacks them...
[The text] consists of three parts: first, the transgression; second, the reprimand; third, the instruction to the assembly at large on the method of receiving [the precepts].
Within this, there are again three sections: first, the method for receiving the precepts; second, from "a woman of noble family" onwards, the explanation of the characteristics of the rite;
third, from "you have already received the full ordination" onwards, the summary and exhortation to uphold [the precepts]. This is the first section.

There are three parts: first, the fundamental rules and rituals for *bhikṣuṇīs*; second, the method for receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*) by *bhikṣuṇīs* from within the assembly of *bhikṣus* at the two seasonal assemblies;
and third, a detailed explanation of their characteristics, which is provided below in the main text.
Next, the precept regarding the ordination of women who have previously married: (12) Those who have already been married have already served a husband;

they are capable of upholding the precepts, and therefore the Buddha permitted their ordination. Those whose age is not yet full [twelve] have not yet established their resolve; since they do not avoid transgressions, it is prohibited to ordain them.
There are five specific conditions: (1) a woman less than twelve years of age; (2) knowing she is less than twelve; (3) ... [text continues].
[The procedure for] receiving full ordination consists of four parts: first, acting as the preceptor (*upādhyāya*); second, performing the *karmavācanā*; third, the conclusion of the *karmavācanā*;

and fourth, the remaining points being the same as previously described. However, the eighth fascicle of the *Mātṛkā-sūtra* states: "If a woman is ten years of age and already has a husband, she may be ordained and allowed to leave the household life.
After she has received the *śrāmaṇerī* precepts for two full years, she may subsequently receive the *śikṣamāṇā* precepts. She must complete these two years before she may receive full ordination."
The full precepts (*upasampadā*). This is called the "Dharma of Correspondence for Two Years.

Next is the precept on ordaining women who have previously married or those subject to the one hundred impediments (*vighna*). The explanation of the intent behind the prohibition is the same as before;

this should also be explained in detail here. For the sake of brevity, the four precepts are summarized. The initial and final [meanings] are the same as the middle two. Alternatively, the previous prohibition may be reduced to twenty.

The age requirement cannot be met; she has already been married. Once the reduction of the required age for ordination has been granted, it is said that other prohibitions (*antarāyika-dharma*) are treated the same as the case of prior marriage.

For this reason, there are two precepts regarding the beginning and the end; the transgressions arising regarding the two intermediate precepts depend on the person who confers them, not on the person being ordained.
Therefore, it is impossible for a transgression to arise based on the causal factor [of the recipient]. How could one say that because she was previously married, she need not train?
Regarding the precept on not revealing the names of the six classes of persons:

Next is the precept on ordaining a courtesan. Although a woman who is addicted to desire is not a formal obstacle to ordination, once she has received full ordination, she may be mocked and wept over by others.

This would result in no small amount of disgrace and entanglement; therefore, one must ensure she is deeply concealed and sent far away. Thus, violating this rule invites censure, as established by the Sage.

This constitutes an offense of confession (*pāyattika*). It requires five specific conditions: first, she is a prostitute; second, one knows her to be such; third, she has completed the full ordination (*upasampadā*);
fourth, she is the preceptor (*upādhyāya*); and fifth, one does not conceal her securely or escort her far away.
Next, one must not fail to sustain disciples through these two dharmas regarding the precepts.

Generally, it is only when one possesses these two dharmas to provide mutual care and nourishment that the path of mutual benefit—the fundamental principle of a teacher’s instruction—is established. These two dharmas are: providing food and clothing to relieve the suffering of the physical form, and instructing with the teachings to enlighten the mind and spirit.
Now, if these two dharmas are deficient, both body and mind will remain unsettled, causing the disciple to become [disaffected].

If one were able to proceed [in such a manner], this would result in deep complications and entanglements; therefore, the Sage established a regulation. There are five specific conditions that must be met:

first, the nun must be pure, so as not to incur an offense by associating with one who has broken the precepts or has been subject to formal censure or suspension; second, she must constantly follow her *upādhyāyī* (preceptor), except when departing due to separation is unavoidable;
third, the *upādhyāyī* must possess the Dharma, as well as robes and food; fourth, there must be no other cause or condition; or, for this reason, two [conditions] may be combined.
Difficult. Fifth, if one does not receive instruction through the two methods, this constitutes an offense.
Next is the rule regarding not following the preceptor for two years: a newly ordained person has not yet attained proficiency and should consult their teacher at all times to achieve self-benefit.
To leave the teacher abruptly without receiving instruction results in a deficiency in spiritual progress; therefore, this must be [prohibited] by the Sage.

The Vinaya regulations state that there are six specific conditions for this: first, the person must be one's preceptor (*upādhyāya*); second, they must be pure, virtuous, and capable of providing guidance; third, the preceptor does not permit the departure;

fourth, the candidate has not yet completed six summer retreats (*varṣa*); fifth, it is a case of dependence; and sixth, the principle of the matter requires it to be so. As for the present mention of "two years," [it refers to the following].
This is due to an error in the text. Fifth, there is no cause or condition, meaning that because of this abiding, two difficulties arise. Sixth, one commits an offense immediately upon departing.

Next is the one hundred and thirtieth precept: the prohibition against keeping a retinue or ordaining others without having requested permission. A person does not know for themselves; it is not their portion.
Regarding one’s own status: the Saṃgha must deliberate upon whether one possesses virtue or lacks it. Now, if one ordains someone without the Saṃgha’s permission, one commits an offense.

Such actions often lead to negligence and harm; therefore, a *thullaccaya* (grave offense) is prescribed. This rule involves four constituent factors: first, the lack of permission; second, the intent to confer full ordination (*upasampadā*);

third, acting as the preceptor (*upajjhāya*); and fourth, the completion of the formal ritual (*kamma*). For the three subsequent precepts, the factor of "completion of the ritual" is not applied; this is a brief explanation regarding the determination of the offense.

The text concerning this matter has three parts: first, those without virtue who cross over others do not know how to instruct them, thereby giving rise to transgressions; second, at that time, various subordinates rebuked [them];

third, from the passage "addressing the bhikṣuṇīs" onwards, it establishes the rule regarding the request to maintain [disciples]. The Saṃgha is sent to deliberate: those with virtue are permitted, while those without virtue are prohibited.
It asks whether the formal act (*karmavācanā*) is established for one who requests [to maintain disciples] without virtue. An ancient commentary states: "Those without virtue who cross over..."
[If one says,] "The person [who acts as preceptor] may separately incur an offense, yet the ritual procedure (*vidhi*) is accomplished;

if that were so, then even a teacher lacking merit would accomplish the instruction. To explain: since a teacher lacking merit has no sense of the duty to instruct a nun at all, the appointment is not validly established.

However, because a preceptor (*upādhyāya*) lacking merit can still cause the candidate to receive the precepts, it is therefore established. This interpretation is incorrect. Whether the ritual is definitively established or not is as explained above.
Next is the precept for ordaining others before twelve *varṣa* have been completed: Those who are young in years and few in *varṣa* have not yet perfected their conduct and virtue;

since their resolve is not yet established, how could they fulfill the role of a teacher? It is necessary that one’s years and *varṣa* be fully completed and that both understanding and practice be complete, so that one is capable of receiving and guiding others.

Therefore, the reasons for permitting [this] are distinguished by four conditions: first, the summer retreat has not yet expired; second, it is for the purpose of receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*);

third, one acts as the preceptor (*upādhyāya*); and fourth, the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) has been completed. There are differences between the male and female ordinations regarding those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and there are likewise distinctions between the preceptors of the two assemblies.

According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, when the bhikṣuṇīs wish to associate with the bhikṣus, they say: "You [bhikṣus] have been [ordained] for five years; you do not require formal dependence (*niśraya*)."
"He took on disciples at the age of ten; we are the same as he. What difference is there? The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, who said:
"From this day forward, a bhikṣuṇī shall not take on disciples until she has completed six years [of training]; only when she has completed twelve years may she take on a following."

Next is the precept against conferring ordination upon those lacking virtue: if one does not establish oneself in practice, how can one save others? Both self and other will suffer loss; therefore, this rule is established.

The specific conditions for this offense consist of four factors: first, the person lacks virtue; second, they receive full ordination; third, one acts as the *upādhyāya*; and fourth, the *karmavācanā* ritual is completed.
This precept serves to distinguish the ignorant from the wise, while the preceding precept distinguished the small from the great. One does not [use] these two...
Regarding the inclusion of the matter: this distinguishes the non-practitioner from the practitioner. Because a nun causes greater harm and loss, she incurs a *thullaccaya* offense in both cases;
whereas a monk, as the one who caused the damage, incurs only a minor offense (*dukkaṭa*).

Next is the precept against ordaining others while slandering the Saṃgha. This was established because one who fails to assess their own lack of virtue and unjustly slanders the Saṃgha causes distress to the community and brings harm upon themselves.
The specific conditions for this offense consist of four factors: first, actually lacking virtue; second, the Saṃgha not permitting [the ordination];

third, slandering unjustly; and fourth, the completion of the speech. As for why there is no formal admonition, the answer is that [the offender] knows they lack virtue and is thus slandering the Saṃgha beyond their proper standing.
Since there is no one else to rely upon, there is no need for admonition.

Next is the precept against ordaining someone without the permission of their parents or husband: Since such a person already has those to whom they belong, it is improper for them to leave the household life;

to grant them full ordination (upasampadā) without authorization and allow them to be seized by others is a disgrace to the monastic community, preventing it from being pure and prominent, and constitutes a transgression of the spirit of the law.

It must not be taken lightly; therefore, the holy regulations must be established. There are four specific conditions that must be fulfilled: first, the person must have a formal affiliation; second, they must be receiving full ordination;
third, one must act as the preceptor (upādhyāya); and fourth, the *karmavācanā* ritual must be completed.
Next is the precept against engaging in mutual affection with a child, as well as delighting in or being prone to anger. To be immersed in desire is already defiling to the path;
how much more so to engage in mutual affection with a male? Furthermore, to afflict oneself and others through delighting in or being prone to anger results in no small degree of harm.

Therefore, this must be strictly prohibited. The specific conditions for an offense consist of five factors: first, being one who is immersed in desire and prone to anger; second, knowing [the other] to be such; third...
Regarding the conferral of full ordination (*upasampadā*): first, one acts as the preceptor (*upādhyāya*); second, the *karmavācanā* is completed;
third, the training rules (*śikṣamāṇā*) are not granted; fourth, the bhikṣuṇī fulfills the training rules for full ordination;

fifth, she single-mindedly aspires for ordination yet craves offerings and does not receive it at the proper time. This constitutes a failure in the master’s method of instruction and guidance. Such is the nature of the transgression.

Because it is a minor offense, it requires a formal regulation by the Noble One. The specific conditions consist of five factors: first, having fulfilled two years of training with pure precepts; second, possessing the requisite conditions for monastic robes;
third, being the preceptor (upādhyāya); fourth, being without other compelling reasons; and fifth, not being one who has already received [the ordination].
Next, taking another’s robe without intending to confer full ordination: previously, the preceptor (upādhyāya) was prescribed; this refers to the teacher of reliance (niśraya-ācārya).
First, one takes another’s robe with the permission to confer full ordination; now, because one does not confer it and thus violates the commitment, it is a *pāyattika*.

There are five specific conditions: first, the training in the precepts is pure and two years have been completed; second, one takes the robe with the permission to act as the preceptor; third, the requisites for the monastic robe are prepared; fourth...
One must not accept [a disciple] without the necessary causes and conditions.
Next, regarding the precepts for ordaining disciples: in general, one who ordains a disciple must know the proper method of instruction.

Since failing to provide such instruction leads to the corruption of conduct according to circumstances, a restriction was established regarding the annual limit. Even if one person were to violate it out of greed, it would thus contravene the holy regulations and constitute a *thullaccaya* offense.

The offense has five constituent conditions: first, having previously ordained someone; second, less than twelve months having elapsed; third, ordaining another person; fourth, acting as the preceptor (upādhyāya);
and fifth, the completion of the three *karmavācanās*. In the text, the point that the offense is incurred upon the conclusion of the *karma* is omitted for brevity.
Next, having completed the primary ritual (*mūla-vidhi*), one should spend the night and then proceed to the community of monks (*bhikṣu-saṃgha*) to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*).

If one goes on that very day, the wholesome mind (*kuśala-citta*) remains continuous; however, if one waits until after the night has passed before approaching, there will be many obstacles and difficulties. Therefore, it is prescribed that this is not permitted; one must approach the Saṃgha after spending the night.

To violate this is to cause distress to the other; the Noble One has prescribed a *pāyattika* offense. There are four specific conditions: first, the original rite has already been completed; second, one does not go that very day; third, there is no extenuating circumstance;
fourth, failing to go and remaining overnight incurs a *pāyattika*. This principle is based on the appearance of dawn (*aruṇodaya*). The text omits certain details for brevity.

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that if dawn breaks, the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) incurs a *pāyattika*, while the other teachers incur a *duṣkṛta*. The *Mātṛkā-sūtra*, fascicle seven, says: "If [the disciple]..."
When a śrāmaṇerī has completed receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*) within the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha, she should immediately receive it from the Mahāsaṃgha during the day;
she should not come at night.
Next, on the day of instruction, she must go to listen to the precepts. Article 130: One who possesses complete virtue and a compassionate heart.

One ought to listen to and accept instruction, and inquire about what has not yet been heard. To now be arrogant toward the Dharma and disregard others by refusing to listen to their admonitions is to lose for oneself the benefits of the Dharma;
therefore, a *thullaccaya* offense is prescribed. This offense requires four specific conditions: first, being appointed by the Saṃgha; second, receiving formal instruction;
third, having no valid reason [for absence]; and fourth, failing to go and listen.
Next is the offense of not requesting instruction on the precepts within half a month. The nun’s requirement for instruction is as previously stated;

however, because she now treats the Dharma with arrogance and looks down upon others, failing to honor and respect the teachings, she violates the original intent of her undertaking. Therefore, this is established as a *thullaccaya* (grave offense). The specific conditions consist of four factors:
first, both Saṃghas must be complete, from a minimum of five members; second, the time for requesting instruction, namely the fourteenth, fifteenth, or tenth day of the lunar month.

Sixth: When the Saṃgha recites the precepts (*poṣadha*), there are three cases where no offense is incurred due to lack of causal conditions. Regarding the four points concerning failing to be dispatched [to another monastery], there are three phrases in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*:

first, the person; second, the establishment of the rule; and third, the incurrence of an offense for violating the instruction if one does not descend [from the seat]. In the commentary on these characteristics, this section and that on the invitation (*pravāraṇā*) do not explain the phrase regarding the incurrence of an offense;

they only explain the preceding two. The explanation of the first [phrase] is self-evident. As for the explanation of the second phrase, the "establishment of the rule," the text states: [The text continues with the specific details of the rule's formulation.]
This is divided into two parts. First, the extensive method of instruction for those who are full [in number] and free from illness.

Second, the method of inquiry for when the bhikṣu-saṃgha is ill, diminished, or otherwise has many individual cases of sickness. Regarding the former, there are four sections: first, the nuns' community appoints someone to go;

second, that person shall request the method of instruction from within the great saṃgha of bhikṣus; third, once they have received the instruction, they inquire below; fourth, [the procedure for] returning.

Regarding the method for taking [a nun] who does not have a fixed date [to depart]: the fourth section concerns the method for hearing of and providing offerings to those who go forth to welcome and escort [the candidate].
The initial text has three parts: first, the citation of the noble injunction, hence the statement, "The World-Honored One has given such an instruction," and so forth;
second, the conditions for the appointment as set forth below; third, the formal procedure for the appointment as stated by the Buddha. Within this formal procedure, there are further two parts.

First is the method for appointing [the instructor]; next, the formal appointment is clarified. This formal appointment is twofold: first, the appointment by means of a *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act);

second, the verbal appointment of an associate. Next is the second part: the method for requesting instruction. Within this text there are also three sections: first, the specific words of the request; second, hearing the assignment of the teaching;
third, the selection of the person to whom one belongs. The remainder of the text is self-evident. The *Mātṛkā-sūtra*, fascicle seven, states: "If on the fifteenth day..."

When a bhikṣuṇī approaches the assembly of the great saṃgha for the time of receiving the precepts, she should immediately request instruction; there is no need to come again at a later time to request it.

Next, regarding not going to the great saṃgha for the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination) ceremony: the intent of the regulation is as before. Furthermore, since the reception of the precepts already depends upon the bhikṣuṇī...

O Kiu, in repenting to eliminate transgressions, one must likewise rely upon [the Sangha]. Therefore, we depend on the Great Monks to bestow their compassionate instruction, so that our practice may proceed without violation and karmic burdens may be extinguished.

There are four conditions for this distinct rite: first, the *an-ju* (rainy-season retreat) must have concluded; second, both assemblies must be complete, harmonious, and free from illness; third, there must be no other cause or condition;

fourth, the person has not been dispatched [to another assembly] and has committed an offense. The root text of the precept consists of three phrases: first, the person; second, the establishment of the rule.

The three offenses of *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. In the commentary, the first phrase may be understood. Regarding the second section on the textual method, there are two parts: first, the detailed procedure for the *pravāraṇā* (self-invitation);

second, the method of inquiry concerning the reduction and elimination of various illnesses. Within the former [the *pravāraṇā*], there are three sub-sections; the first clarifies the method of appointment (*niyoga*). Within this, there are again three parts.
As explained previously regarding the precepts, the second section concerns the procedure for the Saṃgha’s *pravāraṇā* (invitation to point out faults) when visiting the lower assembly.

The monks of the Great Saṃgha must all assemble together; no one may be absent or separated from the group. This consists of two parts: first, the formal observance of dignified demeanor (*īryāpatha*); second, the actual *pravāraṇā*. There are five phrases for concluding the invitation.

First, it is noted that the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha has completed its summer retreat (*varṣā*), which is precisely the time for the *pravāraṇā*. Second, it is further noted that the Great Saṃgha has also completed its summer retreat. It is necessary to state these points because [the *pravāraṇā* depends upon the completion of the retreat].
Regarding the "two assemblies of monks": because a bhikṣuṇī must seek the *prātimokṣa* (exhortation) from both assemblies. Regarding "the three bhikṣuṇīs":

this correctly clarifies the procedure for voluntarily proclaiming one's own faults and requesting the lifting [of the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*] based on charges of what has been seen, heard, or suspected. Regarding "O Virtuous Ones" and below: this is an appeal to the venerable assembly to bestow compassionate instruction.
Regarding the fifth section, "If I should see... and below: this demonstrates one's recognition of one's own faults and their removal through instruction, thereby perfecting pure conduct.

Third, this section below explains the timing for the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination) of the Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha itself. If one does not become fatigued, there is no fault in performing it on the same day.
