The final two sentences describe his exemplary deportment and sublime, wondrous features—qualities that this king lacks—and thus the king exhorts [the assembly] to observe this man from another land.

Therefore, it is said: "Observe that guest. Furthermore, his deportment was orderly and dignified, solemn and impressive to behold. He exhorted all his ministers to together gaze upon these extraordinary signs;
hence, it is said: "Observe that guest. Although the holy practices are many, this one surpasses all others; it is by practicing this path that one attains such results.
The Way establishes one as honorable among men; therefore, it is called "supreme. "Marks" refers to the thirty-two marks, and "excellences" refers to the eighty secondary excellences.

Because these marks and excellences are clearly manifest, they are said to be "most majestic and beautiful. Since the marks and excellences are complete, it is evident that he is not of the common ranks, but must be a descendant of the noble Kṣatriya lineage;
thus, he is not of lowly birth. He is as profound as the great ocean and as firmly established as Mount Sumeru.
Walking slowly like a lion, and gazing like a bull king—therefore it is said, "gazing attentively. Next, the passage concerning "knowing the place" consists of three parts.

At the beginning there was a half-verse; the king commanded his messenger to seek out its location. Next there were three verses; the messenger, obeying the king’s command, sought out and identified its location.
Finally there were two verses; having already found the location, he returned to inform the king. The meaning of the initial passage is clear.
The subsequent passage is further divided into three parts. First, a verse on receiving the command and seeking out the inquiry.

Second, a verse on seeing his deeds—benefiting others with equanimity, restraining the senses without defilement, moving objects through his merit, and remaining unshaken by praise or blame. Third, a verse on tracking him down to discover his location.

The third textual section has two parts: first, a verse on the king’s law; second, a verse on reporting this to inform the king. The fourth section, on paying formal respects, consists of three parts.
The first one and a half verses pay homage and offer greetings. From the second verse, which begins with mutual inquiries, the dialogue is formally established.

Thirdly, as the purpose for coming has been fully expressed, he pays his respects and takes leave. Regarding the first section, it is necessary to inquire after one’s well-being and comfort, such as whether one’s daily life is light and at ease.

In the second section, wishing to establish the dialogue, he first concludes the preceding context and introduces what follows; although he previously offered praise from afar, the doubts in his mind were not yet resolved, and now—

Having received [the instruction] personally, one must present questions and answers; therefore, it is called "rejoinder" (*pratyudgata*). Alternatively, once the inquiries have been concluded, one further resolves lingering doubts;

thus, it is called "rejoinder. Within the section on questions and answers, the text is divided into two parts. First, up to the end of the verses, he asks about what is prayed for within the mind of the noble clansman.
Second, from the prose section below, although he knows the prayer of the clansman, he does not yet recognize its true purpose; therefore, he must relinquish his position.

To verify its reality or unreality, within the preceding section, there is first the question and later the answer. He presents his previous intent face-to-face, while from afar expressing his intention of praise.
Within the question, there are two parts. The first verse asks about what is prayed for in his heart: "I observe your noble conduct during your prime;

by right, you should succeed to the throne and be called King, so that your grace might flow throughout the land. Yet now you have shaved your head and taken up the mendicant's life—what is the purpose of your prayer? This is the first part.
The question concerns the intention behind leaving the household life to practice begging. The subsequent verse asks about his lineage and place of birth:

"Observing you now, O Benevolent One, your countenance is upright and handsome; you must surely be a scion of the noble Kṣatriya clan. Since I have engaged in this dialogue with you, I pray that you will tell me of your original family name and place of birth.
Next, three verses provide the answer. The sequence in the text is not chronological; the first verse answers the latter question first.

The first two phrases answer the previous question regarding the place of birth; hence it says, "There is a land," and so forth. The next two phrases answer the previous question regarding the names of the lineage and father.
His father's name was Sūrya; he belonged to the Solar Clan (Sūryavaṃśa), such as Mahāsammata and others. His place of birth was named Śākya.

Referring back to the preceding section on the "Inferior Śākyas of the North," there follow two verses that respond to the initial question. The first verse concerns abandoning conditions to enter the Path;
the second verse prays for the severance of the source of suffering. Regarding the first, the abandonment of conditions: the cyclic flow of birth and death all arises from accompanying conditions.
To sever the cause of suffering, one must necessarily renounce it; hence it is said, "abandoning those practices," and so forth. The next verse concerns the cessation of suffering:
by contemplating the many faults of desire, one sees that under the previous wheel-turning kings, suffering and its accumulation persisted, and liberation was not attained.

This explains the first line. Regarding "renunciation and peace": this refers to the fruit of Buddhahood mentioned previously. Since cessation and the path have been revealed, one exerts the will to seek them diligently. This explains the second line. [It leads to] the cessation of...

The meeting with suffering is the true nature; it is that toward which the fundamental mind tends. Therefore, it is said that one seeks equality and so forth. This explains the third and fourth lines.

Herein, the contemplation of desire is the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*); the many afflictions are the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*); renunciation is the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*); and peace is the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*). Next, the examination of the real and the unreal consists of two parts:
first, examining and knowing the reality, which corresponds to the aforementioned Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*); second, seeking to be delivered first, which reveals the previous Buddha.
The Way. Having verified that the whole is indeed divided into two, one sets aside the entirety. Within this, there are the dharma, the analogy, and the application.
Once the reality has been verified, one then seeks the fivefold prior measure. The King wished to sincerely address the Bodhisattva, saying: "Bhikṣu, what is your clan, lineage, and noble station?"
You are of royal lineage; by the natural power of your sagely virtue, you ought to preside over the four seas, and there are none among those who look up to the four seas who do not yearn for you.
If you would deign to lower your resolve, we shall surely serve as your vassals. When they met face-to-face to attend upon him, the Bodhisattva replied:

"Among the noble positions in the world, none is more honored than that of a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin), yet I have already renounced even that; how much more so the rule of the four seas? This is why I have left the household life to seek the Way, desiring to deliver [all beings]."
"All of saṃsāra is great suffering; why did you not request me [to come] so that I might first deliver you once the Way was perfected?

Instead, you have merely made this trivial entreaty. The King said, "Excellent! These words are most pleasing. On the day the Way is perfected, I pray that you will first deliver me and the people of this land.
The Bodhisattva granted his consent. The Great King rejoiced greatly, prostrated himself, took his leave, and departed. The third instance of his retreat may be understood accordingly.

Next, the cultivation and realization of equal enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi) is explained. This passage consists of two parts: first, practicing similarly [to others] yet failing to realize the true fruit;

second, from the phrase "At that time, the Bodhisattva... onwards, recollecting the original cause and attaining Buddhahood through cultivation. The former section further divides into two: first, practicing meditative concentration (dhyāna) similarly to others; second, practicing asceticism (duḥkha-caryā) similarly to others.

Regarding the practice of concentration, it further divides into two, namely the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana) and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana). However...

In the remainder of the text, all meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) are fully practiced; here, two are cited as examples, though the others should also be cultivated. Within the section on "non-utility," the text is divided into two parts:

first, explaining the practice of concentration under a false teacher; second, from "At that time, the Bodhisattva... onwards, describing how he departs and does not accept [the instruction]. In the preceding section, there are ten points:
first, citing the false teacher’s instruction for practicing concentration; second, from "At that time, the Bodhisattva... onwards, his going to inquire about and study the Dharma.
Third, from "He replied," he answers regarding the dharmas to be studied. Fourth, from "At that time, the Bodhisattva," he compares the presence or absence [of such dharmas].
Fifth, from "I have now," he explains the cultivation required to attain realization. Sixth, from "At that time, the Bodhisattva," he further inquires about the dharmas to be studied.
Seventh, from "He replied," he answers that there is nothing remaining. Eighth, from "The Bodhisattva replied," he briefly refutes [the opponent's position].
In the ninth section, "Below Ālambana," there is an exhortation to engage in common practice. In the tenth section, "At the Time Below Ālambana," he is revered as being correct.

Next, regarding the two parts on "Refuting the Wrong," first is the comparative evaluation of the refutation, and second is knowing the wrong and abandoning it. Within the former, there are again two parts: first, four phrases concerning the inability to eliminate faults;
second, four phrases concerning the inability to accomplish virtues. "Faults" refers here to the afflictions and calamities of saṃsāra.
"Virtue" refers to the possession of virtue in *nirvāṇa*. As stated in the preceding text, because karma is not severed, it is called "not ceased.

Because the causes have not been eliminated, it is "not departed. Since the characteristics of the fruit of desire still persist, it is called "not extinguished. Because these states revolve in this manner, it is "not at rest."

The subsequent passage does not refer to the attainment of perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), but rather cites its fruit. It is not about the fruits of the śramaṇa; these two [phrases] refer to *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.

The following two phrases refer to *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*. The first phrase discusses the essence, while the second praises its virtues. Alternatively, one may read them as a continuous sequence, saying:
"It is not the attainment of nirvāṇa, nor the place of eternal quiescence," treating them as a single sentence. This is how the former masters have assigned the text and explained it.
Commentary: This is utterly contrary to reason and does not accord with our own school; why then labor over its refutation?

The second [view], which shares the same practice as the Non-Perception [heaven], differs only by lacking the single phrase "attaining perfect enlightenment"; the rest of the text is the same as above.

Regarding those who seek a superior dharma, the ancient commentary states: this refers to those who cling to self-starvation as the path, taking the observation of austerity in worldly affairs to be the ultimate goal.
"Detachment from desire," he said, "is the unsurpassed dharma of rest. Now, the explanation is not so; it is simply that he sought the supreme dharma through desire.

Encountering circumstances along the way, he spent six years without attaining the noble dharma. Therefore it is said: "Even though he did this, he still did not realize the superior noble wisdom and supreme dharma.
That dharma of rest is precisely what is described in the passage concerning his subsequent attainment of Buddhahood. Is this [the practice] of common conduct? It is not rest.

The Method of Resting. Furthermore, when he was relinquishing his heterodox meditative states, he had not yet witnessed the practices of asceticism. Traveling south to Mount Xiangshan, he observed a site and the thought arose as to how [the practice] could be suspended;

he immediately designated this as the method of resting. Subsequently, he joined the ranks of the ascetics, desiring to transform those who followed heterodox paths and lead them back to the True Dharma.
As stated in the middle fascicle of the *Mahāyānopāya-sūtra*: "In the past, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, the Bodhisattva..."
Sāriputra spoke these words: "I have no desire to see this shaven-headed mendicant. How could one who is shaven-headed attain *bodhi*?
The path to *bodhi* is exceedingly profound and difficult to attain," and so on, as explained at length.

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva practiced austerities for six years because of his karmic obstructions, in order to transform the five men and to demonstrate the retribution of his own karma. As for those five men:
The Father King selected five sons from five noble clans and ordered them to serve as his attendants. As for the four daughters, they were present there due to the conditions of that time;
this may serve to manifest the Bodhisattva’s conduct free from defilement, and it may also serve as a distant foreshadowing of the future two assemblies of monks and nuns.

Therefore, the four daughters and five sons are mentioned here. Although he practiced austerities for six years, this was because what he had cultivated was not the true path; it merely increased [his physical emaciation].
[They become] exhausted. Therefore it is said: "Even though you are thus.
Next, following this, there is the section on attaining Buddhahood through practice. This section contains two parts: first, silent contemplation and the weighing of gains and losses;

second, from "At that time, the Bodhisattva... onwards, practicing dhyāna with every morsel of food, severing delusions, and attaining Buddhahood. Within the section on weighing [gains and losses], the text contains...
There are nine phrases. The first four phrases compare and evaluate the ancient path. The next three phrases contemplate the basis for desire.
The final two phrases realize the dharma of the true cause. Within the first four phrases, the first raises the wisdom obtained upon the field of the father-king.
Second, one examines whether this path can bring an end to suffering. Third, one knows that it possesses such capacity. Fourth, by relying upon it, one attains the end [of suffering].
Regarding the subsequent three phrases: the first cites desire as the basis. Desire is the cause of affliction (*kleśa*), while unwholesome phenomena are karma.

Through the mutual reinforcement of these afflictions and karma, one wanders through the various realms of existence. Since it is said: "Is it possible that, by means of desire and unwholesome phenomena..."
Is it possible to obtain the dharma of happiness? It is clearly known that one cannot experience the fruit of happiness through unwholesome causes.
Second, one knows its lack of power. Third, one practices the relinquishment of desire. Can unwholesomeness obtain the dharma of happiness? According to the logic, there is yet another phrase.

The statement that "by relinquishing [food], one immediately attains non-existence" is an abbreviation. Regarding the latter two lines: having awakened to the truth and obtained the necessary provisions, as reflected upon above, the body is dependent and lacks independent power.
If one wishes to exhaust the source of suffering, how could it be achieved through self-starvation? Therefore, it says, "Thus, I do not rely on... and so forth.

In this way, practice depends upon provisions for its completion; if conditions are lacking, one loses the Way. If one does not accept food, by what means can one transcend and ascend? Therefore, it says, "I... and so forth.

Now, regarding "etcetera": next follows the cultivation of dhyāna to attain Buddhahood. Within this section, there are two parts: first, cultivating dhyāna by consuming food; second, severing delusions to attain Buddhahood. In the former, there are again two parts:

first, consuming food; second, cultivating dhyāna. Regarding the text on consuming food, there are three sections: first, explaining the consumption of food, which is the reverse of the previous [section].
Regarding "fasting," the phrase "at another time" means not at the time of deliberation. As for this food—rice and parched grain (*maṣa*)—the remainder of the text mentions milk gruel (*pāyasa*).

The question as to why they differ is as follows: the Bodhisattva first ate rice and parched grain so that his physical strength would gradually increase; only after eating the milk gruel did he achieve Perfect Enlightenment.
The reason we know this is that [if] fasting for six years had been of no benefit from a single meal, it would not have been possible [to attain enlightenment] were it not for a long duration.
He received nourishment. Thus, the *Vibhāṣā* (182) states: After the Bodhisattva had abandoned his ascetic practices, he partook of fine rice, ghee, and milk, and anointed his body with oil;
he practiced the Middle Way. The five [disciples] considered this a lapse and a loss of resolve, and consequently departed.
At that time, there were two women, Nandā and Nandabalā, who simultaneously began to serve him. At that moment, the Bodhisattva...
At that time, he had this thought: "If those five men would not abandon me, how could they allow a woman to come and draw near?
After the Bodhisattva had consumed the milk-rice endowed with sixteen virtues, his physical strength increased further.

He received grass and other items from the auspicious man, and so on until his attainment of Buddhahood. Question: Does the Bodhisattva’s vital energy arise solely from food? Answer: Although the Bodhisattva...
He possessed the strength of Nārāyaṇa. Had he not eaten, it would have been as if he had attained the Way through self-starvation.
To refute such false views, he consumed the milk-rice. The *Third [Chapter on] Cause and Effect* states:
"If I were now to attain the Way with this emaciated body, those non-Buddhists would say that self-starvation is the cause of Nirvana. Although I possess the strength of Nārāyaṇa in every limb..."
Nor did he attain the fruit of the Way by means of this; rather, he thought, "I shall receive food, and only then will I realize the Way.

Second, the five men, not understanding the truth, stubbornly departed. Third, having eaten, his physical strength was restored. Next, he practiced meditation, first clarifying the preparatory methods (*upāya*).
The text on these methods has three parts: first, washing away bodily impurities. Since one intends to purify the mind, one must first remove the impurities of the body.
Next, he wished to proceed to the Bodhi tree; however, as he had not yet attained Buddhahood, he could not yet sit directly beneath it.

Therefore, having sat down and begged for grass, he went to the foot of the Auspicious Tree (Śrī-vṛkṣa) to practice dhyāna. As for his sitting on a seat of grass, first, it was to manifest his own practice of few desires;
second, it was to establish a model for his disciples to follow. The grass was greenish-blue in color, like that of a peacock king.
[His] neck was supple, with blood that was fine and smooth. According to the *Caogu jing* (Sutra on Cause and Effect), he perceived the past through contemplation. He used grass as his seat;
Śakra, having transformed himself into a man, held some pure, soft grass and asked, "What is its name? He replied, "Auspicious. Upon hearing this, the Bodhisattva’s heart was filled with great joy.

I have destroyed inauspiciousness and thereby established auspiciousness. This person should also be requested to be ordained first. Next, the method of sitting is explained: because the body is upright, it is "straight";
because the mind is bound and not dissipated, it is called "right intention"; and because one focuses single-mindedly on a single object, it is named "binding mindfulness before oneself."

The fact that he does not explicitly mention sitting in the *paryaṅka* (cross-legged) posture is an omission; it is logically appropriate for a Bodhisattva to sit in the *paryaṅka* posture. The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 39, asks:
"Among all the modes of deportment (*īryāpatha*), one can cultivate wholesome qualities in each; why then does the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* specify sitting in the cross-legged posture?
It answers: "Because this is the constant deportment of the noble ones (*ārya*). That is to say, the Buddhas of the past and future, numbering as many as the sands of the Ganges..."
Because all disciples of the Buddha abide in this posture while entering meditative concentration. Furthermore, such a posture accords with the categories of wholesome qualities (*kuśala-pakṣa*):
if one walks or stands, the body quickly becomes fatigued; if one leans or lies down, drowsiness and sleep increase.
Only by sitting cross-legged (*paryaṅka-bandha*) are these faults avoided, thereby enabling the cultivation of superior wholesome qualities. [Question: Regarding sitting cross-legged...
What is the meaning [of this]? The answer is: it is the sense of sitting upright with one’s form perfectly complete. The etymologists say:
placing both feet so that the insteps rest upon the thighs, like the coiled body of a dragon, and sitting upright in contemplation;

furthermore, it is explained as crossing the two feet over one another, right and left, and correctly observing the object of focus—this is called *paryaṅka-bandha* (the cross-legged posture). Only this deportment is conducive to the cultivation of meditative concentration. Furthermore...
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Sengqi lü), fascicle 35, states: "The group of six bhikṣus were sitting in the cross-legged posture with their legs tucked under them (*paryaṅka*) inside a meditation cell.

The other bhikṣus informed the Buddha. The Buddha said: 'From this day forward, you must not sit in the cross-legged posture with legs tucked under; you should sit in the full lotus position (*paryaṅka-bandha*)."* (Note: The term *luoma se zuo* [駱[馬*色]坐] appears to be a transliteration or variant for *paryaṅka*, referring to a specific seated posture, often associated with the full lotus or a variation thereof in vinaya contexts.)

Next is the correct cultivation of *dhyāna* (meditative concentration); in the new terminology, it is called *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and insight). There are four distinct types of *dhyāna*. An explanation of these four *dhyānas* is presented through a threefold analysis:

first, the explanation of their names; second, the determination of their essential nature (*svabhāva*); and third, the analysis according to various categories. Regarding the explanation of the names:
in Sanskrit it is *dhyāna*, which is translated here as "meditative concentration" (*jing-lü*). The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, chapter twenty-eight, asks: "By what meaning is this established?"
Therefore, the name "dhyāna" (meditative absorption) is established. The answer is: because by means of this tranquility (*śamatha*), one is able to exercise discernment (*vicāra*).

Tranquility is concentration (*samādhi*); discernment is wisdom (*prajñā*). If that were so, all formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) should also be called "dhyānas," since they too are tranquil and capable of discernment.

Answer: The name is established based on its preeminence, not because of other meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) and so forth. It is like how, in the world, the sun is called "the Radiant One," yet fireflies or candles do not also receive the name "sun.
Question: How is it that *dhyāna* alone is named "the Sun"? Answer: Among all forms of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), only this one encompasses the [eight] factors (*aṅga*);

it proceeds with the equilibrium of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*), and it is supremely capable of thorough deliberation (*vicāra*). Therefore, only this one receives the preeminent name.

Next, the essential nature [of the dhyānas] is set forth. Each of these four dhyānas has two aspects: namely, birth (*upapatti*) and meditative absorption (*samāpatti*). Birth-dhyāna is not necessarily absorption; it is a place of residence.
Absorption-dhyāna, which constitutes the essential nature, is exclusively of a wholesome character (*kuśala*).

Because *samādhi* (concentration) can cause the mental sovereign (*citta-rāja*) to be one-pointed and focused on a single object, it is called "absorption. Its essential nature consists of wholesome *samādhi* among the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*). If [the category] is taken inclusively...

The accompanying factors have the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as their nature, because the form that functions in accordance with them constitutes the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). Question:
If one-pointedness of mind (*ekāgratā*) is itself the nature of *dhyāna*, on what basis are the four *dhyānas* established? Answer:

These are divided into four types of one-pointedness based on the presence or absence of the constituent factors (*aṅga*). Next, there are four sections. First: Which meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) do they subsume?

The factors of the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*). Second, the number of factors in each absorption. Third, the reason for establishing these factors. Fourth, the commonality and specific application across the various stages. Regarding the first gate, there are three types of *dhyāna*:
first, the *āsvādita-samādhi* (tasting concentration), which refers to attachment to pure concentration through feeling associated with craving;

second, the *śuddha-samādhi* (pure concentration), so called because it arises in association with non-attachment and other wholesome, pure dharmas; third, the *anāsrava-samādhi* (untainted concentration), which is not the object of craving.
Therefore, among the three [types of concentration], the latter two include the factors (*aṅga*), whereas the first—the concentration of "tasting" (*āsvādana*)—does not.

According to the second method, the factors of concentration total eighteen: the first dhyāna has five factors: (1) vitarka, (2) vicāra, (3) prīti, (4) sukha, and (5) samādhi; *samādhi* is a specific name for concentration. The second dhyāna has four factors:

(1) adhyātmasaṃprasāda, (2) prīti, (3) sukha, and (4) samādhi. The third dhyāna has five factors: (1) ... [text continues] ... (Note: The provided source text ends abruptly with "一", which corresponds to the beginning of the fourth factor of the third dhyāna, *upekṣā*. The translation reflects the available portion of the text.)

The four factors of the first dhyāna are: 1. equanimity of application (*upekṣā*), 2. right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*), 3. right wisdom (*samyak-prajñā*), and 4. experience of pleasure (*sukha*). The four factors of the second dhyāna are: 1. purity of equanimity (*upekṣā-pariśuddhi*), 2.

purity of mindfulness (*smṛti-pariśuddhi*), 3. neither-pain-nor-pleasure (*aduḥkhāsukha*), and 4. meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Although the number of factors thus totals eighteen, [they are subsumed under the four dhyānas].
In reality, there are only eleven factors. That is to say: the five branches of the first dhyāna;

in the second dhyāna, there is only internal clarity (adhyātmasaṃprasāda), while the remaining three are as before—adding these to the previous makes six. In the third dhyāna, samādhi is as before, while the remaining four are distinct in substance—adding these to the previous makes ten.
Within the fourth dhyāna, non-painful-non-pleasant sensation (aduḥkhāsukhā vedanā) is added, while the remaining three are as before; thus, they become eleven. However...

These eleven [factors] are stated as such because joy (*prīti*), bliss (*sukha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) are explained separately. However, according to their essential types (*jāti*), there are only nine, because joy, bliss, and equanimity are all equally feelings (*vedanā*).

Furthermore, among these nine, mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and feeling (*vedanā*) are the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*); faith (*śraddhā*), pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), and the application of equanimity (*upekṣā-praṇidhāna*) are the great wholesome mental factors (*kuśala-mahābhūmika-dharma*);
and vitarka and vicāra are enumerated as factors external to the universal mental factors. Question: What is defined as a "limb of dhyāna" (*dhyānāṅga*)?
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 80, explains: "Because they are conducive to this dhyāna, they are called 'limbs of dhyāna' (*dhyānāṅga*).
Regarding the third point: although there are four dhyānas, the number of limbs should be the same. Why, then, are there five in the first three and four in the second and those above?

The explanation is that, as previously stated, being "conducive" is the meaning of a "limb. That is to say, each of the four dhyānas possesses its own corresponding set of conducive factors; they do not increase beyond that.

They are not diminished. Furthermore, because the various evils of the desire realm are difficult to sever, difficult to shatter, and difficult to transcend, the first dhyāna establishes five factors as a firm and powerful antidote.

Because the second dhyāna is characterized by intense joy on a heavy ground and is difficult to sever, difficult to shatter, and difficult to transcend, the third dhyāna establishes five factors as a firm and powerful antidote. And the first...
Third, because neither [of these two] possesses such factors as being difficult to abandon, the second and fourth dhyānas each establish four limbs.

Furthermore, in order to counteract the greed for the five predominant objects of desire in the desire realm, five [limbs] are established at the outset; this is to serve as an antidote for those two stages.
Because the five categories of heavy factors are associated with the sensation of joy (*saumanasya*), the third dhyāna is also established as having five factors.

Since neither the first nor the third dhyānas possess these [specific] conditions, the second and fourth dhyānas each have four factors established. Question: Are the factors of the first dhyāna also those of the second dhyāna?
It should be answered by means of four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). There are those that are the first factor but not the second; namely, *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought).

There are those that are the second but not the first; namely, internal serenity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*). There are those that belong to both the first and the second; namely, joy (*prīti*), bliss (*sukha*), and concentration (*samādhi*). There are those that are neither the first nor the second;

namely, the exclusion of the aforementioned factors. Furthermore, it is asked: "If something is a factor of the first [dhyāna], is it also a factor of the third? It should be answered by means of four propositions. There are those that are factors of the first...

It is not the third [dhyāna]. That is to say, applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), joy (*prīti*), and bliss (*sukha*). There are factors that are the third [dhyāna] but not the first:

namely, equanimity (*upekṣā*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and bliss (*sukha*). There are factors that are both the first limb and the third: namely, one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*). There are factors that are neither the first nor the third: namely, excluding the aforementioned characteristics.

He asked again: "If it is the first factor, is it also the fourth dhyāna? He replied: "One should formulate four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*). There are those that are the first factor but not the fourth, namely:
vitarka, vicāra, prīti, and sukha. There are those that are the fourth but not the first, namely: the intermediate feeling (*upekṣā*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), and awareness (*samprajanya*).

There are those that are both the first factor and the fourth, namely: one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*). There are those that are neither the first nor the fourth, namely: excluding the aforementioned characteristics."

Regarding the second dhyāna and so forth, the four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi) should be understood according to the explanation provided for their mutual comparison. In this fourth section, there are eighteen factors of the four meditative absorptions (dhyāna-aṅga) in total.

Among these, the four essential natures of meditative concentration (samādhi-svabhāva) serve as the basis for all stages; therefore, they pertain to all stages and require no further questioning or answering.
Next, there are six types: namely, vitarka, vicāra, and prīti in the first dhyāna; prīti in the second dhyāna; sukha in the third dhyāna; and [the remaining factors] in the fourth dhyāna.

The middle [feeling] is sensation (*vedanā*). These six types of mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) ought to exist in all stages (*bhūmi*); therefore, they are present in all stages without the need for further questioning or answering.

Next, there are eight types: namely, the pleasure (*sukha*) of the first dhyāna; the internal purity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*) and pleasure of the second dhyāna; equanimity (*upekṣā*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), and wisdom (*prajñā*) of the third dhyāna;

and the establishment of distinct objects through equanimity and mindfulness in the fourth dhyāna. An explanation of the reason for this is required. Question: Since pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) and the practice of equanimity (*upekṣā*) exist in all stages, why is it that [only] the first...
In two cases, pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) is established as a factor and not equanimity (*upekṣā*); in three cases, equanimity is established as a factor and not pliancy.

This is because the previously mentioned meaning of "conducive" (*anuloma*) constitutes the sense of being a factor. That is to say, pliancy is conducive to the first two meditative attainments, while equanimity is conducive to the [last] three.

Furthermore, it is for the purpose of eliminating the fivefold body of sensory consciousness (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*) and the associated bodily heaviness (*dausthulya*) of the desire realm, and for the purpose of eliminating the threefold body of sensory consciousness and the associated heaviness of the first dhyāna.
Because the body is coarse and heavy, the first and second dhyānas establish the factor of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).
In the third and fourth dhyānas, there is no coarse body-consciousness nor the bodily heaviness induced by it that must be counteracted; therefore, they do not establish pliancy.

Since pliancy is absent, they establish equanimity (*upekṣā*). Furthermore, the third dhyāna abandons extreme joy, while the fourth dhyāna abandons extreme bliss, in order to relinquish both joy and bliss.

Therefore, equanimity (*upekṣā*) is established [as a factor]. In the first two [dhyānas], joy (*prīti*) and bliss (*sukha*) are not abandoned; thus, equanimity is not established there. Since equanimity is absent, pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) is established [instead].
Question: Faith (*śraddhā*) pervades all stages; logically, it should be present everywhere. Why is it established as a factor only in the [first] two dhyānas? Answer:
It was previously stated that "conformity" is the meaning of being a "factor" (*aṅga*). Since faith conforms only to those two, it is established as a factor. Furthermore, in the first...

In the first dhyāna, vitarka and vicāra are like fire, while the body-consciousness is like mud; these cause the mental continuum to be heated, afflicted, turbid, and disordered, such that faith is not clear and pure, and the factor of faith is not established as a limb.
This is like a facial reflection not appearing in hot mud. Because there is neither fire nor mud in the [next] two dhyānas, the aspect of faith is clear and pure, and faith is established as a limb.
This is like a facial reflection appearing on the surface of clear, cool water. In the third dhyāna...

In the fourth dhyāna, there is an extremely pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*), while there is a superior equanimity (*upekṣā*) that obscures the mental continuum so that the characteristic of faith does not manifest;

therefore, it is not established as having the factor of internal clarity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*). Question: Since wisdom (*prajñā*) is present across all stages, it should also be universally present [as a factor].

Why is it established only in the third dhyāna? Answer: Because it was previously stated that the meaning of a "factor" (*aṅga*) is that which is conducive (*anuloma*). Wisdom is conducive only to the first three [dhyānas]; therefore, it is established only there.
[The factor of] right wisdom (*samyakprajñā*) is not established as a constituent (*aṅga*). Furthermore, in the first dhyāna, coarse vitarka and vicāra obscure right wisdom.
In the second dhyāna, intense joy (*prīti*) obscures right wisdom. In the fourth dhyāna, supreme equanimity (*upekṣā*) obscures right wisdom.

Since the feeling of supreme equanimity is a portion of ignorance (*avidyā*), whereas right wisdom is clarity (*vidyā*), and since clarity and ignorance are mutually contradictory and destructive, right wisdom is not established as a constituent in any of these stages. Second...
The three [factors] are established as limbs because they are qualities free from obscuration. Question: Since mindfulness (*smṛti*) is present in all stages, it should also be universally present.

Why is it established as a limb only in the third and fourth dhyānas? Answer: Since it is said that "conformity" is the meaning of being a limb, and mindfulness conforms to the third and fourth [dhyānas], it is established as a limb.
Furthermore, in the first dhyāna there are coarse vitarka and vicāra, which are like a violent wind; in the second dhyāna there is exultant joy (*prīti*), which is like...

Like waves upon water, they obstruct and conceal right mindfulness; therefore, the latter two are established together. Because these faults do not exist [in the case of mindfulness], mindfulness is established as a factor (*aṅga*).

Next, the text is explained below. Regarding the four meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), there are four sections. First, the initial concentration is explained. The initial concentration further consists of four parts: first, the removal of obstacles to concentration.

Second, the analysis of the attainment of concentration; third, the summary that reveals the attainment; fourth, the explanation of the basis for the attainment. Since it is thus for one concentration, it is the same for all others.
Regarding the first passage, "removing desire-attachment and so forth," the explanation is as before. Furthermore, the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vibhāṣā), fascicle 80, explains:

"Desire" refers to the five objects of desire (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*); "evil and unwholesome dharmas" refers to the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*). Alternatively, "desire" means desire-attachment (*kāmarāga*), and "evil and unwholesome dharmas" refers to...

As for the remaining afflictions of the desire realm, since the root of delusion has been eliminated, one attains concentration (*samādhi*). *Vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought) correspond to the factors of elimination;

a coarse state of mind is called *vitarka*, while a subtle state of mind is called *vicāra*. These are alternative names for *vitakka* and *vicāra*. *Pīti* (joy) and *sukha* (bliss) are the factors of benefit.

Mental gladness is called *prīti* (joy); physical gladness is called *sukha* (bliss). This bliss is *praśrabdhi* (pliancy). "One-pointed mind" refers to *samādhi* (equipoise), which is the basis for those two.
The remainder of the text may be understood accordingly. Next, the second dhyāna is explained; its four textual sections are as before. First, the removal of hindrances is explained.
Vitarka and vicāra disturb the second dhyāna; therefore, they must be eliminated. For example, when clear water is disturbed by waves, nothing can be seen.
Next, the attainment of concentration consists of internal faith as the factor of counteraction. Faith is the aspect of purity, which is called "internal serenity" (adhyātmasaṃprasāda).

Because it is free from external agitation and flows evenly within concentration, it is named "internal serenity. Joy and bliss are the factors of benefit; the explanation is the same [as for the first dhyāna].

The preceding stage: "one-pointedness of mind" (*citta-ekāgratā*) is the basis for those two. The remainder of the text may be understood accordingly. Next, regarding the fourth dhyāna: "joy" (*prīti*) is an obstacle.
Because one perceives many faults in joy, it must be eliminated. For example, when a poor man finds treasure he rejoices, yet once he loses it, his grief becomes even more intense.
By severing both joy and sorrow, one immediately attains bliss. Next, "attaining concentration" (*samādhi*) refers to noble wisdom (*ārya-jñāna*).

What is seen is right wisdom (*samyag-prajñā*). "Guarding" refers to equanimity (*upekṣā*). "Mindfulness" (*smṛti*) refers to right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*). Mindfulness consists in knowing the faults of joy (*prīti*), while wisdom consists in correct discernment.

Equanimity consists in being free from those faults; these three are the factors for removal (*vyupaśama-aṅga*). Because joy is abandoned, mindfulness and wisdom become predominant. "Bliss" (*sukha*) refers to the feeling of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*); this is the factor of benefit (*anuśaṃsa-aṅga*).
The single-pointedness of mind (*citta-ekāgratā*) is omitted here [for brevity]. The rest of the text is easily understood. Next, regarding the four dhyānas, there are four [aspects]:

The bliss obtained in the three dhyānas is indeed beneficial; however, when compared to the fourth dhyāna, it constitutes a significant hindrance. Just as a seriously ill person regards exquisite music as an obstacle to the fourth dhyāna and must therefore eliminate it, so too [must one eliminate the bliss].
If this is so, one should only abandon pleasure (*sukha*); why then is it further said that one abandons suffering (*duḥkha*)? The answer is:
in reality, the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) has already been severed in the first dhyāna. It is only now, upon attaining the fourth dhyāna, that one is said to have severed it.

Because this has already been abandoned, it is said to be "abandoned. This means that a term denoting proximity is used for something distant. Furthermore, another interpretation is that the term "abandoned" is spoken of both together based on the exhaustion of the pair of dharmas.
As for the "pair of dharmas," it refers to suffering and pleasure. At the time of attaining the first dhyāna, although suffering has already been left behind, pleasure is not yet exhausted.
Now, having become detached from the defilements of the third *dhyāna*, both suffering and pleasure are exhausted; thus, they are both said to be abandoned.

[The text discusses] the cessation of sound. Question: Why is it stated again that "sorrow and joy have already been abandoned"? Answer: Because sorrow and joy have already been left behind even before pleasure was severed, it says "already.

Furthermore, the first dhyāna extinguishes the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasya*); the third dhyāna extinguishes the faculty of joy (*saumanasya*); the second dhyāna extinguishes the faculty of suffering (*duḥkha*);

and the fourth dhyāna extinguishes the faculty of pleasure (*sukha*). This is intended to clarify that the four dhyānas sever the four types of feeling (*vedanā*), and thus [the text] summarizes them all together at the outset. Therefore...

Regarding the statement "abandoning suffering and pleasure," etc., this next section clarifies the attainment of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Being without suffering and without pleasure is the limb of benefit (*anuśaṃsāṅga*).

"Equanimity" (*upekṣā*) refers to pure equanimity (*upekṣā-pariśuddhi*); "mindfulness" (*smṛti*) refers to pure mindfulness (*smṛti-pariśuddhi*). These two are the limbs of purification (*vyavadānaṅga*).

The single-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*) is omitted here because it is included by virtue of being free from the eight calamities—namely, suffering, pleasure, grief, joy, inhalation, exhalation, and the two types of discursive investigation (*vitarka-vicāra*). Therefore, it is called equanimity.

"Mindfulness" refers to purity; the rest of the text is easily understood. Question: When a bodhisattva previously cultivated the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana), they had already attained freedom from desire for the defilements of the eight lower stages. How is it that, when about to proceed toward enlightenment, they instead bring to mind the first dhyāna among the [nine] stages and again contemplate it in order to sever the remaining defilements of the lower stages? Answer: Although the prior cultivation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception did indeed sever the defilements of the lower stages, because he followed a false teacher, he did not [realize this]. Thus, he must again apply effort to sever those remaining traces. Furthermore, because he has not yet abandoned the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the form realm, he must cultivate the first dhyāna to sever them. Moreover, because he has not yet severed the afflictions of the formless realm, he must cultivate the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception to sever them. Because he has not yet severed the afflictions of the formless realm, he again brings to mind the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception to sever them. It is for these reasons that he repeatedly contemplates the various stages. As stated in the *Mahāyāna-abhidharma-samuccaya-śāstra*: "The bodhisattva, having already severed the afflictions of the nine stages through the path of seeing, subsequently cultivates the path of meditation to sever the remaining afflictions. This is what is meant. Furthermore, although he had previously severed the afflictions of the nine stages, he did not yet possess the power of mastery over the meditative concentrations. Therefore, he again brings to mind the first dhyāna to cultivate the power of mastery over the concentrations. Because he has not yet severed the afflictions of the formless realm, he again brings to mind the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception to sever them. This is what is meant. Furthermore, although he had previously severed the afflictions of the nine stages, he did not yet possess the power of mastery over the meditative concentrations. Therefore, he again brings to mind the first dhy
Having realized the truth, he is now about to attain Buddhahood. Seeking the fundamental correct cause, he merely wishes to follow the tracks and tread the path;

it is not for the sake of severing the lower afflictions (*kleśa*). As for the statement in the text regarding "leaving evil" and so forth, this refers to the sound of "now leaving" in relation to that which has already been left behind—just as when one says a king has "already arrived," one speaks of him as "arriving now."
Next, he proceeded to the foot of the Bodhi tree. There, through thirty-four moments of mind, he attained Perfect Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Because the Buddha’s body possesses extraordinary and sublime merits, the earth and mountains all shook and trembled;

yet beneath this very tree stood the Vajrāsana, reaching from the surface of the earth down to the Golden Wheel (*kāñcana-cakra*). All Bodhisattvas who are about to ascend to Perfect Enlightenment sit upon this seat before they arise.

The diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) possesses a firm power through its lack of a remainder of support (*anupadhiśeṣa*) and other locations, as it is able to sustain this [attainment].
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 13, states:

"It was heard that after the Bodhisattva realized that the practice of asceticism was not the true path, he then accepted the sixteen-virtue-perfected honeyed milk-rice offered by the sisters Nandā and Nandabalā; having eaten it..."
With body and mind stable and full of strength, he received auspicious *kuśa* grass from an auspicious person and proceeded to the foot of the Bodhi tree.
There, with his own hands, he spread it out and sat down cross-legged, coiling his body like the Nāga King Vāsuki. Having sat down, he made this firm vow:
"If I do not exhaust all outflows (*āsrava*) here and realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, I shall [never rise]."

It shall not arise. At that time, the great earth and all its mountains shook in six ways, like a light boat upon the sea rising and falling with the waves, even as far as the palaces of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods;
they were all shaken like the leaves of a plantain tree blown by a fierce wind.
The Māra King was terrified and, observing the cause of the trembling, saw the Bodhisattva sitting beneath the Bodhi tree, his body upright and unmoving.

He stirred [the earth] and vowed to attain Bodhi. From afar, he left his palace and went to where the Bodhisattva was, urging him to accept the rank of a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*), as is described at length there.

However, although the gates of merit of the Buddha seated beneath the Bodhi tree are immeasurable, for the sake of concise transformation, I shall briefly distinguish the three types of knowledge (*vidyā*).
In explaining these three knowledges, they are analyzed through three sections. First, the explanation of their names. Second...

Second, the essential nature; third, the analysis by way of various categories. Regarding the explanation of the names: first, the "knowledge and realization of past lives" (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñānasākṣātkriyā*).

It is called "past lives" (*pūrvanivāsa*) because it knows events from the prior limit of time. This knowledge is attained through wisdom, and is therefore termed "knowledge and realization" (*jñānasākṣātkriyā*).

Second is the clear realization of the knowledge of death and rebirth (*cyuty-upapāda-jñāna-sākṣātkriyā*). Because one knows in advance the causes and effects of the future limit (*aparānta*) before they have arisen, it is called "death and rebirth.
The explanation of "knowledge" (*jñāna*) is the same as before. Third is the clear realization of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya-jñāna-sākṣātkriyā*).

That which detains sentient beings, causing them to dwell long in birth and death, is termed an "outflow" (*āsrava*). The place where outflows are extinguished is termed "exhaustion" (*kṣaya*). Since this exhaustion results from knowledge, it is called a "clear realization through knowledge. Collectively, these are termed "illuminations" (*vidyā*).

This is because they are thoroughly penetrating and fully comprehending. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 102, states: "These three types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*) are all able to accord with the wearying abandonment of birth and death;
all are able to induce supreme qualities; and all are able to lead toward ultimate *nirvāṇa*.

Therefore, they are called 'clear knowledges' (*vidyā*). Next, regarding their essential nature (*svabhāva*): these three types of clear knowledge have wisdom (*prajñā*) as their intrinsic nature. However, in terms of their specific character as knowledge (*jñāna*), [they are further distinguished].
The first two are conventional wisdoms (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) that, by means of functional observation, discern the events of the past and future limits.

As for the clear knowledge of death and rebirth (*cyuty-upapāda-jñāna*), if it is considered in relation to its fundamental basis, it takes the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divya-cakṣur-abhijñā*) as its essence and takes only the present as its object.

However, according to the retinue induced by this supernormal power, it takes the wisdom associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna-saṃprayukta-prajñā*) as its essence, because it is able to universally perceive future events.

Therefore, the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣur-abhijñā*) cannot know this matter. Because sentient beings possess the three types of karmic conduct, they are born into the good or evil realms according to what their karma evokes.
The divine eye can only perceive form; it does not know speech or intention.

There is a distinct, superior wisdom that is an attendant of the supernormal powers, which arises based on the body of an Arya and is able to know [all these things] completely. This attendant wisdom is also called the "wisdom of death and rebirth" (*cyutyupapādajñāna*).

This knowledge of death and rebirth is induced by the supernormal power of the divine eye; therefore, it is established under the name "knowledge of death and rebirth" in conjunction with that supernormal power.
As for why it is induced by that, it means that the supernormal power of the divine eye is able to know that one dies here and is reborn there; such is this knowledge of death and rebirth.
One also knows that after dying here, one is born there; because the categories of beings are similar, [the karma] is able to project and produce [rebirth].

As for the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣur-abhijñā*), it takes only present form (*rūpa*) as its object. The knowledge of death and rebirth (*cyutyupapādajñāna-sākṣātkriyā*) takes the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) of both the present and the future as its objects.

As for the clear vision of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-vidyā*): if it takes the exhaustion of outflows as its object, it consists of only six types of knowledge, because the exhaustion of outflows is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and these six knowledges take it as their object.

Exclusion: The four [knowledges] of others' minds, suffering, origin, and the path are excluded. This is because the knowledges of suffering and origin take only contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena as their objects, while the knowledge of the path takes conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) phenomena as its object;

the knowledge of others' minds takes both contaminated and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) phenomena as its objects. Since none of these can take unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena as their objects, they must be excluded.
If it is claimed that [the knowledge] arising within the body of one whose outflows are exhausted (*āsravakṣaya*) is of the nature of the ten knowledges (*daśajñāna*), there are next three sections:

first, the difference in their three natures; second, the distinction in the objects they illuminate; and third, the general questions and answers. Regarding the "three natures," these three are all wholesome (*kuśala*).

As for the knowledge of death and rebirth (*cyutyupapādajñāna*), if it were categorized under the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣurabhijñā*) based on the similarity of its flow and type, it would be [unconditioned].

This records the wisdom associated with eye-consciousness. If one takes up a distinct and superior knowledge, it is a retinue of that [wisdom]. According to the theory of retinues, it is exclusively wholesome.
Next, regarding "illuminating the object," the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Furthermore, the supernormal power of the clear realization of the knowledge of recollecting past lives..."

Because one thoroughly penetrates and understands the phenomena of the past limit (*pūrvānta*), the knowledge and vision of death and rebirth (*cyutyupapādajñānadarśana*) is established as clear illumination (*vidyā*).

Because one thoroughly penetrates and understands the phenomena of the future limit (*aparānta*), the knowledge and vision of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayajñānadarśana*) is established as clear illumination. Because one thoroughly penetrates and understands the nature of *nirvāṇa*, it is all likewise called clear illumination.
Furthermore, the first clear illumination consists of knowing, among the past limits of all sentient beings, how by such karma they die here and are born there, [discerning] cause and effect.

Continuity. Next, one clearly understands that among the future limits of all sentient beings, by means of such karma, they die here and are born there, with cause and effect continuing in succession.
Subsequently, one clearly understands that all sentient beings, by means of such a path, can exhaust all outflows (*āsrava*) and sever the continuity of cause and effect;
this alone is ultimate illumination (*paramārtha-vidyā*), while the former two types are conventional illumination (*saṃvṛti-vidyā*). Question: This...

Question: Since they are mundane (*saṃvṛti*), how can they be called "clear knowledges" (*vidyā*)? Answer: Because they can lead to the clear knowledge of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-vidyā*), they are conventionally designated as "clear knowledges," though they are not the true ultimate reality itself.
Next is the question and answer: Question: For what reason are these three among the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) established as "clear knowledges"?

Answer: Because these three possess superior efficacy. That is to say, the realization of the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna-sākṣātkriyā*) perceives phenomena of the prior limit (*pūrvānta*). Deeply...

He gives rise to revulsion. He realizes the knowledge of death and rebirth and perceives the events of the future limit, giving rise to deep revulsion. He realizes the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows. Having already become revulsed, he takes delight in *nirvāṇa*.
Furthermore, first, through clear vision, he perceives his own decline and loss within the past limit and gives rise to deep revulsion.
Next, through clear vision, he perceives the decline and loss of others within the future limit and gives rise to deep revulsion. Finally, having become revulsed—

[The others] are excluded. Since [the knowledge of cessation] has already rejoiced in *nirvāṇa*, the remaining three do not possess this superior function; therefore, they are not established [as such]. The *Abhidharmakośa* states:
"Because of these delusions regarding the limit (*koṭi*) and the three periods of time (*traiyadhvika*), these three types alone are established as 'clear knowledges' (*vidyā*)."

Next, the text is explained. The third illumination (vidyā) has three parts: first, the explanation of the initial illumination. This initial illumination also has three parts: first, citing the wisdom-illumination;

second, the time of attainment; and third, explaining the reason why. Within the first part, there are again three sections: first, concluding the practice to manifest the wisdom; second, citing the objects illuminated;
and third, the section beginning with "knowing the innumerable," which serves as the general conclusion. Regarding the first section: because one has attained the fourth dhyāna, it is said:
Having attained this concentrated state of mind, one becomes free from transgressions and established in practice; hence it is said that "all fetters are eliminated," and so forth.

Because one has severed the three calamities and the four types of sensation, it is said that one "dwells in a place of firm stability. This correctly raises the essence of illumination; hence it is said that one "realizes the knowledge of past lives.

Regarding the second section on the illumination of objects, there are four parts: first, manifesting wisdom by way of the number of births; second, manifesting wisdom by way of time, beginning with the formation of kalpas; third, "I once... [and so on].

The passage beginning with "birth" (*jāti*) and so forth clarifies wisdom (*jñāna*) by way of its retribution (*vipāka*). The fourth section, from "from that end" (*tataḥ paryantāt*) downwards, clarifies wisdom by way of its locus (*sthāna*). The remainder of the text is easily understood.

However, regarding the phrase "when ignorance (*avidyā*) is exhausted, clarity (*vidyā*) arises," this refers to the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*). "When darkness is exhausted, light arises" refers to the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).

It may also be interpreted as first severing defiled ignorance (*kliṣṭājñāna*), followed by severing non-defiled ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*). Regarding the second "clarity," the definitive text is as stated above.

The second section, "Illuminating the Objects," consists of two parts: first, the general, followed by the specific. Within the general, the result is presented first, followed by the cause; within the specific, the cause is presented first, followed by the result.
Next, the third section, "Clarifying," has three parts as mentioned above; its initial part contains only two sections and lacks a concluding statement.

The second section, "Illuminating the Objects," has four parts: first, "contemplating the truths as they truly are"; second, "having already attained [the path], one contemplates the truths below to sever outflows (*āsrava*). This is because...

Previously one knew the truths; now one attains the cessation of outflows (*āsrava*). Hence it is said, "one has already attained," and so forth. As for "according to reality": the outflows themselves are the substance of the outflows. "Knowing the accumulation of outflows" means knowing the cause of the outflows.

"The path leading toward the exhaustion of outflows" refers to the path for severing the outflows. Alternatively, one may know according to reality that the outflows are the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*);

knowing the accumulation of outflows is the Truth of Accumulation (*samudaya-satya*); the exhaustion of outflows is the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*); and the path leading toward it is the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*).

This refers to the abandonment of outflows (*āsrava*) by means of the Truths as objects of focus. Regarding the passage "Third, he acts thus... and so forth: because he abandons the outflows, he is liberated.
"He acts thus" reiterates the prior abandonment of outflows; "observing thus" below refers to attaining liberation.

As for the "three outflows," these refer to the fundamental afflictions (*kleśa*) within the Desire Realm—thirty-one entities excluding delusion (*moha*), together with the ten entanglements (*paryavasthāna*)—which constitute the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*). As for "existence" (*bhava*):

In the form and formless realms (*rūpa-ārūpya-dhātu*), the fundamental afflictions (*mūla-kleśa*), excluding delusion (*moha*), comprise fifty-two entities which constitute the outflows with outflows (*sāsrava*).

Question: Why are the secondary afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) not included in the two higher realms? Answer: Because the secondary afflictions are few in those realms, as beings there lack autonomy (*asvatantra*). Question:

Why are the afflictions of the two higher realms collectively designated as "with outflows"? Answer: Because they are equally indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and operate within the internal door (*adhyātma-mukha*) based upon meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Because it belongs to the [defiled] stage (*bhūmi*) and possesses these three meanings, it is combined with the others into one. There are fifteen types of ignorance (*avidyā*) in the three realms, which constitute the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*).
Question: For what reason is this alone established separately as an outflow? Answer: Because ignorance is able to serve as the root of all existence (*bhava*).
Because ignorance exists, formations and the other links come to be. For this reason, ignorance is established separately as an outflow (*āsrava*).

Question: What is the meaning of "outflow"? Answer: It causes sentient beings to linger and dwell long in saṃsāra, or causes them to flow and wander within saṃsāra from the Peak of Existence down to the Avīci Hell.
Because of that continuity, it discharges faults inexhaustibly through the six wound-gates. Therefore [it is called an outflow].
They are called "outflows" (*āsrava*). They are like water gushing from a spring or milk flowing from a breast. Furthermore, the meaning of being "restrained" is the meaning of "outflow.
Just as when a person is restrained by others, they cannot travel at will; the meaning of being "held fast" is the meaning of "outflow.
Just as when a person is held fast by others, they cannot travel freely through the four directions, so too are sentient beings [held fast] by their various afflictions.
Because they are bound by grasping, they circulate through the various realms, destinies, and births, and are unable to proceed freely toward nirvāṇa.

Regarding the fourth [fruit], although one is already liberated, it is not the ultimate state of the four knowledges. "Already liberated" reiterates the prior liberation; one attains the knowledge of liberation.
This refers to untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) that arises within the person who has attained liberation; therefore, it is called "wisdom of liberation.

As for the statement "my births are ended" and so forth, this means that by the power of the untainted contemplation of internal exhaustion and non-arising, one subsequently utters such words while abiding in the subsequently attained mundane wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-saṃvṛti-jñāna*) after emerging from meditative equipoise.
Thus it is said, "my births are ended," etc. Question: What are the characteristics of these statements, "my births are ended" and so forth?
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 102, explains: It should be stated that [birth] occurs throughout the three periods of time. Why is this?

Since the term "birth" here clearly refers to the four aggregates (*skandha*) of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), practitioners of meditation collectively contemplate these four aggregates of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception across the three periods of time;
by becoming detached from their defilements, they cause both the cause and the fruit of birth to be rendered unobtainable.
It is accomplished; therefore, it is said, "My births have been exhausted. Another interpretation is that it refers exclusively to the exhaustion of birth in future lives.
That is to say, when a practitioner upholds the prohibitive precepts and diligently cultivates the holy life (*brahmacarya*), they do so entirely to prevent birth in future lives.
Since past and present births cannot be prevented, whereas all future births can be prevented, the practitioner prevents them, thereby causing—
Because it will never arise again, it is said to be "exhausted. "The holy life has been established" refers to untainted conduct (*anāsrava-caryā*);

this is the holy life of one in training (*śaikṣa*), not the holy life of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), because the holy life of one beyond training is only now being established. "What was to be done has been accomplished" means:
Because all afflictions have been severed, and because all that was to be done has been fully accomplished, one "does not undergo further existence.
This means that all Arhats are free from further existence; therefore, it is stated generally that they do not undergo further existence.
Furthermore, another interpretation is that if any afflictions have not been severed or fully understood, one does not say, "My births are exhausted," and so forth. If [any such remain]...

Those who have already abandoned and fully understood the afflictions are all collectively described as "my births have been exhausted," and so forth. Furthermore, regarding the distinctions among these knowledges (*jñāna*):
herein, "my births have been exhausted" is the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*); "the holy life has been established" is the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*);

"what was to be done has been accomplished" is the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*); and "there is no further existence" is the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*). Some say that herein, "my births have been exhausted..."

"Exhausted" refers to the full knowledge of the origin [of suffering]. "The holy life has been established" refers to the full knowledge of the path. "What was to be done has been accomplished" refers to the full knowledge of cessation.
"There is no further existence" refers to the full knowledge of suffering. The remaining text is clear. Having reached this point, the outflows are exhausted and delusions have vanished;
knowing that the Way is perfected, he is called the Tathāgata and so forth. Thus concludes the account of the Teacher’s attainment of the Way.

From this point downward, the text transforms beings and delivers people. As we are about to explain the text, we shall first provide a preliminary analysis through four sections: first, clarifying the time when it was not spoken;
second, clarifying the intention for not speaking; third, clarifying the dharma-gates traversed; and fourth, providing a word-by-word commentary.
Regarding the initial periods: for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it is twenty-one days; for this Vinaya, it is six or seven days; for the *Udānavarga*, it is forty-nine days;
for the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, it is fifty-six days; and for the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it is fifty-seven days. These differences exist because the accounts of what was seen and heard vary.
As for the reason why these [specific] durations are not mentioned next, the second fascicle of the *Mahāsaṃghika-vinaya-mātṛkā* asks: "The Buddha [spent] three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*..."
He practiced the bodhisattva path in order to attain the Buddha-way and deliver all sentient beings. Why did he travel through various Dharma-gates for forty-nine days without seeking [the goal]?

Answer: The Buddha first established his own composure, and only then would he deliver others. Therefore, he traveled through various Dharma-gates to enjoy himself and bring his body and mind into harmony;
only after this would he deliver sentient beings. Furthermore, it was for the sake of Kātyāyana and the other five...

Because the faculties of people were not yet mature; furthermore, out of respect for the Buddha-dharma, he spoke with deliberation before teaching. Moreover, it was to fulfill the original vow of King Brahmā.

King Brahmā had vowed that once the Buddha attained the Way, he must first request the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma. For this reason, he waited for King Brahmā’s request before preaching the Dharma.
Next, to clarify the dharma-gates through which he traveled, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (Duo-lun) states: "When the Buddha first attained the Way..."

During the seven periods of seven days, he traversed various Dharma-gates and observed sentient beings. In the first seven days, he entered the Dharma-gate of Joy; in the second seven days, he entered the Dharma-gate of Bliss;
in the third seven days, he entered the various liberations; in the fourth seven days, he traveled into and entered Great Equanimity;
in the fifth seven days, he entered the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination in both direct and reverse order; in the sixth seven days...
He again traversed the aforementioned dharma-gates. During the seventh seven-day period, he observed those among sentient beings who were ready to be transformed;
this Vinaya speaks directly of receiving the bliss of liberation (*vimukti-sukha*) without distinguishing between joy (*muditā*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), and so forth.
From the perspective of principle, the Dharma realized by the Buddha is such that there is nothing that does not transcend obstructions and depart from signs; therefore, it is called "liberation."

Next, the explanation of the textual content is divided into two parts. First, it clarifies how [the Buddha] traveled through various Dharma-gates, experienced the bliss of liberation, took refuge in the Dharma with the two [monks], and delivered his external kinsmen.
Second, at that time, the World-Honored One traveled beneath the *Venuvana* (Bamboo Grove), using the "Welcome" formula and so forth.
Regarding the deliverance of his own kinsmen, the preceding text distinguishes six groups based on their different modes of conversion: first, merchants; second, a tree spirit;
third, a Brahmin; fourth, a Brahmin’s wife; fifth, the sons and daughters of a Brahmin; and sixth, the dragon king Manasvin.

Regarding these six locations: during the first three weeks, he was beneath the Bodhi tree; during the next two weeks, beneath the Nyagrodha tree; and during the final week, at the abode of the Naga King Mucilinda.
Although there are six sites for his transformative manifestations, there are only four realms of rebirth involved:

the first assembly consisted of humans and devas; the second, of non-humans (amanuṣya); the third and fourth [assemblies] were restricted to humans; and the sixth, to animals—namely, humans, devas, nāgas, and pretas.
Regarding the lay patrons: the first section has two parts. First, receiving the bliss of liberation; second, from "At that time, the World-Honored One...
onwards, the second part concerning conversion and deliverance. Within this [second part], there are five sections: first, the tree deity gives rise to faith and exhorts the offering of worship;

second, from "At that time, the brothers... onwards, they accept the exhortation and present their offerings; third, from "At that time, the World-Honored One again had this thought... onwards, the compassionate mind.

[The Buddha] accepted [the offering]. Fourth, from "He received that flour and honey" downwards, [it describes] how he preached the Dharma to transform and deliver them. Fifth, from "At that time, the merchants" downwards, [it describes] how the task was completed and they requested his return.
Regarding the third point, the acceptance of the gift: as for the text's question, "With what vessel shall I receive the food?", it refers to the bowl he used during his time as an ordinary person;
this very bowl became [his] at the moment of attaining Buddhahood. After crossing the Nairañjanā River, it sank into the water, where the Sāgara Dragon King took it away.
He made offerings. Since his own attainment of Buddhahood, no one had ever offered him a bowl; therefore, he asked, "With what vessel shall I receive this?
However, he also recollected that all Buddhas of the past had maintained stone alms-bowls, and thus he said, "I shall not receive it with my hands.
Then the Four Heavenly Kings, knowing the Buddha’s thoughts, each brought a bowl to present to the World-Honored One. Had the Buddha accepted them all, there would have been no need for many bowls.

If he were to accept only one, the benefit would not be universal. To manifest equal benefit for all sentient beings and to demonstrate that there is no need for many bowls, he accepted four in total, combining them into a single vessel.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "The Buddha further reflected: 'If I were to take only the bowl of one king...'"
The other kings could not bear [to offer their own bowls], so he accepted all four bowls. Holding them in his left hand and pressing them with his right, he joined them together into a single vessel.
When the Buddha first attained the Way, he immediately accepted a celestial bowl to eat the food of humans; this was to manifest that he had received the most supreme path among the two realms.
Because the Buddha’s benefits were manifold, he is called the Teacher of Gods and Humans. Regarding the fourth discourse on teaching and transformation, there are eight points within the text.
First is the bestowing of blessings, which is the preaching of the Dharma. Second, from the words "You all" onwards, is the exhortation to receive the two refuges;

because there was no Saṅgha [yet], it does not mention taking refuge in the Saṅgha. As stated in the *Inguoyin* (Causes and Conditions): first, taking refuge in the Buddha; second, taking refuge in the Dharma; third, taking refuge in the future Saṅgha.
Third, at the time following the two merchants, they requested and prayed for the performance of merit. Fourth, at that time, the World-Honored One knew...
At that lower [stage], he bestowed his hair and nails upon them, instructing them to perform offerings. At the fifth stage, the merchants were at a lower level;

although they obtained the hair and nails, they were unable to approach with a sincere heart, for they regarded them as discarded things of the human world and did not give rise to profound reverence.

At the sixth stage, the World-Honored One, knowing the state of the merchants, exhorted them not to give rise to contempt, saying that if they could offer worship with utmost sincerity, they would obtain great merit. At the seventh stage, the merchants...

The people said to the Buddha: "Although we have heard that the merit is great, we are unable to believe it with certainty. Your words must surely not be false; by what proof can we know they are true?
From "The eighth, the Buddha told the merchants... onwards, he extensively cited proofs and verification:

"In the past, when I was a young brahmin (*māṇava*), although I had received this prediction, I had not yet severed all outflows (*āsrava*). Because of my joy at the prediction, I leaped into the air, and even as I did so, I gave away my hair in alms. The assembly... [continued].
People made offerings [to them]. Now that I have attained Buddhahood, I observe with the eye of the Way that they have all entered into *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*; such is the evidence.
How much more so for my own hair and nails today, which are the most honored among all wondrous merits, as my delusions are exhausted and my fruition is perfected?
If one can make offerings to them, the reward will be abundant. Therefore, I now earnestly exhort you. The latter five assemblies are divided into two parts, as previously described.
Next follows the section on saving the inner retinue. This passage consists of three parts: first, the Tathāgata’s contemplation of not preaching;
second, Brahmā descending from heaven to know his thoughts and request the preaching; third, the World-Honored One descending to respond to conditions and proceed with the preaching.
