second, having a seeking mind, as the text says, "desiring to go forth and practice the holy life within the Tathāgata’s Dharma";

third, the necessity of being in the presence of the Buddha, as the text says, "previously addressed the Buddha, saying..."; and fourth, relying on the Buddha’s instruction, such as the command to come. These three types of speech also each have four aspects; the first is going forth...

The characteristics of the household: as the text fully states, one shaves the hair and dons the *kāṣāya*. Second, one faces the various *arhats*. Third, the instruction is bestowed in accordance with the Dharma.

Fourth, one receives the full ordination (*upasampadā*). There are also four points regarding that which must not be transgressed: first, obtaining the Buddha’s permission; second, personally facing Ānanda; third, fully proclaiming the respectful instructions;

and fourth, receiving them upon the crown of the head and practicing them accordingly. This concludes the exposition on the reception of the precepts through the ritual of *karmavācanā* as established from of old.

It is endowed with four conditions, as explained in the *Karmavācanā* for the eight bhikṣus. The text states: "If one receives the full ordination (*upasampadā*), there must be the condition of the fulfillment of the number of monks;
the condition of the successful accomplishment of the formal procedure (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) according to the Dharma;

the condition of the accomplishment of the boundary (*sīmā-bandha*) by obtaining a proper location; and the condition of not forming a separate assembly within the boundary while abiding in the dharma of a bhikṣu."

As for this, when one has reached the full age, possesses no physical impediments or obstacles, and the conditions are complete—when these four factors are present, one is a Great Bhikṣu and may successfully accomplish the root of the precepts.
A person who violates the precepts lacks one of these four and is therefore not a Great Bhikṣu; thus, these four are required for the ritual of ordination to be perfected.

This constitutes the "extinction of disputes" through the five types of presence (*pañca-sammukha*), wherein the object of the dispute is excluded and the remaining four presences are fulfilled. First, the agent...
First, the preceptor who administers; second, the dharma that is administered; third, the place where the dharma is administered, namely the *sīmā* (boundary) being present;

and fourth, the matter for which it is performed, namely the person being present. Now, this act of receiving the precepts is specifically what is performed; therefore, it possesses these four factors and is thus able to engender the precepts.

If the precepts are established, it is due to the completeness of these conditions; hence, this text is cited to explain the meaning of a *bhikṣu*. However, the current interpretation is not so. Upon careful examination of...
The meaning of the text is as follows: this merely serves to distinguish those who incur an offense; it is not intended to explain the full significance of the conditions (*pratyaya*).
The phrase "if one has received the full precepts" (*mahā-śīla*) excludes those who do not possess the complete set of precepts, namely śramaṇas and others, non-Buddhists, and laypeople.

The term "those for whom the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* has been performed" excludes those for whom only the *jñapti-dvitīya* or other [lesser] formal acts have been performed (this constitutes one clause). "Successfully accomplished according to the Dharma" and "having obtained a proper location" together signify that the procedure has been completed in accordance with the Dharma.

The location is not defined by the boundaries of the earth-element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*). As stated in many passages below, all [cases] where the *karmavācanā* is performed by a separate assembly are said to be non-Dharmic;

they do not obtain a valid location. Conversely, when the *karmavācanā* is performed through the harmony of the Dharma, it obtains a valid location; in all such cases, the matter is not discussed in terms of the boundaries or locations of the earth-element.
Regarding those who abide within the dharma of a bhikṣu: this excludes those such as the insane, who do not abide in their own nature.

Furthermore, whether they have received the full ordination (*upasampadā*) or otherwise, these four propositions collectively exclude those who have committed extensive offenses, while including those who abide within the dharma of a bhikṣu through other means of admission, such as being summoned by the Buddha (*ehi-bhikṣu*).

A single phrase excludes those who are deranged and the like. By this, the present explanation possesses thirteen conditions: first, the body is free from prohibitions and obstacles; second, the boundary is established and accomplished;

third, all are assembled in harmony; fourth, the quorum is fulfilled according to number; fifth, the preceptor is requested according to the teaching; sixth, the conditions for the question-and-answer session are complete;
seventh, a teacher of instruction is appointed; eighth, the teacher of instruction conducts the examination; ninth, having completed the questioning, one informs the Saṃgha; tenth...
The instruction is to request [the precepts] from the Saṃgha. Eleventh, the precept master makes the formal announcement (jñapti). Twelfth, he interrogates the candidate before the assembly.

Thirteenth, the formal procedure consisting of one motion and three proclamations (jñapti-caturtha-karman) is completed. These requisite conditions do not deviate from the correct principle; I hope that all students will reflect upon them and thereby attain realization.

Regarding the fourth, the mind and its objects: as previously explained, the arising of the precepts depends on two conditions: first, the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*); second, the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
As for the causal condition, we shall here discuss how the mind establishes its object. Generally speaking, the mind and its objects are opened up into seven categories:
first, compassion; second, the abandonment of evil; third, the cultivation of good; fourth, the deliverance of sentient beings; fifth, the [attainment of] the... [destination].

[The stages of] seeking [the precepts], the sixth, protecting the Dharma, and the seventh, receiving them. Regarding why the initial mind must be characterized by compassion and reverence, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (Duo lun), fascicle one, states:

"Whenever one wishes to receive the precepts, one first provides them with a discourse to guide and enlighten them, saying: 'Now, toward all sentient beings, you must give rise to a heart of loving-kindness and compassion.
Once this superior mind (*adhi-citta*) has been attained, one then attains the superior precepts (*adhi-śīla*). This 'superior mind'..."
This is the general statement. If categorized specifically, there are nine grades. Regarding the "uppermost of the upper grades" of mind:
it means that one perceives these precepts as being difficult to encounter, like a sick person finding a physician or a hungry person longing for food.

Originally, one was without precepts and would have remained submerged in saṃsāra for eternal kalpas; now, wishing to advance to receive them and attain transcendence, the mind must be intensified. The *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* further states:
If one possesses a mind of deep sincerity, there are bodily and vocal actions; if the mind is numerous or frivolous, there are only active deeds and no non-active deeds.
Next, regarding the abandonment of evil: prior to receiving the precepts, one did not abandon various evils, as all objects were conditions for transgression.

Now that the precepts have been received, one establishes a mind of revulsion toward evil; by overturning the previous state of sin, the restraints (saṃvara) fully arise. Although the objects [of transgression] remain...
Generally, these are categorized into two types: sentient and non-sentient. Regarding the objects of sentient beings, the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 1, states:
"From the Avīci Hell below to the Naivasamjñānāsamjñāyatana above, including the trichiliocosm and all living beings up to the Tathāgata, all obtain this precept.
This is because at the time of initial reception, there is no limitation regarding the vow not to kill and so forth. For this reason...
For this reason, there are no sentient beings above whom one does not obtain the precepts. Furthermore, the *Abhidharmakośa* (Chapter 15) states:

"There is no one who obtains the restraint (*saṃvara*) without it extending to all sentient beings. This is because one obtains the restraint only by abiding in a state of virtuous intention toward all sentient beings;
otherwise, it is not so, because the evil intention has not been entirely ceased. It further says: "If..."
A person must not establish five fixed limitations in order to be able to receive the *prātimokṣa* vows.
These five fixed limitations refer to the limitations regarding sentient beings, parts of the body, locations, times, and conditions. Regarding non-sentient things:

from the highest peak of Mount Meru above, down to the limits of the waters below, including all grasses, trees, seeds, the great earth, and sprouts—whenever even a single speck of dust, a single flower, or a single leaf is damaged, or wherever there is any point of destruction, [the vow is incurred].

All such acts are bound up as transgressions. Therefore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "From the three-thousandfold world system down to the adamantine foundation, for every single atom, one precept is obtained above it;
because of this nature of form, it is said that the precepts of sentient beings are infinite, and like the infinite great earth, the infinite precepts are likewise infinite.
The monastics and nuns who have left the household life, the holy disciples of the Buddha, occupy a station more honored than that of devas and humans."

It is truly due to this. Next, regarding the cultivation of virtue: it refers to exerting oneself in the three types of action to bring all the provisions for enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) to full completion.
The *Bodhisattva-kaṇṭhābharaṇa-mūla-karma-sūtra* states: "The precept of gathering virtuous dharmas refers to the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates.
Next, regarding the saving of sentient beings: by means of the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), one vows to rescue all classes of beings, regardless of [their status].

One should impartially assist both enemies and kin. Thus, the *Mūla-karma-sūtra* states: "That which is called loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity extends its transformation to all sentient beings, so that they all attain peace and security.
Regarding the subsequent pursuit [of the goal]: the precepts are the direct cause for advancing toward the Three Vehicles.
I now vow to pursue the enlightenment of the Two Vehicles and the unsurpassed perfect awakening (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* says: "The precepts are..."

Regarding "Supreme Bodhi" and so forth: next, as for the protector of the Dharma, having received it myself, one transmits it to others; in this manner, through successive transmission, the Buddha-Dharma remains unceasing.
This is precisely the meaning of lighting the inexhaustible lamp. Thus, the *Śālistamba Sūtra* (The Sutra of the Final Instructions) says:

"From this day forward," and so on. Next, regarding the recipient: once the various conditions are complete, one should form the intention to receive [the teaching] together; one must then focus one's contemplation and focus one's reflection.

It is attained. Through other perceptions and other volitions, the mind and mental factors thus succeed one another, continuing from moment to moment in a single stream of consciousness, thereby receiving and upholding all sublime merits.
If there were no precepts of the mind, these could not be attained. Among the various realms of existence, only humans may receive them.
Furthermore, among humans, the sense faculties must be complete; within the requirement for complete faculties, there must be no prohibitive obstacles (*antarāya*). Once such obstacles exist—
No [transgression]. When the physical vessel is pure and all conditions are fully prepared, only then does it arise; this is what is conferred upon others.
One must maintain it with clear understanding, opening the path in accordance with the Dharma, so that the discipline (*vinaya*) may first be born.

If there is any negligence or violation, and one merely establishes the method through labor while the ritual rules are applied in vain, the fault lies with the preceptor. Why is this so? Because this precept is the source of all practices; for anyone who cultivates the myriad...

Practice. Taking this as the beginning, the *Śāriputra-parivarta* (The Sutra of the Bequeathed Teaching) says: "Relying upon and because of these precepts," and so forth. Next, regarding the existence of superior conditions, there are two [aspects].
As has been understood above, I now perform this *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) for you before the assembly. This *karmavācanā* possesses great spiritual efficacy;
it can cause the wholesome dharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges to manifest and be perfected within your person. Monks, you shall thereby attain the fruits of the Path.
Fifth, regarding the sequence of events: First, Ājñātakauṇḍinya and others were the first to come forward.
Second, one hundred and ten [monks] attained arhatship through the three refuges and wandered about. Having converted and liberated people, they brought them to the Buddha’s presence.

On the road, they became utterly exhausted and lost their original faith. Consequently, they listened to the arhats, who first shaved their heads and donned the *kāṣāya* robes, after which they received the threefold recitation.

Regarding the *karmavācanā* for receiving the precepts: the third [stage] consists of the three refuges followed by the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*. Therefore, eight years cannot be exceeded. As for the final [stage], the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* states:

"At eight years, one receives the *karman*; at fourteen years, one reveres the Eight Heavy Rules (*gurudharma*). From this, it is known that [the stage of] residing [under the protection of a teacher] belongs to the fourth [year].

Regarding the sixth point, the formal recitation (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*), various masters explain that because the conditions for the "Welcome" (*svāgata*) were powerful and the eight points of respect (*gurudharma*) were felt with such gravity, it was obtained in a single recitation and did not require further formalization.

However, because the mind of one who is exhorted to take the Three Refuges may be arrogant, three recitations are required for an individual; furthermore, for those being ordained, another three recitations are added.

Regarding the formal ritual (karmavācanā): because of the necessity for harmony and consensus, it must be performed four times; once the assembly’s minds are in complete accord, the single performance of the ritual constitutes its completion.

Now, as for the dissolution [of vows], there is no ritual of binding for the other types of undertaking; such a ritual exists only for the formal karmavācanā. The reason for this is that the karmavācanā is performed in the presence of the assembly to manifest harmony, which necessitates a formal binding;

for the others, since they are not performed before the assembly, there are no texts concerning a binding ritual. Regarding the three refuges, the first three are capable of generating the precepts, so they may be recited three times.

It is called a "bond" (*saṃyojana*). If it were merely by virtue of being subsequent to the arising of the precepts that it were called a bond, then the third part of the *karmavācanā* (the formal ritual act) would also have to be called a bond.
Furthermore, the text for the bond of the *karmavācanā* does not recite the preceding ritual;

since this bond occurs after the substance of the Three Refuges, this bond should likewise not recite the substance of the ritual. For these reasons, it is certain that this is not a bond. As for the statement that "there is a bond":

This would result in excessive stagnation of the principle. However, among the various forms of receiving the precepts, the "Welcome" (Svāgata) and the Eight Respectful Precepts (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*) are each easily understood.

As for the Three Refuges, because the mind [of the recipient] is inferior, they are administered to individuals; each refuge is bestowed separately with great care, repeated three times, totaling six cycles from beginning to end, before one is finally able to generate the precepts.

In the *karmavācanā* performed before the assembly, one first makes a formal announcement (*jñapti*) to proclaim the intent; once the announcement has been made and the assembly is aware of it, one then proceeds to perform the actual ritual act. Therefore, as for the act...

As for their substance, there are only three and not four. Thus, those held collectively are three, while those held individually are six; by this it is sufficiently known that the distinctions among the fetters (*saṃyojana*) are explained.

Seventh, regarding the comparative evaluation: among all conditions for receiving [the precepts], the "Welcome" (*svāgata*) is superior, because one attains the first fruit (*phala*), and the Buddha acts as the augmenting factor.

First: the eight *anavasthāpya* [punishments] are ranked second, as they involve receiving the Buddha’s teachings from afar while personally instructing students; next is the threefold refuge, which is applied to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

The *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) is considered inferior because it is employed for ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*). Furthermore, according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*, receiving the precepts through the *karmavācanā* results in shallow merit;
the resulting precepts fail to be firm and stable, leading to various calamities. This constitutes the first type: the weakening of the precepts.

There are four causes for the loss of the precepts: second, renouncing the precepts; third, the transformation of the sexual organs; fourth, severing the roots of goodness. Regarding the contrast between harm and benefit, one is superior while the other three are inferior.

This refers to the period from the time of the "Come Hither" (Svāgata) ordination up to that of Subhadra. The three-refuge ordination ceased after eight years. The eight weighty rules (gurudharma) result in a single attainment without repetition.

The *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal motion followed by three proclamations) may be obtained at all times—whether during the Buddha’s lifetime or after his parinirvāṇa. From beginning to end, the Buddha-dharma relies upon the *jñapti*.
The fourfold *jñapti-caturtha* karma constitutes the fundamental principle of the precepts; it is capable of perpetuating the Three Jewels and bringing about boundless benefit.
Nothing surpasses the *jñapti-caturtha*, for this reason it is the most excellent, the most sublime, and the most venerable.
Eighth, regarding the gradual and sudden: Upon examining the various ways of receiving the precepts, they all arise based on the teachings;

since there is no increase or decrease in their essential substance (*tattva*), none of them constitute an actual "arising" [of the precepts]. Therefore, in terms of their substance, it is clear that there is neither gradual nor sudden. One cannot regard the fifty-two precepts as being gradual or sudden based on their completeness.

Furthermore, if one were to claim that the substance must rely on the five categories [of precepts] to be called "complete," then it could be termed "gradual"; yet such complete possession does not exist.
[The opponent says: "It is hypothetical. How else could it be called 'gradual' (jīan)? Furthermore, at the time of receiving full ordination, one performs the ritual three times;
in the first instance, one receives two hundred [precepts], and in the subsequent instance, one further obtains fifty. It is by such an incremental accumulation that it is properly termed 'gradual.

Since this meaning does not exist [in your view], what would the characteristics of 'graduality' be? How can you establish the names 'gradual' and 'sudden' in vain while there is actually no meaning of gradual or sudden? [The author replies: However, with respect to...

This clarifies the stages; it does not explain them according to their essential nature. Regarding the separate reception [of precepts] in sequence for those of gradual or sudden capacity, this refers to the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual).

In this case, a single reception is both gradual and sudden, while the remaining three receptions are sudden rather than gradual. Question: How is it that the *karmavācanā* is both gradual and sudden? Answer:

First receiving the ten precepts and subsequently receiving the full precepts (*upasampadā*) is called "gradual. Not receiving the ten precepts, but directly receiving [the full precepts], is [sudden].

The full observance of the precepts is called "sudden" (*tun*). Question: Since the reception [of the precepts] is already sudden, what need is there for a gradual process? The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-ābhidharma* (or *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra*), fascicle 1, states:
"Although one receives and obtains the three types of precepts at once, the cultivation of the Buddha-dharma must necessarily proceed by stages.

First, one receives the five precepts to achieve self-discipline; as faith and joy gradually increase, one next receives the ten precepts. Once the ten precepts have been received, the wholesome mind becomes even deeper."
Next, one receives the full precepts (*upasampadā*). Following this sequence, one attains the flavor of the Buddha-dharma; one’s devotion becomes firm and difficult to cause to regress.
It is like traveling across a great ocean, gradually entering deeper and deeper; entering the ocean of the Buddha-dharma is likewise so. If, at one time—

Regarding those who receive the full precepts (*upasampadā*): since they have already lost the proper sequence and violated the rules of decorum (*īryāpatha*), and because sentient beings differ in the timing of their attainment of the Path, it is necessary to follow a sequence and receive them gradually over three stages.
Furthermore, as for the analysis of whether one has transgressed or not: according to the regulations of the *karmavācanā*, there is gradual and sudden transgression;

because one does not transgress gradually, the following text states: "If the *saṃgha* does not bestow the *śrāmaṇera* precepts, the Buddha says that the precepts are nonetheless obtained. There is [a case where] the *saṃgha*...

Regarding the remaining three offenses, they were not established as sudden but rather as gradual. Question: Since the three [methods] such as "Come, O Bhikṣu" (Ehi-bhikṣu) are all permitted as sudden, how is it that the *karmavācanā* ordination was established to be gradual?
Answer: The three [methods] such as "Come, O Bhikṣu" do not restrict one by age; when the conditions are met, the rite is performed immediately, and there is no need for a gradual reception.

As for the *karmavācanā* ordination, it is established that one must have reached twenty years of age; since the age has not yet been reached, full ordination (*upasampadā*) is not permitted. For the time being...
[The Buddha] bestowed the ten precepts, causing them to advance in their practice. If one were entirely without precepts, what could one hope for in terms of the mind?

Regarding the ninth point, "the distinction between the universal and the restricted," this refers to distinguishing [the methods] by way of time, place, and karmic retribution. To speak of "time": the *svāgata* (welcoming) and the three refuges (*triśaraṇa*) cannot exceed eight [precepts];
they are restricted to the period when the Buddha was present and do not apply to later ages. The single method of *karmavācanā* (formal ritual action), however, universally applies to both.

At that time, it was asked: "Since the 'Welcome' (svāgata) greeting is exclusively maintained by the Buddha and does not extend to later generations, why is it that in the *Dharmapada-śāstra* (付法傳), Ānanda also maintains the 'Welcome' greeting when ordaining the assembly of rishis?
The answer is: That instance is based on specific circumstances (*viśeṣa-pratyaya*).

Since the divergent accounts are not authoritative and the original text is not bound [by such rules], the second point of interpretation is difficult to reconcile due to the differences in the traces of the teachings. It is merely a matter of what has been seen or heard.

It is the same; there is this specific distinction. Third, it was to manifest that Ānanda is the custodian of the Dharma-treasury acting as the Buddha’s representative, and thus he was permitted to administer the *svāgata* (welcome) ordination.
Fourth, the timing and the mode of conversion were not according to the usual rule. Fifth, the roots of the rishi had matured, and he was used as a catalyst for this purpose.
Sixth, although Ānanda was ordained, he was not yet equal to the Buddha. Regarding the summary of these points, they are also contained within the first three.

The [formal] ordination (upasampadā) is restricted to this continent (Jambudvīpa). Thus, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 2, states: "The *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) applies to all three continents; other forms of ordination exist only in Jambudvīpa.

Alternatively, based on the underlying principle, the attainment of the Three Refuges (*tri-śaraṇa*) may apply universally, as there is no scriptural prohibition against noble beings (*ārya*) traveling [to other realms].

One should understand both the principle and the text accordingly. Regarding the statement that it is "restricted by retribution" (*vipāka*), this refers to the "Come hither" (*ehi-bhikṣu*) ordination; since these two [methods] are said to be universal, they are compared to the eight [liberations].
Among the bhikṣuṇīs, there is the *svāgata-karman* (the rite of "welcome"). This is clearly established in the *Mātṛkā* and has its own explicit textual authority.

Although the ritual procedure (*karman*) is common to both orders, it differs from the *svāgata*. Because the *svāgata* is capable of being performed as a single ritual act that distinguishes [the two], one order may not perform the rites of the other.

Furthermore, ten persons for the bhikṣus and twenty for the bhikṣuṇīs are not used interchangeably; this is because their purposes are distinct, though their ultimate intent can be understood to be the same.
Respectfully regarding these two sections, the various texts are largely identical. Question: Why is it that women do not receive the three refuges? Answer:
The three refuges were originally established for the community of nuns; because they arrived later, women were thus deprived of this reception. How is this known?

When women sought to leave the household life, Ānanda made the formal request, and Ānanda himself performed the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) for their ordination; it is clear from this that what was done was specifically for the sake of women.

Furthermore, regarding the return to the teaching, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-vibhāṣā* (Duōlùn) clearly demonstrates that [the former] is inferior; this can be understood from the cited text. This refers specifically to those possessing the full precepts (*upāsaka-saṃvara*), and thus it is restricted solely to the Saṅgha.
However, in the case of the fifty-eight [precepts], they always apply generally to female practitioners as well. Yet, there was no one among the monks whom she could not surpass;

for her venerable status was beyond respect, and because nuns belong to a lower order and are female, she was not permitted to enter the Path beyond a certain point. Consequently, she requested permission [to do so].

It is permitted. It must be done with reverence and solemnity; for a man, it is not so, and therefore he does not receive this [ordination]. Above, we have directly based ourselves on the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual); thus, there are four general categories.
Regarding the methods of receiving [the precepts], two are restricted and two are universal. If categorized according to the *karmavācanā*, they are divided into six;
if taken collectively, they become nine. One is universal and eight are restricted.

Regarding the tenth [method], that of being addressed as "Welcome" (Svāgata): receiving the precepts through this address is restricted to the stage of the Noble Ones (Ārya). Only upon attaining the first fruit (Prathamaphala) does one properly merit the address "Welcome.

For those below this level, who have not yet realized the True Dharma (Tattva) and thus cannot move the Buddha to command them by chanting "Welcome," the purpose of the Three Refuges (Triśaraṇa) differs from the explanations of the older commentaries.

For instance, according to the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, after eight years [of practice], only the Three Refuges are employed, while the formal motion and announcement (Jñapti-caturtha-karman) are not yet applied.

Stop. The preceding section was restricted to those within [the stages]. Among the ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) here, could there not have been ordinary persons outside [the formal stages] who entered the Path during these eight years?

Thus we know that this meaning was obstructed and not yet fully established. Furthermore, during the six years, the precept against killing humans was enacted; in the context of that precept, one practices the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).

If those who receive the Three Refuges were considered "inner ordinary persons" (*adhyātma-pṛthagjana*), how could they be practicing the contemplation of impurity throughout this entire kalpa? Therefore...

From this, one knows that it is common [to both stages]. Furthermore, in the Vinaya texts, regarding the "indeterminate stage" (*aniyata-avasthā*), since there is no separate definition provided for it, its meaning is understood as being common.

Moreover, it is said: "Having lost one's original faith, yet clearly knowing one’s resolve for the Path—this is not far from the common [stage] and belongs to the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).

This does not contradict reason. Furthermore, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* speaks of six types of receiving the precepts; when sentient beings possess profound and thick merit and virtue, they are thereby able to attain them.
This precept is firm from beginning to end and free from calamity; yet it does not separately mention the Three Refuges.

As for the "Noble Eightfold Path that cannot be transgressed," its reception applies to a single individual who is certainly at the stage of the first fruit (*srotāpanna*). Therefore, the subsequent text states: "Up to seven births in the human or celestial realms, one then reaches the end of suffering.
It is not known where the five hundred ranks reside. [The questioner] replies: "Their intense aversion to worldly life was identical to [the Buddha's] request."

Leaving the household life is, in its entirety, the principle of the sages; there is no error in this. Therefore, the Śākyas of the royal palace were all sages, which is why King Virūḍhaka suffered the retribution for his harmful learning.
Furthermore, although their understanding may be the same, how could those in a single assembly all be equal to the sages?

What harm is there in allowing that the Śākya clan includes ordinary worldlings as well? As for those who receive the *karmavācanā*, it extends to both sages and worldlings; there is nothing wrong with this, as the benefit is broad and great.
Regarding this dharma:

as for the eleventh person who presides over the rite, if we speak in terms of its underlying principle (*artha*), the precepts exist because of the Buddha; if the Buddha did not appear, this dharma would not exist.

However, if we discuss it in terms of the actual manifestation [of the rite], then the relationship between teacher and disciple differs accordingly. For the "Come hither" (*ehi bhikṣu*) ordination, the Buddha himself presides; for the remaining three, others do.
Question: Why is it that the disciples uphold the teachings while the Buddha himself upholds them? Answer: This is to manifest the objects of his transformation;

furthermore, because the conditions [of beings] differ, the interpretation is made so as to apply to the final age. If only the Buddha were to uphold them, how could this be after his parinirvāṇa? Question: Why is it that the "Come hither" (ehibhikṣu) ordination is upheld by the Buddha alone?
Answer: Because it possesses two meanings: first, it is upheld by the Buddha alone; second, he possesses exhaustive knowledge, perfect majesty, and great power.
It enables sentient beings to transform their worldly attachments into the path to enlightenment. Thus, the *Mātṛkā-sūtra* states:

"Even for one who has studied the Dharma for twenty years, [the teacher] must discern the faculties and nature of the two types of wholesome individuals and administer the medicine according to their capacity, so that they may certainly realize the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) in this very body.

Therefore, the fifty-eighth fascicle of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* says: "The Buddha, the King of Dharma, personally conferred the precepts upon them; there is no case of one in the stage of training (*śaikṣa*) passing away. Thus it is.

The various disciples lacked these two meanings. First, their power of majestic virtue was inferior, as in the case of the bhikṣu in the Mahāsāṃghika school who, though addressed with the "Come, monk" (ehi bhikṣu) formula, did not have his beard and hair removed and his deportment remained impure; the Buddha said, "You may not [attain this]," just as the Buddha’s fearless speech [is definitive].
Second, they were unskilled at discerning the faculties and natures [of others], as the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says regarding Śāriputra’s younger brother:

[The Buddha] taught the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) to his son, and taught the counting of breaths (*ānāpāna-smṛti*) while washing robes. For these reasons, the disciples did not uphold [the precepts].

Thus, it is for this reason that the Tathāgata did not uphold other ordinations. Answer: As for the conditions residing in the Buddha, since the teaching "Come hither" (*ehi-bhikṣu*) was not applicable to him, he likewise did not uphold the others.
Furthermore, regarding the purpose of the Three Refuges, because the capacity [of the recipient] was inferior, they were unable to evoke [the response]. The Buddha [possessed] such [conditions].

The *Mātṛkā-sūtra* further states: First, there are two classes of sentient beings. The first class consists of those who, because they possess karma that obstructs the Path, cannot attain the state of "one who has come well" (*svāgata*) even in their present life;
furthermore, because they lack the causes and conditions for the stage of No-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), they cannot attain the "eight things not to be transgressed.

Regarding these eight things not to be transgressed: the Buddha initially suppressed women and did not permit them to enter the Path. Ānanda petitioned on their behalf, and consequently, the Dharma of Reverence was proclaimed. Thus it was due to Ānanda.

The full precepts are manifested immediately upon these words; therefore, the Tathāgata does not preside over this teaching. According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*, there are ten reasons why the Buddha does not preside:
first, to bestow [the precepts] with impartiality, acting as a teacher for this person without being inconsistent toward that one.
1. Because of equality. 2. To stop quarrels and disputes. If there were distinctions between those who are close and those who are distant, disputes would arise.

3. To stop slander. Non-Buddhists might say: "The Śramaṇa Gautama claims to practice loving-kindness and equanimity; yet he acts as an upādhyāya for one person while not doing so for another, no different from an ordinary person.
4. To establish the three refuges. When performing the *karmavācanā*, it follows the number of the Saṃgha and has no [distinctions].
1. The Jewel of the Buddha. 2. To achieve the four kinds of indestructible faith. 3. To accomplish the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*). 4.

When performing *karmavācanā* (formal ritual acts), if a disciple falls ill, one should attend to them and provide whatever they require; how could this be a matter of exercising arbitrary power? Is this not what the Dharma King ought to do? 5. Not to extinguish the merit of others;
that is to say, when a disciple encounters illness or hardship, providing for their deficiencies does not extinguish prior merit. [If one fails to do so, it would extinguish it.]

Regarding the merits possessed by humans: first, like a *cakravartin* king, when his karma has expired; second, not disturbing sentient beings, regardless of whether they are near or far, because he has accomplished Buddhahood;
tenth, for the sake of reaching the final age—since the Buddha himself does not preside over [the community], who would [preside] after his extinction?

Furthermore, the third volume of the *Shíshí lùn* (Treatise on the Ten Realities) states: "The Buddha does not enter into the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual acts) of the Saṃgha, nor is he the same as any other monks."
Furthermore, because of the distinctions between the Three Jewels, the Buddha is not included within the Saṃgha.

Regarding the twelfth point, similarities and differences: first, let us clarify the Vinaya. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, chapter fifty-eight, there are ten ways of receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*):

first, "spontaneous" (*svayambhū*), which refers to the World-Honored Buddha; he spontaneously attained full ordination without a teacher. Second, the five bhikṣus who attained the Path... [text continues]

1. Attainment through self-vow, as in the case of Mahākāśyapa. 2. Attainment through following the discourse of the Buddha, as in the case of Sūta. 3. Attainment through hearing and receiving the full precepts (*upasampadā*). 4.
Attainment in border regions by means of the fifth [officer] who maintains the Vinaya. 5. Attainment through the eight heavy rules (*gurudharma*), as in the case of Pāṭaliputra.

6. Attainment through being sent by a female from the region of Kāśī. 7. Attainment through the Buddha’s command, “Come, O Bhikṣu” (*ehi bhikṣu*). 8. Attainment through taking refuge in the Triple Gem. 9. Attainment through formal declaration (*jñapti*).

Regarding the statement that one attains [the precepts] through the four *karmavācanās* and yet is called "spontaneous" (*svayambhū*): this refers to the realization of the path of principle being perfected; it is fundamentally without the instruction of a teacher.

Since the *vinaya* discipline is fully complete and does not depend on external conditions, it is called "spontaneous. The *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* asks: "How do Buddhas and *pratyekabuddhas* obtain the precepts?
It answers: "They obtain the precepts without a teacher. It asks again: "Are they obtained from teaching? It answers: "They are not obtained from teaching. Some say they are obtained from teaching.
The Buddha sat beneath a tree in the full lotus posture and said, "I shall not break this cross-legged posture until I have attained the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).

Thus, he achieved perfection through both body and speech. Subsequently, he attained the precepts for the exhaustion of outflows; these were likewise acquired simultaneously. As for "seeing the truths" (*satyadarśana*): having heard the Dharma and reflected upon it, one contemplates the principle of the Four Noble Truths.
Once the principle of the truths has been seen, the category of precepts arises; therefore, it is called "seeing the truths. This refers to his self-vow.
This refers to Mahākāśyapa, who had planted roots of goodness in past lives. Upon hearing a brief word from the Buddha, he resolved his mind and made a vow.
Having completed his vow, he practiced with diligent and arduous effort. When he attained the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), his restraint was fully perfected;

therefore, it is called "self-vow. Understanding that this [attainment] arises from conditions, its names are manifold. From the beginning, it is called "instruction" (*avavāda*). Thus, the treatise says: The Buddha told Kāśyapa...
"Śāriputra, you should give rise to a sense of shame and remorse that penetrates to the very marrow of your bones; you should train yourself in this way.
Based on these instructions, one establishes a solemn vow, which is called "self-vow" (*svapratijñā*) or "receiving the teacher" (*śāstṛparigraha*).

Because one accepts with the mind that the Buddha is the Great Teacher, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Kāśyapa came before the Buddha and said, 'The Buddha is my teacher; I am his disciple. Sugata..."
"Śāriputra is my teacher; I am his disciple. According to the *Mātṛkā-sūtra*, one is established in the higher full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*) based on the name of the subsequent person.

If this is the case, then according to the names of the assemblies for the "self-vow" [ordination] and others, the teachers themselves have not yet obtained the precepts. How then can the *Dharmadāna-saṃgraha* state: [as follows]?
Having made the vow, all the precepts are fully possessed. This answer is spoken in reference to specific conditions; therefore, it is said that they are obtained at the time of one’s own vow.

In various treatises, this is called "receiving from a teacher," which is likewise the case here when explained according to principle. Thus, they are obtained at the time of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
As for the mention of Mahākāśyapa, this is spoken in reference to his clan name. Among the three brothers, he was the eldest and possessed great compassion.
He was "Welcome" (Svāgata); he did not attain this through a personal vow. Furthermore, because his nature was characterized by few afflictions, he was called "The Desireless" (Anicchan).
Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 54, states: "Mahākāśyapa married a golden-hued woman as his wife, yet he felt no attachment or delight; he renounced her and left the household life.
Alternatively, because his body was golden in color, he was named "Golden Kāśyapa" (Kanakavarna-Kāśyapa). Regarding the one who discusses the meaning [of the Dharma], this refers to the śrāmaṇera.

His consciousness was luminous and he was well-versed in the principles of phenomena. At the age of seven, he was able to answer the Buddha’s questions; his words and reasoning were unimpeded, fully satisfying the Sage’s mind.
Consequently, the Buddha permitted him to receive the *karmavācanā* ordination. This was because he had been so from the time of his initial naming; thus it is said, "In debate.
If one follows other schools, the names differ considerably. The *Mātṛkā* says: "Commanded to hear the *Abhidharma*," "Questioning and answering are seen in speech," and "Answering questions."
The *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* asks: "Regarding the distinct names for these [precepts] such as 'joy' (*sukha*) and so forth, they differ from the treatises;

there is no other difference than the six [categories]. They are largely the same as the four parts; their meaning may be understood by analogy. Furthermore, within the context of the *karmavācanā*, when the Saṃgha attains a single assembly, it is called "the bhikṣuṇī receiving the precepts.

Therefore, in the fortieth [section], Upāli asked the Buddha: "Pāṭaliputra, receiving the eight heavy rules (*gurudharma*) constitutes going forth; receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*) makes one a bhikṣuṇī."
As for the other nuns, it is by means of the formal act (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) performed in their presence.

Next, the various treatises are distinguished; the *Mātṛkā-sūtra* is first. There are five [categories] for each of the two assemblies, which constitute the ten types of ordination (*upasampadā*). Regarding the five for the bhikṣus:

[they are] ordination by "Come" (*ehi-bhikṣu*), ordination by establishing [one in] wholesome qualities (*dharmasamādāna*), ordination by command (*ājñā*), ordination by hearing the three-fold formula (*tri-vācaka-karman*), and ordination by formal act (*karman*). In that text, it asks: "What..."

Therefore, it is called "receiving full ordination in the superior manner. The answer is: during the time when the Buddha was in the world, there were those who did not receive the precepts but, while remaining by the Buddha’s side, heard the Dharma and attained arhatship;

these are called "nuns who received full ordination in the superior manner. Regarding the five types of reception—*svāgata* (welcome), *kṣānti-dharmopasaṃpādaka* (establishment in the wholesome dharma), *upādhyāyopasaṃpādaka* (ordination by a preceptor), *śāstṛ-dharma-praheṇaka-karma* (ordination by the teacher’s dispatch of a messenger through formal ritual)—these ten modes of reception are subsumed under seven in meaning, namely: *svāgata*, *upādhyāya*, and [the others].

Regarding the reception of the *karmavācanā*: these three [procedures] apply to both assemblies (*saṃgha*), while the remaining four are restricted. Among those that are restricted, the instruction for the Three Refuges applies only to the monks;
the method for dispatching a messenger applies specifically to the nuns. The methods for the Three Refuges and the dispatching of a messenger are thus restricted.

Having clarified above the instructions for the instruction and the dispatching of messengers, they must now be explained. Regarding the restriction of the instruction to the monks, there are two meanings. First, by means of the *zhang*... [text continues].
As for wisdom, it is strengthened; when answering difficult questions, one is found to be satisfactory, and thus is permitted to receive the precepts.

Second, because a *śrāmaṇera* shares the same physical form as a Buddha, their movements and conduct are identical, and they may engage in dialogue. Women, conversely, are the opposite of this; therefore, they lack this specific reception.

Regarding the dispatching of a messenger, while it is restricted to *bhikṣuṇīs*, it is permissible for both assemblies [of monks and nuns] since the holy life (*brahmacarya*) is equally difficult to maintain; logically, both should be allowed to receive the precepts by dispatching a messenger. However—

When a śrāmaṇera receives the precepts, he must personally approach the assembly; because this involves going to a distant place, there is no such provision for him. A bhikṣuṇī, however, requires two assemblies;
when she approaches the monks and encounters difficult circumstances along the way, an exception is made to allow her to receive them [there].
Next, regarding the attainment of precepts by those of the three vehicles according to the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*, there are nine kinds of "perfect virtues" (*paripūrṇa-guṇa*).
As for these perfect virtues, it means that forty-two thousand merits arise simultaneously, being complete in every respect; therefore, they are called perfect virtues. The verse says:
"One attains perfect virtues based on the seven dependencies. This explains the characteristics of the two types of perfect virtues. Śrāvakas possess seven [dependencies].

Perfect Virtue. There are four ways for a bhikṣu to come forth [into the order]: the three refuges with abbreviated *karmavācanā* (meaning that at the time of the initial formal motion, one obtains [the precepts] upon hearing it);

the extensive *karmavācanā*; the threefold reception for a bhikṣuṇī; and the "Come Hither" (*ehi-bhikṣu*) by sending a messenger (referring to Gopadatta, which is called the Eight Rules of Respect). Regarding the extensive *karmavācanā* above: seven types of śrāvakas obtain the precepts;
the eighth, the pratyekabuddha, possesses limited merit; up to the ninth, the Buddha, who possesses immeasurable merit. Up to...
The section on the conditions for attaining [the precepts] is concluded.

Next, the essence of the precepts (*śīla-tattva*) is elucidated. Now, as for the essence of the precepts, its nature and characteristics are profound and mysterious, and its principles are subtle and hidden.

Were it not for one whose learning exhausts the Tripiṭaka and whose insight penetrates the Five Sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*), there would be no means to fathom its purport or to know the limits of its interpretation. Therefore, in antiquity...

"O eminent and outstanding one, a paragon of the present age! Within this very school, those who have not attained realization do so because the Vinaya lacks a definitive record while the Śāstras contain explicit clarifications.
Since they do not reflect upon this themselves, they constantly rely on others for resolution. Although such reliance may provide the means to establish their practice,"

My principles were obscure and my discipline lax; I subsequently gave rise to a sense of indignation regarding this ruin. Over several years, I have conducted investigations, searching through the sūtras and summarizing the śāstras.
I explored the grand models of the two vehicles and the commoners, scrutinized the old and researched the new, and gathered the great canons of the three and four [schools].

Thus, I have extracted the subtle tenets that support our school and discarded the voluminous texts that deviate from reason. I have composed these "Chapters on Meaning" (Yìzhāng) to transmit them to those of like profession, hoping that all fellow students will [benefit therefrom].
I shall no longer engage in deep study; I hope you will examine this at a glance. It opens up clearly so that there is no need for repeated reading.

Nevertheless, according to its structure of thesis and refutation, the essential meaning is fully attained. Thus, it may be titled the *Treatise on Elucidating the Substance of the Precepts*. As for the analysis within the treatise, it is organized into three sections.
First, the explanation of the names; second, the determination of the essence; third, the analysis by way of various categories.

Regarding the explanation of the names, according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, there are three categories of the precepts (*śīla*). Within these three categories, the characteristics of the restraints (*saṃvara*) are distinguished.

Furthermore, among the three types of discipline (*saṃvara*), one excludes that of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and the path (*mārga*). As for the discipline of liberation (*prātimokṣa*), it prevents transgressions by merely restraining speech;

yet regarding physical actions and mental faults, the Noble Ones permit non-offenses. Regarding the precepts of body and speech: while the names of the afflictions are invoked in relation to their objects, those objects have no boundaries.

The "precept-bird" has limits, yet its objects—whether sentient or insentient—are infinite in number. These precepts pervade the entire *dharmadhātu*; as they arise in accordance with each respective object, they are indeed infinite in number. Though they are infinite...

Categorized, they are twofold: first, manifest precepts (*vijñapti-śīla*); second, non-manifest precepts (*avijñapti-śīla*). First, the individual names "manifest" and "non-manifest" shall be explained;
next, the general term "precepts" as they refer to their objects shall be explained. That which is called "manifest" refers to the physical and verbal activities that produce a representation.
Because it causes others to understand [one’s intention], it is called "informative" (*vijñapti*). As for "non-informative" (*avijñapti*): it arises based on the informative;

it is invisible and non-obstructive, and cannot be manifested. Thus, its essence is termed "non-informative. It is acquired within the continuity of the body and persists even when one enters other states of mind;

it is not called such when it is lost. Next, regarding the general name "precept" (*śīla*) which is the object of this explanation: both this informative and non-informative [action] possess the quality of providing prior defense.

All are collectively termed "precepts" (*śīla*). According to the *Abhidharmakośa*, Chapter 14, there are six general names for them. The treatise states that regarding the specific distinctions of the name "Prātimokṣa-saṃvara" (Individual Liberation Restraint):
first, as for the etymological definition (*nirukti*) of *śīla*, the term *śīla* means "coolness" (*śītalatva*).

Thus, a verse says: "The joy of upholding the precepts brings no heat or affliction to the body; therefore, it is called *śīla*. Second, they are called "Excellent Conduct" (*sucarita*). Third, they are called "the Vehicle of the Three Vehicles" (*triyāna*).
The Noble Ones call them "the wise. Those multitudes praise them as "sublime conduct" (*sucarita*). Third, they are called "action" (*karman*), for both body and speech are that which is performed;
their essential nature is designated as action. Fourth, "restraint" (*saṃvara*) refers to that which enables the body and speech to become supple and conform to the Dharma;

therefore, it is called restraint (these four names apply to both the initial and subsequent moments). Fifth is "individual liberation" (*prātimokṣa*), so named because it is distinct at the first moment.
Because it specifically abandons all evil, it is called *prātimokṣa* (individual liberation).

Sixth, because the course of action (*karmapatha*) reaches its culmination at the first moment, and the intended purpose is fully accomplished, it is called a *karmapatha* (these two names apply exclusively to the initial stage).
Furthermore, the initial stage may be called *prātimokṣa*, while the subsequent stage is called only *prātimokṣa-saṃvara* (the restraint of individual liberation), and not [merely] *prātimokṣa*.
It is called *prātimokṣa*. The treatise states: "From the second moment until it is relinquished, it is not called *prātimokṣa*;

it is called the *prātimokṣa-saṃvara*. (These alone constitute seven names. Furthermore, from the second moment onward, it is called only the "subsequent arising" (*pṛṣṭha*) and is not called a "course of action" (*karmapatha*).
The treatise states: "From the second moment until it is relinquished, it is not called a course of action; it is called the subsequent [arising]."

If the subsequent arising [of karma] is added, there are then eight; alternatively, this subsequent arising may be subsumed under the aforementioned third type of karma, which includes it along with the fundamental [karma] and so forth.
It cannot be called by a collective name. Since the numerical limit has been removed and what arises subsequently is designated as "seven," it is as previously stated.
Next, regarding the determination of its essence: according to the twenty schools of the Nikāyas following the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, this text corresponds to two precepts.
Furthermore, all the Vinaya traditions transmitted from antiquity are subsumed within the Dharmaguptaka school.
It is therefore irrational to claim that [the author] relies on the *Tattvasiddhi* (Satyasiddhi) system, for those people do not investigate the various divisions of the schools.

Rather, because the tenets of the Dharmaguptaka school were widely propagated in the Western Regions while this [Vinaya] was previously transmitted as being prevalent in the Sarvāstivāda school, the present commentary follows the Sarvāstivāda in its entirety.
It is now clarified that these [two] have matter (*rūpa*) as their essence. How is this known? Because the *Abhidharmakośa*, chapter thirteen, states:
"By the power of volition (*cetanā*), there arise separately such and such bodily forms, which are called bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) and vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*).

Since the essence of karma consists of speech and sound—namely, intimation (*vijñapti*) and non-intimation (*avijñapti*)—and both are merely matter, it remains unknown what the meaning of "matter" is; does it possess two natures?
The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, chapter one, states: "Form (rūpa) is characterized by resistance and transformation. If that were so, then atoms (*paramāṇu*) would not be form;

for an atom is, by its very nature, devoid of resistance and transformation. Therefore, it is answered that there is no single atom that exists in isolation; rather, it is only when many atoms aggregate that they constitute [form].
The definition of "obstructive change" (rūpaṇā) is thus established. The five consciousnesses must necessarily rely upon an accumulation [of atoms] as their object.

If this accumulation were such [as you claim], it would follow that it belongs to the past and future; for what is non-material (arūpa) lacks such accumulation. This present understanding is explained by reference to the meaning of "obstructive change" in terms of what has been and what will be.

If that is so, the primary dharma might indeed be acceptable, as it possesses the sense of having been or being about to be. However, since the future has not yet arisen, how can there be "obstructive change" in the sense of "what is to be"? How can this be understood?
"Obstruction" (*āvaraṇa*): Just as firewood, even when it is not currently burning, is still called "firewood," so too is unmanifest form (*avijñapti*) "combustible" despite its lack of resistance.

However, this is not the case for the unmanifest because it lacks the past, future, and those of a similar kind. Thus, there are now two interpretations. First, the master of the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* says:

Because the manifest is subject to transformation and obstruction, that which is acquired in accordance with the manifest is called "form" (*rūpa*), just like a tree; when the tree moves, the shadow necessarily moves along with it.
Next, the master of the *Abhidharmakośa* refutes [the opponent's position] through both reasoning and analogy. First, he refutes the [definition of] the phenomenon (*dharma*), saying:

"If it is because of the informative matter (*vijñapti-rūpa*)—since it is characterized by transformation and resistance—that the non-informative (*avijñapti*) is also called 'matter' (*rūpa*) by following that [informative matter], then this essence of the non-informative is not itself matter.

It is called 'matter' only by following the informative matter; the non-informative is not matter in its own right, but is termed 'non-informative matter' (*rūpāvijñapti*) by deriving the name from the informative matter, rather than being resistant."

[The opponent] follows [the argument]. They also claim that the *vijñapti* (informative action) is called "obstructive" (*sapratigha*). Since obstructiveness is not the same [in both cases], how can matter (*rūpa*) be considered identical?
Next, he refutes the analogy: "For example, when a tree moves, its shadow necessarily follows. Movement arises from the *vijñapti*, yet there is no *avijñapti* (non-informative action).

If [the opponent] also calls it 'matter,' then when the *vijñapti*-matter ceases, the *avijñapti* should also cease—just as when the tree ceases, the shadow necessarily ceases with it. Therefore, the arising of the shadow depends upon the tree; if the tree ceases, the shadow likewise [ceases]."
[The unmanifest] ceases. The unmanifest arises depending upon the manifest; when the manifest passes away, the unmanifest ceases.
Since its cessation is not the same as that of matter (*rūpa*), it also does not accord with correct reasoning. The second [point], "all," is explained by some teachers as follows:
because the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) which serve as its basis are subject to transformation and resistance, the unmanifest [is also considered matter].
[The opponent] says: "That [basis] is also called 'form' (rūpa). The Master of the Treatise objects:

"If it is by virtue of the transformation and resistance of its basis that the unmanifest (avijñapti) receives the name 'form,' then the five consciousnesses, which likewise depend upon the five sense organs, should also be called 'form. [The opponent replies: The five consciousnesses depend upon the five sense organs, yet they do not conform to the nature of the organs."

Regarding how name-and-form (nāmarūpa) is non-manifest (avijñapti) in dependence upon the four great elements (mahābhūta): according to this master’s interpretation, name-and-form follows the great elements;

at the moment an unmanifest [action] arises, it necessarily depends upon the primary elements, just as a shadow depends on a tree, light depends on a jewel, or the five consciousnesses depend on the five sense faculties.
It is not so; it can only act as a contributory condition (*upapattipratyaya*) for their arising. The Master of the Treatise refutes this, saying:

"According to principle, shadows and light should have separate bases in the primary elements (*mahābhūta*). How could shadows and light, which are derivative matter (*bhautika-rūpa*), depend upon trees and jewels? [Having thus refuted it, he explains: By means of the five consciousnesses, their bases are indeterminate;
they may be characterized by resistance (*sapratigha*), namely the sense organs such as the eye, or they may be without resistance, namely the immediately preceding mind (*manas*)."
The basis of the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) is not like this; it is necessarily based on that which is subject to transformation and resistance, and is therefore called "form" (*rūpa*).
Below, the position of the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* school is further clarified. However, according to the *Tattvasiddhi*, the unmanifest is first explained.

The essence of this unmanifest is definitively neither form nor mind; thus, the seventh chapter of the treatise asks: "It is already known that there exists an unmanifest dharma that is not mind; is it now form?"
[Question: Is this [unmanifest action] a mental factor (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*)? [Answer: It is subsumed under the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). [Question:

If unmanifest action were of the nature of form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*), what fault would there be? [Answer: The five factors—form, sound, odor, taste, and tangibility—are not by nature merit (*puṇya*) or demerit (*apuṇya*);

therefore, unmanifest action is not considered to have the nature of form. Furthermore, the Buddha taught that form has the characteristic of being afflicted and disintegrating (*bādhanā-lakṣaṇa*); [if it were unmanifest action,] this characteristic of being afflicted and disintegrating would also apply to unmanifest action.
Because it is unobtainable, it is not of the nature of form (*rūpa*). Next, the precept of action (*kriyā-śīla*) is explained through four sections.

First, the presentation of divergent views: one master holds that its essence consists of both form and mind (*citta*). Thus, the treatise states: "Verbal karma is not merely sound; it must be accomplished by the assistance of mental power.
Therefore, one knows that bodily karma likewise is accomplished by the assistance of mental power. It is clear that the essence of these two types of karma consists of both form and mind."

Regarding the essence [of the precepts]: the second master holds that the mind is the essence. Because the mind is characterized by deliberation and cognition, it can constitute the essence of the precepts;

whereas matter (rūpa) is insentient and lacks cognition, and therefore cannot be the essence of the precepts. Thus, the treatise states: "Apart from the mind, there is no volition, nor are there bodily or vocal actions.

Therefore, one knows that both types of action take the mind as their essence. Second, the refutation of errors: the first master’s position that both matter and mind constitute the essence contradicts the intent of the treatise.
Treatise. The seventh question asks: "Is this body the agent of wholesome or unwholesome [actions]? Since the body itself is not so, it is therefore not that which performs bodily action.
The answer is: "Because it follows the power of the mind, when the body arises in another place, it is able to accumulate karma;
therefore, the accumulation is designated as wholesome or unwholesome. It is not truly bodily or vocal action. Likewise, it is not merely sound or speech. Because...
The power of the mind follows sounds; the accumulation of good and evil through speech is called verbal action (*vākkarman*).

However, the treatises state that the mind can lead the way for action, but they do not take the mind itself as the substance of the performed action. Furthermore, form (*rūpa*) is a material phenomenon (*rūpadharma*), and matter is insentient and devoid of cognition.

Mind (*citta*) is a mental phenomenon (*cittadharma*), and the mind is characterized by deliberation and cognition. To claim that these two combine to constitute the substance [of action] is contrary to correct principle. Thus says the second master.

Regarding the statement that "the mind constitutes the essence," it follows that one must also guard the mind. Since you have already admitted that the mind constitutes the essence, why not guard the mind?
If one does guard the mind, what then? Therefore, the tenth fascicle of the *Śāstra* states: "In the Vinaya, there is no offense committed by the mind alone. It further states:

"If one merely gives rise to an evil thought, one cannot be without fault; however, no formal precept (*śīla*) is established for this, because it is difficult to maintain. One maintains the precepts regarding gross offenses."

It can be prevented. Subtle offenses are certainly removed by [meditative] concentration and so forth. Furthermore, if the essence of morality were the mind, it would have to involve deliberation and cognition;

since it does not involve deliberation and cognition, how could this accord with correct reasoning? Third, to establish the correct position: form (*rūpa*) is the essence of karma. Thus, the second treatise states:
"Non-form phenomena (*arūpadharma*) are the mind and unmanifest action (*avijñapti*). Since it says these two are not form, it is clearly understood [that karma is form].
The precept of action (*karmapatha*) is form (*rūpa*). Furthermore, the seventh treatise states: "Regarding bodily action (*kāyakarman*):
that which is performed by the body is called bodily action. Question: There should be no such thing as bodily action. Why? Because bodily action is defined as the movement of the body.

Since conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) perish moment by moment, there can be no movement. Answer: It is said that when a phenomenon arises in another location, it displaces [the previous state] in that other place. This is what is meant by "bodily action."
This is called bodily action (*kāyakarman*). As for vocal action (*vākkarman*): when the four great elements strike against one another, sound is produced therein;

this sound forms melodies and tones, which serve as designations and names. Sentences function by means of these names. These names and sentences are established upon the basis of sound, and thus constitute vocal action.
Action has no separate essence; it takes sound as its essence. Fourth, the resolution of objections: [The questioner asks: If...
What is it that takes form (*rūpa*) as its essence? Therefore, the treatise says: "Karmic action of speech is necessarily accomplished through the assistance of mental power (*citta-bala*).
The essence of this karma is definitively the nature of sound (*śabda-svabhāva*); the mind is the cause that initiates the karma, not the essence of the karma itself. Question:

The treatise states that apart from the mind there is no volition (*cetanā*), and thus no karmic actions of body or speech. This implies that the mind is the essence of volition; it is clearly understood, therefore, that the two types of karma likewise do not exist apart from it.
Mind. Taking mind as its essence, this [treatise] explains this in order to refute external schools; thus it says:

"All" refers to the fact that, according to the Sarvāstivāda school, apart from the mind-king (*citta-rāja*), there exists a separate mental factor (*caitasika*) called volition (*cetanā*). While volition and mind are simultaneous, they possess distinct entities. Therefore, the treatise states: "Apart from mind, there is no volition.
However, while mind is not necessarily volition, volition is necessarily mind. Furthermore, regarding the tenets established by non-Buddhists concerning body and speech...
Karma does not arise through the assistance of the mind; therefore, the treatise refutes this by stating that there is no bodily or vocal karma apart from the mind.
Next, it provides a detailed analysis through sixteen categories in total: first, the distinction between the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);

second, within the conditioned, the distinction between the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*); third, within the tainted, the distinction among the three aggregates (*triskandha*). The fourth...

Fourth, among the three types [of form] within the aggregate of matter, they are distinguished by their specific natures; fifth, among those three types, they are distinguished according to their categories;

sixth, among those of the nature of outflow (*niṣyanda*), they are distinguished by their moral qualities (*tri-dharmatā*); seventh, among those of a wholesome nature, they are distinguished as being acquired at birth (*upapatti-labdha*) or produced through application (*prayoga*).
The eighth [section] distinguishes based on the locations within the two general categories. The ninth distinguishes based on the great [elements] within those locations.
The tenth distinguishes the beginning and end within the great elements that serve as the basis. The eleventh distinguishes the time of attainment within the end.
The twelfth distinguishes the sequence within the time of attainment. The thirteenth distinguishes the realization within the co-arising.
The fourteenth is the analysis of emphasis within the section on establishing proof. The fifteenth is the analysis of numerical manifestation within the section on non-emphasis.
The sixteenth is the analysis of similarities and differences within the section on enumeration.
Regarding the first gate: both types of precepts are aggregates of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), not the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*).
Since the unconditioned is eternal and these precepts arise from conditions, both of these precepts are subsumed under the category of the conditioned.
This second category consists of conditioned precepts (*saṃskṛta-śīla*), which are comprised within the outflows (*sāsrava*). This is because the various outflows increase in accordance with them.

That is to say, when they are grasped as existence through the condition of craving, they are like dust adhering to a moist garment. However, the untainted higher dharmas (*anāsrava-uttara-dharma*) are not objects of craving;
they can grasp [the mind] like a heated stone, such that the feet do not adhere to it.

The third gate: This impure (*sāsrava*) morality consists of both material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) and mental factors (*citta* and *caitta*) that are dissociated from the mind (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).

These are the causes of morality, but not the actual essence of morality (*śīla-svabhāva*). The reason for this is that because the power of the Śrāvakas is inferior, they merely restrain body and speech;
thus, when they now generate morality, they obtain non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*) through body and speech, thereby protecting the seven branches [of the precepts].
Within the matter of the fourth gate—the body and speech—there are three types in total. First, matter that is visible and resistant, which refers to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Second, matter that is invisible but resistant, which refers to the five sense faculties and four sense objects.

Third, matter that is both invisible and non-resistant, which refers to unmanifest matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*) within the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). As for manifest precepts (*vijñapti-śīla*), they are subsumed under the first two categories of matter.
Regarding "non-informative" (*avijñapti*): it is subsumed under the third category of form. Thus, the *Samyuktābhidharmahṛdaya*, fascicle 3, states:

"That bodily action is visible and resistant; verbal action is invisible and resistant; non-action (non-informative) is both invisible and non-resistant. The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, fascicle 30, says: [same as above].

Excluding non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*), what phenomena are termed "invisible and non-obstructive"? They are not the three types of obstructive [matter]; therefore, they are called "non-obstructive.
Regarding the fifth gate, the specific analysis of the essence of discipline (*saṃvara*): since it is matter, among the categories of contaminated matter (*sāsrava-rūpa*), there are three types:

first, fruition-born (*vipākaja*); second, nurtured (*aupacayika*); and third, outflow-born (*naiḥṣyandika*). Now, these two types of morality (the Prātimokṣa and meditative discipline) are subsumed under the category of outflow-born matter, because they follow from their own kind.
"Arising from causes" means that they are equal, which refers to being of the same outflow (*niṣyanda*). This is because "outflow" denotes a category of similarity.
They are exclusively outflows because the other two categories are exclusively neutral (*avyākṛta*).
The sixth section concerns the physical and vocal aspects, which are virtuous and nothing else. For these two reasons, the *Abhidharmakośa* states:

"That is to say, remaining as before, one sits on a lowly seat—either squatting or kneeling—with body bent and palms joined; furthermore, it says, 'one should arouse a mind of earnest purity and utter words of truth.
Regarding the distinctions of form (*rūpa*), there are twenty in total; among these, eight are shapes: long, short, square, round, high, low, [flat, and convex].

Is it correct? This [definition] applies generally to all three [types of action]. As for their nature, they are restricted to being wholesome (*kuśala*). The "limit" refers to bodily intimation (*kāya-vijñapti*).

The remaining twelve types of action consist of visible forms (*varṇa*)—blue, yellow, red, and white; clouds, smoke, dust, and mist; shadows, light, brightness, and darkness—which are invariably neutral (*avyākṛta*).

Therefore, they are not the essence of the precepts (*śīla*), nor are they vocal intimation (*vāg-vijñapti*). Vocal sound (*śabda*) has eight kinds: first, that which has appropriated primary elements (*upātta-mahābhūta*) as its cause, belonging to sentient beings, is called "sentient-sound" (*sattva-śabda*).
1. Agreeable [sound] caused by appropriated great elements (*mahābhūta*) belonging to sentient beings. 2. Disagreeable [sound] caused by appropriated great elements belonging to sentient beings.
3. Agreeable [sound] caused by appropriated great elements not belonging to sentient beings. 4. Disagreeable [sound] caused by appropriated great elements not belonging to sentient beings.
There are likewise four permutations regarding those caused by non-appropriated great elements; these should be understood accordingly.

Understand this: among these eight types of sound, the first two pertain to all three moral natures (*trividha-svabhāva*), yet when restricted to the wholesome side, they constitute vocal informative action (*vāgvijñapti-karman*);

the remaining six are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), and therefore do not constitute the essence of the precept (*śīla*). Generally speaking, regarding bodily and vocal [action], non-informative action (*avijñapti*) pertains to both natures;

however, as we now clarify the wholesome precept, it is restricted to the wholesome nature alone. Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, chapter thirteen, states: "Non-informative action pertains only to the wholesome and unwholesome natures; it does not exist in the indeterminate."
There is that which is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). The reason for this is that because the power of an indeterminate mind is weak and inferior, it cannot induce a strong karma to arise;
however, when the cause ceases, the fruit may still continue to arise.

The seventh category, wholesome [states], is of two kinds: first, those acquired by birth (*upapatti-labdha*); second, those produced through application (*prayoga*). Both of these types of wholesome minds are capable of giving rise to the precepts (*śīla*).
This is because, for one who has already entered the wisdom derived from hearing (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*), it is a matter of application;

however, the mind that acquires [the precepts] also extends to the wholesome mind acquired by birth. As for the intermediate stage, if one has not yet attained the wisdom derived from hearing, it is exclusively the wholesome mind acquired by birth.

Because it is obtained in the intermediate state. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, fascicle 42, states: "Among the fruits of the various restraints (*saṃvara*), some arise from preparatory effort (*prayoga*) and some arise from innate acquisition (*upapatti-labdha*).
Regarding those produced by a wholesome mind, if the restraint arises from preparatory effort, one first abandons the restraint when the wholesome roots are severed.

However, both the preparatory effort and the fundamental act (*maula*) that sever the wholesome roots are termed 'severing the wholesome roots. It is on this basis that [the text] speaks of 'severing'."

Regarding the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*): when one abandons the various types of discipline (*saṃvara*), if they arise from innate goodness (*upapattilābhika-kuśala*) or from a mind-generated state, then whichever category of mind is capable of producing the roots of goodness, the discipline produced thereby is abandoned at that very moment.
This is because when the primary motivating factor (*samutthāpaka*) is abandoned, its concomitants (*anuvartin*) are also abandoned.
By this, it is proven that [the discipline] is acquired through both types of mind.

The eighth section: A detailed explanation of the vows (*saṃvara*). One acquires [the vow] only with respect to present objects, including the preparatory (*prayoga*), the fundamental (*maula*), and the subsequent (*pṛṣṭha*) stages;

with respect to sentient and non-sentient beings; and with respect to both natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and proscribed transgressions (*prajñapti-sāvadya*). Therefore, the *Abhidharmakośa* (Chapter 4, verse 15) states: "One acquires all two kinds from the present.
Regarding the phrase "all," it refers to the preparatory, fundamental, and subsequent stages; the two kinds refer to sentient and non-sentient beings, as well as natural and...
