If a bhikṣu incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense not shared with bhikṣuṇīs, and that bhikṣu transforms his faculties to become a bhikṣuṇī, he is immediately released. — *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*.
It is also thus. Furthermore, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If one has previously committed an offense common to both monks and nuns, one should repent before the nuns;
if one has previously committed an offense not common [to both], there is no further repentance. The same applies when a monk's gender changes. The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 1, also asks:
"Is it possible for one who has committed a pārājika offense to be granted the going-forth and receive the precepts? The answer is: "Yes, if..."
If a bhikṣuṇī commits an *anekasaṃvāsika pārājika* offense and, having renounced the precepts, undergoes a change of gender to become a male, she may be granted ordination and receive the precepts.

Question: If, because there is no principle of continuity for an *anekasaṃvāsika* offense, it is extinguished [upon the commission], then one who dies or leaves the religious life (*pravrajyā*) should also have their status extinguished;
for in the absence of further transgression, they would be the same as that *anekasaṃvāsika* case. Answer: This is because [the status] is maintained by possessing three factors.

The meanings differ. First, regarding the end of life and so forth, they are identical in that they proceed from a single karma, and not from one's own mind, because this differs from the case where one abandons the path due to the turning back of one's own mind.

Second, regarding the continuity of the object of transgression, there is a difference: whereas for the same offense, continuity of the transgression occurs [in the former], it does not [in the latter].

Third, regarding transformation, there is a difference in that all possess the precepts, whereas at the end of life, one no longer possesses the precepts. As for the third section, if the ritual procedure is not performed, the same offense follows accordingly; that is to say, with respect to—
This is explained within the section on the practice of repentance for residual offenses (*śeṣa-āpatti*).

If one who has committed a different offense changes [gender] while in the midst of performing the formal repentance, regardless of whether the ritual procedure has been completed or not, they become pure provided there is such a mutual transformation, because the root offense has been eliminated and there is no need to continue the practice.
The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (Third Fascicle) states: "If a bhikṣu intentionally emits semen and immediately transforms into a bhikṣuṇī, he is immediately purified."

If one who is undergoing the *ṣaḍrātra* (six-night) penance changes status before it is completed, or if one who is undergoing the *parivāsa* (probation) changes status before it is completed and becomes a nun, they are still considered to be dwelling in purity.
It is the same if a nun changes status to become a monk. Next, regarding the violation of shared precepts:

if a monk who has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense changes status to become a nun at the very moment of the offense, or even if he conceals it for ten or five years before changing status to become a nun—this constitutes one type of the fifteen [cases].

The sun removes the offense. If a bhikṣuṇī commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense and does not conceal it for even a single thought-moment, she shall confess it and undergo the *parivāsa* (probation) for fifteen days according to the rule.
During this period, if on the first or second day she transforms into a bhikṣu, she need only perform the six-night penance; thereafter, her offense is cleared.

By extension of this principle, if one transforms after having already performed six nights of penance, there is no logical necessity to grant another six nights. Question: If a bhikṣuṇī commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense and conceals it...

Regarding "transformation" (parivṛtti): it is not yet known whether one must still undergo treatment for concealment (pārājika-āpatti) or not. The answer is that since one was not treated for concealment while in the status of a bhikṣuṇī, even though one has now undergone transformation, one is likewise not treated for concealment.
Thus, the *Jianlun* (Treatise on Views), fascicle 8, states: "When she was a bhikṣuṇī, she practiced the act of matchmaking; she concealed it and did not disclose it.
Upon transforming her faculties to become a bhikṣu, there is no need for concealment. This differs from the *Shapitanlun* (Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-saṃgraha), which says: "If... [text truncated].
Regarding a prior offense committed with days of concealment, one immediately transforms into a bhikṣu and performs the *parivāsa* (probation) according to the original number of concealed days.

As for the fourth section, the rules for penalties against those who violate the communal sentiment, these are discussed in terms of the seven types of formal acts (*karmas*). An ancient commentary states:

"If, among different offenses, there are seven instances of emotional transgression and they are mutually transformed, then that which has not yet been remediated need not be remediated; however, if it has already been remediated..."

As for this, regardless of whether one has been disciplined or not, there is no need for formal release (*naiḥsargika*). This is because once the fundamental offense (*mūlāpatti*) has been confessed, the disciplinary measures (*daṇḍakarma*) that followed it are automatically nullified.

Furthermore, it is said: "If explained according to the principle, one must remove the prohibitions (*pratikṣepa*) regarding non-approach. Although this specific matter of the offense has been extinguished, one must still confess and apologize to the layperson;
it cannot be concluded simply by that alone. If one claims that the disciplinary measures do not require apology, our current interpretation holds that this is not so, even if the offense...
The offenses have both vanished, yet the methods of treatment still remain. The reason for this is that the seven *karmas* are methods for treating persons;

they do not originally treat the offenses themselves. Once the offense has been expiated, the method remains. Various masters explain the seven *karmas* as follows: in the first four, one first performs confession and subsequently receives release.
Since it has already been granted that the remedial methods (*pratīkāra-dharma*) do not perish once confession has been performed, how can this explanation state that they "accord with the apology"?

Furthermore, regarding the three types of formal accusations (*tri-udghāta*), it is also granted that the offense is extinguished while the remedial method remains; thus, within the "Three Increases" (*tri-vṛddhi*), confession comes first and resolution follows.

Moreover, why does this allow for other remedial methods to accord with the apology as the matter of the offense subsides, yet specifically speak only of the prohibition against reaching the one [offense], even though the matter of the offense has been extinguished, one must still perform confession and apology?

Laypeople (*avadātavasana*) cannot be dealt with so simply; the disciplinary procedures (*dharma-karma*) do not apply to them. However, this [case] is for the purpose of repentance (*pratideśanā*) for laypeople, and it is permitted that the legal procedure does not apply to them.

As for others, they are for the sake of subduing (*vinaya*) people. What loss could there be in the legal procedure? In that case, since the offense is already permitted to be extinguished, how could the disciplinary procedure alone remain?
This matter of the extinction of the offense is not a cause for the loss of the legal procedure; it is like the obstruction of birth by difficulties.

Regarding the method for the disposition of those who have committed a transgression: those who share the same offense ought to be disciplined if they have not yet been disciplined; if they have already been disciplined, they should proceed according to the rules among the *bhikṣuṇīs*.
Once they have been subdued, the *bhikṣuṇī* community shall grant them release. The same applies to the transformation [of status] of a *bhikṣuṇī*.

As for whether the pure dharma of the fifth gate is lost, see the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle eight: when one is a *bhikṣu*, if the three robes and the alms bowl are lost, the rite of formal possession (*parigraha*) is forfeited. Upon reaching the... [text continues].

In the case of a bhikṣuṇī, she should receive the five robes anew. As for any extra robes or alms bowls she previously possessed, she should perform the *śuddhi* (purification) rite again according to the rules for bhikṣuṇīs.
Regarding the seven-day medicine she has received, the formal acceptance (*parigraha*) is lost; the rule requires it to be accepted anew.

Although the original donor does not lose their status as a donor from the previous time and remains the donor now, although the treatise states this, the interpretation of the meaning is not so. It is like when the period of the preceding *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) is transferred.
It is not lost. One may continue to rely on one's original seniority (*vassa*) within the community of nuns. Furthermore, the previous donor is likewise not lost.

How then can it be said that robes and such items alone lose their legal status? Moreover, this transformation does not occur apart from the conditions regarding the robes; for at the time of transformation, how could [the robes] be otherwise?
Furthermore, regarding the method of application: for this reason, when there is a transformation, that which was previously established as a *dharma* remains entirely intact.

The sixth section has two parts: first, concerning the reception of the precepts; second, concerning the delimitation of boundaries (*sīmā-bandha*). Regarding the reception of the precepts, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitation Vinaya), fascicle 56, states:
"If a *śrāmaṇera* receives full ordination (*upasampadā*) and the Saṃgha suddenly transforms [the gender] into a female, he departs beyond the limit of influence (*sīmā-vaśa*)."

One who changes [gender] before the ritual is completed does not obtain the precepts. This is because a *bhikṣuṇī* lacks the principle of receiving the precepts from a male, and furthermore, because the required conditions are not fulfilled.

If one transforms into a *bhikṣuṇī* just as the ceremony is concluding, the *śrāmaṇera* obtains the *bhikṣu* precepts. If it is the disciple who transforms, it is like a *bhikṣu* conferring the precepts upon another;
however, if this *śrāmaṇera* transforms into a female, he does not obtain the precepts because the original basis (*mūladharma*) is deficient. Furthermore, according to the rule...
Because of dissatisfaction. If one undergoes a change of gender at the conclusion [of the ceremony], one obtains the *bhikṣuṇī* precepts.

If ten *bhikṣus* confer the precepts upon a *śrāmaṇerī*, and both teacher and disciple undergo a change of gender, the case is likewise to be treated accordingly. Furthermore, if ten *bhikṣuṇīs* confer the precepts upon a *śikṣamāṇā* as the presiding teachers, if the teacher changes gender, it is not the same as the above case;
however, if the disciple changes gender, it is categorically invalid, because of the male body.

Because it does not rely on the fundamental dharma, the following explains the delimitation of the boundary (*sīmābandha*). According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, the subsequent text poses this question:
"If all bhikṣus perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of delimiting a boundary, and the entire Saṃgha transforms into women, is that boundary called a 'bhikṣu boundary' or a 'bhikṣuṇī boundary'?"

The Buddha said, "It is called the *bhikṣuṇī* boundary. Next, the questions and answers regarding all *bhikṣuṇīs* performing the formal act (*saṃghakarma*) of establishing a boundary were as stated above;

this is called the *bhikṣu* boundary. Again, it was asked: "If, at the time of a *bhikṣu* performing the formal act of establishing a boundary, there are those who turn away [from the assembly] and those who do not, is that boundary called a *bhikṣu* boundary or a *bhikṣuṇī* boundary? The Buddha said, "If the person pronouncing the formal act is male,"

The boundary belongs to the bhikṣus; when it is established for women, the boundary belongs to the bhikṣuṇīs. Next, regarding the boundary-establishment for bhikṣuṇīs, the questions and answers are the same as before.

As for these establishments, they are all said to be completed upon reaching [the limit]. Regarding those who are "corresponding" (i.e., participating), if they have gone far beyond that limit, none of them will succeed.

Next, regarding those of dual sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*), the *Jianlun* (Treatise on Seeing) identifies three types: first, those who can both conceive an embryo themselves and cause another to conceive;
second, those who can conceive an embryo themselves but cannot cause another to conceive; third, those who cannot conceive an embryo themselves but can cause another to conceive.
These three types of persons are all ineligible for ordination and receiving the precepts; if they have already received them, they should be expelled. Next...

Distinguishing the five cases regarding those lacking the [monastic] basis (*amūlaka*): the first four do not involve expulsion because they lack the path [of transgression]; the fifth involves expulsion because the path exists.

According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, if one is bitten by a wild beast, killed by an enemy, or dies of natural decay, such that one can no longer function as a male, one should all be expelled and barred from the community.
Next follows the detailed refutation, which is divided into ten sections. First, three points concerning total silence; second, three concerning the consumption of what is not the Dharma;
third, three concerning the mind’s lack of comprehension; fourth, three concerning the absence of both robes and mental intent;

fifth, regarding those such as the hand-severed, it is because their appearance is loathsome; and as for asuras and gandharvas, they are subsumed under the category of non-human obstacles. The sixth... [text continues].

The first three types of emptiness exist outside the realm of existence (*dhātu*); alternatively, they are adventitious (*āgantuka*) within the scope of seeing and hearing, yet because their realms are distinct, they do not constitute [emptiness].
The seventh threefold [set] is adventitious within the scope of hearing because it does not manifest; the eighth threefold [set] is so because it is free from both seeing and hearing.

The ninth [category] consists of three types because they reside outside the boundaries. Regarding the tenth, those who do not receive the śrāmaṇera precepts have lost the sequential order of entering the Dharma.
Among these ten points, for the fifth there is both attainment and non-attainment; for the tenth, the precepts are attained; for the remaining cases, the precepts are not attained.

Next, the procedure for conferring the precepts is explained. The text is divided into two parts: first, the method of conferring the precepts; second, resolving doubts within the assembly. The first part contains two sections:
first, the delay in the act of receiving [the precepts] due to the failure to comply with instructions, which serves as the introductory context for the inquiry and examination;
second, from the words "The Buddha said," the actual method of conferring the precepts is explained. This section on the method of conferring the precepts has two parts; first, the introduction...

The Dharma establishes the core tenets. Second, from "At that time" onwards, the text correctly explains the conferral of the Dharma. This section on the conferral of the Dharma consists of three parts: first, the ritual procedure for conferring the precepts;

second, from "At that time there was a bhikṣu," which explains the characteristics so that they may be known; third, from "You have now completed receiving full ordination," which concludes with exhortations to uphold [the precepts].
Regarding the ritual procedure for the prior reception [of ordination], there are nine dharmas in total. The first clarifies the initial request for an upādhyāya.
Regarding the Dharma: there is no addition to the meaning of the text. Although the third fascicle of the *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra* asks, "Is one ordained if one does not request a preceptor?

it answers that one does indeed receive the precepts; however, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense for the Saṃgha [to ordain without one]. It is essential that one must request [the preceptor]. Whether such a request should be made has already been clarified above.

Second, as for establishing the location where the person receiving the precepts is placed: this is done so that by seeing their form, wholesome states may arise. One should place them in a visible spot, fearing that [if they were elsewhere], they might hear the Dharma and [thereby] complete [the ordination].

[Objection: It is difficult [to avoid]. One must leave the place where the teaching is being heard. At the third stage, the preceptor (*karmācārya*) appoints a teacher of instruction (*śikṣācārya*). [Question: Why does the preceptor not appoint [the teacher]? [Answer: He appoints the teacher alone. [Objection:

Since the preceptor remains within the assembly, there is no need to appoint [another]. [Reply: The teacher of instruction goes out from the assembly to pose questions and challenges; fearing that he might act arbitrarily, it is necessary to appoint him.

Furthermore, another interpretation holds that the preceptor is precisely the one who should uphold the ritual procedure (*dharmakarma*), and thus there is no need to appoint him; the teacher of instruction is not [the one who upholds the procedure].
Since those who uphold the Dharma must be formally appointed, once a *śikṣācārya* (preceptor) has been so appointed, it is not necessary to inform the assembly.

Furthermore, when posing questions and challenges outside the assembly, there is no assembly to inform. The *karmavācanā* master acts conversely; therefore, he must perform the formal announcement (*jñapti*).

Moreover, since the *karmavācanā* master has not been appointed, there is also concern regarding his acting on his own authority; thus, he must perform the formal announcement. At the fourth stage, the *śikṣācārya* receives the command.

Regarding the interrogation: if one were to interrogate them in the midst of the assembly, they might feel anxious and terrified; therefore, it is conducted in a secluded place so that the mind may be examined with precision.
Within the interrogation, the first part concerns external conditions regarding the robe and bowl; next, one should say, "Lower [your head]," and examine the internal obstacles (*antarāyika-dharma*).

There are three sections in the text for examining these obstacles: first, the instruction to answer truthfully; second, from "What is your name now? onwards, which clearly sets forth the interrogation itself (omitting the thirteen obstacles as they are not relevant to this inquiry).

One must know this: if one does not undergo questioning and interrogation, the reception of the precepts is not accomplished. In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, there is extensive questioning regarding the various obstacles (*antarāyika-dharma*).

One asks only: "Have you never been a bhikṣu before? If one answers, "I have," [one asks]: "Are you pure in maintaining the precepts? When you relinquished them, did you do so with a single-minded focus and according to the Dharma?
Other obstacles are not all questioned. For the reception by a bhikṣuṇī, one asks only about the various obstacles and does not ask about the various difficulties. Third, if...

Regarding the statement "without lowering [the voice]," this indicates the formal procedure for responding to the Saṃgha. Fifth, after the instructor has asked the questions and made the formal announcement (*jñapti*), he calls the candidate forward.
Sixth, upon being called, the candidate enters the assembly; the instructor takes hold of his robe and bowl on his behalf and instructs him to pay homage to the Saṃgha.

Before the preceptor, one kneels with the right knee on the ground and joins the palms. One is instructed to be sincere and to request the precepts from the Saṃgha, thereby manifesting one’s earnestness; for this reason, the request must be made three times.

Seventh, the preceptor makes a formal motion (*jñapti*) before the assembly to interrogate [the candidate], as it is not permissible to act arbitrarily; he consults the Saṃgha regarding whether [the interrogation] may proceed.

Eighth, once the assembly has reached a consensus that it may proceed, the interrogation is formally conducted. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Sengqi lü), fascicle 23, the interrogation is about to begin.
At that time, having been instructed to receive the robes and bowl, he was commanded to answer according to reality, saying: "In the world of devas, Māras, and Brahmās;
among śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, devas, humans, and asuras—if I were not truthful, I would be deceiving them therein."
Furthermore, to deceive the assembly of śrāvakas regarding the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is a grave offense.

Although it ought to have been included in the formal questioning, the absence of the "thirteen obstacles" (trayodaśa-antarāyika-dharma) is omitted from the text; nevertheless, according to the text, these must certainly be questioned.

There is no case where one can achieve the formal act of receiving [the precepts] without having asked [about the obstructing factors]. Although the *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*, fascicle three, states:

"When receiving full ordination, if one confers the precepts without asking about the obstructing dharmas, does one obtain the precepts? Answer: One obtains the precepts; however, the bhikṣus commit a *duṣkṛta* offense, and this [procedure] cannot be relied upon.

The ninth [section] is precisely for the performance of the ritual. When about to perform the rite, one first instructs [the candidate] to focus on the objective sphere and establish the mind, and then recites [the formula].
The Dharma guides and introduces; only then is the Dharma bestowed. Within the Dharma, the *jñapti* (motion) and the *karmavācanā* (formal act) collectively encompass the skillful means (*upāya*).

These are recorded and integrated into the Dharma, which can be understood through careful investigation. Since the rite of ordination (*upasampadā*) is a matter of great gravity, it must strictly accord with the teachings. If the ritual is performed incorrectly or falls into error, the bestowal of the Dharma will not be accomplished.

Both the preceptor and the assembly must clearly discern what is correct and what is incorrect, listening with single-minded attention; only then can the rite be successfully completed. (From the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Part Two).
11. Dividing the Belongings of a Deceased Bhikṣu. There was a śrāmaṇera who had received the precepts. Among the assembly were the group of six (ṣaḍvargika).
The group of six said, "A bhikṣu who has newly received the precepts should not share [the inheritance] with the senior bhikṣus; it should be shared with the śrāmaṇeras. The teacher said:
"Why is this? He replied, "The *karmavācanā* for receiving the precepts was incomplete, and the preceptor did not know what to do. This matter was reported to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "One should ask the bhikṣu who was present during the *karmavācanā* whether that *karmavācanā* was complete. Thereupon, he questioned the various bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus said, "Although we were present during the *karmavācanā*, we did not remember or know [the proceedings]. They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, 'From now on, I allow that when performing a *karmavācanā*, you should listen with a single-minded focus. Do not think of other things; do not perceive other things;

do not contemplate other things. You should concentrate your mind; you should be diligent; you should be respectful; you should reflect. With every thought, you must maintain mindfulness in equal measure, as follows.'"
This is the *karmavācanā* (formal motion). One who performs the *karmavācanā* should speak by distinguishing [the stages], saying:

"This is the first, the second, the third. To speak without such distinction constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "This is the first accomplishment; the second and third are likewise.

The *Samantapāsādikā* (Commentary on the Vinaya), fascicle 17, says: After receiving the precepts, one should measure one's shadow. To measure the shadow means to stand upright and mark the position of the feet.

Regarding the phrase "for the first time" and so forth, it is recorded that one should state the year, month, day, and so on. In the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, chapter seventeen, the Buddha said: "One should instruct them so that they may know. He further stated:
"At the time you receive the precepts now, it is such-and-such a year, such-and-such a month, such-and-such a day, and such-and-such a hour. You should remember this matter for as long as you live.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* (Ten Recitations) is largely the same.

Next, the characteristics of the exposition are distinguished. Within this, there are two sections. First, the prohibition against speaking in response to faults; the five offenses cannot be fully detailed here, so only the first four are manifested.

Second, from "Good son" onwards, the actual exposition. This section is further divided into two: first, clarifying the practice of the four grave prohibitions through cessation and maintenance (*śīla*);
second, the practice of the four reliances through performance and maintenance. The preceding text is further divided into two: first, a general introduction.

The four sections of the prose [explanation] can be understood. Next, from "Now, you all... onwards, the four levels of transgression are listed individually. First, the text on the precept has five parts:

first, "Nothing at all may be done" indicates the strict observance of the prohibitive restraint (*śīla*). Second, from "If a bhikṣu... onwards, it clarifies the commission of an offense; herein there are the dharma, the analogy, and their synthesis.
Third, from "In this regard... onwards, it specifies the duration of the observance. Fourth, "Are you able to observe it? examines the internal state [of the practitioner].
Mind. Regarding the fifth answer, the respondent himself declares the formal undertaking (*yāma*). The three subsequent examples are similar; they differ only in their specific subject matter.

Next, regarding the four reliances (*pratisaraṇa*), there are two parts according to the text: first, the general presentation, which consists of four points that are easy to understand. In contrast to this, the meaning of the four reliances is explained through a fourfold analysis:

first, the explanation of names; second, the determination of their essential nature (*svabhāva*); third, the establishment of their intended purpose; and fourth, their sequential order. First, as for the explanation of the names:
In cultivating liberation, one must necessarily rely upon the provisions (*sambhāra*). To enter the gateway of the noble ones (*ārya*), it is essential that [the practice] arises;

therefore, these four types are the conditions for the arising of the noble ones. For this reason, the *Abhidharmakośa* refers to them as the "noble lineages" (*āryavaṃśa*). Furthermore, in the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, fascicle 181:
Question: Why are they called "noble lineages" (*āryavaṃśa*)? Some say that because they are both noble (*ārya*) and lineages (*vaṃśa*), they are named "noble lineages.

That is to say, they are called "noble" because they are wholesome (*kuśala*) and because they are untainted (*anāsrava*). Furthermore, these are able to produce all dharmas of merit, continuing in succession without interruption;

thus, they are called "lineages. They are also called the "four reliances" (*catvāraḥ pratiśaraṇāḥ*). "Reliance" (*pratiśaraṇa*) means to depend upon or to lean on. Practitioners rely upon these to support and accomplish their own practice. Therefore...
It is said: the four reliances (*catvāri pratiśaraṇāni*). Next, regarding the determination of their essential nature (*svabhāva*):
these four all have non-attachment (*alobha*) as their intrinsic nature. However, this non-attachment is of two kinds: first, contentment (*saṃtuṣṭi*); second, fewness of desires (*alpecchatā*).

Here, the essence of non-attachment refers exclusively to contentment, because the nature of fewness of desires is inferior to that of contentment. The reason for this is that, regarding food, clothing, bedding, and medicine, [one follows...]
Regarding that which has been obtained, one gives rise to contentment in all cases. "Fewness of desires" (*alpecchatā*) refers to the absence of a longing for things not yet obtained;
this is called fewness of desires. Therefore, contentment (*saṃtuṣṭi*) is superior to fewness of desires. Thus, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 181, asks:

Since both fewness of desires and contentment are antidotes to greed and have non-greed (*alobha*) as their intrinsic nature, why is contentment alone designated by the name "noble lineage" (*āryavaṃśa*)?
Is it not [simply] having few desires? Answer: The term "having few desires" involves both faults and exaggerations. Contentment (*saṃtuṣṭi*) is not like this. As for the fault:
it merely speaks of "having few desires," but does not speak of "having no desire. As for the exaggeration: it applies to those who actually have no desire.

Because they are designated as "having few desires," such [craving] does not exist within their joy; therefore, the Noble Lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) are established. Regarding the statement that these are "intentions":
practice depends upon material support, and for that purpose, one must provide for it. Although the conditions for support are numerous, they are essentially limited to the internal and the external.

Since each of these two categories has two aspects, they constitute the four reliances (*catur-niśraya*). Food and medicine are the internal [reliances], corresponding to the body and illness; clothing and shelter are the external [reliances], corresponding to garments and advancement.

...cultivation. Therefore, these four reliances (pratisaraṇa) are established as pertaining to both the internal and external [teachings]. Furthermore, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, chapter twenty-two, asks:

"For what purpose are the four noble lineages (āryavaṃśa) established? It explains that when disciples abandon their worldly requisites and secular occupations to seek liberation and go forth into homelessness under the Buddha, the World-Honored One, the Lord of Dharma, out of compassion for them, establishes two types of aids to the path: first, the requisites for life (*jīvita-pariṣkāra*)...
...complete. Second is the activity (*karma*). The former three are the requisites for the arising of the aids to the path (*mārga-sambhāra*), while the last is the activity that assists the path.
If you can rely upon the aforementioned requisites for arising to perform the subsequent activity, liberation will not be long in coming.

For what reason are these two matters established? It is because one wishes to counteract and eliminate the four types of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) that arise; to remedy these four, the Four Noble Truths (*catur-āryasatya*) are taught.
Regarding the sequence: clothing wards off external cold, while food must provide internal sustenance. The external is explained first, and the internal is discussed subsequently.

Once the conditions for both the internal and external are prepared, one must logically cultivate the Path. Cultivation of the Path relies upon tranquility, which requires staying beneath trees. These requisites for supporting the Path are necessary at all times.
Medicines, however, depend upon the occurrence of illness; because they are infrequent, they are mentioned last. Question: I do not yet know the essential nature of these medicines.
What is this? The answer is that it has been explained since ancient times as the impurity of one’s own body. As stated in the preceding text: "Who could touch their own substance?
Furthermore, regarding the allowance for receiving food before it has reached the ground, the current interpretation is incorrect.

This arose because when the Holy Teaching first emerged, the transmitters did not seek its original intent and instead applied the teachings haphazardly; thus, it has long been practiced. However, the Brahman monks from the West all [hold that...]

It must be kept clean. If one were to consume such filthy and impure things, one would not be tolerated by the community; furthermore, if non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) were to hear of it, they would laugh and slander it excessively.
Therefore, the correct explanation is that this refers to discarded medicine. In Sanskrit it is called *puṇyāhṛta* (translated here as "medicine for rotten food").
This refers precisely to discarded items. Thus, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, chapter sixteen, states: "Medicine that has been cast aside.

Furthermore, when a donor provides the four requisites to the Saṃgha, how could one possibly offer such filthy things to the great assembly? Moreover, the *Bhaiṣajya-vastu* states: "Decayed medicine may be consumed for as long as one lives.
How could this require the addition of a formal ritual (*adhikāra*) before consumption? Based on this, it is certain that [the substance in question] is not excrement.

[The objection regarding] "impurity" can be resolved by citing the relevant passage from the *Śāstra*. Next, the four [points] are listed individually. First, according to the text, there are two parts:

first, the establishment of the superior practice; second, the allowance for the middling and inferior practices. Within the section on the establishment [of the superior practice], there are five points: first, citing the substance of the *pāṃśukūla* (rag-robe) upon which it relies;

second, based on this, the attainment of renunciation, followed by the manifestation of its benefits; third, citing the specific time period; fourth, examining the internal mind; fifth... [text fragment].

The fifth [category] is the formal acceptance through verbal declaration. Next, the opening [of the procedure] follows its respective capacity; there is no need to ask about the maintenance [of the precepts].

The same applies to the [final] three [categories]; they differ only in their specific matters. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* likewise explains twelve rules. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that after the *karmavācanā* is completed, one speaks of the four reliances (*catur-śaraṇa*), followed by the four *pārājikas*, and then the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣas*; each question and answer is as described above.
Next, the concluding exhortation consists of five parts: first, a summary of the fulfillment of the conditions for receiving [the teachings];
second, the exhortation to receive the teaching methods; third, the exhortation to cultivate merit and wisdom, which contains two sub-sections:

the initial separate exhortations regarding merit and wisdom, followed by the summary of the inexhaustible resonance of what has been cultivated, beginning with "You have resolved your mind..."; fourth, that which remains unknown; and fifth, [the conclusion].

[The Buddha] said: "No. Aside from this explanation, he questioned the two masters on other matters. Fifth, fearing there might be faults, he did not establish a rule to prohibit [the action], but rather commanded its prevention.

Next, the section clearing away doubts has two parts: first, clearing away the doubt of the person receiving the precepts; second, from "At that time, Ānanda... onwards, resolving the doubt regarding the *upādhyāya*.

The preceding text has four sections. First, the question concerning the doubt regarding one who has been suspended (*ukkhepanīyakamma*), based on seeing Nandika commit a grave offense and being deprived of his status.

If one returns from having left the path, this is the difficulty of a "borderline offense" (*sīmā-bandha*). Now, if such a person is suspended (*ukkhepanīyakamma*), they do not even count as a bhikkhu.

If one leaves the path and returns, is this the same as Nandika? The Buddha said: "Nandika committed a grave offense; his fundamental practice was false. This is the difficulty of an obstruction to the precepts (*śīla-antarāya*). Is it not so?"

These combined constitute the formal reception [of the precepts]. Now, regarding one who has been subject to the *ukkhepanīyakamma* (act of suspension) and refuses to acknowledge their fault: because the disciplinary procedure is grave, such a person does not count toward the quorum of the Saṃgha;

however, this does not constitute a destruction of the root [of the Saṃgha], nor does it form a "boundary-obstacle" (*paccantika-antarāya*). If they say they do not see [the fault], they are obstructed and must not be ordained;

if they see it, they are not obstructed and may receive the precepts. This is merely for the purpose of subduing an evil person; even if the legal act of suspension is not followed by an apology, the question remains as to whether one who has been suspended may return to lay life. Regarding the legal act of suspension...

"No apology is required. Having relinquished the precepts and returned, one’s seniority from the previous summer retreat should remain intact. [Question: "The summer retreat arises in dependence upon the precepts;

how can they coexist when the formal act of suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*) has been lost? [Answer: "Therefore, no apology is required. [Question: "This bhikṣu was originally subject to the disciplinary measure of suspension for 'not seeing [an offense]'.

Why, after having received [the precepts again], do you ask him, 'Are you able to repent?'? [Answer: "The term 'repentance' here refers to repenting for the original fault of not seeing [the offense]; it does not [refer to the current offense]."
That is to say, first is the confession regarding the offense previously raised; next is the removal of doubts concerning whether one has not yet reached the required age;

next are the three types of doubt regarding the formal inquiry; next is the removal of doubts concerning the preceptor (*upādhyāya*). Since Ānanda was seen to have asked about these matters, the disciple, having thereby formed a thought, subsequently questioned the preceptor:
"If the preceptor’s person is subject to the thirteen grounds for disqualification (*antarāyika-dharma*), and he confers the full ordination upon another..."
[Question: Regarding the precepts, how do we know whether they have been acquired or not? [Answer: He replied: "Before the rules were established, the Saṃgha was without fault.

After they were established, those who [violated them] incurred the fault of the Saṃgha. [Question: Since you speak of "establishment," what kind of establishment is this? [Answer: It refers to the establishment of the thirteen [rules] for the sake of the disciples.
It is difficult to restrain. After this point, it is not permissible to receive [the precepts]. If one should nonetheless receive them, the Saṃgha incurs an offense.

Since it is said that there is an offense, it gives rise to doubt in junior disciples as to whether they have obtained the precepts; thus there is an offense. It is not that they fail to obtain them, yet there is still an offense.
Therefore, four propositions are formulated to analyze this. "One who does not uphold the precepts" refers to those who have committed the grave offenses (*pārājika*) and so forth.

Regarding the first three who obtain [the precepts], it is because they possess a seeking mind. As for the fourth who does not obtain them, it is because they lack any intention to receive them. This is why one asks the *upādhyāya*.
Because this is the fundamental [position], other masters do not agree with it; therefore, it is not raised for questioning. The method for receiving the precepts is now concluded.

Next, the exposition of the *poṣadha* (confession of offenses) is clarified so that understanding may arise. For this reason, the fortnightly discernment of the characteristics of the five categories of offenses is first explained to manifest the timing for listening.
Hence, it is called *poṣadha*. The three methods for the *poṣadha* are explained in detail and gathered together in one place.

It is titled the *Khandhaka*. Within this, there are two parts. First, up to the point where it says "causing the mind not to be distracted," it correctly clarifies the cultivation of the path and that a pure person is qualified to hear the pure Dharma.
Second, from "The World-Honored One was in a secluded place" onwards, it demonstrates the ritual procedure for the aforementioned pure person to recite the precepts.
The preceding section has four parts: first, observing signs and inquiring to gain knowledge; second, from "At that time, King Bimbisāra... onwards, requesting the Buddha to join [the assembly].
[The Buddha] acted. At the third stage, the World-Honored One issued an edict ordering an assembly. At the fourth stage, the bhikṣus personally engaged in the practice of dhyāna.
The preceding passage has three parts: first, witnessing the prior event; second, questioning the attendant minister; third, the minister’s truthful reply.

Regarding the second section on the Buddhas, there are three parts: first, the king requests an assembly; second, [the Buddha] silently accepts the king’s request; third, he subsequently grants the request.
[The text] returns. The third assembly section contains two parts: first, the formal command for the assembly; second, from "At that time, the bhikṣus...
onwards, the assembly in accordance with the instructions. Within this, there are again two parts: the first clarifies the assembly of the bhikṣus;

[it notes that] worldly practice of material giving (*āmiṣadāna*) is precisely the condition for sustaining the Path. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya), fascicle 22, states: "It was not permitted for the bhikṣus to distribute the cloth..."
The *poṣadha* was being recited. The twenty *karmas* had not yet been heard or explained, and the *Prātimokṣa* had not yet been recited while seated in assembly.
At that time, heterodox practitioners and brahmins asked the bhikṣus, "Do you hold the *poṣadha* and other rites? They replied, "We do not perform them, O brahmins."
Out of jealousy and contempt, they rebuked them, saying: "Other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas still observe the poṣadha and other rites;
yet you śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya, who claim to be virtuous and excellent, do not perform the poṣadha and such. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I authorize the performance of the poṣadha and other rites. Just as I have established the precepts, you should recite the *pārājika* rules every half-month."
The Prātimokṣa. The second bhikṣu, out of compassion for the laity, correctly practices the Dharma-giving. Within this, there are seven sections:

first, responding to the request to listen and speak; second, having listened, the following section explains the essence of the Dharma and provides an extensive commentary on the Sūtras, as analyzed in the opening of the school’s tenets.
The third section concerns the ritual for requesting bhikṣus to descend and preach; the fourth section clarifies that the bhikṣus shall descend and proclaim the sound of the Dharma.
In the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, it states that the bhikṣus then chanted together in praise of the Triple Gem, whereupon the Buddha said:

"You should not do so; listen to [the request] from one person. The fifth section distinguishes the appropriate times for preaching; according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* (18), eight [times] are permitted.
On the fourteenth day, the Dharma was preached; on the fifteenth day, the *poṣadha* was held. Regarding the sixth [section], it clarifies the person who preaches the Dharma.
In the *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*, fascicle six, it says: "When the bhikṣus chanted in halves, the Buddha said: 'One should not chant in halves. To chant in halves is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Furthermore, for two people to chant together is also a *duṣkṛta* offense. It is further stated: 'If there is no one capable of chanting within the assembly, one should proceed in order.'"

Item Four: If there are none at all, each person should recite one verse; among them, whoever is capable may be requested to speak. If one is requested but does not speak, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*.
During the *poṣadha*, when laypeople offer robes as alms and wish for a blessing (*svastyayana*), the Buddha said:
"One should provide the blessing. The bhikṣus did not know how to provide the blessing. The Buddha said: "The *karmadāna* (Vina) should be made to provide the blessing."

The seventh period is when the bhikṣus descend to explain the Dharma on the teaching seat; the fourth period is when they ascend to practice dhyāna while explaining the Dharma—this is the speech of the noble ones.
Subsequently practicing dhyāna at night is the silence of the noble ones.
Next, the ritual procedure for reciting the precepts (*śīla*) is explained. This consists of three major sections: first, the mental preparation for the recitation;

second, from the words "At that time" onwards, the formal announcement to the Saṃgha; and third, from the words "By this" onwards, the actual ritual of the recitation. Within this [third section], there are two major parts.
First, the explanation of the introduction (*nidāna*); second, at that time, the bhikṣus wished to chant [the verses], which is explained below as the ritual procedure (*vidhi*).
The text of the introduction has two parts: first, the listing of the eight phrases of the root text; second, the sequential explanation of each *pāṭimokkha*.
Now, intending to explain the text, I shall first establish the distinctions among the types of silent delusive conditions. This distinction will be analyzed through five sections:
first, establishing the general and specific aspects of the questions; second, generating the objects of silence; third, discerning the causes and types of silence;

fourth, analyzing in response to the questions; and fifth, determining whether the concealment is repeated or not. Regarding the first section, as for the general and specific: the introductory questions constitute the general aspect.

The latter eight are specific [cases]. This is because the introduction does not list the names of the offenses but asks generally whether they are pure or not, whereas the remainder all cite specific transgressions and ask about them individually;

thus, one knows they are specific cases. Furthermore, the various questions in the latter section do not interrelate with one another; that is to say, when asking about a *pārājika*, one does not ask about a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* or other categories.

The same applies to the *śeṣa* (residual) offenses and their like; therefore, they also constitute distinct categories. Question: Since the introduction (*nidāna*) lacks both name and category (*nāma-jāti*), how can it constitute a "silence" (*tūṣṇīmbhāva*) offense? Answer:

Although the name and category are not explicitly stated within the introduction, the introduction itself serves as the basis for the two hundred and fifty precepts. Since its meaning is already established as the introduction to the meaning of the precepts, there is indeed the fault of silence.

Therefore, it is said: "I have finished reciting the introduction to the Prātimokṣa Sūtra. Is everyone here pure in this regard? Furthermore, according to the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, even to disparage the introduction constitutes an offense;

if disparaging it is already an offense, how much more so for remaining silent when there is no fault? Moreover, while the introduction poses general questions without listing specific names of offenses, one remains silent only if one remembers, recognizes, and has no doubt;
otherwise, if one does not remember and so forth, there is no such silence. As for the eight subsequent questions, since they do list the names of the offenses...

As for the term "this," it refers generally to both those who remember and those who do not; in all such cases, remaining silent constitutes a transgression of falsehood. Regarding the various offenses involving memory and so forth, silence is committed in two instances.

In other cases where one does not remember and so on, one commits a *duṣkṛta* (light offense) within the specific category; there is no separate aggregate offense, as the transgression exists only in the general sense.

Furthermore, within that general sense, it is restricted to cases of remembering and so forth; in other cases where one does not remember and so on, there is no fault. Moreover, regarding the phrase "in this," it introduces the context of these various precepts. If...

Regarding the remaining eight questions among the *pārājika* and other offenses: the two *aniyata* (undetermined) rules concern offenses committed in private or public places that have been brought forward by others;
these should be examined within the context of the specific facts. Next, as for the "object" (*viṣaya*):

if one commits a single offense and it is questioned three times, is the offense determined based on the individuals involved, or is it determined based on the conditions of the questioning? The ancient interpretation holds that it is obtained from the individuals.

There would be many offenses. It does not follow from that question. Although the one who asks the question is but a single person, it is because the collective sentiment of the assembly has entrusted the inquiry to them. Now, the explanation is not thus;
rather, it concerns the formation of an offense through silence and deception in response to a specific question, not by deceiving the entire Saṃgha.

Therefore, the text says: "For example, as if individual bhikṣus were questioning and answering one another. Since it speaks of "each individual questioning one another," how could one base the determination of the offense upon the Saṃgha? Its...
Regarding the announcement of purity (*śuddhivācanā*): when one speaks before the assembly, declaring oneself to be pure, this is called an "announcement at a time when there is no questioning.

Therefore, it is established according to the person [making the declaration]. Next, concerning the "one who causes [the offense]": if one has committed ten offenses and remains silent within the Saṃgha, does the silence constitute an offense?

Is the establishment of the offense based on what was silently accepted? The traditional interpretation holds that the offense is established based on the questioning; it does not follow from the specific offenses themselves, because the silence is a falsehood toward the Saṃgha.

If one asks [only] when there is something to be asked, then when there is nothing to be asked, there would be no occasion for questioning. Since this is a single [act], how can many instances of silence be produced?

This is not the same as concealment (*paticchādana*). Concealment gives rise to further offenses; thus, according to the duration of concealment, many offenses are incurred. Now, the explanation is that questioning is merely the condition (*paccaya*), while the offense itself is the primary seed (*bīja*).

Logically, the bond (*saṃyojana*) follows the seed; how could it follow the condition? It is just like concealment, which also incurs the bond according to the offense. This silence is precisely what constitutes concealment.
Another name for this is "concealment" (*paticchādana*). Since one does not follow the signs of clarity (*vijjā-lakkhaṇa*), how could silent falsehood be permissible? Question:

If silence is definitively compliant, then those who have attained purity (*visuddhi*) should also incur an offense. Answer: Since purity involves no fault after having undergone questioning, whereas silence is definitively compliant with the commission of an offense, the formal conclusion (*thāpanā*) is like a human body having three limbs:
by performing one prostration, one obtains three merits; how much more so in this case, where the fault of silence results in the formal conclusion of an offense. Next, regarding the question:
Regarding this: when one remains silent after being questioned three times, how many offenses (*āpatti*) are incurred? The traditional interpretation states:

although there are three calls, silence constitutes only a single offense, because they collectively constitute a single formal act (*ekadharma*), just as all three requests (*trayayācanā*) constitute a single formal act.

The present interpretation holds that since there are three questions, and one remains silent in response to each, three offenses are incurred—one for each question—just as in the case of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) where one incurs an offense for violating the admonition at each step.

This also constitutes a single offense of admonition (*tajjaniya-kamma*). Since it arises in accordance with the admonition, does this not follow from the questioning? Next, regarding whether the concealment is grave or not:
although there are general and specific [categories] of purity (*parisuddhi*), one need only disclose them during the *Nidāna* (the introductory section).

When it comes to the specific questions, there is no need to disclose them again, because having already disclosed them, the meaning is the same as being without fault; just as for a person who is pure, there is no fault when questioned.

[This constitutes] an offense. In that case, if one conceals a fault during the introductory inquiry, one may commit the offense of silence; however, during the subsequent eight [sections], one should not further commit the offense of concealment. Answer: Silence is fundamentally a response to a question; yet, to conceal [a fault] at any time constitutes an offense.
This is not the same as making a formal disclosure (*āviṣkaraṇa*); both lead to purification and are without transgression. First, the introduction to the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*).

There must be no further concealment. Should one encounter a subsequent seat [of questioning], there is a fault of silence by principle. Just as in the *pudgala-vinaya* (human dharma), if one confesses first and conceals later, whether the question concerns what was said earlier or what was said later, the fault of silence is equally present.
Whether the questions are asked collectively or individually, one must disclose them all. In response:

In two cases where the conditions (*pratyaya*) differ and the dharmas (*dharma*) are distinct, both constitute the offense of silence for two questions. In cases where the dharmas are equal and the conditions are identical, a collective disclosure suffices; it need not be individual.
Next, the explanation of the eight fundamental points of the text: Whenever one intends to uphold and expound [the Dharma], it is logically necessary to assemble [the community].

Therefore, first, the assembly is clarified as being gathered in one place. Once the monastic community has assembled, the essential tenet must be proclaimed; thus, the second point establishes the manner of such exposition. Following this, the nature of the teaching is revealed.
Since the teaching is intended for sentient beings, the listeners must apply their minds with single-minded concentration; therefore, the third point states, "You all, listen attentively."
Listen attentively to this decree. However, there are those who have committed offenses and are not permitted to hear the precepts.

Therefore, the fourth section encourages those who know they have committed an offense to repent so as to achieve purity; if one’s conduct is pure, such a person is fit to hear the Dharma of the precepts.

Therefore, regarding the fifth point, "one who does not commit an offense," this refers to those taught below who do not offend; their silence indicates purity. Once purity and impurity are known, the response—whether to proceed or not—is indicated.
Thus, regarding the sixth point, "if another asks," this refers to the exhortation below to answer according to reality:

one who has committed an offense should respond by confessing it, while one who has not committed an offense should respond with silence. If one knows of a transgression yet conceals it, it will inevitably result in great harm. Therefore...
The seventh [point], "If such a bhikṣu... and below, concerns those who remain silent when it is appropriate to speak; they share in the fault of impurity, which is a profound obstacle to the Path.

If one can repent their transgression, they will certainly achieve great benefit. Therefore, the eighth [point], "If that bhikṣu... and below, states that because of purification through confession, one attains peace and happiness.

Next, the eight phrases are explained. Although the first two are not in sequential order, the reason for explaining the second first is that it constitutes the essential nature (*dharmatā*) of the teaching being expounded.

Regarding the four sections of the Chinese text: first, the names are raised and explained through their etymological derivations; second, from "self-maintenance" (*sva-dhāraṇa*) onwards, the function of the precepts is praised;
third, from "I shall now" onwards, the method of exposition is stated; fourth, from "therefore" onwards, the conclusion of the exposition and its accomplishment are presented.

In the first section, the terms *śīla* (precept) and *vimukti* (liberation) are explained through their derivative meanings and corresponded individually, as has already been clarified previously in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, chapter eighteen.
It is said: Regarding *prātimokṣa*, by means of this dharma of precepts, one guards the sense faculties and increases wholesome dharmas.
Among all wholesome dharmas, it is the foremost gateway; therefore, it is called *mokṣa*. The *Mātṛkā-sūtra* names it "Most Supreme," as was explained previously.
Regarding the subsequent function: morality is able to protect against the evil karma of body and speech; this is called "self-restraint.

Because it involves restraining oneself and abandoning what is contrary to the essence of the original vow, it is called "upholding" (*dhāraṇa*). When manifested in relation to its characteristics, it is collectively termed "dignified deportment" (*īryāpatha*). This arises from the abandonment of what is improper.
Because one achieves the accomplishment of the rules of conduct (*vidhi*), it is called "self-restraint. One maintains such majestic deportment (*īryāpatha*);

since these rules of deportment are subsumed within the gateway of morality (*śīla*), they are called the "abode" (*sthāna*). Morality can give birth to all practices; thus it is named the "root of practice" (*caryā-mūla*).

Furthermore, among all practices, morality is the most prominent and superior to all other practices; it is termed the "forehead" (*mukha*) that gathers all wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*), thereby accomplishing the aforementioned practices.
Root. Therefore, the *Śāsanāpadeśa* (Teaching of the Last Instructions) says: "If there is no pure precept, all virtuous merits will not arise.
Thus, one should know that the precept is primary. Because it accomplishes samādhi and forms the head of the preceding [practices], the *Śāsanāpadeśa* says:
"By relying on this precept, one attains various dhyānas and concentrations, as well as the wisdom that extinguishes suffering; it can also gather all wholesome dharmas. This is the collection.
Scattered goodness (*vikṣiptakuśala*) and the accomplishment of meditative concentration (*samādhi-siddhi*): these constitute the goodness of collected concentration (*samāhitakuśala*).

Since all forms of goodness do not exceed the categories of the concentrated and the scattered, these two types of goodness exhaustively encompass all practice. Next, regarding the "method" (*vidhi*): although it has not yet been set forth, it will certainly be proclaimed later; therefore, it is said that "it shall be explained.

To indicate this method of explanation, it is said that "it shall be concluded," lest one should transgress by deviating from it later. This is proclaimed for the sake of those who would become bhikṣus.

There are five offenses; therefore, it is said, "One should arouse [the mind]. This is as in the introduction to the precepts (*śikṣāpada*). Next, the five offenses are set forth so that the assembly may hear them together; hence, it is said, "To expound, spread, and reveal.
Having finished explaining the five offenses, they are again summarized and established: "I have finished speaking," and so forth; this is a repeated and detailed analysis.
Furthermore, within each of the five offenses, there are three parts. First, the words "Venerable sirs" constitute the fourth [part].
"Abandoning," etc., refers to what should be undertaken. Next, the presentation of the four precepts is the exposition. Next, "Venerable Sirs," etc., is the repetition.

Alternatively, the character "should" (dāng) in the third phrase may extend through the subsequent clauses. The conclusion is as can be understood. Next, the first phrase of the section on the eon (*kalpa*) is explained.

The details are as explained below. Next, he commands the listeners to straighten their minds and interpret what has been said above; they should contemplate it with a virtuous mind and listen to the Dharma with single-minded focus.

This explains the preceding instruction to "listen attentively. Next, he exhorts those who repent: knowing that one has transgressions, one must perform the methods of confession (*pratideśanā*); for if one does not repent of one's faults, [there can be no purification].

It is not appropriate to hear the precepts [if one has not purified oneself]. Therefore it is said: "The matter of the offense has not yet been confessed. Next, regarding those who manifest purity, there are two types:

first, those who have not committed an offense and are persons of dedicated diligence; second, those who have committed an offense but have already repented and are persons who have confessed their transgression.

These two types of pure persons are capable of hearing the precepts. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, chapter eighteen, states: "Because they remain silent, you should know that I and the other Venerable Ones are pure."
"Purity is like the noble silence. I and the other venerable ones are likewise. Next, regarding answering according to reality:

since people differ in being pure or impure, their responses differ accordingly—some remain silent while others speak. Thus, those who have committed an offense answer by confessing it, while those who have not committed an offense answer with silence.
This is like answering each question individually; this is called "answering according to reality. Next, to reveal the concealment of faults: if...

If one has actually committed an offense yet answers with silence, one incurs the fault of lying. Since it is revealed that falsehood is prohibited by the Dharma, one must respond according to reality;

this serves as a remote support for explaining the obstacles, rather than being direct. Next, to manifest the benefits of repentance: through repentance, transgressions are eliminated and the precepts (śīla) attain purity.
This gives rise to meditative concentration (samādhi) and wisdom (prajñā), ultimately leading to the benefits of the Path. Therefore, it is said: "Repentance brings peace."
[This is] joyful. However, even through repentance, one has not yet attained the state of a noble one (ārya). This is the explanation of Yuan Zizhong.

Next, the ritual procedure for the recitation of the precepts (*śīla*) is clarified. Within this section, there are two parts. First, the method for reciting the precepts when the assembly practices together in harmony.

Second, at that time in Kauśāmbī, following the section on the breaking [of the community] and the improper timing of the *poṣadha*, one should calculate that there ought to be a reduction in the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadhasthāpana*).
Regarding the *poṣadha* ritual, there are three major categories;

however, because the single method of "reduction" is subsumed within the lower category of "prohibitory methods," this text contains only two types of recitations. When compared with the preceding text, these are divided into fifteen sections.

First, the sound of proclaiming the precepts (*śīla*). Second, from "at that time, the bhikṣus... onwards, the determination of the time for the proclamation. Third, from "at that time, the group of six bhikṣus...
onwards, the regulation regarding gathering together in one place. Fourth, from "at that time, the bhikṣus... onwards, the description of the location for the proclamation.
Fifth, from "at that time, the elder bhikṣu... onwards, the clarification of the duties to be performed. Sixth, from "at that time, the lay followers asked... onwards.

The seventh section, "The Procedure for Casting Voting Sticks," explains the origin of the practice. The eighth section, "The Time of the Uposatha," clarifies the essential nature of the Dharma discourse.
The ninth section, "The Time of the Uposatha," opens up the procedure for conveying one's consent and purity.

Tenth: On the day of the *poṣadha*, hearing the abbreviated method for reciting the precepts from below. Eleventh: At that time, the World-Honored One... [and so forth], removing doubts and subduing [the unruly].
Twelfth: At that time, there was a residence... [and so forth], confessing faults to manifest purity. Thirteenth: Regarding visiting monks on the fourteenth day...
[and so forth], concerning whether the new and old [monks] should [perform the rite] together. Fourteenth: The group of six monks... [and so forth], reciting [the precepts] in discord.
Regarding the Vinaya rules: the fifteenth section concerns the method for distinguishing the group of six bhikṣuṇīs from the rest of the assembly.
In the initial text concerning "singing with melodic intonation," the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* records that the Buddha said: "It should be recited directly."

Next, the textual explanation of the timing [of the *poṣadha*] is threefold: first, in relation to days; second, in relation to months; and third, in relation to specific times. The text states: "It is permitted to proclaim the *poṣadha* on the twentieth day.

This clearly demonstrates the distinction between the two dharmas of *poṣadha* and the recitation of the precepts (*śīla*). Regarding *poṣadha*, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (T. 1425) states: "The word 'poṣadha' means 'pure dwelling' (*viśuddhivāsa'), and its literal meaning is 'nurturing' (*puṣṭi*).
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (T. 1435), fascicle 58, asks: "For what reason? Because the Buddha permitted the performance of the *poṣadha*. It answers: "To cause all *bhikṣus*..."
"Kauṭilya, because one dwells securely in wholesome dharmas and abandons unwholesome ones, attaining purity from unwholesome dharmas, this is called *poṣadha*.
The *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*, fascicle six, asks: 'What is *poṣadha*? Every half-month, each bhikṣu reflects upon himself:
"From the previous half-month until the present half-month, have I not transgressed any precepts during the interval? If he recalls a transgression..."
One confesses and repents before a fellow monk who is in agreement. If such a fellow monk cannot be found, one should form the thought:

"If I find a fellow monk, I shall repent of this offense. Furthermore, it is said that because one abandons all evil and unwholesome dharmas, abandons the afflictions and craving for existence, realizes the pure dharmas, and accomplishes the ultimate Brahma-conduct, it is called *poṣadha*.

Next, the second section on the complete assembly of the texts has two parts. First, it clarifies that the group of six monks shared the same mind but differed in form. Second, from "At that time" onwards, it clarifies that Mahākāśyapa differed both in form and mind;
he was not permitted to travel by means of supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), lest those who lacked such powers be confused with him, and thus he was unwilling to go to the discourse.
Therefore, he was ordered to go on foot.
Next, regarding the explanation of the *sīma* hall (*sīma-sālā*): this indicates the location where the recitation of the precepts takes place, but it is not itself a formal boundary (*sīmā*).

Next, there are two types of formal motions (*jñapti*) to be performed; the first is that which should be performed by a junior monk (*navaka*), as it is a manual task that a senior monk (*sthavira*) should not perform.
Next, regarding the six groups of monks (*ṣaḍvargika*), those who are junior should perform what is appropriate for a senior (*sthavira*). They should engage in conversation and preach the Dharma;
those who are junior should not do so. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, chapter nineteen, states: "In a certain residence, Baddhananda was the senior. He announced: 'The Sangha is now ten [in number].'"
On the fifth day, during the *poṣadha* ceremony for the recitation of the precepts, those bhikṣus who did not attend were asked:
"What is the purpose of the Saṃgha’s current proceedings? What business do the bhikṣus have? The bhikṣus replied:

"The bhikṣu so-and-so should be subjected to the formal act (*karman*) of censure (*tarjanīya*), and so-and-so should be subjected to the formal act of separate residence (*parivāsa*). Upāli (Vāḍananda) said: "I do not know."
Regarding the *karmavācanā* (formal ecclesiastical act): the monks asked, "If one does not know the *karmavācanā*, why does one ask the Saṃgha and the monks what action is to be performed?
They reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said, "The Elder (*sthavira*) should recite the *Prātimokṣa*, and the holder of the Vinaya (*vinayadhara*) should perform the *karmavācanā*."
Regarding the origin story (*nidāna*) of the *śalākā* (voting tally): this text should have appeared earlier, while the preceding text should have been explained later.

Why is this so? If there were no origin story, how [could the following be understood]? Since the preceding text already states, "one who possesses the *śalākā*," it is clear that it must be explained first.

Next, the demarcation of boundaries (*sīmā-bandha*) is explained. Within this section, there are two parts. First, the narrative introduction concerning the difficulty of performing the ritual due to the spontaneous gathering [of the assembly].

Second, from the words "The Buddha said" onwards, the actual demarcation of the boundary is explained. This part contains three sections: first, the method for demarcating the large and small boundaries to bring people together under the same Dharma;

second, from the passage beginning "At that time, there were those who felt weary and renounced," the demarcation of the *acīvarāpatti* (non-loss of robe) boundary to ensure robes remain attached to the person; third...

Third: At that time, regarding the two dwelling places, there follows the method for further opening and binding the large and small boundaries (*sīmā*). However, according to the original text, there are three types of boundaries.

The boundary for taking food is explained in the section on the "Method for Medicines" below. The initial text is further divided into three parts: first, the method for binding the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*);
second, from the passage beginning "At that time, the bhikṣus," the method for opening and binding the *śīmaṇḍala* (precept enclosure); third, at that time, the bhikṣus...
The following clarifies the method for dissolving the boundary (*sīmā-bandha*). Regarding the previous procedure for establishing the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*), there are five sections in the text:

first, the regulation for assembling those free from desire; second, the selection of an experienced resident monk to designate the boundaries; third, the instruction for the designated person to proclaim the boundaries starting from the east; fourth, the proclamation itself; and fifth, the formal dissolution of the boundary.

In the fourth section, those of lower rank from among the assembly are appointed to preside over the rite. In the fifth, the actual method for performing the formal boundary-binding (*sīmā-bandhana*) is clearly explained.

First, the meaning of boundary-binding is analyzed through six gates: first, the intent behind the permissions and prohibitions regarding boundary-binding; second, the enumeration of types and the explanation of their names.
Third, its essential nature and characteristics are distinguished. Fourth, whether the dharma arises or not. Fifth, whether it is abandoned or lost.

Sixth, the mutual relationship between the location and the dharma. Regarding the intent of the first section: the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) and the recitation of the *Poṣadha* are precisely the protocols for the dharma of dwelling.

Since one intends to perform them, one must obtain a basis (*āśraya*). Now, this basis extends throughout the entire sphere of conversion; when the entire sphere assembles together, it reaches its limit.

This is a matter of great toil. The Great Sage, out of compassion for those who would otherwise neglect their cultivation, opened the way for them to delimit boundaries within specific locations so that they might all follow the same rules;

thus, the ritual acts (dharmakarma) are accomplished. Once this opening has been made, it becomes the basis upon which the assembly relies; whenever a ritual act is performed, it cannot be successfully carried out without this.

This was the intent behind first permitting [the practice] and subsequently establishing the regulations. Thus, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, fascicle eight, states: "Regarding land that has not undergone formal ritual authorization (*karmavācanā*)."

Regarding the "Non-Appropriation of Monastic Affairs," the following is an exposition of the commentators. This section is provisionally divided into two parts: the naturally established method (*svabhāva-kriyā*) and the formally designated method.
First, the naturally established method is explained. There are four types of natural [boundaries]: first, a village without obstacles; second, a village with obstacles;

third, a forest hermitage (*araṇya*) without obstacles; and fourth, a forest hermitage with obstacles. These are determined according to the persons involved and thus possess spatial divisions; they are not created for the sake of material objects, and are therefore termed "natural."

It is said: "Spontaneous. Next, regarding the method of establishing [the boundary]: when the application of the ritual is limited and defined, with each demarcation being distinct, it is called a "knot" (*grantha*).

Since there are such demarcations, the differentiation between this side and that side is termed a "boundary" (*sīmā*). According to the *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā*, the Sanskrit term is *catur-ama* (translated here as "separate residence").

This means that because the location of this dwelling and the location of other dwellings have distinct demarcations, it is called a "separate residence. There are various types of separate residences.

Regarding their dimensions: the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), categorized by its status, is generally said to have four types. First, when the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) and the distribution of offerings (*lābha*) are separate, it is called "identity of persons and dharmas" (two identities).

Second, when the recitation of the precepts and the distribution of offerings are combined, it is called "unity" (one identity). Third, when the dharma and the food are shared within the same boundary. Fourth, [the identity of both dharma and food].

Three cases involve a common recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) and separate offerings (*lābha*); these are termed "combined" (*saṃgha*). Two cases involve a single legal procedure (*karmavācanā*) within a common boundary (*sīmā*).

Four cases involve separate recitations of the precepts and common offerings; these are termed "combined. Two cases involve a single meal within a common boundary. This one case has no distinct boundary substance; it merely performs the *karmavācanā* for the purpose of distributing food.

Therefore, it is explained according to its status. Next, the minor boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*) also has four types: first, the ordination platform (*sīmāmaṇḍala*), where markers are erected and the boundaries are proclaimed. Second...
Third is the difficulty of establishing a small boundary (*sīmā*) for receiving the precepts; fourth is the difficulty of establishing a small boundary for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*);

and fifth is the difficulty of establishing a small boundary for the invitation ceremony (*pravāraṇā*). Now, regarding the definition of "small" (*kṣudra*): it is called small because the area of the boundary is narrow and restricted, while it is called large (*mahat*) because it is wide and distant. Next, the essential nature (*svabhāva*) shall be distinguished.

First, the natural boundaries are clarified. Within these natural boundaries, the village is first established; therefore, in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations), chapter twenty-two, it says:

"When various bhikṣus are in a village that has no monastery (*ārāma*) and have begun to construct a monastery but have not yet performed the formal boundary-determination (*sīmā-bandha*), at that time, how large should the boundary be?
The Buddha said: "The boundary of the village is the boundary of the monastery. In the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, chapter eight, Upāli [asks the same].

Question: If there is a location—such as a city, town, or village—where the boundaries cannot be determined, and one wishes to perform a *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act), how far should it extend to be considered a properly performed *karmavācanā*, such that the separate groups of monks may see one another and yet the *karmavācanā* is successfully accomplished without the fault of a "separate assembly"?
The Buddha answered: Five *hasta* (cubits) is the measure of a *dhanus* (bow); seven *dhanus* is the space for planting one *āmra* (mango) tree. [Within this distance, the *karmavācanā* is valid.]
Regarding trees: the boundary is defined by the mutual visibility of seven *āmra* trees. For one who performs a formal act (*karmavācanā*) within this distance, it is called a "well-performed act.
Although those in the assembly may not see one another, there is no offense of a separate assembly (*nānāsaṃgha*). This is termed the "boundary of the seven *āmra* trees."
However, there are only seven trees, which together comprise six intervals. Each interval is seven *gō* (bows), totaling forty-two.
