Because the ancient foot-measure was small, one *gō* was taken as nine feet and one *bō* (pace) as six feet; thus, one *gō* equaled one and a half *bō*.
Calculating the total of forty-two *gō*, this amounts to sixty-three *bō*. Because the current foot-measure is large, one [ancient] foot now corresponds to one and two-tenths [modern] feet.

Thus, seven chi and five cun constitute one bow (*dhanus*); five chi constitute one pace (*pada*). One bow corresponds to one and a half paces. Calculating by paces, this amounts to sixty-three paces and [the equivalent] in feet.

Although there are differences between ancient and modern measurements, the calculation of the paces remains the same. This is the measurement of the boundary; it is the same for each of the four sides.

Furthermore, regarding this "assemblage" (*saṃghāta*), according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it refers to a village that can be clearly distinguished—that is, a village where there are no obstacles [to its boundaries].

Regarding the *dharmakṣetra* (boundary) for assembly: according to the *Mahāsāṃghika*, it is based on that which cannot be distinguished, and thus there is an objection [to this]. However, one should simply adopt the sixty-three paces for assembly; the limits for the assembly of *bhikṣuṇīs* should also be clarified in accordance with this.
Regarding the *aranyaka* (forest-dweller) boundary where there is no obstruction, the *Pañcavargīya-vinaya* (T. 1421), fascicle 18, states:
various *aranyaka* bhikṣus did not know how far the extent of their own boundary reached, and they reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said: "The natural boundary (*prakṛti-sīmā*)."

[The distance] from the body [to the boundary] is two *krośas*. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, when there are no villages and monks are in a wilderness area, and they have first constructed a monastery but have not yet performed the formal act of delimiting the boundary (*sīmā-bandha*), at that time, how large should the boundary be? The Buddha said: "It shall be one *krośa* square.
Within this area, the monks should not perform separate *poṣadha* ceremonies or monastic legal acts (*saṃghakarma*). However, the size of a *krośa* is not fixed.
The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (Ji-lü), fascicle nine, states: "Five cubits make one bow; two thousand bows are called one *krośa*.
Calculating one *krośa*, it consists of three thousand paces. Three hundred paces constitute one *li*, which is ten *li*. The *Ratnakaraṇḍa-sūtra* (Za-bao-zang) says:

"Five *li* [make one *krośa*]. These two teachings are not fixed; their aggregations are also too broad. Now, following the *Abhidharmakośa* and other texts, we shall establish a standard that accords with reason. Therefore, five...

One *krośa* consists of one hundred *dhanus*. Each *dhanu* is four *hasta* long; thus, one hundred *dhanus* amounts to three thousand *chi*. Five *chi* constitute one pace (*bu*), which equals six hundred paces.
Three hundred paces constitute one *li*, which equals two *li* and five-tenths. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, one takes the *krośa* in a single direction.

According to the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, one takes the *krośa* from all four directions. Calculating the number of *li* according to these two teachings: [the former results in 2.5 *li*, while the latter results in 4 *li*].
One type [of boundary] is said to be two *krośas*, which is limited to four *li*. Next, there is a difficult point:
according to the *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra* (Jian lun), fascicle 17, the smallest *araṇya* boundary is seven *dhanus* in circumference; one *dhanus* is twenty-eight *zhou*.
If [the residents] do not consent, one may perform ritual acts outside of twenty-eight *zhou*. Calculated, this amounts to one hundred and ninety... [units].
Sixteen *zhǔ*. Since one modern *chǐ* equals one and a half *zhǔ*, the total is two hundred and ninety-four *chǐ*.
Calculating at five *chǐ* per *bù*, this amounts to fifty-eight *bù* and four *chǐ*. This is the same as the measurement for the *āraṇya* robe according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.

Since it has already been stated that they do not agree, it is clear that this is a difficult point. Nevertheless, for one who wishes to assemble the Saṃgha within an empty settlement, it must necessarily rely on the aforementioned boundaries;
"assembling within" refers precisely to this. Regarding the boundaries for the distance of assembling the Saṃgha, this means that while the markers are narrow, the boundary itself is broad.

Alternatively, if the boundary markers are wide but the area to be enclosed is narrow, one should likewise rely on the previously established markers when intending to perform the formal act of demarcation; however, at that point it is not yet a formal boundary.

Regarding the limits of the Great Boundary (*mahāsīmā*) for the subsequent ritual procedure, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* (Wufen lü), fascicle 18, states: "When establishing a boundary according to its distance, the bhikṣus established a boundless boundary.
The Buddha said: 'It is not accomplished, but there is an offense of wrongdoing (*duṣkṛta*). The bhikṣus then established a boundary of twelve *yojanas*, or...
Ten *yojanas*. When going to attend the *poṣadha* ceremony, one may travel for four or five days;

even if one encounters a wild fire, a torrential flood, or bandits who plunder and rob, there may still be the difficulty regarding the holy life (*brahmacarya*), the difficulty regarding the robes and bowl, and the difficulty regarding life itself. The Buddha said:

"If one establishes a boundary of twelve *yojanas* or ten *yojanas*, the establishment of the boundary is not valid and constitutes an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*). Now, I permit a maximum distance of three *yojanas*."

The *Daśottara-sūtra* and the *Dvayāvadāna* also state that it is at most three *yojanas* wide. The seventh fascicle of the *Mātṛkā-vinaya* simply states: "It is heard from afar; one may travel there and return in a single day.
Regarding the establishment of the *mahā-sīmā*, this is called the method of complete correspondence (*sarva-saṃyukta-dharma*). There is no fixed textual authority for this; it merely says:

"The *poṣadha* is recited on the fifteenth day. One should arrive beforehand on the fourteenth day. If the *poṣadha* is recited on the fourteenth day, one should arrive beforehand on the thirteenth day."

Having already spent the night, they finally arrived; this is also similar to other texts. Regarding the boundaries of the *bhikṣuṇī* saṃgha, according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* (Sifen lü shanfan buque xingshi chao), fascicle 4:

"The largest boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) established by *bhikṣuṇīs* is one *krośa*. As for the next, the smaller boundary (*kṣudra-sīmā*), there is the single type known as the *śīlāmaṇḍala* (precept platform).

It is established with marked signs and involves permanent ritual procedures; see the *Jianlun* (Vinayavibhāṣā), fascicle 17. The smallest [boundary] can accommodate twenty-one persons; this is determined by the underlying principle."

One must not extend it further than that, for to do so would again result in obstruction and difficulty. Within a distance of four or five *man* from the center, one may further open up a space of one *vyāma*.

The remaining three small boundaries (*kṣudrasīmā*) are not permanent; they are merely for temporary refuge when the Saṃgha assembles. Regarding the number of people seated, there is no distinct division of space.
As for the nature and form of the boundary, according to the *Jianlun* (Treatise on Seeing), there are five types: namely, square, circular, drum-shaped, semi-... [the text here is incomplete].
The lunar shape is triangular. If the boundary markers have been tied together, even if the markers are later lost, the boundary itself is not lost.
Even if a person digs the earth down to the water’s edge, the boundary is not lost. Its natural demarcation must be taken as a complete circle.

Regarding this, to clarify the distinctions between the characteristics of the natural method of ritual action (*kriyā*), there are four differences in the characteristics of these two types of boundaries. First, the [natural]...
First, there is a difference in whether the *dharmas* (elements) constitute the boundary or not. Second, there is a difference in quantity:

the formal boundary (*kṛta-sīmā*) varies according to the specific matter at hand and is therefore often large, whereas the natural boundary (*prakṛti-sīmā*) is otherwise and thus singular. Third, there is a difference in breadth: that is, the natural boundary was formerly broad but is now narrow.

Originally, it should have been unified; therefore, it is broad. Because the assembly was difficult to gather, the boundary for the formal act (*karmavastu*) was opened while the conclusion remained restricted.

Had it followed the original assembly, I fear the conclusion would not have been achieved; thus, the demarcation of the "empty village" (*śūnyagrāma*) was established. Consequently, the current narrow procedure is contrasted with the original; because the opening and the conclusion differ, it is narrow.
Nevertheless, compared to the present assembly, they possess relative breadth and narrowness, and the four [aspects] are unequal in strength. If one looks back to the initial assembly, it is also...
There is no distinction between strength and weakness. For those gathered here now, [the procedure] is naturally weak; because it is weak, the ritual of the Dharma is extremely narrow.

One may only perform the *sīmā-bandha* (boundary-binding), but one cannot perform other [rites], nor is there the *chanda* (consent) for the Dharma. Because the performance of the rite is strong, the application of the Dharma is extremely broad, extending down to the *sīmā-vimokṣa* (dissolution of the boundary) and including the general *chanda*, etc.
Regarding the presence or absence of subsequent rites: [this refers to] the question concerning this performance of the rite within the place where the boundary is bound.
Does it arise from an existent dharma? Or does it arise from a non-existent dharma? Answer: In this context, no distinct dharma arises.

This is because the method of the Sūtra differs from that of natural occurrence; for example, as with the category of sentient beings, there is a separate performance of karma that gives rise to non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), and therefore there is acquisition (*prāpti*).

Having obtained this method for establishing the boundary (*sīmā-bandha*), it does not belong to any individual person. Since the location of the boundary is insentient matter, to what could it possibly be attached?

It is simply that which has undergone the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*) and where the place was formally designated. Therefore, the subsequent text states: "The boundary being present" refers to that which is within the ritual procedure;

those who establish such restrictions—such as the cases of receiving and keeping robes and bowls, or the separation from the community—are all instances where the formal rite has already been performed.
It is said that there is no offense. Since these are non-sentient things, no dharma can arise from them. If that is so, how do we interpret the seventeenth fascicle of the *Śāstra* which states:
"Once a boundary has been established, if a pit is formed by water washing away the earth, and there is a place where water flows, one should recognize that location and erect a pillar there"?

Question: Is it permissible to perform ritual acts (*dharmakarma*) within the area above? Answer: Because one knows that the location is entirely included within the boundary markers, regardless of whether it is high or low, shallow or deep, it all constitutes a single boundary (*sīmā*).
Next, regarding "abandonment and loss": if the Saṃgha intentionally abandons its residence forever.
Regarding the realm that serves as the basis for the boundary: once one has left that realm, it is lost. Thus, in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, chapter forty-seven, it says:

"There were some bhikṣus who abandoned their monastery and departed, thinking: 'I shall never return to this place. This is called abandoning the boundary; it is not what the Buddha called abandoning [the precepts]."
Furthermore, there were fifty-six [cases]. While Śāriputra was traveling, he came upon an empty monastery along the way.
On the day of the *poṣadha*, he did not know which part was within the boundary (*sīmā*) and which part was outside the boundary. He reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:

"If there is an abandoned empty monastery, it is called entirely outside the boundary. Within it, one may perform the *poṣadha* according to one's wish. If that is so, how [should it be done]? Below...

Regarding the phrase "in a monastery that has been dismantled": it is suspected that there may be a pure site (*śuddhasthāna*). The Buddha said: "Having dismantled it, one should re-establish and then dismantle it again.

This passage has been incorrectly applied by all the ancient masters. Regarding the subsequent phrase "it is suspected that there may be a pure place": if there is none, one says "there is none"; if there is one, one says "there is."
Regarding the location, it is not known how [it should be]. The Buddha said: "Re-bind. This refers to the text of this own school (*sva-nikāya*);

yet, even while using it erroneously, one speaks of the texts of other schools (*para-nikāya*) as if they could be fully detailed. If one discusses the two assemblies (*dvaya-saṃgha*), re-binding does not constitute a loss; this is stated in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (Jianlun), fascicle 17.

If a bhikṣu has already established a boundary (*sīmā-bandha*), he may establish a separate boundary for bhikṣuṇīs within that which is not a boundary for bhikṣus. Regarding the bhikṣu and the bhikṣuṇī...
The same applies to the boundaries of the *dharmadhātu*. If a bhikṣu who is not in accordance with the Dharma resolves the boundary with an evil mind, the resolution is likewise not established;

this is analogous to the resolution of purity (*śuddhi*). Next, regarding the correspondence between the three types of formal acts—*jñapti*, *jñaptidvitīya*, and *jñapticaturtha*—and their application to specific locations:

first, regarding the act performed by nature (*svabhāva-karman*), the two stages of *jñapti* and *jñaptidvitīya* apply universally. Although *jñaptidvitīya* applies to both types of locations, the act performed by nature is extremely restricted, applying only to the establishment of the Great [Boundary].
The *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* for the small boundary (*kṣudra-sīmā*) exists because it is based upon this fundamental [procedure]. It is performed within the natural state (*prakṛti*).

Next, regarding the formal procedures (*karman*) within both the large and small boundaries, the three types of formal acts (*trividha-karman*)—the *jñapti*, the *jñapti-dvitīya*, and the *jñapti-caturtha*—possess both general and specific applications. For instance, in cases such as receiving [the precepts] or performing confession (*pratideśanā*), the *ekajñapti* (single announcement) applies to both locations.

[Specific applications include]: the relinquishing and receiving of the *kaṭhina* robe; the examination of qualifications (*guṇa-parīkṣā*); the settling of disputes (*adhikaraṇa-samatha*); the *mūla-niḥsargika-pāyattika*; the *tṛṇa-praticchādana* (covering with grass); the formal assembly (*saṃgīti*); and the distribution of alms bowls (*pātra-caryā*) to prevent mutual disturbance.

The *jñapti* (motion) pertains exclusively to the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*). Within the two stages of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations), the returning of robes, the six-year rule for separation from robes, and the carrying of staffs and nets apply to both boundaries.

The procedures for assigning duties, the formal establishment of purity, the "learned family" (*śaikṣa-kula*), the insane, the gathering of robes, the overturning of the bowl, using old [robes] to maintain new ones, not bowing, the distribution of robes, the four months, the eight virtues, and so forth, pertain exclusively to the great boundary.
Within the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, the conferral of ordination and the removal of offenses apply to both.

Regarding the two realms (*dvisīmā*), there is mindfulness and freedom from delusion. Matters concerning offenses (*āpatti-sthāna*) and the seven types of formal acts (*saptakarman*) are restricted solely to the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*).
*The Record of the Opening of the Sectarian Principles of the Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, Fascicle Seven, Part One;
*The Record of the Opening of the Sectarian Principles of the Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, Fascicle Seven, Part Two.

Next, the text is explained below. Regarding the term *gandi*: the Sanskrit pronunciation is incorrect; it should properly be *bherī*. *Gandi* and *bherī* are translated here as "striking the *gandi*.
The wood used for striking and the method of striking are as usual. According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, chapter eighteen, one should announce that "the time has arrived."
If the *ghanṭā* is struck, or a drum is beaten, or a conch shell is blown, it was not known who should strike them. The Buddha said, "A *śrāmaṇera* or a park-keeper should strike them.
They then struck them many times. The Buddha said, "One should strike three times. If there are no *śrāmaṇeras*, a *bhikṣu* may also strike them. [Question:

Why was the boundary established and the rule made that everyone must assemble, and that giving one's consent (*chanda*) is not permitted? [Answer: There are three reasons for the dissolution [of the boundary].

The meaning is as follows: First, because it is naturally without boundaries and is weak, it does not encompass other dharmas; yet, because it relies on the strength of the boundary (*sīmā*), it is able to encompass the two types of *saṃgha-sīmā*.
This is the foundation of communal harmony (*saṃgha-sabhāgatā*) and, by principle, ought to be strictly regulated. Therefore, the dharma of granting consent (*chanda*) is not permitted for it.

As for the remaining *karmans*, they are not the foundation of communal harmony and do not require urgent regulation; thus, granting consent is permitted for them. Third, this ensures that the characteristics of the boundaries are recognized, so as not to obstruct monastic affairs. The rest...
The Dharma is the opposite of this; therefore, it permits the granting of consent (*chanda*). Next, one must appoint a person to proclaim the boundaries (*sīmā*).

One who has resided there for a long time must be selected for this task, as they will know the precise extent of the boundary divisions. Even if the person is not a former resident, they may still qualify provided they possess such knowledge.

Regarding the boundaries to be proclaimed, twelve types are fully enumerated in the text. For example, when pointing to a mountain, one must specify "the eastern side of such-and-such a mountain"; if one does not point specifically, [the proclamation is invalid].

To speak directly, the principle of a "mountain" is not established. As it is with mountains, so it is with other similar phenomena. In the *Jian lun* (Treatise on Seeing), there are seventeen categories, and among them, eight are characterized by boundaries (*dhātu-lakṣaṇa*).
These are: mountains, forests, rocks, trees, paths, enclosures, rivers, and waters. Regarding the characteristic of a mountain: it may be as large as Mount Sumeru.
Regarding the boundary markers of stones: the large ones are as big as an elephant, and the small ones weigh thirty *cheng*.

If one cannot find natural stones, it is permissible to install separate ones. Regarding the boundary markers of forests: if they are grass thickets or bamboo groves, they cannot serve as boundary markers because their substance is empty and insubstantial.
As for large forests, they may extend up to a hundred *yojana*; as for small ones, they must consist of at least four trees joined together. Furthermore—
Regarding what is called a "grove": as for the characteristics of trees, one must not take a withered tree as the defining characteristic.

They should be as large as a Jambu tree, or at the smallest, eight inches high and as thick as a needle. If there are no naturally growing trees, it is also permissible to plant them. Regarding a "road":

except for paths leading to fields, water sources, and the like, a path that reaches its end is not permitted; however, a major road used by carts or pedestrians—even if it is short, extending only through three or four villages—is permitted.
Regarding ant-mounds: the large ones are like mountains, while the small ones are eight inches high. Regarding rivers:

if one favors the transformation of the king’s governance and it rains once every five days, this rain cannot serve as a boundary marker for the river water. If there has been no rain for four months and the flow continues without interruption, with the water reaching a depth of two feet, it may serve as a boundary marker.
Regarding water features: natural pond water may serve as a boundary marker, provided it is continuous. If it is... [text ends]
Water enters the field; or one may use a vessel filled with water as a marker, provided it does not create a fixed boundary mark.

Once the markers are known, if there is no *sīmā-kṣetra* (precept-field), simply install a single-layered marker and perform the formal proclamation (*karmavācanā*) as usual. If there is a *sīmā-kṣetra*, one must erect three layers of markers.

First, having proclaimed the boundaries of the *sīmā-kṣetra* and completed the binding, next bind the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*). First, proclaim the outer boundary of the great boundary once around, saying: "This..."
This is the outer boundary marker. Next, chant the inner boundary marker once around, saying: "This is the inner boundary marker of the great boundary.
Next, state them together: "This is the inner marker; that is the outer marker. This completes one circuit of the inner and outer markers of the great boundary.

This was repeated up to three times. If the boundary markers do not appear clearly or if they are not proclaimed, the formal act of establishing the boundary (*sīmā-bandha*) is not accomplished as a whole.

Thus, in the *Pañcavargika* and the *Aṣṭādaśa-vargika*, the Buddha said: "If the boundary markers are not proclaimed, the establishment of the boundary is not accomplished; one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The bhikṣus used sentient beings, fire, or smoke as boundary markers, such that two boundaries were joined together or their markers overlapped. The Buddha said:

In all such cases, the boundary is not established, and one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense. Regarding this and the various schools' methods for proclaiming the boundaries (*sīmā-uddeśa*), none of them mention "three" [recitations].

According to the underlying principle, a single proclamation suffices for its accomplishment; however, because the ritual practice has already become established, three proclamations are maintained together.

Furthermore, within the assembly, the person appointed to administer the rite (*dharmakara*) must not be the same as the person who proclaims the boundaries, nor may the person proclaiming the boundaries jointly perform the administration of the rite. For these reasons...
Because of the meaning, the texts are cited separately in five parts and sixteen sections. First, one bhikṣu should proclaim the boundary markers of the four directions;

furthermore, another bhikṣu should proclaim the exclusion of the interior land. Next, one bhikṣu should address the venerable Saṃgha, saying, "May the Saṃgha listen," and so forth. Finally, the formal ritual procedure is performed in fifteen steps.
Second, regarding the recitation of the characteristics of the names of those involved in the *karmavācanā*: since there are no [specific] names here, one must not arbitrarily rely on other sections.

As for the phrase "residing in the same dwelling place" (*ekāvāsa*), this refers to the commonality of location in contrast to two distinct dwelling places. Regarding the statement "originally separate, now the same":

because those [cases] cannot be called "residing in the same dwelling place," this is said to be "residing in the same dwelling place" because they were originally the same and are now the same; thus it is called "reciting together."
Regarding the precepts (*śīla*): this refers to the commonality of these dharmas.

Next, the boundary for the precepts (*śīlā-maṇḍala*) is explained. First, its meaning is interpreted through a fourfold analysis: first, clarifying the intent of the opening; second, explaining the name of the separate field;
third, determining the location for its placement; and fourth, distinguishing the sequence of the formal ritual (*bandhana*). As for the "intent of the opening":
The monastic residence within the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) is vast and distant, and as various separate matters frequently arise, it is somewhat difficult for all to assemble.

Therefore, this is permitted: within the great boundary, a separate *sīma-kaṇḍa* (precept field) is established. Thus, when performing acts such as receiving the precepts, one does not trouble the great assembly.
This is just as when matters involving four or more persons arise in the texts; the permission to establish them separately is precisely for the benefit of the bhikṣus. Next, the names are explained:
This is why it is called the *sīmā* (precept-field). Originally intended for individuals, it serves to extinguish evil and generate goodness, and to exclude defilement while selecting purity;

thus it is termed a "field. It is like a secular field, receiving its name from a metaphorical analogy. Question: Other boundaries (*sīmā*) also possess this same significance; why are they not given the name "field"? Answer:

The Great Boundary (*mahāsīmā*) is fundamentally for the residence of the Saṃgha as a whole; it does not specialize exclusively in extinguishing evil and generating goodness. Therefore, it is not designated as a "field."

As for the names: although other minor boundaries (*kṣudrakasīmā*) also eliminate evil and generate good, they are difficult to distinguish individually, are not established as long-term procedures, and lack boundary markers;
thus, they are not given the name "site" (*kaṭhina*). Next, regarding the establishment of the location: concerning the *śīlakaṭhina* (precept site), it must be within the boundary.

This is because the assembly of the boundary is difficult to gather, so the establishment of the *śīlakaṭhina* is permitted; therefore, one knows it must be inside. Furthermore, the *karman* text states:
Regarding this dwelling place, when a bhikṣu announces the boundary markers of the small boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*) of the four directions, what is the case for one who is outside?

It is said that there is no formal demarcation (*saṃskāra*) for a *sīmāmaṇḍala* (precept platform) in such a location; although it is not established as a residence, it is nonetheless considered within the interior of another dwelling place.

Furthermore, what is the case for one who is outside? Since the lower boundary (*sīmā*) and the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) mutually involve being seen or heard, the Buddha prescribed that they must be summoned. (From the *Mātṛkā-sūtra*, fascicle [number]).

One school says: "Outside [the monastery], one does not further establish a great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), but establishes only a small boundary (*kṣudra-sīmā*); yet even so, one cannot receive full ordination (*upasampadā*).

Regarding the sequence of priority, various transmitters of the Dharma say: "There is no explicit scriptural authority for this; it should be great first and small later, because the ordination platform (*sīmāmaṇḍala*) is established within the great boundary.
Now, my interpretation is not thus. Since the ordination platform is established within the great boundary, according to principle, the...

The site must first be demarcated. Thus, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, chapter sixteen, states: "One should first perform a formal motion with a second proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) to relinquish the boundary of the monastery (*saṃghārāma-sīmā*).

Having dissolved it, one then demarcates the boundary for the ritual enclosure (*sīmābandha*). Once the ritual enclosure has been demarcated, one again demarcates the boundary of the monastery. The *Mātṛkā-vinaya*, fascicle two, says:

Regarding the dissolution of boundaries, one first dissolves the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) and subsequently dissolves the small boundary (*khuḍḍakasīmā*). Regarding the establishment of boundaries, one first establishes the small boundary and subsequently establishes the great boundary.
This is largely the same as in the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*; it cannot be recorded in full detail.

Next, the text is explained. This section is divided into two parts: first, citing the conditions to introduce the formal act (*karmavācanā*); second, from "In this manner... onwards, the actual method of the formal act is clarified.
The boundaries and details of the formal act should be understood as previously described. Question: Why is it not stated that they must be at the same dwelling place? Answer:

Because a *sīmāmaṇḍala* (boundary enclosure) does not exist there; it is not intended for habitation. Since it is not for habitation, the requirement of being at the same dwelling place is not mentioned.

As for why it is not said that the *poṣadha* (recitation of the precepts) is the same [as the formal assembly], the answer is: there is no *sīmāmaṇḍala* (boundary enclosure) where the *poṣadha* is not recited.

Why would the establishment of the *poṣadha* ceremony fear that the great assembly would become weary? One is permitted to go to the *sīmāmaṇḍala* to recite the *poṣadha*. However, in such a case, the *sīmāmaṇḍala* itself does not arise [as a formal boundary].

If it were for the sake of a separate *karmavācanā*, one should instead say "identical *karmavācanā*. To explain the term "identical" (*sādhāraṇa*) in the context of the *mahā-sīmā*, it refers to the "identical *poṣadha*";

thus, there could be cases where the fundamental boundary (*mūla-sīmā*) and the distinct boundary (*visama-sīmā*) share the same *śīma-kuṭi*. If one were to say "identical *karmavācanā*," it would be feared that this would also apply to the *mahā-sīmā*, which likewise requires the fundamental and distinct boundaries to be identical.
For this reason, it is not said to be "identical *karmavācanā*. Furthermore, the establishment of the *mahā-sīmā* is for the purpose of providing a place for the Saṃgha to dwell.
Furthermore, because one wishes to include people so that they share the same Dharma, it is necessary to say "residing in the same place" (*ekāvasatha*).

Since there is no *sīmā* (boundary) where one does not reside, [if this were omitted], one would not wish to include people so that they share the same Dharma; therefore, it is not said "residing in the same dwelling place. [The phrase] "identical *karmavācanā*" (*ekakarma*) [is used].

Next, the explanation of the dissolution of boundaries (*sīmā-vimocana*) is clarified. Formerly it was said that this single method of dissolution applies both to the *śīma-kuṭi* (precept field) and the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*). Now, I say this is not so;
it only dissolves the great boundary and does not dissolve the *śīma-kuṭi*, because the texts concerning their formal establishment (*bandhana*) and dissolution (*vimocana*) are not analogous.

This single case of establishment alone is paired with its dissolution for the sake of distinction; as for the other three [types of boundaries] and the *śīma-kuṭi*, there are no texts for their dissolution. From the perspective of the underlying principle (*artha*), one who wishes to...

Regarding the dissolution of the *sīmā* (boundary): it should be performed by reversing the procedure for its establishment. The reversal is stated as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen. This is the *śīlākṣetra* (precept-boundary) of the monks at this residence.
If the time has come for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, being patient and willing, grant its consent. This is the formal motion (*jñapti*) for the dissolution of the *śīlākṣetra*.

Venerable Saṃgha, listen. This is the *śīlākṣetra* of the monks at this residence. The Saṃgha now dissolves the *śīlākṣetra* at this place. Which elders among you consent to the Saṃgha [dissolving] the *śīlākṣetra*?"
Those who approve of this dissolution of the *sīmā* (boundary) remain silent; those who do not approve should speak. The Saṃgha has approved; the dissolution of the *sīmā* at this place is concluded.
Since the Saṃgha has approved by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld. As with the dissolution of the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*), the reverse procedure is likewise the same.

Exegesis of the Text, Part One: First, the analysis of the conditions for the dissolution [of the boundary]. In the sixth fascicle of the *Mātṛkā-sūtra*, there are two conditions for the dissolution of the boundary (*sīmā*):

first, when the markers (*nimitta*) are destroyed by flooding and their locations can no longer be known; second, due to the threat of bandits, the bhikṣus all depart outside the boundary. Next, the method for dissolution is clarified.

Since the markers were established at the time of the formal binding (*bandhana*) so that the boundaries could be recognized, they must now be established for the purpose of dissolving them. To relinquish the characteristics of the boundary, one simply dissolves it.
There is no need for a formal proclamation.

Next, the *acchinna-cīvara-sīmā* (the boundary where robes are not lost) is explained. The natural *cīvara-sīmā* has already been clarified above; now the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*) is distinguished.
First, its meaning is interpreted through a twofold classification: first, the correct definition of the robe boundary; second, the lifting of the robe and its determination before the Saṃgha.
Regarding similarities and differences: first, we clarify the robe-boundary (*cīvara-sīmā*). This is analyzed through three sections: first, the intent behind opening and binding the boundary;

second, the explanation of the term "robe-boundary"; third, what is excluded from the village and what is not. In the first section: the three robes are prescribed for possession as a matter of principle, for they ought to accompany the person. If one is now far removed from them, how can one fulfill the duty of maintaining and protecting them?

Furthermore, since a bhikṣu’s practice of recitation and meditation must not be interrupted, yet the boundary is wide while the monastery (*ārāma*) is narrow, there would be obstructions [if they were not separated].
Therefore, the Noble One permitted [the practice] and established the *cīvara-sīmā* (robe-boundary) upon the *saṃgha-sīmā* (monastic boundary), so that the entire area would be common to all.

Thus, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, fascicle eight, states: "Śāriputra was observing the rains retreat in the village of Nāla. Every day he went to the Bamboo Grove to pay homage at the feet of the World-Honored One.
It happened that it rained continuously for seven days. He thought to himself: 'My body is now weak, and this saṃghāṭī robe is heavy.'"
He wished to take it with him, but as it was rained upon, it became heavy. He thought, "If I do not take it with me, I might fail to return, and I would then incur a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
He decided to leave it there until the weather cleared and went to visit the World-Honored One. On the way, he encountered non-Buddhist practitioners and engaged them in discussion.

The Buddha asked why he had not been seen for many days, and [the monk] explained the aforementioned matter in detail. The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus: "From this day forward, at Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove Monastery..."
In the village of Nāla, the boundary for "leaving one's robe" (*acīvaravippavāsa*) was established. Now, the monks dwell in peace and comfort;

the ritual procedure (*kamma-vācā*) may be understood. Once the rule against losing one's robe has been enacted, this road leading from Rājagaha to the village of Nāla—measuring twenty-five cubits on each side—is designated as the boundary.
If the robe is within the road, one may stay up to two [cubits] to the left and right of the road.
Fifteen cubits [is the distance]. If one leaves the robe in Rājagṛha and reaches the village of Nāla, there is no offense.

It is the same if one leaves the robe in the village of Nāla. Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu at the Jeta Grove Monastery who, after his meal, wished to go to the Kaṇṭaka Forest to practice meditation.
He then had this thought: "If I should stay overnight there, I might lose my *saṃghāṭī*. He immediately took his three robes and encountered...
Having seen the World-Honored One, he questioned the Buddha, who, having understood, declared:

"From this day forward, from the Jeta Grove to the Āmrapālī Grove, and including the Eastern Monastery, the Western Monastery, the Eastern Forest Monastery, the Western Forest Monastery, the Royal Garden Monastery, and the Śalavana Monastery at the Staff-Counting Stūpa—all these shall equally observe the rule of 'not losing the robe' (acīvarāpanna). Now, O Bhikṣus..."

One attains dwelling in peace and happiness. The *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) is as stated in the text. However, one should not establish a boundary for a forest hermitage (*araṇya*) that extends into a village settlement.

One should establish a boundary for a forest hermitage that extends into both a forest hermitage and a village settlement, or establish a boundary for a village settlement that extends into both a village settlement and a forest hermitage; only in this case is the boundary broad.
Regarding the *āveṇika* (monastery enclosure): one may establish a *saṃghāṭī-sīmā* (robe-boundary). This is intended so that within the *saṃgha-sīmā*, there may be a single robe-boundary.

Whether this *āveṇika* looks toward the *saṃgha-sīmā* and is equal to it or wider than it, these two robe-boundaries do not require further establishment; if one were to establish them in relation to each other, it would conversely result in restriction and obstruction.
This does not mean that all robe-boundaries must be formally established. Next, to explain the name: it is because this ritual (*dharma*) is added [to the boundary].
Regarding "the robe being held by a person": since there is currently no offense for being separated from it, it is called the "boundary where the robe is not lost.

Alternatively, it may be understood that after the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) has been performed, one may go far away; as long as one does not leave the boundary, the robe still belongs to the person.

Therefore, it is called the "boundary where the robe is held. Next, regarding the phrase "excluding the village": when performing the ritual, is it because a village exists that one must say "excluding the village," or is it permissible [to omit it] when none exists?

"Village," or alternatively, "excluding the village. Regarding the traditional interpretation of the village boundary (*grāma-sīman*): it was held that whether a village actually exists or not, one must always exclude it.
Our current explanation is not so. If a village currently exists, it is necessary to state that it is excluded; if no village currently exists, there is no need to exclude it.

If one were to establish the boundary by stating an exclusion for a place where no village will ever exist, this would mean the matter does not accord with the Dharma; how could such a thing be established? It is like [the case] in Campā, where [there was no village].
Treating a disease with waves, being rebuked by a guest, non-concealment and concealment—these and other such cases do not hold.

Instances of this are not limited to one. Question: For what reason is the village excluded from the *cīvara-sīmā* (robe-boundary)? Answer: A village is the dwelling place of laypeople, whereas the robe follows the bhikṣu;

since their respective domains and essential natures are contradictory, it must be excluded. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*, there are five reasons why a single settlement (*grāma*) must be excluded: [it causes] distraction.

It is indefinite. The robe-boundary (*cīvara-sīmā*) is fixed. There are five reasons for this: first, to eliminate slander; second, to eliminate strife and contention; third, to protect the holy life (*brahmacarya*);

fourth, to eliminate suspicion and resentment. Furthermore, regarding the two types of formal acts (*karmas*) concerning the Sangha’s robes, there are cases where they are removed and cases where they are not.
The traditional explanation states: both involve restraining laxity through urgency. As for the removal or non-removal of the robe, the fault lies in treating what is distinct as if it were not.

Therefore, one must exclude the village and proceed directly to the emergency site. Since the Saṃgha incurs a fault for not assembling within the same boundary, one does not exclude the village but proceeds directly to the emergency site by remaining within the same [monastic] boundary.

Furthermore, it is explained that once the Saṃgha boundary has been opened, it need not be reopened; thus, the robe boundary is not excluded for the same reason—it is an opening that need not be reopened.
For this reason, it must be excluded. According to our current interpretation, since the two boundaries of the Saṃgha and the robe are distinct, the [village] is excluded.
With the exception of the specific case [of the robe], furthermore, the act of laying aside one's robes is fundamentally incompatible with the village boundary (*grāmasīman*);

thus, even though the establishment of a dwelling place (*āvāsasīmā*) is permitted, it must still be excluded. However, this is not incompatible with the monastic boundary (*saṃghasīman*); because they are not incompatible, it is not excluded.

Next, the similarities and differences are clarified through a threefold analysis. First, the breadth and narrowness, as well as the quantity; second, the compatibility or incompatibility of their characteristics;
third, the presence or absence of their functional spheres (*śakti-vibhāga*). Regarding "quantity," when comparing monastic robes (*saṃgha-cīvara*), there are three possible positions:

first, the two natural [categories] differ in five ways; second, when comparing the natural [category] of the robe with that of the Saṃgha, the formal procedures (*karmavācanā*) likewise differ in five ways.
Third, by means of two [factors] acting as mutual opposites, three propositions are established to distinguish the first five cases: First, the Saṃgha is broad while the robe is narrow;

this refers to the gathering of the Saṃgha within an araṇya (forest hermitage), whereas the gathering of robes extends for one krośa (one *krośa* = eight *pādapa* intervals). Second, the robe is broad while the Saṃgha is narrow.

Just as the monastic robe is gathered within the boundary of a monastery (ārāma), there is a sphere of influence (sīmā) outside the boundary; this is the third case where the robes are shared equally among the monks.

This sphere of influence of the monastery is equivalent to the extent of seven trees. The fourth case is where one monk possesses many robes, like having many households within the space of seven trees.
Regarding the fifth point concerning robes: one robe for a single monk versus many for a community (*saṃgha*). It is like a great tree in an open space spanning a hundred *yojanas*.

A bhikṣu may, through his excellence, be permitted to protect a robe that extends [beyond himself]; however, for the *saṃgha*, there is a limit to its multiplicity. Some say: "Because the characteristics of the *ārāma* (monastery grounds) are broad, it is 'one robe';

because there are many [monks] within it—sixty-three paces—it is 'many for the *saṃgha*. This is not reasonable. If within this *ārāma* there is that which can be distinguished, [it would be sixty...]
Three steps; there must not be more. If they cannot be distinguished, how could many robes belong to one monk? Regarding the five subsequent positions:
first, the monk is wide and the robe is narrow, like a large boundary and a small monastery (*ārāma*). Second, the robe is wide and the monk is narrow, like a large monastery and a small boundary.
Third, both are equal, like the influence-area (*sīmā*) of a monastery. As for establishing the boundary for the Saṃgha, this is the fourth [position]; the monk is three [times the size].

Regarding robes: first, because there is a *sīmā* (boundary for formal acts), there are five; second, because the Saṃgha is one while robes are many, and because there is no *sīmā*, the Saṃgha is one;

third, because there are several distinct boundaries within a monastery (*ārāma*), robes are many. As for the three subsequent positions: first, the Saṃgha is broad while the robe is narrow, meaning it excludes the outer boundaries of the villages.
Because the area where [the robe] has been removed lacks the boundary for the robe (*cīvara-sīmā*). Second, there is the boundary of the Saṃgha (*saṃgha-sīmā*) and the boundary of the robe;

first, because there is a *śīlākā* (ordination platform), the Saṃgha is threefold and is comprised by the formal act of delimitation. As for the robe boundary, since there is no village, it is said to be "one" robe boundary; thus, the three are equal, meaning that there is no *śīlākā*.
Within this, it is not permissible for the robe boundary to be wider than the Saṃgha boundary, because the formal act for the robe depends upon the Saṃgha boundary. Furthermore...
The robe-boundary (*cīvara-sīmā*) arises by depending upon the provisional monastic boundary (*sāṃghika-sīmā*). Furthermore, one may not perform formal ritual acts (*karmavācanā*) with the robe;

it is naturally established in relation to the Saṃgha. Regarding the subsequent "consent" (*anujñā*): the two types of natural [boundaries] possess three common characteristics, and thus consent is not possible between them.

First, the regulation for the robe follows the person, whereas the Saṃgha follows the location; since the robe and the Saṃgha are distinct, how could they grant mutual consent? Second, each is independent and does not depend upon the other. Third...

Regarding the presence or absence of *śakti-vibhāga* (spatial influence): the next two methods of procedure (*karmavācanā*) are the inverse of the three meanings mentioned above, and thus they are mutually compatible.

First, because a robe follows the person in times of urgency, it is permitted to transition from urgency to non-urgency; it may be formally established (*bandha*) within the Great Boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), and for this reason, it is compatible.

Second, a robe necessarily depends upon the Saṃgha, whereas [the other] lacks spatial influence in both respects; since these are naturally distinct procedures, and as the existence or non-existence of the Dharma differs, they cannot be mutually compatible.

Correct. Having clarified what is permissible and what is not, we next consider the presence or absence of the *śakti-bhāga* (the functional sphere). Regarding the boundary of the Saṃgha (*saṃgha-sīma*), it is determined by the spatial limits;

whether it is established by a physical enclosure or by formal ritual action (*karma*), in both cases there is no *śakti-bhāga*. The boundary for robes (*cīvara-sīma*) is the opposite: logically, it should possess a *śakti-bhāga* in both instances.

However, because it is established by natural extension (*prakṛti-sīmā*), the robe is contained within the person’s space and is not fixed; since it is unfixed, this exception is granted, and the *śakti-bhāga* is established.
Regarding the *dharmakāya* robe boundary (*cīvara-sīmā*), it is established by relying on a physical location; since that location is fixed, it possesses no "sphere of influence" (*prabhāva*).
Furthermore, one may establish a robe boundary based on a provisional monastic boundary (*saṃgha-sīmā*). However, if the basis (*āśraya*) does not exist, how could the dependent (*āśrita*) exist?

Next follows the explanation of the text. The text is divided into three parts: first, the method for establishing boundaries where there is no village; second, the method for establishing boundaries where there is a village;

and third, an analysis of whether one may advance [the boundary]. Regarding the section on "no village," there are two parts: first, citing the causal conditions; second, the formal ritual procedure. The *Mātṛkā-sūtra*, fascicle 2, states: "First establish the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*);

afterwards establish the 'non-forgetting-of-clothing' boundary (*a-niśrita-cīvara-sīmā*). First relinquish the 'non-forgetting-of-clothing' boundary; afterwards relinquish the great boundary. Next follows...
The Method for Establishing Boundaries Within a Village (*grāma-sīmā-bandha*). First, the occasion (*nidāna*) is presented; next, the method of establishment is explained. Question:

Why is there a village within the boundary? Answer: The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (or *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*), fascicle four, states: "Because of the majestic power of the boundary, evil cannot find an opportunity. Furthermore, being within the boundary, it is protected by benevolent deities.

Therefore, for the sake of the donor (*dānapati*), one establishes the boundary encompassing the settlement. Next is the analytical examination, which consists of four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*); only the explanation is provided here.

Understood. Next follows the third section: the method for establishing and dissolving the large and small boundaries (*sīmā*). This section is divided into four parts: first, the establishment and dissolution of the large boundary;
second, from "At that time there were two monasteries" onwards, the detailed analysis regarding food; third, at the time of the *poṣadha* day...

The following section explains the dissolution of the minor boundary (*kṣudrakasīmā*). Regarding the fourth period, when the heavens sent down a torrential rain, the *Abhidharma* provides a detailed analysis.

The initial text consists of four parts: first, it clarifies the *dharmabhakta* (Dharma-food) and *piṇḍapāta* (alms-food). Second, the section on "being within the same boundary" is divided into five parts:

first, it cites the previous distinction; second, from "the bhikṣus... onwards, it reveals the *chanda* (consent); now, because they act together for the sake of the Dharma-food and mutually share [the offerings], they rely upon one another. Third, the various... [text continues].
First, the bhikṣus request the teaching based on the circumstances. Second, from "The Buddha said" onwards, the previous distinctions of the past are explained.

Third, from "They should all assemble" onwards, the opening and closing of the boundary are established; the current method for establishing the boundary and its specific limits have been explained in detail above.

Fourth, the food is common but the boundary for the Dharma is separate. Although the food may be abundant, there is a deficiency in the Dharma. The explanation of the text follows the pattern above. Fifth, the food is common but the boundary for the Dharma is separate.

It is precisely because food is scarce while the Dharma is abundant that this regulation must be established. This food belongs to the permanent endowment (*saṃghika*) and cannot be distributed at will;

unless a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) is performed, there is no way for it to be shared. It is just as when the Saṃgha receives offerings: they belong to the ten directions [of the Saṃgha] until the ritual is completed, at which point they may be claimed as one's own.
As it is with material objects, so it is with food. There is no separate boundary here, nor is there a need for a formal act of "releasing" (*visarjana*); one simply desires—

Regarding eating together: perform this *karmavācanā*. The explanation of the text follows the previous [section]. Fourth, combining the first two cases and resolving them as two distinct [sections], the same should apply to the latter two;
their absence from the text is merely an abbreviation. Next, to briefly examine the types of food: if it is food obtained according to circumstances...

If they each eat it, this would deviate from their original agreement; how could it constitute eating together? If one were to go back and forth to deliver it, there is also fear that the time would pass.

Therefore, one should merely perform the verbal agreement (*mukha-saṃvāda*); thus, neither party commits an offense. Although this method is employed, it applies only when the food is small in quantity.

If the food is large, such communication is not permitted. This is called counting people within a minor boundary (*kṣudra-sīmā*). One first establishes [the boundary] and subsequently releases it; having released this minor boundary:

People are bound by their association with a specific location; since this person formed the bond, it is this same person who must release it. Because the ritual act (*dharmakarma*) performed for a temporary purpose ceases upon departure, how can a second person subsequently dissolve this boundary?

This differs from the case of a *sīmāmaṇḍala* (precept field), where the ritual is performed permanently and is accompanied by permanent boundary markers, such that a subsequent person may formally recite the dissolution.
Next, we shall briefly analyze the legal principles regarding these matters: first, concerning rivers; second, concerning distant roads.
Next, the essential nature of the method for reciting the precepts (*śīla*) is explained. Before interpreting the text, it shall first be analyzed through four topical gates:

first, concerning time; second, concerning place; third, concerning persons; and fourth, concerning the dharma. Regarding the first, time, there are four factors: namely, year, month, day, and hour. As for the year:

the twenty-three large and small years within a single cycle are easily understood. As for the month: this refers to the dark and light fortnights (*kṛṣṇa-pakṣa* and *śukla-pakṣa*). As for the day: [text continues]
The fourteenth, fifteenth, and sixteenth [days] are established as a constant rule according to one’s place of residence. Regarding "time," it encompasses both day and night;
however, this text mostly speaks in terms of the night, as seen in the text itself because of the lighting of lamps.

Furthermore, because the night is generally more tranquil and listeners gather [at that time], this text—though understood to refer to the night—incurs no fault if applied to the day as well. Thus, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "From now on, I permit..."
There are two times for the *poṣadha*: first, before the meal; second, after the meal. One [period] lasts for one day and night. Next, regarding the place (*sthāna*):

because individuals may belong either to the Saṃgha as a whole or to a specific group, the place encompasses both formal ritual sites (*karmabhūmi*) and natural boundaries (*prakṛtisīmā*). Within these formal ritual sites, there are further distinctions between large and small;

the principle of the "large boundary" (*mahāsīmā*) is all-pervasive, while the "small boundary" (*sūkṣmasīmā*) is restricted to a specific number of persons. Next, regarding the persons (*pudgala*): excluding the three lower groups of practitioners, because...

It is not that which is held [as the primary authority]. There are three stages for possessing the precepts (*śīla*), and in all three, the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) is taught. The Saṃgha has four distinctions; it is subsumed under the "four-person Saṃgha.

Furthermore, within the Saṃgha, there is a distinction between the extensive and the abbreviated according to the meaning. From three persons downward, it is merely the abbreviated method. If one discusses the reduction of the non-seasonal [recitation], this is based on the recitation by the Saṃgha.
Moreover, there must be a person who recites the precepts; the Elder who recites the precepts should perform the recitation. (The *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, fascicle 5).

19. It is said: At a certain residence, a *poṣadha* ceremony was being held with Upananda serving as the senior elder (*sthavira*). When the community of monks requested him to recite the precepts, he replied, "I have forgotten them.
The monks said, "If you have forgotten them, why do you occupy the seat of the senior elder? They reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said, "The senior elder should recite the precepts;

if he does not recite them, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. The monks did not know the limit [of what constitutes] being a senior elder. [The Buddha continued: "How many [qualifications] constitute being a senior elder?"
[The assembly] sat down. The Buddha said, "Those who are above others are all called *sthavira* (senior elders).

Furthermore, if the *sthavira* is unable to recite [the precepts], the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, fascicle 34, states: "The senior elder of the Saṃgha should recite the precepts. If he is unable, the next senior elder should recite them.
If he too is unable, it should continue until someone capable can recite them. Moreover, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, fascicle 19, states: "The various bhikṣus..."
Previously, they did not invite [the preceptor]. The one reciting the precepts delayed the *poṣadha* ceremony because of this and reported it to the Buddha.

The Buddha said: "One should first invite the person who will recite the precepts. The *Ekottarika Āgama*, fascicle 44, states: "I now authorize the *sthavira* (senior elder) to recite the prohibitory precepts.

If the *sthavira* of the Saṃgha is incapable of reciting them, I authorize a *dharmadhara* (one who upholds the Vinaya) to recite them. If there is no such person, then whoever is able to recite the precepts with fluency and mastery [should do so]."

When chanting this, one should recite the *Poṣadha* (precept-recitation). Next, regarding the clarification of the *dharma*: the categories of *dharma* encompass three types, namely, mental intimation (*manasikāra*), the threefold verbal formula (*trivācika*), and formal ritual action (*karmavācanā*).
Within these *karmas*, there are further three stages; because this regulation is for constant practice, it consists merely of a single formal announcement (*jñapti*).
Next follows the explanation of the text, which is divided into three parts: first, the single announcement (*ekoddeśa*) for gathering the assembly;
second, from "At that time, on the day of the *poṣadha*" onwards, the formal exposition of the essence of the *poṣadha* ritual; and third, from "If there are three persons...

onwards, the clarification of what constitutes proper and improper conduct. The initial announcement is self-evident; furthermore, if there are other ritual matters, they must all be performed prior to the announcement. (From the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*)
19. It is said: At that time, the bhikṣus first recited the precepts and afterwards performed the various *karmans*.

The group of six bhikṣus departed as soon as the recitation of the precepts was finished, failing to remain in harmony with the Saṃgha. They reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said: "One should first perform the various *karmans* and then recite the precepts;
by doing so, one maintains the unity of the Saṃgha. From now on, you must not depart. Next, it is explained that the essence of the Dharma has three aspects.

Regarding the various procedures for the *pratideśanīya* (confession before the assembly), the *manasikāra* (mental recitation), and the abbreviated *saṃgha-vyavahāra* (formal acts of the community): first, prepare the necessary materials. Strike the gavel to assemble the community;

this is not restricted to the fully ordained monks (*bhikṣu*), as śrāmaṇeras must also be assembled. Once the assembly has gathered, they should examine one another. If anyone has seen or heard anything [of improper conduct], they should be summoned to investigate the matter.
The sequence of what is to be abolished or established can thus be determined. One should then prepare pure water and fragrant liquid, light lamps, and arrange the *śalākā* (voting sticks).
*Śalākā* means a tally stick. There were five types and eighteen [varieties]. The bhikṣus then made tally sticks of gold and silver. They reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"One should use copper, iron, ivory, horn, bamboo, or wood, excluding those from trees that are tainted by poison.

The bhikṣus made some short and some long. The Buddha said: "The short ones should be the length of five fingers; the long ones should be the length of a fist or one cubit (*hasta*). They must not be thicker than [the width of the fingers]."
The little finger [should be used]; it must not be thinner than a *kṣura* (razor). It should be dyed and placed together with the others, suspended above the *poṣadha* hall.

The *Saṃghāṭi-vinaya* (Monastic Code), fascicle 27, states: "When one wishes to recite [the names], one should first wash [the fingers] clean. Having washed them, one should grasp the counting-stick (*śalākā*).

If there are [fragrant substances available], one should bathe the counting-stick with scented liquid. Those others who wish to grasp the counting-stick should do likewise. It further states: "Sprinkle scented liquid upon the ground and scatter flowers."

Ran-deng (Dīpaṃkara) stated in the thirty-fourth [section]: "One person should go out and one person should collect [the ballots]. One must not walk with the head covered or the shoulders covered while distributing the ballots.
One should remove one's leather sandals and bare the right shoulder; the person receiving the ballots should do likewise. First, those who have completed the full preparations [should proceed]."

[The procedure for] the voting sticks (*śalākā*). Having distributed the śrāmaṇera voting sticks, one announces: "There are so many persons seeking full ordination (*upasampadā*), and so many śrāmaṇeras combined;
there are such-and-such people. Next, regarding those who perform the rite face-to-face (*pratyekamukha*): because it is not a formal assembly (*saṃgha*), they may not question one another.

Since the declaration of purity (*pariśuddhi*) is identical to the Dharma of the Saṃgha, one must personally declare one's own purity. Next, regarding the person who performs the rite through mental recitation (*manasikāra*): this is because there is no counterpart present.
It is stated that "mental intention" (*cittābhisaṃskāra*) is termed "desire" (*chanda*). Because it manifests purity and is identical to that of the *saṃgha*, it must be explicitly mentioned.

Next is the section on what is permissible and what is not. This text has two parts: first, an explanation in contrast to the previous three positions; second, a specific determination of what is permissible and what is not. The first part consists of two sentences. The first sentence concerns what is "unlawful and separate" (*adharmika-vibhakta*):

when the assembly performs the formal announcement (*jñapti*) for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), it should be performed by four persons; if now it is performed by only three, this is therefore unlawful.

Third, furthermore, it is not the Saṃgha; it does not constitute the granting of consent (*chanda*), which is precisely a separate assembly (*pṛthag-varga*). The next two lines below concern the "separate assembly regarding the Dharma" (*dharma-pṛthag-varga*);
because it accords with the three-fold formula (*tri-avavāda*), this Dharma should not accept consent, which is precisely a separate assembly. Next, the specific textual passages are fourfold:

first, the offense committed by the group of six (*ṣaḍvargika*); second, the bhikṣu’s report to the Buddha; third, the Buddha’s prohibition that it is not permitted; fourth, as in the case of the offense.

This section on "Manifestation" consists of three parts: first, the enumeration of the four numbers; second, the listing of the three types of illegality; and third, the explanation according to the words. Regarding the two types of illegality:
first, if the Saṃgha has not assembled, one performs the formal announcement (*jñapti*) in that place; second, one receives the announcement from three persons.

If a fourth person intends to announce the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), this is called an "illegitimate separate assembly. If all four persons have assembled, yet one repeats the action while leaving the announcement aside—or perhaps it is the four persons themselves—[this constitutes another case].
If they perform the threefold proclamation together, this is called an illegal concordant assembly (*adharma-sāmagrī*).

If four persons do not assemble but perform a formal motion (*jñapti*) as a formal motion, or if three persons or fewer accept the consent (*chanda*) and perform the ritual, this is called a legal separate assembly (*dharma-bhinna-gaṇa*). Regarding "acting as one":

if four or more persons all assemble and perform the formal motion, or if three persons or fewer do not accept the consent but perform the threefold proclamation and mental recitation together—this is [the case].
This is called the "conjunction of dharmas. Whenever one points out what is incorrect, it is intended to cause the consciousness to recognize the error so that it may be abandoned.

When one reveals what is as-it-is (*tathatā*), it is intended to cause one to realize the truth and follow it in practice. Whether this is accomplished through such revelation is to be understood according to the text. Nevertheless, the Buddha revealed these dharmas and taught the *Poṣadha* (confession) through their conjunction.
This is intended to cause the bhikṣus to recognize the commonality of their practice; therefore, it is said: "This is my teaching.
Next is the procedure for granting the purity of *chanda*. This section contains three parts: first, the granting of *chanda* prior to the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*);

second, at the time of the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), the granting of purity and the subsequent recitation of the precepts; third, from the point concerning the group of six (*ṣaḍvargika*) monks, the detailed analysis.

Proceeding forward, the preceding text contains four sections. First, the method for granting consent (*chanda*) when the illness is light. Second, the method for assisting one who is unable to do so [as mentioned above] to go to the assembly.
Third, the method for surrounding those whose illness is severe, as indicated by the passage beginning with "If [the patient] is...

Fourth, the method for many patients going out of the boundary, as indicated by the passage beginning with "If there are many sick people...". This explanation of the meaning is analyzed through seven gates; first, the opening [gate].

[This consists of] seven sections: first, the general intent; second, the explanation of the names; third, the determination of the conditions; fourth, the application according to time; fifth, the application according to place;

sixth, the application according to persons; and seventh, the application according to the Dharma. Regarding the first section: if the Saṃgha performs a formal act (*dharmakarma*), it is logically necessary that all follow it in unison; if there is any discordance in their intentions, [the act is invalid].
A formal assembly (*saṃgha*) is not established. However, within that assembly, body and mind are distinct. The body serves as the condition for the exclusion or inclusion [of members].

Once the singular mind has gathered its intentions and arrived, it is termed "acting in concert" (*samāna-kārya*) with the Saṃgha. Since there is no violation of the rule against separation, it is permitted to grant one's consent (*chanda*).

Next, regarding the explanation of the term: as for "consent" (*chanda*), its meaning is "that which is desired or required. Thus, the *Gāthā-śāstra*, fascicle six, asks: "For what reason is it so named?"

*Chanda*. *Chanda* refers to the joy in performing one's duties and the shared delight in accordance with the Dharma. Regarding the *yathādharma-saṃghakārya*, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya), fascicle 58, states:

"The dharma of *chanda*: 'chanda' means the arousal of the mind. In matters concerning the Saṃgha according to the Dharma, to accord with the Saṃgha’s rules and grant one’s *chanda*—this is called the dharma of *chanda*.
The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* (Realization of Truth), fascicle 7, states: "That which the mind requires is called *chanda*. However, when it comes to granting it, [one must act] oneself..."

There are cases where one person depends upon another, such as the rules for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) and the invitation for criticism (*pravāraṇā*), which are established as constant practices; if one were not to perform these, the Saṃgha would certainly impose a penalty.

Alternatively, there are matters where the Saṃgha requires an individual, yet that individual does not depend [on others], such as the rituals for receiving ordination, confession, and the treatment of those who require discipline;

if one were not to perform these, the Noble Ones would not impose a penalty. Although there may be expectations regarding whether something is required or not, the Saṃgha nevertheless maintains [these rules].
All must assemble together. Regarding the determination of the conditions (*pratyaya*): this text specifically permits [the action] for the sake of illness;

however, matters such as attending to the sick or serving the Three Jewels that do not contradict the teachings are all included within the scope of what is permitted. For example, regarding the failure to grant one's consent (*chanda*), the *Prātimokṣa* states:

"If it is for the sake of the Saṃgha’s affairs, the Stūpa’s affairs, attending to the sick, or for the sake of remorse regarding the precepts, or for the purpose of making robes, it is likewise permissible."
Next, regarding the time: this refers to the times for performing the *karmavācanā* (formal acts) such as the *Poṣadha* (confession of precepts) and the *Pravāraṇā* (invitation to admonish).

The meaning of "time" is not fixed; it is distinguished according to the specific dharma. Therefore, the text below states: "At the time of performing a *karmavācanā*, one should grant one's consent (*chanda*). Next, regarding the place: this refers exclusively to formal ritual procedures (*dharmakriyā*).

Since there is no [granting of consent] within the state of natural boundaries (*sīmā*), one may not receive consent at the time of establishing a boundary. However, within formal ritual procedures, there is furthermore...
Regarding the large and small [assemblies]: within the small assembly, the *śīma-kaṭhina* (boundary) is excluded; the remainder constitutes those who are without desire (*an-icchā*).

Thus it can be understood. Next, with respect to persons, there are three types. First, the person capable of giving consent (*chanda-dātṛ*); this refers to the two higher assemblies (*saṃgha*), and not the three lower groups.

Within these two assemblies, the individual must be one who accords with the Dharma. Second, the person receiving the consent (*chanda-grāhaka*); this refers exclusively to the *saṃgha*, and not to the two lower positions. Therefore, the text says:
Regarding one, two, or three people, they are not permitted to receive the *chanda* (consent). The Saṃgha has four distinct categories, all of which generally include the inclusion of *chanda*.

However, for a small portion of the fourth category, there is no *chanda* within the boundary (*sīmā*). Thirdly, regarding the person who holds the *chanda*, I shall explain according to the text. Next, concerning the application of the Dharma (*dharma*), there are two positions.
First is the "Dharma that ought to be performed. Within that which ought to be performed, there are three positions: namely, the recitation of the *Poṣadha* (precepts), the first.

The Dharma-discourse includes the *śīla* (precepts), the *karmavācanā*, and the *pravāraṇā*. One category of *pravāraṇā* consists of both the *pravāraṇā* itself and the *karmavācanā*; all other dharmas consist exclusively of the *karmavācanā*.

However, the three stages of the *karmavācanā* universally include the transmission of consent (*chanda*), with the exception of a small portion of the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal motion followed by one proclamation) and the delimitation of boundaries (*sīmā-bandha*), which do not require consent.
The second method, the procedure for granting consent, shall likewise be explained according to the text.

Next, the explanation of the text follows. The initial section has three parts: first, the presentation of the monastic duties; second, the citation of the reasons for non-attendance starting with "There being differences... and so forth;

third, the opening of the method for granting *chanda* (consent) starting with "The Buddha said... and so forth. Within this [third part], there are again three sections: first, whether the granting is valid or invalid;
second, whether the holding of the *chanda* is valid or invalid starting with "If the monk who receives the *chanda*... and so forth; third, the person who receives the *chanda*.

The following section explains what is established and what is not. The initial text has two parts: first, the presentation of the dharmas intended to be established; second, the negative formulation "if not," which serves as a counter-illustration of what is not established.
Within the former, there are again two parts: first, a general statement of what should be granted; second, a specific enumeration of the dharmas intended [to be established].

The *chanda* (consent) procedure consists of five types. Of these five, four are abbreviated and one is extensive; the abbreviated ones exclude those with serious illnesses while permitting those who are light in illness.

The single extensive type applies to those who are neither ill nor have a specific condition. Regarding the failure to accomplish [the act]: if one does not manifest the physical signs (*kāyasaṃskāra*), it is the opposite of the fourth type;

if one does not speak verbally (*vāksaṃskāra*), it is the opposite of the other four types. Such cases do not constitute [valid] accomplishment and one must again grant the *chanda*. Since the *chanda* procedure is thus, [it applies to] the following...

The same applies to the *pāriśuddhi* (declaration of purity). This is likewise stated for the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to admonish) up to its conclusion. Next, there are three stages to the transmission [of the *karmavācanā*]:

first, at the patient’s location; second, reaching the middle way; and third, reaching the midst of the Saṃgha. Regarding the first, at the patient’s location, twenty-seven persons do not constitute a valid transmission of the *chanda* (consent).

Below, in the section on the *pravāraṇā*, there are twenty-five; this is a brief summary that omits those with supernormal powers (*ṛddhipāda*) and those who have transcended seeing and hearing. This...

There are three middle positions. In the first, there are seven persons; that is, having already accepted the *kāmāvacara* [precepts], if one subsequently speaks for oneself, etc.—the nineteen [cases] below apply generally as well as regarding the time of giving.
In the third, one is separated from seeing and hearing; this single type is restricted solely to the time of giving.

The reason it is restricted solely to the time of giving is that, although one is separated from [the precepts] after having accepted the *kāmāvacara*, one does not lose [the precepts] through seeing or hearing. Therefore, we know that at the time of receiving [the precepts], one may not be separated from seeing and hearing. The rest...
"Abiding in the place" means going outside the boundary. Therefore, it is said in the *Mahāsaṃghika-vinaya*: "If one goes outside the boundary.

Furthermore, according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Sifen lü), fascicle 39, one who has granted consent (*chanda*) may not go outside the boundary; thus the text says: "The Buddha declared: 'From this day forward, one who has granted consent shall not go outside the boundary.
One who violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense. Moreover, one may not receive the consent of those outside the boundary. Question: Since other activities are already... [text ends]
[The questioner asks: "One has exited the boundary. Why, then, do you further clarify the loss of the *sīmā* (precept field)? [The answer:

The reason for saying "precept field" (*sīmā*) now is that although one has indeed already exited the boundary, because this is a separate place of practice within the interior of the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*), [the status] may not necessarily be lost from the perspective of the mind; therefore, it is clarified once more.

Regarding the thirteen grounds for disqualification (*antarāyika-dharma*) and so forth, if there is a person with such faults who does not know [of them], they must make a formal declaration (*svavacana*). If they know [of their own faults], it is not necessary [to rely on another].

He himself said: "When asked why there is no mention of the three [cases] such as insanity, he replied: 'These are cited by way of a single representative example; the principle is not fully exhaustive.
What is absent from the text is omitted for brevity, though it exists in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*.

Regarding the question below concerning those who do not count toward the quorum, there are further cases such as nuns and others who live separately, those who are concealed, and those who are the object of legal action. Why, then, do these seven persons not come? He replied: [as follows].

Regarding those for whom [the offense] is committed: because they have become holders [of the precepts], it does not exist. For the six types of persons, including nuns and so forth, it is logically present but is generally omitted;

the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* fully addresses these questions. Among them, the six persons are: one who has passed away, one who has gone to another place, one who has renounced [the training], one who has entered a non-Buddhist path, one who belongs to a different community (*nikāya*), and one who belongs to a separate faction (*pṛthag-bhūta*).

When the light of dawn appears, why are these [six factors] not included among those that are "insufficient"? The answer is: these [six] are established based on the loss of the boundary of desire through coming and going;
therefore, there are cases such as death and the passage of time. Those [factors] that are "insufficient" do not rely on coming and going, but are explained solely in terms of their essential nature;
