therefore, these six are not present there. Next, regarding the "monks in the midst of the Middle Way": even if one is separated from the constant path of seeing and hearing desire, one does not lose [the precepts].

One maintains the desire [to see or hear]. Since this is a mission involving coming and going, how could one possibly be separated from the path? If one were to see or hear [the object], it would immediately cause the desire to be lost.

For this reason, it is known that within the path there is no separation from seeing or hearing. If that is so, since seeing and hearing are absent within the path, it is said that "it is also like this.
Answer: In truth, seeing and hearing are restricted; they are not permissible during the time of receiving [the precepts]. It is not appropriate to exclude only this one factor. It is...

Therefore, looking back at the preceding stages as a whole, it is said that "it is also thus. Furthermore, within the *saṃgha*, there is likewise no separation from seeing or hearing, because [the rules] are restricted to the time of receiving [the precepts].

Moreover, this interpretation holds that all three stages are explained in relation to the act of receiving. Since it is so for what is received by the sick person, it is the same for the *saṃgha* in the interim.
To examine the errors and follow the text, this explanation is the most excellent. Thus, regarding the *pravāraṇā*, the text says:

If one has already arrived at the bedside of a patient who then passes away, according to the principles of both [the *Vinaya* and the *Abhidharma*], it would not be appropriate for the *chanda* (consent) to remain.

However, ancient masters state that within the *saṃgha*, there are four ways in which the *chanda* is separated from sight or hearing: first, concealment; second, departure; third, being obstructed by a barrier; and fourth, sitting at a distance.

This discussion is insufficient on its own and does not concern the loss of *chanda*. Next, the establishment or non-establishment [of the *chanda*] will be explained, as can be understood from the text.
Next, regarding the assembly and so forth, it is fully explained in the text. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, chapter eighteen, states:

The Buddha said, "The entire community should go to the sick person's location to have the *poṣadha* (recitation of the precepts) performed. The monk who recites the precepts should sit in the center and recite them, causing the sick monks to face the reciter.
Furthermore, there were some sick monks who were unable to face the reciter and instead sat or lay down with their backs turned. The Buddha said:
One should go outside the boundary; however, the *poṣadha* may not be performed there. It must be performed within the boundary.
Performing the *poṣadha* as a separate assembly (*pṛthaggaṇa*) follows the same procedure as the rite for granting purity (*śuddhi*).
Next, regarding the "non-acceptance" [of the invitation], the text contains nine items: first, the desire for purity so that the Dharma may proceed; second, the inability to state [the fault].

The first section concerns the formal declaration of the *chanda* (consent). The third clarifies that the *chanda* and purity (*pariśuddhi*) must not be lost. The fourth concerns the quantity of the *chanda* to be received.

The fifth further clarifies the ritual procedure for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*). The sixth concerns the method for transferring the *chanda* and purity. The seventh concerns whether or not one may address the name of the *upādhyāya* or *ācārya*.
The eighth concerns whether or not one may go to deliver the formal declaration. The ninth establishes the rules regarding going and sitting. The initial text combines the *chanda* and purity.

This is established so that monastic affairs are not delayed and whatever is undertaken may be successfully accomplished; therefore, it is prescribed that when one intends to grant *pāriśuddhi* (purification), it should be granted together with the *chanda* (consent);

and when intending to grant the *pravāraṇā* (invitation for criticism), it should likewise be granted together with the *chanda*. Furthermore, regarding the subsequent permission to state the specific matter:

this is also to prevent the delay of monastic affairs, so that the Saṃgha may uphold the Dharma without obstruction, and to eliminate what is contrary to the Dharma (*adharma*), ensuring it does not accord with personal bias. For these reasons, it is simply stated as follows: [as in the original text].

Regarding the matters of the Dharma and the Saṃgha, and the granting of consent (*chanda*) and purity (*śuddhi*): since it is not permitted to state the specific matter [in the formal motion], how can one grant consent for the *pravāraṇā*?

Answer: It is not permitted to state the specific matter; that is to say, one must not state the specific business being conducted within the Saṃgha. As for the *pravāraṇā*, one declares one’s own state of mind.

Even if the Saṃgha raises a charge against one, this is not the same as stating the specific business performed by other members of the Saṃgha. Furthermore, regarding the loss of the granting of consent and purity: [the following applies].
This is because there were obstacles on the road, preventing them from coming to the Saṃgha; they came from outside so that the Dharma might not be lost.
Regarding the quantity of those who receive the *chanda* (consent): these texts all state "many people" and so forth, as one cannot record their names, surnames, or physical characteristics;
the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* is likewise. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, fascicle 27, states: "When receiving the *chanda*, one should reflect within oneself..."

Only those who can transmit the *chanda* (consent) may do so; one must not take the consent of the entire assembly. To obtain the consent of at least three people, regarding the number of persons to be gathered, the *Ji-lü* (Mahīśāsaka-vinaya) further states:
"From this day forward, it is not permitted for those who have transmitted their *chanda* to perform the *poṣadha* in numbers greater than or equal to [the original assembly].

If those who have transmitted their *chanda* perform the *poṣadha* in greater numbers, it is a violation of the *vinaya*. (Pañcavargika-vinaya 19). Now, it is permitted for many bhikṣus to assemble together.

The Venerable Kāśyapa has come with pure intentions. For this purpose—gathering for the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*—a large number is required. As for other matters of the Dharma, it does not matter whether they are many or few.
Regarding the ritual procedure for the recitation of the precepts: it is established for the sake of the recitation so as not to constitute a separate assembly (*nānāsaṃvāsika*).

With the exception of these [authorized] persons and the master of deportment (*airyāpathika-ācārya*), if there are others sitting or standing, they all constitute a separate assembly for the recitation of the precepts; those who forget, err, or fail to transmit [the text] may [be dealt with accordingly].
[The text] says: "Know [this]. Next, the transfer of the desire (chanda) is as stated in the text. When previously addressing a sick person, there were both extensive and abbreviated forms;

however, when transferring the desire for one who is not sick, it must always be done extensively. The *Mātṛkā-sūtra*, fascicle 8, states: "One who takes the desire speaks to one person, and thus it is passed on in succession until the seventh person;

all may thereby obtain the purity (viśuddhi). This is called the 'Method of Sevenfold Correspondence' (*saptaka-yoga-dharma*). It is not the same as the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* regarding the loss incurred by transferring [the desire]."

Regarding the *yok* (consent): The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that the Buddha said, "From now on, one must not grant consent (*yok*), self-confession (*pravāraṇā*), or the removal of offenses (*āpatti-vinodana*) through a succession of intermediaries.

One who violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense. Furthermore, one must not utter the names of the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) or the teacher (*ācārya*). The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* says: "If someone asks you, 'What are the names of your preceptor and teacher?
you must not state the names of the preceptor and teacher directly. You should [respond as follows]..."

The purpose of the explanation is to cause understanding. Next, having finished conveying the *chanda* (consent), one must go into the midst of the Saṃgha; if one’s intention was previously harmonious, there is no offense.

Even if one is separate from the assembly, it is only for the sake of concluding the matter that one should listen to the *Prātimokṣa*. Not going would be a violation of the instruction; therefore, such a person is dealt with according to the Dharma.

Thus, having finished conveying the *chanda*, not going does not constitute an offense. As for those who are separate [from the assembly], they receive the *anujñā* (authorization); if the matter is concluded and they do not return, they should remain in retreat during the summer rains.

It is not broken. The old commentary states: "When the matter is concluded in the future, the summer retreat (*varṣa*) is not immediately broken. To clarify that this is not so: when one receives a formal authorization (*ādeśana*) for a specific matter, it is granted according to the nature of that matter.

Once the matter has ceased and the legal basis (*dharma*) has vanished, one does not return to break the summer retreat. This is because the expression of one's intention (*chanda*) is intended to convey one's state of mind, rather than being strictly dependent on the matter itself;

therefore, at the time of expressing the *chanda*, one does not mention the specific matter. Next, regarding the matter of the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), one must go to the assembly and listen. Both [the *chanda* and the *poṣadha*] require attendance.
Regarding the four propositions, they may be understood according to the text.

Next, the brief exposition consists of three parts: first, the clarification of the abbreviated conditions; second, from "From this day forward" onwards, the demonstration of the time for performing the ritual;

third, from "That bhikṣu" onwards, the formal explanation of the abbreviated recitation. Among the preceding texts, those that are grave are termed "difficult cases," while those that are light are "other conditions."

Regarding "one who is ill among the eight difficulties," this refers to the preceptor of the *poṣadha*. Regarding "one who is ill due to other circumstances," this refers to the rest of the assembly of monks.

As for "difficulties," it means that there are many laypeople residing at the dwelling, which hinders the recitation of the *poṣadha*; or there may be wicked people who come to the seat and seize a bhikṣu.
At such a time, as long as the dawn has not yet appeared, one must perform the *karmavācanā*; once the dawn has appeared, [it is no longer permissible].

Because it would immediately be lost. Next, the correct explanation follows. The brief text is divided into two parts. First, seven summaries are made: first, "direct departure"; second, there are five kinds;
and below, three positions are established. These five summaries precede the preceding text. The difficulty of the first phrase has not yet arrived and should be explained in detail.

This is the full explanation (*pṛṣṭha-vyākhyāna*) of the *naiḥsargika-pāyantikā* rules; it is called a "detailed explanation" because it is the detailed portion within the summary, and not [the other kind].

The five offenses are explained in their entirety. The reason for this is known from the subsequent sentence, which states that the ninety [offenses] are fully explained; this serves as proof that the preceding sentence refers to the *pāyattika* (or *pratideśanīya*) offenses. Question:

Why is there no detailed explanation of the *saṃvara-śikṣāpada* (rules of training) and the seven methods for settling disputes (*saptādhikaraṇa-samatha*), yet it is said that "the Saṃgha always hears them"?

Answer: If one were to explain the rules of training, they would constitute the five categories of offenses already mentioned; thus, even if the remaining seven rules were included, they could not be termed "abbreviated. As for the other sentences...
This can be understood as follows: it consists of seven summaries (*piṇḍa*). First, because there is no uncertainty regarding the true departure (*yathābhūta-gati*), there are six summaries.
One is direct departure; next is alternating error. The preceding seven constitute the "three and five. The original seven proceed from conditions toward urgency;
now these "three and five" proceed from urgency toward relaxation. The first five form the single sequence as the head, extending to thirty in total; this is still within the summaries.

Because it is extensive, it is called the "Extensive Exposition" (*vaipulya*). The fifth [section] merely omits the extensive version for brevity; although the text is extensive, its name is taken as "Numerical Categories.

Since what is taught does not differ from what was previously heard, it is called "Constantly Heard by the Saṃgha" (*saṃghānuśruti*). The following two sets of five can be understood accordingly. In the *Mātṛkā* for Bhikṣuṇīs, there are only two sets of five, as the six [categories] have been abbreviated.
Next is the removal of doubts and subjugation. This section contains five parts: first, establishing the regulations to remove doubts; second, from "At that time, the World-Honored One...
onwards, the method of self-accusation (*pratideśanīya*); third, from "At that time, on the day of the *poṣadha*... onwards, regulating the ignorant by relying on the wise;
fourth, from "At that time, Nanda... onwards, the subduing of disciples; fifth, from "At that time, there was one... onwards, the honoring of those of virtuous character.

The preceding text consists of four parts. First, the establishment of a regulation to remove doubts for the sake of purifying the assembly. Second, there are three types [of individuals] listed below for detailed analysis;

because the first type involves confusion, the procedure must be performed, whereas for the latter two—those with insanity and illness—there is no confusion and thus it is not required. Since this is the case, the other two categories are likewise so.

how could this [present case] not be considered appropriate? On the second day of the *poṣadha*, if the entire Saṃgha has committed an offense but does not recognize its name or characteristics, one should inquire about the confession.

"Not recognizing the characteristics" means not knowing the extent or nature of the offense. This is taught as a way to perform the rite of confession and inquire about the ritual procedures.

However, there is only the day for reciting the precepts (*poṣadha*), but no specific time for reciting them. Because one fails to recognize the offense and instead gives rise to a sense of purity based on attachment, it is said that one must not be forceful.
Urging one to repent.

Next, regarding the relationship between the visiting and resident monks, there are four sections in the text. First, it discusses whether the dates of arrival coincide or not, and whether those arriving are few or many, clarifying what is appropriate and what is not;
this contains thirty-six propositions. Second, it discusses the day of the *poṣadha* ceremony, descending into the monastery grounds, and their mutual [interactions].

Regarding "seeing, hearing, and doubting," there are forty phrases. In the third section, concerning the mutual seeing, hearing, and doubting between those residing in different locations, below the great boundary (mahā-sīmā) and the ritual site (sīmā-maṇḍala), there are twenty-four phrases.

In the fourth section, concerning the mutual seeing, hearing, and doubting between those residing in different locations, within the boundary and outside the monastery grounds (ārāma), there are twenty-four phrases.
The first part consists of two sections: first, a detailed explanation of what is appropriate and inappropriate; second, [the section on] what is appropriate.
Whether following or not following [the rules], one incurs the offense of a malicious mind. The preceding text has three sections, each consisting of twelve phrases.
The first explains how, when the days of the observance are different, there are variations in the number of arrivals—few, many, and so forth—forming twelve phrases.

The second explains how, when the days of the observance are the same, there are variations in the number of arrivals—few, many, and so forth—due to mutual ignorance of one another, forming twelve phrases. The third section, consisting of twelve phrases, differs precisely in that it concerns knowing the future arrivals.

In the first twelve [days], there are two [sections]. Six phrases refer to the fourteenth and fifteenth days, forming one "six. Next, the fifteenth and sixteenth days form another "six. In the first six, there are two positions.
Three phrases refer to the beginning of the third [section]: the guest is the fourteenth day, and the resident is the fifteenth day.

Regarding the guest's presence—whether it be slightly less or equal, or more or equal—the guest must conform to the resident. If the resident must go outside, the next three [phrases] concern the resident on the fourteenth day.

The guests number fifteen. Among the guests, there are those who are slightly fewer and those who are equal in number. The rule is that the guests must go outside; if the number of new arrivals exceeds the old residents, one must follow the guests.
Next, in the sixth [section], there are only [the following]: in the latter three, the guests are sixteen and the old residents are fifteen; the first three are omitted. The guests are fifteen.
The former [version] consists of sixteen [sections]. Question: The former version speaks of "guests arriving" and so forth; this establishes the guest as following the former.

Why, then, does the latter version speak of "the former arriving" and so forth, yet not establish the former as following the guest, but instead requires the guest bhikṣu to go outside the boundary to recite it?

Answer: This is intended to clarify that the former is strong and the guest is weak; thus, there is a case where one is established and another is not. Furthermore, in the subsequent section on the same day:

"The new arrivals are equal in number to the residents; how then can the residents be regulated? Furthermore, one speaks again for the sake of the new arrivals. Answer: "Below, the ritual procedure is performed on the spot so as not to cause excessive trouble or disturbance.

Although the new and the old are equal in number, it is for the sake of the new arrivals that the rite is repeated. Again, he asked: "In the case of those who are not equal, why is there no mention of 'new arrivals'?
Is it that the new arrivals are compared to the old, or the old to the new? Answer: "It is to distinguish between strength and weakness that the comparison between new and old is established."
If the newcomers and the residents look toward one another, there is then no distinction between strong and weak; it may be that they are combined, though the text omits this for brevity.

Next, the twelve phrases consist generally of four sets of three: the first three concern the residents looking toward the newcomers; the next three concern the newcomers looking toward the residents;
the next three concern the residents looking toward other residents; and the final three concern the newcomers looking toward other newcomers. [Question: Why do those from outside enter the boundary?
[Question: There is no offense. One may separately grant the *pārisuddhi* (declaration of purity). [Answer: Because the mind has no separation, there is no offense toward the Saṃgha. [Objection:

If that were so, then other legal acts (*dharma*) performed toward the Saṃgha should likewise be without offense. [Answer: The procedure for the *Poṣadha* is established such that all must follow it together. Because the mind is directed toward the Saṃgha, there is no offense.

However, regarding other legal acts performed apart from the assembly, if one acts separately, it is not in accordance with the rule; even if the mind is directed toward the Saṃgha, it remains within the limit of an offense.

The subsequent twelve points are explained by reversing the preceding ones: the first three concern the new members looking toward the old; the next three concern the old members looking toward the new;

the next three concern the new members looking toward one another; and the final three concern the old members looking toward one another. Regarding the conclusion on the offense: this applies across all the aforementioned stages.

Whether one should have emerged but did not, or should have acted but did not, because they failed to assemble, they intentionally employ the Dharma with an evil mind for the purpose of destroying others. Thus, an offense is incurred.
[If one] commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense due to indolence, but does not act with the intent to cause schism, one incurs only a *duṣkṛta*.

Next, the second section contains four items, each with ten phrases: 1. A visitor perceives the signs of a resident; 2. Regarding "there is a residence," etc., the resident perceives the signs of a visitor;
3. On the day of the *poṣadha*, etc., the visitor hears the voice of a resident; 4. Regarding "there is a residence," etc., [the resident hears the voice of a visitor]. Each of these has ten phrases.
Section. Previously heard of as the "Guest Sound. The first text consists of ten phrases, divided into two groups of five. The first group, "Seeing Without Doubt," contains five items.
Within the first four, the first three constitute non-achievement with fault;

the fourth constitutes non-achievement without fault, because it was not accumulated and thus is not achieved. This means that there is no transgression and no offense. Within the former [the first three], there are again two parts. The first...
In two cases, the offense is not established as light because of negligence; in the third case, the offense is not established as grave because of an evil intention.
Next, regarding the five types of doubt arising from seeing: having seen [the person], one conceives a doubt as to whether they are a *bhikṣu* or a *śrāmaṇera*. The formulation is the same as before.

Therefore it is said: "It is also like this. As it is with the first ten, so it is with the remaining ten; they are all the same. Next, regarding the three texts, there are likewise four stages as before, differing only in that the phrases are fewer.
In the first text, there are six phrases, divided into two groups of three. Within the first group of three, there are three instances of seeing [the boundary] without doubt.
Among these three, the first two constitute [a valid boundary] despite the presence of faults, because they are distinct boundaries (*sīmā*). Therefore, they are established; one should call [them].

If one does not call [the assembly], there is an offense. When the third call is made and the formal act (*karmavācanā*) is performed, it is established and there is no offense. Next are the three phrases concerning seeing and doubting;

the composition of the text is the same as before. Since this is the case for the first six, the remaining six categories are likewise so. The subsequent four texts are to be understood according to the principles explained previously.

Next is the explanation of the method for departing during the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*. The group of six bhikṣus, being aware of their many transgressions and fearing disciplinary action by the Saṃgha, departed while the *Prātimokṣa* was being recited.
This section is divided into two parts: the first nine cases concern themselves, and the subsequent nine cases concern others. The interpretation of the text is self-evident.

Next is the section on distinguishing [the rules] for other assemblies. This passage contains two parts. First, the distinction regarding other assemblies: although a *bhikṣuṇī* may possess the full precepts, she is not permitted [to recite them] due to the difference in form.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that it is permitted for a *bhikṣu* to recite the *bhikṣu* precepts in the presence of a *bhikṣuṇī*, but it does not permit a *bhikṣuṇī* to recite them.

If a *bhikṣu* forgets [the precepts], he may listen to a *bhikṣuṇī* orally transmit them; the *bhikṣuṇī*’s case is the reverse. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, fascicle 27, states: "From this day forward, it is not permitted..."
To explain the names of the five categories of offenses to those who have not yet received full ordination is permitted; one may instruct them, saying:

"You must not engage in unchaste conduct, you must not steal, you must not kill living beings, and you must not speak falsely. In this manner, a bhikṣu may provide such instruction. Second, with the exception of persons, it is permissible to teach the rest without incurring an offense.
Next is the *akāla-poṣadha* (non-timely confession of precepts). Excluding the fourteenth, fifteenth, and sixteenth days, performing it on any other day constitutes the non-timely.
This is because for many days the community of monks had been in conflict; as their minds were estranged, they could not achieve harmony. Now that the dispute has been extinguished—

It returns to being of one flavor. Were it not for the formal act (*karmavācanā*), there would be no means to manifest this externally through ritual form. Within this, there are three sections: first, the formal announcement (*jñapti*) regarding the settlement of disputes;

second, the inquiry as to whether [the assembly] should respond or not; third, the announcement that this is an untimely recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*). This announcement serves as a substitute for the standard announcement for the recitation of the precepts.
If one considers the recitation according to the specific time, all texts—excepting only those concerning new and resident monks—contain these elements in their entirety, as clarified above.
The preceding section concludes the exposition on the Dharma of Precepts (śīla-dharma).

Next are the two *khandakas*, which together clarify the avoidance of transgressions. Since the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*) prevents [transgressions] before they arise, it first clarifies the formal commitment to this dwelling;
thus it is called "retreat" (*an-gi*). It extensively explains the four types of methods for the rainy season retreat, all of which are gathered in one place and designated as such.
The *Cīvaravastu* (Section on Robes) is divided into three major parts: first, the arising of faults during travel; second, the reproaches from householders at that time;

and third, the establishment of prohibitions by the World-Honored One for the monks below that point. Regarding the traveling [monks], one should understand how they incurred faults by violating the rules for the retreat (*vassa*).

The text on the reproaches is divided into three sections. First, the reproaches from laypeople (*avadātavasana*), which is further divided into three sub-sections. First, the [reproach of] grasping...
What has been done should not be censured. Next, regarding "the various non-Buddhists" and below, he censures by using external cases to illustrate internal ones.
Next, regarding "down to insects and birds" and below, he censures by using lower cases to illustrate higher ones. Next, the censure of the bhikṣus and the censure of the Buddha follow the text.

Next is the explanation of the establishment of the rules, which is divided into six parts: first, the method for concluding the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat); second, from "if the *varṣā* is completed" and below, the method for distributing summer quarters; third... [and so forth].

Third, at that time, Śāriputra [discusses] whether one may enter [the village] after descending from the *āvāsa*. Fourth, at that time, the bhikṣus [discuss] establishing the place of dependence (*niśraya*) after descending from an open space.
Fifth, at that time, there was a donor who invited [the monks]; [the text discusses] whether one may enter outside the boundary.

Sixth, at that time, in Kauśāmbī, [the text] clarifies the meaning of whether or not to turn away from an invitation for the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat). First, explain the initial passage. Within the text:

This is divided into two parts. First, turning the detrimental toward the beneficial, the teaching is promulgated in its entirety. Second, after identifying the person upon whom it relies, the rules for the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) are set forth.
Because the *varṣā* accords with the Dharma, the Buddha declared it "permitted" (*anu-jñāta*). Yet, if one violates what has been permitted, it is termed a "prohibition" (*pratiṣedha*).
In response to this, the general meaning of the *varṣā* is presented, and the definition of *varṣā* is explained through a fourfold analysis. First, regarding...
At that time, the second [section] concerns the place, the third concerns the person, and the fourth concerns the Dharma.

First, regarding the time, there are three points: first, that the summer retreat (*varṣā*) is observed in the summer and not in spring or winter; second, that although the summer consists of four months, the intention is to observe it for three;
and third, whether or not an intercalary month within the summer is included in the count. Regarding the first point, the question is raised by citing three [cases].

Question: At that time, one ought to apply the prohibitions universally. Why is it that the summer retreat (*varṣā*) is prescribed but not the spring or winter? Answer: Faults arise more frequently during the summer than at other times.
Although the formal practice of cultivation is equally suspended during all seasons, the summer incurs greater censure and reproach due to various faults such as the rain;
thus, because the tendency toward the corruption of conduct is more prevalent, it is specifically restricted. During other times, the tendency toward the corruption of conduct is less frequent.

It would have invited further censure and was trivial; therefore, it was not established as a rule. For this reason, the text states: "I permit the bhikṣus to observe the three-month summer retreat (varṣā).

While staying during the summer, there is much benefit for the persistence of the Dharma; since there is a benefit in staying, there is also a benefit in departing. At other times, the benefit is slight;
while staying, there is no such benefit, and since there is no benefit in staying, how could there be one in departing? [End of] Question on Summer Retreat.

The offense is grave. Regarding the statement that "entering the summer retreat (*varṣā*) is not for other times," why is it that when a nun travels during the three seasons, she incurs a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation), whereas for a bhikṣu it is a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense)?

Answer: There is a distinction between the two meanings of "entering the retreat" (*anugata*) and "traveling" (*cārikā*). There are those who do not travel because they have not entered the retreat; there are also those who, having entered the retreat, nevertheless travel.
For this reason, in the Vinaya for nuns, separate precepts were established for entering the retreat and for traveling. Thus, one should know that [the offenses] are not identical.

Section Two. Question: Why is it that although there are four months in the summer retreat (*varṣā*), only three are formally concluded? Explanation: There are two reasons. First, to provide an opening for those who are unable to fulfill the full term.
If one lacks the necessary conditions, one concludes the retreat early; if one possesses the necessary conditions, one concludes it later.

If one were to conclude the retreat for the full four months, it would only be successfully accomplished on the sixteenth day of the fourth month; from the seventeenth day onward, [the retreat] would immediately [be considered terminated].

It was not established as a fixed rule because the teaching was too strict and its practice difficult to maintain constantly; therefore, it was permitted to deliberate for one month on whether to proceed.
For this reason, in the text, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana arrived on the seventeenth day, and the Buddha said, "I allow you to observe the later retreat (*paścimikā varṣā*).

Second, it is to reward their labor. If it were fixed that the retreat must be entered on the fourteenth day, those with physical bodies would have no days left to receive such reward. Therefore, it was permitted.
One month of the summer season is used to provide rewards for the five benefits. Thus the text says: "If one enters the *pūrvavārṣika* (early rains retreat), one dwells for the first three months.
It further states: "Not receiving the *kāṭhina* robe for one month. Third gate: Regarding whether or not to calculate the intercalary month.
The original regulation for the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) pertains to the summer period; therefore, when there is an intercalary month (*adhika-māsa*), it is included within the summer.

Thus, according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya-śāstra*, even with an intercalary month during the summer, one may still keep the rain-clothing for a total of one hundred and twenty days. Since the allowance to store rain-clothing already permits the inclusion of the intercalary month, how could the regulation for the *varṣā* retreat—which is established for the purpose of cultivation—be set aside as incidental?
Furthermore, another interpretation holds that the path of cultivation requires urgency; therefore, a longer duration is considered virtuous. It is not [the case that]...

If one were to count the intercalary months until they total three full months, since counting them is not permitted, then departing the boundary during an intercalary month within the period of the rains retreat (*varṣā*) would not constitute a violation of the summer retreat.
In response to the question regarding staying overnight outside [the boundary], this does not constitute a continuous connection [to the retreat] while remaining at the designated location.

Therefore, the summer retreat is broken. In that case, if one encounters an intercalary month while observing the *ādeśana* (the formal request for permission to leave), may it also be included within the retreat?

Answer: Since the summer retreat is restricted to a specific location for the purpose of practicing the Path, the intercalary month is naturally included. However, the *ādeśana* is specifically permitted for particular circumstances; therefore, it follows only the [actual] days.

In that case, if there is an intercalary month during the summer, and the intercalary month is subsumed under the summer, would the "five matters for rewarding labor" also apply for two months? No, because the six months are not uniform. This is the explanation.

The five benefits are broad; they do not include either [the practice of] *śikṣādattaka* or *sārdha-vihārin*. When the number of intercalary months completes one month or five months, one immediately relinquishes the retreat, as it is not the same as the formal *varṣā* (rainy-season) retreat.

Furthermore, another interpretation holds that the five months include the intercalary month. Since it is stated that "the four winter months are complete," this is determined by way of time; thus, we know that it includes the intercalary month within the first month.

Because it is restricted to the remainder of the summer following the intercalary month, it does not include the intercalary month. Since it is said that the *varṣā* includes the intercalary month, if there is an intercalary month during that period...
In the fifth and sixth months, one must certainly remain for one hundred and twenty days. If there is an intercalary fourth month, there are three ways to establish the boundary (*sīmā*):

if the boundary is established during the first four months, one remains for one hundred and twenty days; if it is established during the latter four months, the duration is indefinite according to the number of days remaining;

if it is established in the fifth month, the duration is fixed at ninety days. Within this period, there may be cases where one departs after an interval of one month from the commencement of the rains retreat (*varṣā*).
Regarding the interval of one day: it is as if one person concludes on the thirtieth day of the fourth month, while another concludes on the first day of the fifth month;
this is called an interval of one month. If we discuss the departure, the former person departs on the final day of the seventh month, while the latter departs on the first day of the eighth month;
this is called an interval of one day. This also applies if one concludes on the thirtieth day within an intercalary month. All [cases] are the same.

This is the same as on the first day of the fifth month. It may also be said that the *anvāropana* (the formal commencement of the rains retreat) is separated by twenty-nine days, and even if one departs for as little as one day, it remains simultaneous [with the original date].
If it falls during an intercalary seventh month, there are two possible positions for the commencement:

staying for ninety days from the sixteenth day prior to the first day of the fifth month; or staying for one hundred and twenty days from the second day thereafter through the fifteenth day. This is so.
Among these, there may be cases where the commencement of the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) is separated by one day, while the departure is separated by one month.
For example, suppose one person begins the *varṣā* on the first day of the fifth month and another on the second; this is called "commencing the *varṣā* with a one-day interval.

The former person may depart on the first day of the intercalary seventh month, while the latter departs on the second day of the eighth month. Because an intercalary month occurs in the interim, it does not constitute a full [counted] day.

Regarding the term "departing at a time separated by one month," and so forth, up to "having the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) separated by fifteen days" and "departing at a time separated by one month," etc.:

next, concerning the gate of location (*sthāna-mukha*). Now, one who observes the *varṣā* must rely upon a boundary (*sīmā*). The reason for knowing that one relies upon a boundary is stated in the text: "First..."

The feet enter within the boundary (*sīmā*). Furthermore, one receives [the invitation] and goes outside the boundary. Also, regarding whether or not a formal invitation (*pravāraṇā*) is valid when one turns one's back [to it], it says:

"The *poṣadha* ceremony within and outside the boundary. It further states: "The Sangha in this and that boundary is split," and so forth. Moreover, in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, chapter fifty-three, it asks:

"Is there a case where a single bhikṣu observes the rains retreat (*varṣā*) in four different residences, yet is still said to be observing the retreat? The answer is: "If the bedding, wooden materials..."

Connecting the four boundaries, one dwells within them; this is termed "the rains retreat" (*varṣā*). Again, it was asked: "In which places should a bhikṣu be given the offerings for the rains retreat?
The answer was: "In all four places, he should be given an equal share. Again, it was asked:

"Is it permissible for many monasteries to collectively establish a single boundary for the rains retreat? The answer was: "It is termed 'the rains retreat'; the bhikṣus should reside in whichever monastery [is designated]."
[Question: "In a neighborhood (*gāma*)? [Answer: "One may dwell according to one's inclination. [Question: "If that is so, how is it? [Text says: "A certain monastery (*ārāma*), etc. [Answer:

This refers to citing a location in order to determine its boundary (*sīmā*). Now, there are two kinds of boundaries: those established by nature (*prakṛti-sīmā*) and those established by formal ritual (*karmavācanā-sīmā*). In both of these locations, the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) is valid. [Question:

"If one observes the *varṣā* based on a natural boundary, is it possible to establish a formal boundary within it? [Old Interpretation: "It is not possible to establish one. If one were to establish it, it would immediately be invalidated."
In the summer, the *Vinayavibhaṅga* states that once the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) is completed, one should establish the boundary (*sīmā*).

If this were so, then if one were previously within a naturally established robe-boundary (*cīvara-sīmā*) and suddenly establishes a robe-boundary [of the new type], one would also lose the robes. Answer: This is not analogous.

Because the original undertaking of the robes does not depend upon a naturally established robe-boundary, even though a boundary is now established, the formal act of undertaking (*samādāna-dharma*) is not lost. Furthermore, the method of the *varṣā* retreat does not consist of being restricted to a fixed boundary; entering the boundary constitutes its completion.

Because one enters the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat), the boundary is established; thus, to break it is to violate the *varṣā*. Question: If one enters the *varṣā* at a place where no formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) has been performed, may the boundary be dissolved?
Answer: It may not be dissolved. For if it were dissolved, the *varṣā* would be violated. The text states: "When the *varṣā* is concluded, the boundary should be dissolved.

If that were so, then by dissolving the boundary for not losing one's robes (*acīvarāpatti*), one would necessarily lose one's robes. To this it is replied: The *varṣā* is established by depending upon the boundary. Now, if the boundary is dissolved, the basis [of the retreat] is lost.
Upon disbanding [the boundary], it is immediately destroyed. Receiving robes does not depend upon a boundary; even if the boundary is disbanded, the reception of the robes is not lost.

Furthermore, because it is restricted to a specific location, entering a boundary or a monastery garden constitutes the formal summer retreat (*varṣā*). However, the reception of robes is not restricted by boundaries; therefore, entering a boundary does not constitute the reception of robes.
Even if one disbands the robe-boundary, the method of reception is not lost. Now, the current disbanding is not like this; during the summer, the tying of knots is disbanded all at once.

The summer retreat (*varṣā*) is not broken. If one asks how that is so, the text states: "When the *an-ku* (summer retreat) is completed, one should perform the *kṣaya-jñapti* (declaration of completion).
If one performs the *kṣaya-jñapti* before the *an-ku* is completed, one incurs only the offense of *na-pratirūpa* (inappropriate conduct), but the summer retreat is not actually broken.

This is just as when there are a hundred persons subject to prohibitions; although those who receive ordination incur the offense of *na-pratirūpa*, it does not prevent the arising of the precepts. This case is also like that. Such is its category.

This is indeed many. If one were to argue that the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) is dissolved simply because the boundary (*sīmā*) is broken—then, for example, when the boundary of a monastery (*vihāra*) is destroyed, the summer retreat would also have to be lost.
Conversely, if one argues that although the monastery is destroyed, the summer retreat is not lost because one has not left the location (*sthāna*), [then...]

The present boundary is likewise. Even if one were to untie the knots [of the boundary], they would not depart from their location; how then could the summer retreat be lost? Furthermore, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states:
"If a nun relies upon a bhikṣu for her rains retreat, and during that retreat the bhikṣu dies, renounces the path, or departs for another place, the nun must not leave.
Within a distance of three *yojanas*, if there are monks residing there, she may go to them every half-month to inquire about the *poṣadha*."
By this it is proven that both [the beginning and the end] of the *saṃghāṭī* robe-binding ceremony are attained.

Furthermore, regarding those who perform the *saṃghāṭī* binding during the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat), such binding is entirely invalid. Just as when the *varṣā* is concluded, four matters ought to be performed;

however, with the single practice of *pravāraṇā* (the invitation for criticism) replacing the place of the *poṣadha* (recitation of the precepts), one proceeds with the sound of permission and performs the remaining three dharmas toward the conclusion. Whether it is actually completed or not yet completed depends on whether these are necessarily finished.

If one accepts a *guṇa-cīvara* (extra robe) with the common consent [of others], it is not established. If the acceptance is not yet complete and there is a release of the bond (*saṃdhāna*), how can the release of the bond be established?
Although this explanation exists, for now, the previous interpretation is taken as correct.

Next, regarding the persons concerned: this refers to the five groups of monastics, all of whom must observe the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat). As is fully demonstrated in the *Bhikṣuṇī-prātimokṣa*, the specific categories of offenses are clearly set forth.

Since their advancement in practice is no different [from that of monks], it is evident that they are subject to the same prohibitions, and their censurable transgressions are likewise equal. Furthermore, in the twenty-fourth fascicle of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Upāli asked the Buddha:
"Who should observe the *varṣā*? The Buddha replied: "The five groups of monastics should observe the *varṣā*. The question was the same for all, and the *varṣā* is observed equally by them all.

"One should count the years. The answer is: "One counts the years of *vassa* (the rainy season retreat). There is a distinction between these two meanings; one cannot equate the *vassa* with the counting of years.

Furthermore, [the calculation] must be divided based on the fulfillment of the full precepts (*upasampadā*); since the status of a teacher differs from that of a novice (*śrāmaṇera*), the latter does not count the years."
Next, regarding the definition by dharma: there are two types of dharma, namely the former and the latter. On the sixteenth day of the fourth month, the single day is designated as the former;
from the seventeenth day onwards, it is collectively termed the latter. This distinction between former and latter is established based on rewards and punishments.
However, if one refers to the formulation of offenses for bhikṣuṇīs, only the sixteenth day of the fifth month is considered the latter. All that has been stated above...

Regarding the preceding [discussion], this refers to the determination of the offense. The former is a *duṣkṛta* (light offense) and the latter is a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation). Now, having fixed the sequence of before and after, we shall explain it according to the previous principle.
If clarified by way of the time of the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*), if there is no intercalary month, the observance is completed within thirty-one days;

if there is an intercalary fourth month, it is completed within sixty-one days. Why is it that the observance is accomplished over such many days? The answer is: because of the permitted number of days.
These are all within the period for establishing the boundary (*sīmā-bandhana*). Furthermore, because the subsequent three months are fully completed, the text below states:

"Those who observe the later retreat (*paścima-varṣā*) dwell for the latter three months; they obtain the *pravāraṇā* according to the earlier retreat, yet they do not [perform] the *pravāraṇā* themselves.

They dwell for several years awaiting the completion of the days, which differs from the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*. Only on the sixteenth day of the fourth month and the sixteenth day of the fifth month is the boundary formally established."
Regarding the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat): Thus, the twenty-seventh [section] of that text states:

"If a bhikṣu is traveling and has not yet reached his dwelling place when the day for entering the *varṣā* arrives, he may immediately enter the retreat by the roadside, relying on a tree, a vehicle, or similar objects. When the dawn light appears, he proceeds to his actual dwelling place."
Upon arriving for the later retreat (*paścimā varṣā*), one should expose the right shoulder and so forth, and perform the formal declaration of the retreat (*varṣopagamana*) three times.

If a bhikṣu who has been traveling does not accept the retreat on the day of the earlier retreat (*pūrvā varṣā*), he commits one *vinayātikrama*. If, upon reaching his place of residence, he does not accept the retreat on the day of the later retreat, he commits two *vinayātikramas*.
Furthermore, according to the *Ekottarika-āgama*, an additional case is added: the meaning should be summarized as follows—[if he fails to do so] during the four months [of the rainy season].
The sixteenth day is the beginning; from the seventeenth day onward is the end. Among these, the sixteenth day of the fifth month constitutes the latter [part] of the interval.
However, according to the method of formal establishment (*bandhana*), there is no such intermediate period. Other meanings shall be explained in their respective textual passages.

Next, the text is explained. The exposition is divided into four parts: face-to-face confession (*pratimukha*), mental recollection (*manasikāra*), success through forgetfulness, and the boundary (*sīmā*). Regarding the first, face-to-face confession, there are two sections: the preliminary and the subsequent.
Within the preliminary section, the person upon whom one relies for the formal declaration (*jñapti*) refers to the individual before whom the confession is made.

In the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, chapter nineteen, the ritual deportment (*īryāpatha*) is fully detailed; here, the text is abbreviated. There are five elements to the formal procedure (*karmavācanā*): first, requesting the [monk] to maintain mindfulness; second, ...
[The sequence: First, one states one's own name. Third, the phrase "in a certain village," etc., clarifies the location upon which the practice depends;

this refers to naming the place according to the specific circumstance, so there is no need to list every detail, as seen below in the text regarding mountain caves, trees, open spaces, woodcutters, and so forth.

Fourth, it correctly explains the ritual procedure (*vidhi*): one makes a formal commitment (*samaya*) to dwell here. The former [term] distinguishes itself from the latter; "three months" excludes the fourth month.

"Summer" (grīṣma) refers to the exclusion of spring and winter. "Dwelling in retreat" (varṣā) signifies fixing the mind on remaining in one place. Regarding the "five types of dwellings" and so forth, these refer to the maintenance of necessary requisites;
this is intended to ensure that the monastic community from the four directions does not lose the benefit of their use. Because it is essential to be diligent, the number reaches three.
If one is observing the retreat within a village or similar location, the phrase regarding the maintenance of requisites is unnecessary, as [the conditions] are not...
In the quarters of the Saṃgha of the four directions, it is not permissible to act as a messenger for laypeople (*avadātavasana*).

According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, fascicle 24, when the Elder (*sthavira*) wishes to announce the commencement of the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*), he rises from his seat, assumes the proper deportment, and makes the announcement three times before the junior monks (*navaka*). Having finished speaking, the junior monks respond.
The Elder Mofangyi said: "Receiving and upholding [the precepts] from a junior monk is performed in the same manner as when facing an elder;
the only difference is that one says 'we mutually offer [ourselves]' to the elder, and the two feet [are positioned differently]. He further asked about those who uphold the Vinaya:

since the summer retreat must necessarily rely on a fifth Vinaya master, the practitioner of the ritual should pose the question according to the text. The rules for nuns are the same. Regarding the "last three months," it refers to the three [months].

Regarding the "moon" (the lunar month): this refers to the period from the seventeenth day onwards. The ritual procedure is the same as before; the only difference is that one refers to the "latter three months.

Therefore, it is said, "it is also like this. Next, regarding the "mental recitation" (*manasikāra*): since there is no *bhikṣu* available to perform the rite in their presence, although it is called "mental," it must nonetheless be spoken aloud.

Regarding the method of speaking aloud, there is no explicit text in the Vinaya; however, following the procedure for "confession in the presence of another" (*pratyakṣa-vinaya*), one should omit the first phrase.
This refers to cases such as being in a village or similar location. Furthermore, excluding the phrase regarding material requisites, one asks:

"If one has already performed the mental resolve for the *vassa* (rainy-season retreat), may one also perform the mental resolve for receiving [the day]? The answer is: "The *vassa* is the primary practice; its conclusion has a fixed limit. One fears violating that limit."

Therefore, it is permitted to perform the formal act through mental recollection (*manasikāra*). Receiving [the invitation] from Japan constitutes a distinct condition; it requires that the matter be formally stated and another person be requested to deliberate upon it.

Thus, there is no mental recollection [of the specific details]. Regarding "forgetting and yet accomplishing": this refers to one who has come from abroad for the purpose of the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat). Since there is no one to whom he can report his arrival, he forgets to perform the mental recollection.
The Buddha, seeing that this was consistent with the circumstances, also granted that the accomplishment was valid. Therefore, it is said: "If it is for the sake of the *varṣā*..."

Upon arrival, it is established. Regarding the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat), according to the text, this refers to one who has come from outside; for one who was already within this boundary, the allowance for forgetting [the formalities] is not granted.

However, when sought through the underlying principle (*artha*), it is universally granted without error. First, the rule regarding forgetting is the same as the second case: because the purpose is to remain settled and not depart.
Thirdly, the text relies on those who have come from outside as the basis for granting the exception. Once this single exception is granted, all instances of forgetting may proceed accordingly.
Furthermore, within the text: "Is it for one who has no basis that one may declare [the offense], or is it forgotten and not brought to mind? How could it be necessary that there be no basis?
If one who has a basis were not permitted to forget, then the allowance for forgetting would not apply;

yet, since the allowance for forgetting does not distinguish between those with a basis and those without, it is clear that this refers to the *dharmadhātu* (the realm of phenomena), and does not exclude those who have come from outside this location. Thus, the five-part [vinaya] and the ten... [etc.]
9. It is said that there was a bhikṣu who, having finished distributing the rooms and bedding, did not form the thought, "I am now observing the rains retreat," nor did he speak the words aloud.
Later, doubt and regret arose within him: "I have not formally entered the retreat; does this count as having entered the retreat? He reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said:

"If one has accepted a room and bedding for the purpose of the rains retreat, even if one has not formed the intention or spoken the words to enter it, it nevertheless constitutes entering the retreat."
This is termed the "rainy-season retreat" (*varṣā*). Next, the clarification of the boundary (*sīmā*) follows. The boundary is divided into two types:

the formal boundary (*karmasīmā*) and the natural boundary (*prakṛtisīmā*). Furthermore, regarding the term "garden" (*ārāma*), it does not refer to a garden for vegetables or fruit; rather, it refers to the very substance of the monastery.
In Sanskrit, *saṃghārāma* is incorrect; this should be translated as "monastic garden. It is also like the Anāthapiṇḍada Garden.

It is not distinct from the *ārāma*. For this reason, it is known that "boundary" (*sīmā*) and "garden" (*ārāma*) are one and the same. Furthermore, what is now called a "temple" (*si*) refers to a public institution;
it is also another name for a communal garden. Moreover, "temple" (*si*) can mean an administrative office; this is based on distinguishing between the garden and its boundaries.

There are two cases where both feet enter [the boundary], and one case where one foot enters [the boundary]. Thus, according to the specific circumstances, there are four divisions. Regarding the first case, where both feet enter the boundary:

previously, it was permitted that entering the boundary was accomplished even if forgotten; however, because this state has persisted for a long time, this specific thought arises. The Buddha has permitted its accomplishment.
"Now I have entered the boundary, and my mind truly does not forget it; however, because time was short, I did not have the opportunity to perform the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*).

I do not know whether this constitutes a valid *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) or not. The Buddha said: "Although you did not perform the ritual, this is not the same as the first two cases. Furthermore, since you remembered it without forgetting, it differs from the third case.
Nevertheless, because this mind—which originally arose—corresponds with the boundary, it is also declared to be accomplished. Next, enter..."
Regarding the principle of the monastery: if one foot enters the boundary while the other remains outside, it is judged as "both entered," according to the previous ruling.

[The questioner asks: "If I enter with only one foot, I do not know whether the formal act is accomplished. The Buddha said: "At such a time, when the deadline is drawing near and the urgency exceeds what was before, even if one acts according to one's original intention, the accomplishment is permitted.

[The questioner asks: "If entering the boundary with one foot is permitted to constitute the establishment of the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat), then exiting the boundary with one foot should constitute a breach of the summer retreat."
The explanation is intended for further benefit; thus, what is easily established becomes difficult to refute. If one were to reverse the previous statement, it would impair their practice.

If that were so, it would be like entering a pure ground (*śuddhāvāsa*): likewise, it is the same as the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat). Entering once constitutes contact; exiting once exempts one from the overnight stay. Each follows its own benefit and is not identical to the *varṣā*.
Contact requires double entry; exiting once exempts one from the overnight stay. Subsequent entry into the monastery garden is also the same.

Although the commentary on the text is thus, it shall next be explained by way of its meaning. There are three gates for explaining the meaning: first, enumerating the number of dharmas; second, determining their sequence;

third, distinguishing between the new and the old. Regarding the first gate, as for the dharmas: according to the restrictive rules (*niyama*), there are only two—*karmavācanā* (formal ritual action) and *manasikāra* (mental recitation).

According to the permissive rules (*anujñā*), there are four, adding *vismṛti-saṃpādana* (accomplishment through forgetfulness) and *sīmā* (boundary). Alternatively, including the boundary, they may be divided into four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Thus, there are seven dharmas for the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) in total. Regarding "before and after," this refers to the sequence of the retreat in relation to the formal procedures (*dharma*).

Because these seven types [of methods] apply to both the preceding and succeeding periods, they are universally applicable across both. However, when distinguished by the specific days, there are cases of universal application and limited application.

That is to say, the formal act (*karmavācanā*) and the mental resolve (*cetanā*) extend even to the sixty-first day; whereas the forgetting of the completion and the boundary (*sīmā*) are restricted solely to the first and last two days.

Accomplishment refers to having already reached the seventeenth [day]; one’s clarity is not yet equal to that of the preceding stage, yet there are still days remaining, so one does not worry about losing the subsequent stage.

If one considers the middle position in terms of both general and specific applications, the first two stages apply to all three [periods], while the remaining five are restricted; since the preceding and succeeding stages thus have their respective positions.

Regarding the clarification of the horizontal and vertical [arrangements] of the *dharmas*: if one takes four *dharmas* and divides them into eight by way of preceding and succeeding [periods], with only the first two in the middle, they total ten.
If separated to form seven, there are fourteen in the preceding and succeeding [periods], and likewise the first two in the middle, totaling sixteen.

Calculating all together, there are eighty *anvārakas* (summer retreats) across the five groups. Next, regarding the new and old: the first three *anvārakas* apply to both new and old; this does not depend on [the specific category].

Those who come from outside this boundary all achieve [the formal act of] *sīmā-bandha* (boundary-establishment). However, for those who already resided within the boundary prior to their arrival from outside, this principle does not apply;
therefore, it is said that one who comes specifically for the purpose of *vassa* (the rains retreat) shall thereby complete the *vassa*.
The section on the distribution of rooms has three parts: first, the introduction of the occasion; second, from "From now on" onwards, the selection of qualified persons for the task;

third, from "The distribution of rooms" onwards, the ritual procedure for the assignment. Within this [third part], there are four sections. The first is the formal assignment itself. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Sengqi lü), fascicle 34, states:
"For those who are far away, the distribution takes place on the tenth, twentieth, or thirtieth day of the fourth month; for those who are nearby, it takes place on the fourteenth or fifteenth day."

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, chapter twenty-five, states: At that time, the bhikṣus were distributing the monastic bedding daily. The Buddha said, "This should not be done. Listen: at the end of spring, one should distribute the bedding;
on the first day of summer, one should enter the rains retreat (*varṣā*). One should use only those monastic quarters belonging to the Saṃgha from the four directions that are pure.
Therefore, it says: 'If wicked bhikṣus come, one should not give [the bedding] to them. There is no text here regarding giving to śrāmaṇeras. [Regarding] receiving the precepts..."
Regarding the Dharma: one who is capable of protecting [the property] may be permitted to give it. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Sengqi lü), fascicle 34, states:

"One must not give a room to a śrāmaṇera. If the teacher says, 'Simply give it; I shall take care of it,' then it should be given. The second period concerns the various bhikṣus gathering at locations such as the *duji* (assembly hall) and so forth, where they should not divide [the property].
The third period concerns the various bhikṣus recording the places for dividing and residing. The fourth [period] concerns those bhikṣus... [and so forth].
Regarding the ritual for the transfer and use of bedding and requisites: "fixed bedding" refers to a case where the intention of the donor is restricted to a specific location;
"unfixed" refers to a case where the intention of the donor is not so restricted. This is the distinction between the two.

Next, the section on miscellaneous dwellings has seven parts: first, opening the subsequent dwelling; second, listing the two types of peaceful abodes; third, allowing for prior or subsequent occupancy;
fourth, the limits of years according to the merit of the dharma, which necessitates taking the final [term]; fifth, what should be sent away and what should not; sixth, receiving divisible items;
seventh, whether or not to take bedding and furniture.
Next, the section on the dwelling has two parts: first, clarifying the location; second, from "At that time, the cowherd... onwards, clarifying the person.
Although it is said to rely on the person, one must necessarily take up the location; as for the location, it does not depart from the ritual procedure, which is spontaneous.
Next is the method for departing from the boundary. This section is divided into four parts: first, the method for receiving the *pārivāsika* (the day of departure);
second, from "At that time, the World-Honored One" onwards, it concerns the allowance for shifting the summer retreat (*varṣa*) due to the difficulty of protecting the Saṃgha;

third, from "At that time, the bhikṣus at the residence" onwards, there are four phrases of text concerning the noble permission to go directly for the sake of harmonizing the Saṃgha; fourth, at that time, there were certain... [bhikṣus].

The World-Honored One accepted [the seven-day leave]; if the period was not completed by the end of the seventh day, it would constitute a violation of the precept. The first section contains two parts:
first, the procedure for receiving the seven-day leave through face-to-face declaration; second, the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for the one-month leave.

First, a general explanation of the meaning is provided through a sixfold analysis. First, determining whether the object of focus (*ālambana*) accords with the precepts or not. Second, clarifying the combination or separation of objects of focus.
Third, whether the reception is obtained in advance or not. Fourth, whether a double reception is permissible or not. Fifth, whether the objects of focus mutually constitute one another or not.

Sixth, whether the object returns once the matter is concluded or not. Regarding the first gate, as for the "object": when receiving [the precepts], the formal act (*karmavācanā*) must necessarily accord with the precepts. For...

Regarding "unlawful [conditions]" and so forth: if one proceeds with the formal ritual (karmavācanā) under such conditions, it is not accomplished. Although the conditions for the meaning [of the ritual] are immeasurable, they are summarized into five.
First, the condition of the field of the Three Jewels, as explained in the text. For instance, the monk Kāla had business requiring him to go among the forest trees;

furthermore, unfaithful great ministers seized the robes and other requisites—such as food and drink—belonging to the Buddha and the Saṃgha, and harboring evil intent, they wished to excavate the Jetavana.

The thorough channeling of the Huan River is the condition for the Buddha and the Sangha. Furthermore, the text states that reciting sixty kinds of sutras, such as the *Brahmajāla-sūtra*, in search of others with whom to recite together is the condition for the Dharma.
Moreover, the sixth fascicle of the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* says: "During the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*), there are no [external] affairs."
One must not stay outside the boundary for even one night. If there is a necessary matter, one should receive the seven-day authorization (*saptāha-vidhi*).

Whether it be for the sake of a stūpa or for the sake of the Dharma, on account of such causes and conditions, it is permitted for the two groups of renunciants and the five groups of lay followers to go forth. The conditions for generating the wholesome and extinguishing the unwholesome are as stated in the text.

Receiving the precepts and performing repentance for the arising of wholesome states are the three paths for extinguishing evil. The causes and conditions regarding the illness of a layperson are as stated in the text.

Regarding the illness of a faithful upāsaka, or matters of grief and distress concerning parents, or matters of benefit, as well as that which the *Vinaya-śāstra* says—such as for the sake of the illness of one’s upādhyāya or ācārya—the four types of laypeople create meritorious conditions as described in the text. [The same applies to] a great minister.

They are capable of performing acts of benefit or harm. Because the kindness of parents is profound, whether one has faith or lacks faith, it is permitted for them to receive [the precepts] for a limited period.
For other laypeople who possess faith, they are permitted to go [to the preceptor] as described in the text.

When a donor invites a bhikṣu, saying, "I wish to give [offerings]," these five reasons for seeking robes, bowls, and medicinal herbs for oneself are as described in the text. One should not do so solely for the sake of food and drink; therefore, one should accept [the invitation].

One may go for seven days for the sake of robes, alms bowls, and so forth. Although it is permitted to go for the sake of robes and bowls, one must do so for the purpose of receiving offerings in accordance with the Dharma;
if it is for the purpose of seeking profit through trade, one should not go. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, chapter nineteen, states: "Whether there is an invitation or no invitation..."
Furthermore, it is permitted to go outside the boundary for all purposes, provided one returns within seven days. It is further stated:

"From now on, if there is business concerning the Buddha, Dharma, or Sangha, or private matters, beyond the seven-day limit, it is additionally permitted to perform the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (motion and second resolution) to receive [permission] for fifteen days or one month.

Regarding subsequent circumstances involving separation or reunion, one should perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) according to the specific conditions; even if many such acts are performed, they will certainly be valid. As it says:

There is no fault even when conditions coincide, just as in the case of the "remorse for leftovers" (*śeṣa-parivāsa*) or the three types of *utkṣepaka* (suspensions). Question: If the conditions are equal in length, it may be appropriate to combine them;

however, can one obtain [the full duration] by piling up many short conditions to reach a long one? Answer: The text states that if it does not reach seven days, one must receive [the *poṣadha*] again.

Fifteen days or one month are now obtained by piling [the days]; therefore, since it does not reach [the limit] through combination, what fault would there be? Next, regarding receiving [the *poṣadha*] while suspended (*pralambita*).
As for this: if one relies on prior conditions, it must necessarily manifest in the present;

if one were to point toward the future in advance and receive [the precepts] beforehand, it would not be valid—just as in the case of the "disease of non-lifting" (*an-uddharaṇa*), where performing the *pārivāsika* or *āvarhana* rites while under censure (*ākrośa*) does not constitute success. There are many such instances.

If one considers the day of actual application, there is logically a sense of "anticipation," just as although one has obtained the Dharma, one does not immediately complete its practice. In that case, the principle should also apply to the seven-day medicine (*saptāha-bhaiṣajya*).

However, the answer is that because the medicine is prepared according to the ritual procedure, it is permitted for seven days; therefore, from the day the addition of the ritual is performed, it is established as a formal acceptance with the original intent of departing the boundary.
Thus, departure from the boundary is set as the limit. Regarding the subsequent question of whether one should receive [the precepts] again:

the traditional commentary states that since the establishment of the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) is for the purpose of cultivating the path with single-minded devotion, why would it be necessary to receive them again? For this reason, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* permits receiving [the *saptarātra-anujñā*] for only one period of seven nights, and does not allow it beyond that.
One receives [the *pārivāsika* status] for two periods of seven nights. Thus, we know there is no repetition. Furthermore, the text states: "First, one goes out for seven days.

If those seven days are exhausted, one should receive [the status] for thirty-nine nights and go out. If those thirty-nine nights are exhausted, one should break the *varṣa* (rainy season retreat) and go out.

According to the meaning of this passage, we know there is no repetition. If one were permitted to receive it repeatedly, what would be the reason for going out on the day of receiving it? The answer is: to break the *varṣa*.

[The text] ends here. If one were to cite further passages, they would mostly establish [rules] based on specific circumstances; there is the principle that those who have already received [the precepts] do not receive them again, which is refuted according to the occasion.
I shall not explain this at length. Now, I resolve that it is not so. Originally, because faults arose from wandering about, the rule was established to require *varṣā* (the rains retreat).

Now that the retreat has been entered and one advances in cultivation, it is clearly free of transgression. It is simply for the sake of the two benefits (*svārtha* and *parārtha*) so as not to be in vain. The Sangha grants...
Regarding the Dharma: since it is not a matter of exclusive intent, what hindrance is there to receiving it again? The text merely states that the Buddha has not yet permitted such a thing to go;
it does not say he has not yet permitted going again. For this reason, we know that one may do so whenever there is a valid cause.

Furthermore, if the Saṃgha has urgent business and permission has been granted to manage it, and the matter is not yet concluded, how could one simply terminate it? Moreover, in this text, the causes and conditions are enumerated... [the text continues].

It is brief; it simply says to allow them to go, and does not mention any prohibition against returning. Furthermore, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* permits one to stay near a holder of the Vinaya for seven days to travel back and forth.

How could there be any prior doubt regarding the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*)? Thus, one is permitted to go and inquire. If there is a need for a final decision later on, one should not fail to send someone to consult him.

Such a meaning of severance remains obstructed and unpenetrated; yet, if one exhausts its ultimate purpose, all true benefits will be attained. Furthermore, if it were not permissible to receive [the precepts] again, the ritual procedure would be invalid.
If this performance is invalid, why would it not be included among those cases? How, then, is it to be understood? The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā* states:

It is permitted for one week, but not for two weeks. Furthermore, the seven-day period is received for the purpose of extinguishing disputes, even to the point of causing those who have caused a schism to settle and depart.
This differs from the *Śāriputra-vinaya* (Ten Recitation Vinaya); they are distinct and cannot be conflated. One must not use the separate texts of other schools to confuse these ritual procedures.

If one were to dismiss this case as being similar to the *Śāriputra-vinaya* and thus not requiring repetition, then this present text serves as a reconciliation, whereas the former [text] does not accept that position.

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations) is likewise. Since these [texts] are already dissimilar, it is clear that they belong to different schools (*nikāya*). Furthermore, upon examining the meaning of those passages, their intended significance appears to differ.
Regarding the prior reception of one or seven days [of probation]: once the period is completed, one receives it again; it should not be added twice before it has been used.

Moreover, as for the matter of not being resolved—sending away one who causes schism—it is merely because the purification of the matter is difficult to achieve and the time of its resolution is unknown; therefore, one sends away the one who caused the schism to establish peace. It is not... [the end of the sentence].
One must receive the formal authorization (*jñapti*). Regarding the subsequent conditions for mutual fulfillment: the ritual of receiving the authorization is established based on the actual facts;

since these facts vary in duration, they are categorized into three grades. These three grades of conditions must not be confused or interchanged. If the conditions and the ritual are confused or interchanged, none shall be valid.

Even if only two or three days remain before the end of the summer retreat (*varṣā*), if one encounters a long-term condition, the *karmavācanā* (formal motion) must be added; otherwise, it shall not be valid.
Seeing that the day was nearly spent, one should immediately depart using the *pratimukha* (face-to-face) procedure. Departing in this manner constitutes a violation of the summer retreat (*varṣa*).
Just as with the seven-day medicine or the lifetime medicine, it is not strictly necessary to consume them for seven days or for the remainder of one's life before adding the two procedures;

even if there is only a small amount, the two procedures are added. This case is exactly the same: one adds the procedures according to the specific circumstances. Furthermore, after obtaining the [medicinal] substance, one uses it...

Nor do they alternate with one another. For example, if one acts as a *karmadāna* for the Buddha’s reception [of offerings] and then proceeds to manage the affairs of the Saṃgha, each such deviation cannot be recorded in full;

however, in any case where this occurs, the summer retreat (*varṣā*) is entirely invalid. If there are originally many conditions, and one adds yet another practice, even if these are applied unevenly, the summer retreat is still not broken.
The reason for this is that all these conditions possess their own established rules; one should act according to the original conditions and manage the affairs accordingly.

All such persons obtain [the status]. Regarding "returning after the matter is concluded": an ancient commentary states that once one has received [the *pravāraṇā*] and gone outside the boundary, one must return when the matter is finished.
