If it is surplus material, although it was previously purified through the rite of *deśanā*, if it is later made into a robe and accepted as one's own possession, the method of purification is lost. This...

If one discards the robe later, it must be re-consecrated (*śuddhi*). However, if its color fades or if it is further enhanced with dye, the original consecration is not lost. According to the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*:

"If a robe becomes old and its color fades over time, the formal holding (*dhāraṇa*) is not lost. Furthermore, it is said that if it is later dyed with a superior color, the consecration is likewise not lost."
Next follows the commentary on the text. There are eight sections within the text. First, the field [of merit] is shown to Ānanda, instructing him to emulate the making of robes.
This section contains four parts: first, showing the field and instructing him to emulate it; second, from "At that time, Ānanda" onwards, he receives the command and is taught how to make them;

third, from "At that time" onwards, the Buddha praises Ānanda, citing his similarities with those of the past and future, so that he may develop reverence for him across all three periods of time; fourth, from "From this day forward."
First, the permission to cut and sew [the robes]. Second, from "Then the bhikṣus... onwards, the explanation of the number of strips. Third, from "At that time, the bhikṣus...

onwards, the method for wearing the robe. Fourth, from "At that time, Śāriputra... onwards, the regulation of the hook-fastening method. Fifth, from "At that time, the World-Honored One was in Rājagṛha...
onwards, the regulation of the number of patches on the robe. Within this fifth section, there are four further parts: first, seeing the faults of possessing too many robes.

1. Recalling the restriction. 2. At that time, [the Nāga king] accepted the gift of the Āmra grove; *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, chapter 20. The Buddha said: "Simply offer it to the Saṃgha; I am included within the Saṃgha.
The daughter of the Naga (Nandā) received the instruction and immediately offered it to the Saṃgha. 3. At that time, [the Buddha] gave rise to a thought regarding his place of residence.
4. When the night had passed, he informed the assembly and established a regulation. 6. At that time, in another dwelling place, [the text] clarifies...
[Is it] appropriate or not? At the seventh [occasion], the World-Honored One was at Pāṭaliputra and established the measurements for robes.

At the eighth [occasion], the World-Honored One further clarified whether it is appropriate or not. Within this, there are four sections. First, there are three statements clarifying whether it is appropriate to keep [the robe].

Second, from "At that time" onwards, it is explained that the upper garment must not be used as a lower garment. Third, from "At that time, the bhikṣu" onwards, there are ten matters concerning laypeople.
The Dharma may not be employed. Regarding the four seasons, there are ten matters below concerning which the dharmas of external paths (tīrthika) may not be employed.
Third, the third section clarifies the acquisitions of the Saṃgha at improper times (*akāla*). Within this text, there are four parts: first, the rules for acquisitions of the Saṃgha;
second, "At that time, the World-Honored One was in Śrāvastī," and so forth, wherein the two assemblies manifest the aforementioned acquisitions of the Saṃgha; third, [the section on] various...
A bhikṣu should reflect in this way regarding whether or not to grant [the precepts] to those who have committed transgressions and so forth.

Fourth: at that time, the Buddha was in Śrāvastī; the following concerns the methods for tending to the sick, rewarding labor, inquiring about debts, and so forth. The preceding text has two parts: first, the methods subsumed under each individual section;
second, from "At that time there was another resident... onwards, the methods subsumed under the two sections. The former part further has two divisions.

First, regarding the property of a donor (*dānapati*), it clarifies that it belongs to the Saṃgha. Second, from "At that time in Śrāvastī" onwards, regarding the property of deceased bhikṣus, the principle is the same:
it belongs to the Saṃgha. The preceding text has three parts: first, citing the initial occasion and the method of distributing by counting people and casting lots;

second, from "when the bhikṣus were dividing the robes" onwards, the methods such as performing the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) for distribution; third, from "at that time there was a residence" onwards.
Is it permissible to divide and receive [the portion]? The preceding text further divides into three parts. First, the permission to receive and divide the alms.

Second, from "Furthermore, if one does not know" onwards, this demonstrates the method for casting lots (*śalākā*). Third, from "At the time of distributing the objects" onwards, this clarifies the case where a guest arrives;

there are eight phrases, of which the first four indicate that [the portion] should be given because the distribution is not yet finished. Within these, the second and third phrases merely correspond to the preceding formalities. Furthermore, there is...
There is a slight distinction, but they are not entirely different. The latter four [categories] should not be granted, as they have already been concluded.
Because there are two or more persons, there is the designation of "casting lots" (*śalākā*); because there is only one person, there is the title of "receiving the portion with joy."

This does not refer to the initial stage of making a mental determination regarding the distribution of the Dharma. If there are others who arrive after the distribution has already been completed, it is not appropriate to give them a share;

if they arrive before it is completed, then it is appropriate to give them a share. The subsequent phrase is also like this. Next, there are two sections of text concerning the ritual procedures for performing the *karmavācanā* (formal act) and other methods:

first, citing the circumstances to demonstrate the method, as in the case where robes such as those made of *vāśu* were brought by mistake; second, clarifying the ritual protocol for the three methods of distribution and inclusion.

Within the legal procedures for the Saṃgha, there are two types of *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (formal acts consisting of one motion and one announcement). The first is the *jñapti-dvitīya* for appointing a person; the text explicitly states "one should hold [the robe]" and so forth, citing the method for assigning the distribution.

Although the procedure for appointing the distributor is omitted here, it is established by analogy with the *jñapti-dvitīya* for persons. Both the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* and the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* contain the full textual account.

Among those who distribute the rice porridge and so forth, there is also the expression "distributing the robes. Furthermore, when Trapusa oversees the affairs of the Saṃgha, there is also the formal procedure of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a motion followed by one proclamation).

In the second instance of the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* for distribution, the wording is inverted; therefore, it says "one should hold [the robes]," and so on. If this were to follow the correct sequence, it should say:

"By means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*, one should hold the robes and give them to a single bhikṣu to distribute. Its essence is the method of entrustment and distribution. Moreover, as for the distribution...

The note regarding the robes of the deceased refers to the preceding passage. As for the text stating, "The Saṃgha now gives [the robes] to bhikṣu so-and-so," this is because they have been entrusted to a specific individual;

thus, there is no distribution among the four quarters. Regarding how that person should give them, one person should be appointed from within the Saṃgha through *karmavācanā* to perform the distribution.

This is not the formal text. The term "Saṃgha" here excludes transfer to a private individual and instead requires that they be returned to the community. Therefore, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, fascicle 28, states:
If a bhikṣu receives a robe through a formal act of the Saṃgha (saṃgha-karman) and, having taken it, refuses to return it, saying:
"This is truly a gift; it is well given, well received, and the matter is properly settled according to the Dharma; it has been finalized within the Saṃgha. Why should I return it? the Buddha said:

"That bhikṣu should be instructed as follows: 'This gift was given for the sake of purity. It would be good if you were to return it. If you do not return it, [you should be dealt with accordingly].'"

One should forcibly take back the items and perform an auspicious confession (*kṣānti*). Once the items have been returned, one should follow the instructions given; this constitutes the method of distribution (*vibhāga-dharma*).

There is no need to laboriously perform another formal act (*karmavācanā*). The *Tiyi* (The Body) states: "The person appointed for that purpose must further perform a formal act of two announcements (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) regarding the distribution of the items.
Since these are monastic property, it is improper to divide them arbitrarily. Therefore, the text says: 'One should take the robes and give them to a single person.'"

The Buddha commanded that the distribution be carried out through a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation). Now, to explain this: it does not constitute a separate ritual act; rather, it simply refers back to the aforementioned *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*.

One holds the robes and gives them to a single bhikṣu, who then proceeds directly to distribute them without the need for further formal procedures (*dharmakriyā*). If there are five or more people, both of these methods are complete;
however, with only four people, the appointment and entrustment are not accomplished, as the number of monks required for the appointment and entrustment is not fixed. Thus, the Saṃgha...

It must be handled through a formal ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*). The procedure should be stated as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen. Whatever robes or non-robes are present at this dwelling place should be distributed by the Saṃgha currently before us.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent. Now the Saṃgha currently before us shall distribute the clothing and requisites.

This is the motion (*jñapti*). The formal act is accomplished according to the motion. The reason for this is known from the *Mātṛkā-sūtra*, chapter eight, which states: [The text continues with the citation from the Mātṛkā-sūtra.]

Regarding the fourfold communal procedure (*catuṣka-saṃvāsa-dharma*): when five persons live together and one person passes away, the remaining four perform the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) to divide [the deceased’s] property.

This text does not state that it is to be transferred successively to one person. Regarding the fivefold communal procedure (*pañcaka-saṃvāsa-dharma*): the five persons perform the ritual to divide the property of the deceased bhikṣu;
the four persons perform the ritual to bestow [their shares] upon one person, who then in turn bestows them upon the Saṃgha. Subsequently, the entire body [of the Saṃgha] may divide them together.
Since it was only upon reaching five people that the words of "transference" (turning over the ritual) were uttered, we know that for two types of rituals, five or more persons are required.
In the case of a novice (śrāmaṇera) acting as an agent, although his person does not count toward the legal quorum, he must simply be present within the boundary at the time the ritual is performed.
This shall immediately pertain to the Dharma, and one shall likewise obtain one's share. Next is the procedure for the three statements in the presence of a counterpart.

The ritual formula should be recited as follows: "Two elders, please bear this in mind: whatever robes or non-robes exist in this residence are to be distributed among the present Saṃgha; however, there is no Saṃgha present here."

"This is our portion" (recited three times). However, because the ritual is performed by an individual and the legal authority is weak, it is necessary for each person to personally declare their intention.

This is similar to the procedures for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) and the invitation to criticism (*pravāraṇā*), where one expresses both the intent and the substance. Furthermore, according to the scriptural text, while the mutual acceptance through the three-fold formula is common to both parties, the distribution of the portions differs.
The old commentary states: "Since this text does not say that each person must accept the portion through the three-fold formula, there is only one [portion]."
When people perform the ritual (*dharma-karman*), if they say, "This is our shared portion," it is indeed a shared portion;

there is no need for mutual performance, unlike the *pravāraṇā* ceremony where each person individually expresses their purity. This interpretation is incorrect, for the *Mātṛkā-sūtras* all contain statements regarding mutual exchange of speech.
Furthermore, in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, fascicle 28, there is a textual passage concerning the formal procedure (*karmavācanā*) for "this" and "that," which cannot be recorded in full here.

Next, regarding the method of mental recollection (*manasikāra-dharma*), one should say: "In this residence, whatever robes or non-robes are present, the Saṃgha should divide them; however, there is no Saṃgha present in this place."

This is my threefold explanation of the "this is my portion" (*idam me bhāga*). Next is the establishment of the "not [formally] stated" (*anukta*), which consists of twelve phrases. The first six pairs concern whether it is established through *saṃgha-karman* (formal act of the community).

The latter six concern whether it is established through the three utterances (*trivācika*) or mental recollection (*manasikāra*). Alternatively, the former six may be understood as concerning *karman* and face-to-face procedures (*pratyakṣa*).
[The first] three are non-establishment; because even two or three people must divide [the food], they are likewise non-establishment.

Next, regarding the six cases concerning the establishment or non-establishment of receiving through mental intention (*manasikāra*), when one person alone receives directly without dividing, [it is established]. Among these two sets of six, in each case the first three are non-establishment and the latter three are establishment.
Furthermore, among the four sets of three, in each case the first two constitute an offense and the third does not constitute an offense.

Next, the treatment of the property of a deceased bhikṣu is explained. Its meaning is the same as that of the "non-timely monastic gift" (*akāla-saṃgha-dakṣiṇā*). First, its meaning shall be clarified.
According to the preceding and following texts, there are five categories of legal inclusion: first, inclusion by the harmonious assembly; second, inclusion by the law of the heterodox or orthodox;

third, the law regarding death while in debt; fourth, the law regarding death while under formal suspension (*ukkhepanīya-kamma*); and fifth, the law regarding death while without a fixed residence. The meanings of the latter four sections shall be explained according to the text, as they all...

There is a textual passage that facilitates the explanation of the meaning. Regarding the first section on meaning, there are two cases: those where the requirements are complete and those where they are not.

As for the death of a *śrāmaṇera*, there is no explicit text in this Vinaya; however, in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* (T. 1421), fascicle 20, the procedure is identical where the requirements are complete.

The text states: "A certain *śrāmaṇera* passed away. The bhikṣus did not know how to dispose of his belongings. They reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said: 'If he had already given [the items] during his lifetime...'"
A person should give it to them. If they did not give it away during their lifetime, the *saṃgha* present before them should divide it. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* is largely the same.
In the thirty-first [chapter] of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, regarding the death of a *śrāmaṇera*, the bhikṣus asked the Buddha:

"To whom do these robes, bowls, and belongings belong? The Buddha said: "They belong to the *upādhyāya*. According to the underlying principle, the *upādhyāya* should distribute them to the *saṃgha*; the *upādhyāya* may not [retain them].

He shall take them and incorporate them into himself. Within the section on "Possession," there are categories of pure and impure. Regarding the impure, there are three types: first, death due to committing a grave offense (*pārājika*).

There are three cases for committing a grave offense: first, when one has not yet been expelled, the principle is the same as the standard regulation; second, when one has already been expelled and enters among lay relatives; third, regarding a novice (*śrāmaṇera*) in training.
According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, chapter twenty-eight, at the time of death, the present community (*saṃgha*) should divide the robes and bowl.
I. Objects. II. The four bases for offenses, such as censure (*tarjanīya*), as well as the *parivāsa* (probation) and so forth, are adjudicated according to their common purity.

III. Death while under suspension (*ukkhepana*), as explained in the following text. Next, regarding death after purification, there should be four sections: 1. Determining cohabitation and shared life; 2. Determining the distinctions between heavy and light [offenses];
3. Clarifying the care of the sick and the distribution of labor; 4. Distinguishing whether the assignment of property is valid or not. These three [sections] follow below.
Section on the Gate. This shall also be explained according to the text. First, regarding those who have made a "joint vow" (*sahaja*):

if, from the outset, one has made a commitment for one matter or more—regardless of the number—and all have joined together in this commitment, then after the commitment has been made, if one dies or abandons the path, their property and belongings should be divided equally and entered into the Sangha.
If one violates the commitment, they commit an offense proportional to the value [of the goods]. If one is not a joint-vower but falsely claims to be so, it is according to that [deception].

Regarding the acquisition of objects: one also commits an offense by calculating their value. Furthermore, if a teacher has no intention [to give] but provides an object to a disciple, that which has already been given belongs to the disciple;

that which has not yet been given belongs to the Saṃgha. Next, the determination of gravity and lightness: within this, the textual meaning comprises three parts. First, listing the thirteen chapters and establishing them as belonging to the intent of the Saṃgha.

Second, it is necessary to distinguish and determine the two categories of gravity and lightness. Third, the separate explanation according to the text, including what is consistent with the division and what is inconsistent.
The first thirteen chapters concern the saṃghārāma, up to the many robes, alms bowls, and *niṣīdana* mats.

Regarding the reason for entering the Saṃgha: all who have joined the monastic order share the same practice as water and milk; they coordinate their three karmas and equalize the six points of harmony (*ṣaḍ-samagra-dharma*). Once born into this state, whatever they produce is gathered under the laws of the Saṃgha;
thus, even upon death, their belongings must be returned to the community. Even if they were to offer them to the Buddha or the Dharma, the bhikṣus [must still return them].

There is no inheritance. This applies even to kings, ministers, and relatives; it is all likewise. Because there is a distinction between the ordained and the laity, and their respective statuses differ, they cannot rely upon one another.
Upon death, one does not enter into the other's estate. Therefore, it is said that whether one has many acquaintances or none at all, everything belongs to the Sangha.

Next, the gravity [of offenses] shall be determined. For the time being, these categories are established as three: first, items that the Buddha prescribed for possession, such as the three robes and their like;

second, items whose possession is not permitted, such as fields, houses, gardens, groves, slaves, and their like; third, items whose possession is permitted, such as extra robes, alms bowls, precious objects, medicines, and their like.
Among these three types of items, the first belongs to the light category because they are essential requisites for the Path; the second belongs to the heavy category.
Because the hindrance to the Path is profound, this is summarized into two gates: the light and the heavy. Within the third category of objects, three distinctions are made:

first, lightness and heaviness by nature; second, lightness and heaviness by substance; and third, lightness and heaviness according to utility. Regarding "lightness by nature," this refers to the ten types of robes and the threads used for them.
Since the robes produced from them are already limited to the category of light items, how could the constituent threads themselves not be included?
"Weighty" refers to items such as various coins and treasures, food, medicine, dyeing materials, cauldrons, pots, jars, and bowls—specifically sixteen such items.
"Light in terms of substance" refers to all personal belongings such as skirts and shirts.

"Heavy in terms of substance" refers to items such as large woolen rugs, large and small tents, screen-walls, tables, and fans. "Light in terms of utility" refers to items such as clothing chests and alms-bowls.

Regarding items such as needle cases and razors, the phrase "according to their use" refers to things like door-curtains, beds, canopies, curtains, screens, tables, carts, litters, combs, and awnings.
Now, by classifying these according to their nature and function, the three light items are subsumed under the first category.
Those items where the nature and function both follow the heavy classification are subsumed under the second heavy category. Next...
Third is the detailed explanation according to the text. Among the preceding thirteen chapters, they are condensed into nine sections:
the first six are grouped as two pairs to form three; the ninth and tenth are combined; and the remaining five remain as five. Thus, they are collectively categorized by means of these nine gates.

In the first gate, there is no further distinct meaning beyond its entry into the "heavy" category. Regarding the second gate, which pertains to items belonging to individual rooms, this refers to the furnishings within the rooms.

Regarding items such as cloths or screens, or objects that have been relinquished, if one builds a dwelling for oneself and the owner dies before the dwelling is completed—whether those items have been transformed or not—they are all to be adjudicated according to their current status of lightness or gravity.
Since both the items and the dwelling belong to the bhikṣu, this differs from cases where they are relinquished to the Buddha, the Dharma, or an individual;
for if the items belong specifically to an individual, they enter into that person’s possession. Third.

The gates, vases, poor-quality items, and horned vessels, etc., all have fixed quantities according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*. This differs from those [rules] where everything is considered heavy.
Regarding various heavy objects—namely, tables, benches, medicinal herbs, dyeing liquids, wood, stones, and so forth—the fourth section treats them all as heavy.
Regarding the rules on leather, it says: "Brocade mattresses, multi-colored bedding, and woolen carpets; if one uses otter fur for a mattress... [The Buddha said...]
It was said that this was improper. Regarding the fifth gate, the *ilindata*: tradition says it refers to a walking screen, or perhaps it is the skin of a deer king.

A *moraka* is a small canopy; a *mora-moraka* is a large canopy, or perhaps it belongs to the class of *tappas*. As for *kūṭāpa*, it refers to a solid-colored [woolen cloth] suitable for the Dharma robes;
therefore, its distribution was permitted. Blankets (*śāṭī*) are also of this substance; those that are light and thin are [suitable].

Regarding those who wear garments with pleats and folds: even if they exceed the prescribed measure, they may still be categorized as light. This differs from the five-fold woolen blankets (*pañcaka-paṭa*), which all fall under the category of heavy bedding and must be divided among the community.
In the sixth section, the *nīla* (blue/black) person falls under the category of heavy property; all their private belongings enter into the private use of that individual.

Upon death, they pass to their relatives. If there are no relatives, it is permissible for the Saṃgha to use them. The third fascicle of the *Mātṛkā-vibhaṅga* states: "If there are male or female slaves..."

One should release them and let them go. If they are not released, one should employ them as *śrāmaṇeraka* laborers for the Saṃgha; camels, horses, oxen, and donkeys shall be used for transporting goods for the resident monks of the monastery.
Seventh gate: Water jars and basins. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, there is a fixed number;

by this standard, all such items constitute a heavy offense (*sthūlātyaya*), regardless of whether they are many or few, large or small. Eighth gate: The five types of metal implements and tools should be distributed.
There are two categories: first, those that constitute the vessel itself and must all be placed inside [the robe]; second, those things contained within the vessel that may be divided.
These refer to the razor, the alms bowl, the needle, and the needle case. Since the substance [of the case] is like a needle case, it should be divided; the same applies to the sheath for the knife.

As for the small knife and the scissors, the *Mātṛkā* (Third Scripture) states they are divisible; the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* are likewise. Regarding the incense burner, there is...

Regarding the distribution: it is not the same as [the case of] those who are capable of making offerings. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "Iron, copper, stone, and ceramic utensils are all permitted to be divided.

The third fascicle of the *Mātṛkā-sūtra* also says: "Incense burners may be divided. Furthermore, within the section of the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* concerning light objects that may be divided, there are also mentions of incense burners, incense spoons, and incense vessels.
Since these texts are authoritative, their principles are difficult to contravene; the only exception being those items specifically designated for the worship of the Buddha.

Regarding that which is "not subject to redistribution": this [item] belongs exclusively to the Buddha and must not be divided at will. Since the incense burner is the primary object, the same principle applies to its accompanying items.

Furthermore, the text states: "There are also items that should not be divided. What are they? When the person who was filial is present, all the scriptures and Vinaya texts should be distributed to those capable of reciting them.
If there is no one present among the *saṃgha* to whom they may be distributed, they should be given to those capable of recitation."
Regarding the reciter: these items may not be divided or sold. Since this is the case for both the Sūtras and the Vinaya, it should likewise apply to the commentaries and their containers.
As for the scripture racks, they are not fixed; those that originally belonged to the Sūtras follow the Sūtras. If they belong to a person, they should be included among the heavy [category].

The ninth category consists of all items that accord with the Dharma, which are all collectively included in the light [category]. Furthermore, the water-strainer is essential for the path; by principle, it should be included in the light [category].
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that those who care for the sick should be rewarded. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* permits the distribution of leather sandals.

Thus, one knows that boots, shoes, and slippers are all treated in the same manner. Since bowls may be distributed, it follows that items such as bowl-rings (*kañcī*), spoons, and chopsticks are likewise so.
This text permits the distribution of *kūpya* vessels; these are of the same category as bowl-rings. These points are presented here in a general summary rather than in full detail.

Next is the procedure for the inclusion [of property] by the two assemblies (*ubhayasaṃgha*). Within the previous category of inclusion, there was the property of lay donors (*dānapati*) and the property of deceased persons;

now, within these two assemblies, it is likewise the same as before. First, regarding the property of lay donors, the distribution is as described above. Second, regarding the property of deceased persons, it can only be appraised and recorded by those who possess faith;
for fear that the property of the Saṃgha might be lost, it is given to whichever of the five groups of monastics arrives first. This is the ancient interpretation.

It is said: regardless of whether the offense is grave or light, all shall enter the prior possession. However, for light offenses, one does not wait for formal legal procedures; they enter the person immediately.

As for grave offenses, because they do not pertain to personal property, they are disposed of according to who arrived first, and thus revert to the common property of the Sangha (*sādhāraṇa-vastu*). It is in accordance with this principle that [the rule] is established.

The property of the deceased is also the same as that of a *dānapati* (donor). However, because laypeople do not understand the rules for making offerings, they may think there are two sets of rules for its distribution.

To clarify that this is not so: this is a case of property belonging to those without a fixed residence (*anālaya*). Since the two assemblies (*dvaya-saṃgha*) do not share it equally, it is not a matter governed by the rules for the two assemblies.
Fearing that the property of the Saṃgha might be lost, one should dispatch it to those who arrived first. Once those who arrived first have received it, they must...

Investigate the matter. If it is the property of a bhikṣu, send it to his home temple if its location is known; if the location is unknown, deliver it to a nearby monastery. The same applies to the death of a bhikṣuṇī.
This is done only for fear of losing monastic property, requiring that what was previously brought be handed over.

It is not because what was previously brought is entitled to receive it. If it were something that should rightfully be received because it was previously brought, then even heavy items should be included; why would only light ones be so? Furthermore...
If there is someone to take it, it must be formally added [to the inventory]; since it is property belonging to the Saṃgha, how could it be entered [into the records] arbitrarily?

If no one comes to claim it, it should be sent to a nearby location. One should simply take the nearest place, making no distinction between monks and nuns. Although it has been received at the nearby location, it is not yet to be entered [into the inventory] immediately;

one must first inspect the items and dispose of them as previously prescribed. Thus, the *Śāriputrābhidharma* (or *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*), chapter fifty-seven, states: "A certain bhikṣu died. This deceased bhikṣu..."
The Bhikṣu [Kātyāyana] entrusted his robes and bowl to a bhikṣuṇī’s vihāra and did not know how to report this to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"If a bhikṣu dies before having entrusted his robes and bowl to a bhikṣuṇī, the present community of bhikṣus should divide them. It is the same for property entrusted by a bhikṣuṇī to a bhikṣu.
Since both communities understand the Dharma and do not share the same dwelling as laypeople, they should be returned to their original owners."

Regarding the places [of residence], they are divided according to their respective classes. Since it is thus that they mutually entrust [their belongings] to one another, it is likewise the case for mutual debts.
Furthermore, according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, fascicle 20, there is also a method for monks and nuns to mutually take charge of one another's property. The text states:

"If a monk passes away at a monastery where there is no other monk during a time that is not the period of the rains retreat (*varṣā*), the bhikṣuṇīs should divide [his property]. If a bhikṣuṇī passes away at a monastery where there is no other bhikṣuṇī during a time that is not the period of the rains retreat..."

During the period of residence, if a bhikṣuṇī passes away and there are no other bhikṣuṇīs present, the bhikṣus should divide her belongings. This applies equally to whatever offerings are received during the rainy season retreat (varṣā).
Next is the second [section], the "Manifestation of the Gift," which consists of three parts. First, the announcement of the three-month seclusion;

the *Daśabhāṇavāra* (Ten Recitations), chapter five, records that the Bhikṣus established a regulation because they were accumulating many robes. He said, "I wish to remain in meditative seclusion for four months.
I require that the Bhikṣus not come to my location, except for those who bring food and the Bhikṣus who attend the *poṣadha* ceremony. Thus the Bhikṣus established the rule.
Having made the regulation, he informed the Buddha. This does not apply to these two individuals; as for the former *Ti-ji*, even *Ji* would permit it (*Vibhāṣā* 26).
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "I wish to remain in meditative seclusion for two months. You need not assemble to question me, except at the time of bringing food or during the *pravāraṇā* ceremony.
At that time, the World-Honored One entered his room and sat in meditation. [Someone] asked: "For what reason has the World-Honored One been in meditative seclusion for so long?"

"Is he sitting? [The question was asked. The answer was: "The Buddhas of the past and future, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, by the very nature of reality (*dharmatā*), all ought to sit in meditative composure (*pratisaṃlayana*) in this manner.
Some say it is because he wishes to preach the secret Dharma to the various devas; some say it is to sever the pride and laxity of the bhikṣus;

others say it is because he wishes to preach the sublime Dharma to sentient beings in other realms (many such explanations exist and cannot be recounted in full). The Venerable One said: "By virtue of..."
There are two causes and conditions for the Tathāgata’s remaining in meditative seclusion for two months: first, because he personally experiences the great joy of the Dharma;

second, out of compassion for all sentient beings. Second, from the passage beginning with "At that time, the Elder... [it is shown] that, having understood the Buddha's intention, they paid homage, visited him, and offered praise.
Third, from the passage beginning with "At that time, the bhikṣus... [it is shown] for the purpose of establishing the practice of the equal distribution of robes and the practice of giving.
It is sent to a bhikṣuṇī as a non-clothing gift; for this reason, it is called a "gift before the two assemblies.
Although it also applies generally to the Buddha and the stūpa, because the Saṃgha is the primary recipient, it is explained here specifically in terms of the Saṃgha.

Next, the third section provides a detailed analysis of what should and should not be given. This passage consists of two parts: first, the determination of what should or should not be given in relation to the seven classes of followers;

second, from the section on Śāriputra onwards, the clarification of what should or should not be accepted. In the first part, those such as the *pratyekavihārin* (one living separately) are treated the same as those who are pure (*pariśuddha*).

Next, regarding the seven types of formal acts (*karmas*), because their transgressions are grave, one does not give them with one's own hand. Finally, for laypeople (*avadātavasana*), one compensates them according to the labor performed.
Next, regarding the śrāmaṇeras: if the Saṃgha is in harmony, they should be given an equal share; next, half [of that]; next, one part out of three.
Thus, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya), fascicle 27, states: "The bhikṣus thought thus: 'The Buddha said they should be given, but we do not know how much.
They informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said: 'Whether the śrāmaṇeras are standing or sitting, or according to their order, the various donors...'"

If lay donors (*dānapati*) personally distribute gifts, they may assign some to the *śrāmaṇeras*. If the donors do not distinguish between recipients, the property shall be divided into four parts, with one-fourth given to the *śrāmaṇeras*.
If they are unwilling to do so, it should not be divided; although this is property belonging to the Saṃgha, it is not to be allocated separately. A *śrāmaṇera* should train in this manner.
According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, fascicle 53, [the *śrāmaṇera*] shares equally with the *bhikṣus*. Next, [concerning] the monastery (*saṃghārāma*).

Although a person may not be a monk, because they have rendered service to the Saṃgha, they must also be given [a portion]. Since the status of the laity differs from that of the monastic community, and furthermore differs from that of a śrāmaṇera, one additional portion is given outside of the four [standard] portions.
It is improper to distribute it if it is not given. Next, because of the gravity of parental kindness, it is permitted.

Next, regarding borrowing another's robe: in the twenty-first [section] of the *Pañcavargika*, Maudgalyāyana said to the Buddha, "I pray that the Buddha will permit me to manifest through transformation..."
An iron cage. It encloses that great city. The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana: "Though you possess supernormal powers, how could you possibly alter this karmic cause and condition of fixed retribution?

The Buddha has declared that after seven days, King Virūḍhaka shall suffer the consequences for his crime against the śrāmaṇeras, and his entire retinue, both great and small, shall likewise lose their lives.
When the king heard this, he thought to himself: "The Buddha’s words are never empty. Other sufferings may yet be endured, but only [this one remains]..."
Fearing the fire, he immediately took his kinsmen and boarded a boat to enter the river. When the seven-day period arrived, the waters suddenly surged and overflowed;
consequently, they were all submerged and drowned at once. Next, regarding the taking of another's robe, it must possess seven qualities.

These are the "great kinsman" and the seven qualities; if these are lacking, one should not take even a robe to assist oneself. As for one who does not become angry, this is a "minor friend"; therefore, it is said that one should not take [the robe].
Next, regarding the methods for rewarding labor and so forth, the text is divided into seven sections: First, the method for distributing rewards for labor;

Second, from "At that time in Śrāvastī... onwards, showing what robes should be granted; Third, from "The Buddha permitted the granting... onwards, clarifying whether the merit is complete; Fourth, from "If a sick person...
onwards, concerning whether the bestowal is accomplished; Fifth, from "That sick bhikṣu... onwards, further clarifying the objects of reward. [Sixth... Seventh...]

Sixth, at that time, the method for the death of a subordinate who has died owing a debt. Seventh, the method for questioning the details regarding the two days [of service] concerning the subordinate who attends to the sick.
In the first section of the text, the meaning of rewarding labor is explained through a fivefold analysis. First, the intention for which rewards must be given. Second, the object...
Regarding those who are to be rewarded: first, whether they should be rewarded based on their virtue; second, the objects to be rewarded; third, the ritual for distributing the rewards;

and fourth, the procedure for the distribution of rewards. As for the intent of rewarding in the first section: that caregiver harbors compassion for the patient and serves them with diligence day and night, never declining labor or weariness.
Furthermore, by upholding the holy teachings and attending to the patient, they have rendered a service; how could it be permissible not to reward them? Therefore—
[Saṃghika] 31. A bhikṣu who tended to the sick spoke with resentment, saying: "I have not shunned cold or heat;

I have undertaken various arduous tasks, seeking out decoctions and medicines, even to the point of clearing away the vessels for excrement and urine. This is indeed the case. Is it right that I should receive these things individually, or should they be received by the Saṃgha?
The bhikṣu reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said: "Tending to the sick is extremely difficult. One should be granted the three robes, a bowl, and whatever [other requisites are needed]."

Regarding the "residual medicine" (*ucchista-bhaiṣajya*): The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations), fascicle 28, states: After the robes and bowls had been distributed among the Saṅgha, someone asked, "Which one is the sick bhikṣu?
A certain bhikṣu replied, "It is I. The Saṅgha said, "Carry this dead person away. The bhikṣu said, "Venerable sirs, I am not a *caṇḍāla*, nor do I have leprosy.
Since the robes and bowls were distributed by the Saṅgha, why must I carry a dead person away? This person...
"While he was alive, he respected and cherished me; I have now fulfilled my debt to him. As for this dead man, whoever wishes to take him may carry him away.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said: "The six personal effects should first be given to the sick bhikṣu."

Other light items should be divided among the Saṃgha. Regarding the second section on those who tend to the sick: this applies to all seven classes of followers. If a *bhikṣu* dies, two groups receive [the inheritance]:
the *bhikṣus* and the *śrāmaṇeras*. If a *bhikṣuṇī* dies, three groups receive it. This is because the labor of mutual care among the remaining groups is not sufficient to qualify them.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, fascicle 20, states: The Buddha said, "If a *bhikṣu* passes away, his robes should be given to two people: the *bhikṣus* and the *śrāmaṇeras*."
Even toward one's parents or brothers, [the robe] should not be given. If a bhikṣuṇī passes away, one should give robes to three people:
the bhikṣuṇī, the śikṣamāṇā, and the śrāmaṇerī. Regarding the distribution of items for nursing care among the bhikṣus, they gave one-third to the śrāmaṇeras;
the Buddha said that these should be distributed equally. (Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya 54). When a layperson or a bhikṣuṇī provides nursing care...

One who is ill should not be given property by the attendant; it should be given to those who are observing the rains retreat elsewhere or to those who have already completed their retreat or are about to do so.

If a śrāmaṇera attends to the sick, the great bhikṣus and others should provide for him. Regarding the third section, which concerns merit (*guṇa*), there are five kinds of merit as stated in the text (Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya, Chapter 31).
Those who should not receive [the property] are those who merely perform temporary tasks, those who act out of a desire for pleasure, or those who seek merit.

Regarding "making what was not made" and "what should be obtained": the Buddha said that because he wishes to provide benefit, even down to a single lamp-wick, whatever is necessary for a sick person to recover should be obtained.
If one seeks medicine for a sick person, or for the sake of stūpa affairs or monastic affairs, it is said that it should be given (*Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* 54).
When a caregiver goes beyond the boundary and the patient dies, [the Buddha] said... [text ends].
If one departs for the actual purpose of attending to the illness, one should give [the robe]; if one departs for any other purpose, one should not give it.

The twentieth fascicle of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "There were certain caregivers who, either on behalf of the patient or as companions to the physician, departed. Subsequently, the patient passed away."
Others obtained his robe and bowl. The Buddha said: "One should not give them to just one person; they should be given to those who provided ultimate care for the sick.
The fourth section concerns five grades of objects. First, regarding the substance of the object: according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, six items should be given.
These six items refer to the three robes, the bowl, the water-strainer, and the sitting mat (*niṣīdana*). This text, however, mentions only the robe, the bowl, and the sitting mat.
There are also six types of containers for storing robes: bamboo tubes, baskets, and so forth. These six are common to both nuns and monks;

the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* mentions only the three robes and the alms bowl, while the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* adds "medicines received for later use" to the list. Second, regarding presence or absence, one should bestow [the reward] according to what is present;

if something is absent, it is not improper to fail to bestow it. Third, among those items that are present, there are those currently on hand and those not currently on hand; those currently on hand must be bestowed, while those located in other monasteries may be accounted for accordingly.

It then belongs to that Sangha. *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-vibhāṣā*, fascicle 4: "If a bhikṣu has sewn his three robes together, and for some reason tears them apart to carry them separately while traveling to another location, this is called 'not being separated from one's robes overnight.
If the bhikṣu dies, it further states that within the original boundary (sīmā), a formal act (*karmavācanā*) should be performed regarding these robes;
furthermore, it states they should be given to the attendant who nursed him, because originally they were a single set of robes held in common."

Therefore, the Vinaya Master says that the latter is the definitive meaning. He further states that one may stay overnight separated from the robe after having obtained the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual).

This robe should be given to the attendant who nursed the sick person, because the robe belongs to the deceased bhikṣu. Fourth, regarding whether the robe is held or not held among those present: it should be given to the one who holds it.
Fifth, for one who does not know whether it is held or not held, one should assess the three grades of care provided by the attendant and bestow the three grades of robes accordingly.

The ritual procedures for the five gates consist of four parts. First, the distribution of items to be rewarded. When one is about to perform the ritual act, the community of monks must first determine the gravity of the offenses and the items that should be rewarded;
the method for this distribution should be understood as it is normally practiced. Second, the place of distribution. This refers to locations other than before a corpse.
According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations), chapter twenty-eight, the monks of Kośala distributed the robes and bowls before the deceased monk. This is [the second part].
The bhikṣu stirred and spoke to the other bhikṣus: "Venerable Elders, do not divide my robes and bowl.

The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said: "Do not divide them right there in front of the corpse. Once the corpse has been removed, if the Saṃgha is in another location, they should be divided there.
The *Mātṛkā Sūtra*, fascicle three, states: "First, having taken the deceased away and hidden him, the Saṃgha returns to that place."
In the monastery, once the *sāṃghika* monks currently present have assembled, they should take the property of the deceased monk and place it before the Saṃgha for distribution.

Although their physical locations differ—meaning that while one is within the *mahā-sīmā* (great boundary), the other is on the *śīma-kaṇḍaka* (precept platform)—the latter is a place where distinct practices are performed, and thus the items should not be divided there.

Therefore, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, chapter twenty-one, states: "There was a residence where the Saṃgha obtained cloth suitable for distribution. A single bhikṣu took it and went to the *śīma-kaṇḍaka*..."
On the altar, one person alone takes possession [of the items]. The Buddha said this should not be done; it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. The items should be divided among the monks present.

If there are three or fewer persons, the location and the nature of the object are both considered. Regarding the three types based on persons: this refers to when the Saṃgha consists of more than one person.

There are two distinctions within the Saṃgha: namely, groups of four or five persons. Regarding the four types based on the Dharma: if there are five or more persons, they must perform the three formal procedures (*trividha-karma*) in their entirety.
This refers to the distribution of rewards and the assignment of persons. For three individuals, there is the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (formal act consisting of a motion and one announcement);

for four individuals, the single formal act (*ekakarma*) is performed directly as previously clarified. The procedures for face-to-face (*saṃmukha*) and mental recollection (*manasikāra*) should be understood by analogy with this principle.

If there are four or fewer, it is consistent with reason that they may orally agree upon the distribution according to the intent of the procedure for collecting goods. Next, the text is explained; therein are two parts. First:
The Method for Attending to the Sick. Second: At that time, there was a bhikṣu who... [follows the instructions] to attend to the sick. The preceding section has two parts:
first, the Buddha himself attends to the sick and establishes the rule; second, from "At that time, the World-Honored One" onwards, he establishes the method for attending to the sick.
Regarding the former section on attending to the sick: *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, chapter twenty-eight. The World-Honored One was inspecting the monks' quarters when he saw a sick bhikṣu lying down.
Amidst filth and excrement, he had fasted for seven days. The World-Honored One asked, "Is there anyone with you, such as a companion? He replied, "No; I am merely solitary and suffering.

The World-Honored One wished to offer him a robe, but Ānanda requested that it be set aside. Ānanda prepared a shelter for him, the World-Honored One poured water [for bathing], and once everything was settled, he preached the Dharma.
The bhikṣu attained the purity of the Dharma-eye. This bhikṣu was thus without a teacher, nor did he have a fellow teacher or a cellmate.

The Venerable One assembled the community and addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "You have each come from different clans and different families; out of faith, you have left the home life for the homeless state.
You all now share the same clan: that of the Śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas. If you do not look after one another, who then shall?

If a bhikṣu falls ill, the upādhyāya and others—even those sharing the same cell—must look after him. Whoever fails to do so commits a *vinayātikrama* (offense against the discipline). If there is no [one available]..."
The Saṃgha should appoint someone to look after him. If they do not appoint anyone, the entire Saṃgha commits an offense.
The Buddha said to you, "Go back and look after the sick bhikṣu in your original cell. Not far from the Buddha, he manifested as a sick śrāmaṇera.
The Buddha said, "Go and look after this sick śrāmaṇera; this shall be your meritorious punishment. He asked whether he was making progress in his nursing, as detailed in the text. [He replied: "No."
This can be explained extensively; here, I have cited it briefly. In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it is recorded that one attained arhatship upon hearing the Dharma.

The text on the establishment of the rules consists of three parts: First, the rule for tending to the sick. Because the compassionate mind with which one tends to the sick is equal to the mind with which the teaching was established, it is said: "Those who wish to make offerings to me should make offerings to the sick.
Second, regarding the permission for those [monks] to be present, the text distinguishes the seven classes of followers (the seven *saṃghas*). Third, concerning the sick person...

There are five matters concerning the examination of ease or difficulty [of care], which follows below. Next, the text on caring for the sick in accordance with the teachings consists of three parts: first, caring for the sick in accordance with the teachings;
second, from "At that time, the bhikṣus... onwards, the praise by the Noble One (the Buddha);

third, from "He took the deceased bhikṣu... onwards, the method for distributing rewards for labor. This section contains three parts: first, a general statement that [the property] belongs to the Saṃgha, hence it says, "The Saṃgha should divide it. Second... [text continues].

Second, from "At that time, the World-Honored One" onwards, the specific method for distributing rewards is shown. Third, from the commentary on the sub-section below, the method for allocating and collecting [the property] is clarified.

The initial passage is understandable. Regarding the text on rewarding labor, there are three parts: first, the presentation of what should be given; second, the relinquishing of items and their entrustment to the Saṃgha.

As for the text, it refers to "robes, bowls, and so forth" based on what is currently present; however, according to principle, the items mentioned should correspond to the actual objects. Furthermore, since the deceased’s belongings are numerous, [the text uses this general phrasing].

It cannot be explained one by one. According to the previous rule regarding what the *saṃgha* obtains, it says: "If it is cloth or not cloth, there is no hindrance; the substance has its own established definition and is not distinguished by whether it exists or not.
For those who recite according to the literal text, the legal procedure (*dharma*) will certainly not be accomplished.

Third, within the *saṃgha*, the procedure for bestowing rewards is performed below. Within this procedure, the items are listed according to whether they exist or not; the subsequent distribution and inclusion can be understood accordingly. *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*. Correct.

Within the *karmavācanā*, if there is mention of "robes" or "non-robes," the principle allows for either a face-to-face (*sammukha*) or mental (*manasikāra*) procedure; their absence here indicates brevity.
Next, he shows the robes that should be given, namely those which are to be constantly worn.
Next, regarding the qualities, they are as explained in the text and their meaning.

Next, the basis of attribution is clarified through a threefold classification: first, the distinctions of the basis of attribution; second, the wholesome and unwholesome; third, the accomplished and unaccomplished.
Regarding the first, the distinctions, these are divided into four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). For instance, when a person manifests an object, the object may or may not be manifest.

If the person is present but the object is not, or if both the person and the object are not present, these three cases do not permit immediate bestowal; therefore, they must be designated as "entrusted" (*pariṇāmanā*).
If both the person and the object are present—such as a robe or bowl that is capable of being transferred—that constitutes a formal bestowal (*dāna*) and does not require designation as entrusted.

Furthermore, regarding items such as servants, fields, or houses that cannot be transferred, they must be both "belonging" (*śeṣa*) and "transferred" (*pariṇāmita*); this is what is meant by "both belonging and transferred.

Conversely, it should be understood that if something is neither belonging nor transferred, it is not so designated. Next, concerning the wholesome and unwholesome: these pertain to both what belongs and what does not belong.

Regarding the wholesome and unwholesome within the context of what belongs and is transferred—for instance, there may be a bhikṣu who knows for himself that he has accumulated [wealth] and is on the verge of...
Ultimately, one feels shame and remorse. To break through stinginess and practice giving—such as bestowing gifts upon the Triple Gem and others—is called "wholesome.

For example, if a bhikṣu fears that the Sangha might receive something later, he immediately resolves to give it to his own relatives; although this constitutes an act of transfer, it is called "unwholesome.

Regarding what is wholesome or unwholesome within that which is not [formally] transferred: it is like being mindful of the necessities of life, or having faith in the Buddha’s majestic power and benefit, or entering into the profound benefits of the two types of Sangha.
The benefit is greatest. I shall now simply follow and obey the holy teachings; practicing one's own deeds is what is called "good.

If one has accumulated many possessions since birth and, when afflicted by illness, wishes to cultivate merit but only briefly gives rise to a mind of renunciation—only to later feel regret and longing—fearing that once the affliction is removed there will be nothing left to give, and thus passes away, this is called "unwholesome. Next...
Regarding success or failure: one who makes a formal dedication with a resolute mind, free from regret or change of heart, achieves success in all cases.

Thus, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Sengqi lü), fascicle 31, states: "If there is a firm dedication, saying, 'Whether I die or live, I give this,' and the mind is determined to bestow it, it should be given;
such a resolute intention succeeds. As for the instruction: "I [give] this much..."

Regarding the use of materials for the creation of images and the construction of temples, one should have them made quickly so that I may see them. For those who resolve with such determination, all things are accomplished.
However, if one says, "I shall create scriptures, images, and so forth after my death," and thus makes such a formal entrustment, it will not be accomplished.
Therefore, it is said: "If I give these after my passing, or if they do not return to me while I am alive. The Buddha said: "One should not act in this manner."
[The items] should be distributed before the assembled Sangha. Furthermore, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, chapter twenty-one, states:

"There were certain bhikṣus who, while still alive, made dispositions regarding their clothing and requisites, saying: 'After my death, I give these clothing and requisites to such-and-such a person; these clothing and requisites shall be used in such-and-such a manner.
The Buddha said: 'This should not be done. [To do so] constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. The giving is invalid; the use is invalid.'"

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations), chapter thirty-nine, states: There was a certain sick person who said to his attendant, "If you can look after me well and love me dearly, then when my life comes to an end, all my possessions shall be given entirely to you.
Having spoken thus, he passed away. When the Saṃgha assembled intending to divide the property, the attendant recounted the words of the sick man in detail.
A bhikṣu reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "There is no such death [where one's estate goes to another by mere verbal promise]."

The property should be given to the Dharma; the physical items should be divided among the Saṃgha. Since it is stated that after death [the deceased] no longer exists, it is clear that any disposition made for such things as plastering the tomb, burial shrouds, or coffins is entirely ineffective.
Next, the three phrases concerning the re-appropriation of items are clarified once more: first, receiving what is not good; second, sending it elsewhere; third, measuring the quantity and quality.
Next, the section on debts is clarified, which explains the method of distribution (*vibhaṅga*) and may be divided into two gates. The first gate first clarifies the method for repaying debts.
The text states: "Whom do you owe? This refers to cases where a sick person owes the Three Jewels, other individuals, or heavy and light items. One must repay each according to its relative weight;
however, if there is no item of equivalent value, it is also permissible to repay by mutual substitution. According to principle, any outstanding debt should be repaid first.

Because it was for the benefit of the deceased, what was returned remains as a surplus; therefore, one should follow the standard procedure by stating, "I shall repay this with a long robe (*atirekacīvara*) after selling it.
If there is no such robe, one should sell the three robes (*tricīvara*) to provide the payment. Second, the method for claiming debts is explained in the text: "Who owes you?

This means that if the property of the deceased is owed by the Sangha, the Buddha, or an individual, it should all be claimed, as it rightfully belongs to the Sangha. If the value of the debt and the goods are equivalent, each [party] should...

It follows its original nature; even if it is subsequently recovered through mutual searching, it still follows its original nature. If the permanent monastery (*sāṃghika*) owes a heavy debt, it shall follow the creditor into the light category [of property].
However, that which must be taken and entered into the *pratyutpanna-saṃgha* (the present monastic community) is as stated in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, chapter fifty-seven:

"A bhikṣu borrowed robes and bowls from the fourfold monastic community for personal use. When this bhikṣu died, he informed the Buddha. The Buddha said: 'As for the property of the fourfold monastic community, calculate it...'"
One should return directly. The items should be divided among the monks present. If the monks present have carried heavy or light goods, one must deduct [the value] and reclaim them;
the heavy items shall be assigned to the permanent endowment (*sthavira*), while for the light items, a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) shall be performed.
Next, inquire of the patient in detail for two days as prescribed in the text.

Following this, the fourth section clarifies what is appropriate and what is not; since these are miscellaneous rules (*miśraka-dharma*), there is no fixed sequence. One should understand them according to one’s own inclination and in accordance with what is essential.
Next is the fifth [type of] giving, that which is given in the presence [of the recipient]. This section contains two parts.

In the first part, because it is given in the presence [of the recipient], it must be said that [the portion] is taken from multiple locations. If each [monk] takes half, and if the Sangha receives it at that time, it must be distributed according to the Dharma;

those who do not receive it according to the Dharma do not logically deserve to obtain it. The old commentary states: "Since this is an object obtained by the Sangha at this time, it is said that they take half. As for 'in the presence'..."

"To take both [types of robes] according to the donor's intention is without fault"—this explanation is unreasonable; there is no need to elaborate on its refutation. The eater should consume [the food] according to the donor's offering.

Next, the acceptance of the summer robe (*kāṭhina*) is first permitted; that is, the prohibition against exceeding [the limit] is relaxed. In truth, this relaxation should have been stated previously.

Next, regarding the alms received by the Saṃgha during the six periods of the day, there are three sections in the text. First, the pair of clothing and food; within the section on clothing, there are three points.

The first point concerns the authorization for assignment (*pariṇāmanā*). The second point concerns the assignment of uncut cloth (*maṇḍala*). The third point concerns the recipient’s forgetfulness of the assignment, as both are divided through formal ritual action (*karmavācanā*);

even when one is not present within the boundary (*sīmā*), the division is valid. Because of the labor involved at this location, it is permitted to take possession through assignment. This also applies to food.

One should eat according to what has been offered. Next, Śāriputra, this is an offering made in person at an improper time; it should not be governed by the rules for [offerings] made at the proper time.
Next, one bhikṣu should take it into his mind; however, it is clearly known that when there are many [monks], one must perform the *pratyakṣa-karman* (formal act before witnesses).
Next is the seventh section on the inclusion of the correct and the false. This passage contains two parts. The first consists of ten phrases concerning non-timely gifts to the Saṃgha;

the second consists of six phrases concerning timely gifts made in the presence [of the recipients]. The first part has three sections. The first has six phrases regarding a donor bringing goods to give to the Saṃgha;
the next has three phrases concerning the persons of the three groups; and the final phrase concerns the pure Saṃgha entering the house for the distribution [of the goods].

Regarding giving (*dāna*), the preceding text has two parts: the first three cases concern the Sangha, while the subsequent three concern individuals. Alternatively, these six may be understood as distinguishing between giving at the proper time and giving at an improper time.
The first three cases concern the object of the gift, whether it has been acquired or not yet acquired, and whether it is already obtained or not yet obtained.
The first phrase is divided into two parts; the second phrase questions the donor; and the third phrase is the same as the previous two. The reason for dividing it into two parts is that this...
Regarding the property of the Saṃgha, both the orthodox and the heterodox have a share in it; it is not permissible to apportion it among those present. One must perform a *karmavācanā*.

Once the *karmavācanā* has been performed, since the orthodox and the heterodox cannot satisfy one another, it must be divided into two portions, each of which shall proceed to their respective groups to perform the ritual.

Regarding those who obtain the Dharma, it is as clarified in the regular [explanations]. Next, the three *saṃghas* have already been divided; based on the objects [of the division], they are categorized as three.

Since the objects have already been split into two portions, when one arrives at the faction of the heterodox (*yāna*), one naturally deserves to receive a share; therefore, no share is given to those who departed. Logically, there should be another three cases:

for those who return from the heterodox to the orthodox, they should be granted a share by the incoming party. That this is not mentioned in the text is due to abbreviation. These are the six [cases].
Section on the Handling of Property by the Righteous Assembly and the Heretical Assembly. There should be another six [sections].
The first three sections are as in the first three above; the subsequent three sections are as in the last three above. Next, regarding the property of the deceased, there are initially two sections.
If an object enters the category of the heterodox (*yī*), it is because its original mind turns away from the orthodox toward the heterodox; there should likewise be two further cases:

when one returns from the heterodox to the orthodox, the object enters the category of the orthodox. That these are not mentioned in the text is due to abbreviation. Furthermore, this is based directly on the clothing and belongings carried by the body, judging the destination of entry according to the turning or turning away of one's own mind.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations), fascicle 28, states: The Buddha said, "There is a bhikṣu who has received the dharma..."
If a monk who does not follow the Dharma dies while staying among monks who do follow the Dharma, he leaves instructions that his robes and bowl should be taken away.
If the monks who follow the Dharma take them, it is well; if they do not take them, they should use them for the bedding and furniture of the Saṃgha’s lodgings in the four directions.
The same applies in reverse if a monk who follows the Dharma dies among a community of monks who do not follow the Dharma. Furthermore...
There is a monk who upholds the Dharma (dharmika) who expels another monk. That expelled monk goes to those who do not uphold the Dharma (adharmika) and says:
"Venerable sirs, please remove my offense so that I may become pure; I shall then act as one who does not uphold the Dharma.

If he dies before his offense has been removed, the monks who uphold the Dharma should take back his robes and bowl. If he dies after his offense has been removed, his robes, bowl, and belongings belong to those who do not uphold the Dharma.
"O monks, there are monks who do not accept the Dharma. Suppose a monk who has been suspended goes to those who accept the Dharma; it should be understood that he must state his case.

Next, suppose one who has been subjected to the *ukkhepanīyakamma* (act of suspension) dies. He shall be assigned to whichever community of monks performed the same *kamma* against him—namely, those who were co-suspenders."
Since the attainment of the Dharma and material wealth are distinct, for what reason should one immediately take possession of property after death?

If that were so, when one person who has been subject to a formal act of suspension dies, into whose share should it enter? If one person has been suspended, it enters the Saṃgha capable of carrying out the formal act;

however, anyone who participated in the assembly carrying out the formal act is entitled to receive a portion. Therefore, it is said: "It should be given to the Saṃgha that was collectively subjected to the same *karmavācanā*. This means:

This is because they are the Saṃgha that has performed those meritorious functions; thus, it should be understood that next follows the face-to-face giving (*saṃmukha-dāna*). Next is the giving in the presence of the assembly (*sāṃmukhika-dāna*).

Regarding the first three types, which concern the Saṃgha, the distribution of items—whether already acquired or not—is determined by the specific circumstances of the labor involved, and the items are divided among the members present.

Regarding the next three types, which concern individuals, the distribution is likewise determined by the specific circumstances of the labor, and the items are given to those who have departed. If, however, the group of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) takes possession of the items, [the rule is] contrary to...

"Yea" returns to the correct [category]. There are further three phrases, which are also divided among those who go away. Furthermore, by inferring through their meaning, there should additionally be six;
when the correct and the erroneous are viewed in relation to one another, they do not apply to those who come. These and other such matters are all omitted.
Next, the eighth section generally explains the eight kinds of giving. The text is divided into three parts. First, the eight are raised collectively;

following the ritual procedures for a single direction, their external giving is manifested, and by distinguishing the mind according to its objects, these eight are briefly indicated. Giving one’s own property to others is termed "giving" (dāna), and three [of these] are specifically designated as such.
Second, the eight types of giving are enumerated: first, the *bhikṣu-saṃgha*, which includes four varieties—namely, the two types of *saṃmukha* (present) and the two types of *saṃgha*.
It is obtained. Second, the *bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha* is also fourfold as described above. Third, the two assemblies (*ubhaya-saṃgha*) also comprise these four types;

when the two assemblies are present, they must each be counted separately, with the two groups divided equally. Fourth, the *cāturdisa-saṃgha* (the Saṃgha of the four quarters) refers to the permanent endowment for the four directions;

in principle, this includes both one assembly and two assemblies. If a gift is made to the two assemblies, it should be divided into two portions. Fifth, the *sīmāntara-saṃgha* (the Saṃgha within a boundary); whichever boundary it may be, [it should be]... when the time comes.

1. It may be obtained within the boundary (*sīmā*), because the location is fixed; the number of people shall divide it. Those who are of the same *karmavācanā* (formal act) as the Sangha—meaning all those who participated in the *karmavācanā*—are entitled to share in the portion.

This principle applies equally to both the one-section (*ekadeśa*) and two-section (*ubhayabhāga*) Sanghas. Since the restricted rule is taken as authoritative, the number of people shall divide it. 2.

"Calling out by name" means that names are recorded and the items are given specifically to each individual. 3. "Giving to one person" refers to cases where the item is delivered directly to a single recipient.
The three explanations are understandable.

Next is the method for the ninefold pure gift (*navavidha-śuddha-dāna*); its meaning is explained as above. Regarding those who perform the ritual procedure, they should recite according to this text.

Next is the tenth [section] concerning whether the acceptance is accomplished or not; within this text there are two parts: first, regarding a bhikṣu; second, regarding a layperson (*avadātavasana*). The former...

The text consists of twenty-four phrases. The first twelve concern the borrowing of robes. In the first six items, there are three cases of "incomplete taking," because the one to whom the borrowed robe is given acts with the intention of a kinsman or friend.
Next, there are three cases of "taking," because the one who lends the robe acts with the intention of a kinsman or friend.
In the subsequent six, the first three are "incomplete acceptance," because the person to whom it is given is not the owner of the robe. Next, there are three...

[The first] six [cases] of the first three [sets of] twelve phrases do not constitute [an offense], because one is able to give this robe to the person who is its owner. The latter twelve phrases involve sending the robe to a beggar;

of these, the first three of the first six do not constitute [an offense], because the gift belongs to that beggar. The next three constitute taking [the robe]. The latter six of the latter six do not constitute [an offense].

Because the lower three [levels] are established, next comes the property of the lay devotees (*gṛhapati*). Since it is determined by a mind of relinquishment, its use is permitted. The section on the rules for robes (*cīvara-dharma*) is concluded above.

Next is the *Bhaiṣajya-khaṇḍaka* (Section on Medicines). It is called "medicine" because it possesses the capacity to treat ailments. There are four types of medicine, beginning with that taken at the proper time (*kāla-bhaiṣajya*).
The term *khandhaka* refers to a collection gathered in one place; this is a specific name for the period of concealment and so forth, while "medicine" is used as the general designation.

The main text is divided into two parts: first, the exposition of the regulations; second, from "At that time, the World-Honored One... onwards, the exposition of the permissions granted in the preceding text.
First, the explanation of begging for food, which is the second reliance (*niśraya*). Regarding "Kubadara rice": according to the *Jianlun* (Treatise on Seeing), this refers to millet porridge;
"tiaobu" refers to green bean soup; "jiluo" refers to a bamboo lute. Next, the explanation of putridity, which is the fourth reliance.
The medicinal substances for putrefaction have already been analyzed as previously explained.

Next, the four types of medicine will be opened up for discussion. First, the meaning of "medicine" (bhaiṣajya) shall be elucidated through a fourfold analysis. First, the explanation of the name; second, the determination of its essential nature (svabhāva).
Third is the method for purifying [the medicine]; fourth is the meaning of consuming it after it has been mixed.

Regarding the explanation of the names: the general explanation of the names of medicines has already been distinguished as previously set forth. As for the meanings of "medicine," there are four different types.
Regarding the term "time" (*kāla*) and so forth: from after the appearance of dawn until before midday is the time for eating, which is designated as "time.

Medicines permitted to be consumed during this period are called "timely medicines" (*kālabhaiṣajya*). From after midday until before the appearance of dawn is not the time for eating; it is called "non-time" (*akāla*).
Because they are permitted to be consumed during this non-temporal interval, they are called "non-timely medicines" (*akālabhaiṣajya*). The Noble One [the Buddha] limited them to seven.

That which is taken daily is called "seven-day medicine" (*saptāhika-bhaiṣajya*). Because it is permitted to be taken for as long as one lives, it is called "lifetime medicine" (*yāvajjīvika-bhaiṣajya*). Regarding the substance of lifetime medicine, there are three aspects:
primarily taking the physical body (*rūpakāya*) as the basis, while also clarifying the relationship between medicine and illness.
Next, regarding the determination of the substance (*dravya*): "timely substance" refers to the five kinds of *pūjani* and the five kinds of *khādaniya*.
Furthermore, the text mentions that sugarcane was obtained, and the Buddha declared it permissible as "timely food. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, fascicle 28, states: "Regarding the rules for medicine:
'timely roots' and 'non-timely roots' include radish roots, onion roots, and even lotus roots and so forth; such things are categorized together with [other] foods."
These are called "timely roots. As for "untimely roots," they include the *vāṭa* root, the *pipphala* root, the *nyagrodha* root, and so forth.
Any such [roots] that are not combined with food are called untimely roots. The same applies to stalks, bark, leaves, flowers, and fruits.
Regarding "gruel" (*pāna*), there is timely gruel and untimely gruel. Timely gruel refers to all rice-based liquids and flour-based drinks.

Broth, milk, curd, and fermented grain-drink—these are called "timely drinks" (*kālika-pāna*). As for "non-timely drinks" (*akālika-pāna*), they consist of all beans and grains such as wheat, provided they have no husks;
as well as ghee, oil, honey, and rock sugar—these are called non-timely drinks.
