If a bhikṣu is ill and a physician says that he will live if given food but will die if not, one should wash a vessel clean seven times, fill it with non-grain substances, place them in a fine cloth bag, and tie it shut.

Boil them in a vessel so that they do not break apart, and give the resulting substance as a drink later on. Furthermore, regarding these eight kinds of fermented liquors (*pāna*), the Buddha stated that drinking them outside of the prescribed time (*akāla*) is permitted.

Question: The substance of the fruit is a "timely medicine" (*kālabhaiṣajya*), yet it is permitted to drink the fermented juice (*pāna*) outside of the prescribed time. Since cooked rice is also categorized as a "timely [medicine]," why is the fermented juice of rice permitted to be drunk outside of the prescribed time?

Answer: There is a specific principle within the fruit itself: the juice and the fermented liquid may be drunk outside of the prescribed time. However, when rice is used, external water is added to the fermenting mass. Because of this addition of water, the fermented juice of rice is permitted to be drunk outside of the prescribed time.
It is also subsumed under "timely food" (*kālabhojana*). If that is so, then rice is [the base] for external water; when juice is added, it is subsumed as timely food.

Fruit juice likewise relies on water [for its purification]; how could it not be categorized as untimely? This objection fails to grasp the essential point. Rice becomes juice by being mixed with water; without water, it is not juice.
The juice of fruit uses water for purification; even without water, it naturally constitutes juice. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that these are simply the five grains.

Regarding fruit juices (*phala-pāna*): because they provide substantial nourishment, they were not permitted [as non-time food]. However, since fruit juices are not derived from grains and their nutritional support is weak, they were opened for consumption.
Thus, the *Viniścaya-śāstra* (Jian lun), fascicle 17, states: "All tree fruits may be used as non-time juice, with the sole exception of the seven types of grains.

Furthermore, it is explained that ordinary food provides only a subtle benefit to the body and lacks the fault of being "conscious" (i.e., fermented). Therefore, the World-Honored One permitted its drinking outside of the proper time. If...
Regarding the strengthening of the body, if food incurs criticism, the World-Honored One prohibited it.
As for the substance of the seven-day medicine, it is like the five kinds of *śyāmāka* grain and the five kinds of fat. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, fascicle 2, states:

"The five kinds [of dairy] such as ghee (*sarpis*), and the five kinds of fat—these medicines are pure and free from the odor of food; they may be accepted all at once and consumed for seven days. Therefore, it is so named.
Regarding the seven-day medicine and the lifetime medicine, the text states that those which are unfit to be used as food include all pungent, salty, bitter, and so forth substances.
The *Cīvaravastu* specifies these as myrobalan (*harītakī*), emblic myrobalan (*āmalaka*), black pepper (*marica*), long pepper (*pippalī*), ginger (*śṛṅgavera*), salt, and the like.
These various medicines, being devoid of the quality of food, may be accepted at once; a sick bhikṣu may take them for the rest of his life. This is called a lifetime medicine.

Next, regarding the method for purifying: the purification of *kālika-bhaiṣajya* (medicines taken during the day) follows the text. As for *vikālika-pāna* (beverages taken outside the designated time), one must necessarily verify that they have been purified with water.
To eliminate craving for the flavor, they may then be consumed. Thus, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, fascicle 26, states:
"If grapes have not undergone fire-purification (*agnipariśuddha*), or if the juice has not been purified with water; or if the grapes have been purified but the juice has not."

If the juice has been purified (*kappiya-kata*), but the grapes have not been purified, neither should be drunk. If the grapes have been purified, and the juice has also been purified, it should be drunk.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Sengqi lü), fascicle 29, states: "If one brings juice, it must be purified.
If there is residual water remaining at the bottom of the vessel, this is called 'purified. If rain falls into it, this is also called 'purified. Or [if] the juice..."

If a *kappiya-kāraka* (one who makes things permissible) wishes to depart without having performed the purification (*kappiya-karaṇa*), one should immediately accept [the food] and make a formal notation (*saññā-vidhāna*), saying: "The pure substance herein shall be accepted by me.

If there is a reason why it cannot be accepted at that time, and one fails to make the notation and lets it remain for even a moment longer, it may not be accepted, because its nature has become mixed with that of *kāla-bhojana* (food permitted only during the day).
As for the seven-day medicine (*sattāha-bhesajja*), it must likewise be purified; it is distinct from *kāla-bhojana*. Water...
It becomes pure by dripping [rainwater] upon it; only then may one eat it. Thus the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If a cartload of stone honey (*śarkarā*) is rained upon, it is then called pure.

If water remains in a boat, or if water remains after a pure person (*pariśuddha-pudgala*) has washed their hands, both are collectively called pure. If it is mixed with [impure substances], one must likewise mark it and maintain mindfulness of its status.
The tenth fascicle of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* says: "When a bhikṣu is begging for food and receives a great deal..."
Regarding ghee: when a novice or a monk with little knowledge uses fine woolen cloth to filter it thoroughly, the ghee may be accepted for seven days.
If there is a specific circumstance, one must not fail to perform the ritual before midday. One should say: "This pure substance has arisen within me; I shall accept it as a seven-day medicine.
If one forgets to accept it by mistake, or if the time passes without performing the purification (*pariśuddhi*), it is called impure. If [the quantity] is large...

Regarding the acquisition of oil and fish fat, it is as explained in the section on *sarpis* (clarified butter). The meaning of "medicines for the duration of one's life" (*yāvajjīvika*) should be understood by analogy.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, fascicle ten, states: "If a bhikṣu has received a large amount of sugarcane while eating and has leftover stalks, he may process them into syrup and accept them during the night."
If one does not finish drinking it, one may receive it as stone honey (*śarkarā*) made beforehand for seven days. If the stone honey is not finished, one may burn it to ash and receive it for life.
If there is a matter that prevents one from pressing [the juice], one should instead purify it with water before midday, making this declaration:
In this regard, if pure substances arise, I shall accept them.

Next, concerning "mixing together": it refers only to the mixing of the four medicinal drugs, all of which should be taken according to whichever is strongest; for instance, because there is *kṣīra-nī* within stone honey (*śarkarā*).

The Buddha said, "The ritual procedure should be performed in this manner. By extension of these principles, all other cases are likewise so. (Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-vibhāṣā, fascicle 6). According to the *Xiāngzhùchéng* (On Mutual Assistance and Completion), it says:

"If one uses a *kālika-bhaiṣajya* (medicament for the day) or a *yāvajjīvika-bhaiṣajya* (medicament for life) to assist in the preparation of a *saptāhika-bhaiṣajya* (medicament for seven days), and one consumes it as a *saptāhika-bhaiṣajya*, there is no transgression.
This is because the potency of the *saptāhika-bhaiṣajya* is predominant, and because it has been assisted by [the other substances]. It is like using clarified butter (*ghṛta*)."

When meat is boiled, the broth from these medicinal balls (*sukhāra*) may be taken as a seven-day medicine (*saptāha-bhaiṣajya*). Alternatively, by means of a daily medicine (*kālika-bhaiṣajya*) or a seven-day medicine, it may be transformed into a lifetime medicine (*yāvajjīvika-bhaiṣajya*);
there is no fault in taking it as a lifetime medicine. Or, by means of a lifetime medicine or a seven-day medicine, it may be transformed into a daily medicine;
one may take it as a daily medicine because of the predominance of its potency and because they mutually assist one another in their formation. If [the substances] are divided...

Regarding "those of equal potency": one determines [the classification] according to the name, just as with honey pills (*śarkarā-guḍikā*). Although their potencies are equal, because they are determined by their names, they are taken as seven-day medicines (*saptāha-bhaiṣajya*).

This is like the five-stone powder (*pañca-śilājatu-cūrṇa*), which takes its name from the stone; it is taken as a lifetime medicine (*yāvaj-jīva-bhaiṣajya*). This textual passage harmonizes [the categories] based on the substance being predominant.

If, however, one follows the potency, then as when poisonous substances are mixed with other medicines, [they would all be classified differently]. None of these [would be considered seven-day medicines].
It is the sustenance for abiding. It should be taken as a medicine for life-long use.
*The Record of the Opening of the Sect of the Four-Part Vinaya*, Fascicle Eight, Part One;
*The Record of the Opening of the Sect of the Four-Part Vinaya*, Fascicle Eight, Part Two.
Next, the explanation of the text follows, divided into fifteen major sections: First, the primary section clarifying medicines for as long as one lives;

Second, from "At that time, Śāriputra... onwards, concerning whether other dharmas should be [permitted]; Third, from "At that time, the World-Honored One... onwards, concerning the prohibition of the five kinds of meat;
Fourth, from "At that time, the World-Honored One was at Vārāṇasī... onwards, concerning the donor’s invitation to the Dharma; Fifth, from "At that time, the World-Honored One was at... onwards...
In Śrāvastī, [the Buddha] explains the seven-day medicines. Sixth, regarding the time-medicine, he explains the meaning of taking them in combination.

Seventh, regarding the bhikṣu suffering from a wound, he clarifies the miscellaneous rules thereon. Eighth, regarding the World-Honored One suffering from wind-disorder, he prohibits the two internal [medicines] and briefly clarifies the pure places.
Ninth, regarding the World-Honored One being at Vaiśālī, he permits the consumption of the three [kinds of meat].
10. At that time, the World-Honored One, descending from Vaiśālī, permitted the purification of food by lay attendants (*upāsaka*).

11. At that time, the World-Honored One, descending from Āmra, authorized the eight kinds of fermented drinks (*aṣṭavidha-pāna*). 12. At that time, the World-Honored One, descending from this dwelling, clarified the rules regarding what is permissible and what is not.
13. At that time, there was a monk who had vomited; [the Buddha] permitted medicine to be placed on purified ground (*pariśuddha-bhūmi*).

Section Fourteen: At that time, the method for protecting the purity of impure ground. Section Fifteen: At that time, the miscellaneous rules concerning the six groups of monks ascending and descending.
The preceding twelve sections are easily understood. Now, the thirteenth section, "Establishing Medicine on Pure Ground," is explained.

This section contains two parts: first, citing the circumstances to inform the Buddha; second, from the words "The Buddha said" onwards, the opening of the rules for establishing pure grounds. The opening text:
There are three parts: first, the opening of the precept against its specific object; second, the fourfold classification of the distinctions regarding purification;
and third, the resolution of doubts starting from the section on "the bhikṣus.

Regarding the first part, the explanation of the meaning, there is a threefold analysis: first, the intention behind the opening and the definition of the name; second, the determination of the two internal bases.

Third, regarding the method for binding [the precepts]: first, as for the underlying intention, it is because the karmic power of practitioners differs that the Great Sage established varying rules of permission and prohibition.
For instance, those of superior capacity are capable of practicing alms-gathering and do not require the accumulation of stored goods.

Those who attain realization on their own practice the Path; those of middling or inferior capacity have limited strength and must rely on external resources. If they were not permitted [to do so], there would be no means for them to advance in their practice.

Initially, the establishment of "pure grounds" (*śuddhasthāna*) was permitted due to the circumstance of illness; once established, it benefits all three grades of practitioners alike. This is indeed the Great Sage’s [teaching].

Guiding and comforting beings according to their circumstances, each in accordance with their individual faculties and needs, this Dharma was established. Determined according to its specific category, it restricts food for the sake of the Saṃgha;

by means of the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual), it is designated as "binding. Since there are differences regarding the food of individuals, there is no fault in keeping it overnight or cooking it; eating it incurs no offense.

It is designated as "pure" (śuddha). The name is established based on its location; therefore, it is called the "purification of the site" (*śuddhasthāna*). Next, regarding the determination of the two internal sites (*adhyātma-sthāna*):

the traditional interpretation states that "site" (*sthāna*) refers to a long-term residence, while "monastery" (*ārāma*) implies the presence of enclosures and obstructions; thus, both a single site and a single monastery each possess two internal sites.
If this is the case even when they exist separately, how much more so when they exist together? This can be understood from the cited evidence. Excluding the self-substance and the open ground:

first, it is not a place where the Saṃgha dwells for long, as it lacks the sense of accumulation; second, furthermore, there is no possibility of censure or disgrace; therefore, there are no two internal [factors].

Regarding the term "its own substance" (*svabhāva*), this distinguishes it from the boundary (*sīmā*). Regarding the term "open space" (*abhyavakāśa*), this differs from a monastery (*ārāma*). Now, we shall explain whether there is a boundary distinct from this monastery, or not.
The reason for this is that a monastery is established for the residence of the Saṃgha; as the text states: "the same place of residence."
The Great Boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) is fundamentally for the sake of the Dharma. It is stated in the joint formal act (*sahita-kamma*): "There shall be a single recitation of the *Poṣadha*.

Since a monastery (*ārāma*) is a residence for the Saṃgha, it is not a place for preparing food; for if food were prepared therein, it would give rise to public reproach. As stated in the preceding text: A bhikṣu placed food and drink on the open ground without securing them well.
When a cowherd or a shepherd took the food away, or if a thief carried it off, the bhikṣu informed the Buddha. The Buddha said: "It should be kept..."
In a quiet location at the edge of the quarters, one should designate a clean kitchen (*śuci-kūṭī*). One must not send [the meat] from a *nīla* (blue/green) area; it should be kept on open ground.

If it is within the boundary (*sīmā*), it should be sent outside the boundary. Furthermore, this text states that it is permitted to designate a clean area (*śuddha-bhūmi*) within a monastery (*saṃghārāma*).

Moreover, the three aforementioned types of purity refer to areas that are part of the monastery but not part of the formal boundary. It is also stated that one must not designate a superior room as a clean area. Furthermore, regarding ghosts...
Regarding the temple building: why must there necessarily be a great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*)? According to this principle, it is a matter of not establishing boundaries within a monastery (*ārāma*).

This is simply because the monastery has obstructions that block the view of the courtyard’s features, thereby inviting criticism regarding the boundary. Furthermore, whether the view is narrow or wide, how could one avoid generating slander by defining the limits?

Moreover, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Sengqi lü), fascicle 31, states: "At that time, food was being prepared inside the monastery; the kitchen broth and water used for rinsing vessels flowed out as foul water."
When he went out into the street, he was censured by the people of the world, who asked: "How can a śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas, not have a separate kitchen for his dwelling?
The bhikṣu informed the Buddha. The Buddha said: "It is not permissible. Even if the dregs of the gruel flow outside, it is a *vinayātikrama* (offense against the discipline).

Furthermore, according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, initially [the Buddha] permitted [cooking] within the room after performing the formal act of *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a motion followed by one proclamation) to purify the site; later, due to public censure, he prohibited it. Moreover, in the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, fascicle... [text continues].

Regarding the ninth point: "The smoke from the monastery quarters does not cease, for various kinds of food are constantly being prepared; these are made by others, and a practitioner should not eat them.

Since it is thus stated that there are two types of *ārāma* (monasteries), how is it that in both the preceding and following passages it is said that one must not stay overnight or cook within the boundary?

This refers exclusively to the *saṃghārāma-sīmā* (the boundary of the monastic compound), not to the *saṃgha-sīmā* (the boundary encompassing the community). Therefore, the preceding text states: [as cited above].
This is the boundary of this monastery; it is not the boundary of that monastery. Furthermore, within a monastery there is a boundary, and the boundary is coextensive with the monastery.

When one says "the boundary," it refers to the monastery itself; thus, for a solitary boundary, there is no offense. Moreover, regarding the terms "above" and "below" used here, these all refer to the formal establishment of the offense (*sāpattika*).

The text specifically opens the section on the establishment of boundaries by referring to them collectively as *ārāma* (monasteries). Question: Why is it that one may not stay overnight on pure ground (*śuddhasthāna*)? Answer: Observing the cooking [of food] does not constitute an offense.

Regarding "cooking": the answer is that it is an offense for cooking because it incurs public censure when staying in the same place as human food. It is permitted because there is no censure when the matter does not persist over a long duration.

Furthermore, another interpretation holds that "cooking" refers to the location and "staying overnight" refers to the person; since cooking pertains to the location, one does not commit the offense of cooking while merely supervising the cooking.

Since staying overnight pertains to the person, one commits the offense by being in the same place as the food. Moreover, because cooking pertains to the location, [the rule applies] regarding what is not...
Cooking on pure ground: even if there is no bhikṣu present, one still commits the offense of cooking indoors, because the food has been kept overnight by someone [who was not a bhikṣu].

If one keeps it overnight on impure ground, provided there is no bhikṣu present, one does not commit the offense of keeping food overnight indoors. Regarding the subsequent formal act of binding (the *sīmā*): in principle, it should not be performed from a distance.
The mention of "in the center" serves to distinguish it from human habitation; thus, it says, "The Saṃgha now establishes this place as a pure ground (śuddhasthāna).

This particular location does not necessarily depend solely on the arising of a formal boundary (sīmā); it may be either the boundary itself or a separate area, both of which are permissible, just as in the case of establishing a garment-boundary (cīvarasīmā).

Next is the procedure for the *kaṭhina* robe. *Kaṭhina* is a Sanskrit term; in this language, it is called "the robe that rewards the good and punishes the evil.

"Reward" refers to the five privileges obtained by those who observe the earlier *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat). "Punishment" refers to those who enter the later *varṣā* or break the retreat, who do not obtain them. Furthermore...
It is said that if one receives this *kaṭhina* robe, it can produce five kinds of beneficial merit (*guṇa*). It is called the "merit robe" because its name is derived from its functional efficacy;
it is also called the "solid robe" because when it is made, it is composed of many pieces of cloth, hence it is termed "solid.
A detailed explanation of the ritual procedures for receiving and relinquishing it, collected in one place, is called a *khandhaka*. This text is divided into two parts.
The first section clarifies the ritual procedure for receiving robes (*cīvara*). The second section concerns the method for relinquishing robes as practiced by the group of six monks (*ṣaḍvargika*).

The preceding text is further divided into three parts: first, it clarifies the circumstances for receiving robes; second, it explains how the Saṃgha should receive them through formal relinquishment.

The former part is divided into three sub-sections: first, it uses the monks of two countries as the introductory context; second, from the passage "At that time, the World-Honored One... onwards, it demonstrates the conclusion of the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*).
There are four matters that should be performed because of receiving robes; these follow the sequence of the remaining three [categories].

The first applies to all three days—the fourteenth, fifteenth, and sixteenth—while the other two matters are restricted to the sixteenth day alone. Regarding the third [category], there are five matters, which are explained below as the five benefits.
This section contains two parts: first, receiving the robe for the sake of the five matters; second, having received the robe, being permitted to perform the five matters.
Next is the procedure for receiving [the robes]. First, one should understand its meaning through a fivefold analysis: first, the time of receiving; second, the place of receiving;
third, the person who receives; fourth, the matter of the robe; and fifth, the clarification of the ritual. Regarding the first, the time, there are two parts:

first, the time of receiving the robe; and second, the time of obtaining the benefit. As for "the time of receiving the robe," according to this Vinaya text, it is restricted solely to the sixteen days [of the rainy season retreat], because...

The fifteen-day *varṣā* has not yet concluded; because the labor [of the robe-making] would not be fulfilled, if one were to receive it on the seventeenth day, it would already be past the subsequent period, as there are no five months in the winter season.
For this reason, the text states: "It is permitted that when the four months of winter have ended, the Saṃgha should bring forth the *kaṭhina* robe.
It further says: "From now on, it is permitted that after the *pravāraṇā*, one shall not receive the *kaṭhina* robe, but may receive it for one month."

The *Kaṭhina* robe [period] lasts five months. Furthermore, according to the *Vinaya-vibhaṅga* and the *Vinaya-saṃgraha*, those who enter the later retreat (*paścima-varṣā*) are not permitted to receive the robe;
thus, it is known that the time for receiving it is strictly limited to sixteen days. Next, regarding the time for obtaining the benefit, it is strictly limited to five months.

The intermediate eight days of relinquishment (*utsarga*) are indefinite in length. Next, regarding the location, this refers to the formal ritual boundary (*karmabhūmi*), which is large rather than small. Large...

The essential point here is that the realm and the persons must differ; otherwise, the realm and the persons cannot be established. According to the *Jianlun* (Treatise on Views), there are eighteen [cases]. If the designated location is not complete, five persons may be summoned.
The assembly of monks from other monasteries may suffice for the count to receive the robe; visiting bhikṣus may not receive it. There are three subsequent types of persons:
first, the person who receives the robe; second, the person who holds the robe. (2) Initially, these were categorized separately as "the receiving person," referring to the five assemblies.

Among these, the first two [cases] do not apply to the latter three. According to the *Jianlun* (Treatise on Views), four bhikṣus and one śrāmaṇera were about to conclude their summer retreat (*varṣā*).

They intended to confer the full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon the śrāmaṇera so that they could reach the required number of five to receive the robes; thus, the newly ordained person also fulfilled the requirements for receiving them.
The same applies when there is one bhikṣu and four śrāmaṇeras. From this, it is known that a śrāmaṇera has no right to receive the robes.

Within those who are in *anvāsa* (the period of temporary residence), there are those who are settled and those who are unsettled. Those who are unsettled do not obtain [the robe], because they have not completed their *anvāsa*.

Within those who are settled, it is restricted to the former and not the latter. Within the former, one takes the case of one who has successfully [completed the ceremony] and not one who has broken it. Within those who have succeeded, there is the one who possesses the *saṃghāṭī*.

It is obtained. As for the *kāṭhina* robe, it must be within the boundary; though within the boundary, it must be before the Saṃgha. As it is said, one who intends [to leave] is not permitted to receive the robe.
Regarding the two persons who hold the robe: this refers to those who have taken up the summer retreat within the same boundary and possess virtuous conduct.

Regarding the ten rules, one who possesses the five virtues is appointed; that is to say, one who has not [previously] accepted [the robe], and so forth, and who knows whether [a robe] has been accepted or not yet accepted.

Although there is no explicit text for this, the meaning should likewise be so. Third, regarding the distinction between the Saṃgha and the individual: this refers to the Saṃgha and not the individual. The Saṃgha consists of four persons;

since the formal act (*karmavācanā*) performed by the Saṃgha must necessarily possess these five [virtues], the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* asks: "How many persons may receive the *kaṭhina* robe? At the minimum, five persons."
Regarding the "subsequent robes," their substance must be the three robes (*tricīvara*). Only when they are complete with the four requirements can they be obtained;

if they are deficient in these or consist of other types of cloth, they do not constitute a valid acceptance. The *Vinaya* cites that five-strip robes (*pañcakaṣāya*) are not permitted to be made as a single seamless garment (*saṃkakṣikā*).

Regarding the merit robe (*kaṭhina*), it must necessarily be cut into pieces; thus it is said that the five strips are cut to form ten sections. The *Saṃghabhedavastu* (or *Karmavastu*) states that even a robe of reduced measurement does not constitute a valid acceptance. This discusses the quantity [of the cloth].
Regarding this, the minimum is three persons. Furthermore, the request must also accord with the Dharma; otherwise, it will not be valid, as stated in the text.
If one obtains [the requisites] before they are completed, one must have them made. The text merely states that through a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*), a monk is appointed to perform the work.

There is no *karmavācanā* text for this. In the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, chapter twenty-two, it states that one, two, three, or even many people may be appointed through a formal motion (*jñapti*) to assist [the officiant].
The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* also says: "One, two, or three persons. Subsequently, the application of the rule follows the text.

Next follows the explanation of the text. The text is divided into two parts: first, showing the correctness and incorrectness regarding the substance (*dravya*) and color (*varṇa*) of the robe to be made;

second, from "At that time, there was another residence... onwards, clarifying the method for receiving the robe. The former part is further divided into two: first, the correctness and incorrectness regarding the substance; second, from "At that time, the group of six [monks]...
onwards, clarifying the correctness and incorrectness regarding the color. The former of these has three sections: first, citing the correct manner in which the acceptance is accomplished; second...
How is it that the Saṃgha does not constitute a formal act of censure (*otarana*)? It is not non-constitutive when there is a fault. Third, how is it that the acceptance constitutes a formal act?

This refers to the prior substance of the censure; as it should be according to the Dharma, it is accepted in accordance with the rules. The preceding text has three parts: first, a general statement on what should be accepted; second, a specific clarification of what is in accordance with the Dharma.
The three [sections] constitute the section on "Acceptance. In the second [section], the section on "Specifics," there are three parts: first, clarifying the substance of the robe;

second, clarifying the proper manner of seeking it, as indicated by the phrase "not... below"; third, indicating the characteristics of what should be accepted, as indicated by the phrase "on that very day... The first part, concerning the substance, consists of three sentences. The first sentence is termed "new robe" in general because it is obtained for the first time.
Regarding the two types of new substances, the following two robes are distinguished: the first is obtained from another person, hence it is said...
If a donor offers robes, these are received because the Buddha permitted such gifts. Second, one may collect discarded remnants to serve as dharma-robes;
therefore, it is said that "rag-robe" (pāṃśukūla) refers to this prescribed garment. Third, one performs the ritual of purification (*kappiya-karaṇa*) for these in the same manner.
Regarding the new and old among the aforementioned robes: for these new and old garments, the precept requires that new material be patched on to constitute purification, or they may be washed first.
Accepting [the item] constitutes purification. Next, one seeks five phrases. Since this is not for the purpose of divination, one does not employ the *yāmi* (command) formula.

According to the two preceding texts, one should add the phrase "not being deceitful or crooked," because it is obtained according to the standard ritual. One does not judge movement by signs or silence, saying "it is not agitated" or "it is obtained.

Because it is not one of the fifteen [grounds for forfeiture], there is no transgression regarding the overnight stay; since it was never subject to forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*), purification is performed.

Next, one should receive [the robe] according to four points: first, it must accord with the Dharma; second, it must have the prescribed number of strips, hence it is called "five strips" (pañcakaṇṭhaka), or ten intervals, and so forth;

third, because the ritual for its preparation is taught, such as washing and dyeing; fourth, because the manner of receiving it is taught, one must stand before the Saṃgha. The subsequent [sections on] binding [the robe] are easily understood.

Next, regarding the section on non-attainment (*asiddhi*), there is an objection concerning the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*). As for the absence of the *saṃghāṭī* robe, it is because there is no purpose [for it].
Next, one should receive [the precepts] in accordance with the Dharma as prescribed in the text. Next, the color may be known.

The text concerning the receiving of robes consists of five sections. First, citing the circumstances to inform the Buddha. Second, from "The Buddha said" onwards, demonstrating the method of reception. Third, from "At that time, Upāli" onwards, answering questions to resolve doubts and obstructions.

Fourth, from "If one obtains" onwards, distinguishing between what constitutes a valid completion and what does not. Fifth, from "Those six groups of bhikṣus" onwards, indicating the proper time for receiving benefits.
Regarding the first section: having obtained the robe, the method for maintaining it was not yet understood; therefore, he sought to demonstrate the proper model for practice. Thus [the text begins].
One must first announce to the Sangha. Next, the text on the Dharma-procedure has four parts: first, making it known to the white-robed Sangha whether [the robe] has been accepted or not;
second, from "In this manner" onwards, appointing a person to guard the robe; questioning the reason for the *pravāraṇā*; first appointing and then announcing.

This acceptance of the virtuous robe (*guṇavastra*) follows the sequence of announcement first and appointment later, because it is a formal act of *pravāraṇā*. In contrast, for laypeople, one appoints first and then announces, so as to allow them to know whether it has been accepted or not.

Therefore, it is essential that one first makes a formal announcement before assigning the task. "The three virtuous ones, the Saṃgha, listen" and so forth, is for the purpose of emphasizing this formal act (*karmavācanā*) of entrusting the robe to that person.

Regarding "one who maintains [the robe] at this residence," it means that such a person shall not receive the benefits of the robe. From "that bhikṣu" onwards, the text correctly clarifies the method of receiving [the robe];
the textual passage has three parts: first, the person holding the robe places the pattern of the robe on both sides, and according to what is obtained by hand, he speaks as follows.
This is the place for the formal conclusion. The ritual for receiving the precepts is recited three times. Next, the assembly of monks below [the preceptor] accepts them.
To demonstrate that the holding and receiving accord with the proper ritual, it is said: "It has been well received. Regarding the merits contained herein, this refers to the five benefits;
since there is no fault or loss, a beautiful reputation manifests outwardly, hence the term "renown. Because I have obtained this name, it belongs to me. Next, he replies: "So be it."
This refers to the person holding the robe speaking and giving his consent. If there is one who wishes to receive it, he should act in this manner;

if there is no one to receive it, he should remain silent and let the matter pass. Next, Upāli saw these nine statements and, having conceived a doubt, posed a question. The Buddha answered to clarify the matter for him.

Therefore, the formal acceptance (*pratigraha*) is not for what has passed or what is yet to come. Next, regarding the robe being completed before the time for receiving the benefit, it may be understood from the text.

Next, the section on relinquishing the robe (*cīvara-pratyādeśana*) consists of two parts: first, the forfeiture due to the lapse of time; second, the detailed explanation of the methods of relinquishment based on eight causes and conditions.
The preceding text consists of five parts: first, not relinquishing [the object] and reporting it to the Buddha; second, from "The Buddha said" onwards, demonstrating that such an action is improper;

third, from "From now on" onwards, distinguishing the timing of the relinquishment; fourth, from "It should be done thus" onwards, prescribing the method for relinquishment; fifth, from "If not" onwards, concerning the transgression of the time limit.

The determination of the offense. The fourth section, the text on the ritual of relinquishment (*pratyākhyāna-dharma*), has two parts: first, the preliminary preparations (*pūrvakalpa*); second, the formal body of the ritual procedure (*karmavastu*).

The preliminary preparations apply universally to all rituals; if they are deficient, the ritual act will not be accomplished. These preparations consist of six points. First, the assembly of the Saṃgha as described in the text:
"One should spread the seats and strike the *ghanṭā*; everyone should gather together in one place. It further states: "All who should come must come."

When those [monks] have come to face this assembly, one must know the number of those gathered. The extent of their gathering depends on the requirements of the specific function; if there are too few, the rite is not accomplished.
Second, when two or more are assembled as prescribed by the text and present before the assembly, one who ought to be rebuked must be rebuked.

This gathering of the Saṃgha in harmony has two aspects that cannot be considered as one: namely, there may be a gathering of the Saṃgha that is not in harmony, or there may be harmony while the Saṃgha is not [fully assembled].

[The assembly] gathers. Thus, one knows that the gathering of the Saṃgha is determined by number, as stated in the text. As for "the Saṃgha," it refers to four or five persons who are harmonious and of like mind, as stated in the text.
Regarding "harmony": there is a single *karmavācanā* and a single recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*. Third, those who have not yet received the full ordination (*upasampadā*) must depart;

because they are of a different class, they do not constitute a legal assembly. Fourth, those who do not attend must announce their consent (*chanda*). As the text says: "Those who should give their consent must give their consent."
Come. Now, although the previous section on calculation also included the desire [to act], it was explained separately because the matters concerning desire are distinct;

thus, it is clarified again here. Fifth, one asks about the action to be performed, saying: "What is the Saṃgha doing now? Sixth, one answers the action to be performed, saying: "The *kaṭhina* robe is being spread.

However, it should be understood that these questions and answers have both general and specific applications. Next, the formal announcement (*jñapti*) is as stated in the text. (From the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, Five-Part Vinaya)
The formal act of relinquishment (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) is abandoned.
Next, the abandonment is explained in detail. The text is divided into three parts: first, the direct explanation of the eight abandonments;
second, the six matters concerning the mutual distinctions of errors below; third, the two types of ultimate loss explained below. Among these, the former eight and the latter...

Second, ten [cases] are manifested according to their specific matters. Regarding the essence of relinquishment (*tyāga*), these stages are condensed into three categories. Among the eight [cases], the first six require mental relinquishment;

the next two are both relinquishments through formal ritual action (*karmavācanā*); and of the final two, one takes the case where a monk holding the robe goes outside the boundary to relinquish it, while the case where the Saṃgha acts in harmony to relinquish it together is the same as the preceding.
The preceding text has four parts: first, the introduction; second, the enumeration; third, the explanation.

There are four types of relinquishment through formal resolution (*saṃkalpa*). Regarding the first, "relinquishing through departure": this refers to the intention to depart for good with the mind, forming the resolve not to return.

This resolve may be made at the time of receiving [the robe], or it may be made when one intends to depart; subsequently, because one has formed the mental resolve to leave, it is called "relinquishing through departure. Regarding the second, "having finished":

originally, one resolves to relinquish [the robe] once the making of the robe is finished, and now that the making of the robe is finished, one subsequently resolves to relinquish it. Regarding the third, "not having finished": originally, one receives the robe...
The purpose was to make a robe. Now, having gone outside the boundary, he has set his mind at rest and does not make it; furthermore, he does not return to the boundary where the robe is kept.

Although the robe is not finished, because he maintains his original resolve, this is called "abandonment by non-completion. As for the four losses: the original resolve was to go outside the boundary.

It was for the purpose of making robes. Once the robes were finished, if they were lost, there would have been no need for the benefit of the robe-offering. Now that they are lost, one must seek them again; therefore, it is called "losing and relinquishing. Regarding "the five expectations being severed":

originally, when one intends to receive a robe, there is a place from which one expects it. If this expectation is not fulfilled, yet there is a continuity [of expectation], one does not relinquish it.

However, if the expectation from the previous household is severed and no subsequent expectation arises, since there is no longer a continuity of expectation, one says, "I relinquish the *kaṭhina* robe," and later arrives [at another place].

Regarding the "place of expectation": one originally intended to relinquish [the robe] upon reaching that place, yet subsequently made a formal resolution (yācana) and relinquished it. Regarding the "sixth, hearing": one originally intended to make a robe and planned to relinquish it immediately upon hearing [the announcement];

now, having heard that the Sangha has emerged, one makes a formal resolution and relinquishes it. The ancient commentary states that this "hearing" applies to both the literal and the figurative. Question:

If "hearing" refers to hearing that the Sangha has relinquished [the robe], then once the Sangha has completed the relinquishment, what further need is there for a formal resolution? Furthermore, if there were no formal resolution, one should not lose [the robe]. Answer: It is called "hearing."
A specific individual within the Saṃgha does not receive the benefit of the robe; therefore, it is called "the robe being issued from the Saṃgha upon hearing.

Now, let us explain this: this "hearing" is hollow and not real. The Saṃgha has not actually relinquished [the robe]. There is naturally a requirement for "hearing," but because someone erroneously transmitted it as being merely a "requirement," it was lost.

If it were real, it would simply fall under the seventh category, "concealment. How could one who is already concealed further require a formal resolve (*cetanā*)? Furthermore, the text explicitly states: "The assembly of monks..."
Regarding the relinquishment of robes: one must not say, "This belongs to a specific person within the Saṃgha. The aforementioned six types of relinquishment occur because of a malicious intention;

however, if there is no such intent, there are six cases where the robe is not lost. As for the seventh case, "leaving the boundary": having accepted the robe, if one leaves the boundary and the Saṃgha performs a formal act of relinquishment (*dharmakarma*), that person remains outside the boundary and loses the robe by hiding there in the dark.
If they do not know of the relinquishment, they incur no offense regarding the acceptance of the benefit. The eighth case is "going out together."
Having received [the robes], one makes them into a garment. Whether the work is finished or unfinished, one returns to the original residence and performs the formal act of relinquishment;
therefore, it is called "commonly exiting. Next, the second section contains five items: the first has two sets of six; the second has four sets of fifteen;
the third has twenty-four; the fourth has three sets of nine; and the fifth has two sets of five. These five sections together total one hundred and one.
There are eighteen phrases. First, I shall explain the initial section. Herein, the first six phrases concern robes not yet obtained; the subsequent six concern robes already obtained.
There should also be a combination of both obtained and not obtained, but it is omitted from the text for brevity. Question: Since the first six concern robes not yet obtained, [how is this so?]

How can there be [the categories of] completion and so forth, given that there is renunciation? Answer: Because there was no initial acceptance, it is said that [the robe] has not yet been obtained. Later, when it is obtained and the robe is subsequently made, completion and so forth occur.
Herein, for the time being, two sets of six are established according to the distinctions of the stages; this interpretation based on the text does not contradict [the principles].

Regarding the Great Principle (*dàlǐ*): there is no need to further pair it with "concluded" (*jìng*) and so forth; by excluding these two-by-two, its many sixes are established. Next is the second position, namely:
having obtained the robe, not yet having obtained it, and both having obtained and not yet having obtained it—each constitutes fifteen. As the text says, "the eight above are mutually intermingled":
among those eight, the seventh is restricted solely to outside the boundary (*sīmā*). This hidden loss does not apply within the boundary, because [it has] come [from there].
Emerging together within constitutes the eighth. If they do not harmonize, the separate assembly is not established.

The remaining seven types apply both inside and outside the boundary; since there are seven for each—inside and outside—they total fourteen. The "concealed and submissive" applies only to the outside, thus making fifteen propositions in total.
Regarding the first, second, and third positions: the initial twelve propositions are formulated based on a single family, viewed through three positions and four propositions.
The first four phrases refer to obtaining the garment one hoped for. The next four phrases refer to not obtaining the garment one hoped for, as well as obtaining a garment that was not hoped for.

The final four phrases are all cases where, at the place of expectation, one obtains it and one does not obtain it; therefore, they are collectively termed "obtaining the garment one hoped for" and "not obtaining the garment one hoped for.
These three positions each have the distinctions of completion, non-completion, disappointment, and abandonment; thus, they constitute twelve [cases].

Regarding the departure to hear [the proclamation], it is because they depart together from the boundary and do not face the robe; therefore, it does not exist. Next, the twelve phrases of the ritual procedure are the same as before.
According to tradition, the difference lies only in the fact that it arises in relation to many members of the assembly. Next, the fourth position is also determined by this.

Regarding "the robe not yet obtained" and so forth, there are nine permutations for each. The first set of nine consists of three cases each for hearing [of the robe] within the boundary, hearing it on the road, and hearing it upon arrival at that place, as described in the text.
These are contrasted with the making of the robe; however, because there is no seeking of the robe, there is no expectation or cessation regarding the other two categories of substance.
As for the next five positions, the first five involve traveling to another region, and thus there is no necessity of departure.

Since he originally did not seek robes, there is no expectation or interruption [of the *kaṭhina*]. Because his body is outside the boundary, there is no "joint emergence. However, the five [cases] follow the sequence of the text;
the latter five differ only in that they prioritize the delight in tranquility. The second and third positions follow the text.

Originally, this was for the sake of this person guarding the robe so as to benefit others; now that the fundamental [condition] of staying overnight outside has occurred, all others lose [the benefits]. Above has been the *kaṭhina* rule.
[End. ● Next is the eighth *khandhaka*, which clarifies the communal regulations (*saṃghadharma*).

This [section] concerning Kauśāmbī, based on the ability to uphold virtuous conduct and the maintenance of the community’s protocols, should be named the *Saṃgharakṣa-khandhaka*. Furthermore, regarding the matters to be adjudicated therein, it concerns disputes.
*Kaṇḍa* (Section). It is named after the place where the dispute arose and the location where the protection of the community’s conduct was taught; thus, it is called Kauśāmbī.
It elucidates the extensive rules and protocols for the virtuous conduct of the community gathered in one place, which is termed a *kaṇḍa*.
Within this, the main text is divided into three parts: first, the presentation of the dispute to explain the principles and facts; second, from "At that time, the World-Honored One... onwards...

The method for settling disputes through silent censure and abandonment (*tūṣṇīka-prasrabdhi*) has been concluded. Third, at that time, the Buddha addressed Upāli, providing the rules for protecting the Saṃgha so that they might be observed and maintained.
The preceding section consists of four parts: first, the presentation of the dispute; second, the timely accusation of the offense.

1. The lower section details the report made to the Buddha. 2. The Buddha’s three statements below indicate whether the action was appropriate or not. 3. At that time, the World-Honored One went to [the place where] the *ukkhepanīya* (suspension) had been imposed, to exhort those in dispute toward reconciliation.
The preceding text is further divided into four parts: A. Granting the *adarśana-utkṣepaṇīya-karman* (formal act of suspension for failure to see an offense) to a bhikṣu who has committed an offense;

regarding this offender, there is no fixed explanation in the text, and it is provisionally treated by way of the analogy of shaving. Its appropriateness or lack thereof is discussed. B. The bhikṣu who has committed the offense... [text continues].

1. The one being censured (*pārivāsika*) himself declares that he has not committed an offense and refuses to submit to the formal act of suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*). 2. He then descends [from his status] and seeks companions to incite a dispute. 3.
Those individuals, having been suspended, form a separate faction and cause a schism. 4. Next, they inform the Buddha, and the Buddha’s reproach may be understood as follows.

Next, regarding whether the shadow [of the *karmavācanā*] should be valid or not, the text is divided into four sections: first, demonstrating whether it is valid; second, how the dispute increases when that person is suspended (*ukkhepanīya*);
third, how the assembly does not know the method of supervision; and fourth, showing the appropriate place for settlement. In the preceding section, there are two parts:

first, a general demonstration of the invalidation in response to the one who performs the suspension, meaning that within a single boundary (*sīmā*), both parties perform the ritual (*dharmakarma*) in relation to one another.

It is not established; therefore, it is called "breaking the Saṃgha. Next, the passage beginning with "If that person" clarifies whether [the act] should or should not be so considered. This section contains three parts. First, the presentation of what should be established.
The father says, "If that person," because he does not address the one who was cited, he uses the term "if that person. Regarding "what that person was cited for":

if they do not falsely seek companions as I have described, but remain in a single harmonious union, they achieve [their goal] without transgression. As for "you all": [this refers to those who follow such a person].
Because it corresponds to the ability to perform the formal act of suspension (*ukkhepana*), it says, "You [should] perform. "You" refers to those capable of performing the act.

As I have taught, one should seek a worthy companion, assist one another in harmony, and thus accomplish the rite without transgression. Next, for what reason is this established? Following this, there are two sections below that provide the explanation.

Within the explanation, first the distinction is raised: the performance of the suspension is not the same as the abandonment of the community. This passage consists of five sentences: the first is the enumeration of the number.
Second is the subtle inquiry; third, the listing of the two names; fourth, from "How so?
onwards, the explanation of the distinction between the two; fifth, from "For what reason" onwards, the conclusion.
Next, its commonality is raised to manifest that it causes one to practice; the text follows this principle.
The preceding section should also consist of five parts; however, because a minor inquiry is omitted, there are only four, which are the same as above.

The three subsequent passages can be understood accordingly. Next, the text on exhorting reconciliation has two parts: first, private exhortation; second, from "At that time" onwards, public exhortation in person.

Within the former, there is first the exhortation regarding the one who has been accused. This passage contains five sections: first, exhorting the offending bhikṣu to recognize his transgression and repent. If...

Regarding the phrase "not seeing [the offense]," etc.: the Sangha is universally esteemed by the kingdom as the Three Pitakas; this is truly something to be feared. One ought to acknowledge one's guilt.
Second, regarding that bhikṣu who has committed an offense, the following encourages reflection: the Sangha possesses great power and majesty;

if you do not acknowledge your guilt, they will certainly bring a formal charge against you. Third, regarding that bhikṣu, once the formal charge and disciplinary action have been carried out, the thirty-five [qualities] will certainly be forfeited.
[The section on] the matter. Fourth, if that bhikṣu [is not compliant], since they do not engage in the same activity, a dispute arises and a schism is formed.

Fifth, if a bhikṣu [is heavy with faults], the following exhorts him to see his own offenses for the sake of harmony and benefit. Next, the exhortation to those who can censure is also fivefold as before.

Next, the general exhortation regarding both the censurer and the censured consists of two parts: first, the introduction; second, the verses. The introduction has three sections: namely, the three exhortations and the three roots. First—
First, the extensive prose: This refers to citing secular matters concerning laypeople who, despite harboring such heavy resentment, still relinquish their discord;
how then can you cling to what is light and refuse to let go? When the World-Honored One exhorted them in this manner, the bhikṣus did not accept it.

He exhorted them a second and third time, with the extensive prose being the same as before. Next, the verse section is divided into two parts. First, the twelve verses generally exhort both the parties capable of and those involved in the cessation of strife and lingering resentment. Furthermore—

Now, his actual practice is manifested outwardly, matching his attire. The following four and a half verses describe the etiquette for leading and correcting the assembly according to the specific teachings, as well as the manner of his harmonious coming and going.
There are nine sections in the preceding text: first, one verse that casts a shadow toward the ultimate, citing the heavy to explain the light;
second, one verse that recites the previous abandonment of resentment, using the secular to illustrate the supramundane; third, one [verse]...

The first verse reveals that enmity arises from contention. The second verse demonstrates how patience eliminates enmity. The third verse shows that one who is free from enmity finds personal contentment. The fourth verse shows how patience benefits both oneself and others.
The fifth section consists of two verses encouraging the knowledge of firm dharmas. The sixth section consists of two verses encouraging the cultivation of superior practices.
The seventh section consists of two verses encouraging the practice of wearing the same garment [of discipline]. The first phrase of the initial verse directly addresses contention.
Thus, a foul reputation spreads far and wide. The second verse states that one is unable to practice the supreme Dharma of patience.

The following two verses explain that the schism in the Saṃgha was not caused by a major matter, but resulted from a minor provocation. The five subsequent verses explaining these characteristics are easy to understand.
Next is the seventh section, "The Non-Solid Dharma. This passage has two parts. The preceding verse identifies what is not solid so as to cause its abandonment;

that is to say, because it increases strife and enmity and causes the cycle of birth and death to never cease, it is called "non-solid. Because fools do not understand this and instead claim it to be superior, it is called "proclaiming solidity."

Patience can eliminate enmity and forever sever the retribution of suffering; therefore, it is steadfast. Furthermore, it is said that fools do not understand this and regard it as inferior; thus it is called "seeing what is not firm.
Because the mind is thereby deluded regarding the principle of right and wrong, it does not accord with the holy teachings; hence it is said, "they do not understand," and so forth.
The subsequent verse clarifies that this is intended to induce cultivation, whereby the mind thoroughly comprehends the principle of right and wrong. Understanding...

Holding [the precepts] is beneficial; knowing [their] violation brings loss and damage. Practicing in accordance with the teachings is therefore called "firmness" and "knowing firmness," and so forth.

Next, regarding the eight superior practices (*aṣṭau viśeṣa-caritāni*), the former is not like the latter. Each consists of a metaphor in the first half and its application to the Dharma in the second half.

For a monk engaged in strife, the three poisons are like arrows; lacking within him the courageous resolve for counteractive measures is equivalent in meaning to "holding loosely. His intention is to cause harm.
That poison arises from the mind; it first destroys one's own goodness, hence it is said that one "injures one's own hand.

When a śramaṇa joins his palms, he is like a person who, being not virtuous, joins his palms with a loose grip, thereby increasing his time in hell; by joining his palms with such a loose grip, he injures his own hand. The next verse says:
"All virtuous bhikṣus always take the three virtues as their core, never indulging in the three poisons; therefore, it is said that if one can grasp well..."

"Arrow. Internally, one should diligently practice self-mastery and cultivate its antidote; this is synonymous with "grasping firmly. Once the wholesome cause is established, one will not be harmed by the poison;

hence it is said, "one does not injure one's hand. If a śramaṇa can properly apply himself—skillfully grasping the arrow firmly—he shall be born in a good realm and, as stated above, "not injure his hand.
Subsequently, the nine practices are identical to the external application; likewise, first...
It is not the ultimate reality. Although one may endure and submit to them, the afflictions and delusions are not eliminated; hence it is said, "Although there are [robes]," and so forth.
Because they do not eliminate the conduct of enmity and harm, they are inconsistent with the robes; hence it is said, "They cannot," and so forth.

Next, if one can eliminate the fetters, maintain the precepts without transgression, and remain free from resentment and strife, such that one’s own person is at ease and secure, then one’s internal practice accords with the external robes. This is what is called "leaving home" and "entering [the order]."

This is the Way-person (*mārga-pudgala*). Next, the ritual for traveling among the multitude is clarified. Within this section, there are two parts. The first two and a half verses concern the rules for departing or remaining when a companion cannot be found;
although the initial verse states that one suffers no loss to oneself even if lacking a virtuous companion, one must nevertheless be careful in mind and not associate with the foolish.
The subsequent one and a half verses state that since one lacks a virtuous companion, one should fear being encroached upon by the foolish and thus ought to abandon solitary travel.
Like an elephant on a mountain peak. The following two verses clarify the conditions of having or lacking a companion, and the resulting states of progress or lack thereof.
Since the preceding verse established that one who has obtained a good companion can manage the multitude, they should be skillfully guided so as to remain free from anxiety and distress.
The subsequent verse shows that one without a companion cannot manage [the multitude] and should likewise quickly depart, just like the wild elephant mentioned before.
Next, the explanation of the text on settling disputes consists of two parts. First, the explanation of the expedient means for settling disputes;

second, from "He forms this thought" onwards, the actual explanation of settling disputes. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, the Buddha’s silent relinquishment as an expedient means for resolving the matter;

second, from "At that time, in Kauśāmbī," onwards, the collective censure by the people as an expedient means for suppressing the offense. Next, the text on the actual settlement has four sections. The first explains the [matter] being...

First, he reflects on his transgressions and prostrates to confess his sins. Second, the World-Honored One instructs the subordinates that taking refuge in the Buddha with the mind constitutes the definitive resolution.

Third, if those bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs [commit an offense], they are instructed by the Saṃgha to seek absolution. Fourth, the Buddha states that it is not the proper time for a formal assembly (saṃghakamma).
The preceding text has three parts: first, due to the severance of benefits, one approaches the Buddha to request extinction; second, at that time, Śāriputra...

The procedure for the fourfold assembly to request [the adjudication of] a dispute concerning a monk. Herein, because there are requests from the fourfold assembly, the text is divided into four parts. First, regarding the request by monks, there are four points:
namely, knowledge of what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma, the location, the offerings, and the conduct of sitting and rising. Regarding the request by nuns, there are two textual sections:

namely, Dharma and non-Dharma, and the instruction based on the location; these constitute the third and fourth [sections]. Second, within the requests by the laity, each textual section consists of two parts, concerning knowledge...

Regarding the Dharma, the non-Dharma, and the benefit for beings: thirdly, at that time, the suspended bhikṣu descended [from his position] and, having personally verified that he was not guilty of the offense, reported it to the Buddha.
Next is the determination of the resolution of suspension, as in the text. Next is the untimely formal assembly; the text has three parts as above.

Next, the ritual procedure (*vidhi*) is shown. The text is divided into two parts. First, the matters to be managed are presented; this includes cases where there is something that ought to be treated but has not been.

Second, from "The Elder... onwards, the qualities of the person who manages these matters are clarified; this includes what ought to be done and what ought not to be done. The first part has three sections:
first, the enumeration; second, the inquiry; and third, the listing. Among these five persons, although the first three may have actual transgressions, or perhaps the assembly is incomplete, or...
When the Saṃgha is not in harmony, one should not immediately administer discipline; to do so would result in a schism in the Saṃgha. One should merely console them, saying:
"If you perceive your fault, you ought to confess it. Regarding the latter two individuals, once the assembly is full and in harmony, they must necessarily be disciplined and subdued.
If one were to neglect them and fail to discipline them, one would not fulfill the virtue of rectifying the community. The first offender is precisely the subject of this introductory narrative.
This is not a case where treatment is appropriate; rather, such treatment would result in strife. Because of this single instance, the remaining four types of offenses are enumerated.
The offense of the first person is a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation) and so forth; the second is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (offense requiring suspension), hence it says "to be confessed before the Saṃgha.

The third is the offense of begging for a bowl, hence it says "to be repented before this Saṃgha. The fourth is the "treatment of the evil horse" (*aśvavada-dharma*). When this person commits an offense, the nature of the offense is not void, and the assembly perceives it all.

Upon hearing this, one must immediately impose punishment. Furthermore, because he refuses to acknowledge the Sangha’s decision as insignificant, and since he does not submit to his own guilt, he is cast out like a wicked horse;
this applies not only to this assembly but to other assemblies as well. Therefore, it is said that "wherever you reside, they shall likewise censure you.

This has the same meaning as "speaking for oneself" (*svavāda*) and "seeking a formal hearing" (*samanubhāṣaṇā*). Thus, when it says "one should not seek a hearing," this is itself the granting of a hearing. In the text:

There are three [types of formal acts]: namely, those consisting of the Dharma, the simile, and the combination. The five [cases] refer to being accused for not seeing [an offense]. When one has actually committed an offense in private and is accused by another, yet refuses to acknowledge and submit, one is therefore subjected to a formal act of accusation and discipline.

Furthermore, regarding the "treatment of a wicked horse": this refers to one who acknowledges neither the matter nor the offense. The second type of formal act of accusation and discipline refers to [this case].
The text cites the matter but not the offense.

Next, it clarifies whether or not one should perform [the prescribed action]. This section is divided into two parts: first, the clarification of whether or not one should perform it; second, from "At that time" onwards, the exchange regarding its excellence.
The preceding section has five parts. First, after Upāli has seen the principle of what is to be abandoned, he asks whether there is a corresponding treatment for the matter.
Joint governance. It is not yet clear how many qualities one who wields this authority must achieve to be capable of protecting the Dharma and rectifying the assembly.
Next, the Buddha’s answer lists five [qualities]: three subtle and four intentional actions, which are then enumerated individually as follows. First, regarding what is real and what is unreal:

"real" refers to that which should be done when there is an offense, and that which should not be done when there is no offense. Second, from the passage beginning "That bhikṣu..."—although the matter may indeed be real, it should...
One should contemplate whether an action is beneficial or not. "Beneficial" means that because one contemplates the faults [of the object], evil is transformed into goodness;

this is what should be done. "Not beneficial" refers to failing to contemplate the faults and instead giving rise to anger and contention. Third, regarding the lower matters—even if they are beneficial, a bhikṣu must further contemplate whether the time is right or wrong.

"The right time" means when the required number is complete, the assembly is harmonious, and the matter accords with the Dharma and should be performed. "The wrong time" means when the number is incomplete.

1. Dissension. The matter is not in accordance with the Dharma and should not have been done. 2. That bhikṣu, although he knows it is the proper time, must further observe whether the Saṃgha is in harmony or divided.
3. If a bhikṣu performs an action, one must examine below whether there are associates [for the offense]. This, compared to the preceding conditions, constitutes a real transgression;
because the four factors mentioned below are lacking, it results in a schism in the Saṃgha. 4. Upāli, etc., concludes.

Next, he asks about the excellence [of the teaching]. The first half of the verse acknowledges the words: the Buddha spoke to the Saṃgha regarding the principles and matters to be abandoned, as well as the conduct of the leader of the assembly for providing protection and rescue;
thus it says, "he spoke these words for the Saṃgha. This acknowledges the preceding speech.

Because its benefit is inexhaustible and can cause bhikṣus to take it forever as a guide for their minds, it says, "because its meaning and benefit are definitive. The second half initiates the question; the first phrase...
[He] does not know. Furthermore, what further excellence is there that is worthy of upholding the supreme Dharma and managing affairs within the assembly?

Therefore it is said: "How can one know the excellence? The next phrase [expresses] ignorance. How can one recognize the principle of what is to be abandoned and, through the Dharma, reach a definitive judgment, thereby becoming capable of protecting the Dharma?
Therefore it is said: "The bhikṣu attains firm persistence. The subsequent answer consists of two parts: first, the seven-syllable verse answers the initial question; next...
The five-character verses answer the subsequent questions. The preceding text is divided into six parts. The first consists of two verses that manifest the excellence of his practice.

As he is about to rectify the masses and perpetuate the Dharma, his practice must transcend that of ordinary beings; for if his conduct were to conflict with reality in any matter, who would follow and revere him?

Therefore, it is necessary first to clarify the excellence of his observance of the precepts. Although his practice is excellent, if he lacks understanding, he will lack the capacity for decisive judgment. [Sudu]... [text continues].

The virtue of things is elucidated by this second single verse, which clarifies the excellence of understanding. Once the practice of understanding is complete, one is capable of making decisive judgments;
thus, the third set of three verses clarifies the excellence of decisiveness, wherein one holds the principles of judgment for the assembly without any doubt or hesitation.

When making decisions within the assembly, one ought to be humble and respectful; if one were instead arrogant and haughty, it would conversely invite derision. Therefore, the fourth single verse [addresses this].

The first [verse] clarifies superiority in being humble and lowly; having already established modesty and respect, one is able to rectify the various teachings. It is logically necessary to understand affairs, because [otherwise] complaints and disputes over right and wrong would arise.
The fifth pair of verses clarifies superiority in harmonizing sentient beings;

having already possessed the previous five qualities, one is capable of presiding over the assembly and can cause the True Dharma to abide for a long time without extinction. Therefore, the sixth single verse clarifies superiority in upholding the Dharma. Next, I shall explain the text.

The first phrase refers to the purity of the inner mind; the second phrase refers to the external appearance being worthy of observation. Because of this, enemies are unable to utter words of reproach.
In the first phrase of the following verse, one is able to remain free from resentment. The second phrase distinguishes the person by their conduct and designates them as "that one" (the other).
Because that leader who governs the assembly maintains pure conduct and is without transgression, they are able to attain [this state]; it is for this reason that others do not slander them. Next...
Regarding "one who possesses clear understanding": the first phrase restates the preceding practice as accomplished; the second phrase explains being free from doubt and obstruction;

the third clarifies decisive resolution. Within the text, there are two parts. The first verse establishes the thesis of decisive resolution. Although one may be fearless in private, one is not yet fit to uphold the Dharma;

it is necessary that one’s mind be at ease within the assembly before one can provide protection and guidance. Therefore, it is said: "not fearing when among the assembly," and "residing in the assembly to adjudicate principles. Form...
The mind is as it always is; therefore, it is said that there is no change. Whatever determinations arise are all in accord with correct principle;

therefore, it is said that they are not lost, and so forth. The next two verses correctly clarify these determinations. Herein, the first phrase poses the question, while the remaining three phrases provide the answer.

Because there is internal, swift discernment, it is said that he answers promptly, and so forth. Furthermore, because there is the capacity for broad vision, it is said that he acts according to the occasion, and so forth.
The mind remains free from change or fear; therefore, it is said that "the responses are equal. Next, "humble" is as can be understood. Next, regarding "taming beings":
this refers to the fundamental origin of affairs. By subtly analyzing grievances, one ensures that the enemy cannot gain the upper hand.
When practicing this method, it truly serves as a model for all people, such that none fail to look up to it; hence, it is called "taming many people. Next is "upholding the Dharma."

As for this person: since their virtuous conduct is thus, they are fit to serve as a teacher and instructor. When upholding the community and adjudicating principles, they first respond according to the Way; therefore, it is said, "Always [acting] with equality," and so forth.

Next is the response concerning the matters to be deliberated, which also consists of six parts. First, there are two phrases concerning the knowledge of what constitutes an offense and what does not. Second, there are...

There are four statements. [The first] concerns knowing whether one has repented or not; it consists of two or three statements. [The second] is to exhort those who know how to repent; it consists of three statements.

[The third] is being able to accept the Sangha’s command; it consists of three statements. [The fourth] is being able to abandon arrogance; it consists of three statements. [The fifth] is concluding with the protection of the Dharma; it consists of two statements. Regarding the initial text:

"If one commits such an offense" refers to the two types of offenses—those of omission and those of commission. This refers to the aforementioned five kinds of offenders; if they do not commit [the offense], they obtain [the precept].

Regarding "offense": it refers to one who is diligent and focused; by not committing what is non-offensive, one attains purification and extinction [of faults]. The subsequent text takes up this defilement regarding the aforementioned offender. There are two types of offenses:

those of omission (*saṃvara*) and those of commission (*asamvara*), which are referred to as the "two. Since both of these are fully understood, it says "knowing both. Knowing the defilements, one performs repentance and eradicates them.
This refers to one who has committed an offense and now regrets it. The next two phrases indicate the signs for the community to expel such a person.

"One who knows their defilement and regrets it" refers to those among the five types of persons where the first three do not regret, and so forth; the latter two are explained according to the text as exhortations to know [the truth].

Next, "receiving the Sangha’s command" refers to a person of faith; because they possess faith, they can act upon the words of the assembly. The final two passages below are easily understood. Above...
The section on protecting the communal rules is concluded.
Next, the rules maintained at Campā are explained. If named according to the subject matter, it should be called the *Karmavastu* (Chapter on Ritual Acts).

However, as it is titled here based on the location where it was taught, it is called "Campā. It extensively clarifies the ritual acts (*karman*) and the characteristics of what is improper. [End of] Collection.
In one section, it is titled *Khandhaka*. Within this, the main text is divided into three parts:

first, whether those who have been disciplined for an improper act are cleared of suspicion; second, from "At that time, these resident bhikṣus... onwards, raising the matter to inform the Buddha and inciting his rebuke; third, from "He addressed the bhikṣus...
onwards, extensively explaining the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) according to its characteristics of being improper. Regarding the preceding text:
Three points: first, the suspension of offerings; second, that visiting bhikṣu being subject to disciplinary measures for minor offenses;
third, whether the doubts in that bhikṣu’s mind are resolved.
Next, the text for addressing the Buddha consists of two parts: first, the resident bhikṣus’ formal request to awaken [the Buddha’s awareness];

second, when those visiting bhikṣus respond to the questions below by confessing their own words, thereby effecting the reprimand. The preceding section contains five parts: first, approaching the location;
second, from "At that time, the World-Honored One... onwards, inquiring whether they are at ease; third, "You, bhikṣus, from where..."; [fourth, ...]; fifth, [conclusion].

First, [the monk] comes down and asks about his place of origin; second, he answers by recounting the matters above. Fourth, the Buddha tells that bhikṣu [to stop], below which the Buddha judges it to be unaccomplished.
Fifth, "You, bhikṣu, may go back," below which the Buddha acts as his companion. The subsequent passage also consists of five parts: first, explaining the approach; second, asking whether he is well;
third, asking about his place of origin; fourth, asking "In that place, is there... and so forth, which asks about what was obtained.
He says: Fifth, at this point, he distinguishes the censure below.
Next, he extensively clarifies what is not as it should be below. Now, wishing to explain the text, he analyzes it according to four sections. First is the classification of the scriptural text.
Second, determining the intent of the treatise; third, regarding the presence or absence of conditions; fourth, the word-by-word explanation.
