In the first section, there are eleven general categories according to the specific distinctions of the conditions: first, a brief presentation of the offenses and their formalities (*karmavācanā*) in relation to conditions, indicating what is appropriate and what is not;
second, the four cases of a quorum, which clarify what is appropriate and what is not by examining the requirements for a full assembly; third...

1. At that time, the group of six bhikṣus [discussed] the determination of whether a formal assembly (*saṃgha*) had been constituted or not, and whether the one for whom the act was performed was a member of the *saṃgha* or not. 2.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus [discussed] that the procedure of repeated authorization (*anujñā*) and the method of layering [the robe] may not be performed again.

3. At that time, the Buddha said, [passage] below, clarifying the boundaries of the four types of usage for the *saṃgha*. 4. At that time, the group of six bhikṣus [discussed] the formal initiation [of a candidate].

The seventh [section] concerns whether it is appropriate to apply a remedy when it does not correspond to the illness; at that time, Upāli asked below whether a medicine was improper for a disease and whether one should administer it.

The eighth [section] concerns the difficulty of accomplishing formal procedures (*karmavācanā*) before a community when faced with specific circumstances; at that time, there was another residence where...

The ninth [section] concerns manifesting the lack of essential understanding regarding the body of the Dharma and the difficulty of communal disputes; at that time, there was a residence where the community of monks...
The same. Tenth: At that time, Vajrapāṇi asks below whether those who have attained the Dharma should be understood or not. Eleventh:
Vajrapāṇi asks again below whether such a person should be expelled or not.
The essential meaning of the second section is as follows: In the first passage, four types of "non-[proper action]" are briefly enumerated in relation to the conditions.

Next, regarding the two pairs of dharmas and non-dharmas, one should not act in two ways; rather, one should act according to what is appropriate. In the second passage, that which completes the quorum is "proper" (*yathā*), while that which does not complete it is "improper" (*na-yathā*).

That which is not subject to censure does not constitute [a formal act]; whereas when one censures that which is subject to censure, the censure is established and the impropriety is halted. The second... [text continues].

In the third section: although groups of six, two, three, or one bhikṣus exist, they are not the *saṃgha*; therefore, when one accuses another of being two, three, four, or more, or even if it is indeed a *saṃgha* yet proceeds with an accusation, that which is done is incorrect.
This is merely an accusation of what is wrong. It differs from the "clarification of the *yathādharma*" (acting according to the Dharma).
As for the *yathādharma*, since the *saṃgha* must perform the formal act (*karma*) of two, three, or one [members], it is called *yathādharma*. In the fourth section, its governance is entrusted.

When a person extinguishes their offenses, they dispute even more; one must not perform the formal act (karman) again. To increase or add to the established rules is likewise to raise an objection. One does not discern what is "as-it-is" (yathābhūta).

That which is "as-it-is" refers to acting directly according to one's condition, because it is not performed repeatedly; thus it is "as-it-is. Fifth, by relying on the application of the Saṃgha, the boundaries are clarified.
According to those boundaries, whether full or deficient, right or wrong is determined. In the subsequent text, the characteristics of right and wrong manifest the essence. Eighth.

In the texts, they likewise merely cite what is "not-so" (*na-yathā*). As for that which is "as-it-is" (*yathā*), because it gathers all things in total harmony and does not fall into the category of "not-so," it is termed "as-it-is.
Thus, when the various texts distinguish between "as-it-is" and "not-so" as relative opposites, these constitute twenty-two dharmas.

Now, for the sake of brevity, there are only nineteen; however, according to the intended meaning of the various texts, they must all be presented in pairs to reveal their significance, thus there are only eleven.
The Third Gate: Among these various texts, the second and fifth lack a specific introductory narrative (nidāna); the Buddha explained them directly.
The seventh and eleventh rely on questions and answers posed by Upāli to clarify what is not the case. As for the remaining six texts, all possess an introductory narrative;
in each, a bhikṣu raised a matter based on a specific event and reported it to the Buddha, who then provided a detailed explanation. This also serves to demonstrate...
Regarding the characteristics of the various factors that make it difficult for the *dharma* to be accomplished:
the fourth section, the explanation of the text, first interprets the initial passage. This passage contains three parts. First, a general enumeration of the number;
thus it says, "He addresses the assembly," and so forth. Second, the listing of their four names. Here, the first phrase directly states "an illegal *karmavācanā*. Correctly...
This matter of dependent origination is not [the case]. Alternatively, since it is not listed separately, it may further include other "non-[cases]. Regarding the three subsequent phrases:

because the person upholds the Dharma, the person and the Dharma are made to intersect in order to clarify that the words of the text are not the Dharma. "A separate assembly" (bhedasaṃgha) refers to both person and Dharma being non-[concordant].

"Non-Dharmic concordance" (adharmasāmagrī) refers to the Dharma being concordant while the person is not. "Dharmic separation" (dharmabheda) refers to the Dharma being concordant while the person is not. Above...

The four phrases that follow: if one clarifies the separation of person and dharma, there are seven [categories]. The third is the middle and lower; it concludes by indicating what is appropriate and what is not.
Within this, five "non-[factors]" are extracted to constitute the two non-[factors] of person and dharma.

Regarding the phrase "not the dharma," this refers to the "not the dharma" within the first three phrases. Regarding the phrase "separate assembly," this refers to the "separate assembly" within the second and fourth phrases. All of these...

There is no formal procedure (*vidhi*). Therefore, it is said that "it should not be performed. Regarding the statement that "a legal *karmavācanā* (formal act) and a harmonious *karmavācanā* should be performed":
"legal" refers to the "legal" in the fourth phrase; "harmonious" refers to the "harmony" in the third phrase. Because these possess a formal procedure, it is said that "they should be performed.

Herein, what is not the essence constitutes the four types of non-validity. Below, there is merely a summary indicating what should and should not be done, which is not like the aforementioned [invalid] cases.

Regarding the characteristics [of these acts]: how is this known? The text states that among these two types of *karmavācanā*, one should not perform an illegal (*adharma*) *karman* or a *karman* performed by a separate assembly (*nānāsaṃgha*).

How could an act be illegal if it is not performed apart from those who hold authority? If it is performed by those who are in harmony, then that is precisely the third case of being performed by individuals;
as for the second case, how could one simply say it is an illegal *karman* and thus should not be performed?

The acts of formal motion (*jñapti*) and so forth separately constitute the substance of the two non-entities (*advaya*). Since these two non-entities lack a distinct substance, the two "as-it-is" (*tathatā*) states are likewise so.

Although the commentary explains it thus, one must analyze it by means of four gates: first, the Sangha who performs the act; second, the Dharma which is performed; third, the place where the Dharma is performed;

and fourth, the matter for which it is performed. Regarding the first, concerning the Sangha: because the conditions depend upon the persons being disciplined, these are the four types of individuals.

Regarding the principle of the Sangha’s inclusion, there are actually four types of Sangha. Among these, there are cases where the four types of Sangha collectively perform the three formal procedures, such as the *jñapti* (motion).

These three procedures—*jñapti*, *jñaptidvitīya*, and *jñapticaturtha*—all possess the four kinds of non-validity (*avaiyāpṛtya*). Although there is a difference in breadth or narrowness when viewed from the perspective of the Sangha performing the formal act, if one discusses the four kinds of non-validity themselves, they apply universally to all four types of Sangha.

Next, regarding the formal procedure itself: since the basis for the motion concerns the person being disciplined, this is a *jñapticaturtha* (four-part) procedure; in principle, the four kinds of non-validity pervade it entirely.

This applies to the three types of formal announcements (*jñapti*) and so forth. To take the single announcement (*ekajñapti*) as an example: if there is an increase or decrease in the wording, or if the matter is incorrect, this constitutes the first fault.
If one performs it at a place where a single announcement should be made, yet a separate person presides over it, this is the second fault.

If one performs it at a place where a single announcement should be made, yet two people together preside over it, this is the third fault. If, however, one performs the announcement in accordance with the proper procedure for an announcement, [it is correct].
Regarding the fourth "non-validity" (*asādhū*) due to being performed by a separate assembly (*pṛthag-varga*): there are four types of non-validity.

First, if the substance of the dharma is increased or decreased, or if the matter itself is improper, this is the first non-validity. Second, if one performs a formal motion (*jñapti*) for one matter but performs the ritual act (*karmavācanā*) for another, it is called "unlawful" (*adharmika*);
because it is performed by a separate assembly, it is an "unlawful separation. This is the third non-validity.
As for "that which is not the Dharma" (adharma), it is the same as before; because it is performed by a group of people together, it is an "unlawful benefit.

Regarding the fourth "not [the Dharma]," if one performs a formal motion (*jñapti*) according to the method of a formal motion, or performs a *karmavācanā* according to the method of a *karmavācanā*, it is called "Dharma. However, because it is performed by a separate assembly (*pṛthaggaṇa*), it is "Dharma with a separate assembly.
By this, one should know that the three methods beginning with the formal motion each possess four types of "non-[Dharma]. Next, regarding the location, it explains them generally.

Regarding the two matters of location and substance within these four locations, there are four types of "non-[application]" (*aprāpti*). When considering the dharma in relation to the location, there is both pervasiveness and restriction.
As for the four types of non-application, they actually pervade all locations. Next, regarding the substance, the general explanation identifies three kinds:

first, matters concerning sentient beings and the path, such as receiving the precepts, observing the days, censure, concealment, and so forth; second, matters concerning non-sentient things... [text fragment].

Regarding sentient beings: such as the demarcation of boundaries and the purification of sites. Regarding the combination of sentient and non-sentient: such as robes separated while staying in one place.
These three types are the objects of action; when wrongfulness arises in relation to these objects, each and every case is fully endowed with the four factors.
Next, the second passage is explained. This section is divided into three parts. First is the enumeration of the number. The text states: "There are four full numbers.
This means that by means of four phrases, the meaning of "full numbers" is explained. If the text were exhaustive, it should have stated: "There are four full numbers and non-full numbers.

However, here the non-full numbers are omitted and only the full numbers are explicitly clarified; therefore, it says, "there are four full numbers. An ancient commentary states: "It is not the case that all four..."
"Full. Because it receives its name from the beginning, it is called "the four fulls. This explanation does not take the original text of the first phrase as its basis;

it merely lists three persons, omitting them for brevity. It obstructs reaching the actual substance of the dharma. Alternatively, one might add "correct" based on the meaning for those who possess [it].
Since the original text already lists three persons, how can it then say, "it receives its name from the beginning"? The second [section] lists its four names, and the third restates...
This is the explanation of the names. In the first phrase, the four *karmavācanā* (formal acts) involve persons whose transgressions of mind are slight;

because the punishment is not severe, they attain the status of a full quorum (*pūrṇasaṃkhyā*), as their bodies are capable of performing the ritual acts and do not require formal censure. In the second phrase, those whose bodies lack the complete precepts do not attain the status of a full quorum.

Because the matter is of great importance, the censure is permitted. This censure, according to the text, refers to the underlying meaning: it is a censure arising from the fear that the Dharma will not be successfully accomplished.
According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, this refers to a case where the mind does not intend to receive [the precepts]. Thus, the fifty-seventh [section] states:
"There may be a śrāmaṇera who, at the time of receiving full ordination, feels regret and does not intend to receive it, saying: 'I do not intend to receive full ordination.'"
Regarding the statement "accomplishing the prohibition for a śrāmaṇerī": this applies when she receives the six rules (*ṣaḍ-dharma*), or likewise when she receives full ordination (*upasampadā*).
When a bhikṣu confesses a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense and undergoes the *parivāsa* (probation) and so forth, as well as when appointing an administrator (*vaiyāvṛtyakara*), one should say:

"I do not accomplish the prohibition. In the subsequent phrase, both [the former and latter cases] are not permitted. Twenty-eight types of persons are listed in detail; in the subsequent phrase, all are permitted, as can be inferred by analogy with what is virtuous.

The six beginning with Kiu (Gautama) correspond to twenty-eight individuals. First, the "virtuous bhikṣu" corresponds to the aforementioned twenty-two. This is an explanation based on general categories.

If explained specifically, it includes the virtuous ones, the eighteen bhikṣus and the four types of bhikṣuṇīs, as well as the virtuous ones, the three types of *karmavācanā* (formal acts of accusation), the two types of *nihsargika-pāyattika* (expulsion) bhikṣus, and the remaining seventeen.
Next, those who "dwell within the same boundary" (*sīmā*) correspond to the two preceding individuals. Those who "dwell within the same [boundary]"...

As for "those who abide": this refers to those who, having previously been in separate *pravāsanīya* (banishment) within the same boundary, now extend their hands [in greeting] and turn back; it reverses the previous *sīmāmaṇḍala* (boundary). Next, there are three persons;
they directly face one another, totaling six, and even speak to bystanders—this reverses what was previously done. This refers to the person performing the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act).

Regarding the person against whom the reproach is directed: it does not constitute a valid reproach if they cannot be censured. Since this has already established that a reproach is valid when the signs (nimitta) and the counterpart (pratipakṣa) are present, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, chapter twenty-four, states:
"If a bhikṣu within the same boundary reproaches [the offender], such that the bhikṣu is made to sit and hear it, it constitutes a valid reproach; it is to be judged according to this."

Although at the time of the *kukkucca* (reproach), one does not speak directly to the person performing the *karmavācanā*, but rather sits together with the bhikṣus to deliberate on what is right and wrong, this also constitutes a limit of reproach.
Next, the meaning should be analyzed by means of six gates: first, the correspondence between the full [number of] reproaches; second, the determination of the number of persons.
The third concerns the Saṃgha; the fourth concerns the Dharma; the fifth concerns the location; and the sixth concerns the matter. Regarding the first gate:
if, for the time being, one contrasts the "complete" with the "incomplete," then that which is complete in number is correct, because it is appropriate to reprove [the offender].
If there is reproval but it is not stopped, it is incorrect. That which is incomplete in number is incorrect, because it is not appropriate...
"Rebuke. Thus, it does not constitute a rebuke; it does not stop that which is non-substantial. Among these four phrases, the first and the fourth are both complete numbers (*pūrṇa-saṃkhyā*).
If one considers the rebuke itself, there are cases where it is appropriate and cases where it is inappropriate. As for the second and third phrases, neither constitutes a complete number.

Regarding their substance, there are likewise cases where they are appropriate and cases where they are inappropriate. Furthermore, when contrasting the appropriateness or inappropriateness of the rebuke with whether the number is complete or incomplete, it is said to be "appropriate."

Within the [category of] "reproving," there are those that are complete and those that are incomplete; these correspond to the two sets of four phrases. Within the "not to be reproved," there are likewise those that are complete and those that are incomplete;
these correspond to the first three sets of two phrases. Now, as for this statement regarding "those who should be reproved," it is not yet known what kind of reproval this refers to.

The answer regarding the "reproach of one who contradicts the intent" (*pratyanuyoga*) is twofold: first, reproach due to a divergence of intent, which constitutes the reproach of forming a separate assembly (*pṛthaggaṇa*);

second, reproach due to a commonality of intent, which constitutes the reproach that does not cease. This present reproach refers only to the reproach that does not cease due to a commonality of intent;
it does not concern the reproach of forming a separate assembly due to a divergence of intent. The reason for knowing this is as in the second phrase [of the *Pratimokṣasūtra*].

If one fulfills the quorum, then although the act of censuring is accomplished, it does not constitute a *na-pratinihsargika* (non-abandonment) offense; nor does it constitute a *nānā-saṃgha* (schism).
Since this first phrase is thus, the remaining phrases should be understood by analogy. Regarding the determination of what is appropriate or inappropriate when considering both types of censure:

because the first phrase concerns the person being disciplined, it does not constitute a *na-pratinihsargika* offense, yet because the quorum is fulfilled, it does constitute a *nānā-saṃgha*. Since the text refers to the initial censure, it states that it is "inappropriate."
In the second case, because the required number is not met, the censure does not constitute a formal schism; however, since censuring is permitted, the censure is established and cannot be halted.
In the third case, because the number is not met and censuring is improper, the censure does not constitute a formal schism, nor does it constitute a valid censure.
In the fourth case, both conditions are fulfilled: because the number is met, the censure constitutes a formal schism, and because the censure is appropriate, it constitutes a valid censure.
Cease. Next, regarding the number of persons: in the first clause, three persons are enumerated;

alternatively, there may be four, making nine persons in total when combined—namely, adding the four [periods] such as *parivāsa* (probation) and so forth, along with the *āpattisthāna* (the locus of the offense).
In the second clause, there is only one; yet in terms of its meaning, it applies to both male and female rebirths. In the third clause, twenty persons are enumerated in the text.
8. These must exclude the four [procedures] beginning with *tarjanīya* (reprimand), the four beginning with *parivāsa* (probation), and the *āpattisthāna* (place of offense).

If one performs these nine matters in relation to [a single individual], there would be thirty-seven people in total; however, this would not constitute a full quorum, nor would it be appropriate to perform the reprimand. Therefore, the text below states:

"The four beginning with *parivāsa* cannot mutually act as the presiding authority (*dharmakara*) to complete the quorum. Since this is the case for the four beginning with *parivāsa*, the same applies to the *tarjanīya*.
These five categories consist of these nine types of persons, all of whom forfeit thirty-five matters.

If one excludes these nine, and further excludes those who act on behalf of the community (*saṃgha*)—provided there is no other specific purpose for their action—one arrives at twenty-eight persons when considering them in relation to the remaining rules.

This constitutes the fourth phrase. That is to say, excluding the nine [cases] such as "reproach" (*tarjanīya*) and so forth, when considering other factors in general, one reverses the preceding twenty-eight [cases] by means of the six [categories] such as "virtuous bhikṣu" and so forth;
this is the fulfillment and combination of reproach. If, however, it is in relation to the nine [cases] such as "reproach" and so forth...

Regarding the total of thirty-seven individuals, there are seven persons who should have the seventh added; they are not subject to disciplinary punishment. By this single phrase, nine persons are excluded.
Next, concerning the *saṃgha*: the first phrase is as listed in the text. As for those added by way of meaning, they apply only to the two types of *saṃghas* of fifty members;
they do not apply to a *saṃgha* of twenty members. Within a *saṃgha* of four members, eight [cases] are excluded.

Regarding the first case, once the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) has been performed, the remaining procedures apply universally. Regarding the second case, it applies exclusively to a community (*saṃgha*) of ten persons;
it is entirely absent from a community of five persons, and partially absent from the other two types of communities as well as from half of the five-person group.

Regarding the third case, if one considers twenty-eight persons as the "concordant" category, then it is said that the four types of communities, when incomplete, do not constitute a valid basis for censure. This is according to the underlying principle.
Adding nine people to make thirty-seven applies only to the assembly of twenty monks and partially to the assembly of four monks;
it cannot exist at all in the other two assemblies of fifty monks each. As for the fourth case, if one looks from the perspective of six people, it becomes twenty-eight.

This applies to all four types of saṃgha. As for the seven [karmas] that correspond to thirty-seven [procedures], they exist only within the twenty-member saṃgha and a portion of the four-member saṃgha;
the remaining two saṃghas (the ten-member and the fifty-member) cannot possess them. Next, regarding the application of the dharma:
in the first clause, nine *jñapti-caturtha* karmas must be excluded; if one considers these nine dharmas as being performed, they are subsumed under the third clause, with the exception of these.
Regarding the nine procedures (*karmas*): they have already been explained as being common to the three types of procedures, such as the *jñapti* (motion) and so forth.

In the second case, there is only the preceptor (*śikṣācārya*). This includes one *jñapti* alone and one *jñapti-caturtha* (four-part motion); these apply to the conferral of ordination for both assemblies (*saṃghas*), totaling four procedures. Among all other procedures, none of these may be present.
In the third case, if one considers it in relation to the twenty-eight persons, it constitutes a "concurrent" category, thus applying to all *jñapti* procedures and so forth.
Regarding the three dharmas: if one adds nine persons according to their meaning to make thirty-seven, this applies only to the nine dharmas such as censure (*tarjanīya*) and so forth;

it does not exist among the other dharmas. In the fourth case, if one reverses the twenty-eight by means of six, it then applies universally to all three dharmas, such as the "pure" (*śukla*) and others.
If one reverses the thirty-seven by means of seven, it applies only to the nine [dharmas] such as censure and so forth, and not among the other dharmas.

None. Next, regarding the locations (*sthāna*): the first phrase applies universally to all locations; that is, the two pairs of phrases beginning with "stage" (*avasthā*) are restricted to the *dharmadhātu-kriyā*.

Within this *kriyā*, they pervade all great boundaries (*mahā-sīmā*) and small boundaries (*kṣudra-sīmā*). The remaining two [phrases] apply generally to both types of small boundaries, as well as being absent within their own essential nature (*svabhāva*).
As for the third phrase, if one takes the twenty-eight persons as the "concurrent" (*sahita*) category, it pervades all *kriyā*s within their respective essential natures.

If one applies the meaning to nine persons to constitute thirty-seven, this refers to removing a small portion from within the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) and the site for the observance of the precepts (*sīmā-maṇḍala*).
The fourth phrase is the inverse of the third meaning, which can be understood accordingly. Next, regarding the application to matters:

with respect to the category of sentient beings, paths, and affairs, one excludes the nine dharmas such as censure (*tarjanīya-karman*) and so forth. If these nine are performed, they are subsumed under the third "concurrent" category.

Apart from these nine cases, [the offense] applies universally to other matters. The second phrase is restricted solely to the path of intentional action; the remaining two phrases are entirely absent.
The meanings of the third and fourth phrases may be inferred accordingly. Next, regarding the three entities that have not yet formed a *saṃgha*, the text is divided into four parts.

First, the misconduct initiated by the group of six (*ṣaḍvargika*); this section contains thirteen phrases, meaning there are four phrases each within the first, second, and third [categories]. Within the *saṃgha*, however—

Because there is one [case], there are thirteen [sentences]. The second [section] regarding the white [action] to the Buddha should also be stated in full; however, for the sake of avoiding prolixity, it is merely indicated briefly.
From the third [section] where the Buddha speaks downward, its invalidity is demonstrated through the full thirteen sentences.

The fourth [section], beginning with "If one person," determines that it constitutes an illegal act, also consisting of thirteen sentences. Among these thirteen sentences, the first twelve are based on the nature [of the offense].

Regarding the term "Saṃgha": although the substance of the thirteenth phrase is that of the Saṃgha, because that which is being performed is [for] the Saṃgha, it constitutes an illegal act (*adharma*).
The text should have cited an example; its absence here is an abbreviation. Next, the meaning is explained through four gates. First, concerning the Saṃgha:

the intent of this passage is primarily to define the Saṃgha as consisting of four persons, and to distinguish that with three persons or fewer, it is not the Saṃgha and thus should not perform formal acts (*karmas*). If...
When there are four persons, although their physical form constitutes a *saṃgha*, because the action performed is that of a *saṃgha*, it nevertheless becomes an illegal act (*adharma*).

If one applies this principle by analogy to cases involving five persons or more, the other three types of *saṃghas* likewise become illegal; for while five persons should uphold the legal procedure (*dharmakarma*), four persons do not constitute a *saṃgha*.
This same logic applies by extension to groups of ten, twenty, and so forth. In the present text, however, it is stated directly that four persons constitute a *saṃgha*.

One should uphold all dharmas; therefore, they are explained selectively. Next, regarding the dharma: because the text relies on the treatment of persons, it specifically refers to the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations).
It does not, however, exclusively refer to the *jñapti* and the other three [proclamations] such that one may claim anything other than the *jñapti-caturtha* is invalid.

One should simply know that if the substance [of the act] has not yet been completed, any performance by the Saṃgha constitutes an illegal act (*adharma*). Next, regarding the location: the text is based on the treatment of persons.

This appears to be a specialized method of ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*). Within this ritual procedure, the meaning of "large" excludes "small," though by extension it also applies to the small boundary (*sīmā*) of one's own person.

This is because for those with fewer than three [monks], any location would be unsuitable. Next, regarding the matter itself: according to the text, it refers to the person being disciplined, which is a circumstantial matter (*vastu*).
However, if judged by the underlying principle, the other two [types of boundaries] are also applicable.

Next, the method for the fourth layer of compounding [the rules] consists of three parts. First, the offenses committed by the group of six (ṣaḍvargika), namely: the seven [rules] such as censure (*tarjanīya*) and so forth;

the four [rules] such as separate residence (*parivāsa*) and so forth; and the seven *vinayas*. These eighteen rules are discussed in terms of treating the person, extinguishing offenses, and settling disputes.
Next, they report this to the Buddha. Next, he declares that it is improper. The fourth part, which is a brief judgment that the action is invalid, is omitted. Furthermore...
"Non-existence of such [a person]" is also an abbreviation. Next, the meaning is analyzed by means of four gates. First, regarding the *saṃgha*:

according to the text, those who govern people and so forth—namely, the eighteen dharmas—are subsumed under the *caturvargika-saṃgha* (the community of four persons) and the *viṃśativargika-saṃgha* (the community of twenty persons).

By extension of this principle, it also applies to the fifty-two types of *saṃgha*. This is because those who perform the ritual twice would both incur the fault of invalidity. However, within the *caturvargika-saṃgha*, that which...

The matters upheld by the *bhikṣu* are numerous, and the heavy offenses (*guru-apatti*) are likewise numerous. For the other five groups [of practitioners], the matters upheld by the threefold *saṃgha* are few, and the heavy offenses are likewise few.

Next, regarding the application of the *dharma*: although the text cites eighteen instances based on specific conditions, in principle the meaning extends to the three types of *dharma*-essences—such as those beginning with "self"—and the three types of formal acts, such as the *jñapti*.
These are enumerated collectively according to their stages. If one searches through the various preceding and succeeding passages and compares them...

Regarding the formal procedures (*karmavācanā*) for establishing the Dharma, there are one hundred and fifty-seven in total. That is to say: forty *jñapti* (formal motions), seventy-one *jñapti-dvitīya* (motions followed by one proclamation), and forty-six *jñapti-caturtha* (motions followed by three proclamations).

If these are categorized according to the two assemblies of monks and nuns, and explained in terms of both general and specific applications, they constitute two hundred and seventy-eight formal procedures.

These include forty *kevala-jñapti* (simple motions); the two [procedures] common to both physical and legal matters; the appointment of a teacher of instruction (*śikṣācārya*); the summoning of the assembly; and the preceptor of the precepts (*upādhyāya*).
Questioning and Refutation (two sections; combined total of six). Declaration for the Non-Timely Assembly for the Recitation of the Precepts. Non-Timely Recitation of the Precepts.

Two Declarations for the Extended Recitation of the Precepts (combined total of seven). Declaration for the Monastic Confession and Disclosure (two declarations; combined total of seven). Declaration for the Invitation (Pravāraṇā). Abbreviated Declaration for the Invitation.

Three Declarations for the Postponement of the Invitation (combined total of five). Receiving Confession. Circulating the Alms Bowl. Receiving the Kaṭhina Cloth for Causing Discord or Provocation, as well as its Relinquishment (combined total of six). Manifestation.

In the *Prātimokṣa*, there are five formal motions (*jñapti*): the motion for settling disputes (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*), the motion for the assembly to be informed, the three motions for sending away [the offender], and the three motions for the "grass covering" (*tṛṇaprastāraka*).

In the Council of Five Hundred, there were six formal motions: one for appointing the assembly, one for the formal gathering itself, and two each for the questions and answers between Upāli and Ānanda.
Within the *Saptashatika* [Karmavācanā], there are five types of *jñapti*: first, the *jñapti* for the formal assembly; second, the appointment of the assembly; third, the actual assembly;

and fourth and fifth, the respective question and answer. There are forty-three instances of the *ekajñapti* (single-announcement) as previously established. Now, by condensing the three *jñaptis* of the *pravāraṇā*, their essence is unified into one.

Furthermore, within the *Saptashatika*, the three *jñaptis* for the public recension of the Dharma share the same essence as the three *jñaptis* for the private discussion of the Dharma; therefore, they are not separated.
Having removed these five, the *jñapti-caturtha* (four-part) formal acts are increased by adding two *jñaptis*, making forty. Within these forty, the *bhikṣuṇīs* receive the questioning;

the *jñaptis* are restricted to the *bhikṣuṇīs*. Among the eleven *jñaptis* for the formal act of binding (*bandhana*) within the assembly, ten are restricted to the *bhikṣus* performing them, while the remaining twenty-eight apply to both divisions (*ubhaya-saṃgha*).
This constitutes fifty-six *ekajñapti* (single-part) formal acts. Together with the twelve that are restricted, there are sixty-eight *ekajñapti* formal acts in total.

The *jñapti-dvitīya* (one motion and one proclamation) [karmas] are seventy-one. Regarding the two types of rooms, there are two methods. Returning robes has two aspects: transference and returning the value;

as well as being apart from the robe. Holding the alms bowl for six years (seven). The family under restriction, the insane, and the overturned bowl. Not bowing, relinquishing instruction, relinquishing, and releasing (ten).

Establishing the great and small boundaries (eight), including the inclusion of the *poṣadha* hall. Robe-boundaries, the three pure grounds, storehouses, and their release—these together total twenty.

Sixth: The distribution of the Sangha’s virtuous offerings (*śīlāṃśa*) involves two types of entrustment and direct appropriation of shares. The same applies to the property of the deceased. Regarding the method for rewarding labor, there are two [sections].

(Six) For four months of communal residence, one receives the staff, the water-strainer, and the pouch; one may accept invitations to maintain a following. Because of this, a dwelling may be given to a layperson (*gṛhapati*).

One may also perform repairs together with them and entrust the virtuous robe (*śīlaka-cīvara*) to them. It is permissible to appoint a person to oversee all six matters. Alternatively, one may assign tasks according to their specific categories.

One may also be appointed to depart from the *pravāraṇā*. The *Śāriputra* is appointed to oversee the one who has transgressed during the *pravāraṇā*. One is appointed to instruct the *bhikṣuṇīs*. The *bhikṣuṇīs* appoint someone to request instruction.
One is appointed to go among the *bhikṣus* for the *pravāraṇā*. One is appointed to prepare the *kaṭhina* robe. One is appointed to guard the *kaṭhina* robe.
Appointing a person to guard the storehouse; appointing a person to distribute bedding and furniture; appointing a person to perform penance for laypeople;

appointing a person to inform households whose *pātra* has been overturned; appointing those who distribute [alms] and so forth; appointing a person to take the *chanda*; appointing a messenger to confer the precepts; appointing a person to attend to and repair rooms;

appointing a person to distribute robes, rain-cloths, and rice-gruel, etc.—these, such as the case of Trapusa, constitute one [category], totaling sixteen. Herein is explained the relinquishing of the overturned *pātra*, according to the teaching.
The relinquishment (*pratikṣepa*) and the resolution (*visarjana*); the two types of robe-keeping within the *sīmāmaṇḍala*; the *poṣadha-hall*, the pure ground (*śuddhasthāna*), and the storehouse;

the remaining three great boundaries (*mahāsīmā*); the acquisition [of robes]; the making of the *guṇavat-cīvara*; the rewarding of the administrators (*vaiyāvṛtyakara*); the distribution of robes from the gifts to the Saṃgha;

and the two portions for the deceased—these seventeen dharmas should be included according to the texts, though their formal bodies (*dharmatattva*) are briefly absent. The old edition lists sixty-one *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (formal acts consisting of one motion and one proclamation), to which [the following] should be added:

Returning robes; transferring [robes] where there is no village; the robe-boundary and its dissolution; distributing the gains obtained by the Saṃgha; the formal establishment of persons and things; the respective methods for taking possession; appointing a person to assign rooms;
appointing a person to perform penance for laypeople; appointing a person to guard the storehouse; and the relinquishing of the storehouse.
The awarding of robes to those who have been recognized for their merit constitutes seventy-one [items].

Among these, the non-prostration, the dismissal of the instructor, the request for an instructor, the dispatch of one to the community of monks, and the authorization for anyone to be dispatched as a preceptor for ordination—these five together constitute the rules for the nuns regarding the dispatch of an instructor.

The dismissal of the instructor by the nun and the dismissal [of the candidate] constitute three [items], which are the rules for the bhikṣus. Excluding these eight rules, the remaining sixty-three apply to both [orders].

The *bhikṣu-prakīrṇaka* consists of one hundred and twenty rules; when combined with the eight *niyata-dharmas*, they total one hundred and thirty-four. There are sixteen *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* and forty-six *jñapti-caturtha-karman*.

Regarding the *dvādaśa-sapta-dharmas* concerning the violations of admonitions by monks, nuns, and śrāmaṇeras, these amount to twelve, but when including the *vyutthāna* (rehabilitation) procedures, they become fourteen.

Furthermore, there are the *upasampadā* (full ordination) for monks and nuns, the six *dharmas*, the three [procedures] such as *parivāsa* (probation), the five [procedures] such as *mānāpya* (penance), and the three [procedures] such as *smṛti-vinaya* (settlement based on mindfulness). And...

The fourth section concerns the resolution of offenses. The commission of grave offenses (pārājika) and the acts of immediate retribution (ānantarya), etc., are combined as one. There is the formal act of banishment for those who have committed a grave offense after having been subject to the training of repentance (śikṣādattaka-śikṣā), and the formal act of banishment for śrāmaṇeras—these constitute five [categories].
For bhikṣuṇīs, there is the half-month [probation] and the returning to the original status; there are three methods for the removal of offenses.

These three, including the half-month [probation], along with the resolution of the banishment of śrāmaṇeras and the formal acts of banishment for those in border regions, should logically be included according to the texts, though their essential nature is omitted here. [Old] (Note: The term "舊" at the end likely indicates that this is an excerpt from an older commentary or a fragment.)

There are forty-one cases of the *jñapti-caturtha* (one motion and three proclamations). Now, excluding the formal act (*mūla-karman*), since the three proclamations within the formal act are not separate from the *jñapti-caturtha*, why are they listed separately?
Furthermore, adding the three [cases] such as the nuns’ half-monthly [confession], because the officiants differ; plus the revocation of the suspension of a *śrāmaṇera*;
and adding one each for the suspension itself and the "original day" (*mūla-tithi*)—thus making forty-six. Among these, there is no...

There are six types of admonition (*codanā*), and with the six dharmas added, there are seven; these are restricted to the *bhikṣuṇī* discipline. For the *bhikṣuṇī* ordination, there are four original [procedures];
the four dharmas for the removal of offenses (*āpatti-vyutthāna*) are restricted to the *bhikṣuṇī*. The five procedures, such as separate residence (*pṛthag-vāsa*), belong to the *bhikṣu* discipline.
Excluding these sixteen, the remaining thirty dharmas are practiced by both divisions (*ubhayasaṃgha*). Thus, there are sixty dharmas. Adding the sixteen that are restricted makes seventy.

There are sixteen *jñapti-caturtha* (motions followed by three proclamations). In this context, it is not permissible for any single dharma to serve as the opening [motion] while subsequently performing other dharmas;

all such cases would be invalid. Furthermore, one may apply these dharmas to the Saṃgha. It should be clarified that there are five types of persons who should preside over the proceedings, and eight types of proceedings to be presided over. These are: the two *jñapti-caturtha* motions within the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination);

the two *jñapti-caturtha* motions within the *upasaṃpadā* (ordination)—namely, the *catur-varga* (four-person) and the *pariśuddhi* (purification) procedures; and the four *jñapti-ekavācika* (motions followed by one proclamation) within the ordination. This makes forty [instances].

It should be performed. There are only six categories of receiving the precepts; these six dharmas are identical to the substance of receiving them from a borderland community. Within the application of the Sangha, there is a distinction:

according to the substance of the dharma, it is the same as a community of twenty persons. For two *jñapti-caturtha* (motions followed by three proclamations) and the remaining one hundred thirty-seven dharmas, these are performed by a group of four persons.
Whichever single dharma serves as the head, by performing the remaining dharmas again in accordance with that, they are then completed.
One hundred and forty-six non-faults. Since this one case is thus, the remaining categories are likewise so; they total one hundred and forty-seven items.
Regarding the one hundred and forty-six non-faults, the remaining five persons and others are presided over by the three types of Saṃghas;

each should be clearly understood as being subject to re-administration. Question: It is not yet known whether the fundamental validity is established when the remaining dharmas are re-administered. One interpretation holds that the fundamental [validity] is indeed established. [This is] a rebuke.

The formal act of *tarjanīya-karman* (reproval) is accomplished because the medicine and the illness correspond. However, if one were to perform a *pravāsanīya-karman* (banishment) or other such acts again, seventeen [instances] would be invalid because the medicine and the illness do not correspond.
Therefore, the text states: "One should not perform a *pravāsanīya-karman* after having already performed a *tarjanīya-karman*, and so on, up to the *tṛṇaprastāraka* (covering with grass).
In this context, calculating the legal procedures (*dharma*), there are three hundred and twenty-four [rules], consisting solely of the root [offenses].

There are eighteen dharmas that constitute the remaining three hundred and six improper acts. Furthermore, although the preceding dharma has been completed, the matter is not yet finished—such as when it is said that the *zide* robe, the formal acceptance (*pratigraha*), the confession (*pratideśanā*), or the announcement (*jñapti*) are still pending.
If one were to perform these again, it would immediately constitute an improper act; however, once that dharma is concluded, [the matter is finished].

The matter may also reach its conclusion. This is as in the case of relinquishing the *guṇavat-cīvara* (virtuous robe), or the dissolution of boundaries (*sīmā-bandha*) and similar acts; even if these are performed again, the prior ritual act remains valid.

Furthermore, this is explained with reference to the underlying intention (*citta*). If one’s fundamental intention is to harbor malice toward another and intends to subject them to further punishment, then [the act] is not accomplished—just as, for example, the dissolution of purity (*śuddhi*) performed with a malicious mind is not accomplished.
However, if one’s fundamental intention is simply to issue a formal reprimand (*tarjanīya-karman*), [it is valid].

This procedure is concluded. Fearing that it might not be accomplished, [the rules] such as the repeated imposition of *pravāsanīya* (banishment) and so forth—seventeen in total—are established; thus, the preceding procedure is perfected.
To perform them repeatedly is improper. According to the text, there are eighteen; since the explanation is thus, they are extensively applied to one hundred and fifty-seven cases.
The same applies to the emphasis on meaning (*artha*). Next, regarding the application to specific cases (*sthāna-vastu*), one should understand it by analogy.
Fifth, the four types of Saṃgha are explained; first, their meanings are elucidated through a threefold analysis: first, enumerating the numbers and explaining the names;
second, defining their essential characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*); and third, analyzing them through various categories.
Regarding the enumeration and explanation of the names: although the Dharma accomplishes its purpose through the Sangha, the Sangha functions according to specific matters.

Briefly enumerated, there are four types, namely those consisting of four, five, ten, or twenty members. The explanation of their characteristics and the clarification of their names are as distinguished above.

Next, to clarify the essence [of the Saṃgha]: this refers precisely to the essence of the Saṃgha as the five aggregates of wholesome phenomena (*kuśala-skandha*). The Saṃgha achieves harmony by upholding the Dharma;

regarding the essence of this harmony, according to the Sarvāstivāda school, there exists a distinct "nature of harmony" (*saṃgraha-dharmatā*) among the non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
This nature of harmony is the very essence of the Saṃgha, because when the Saṃgha is split, this nature is abandoned. Alternatively, this nature of harmony is simply the assembly itself.
It is subsumed under the category of "homogeneity" (sabhāgatā). The schism of the Saṃgha is not included among those [states] that are acquired.
Next, there are four sections: first, the reason for establishing the four; second, whether they exhaustively include the Saṃgha; third, the relative relationship between persons and dharmas.
Fourth, the scope of the application of the positions.
Regarding the first gate: as for why four [monks] are required, the ancient commentators explain that the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*) is only perfected when there are at least four persons;

it is only then that one can expel offenses and settle disputes, and thus is designated as a *saṃgha*. For example, in the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*, one person presides over the recitation while another...

The Elder: One person proclaims the formal announcement (*jñapti*), three persons uphold the assembly; down to the case where even a single person listens to the precepts, it requires the harmony of four persons before one may be designated as a *saṃgha*.
If there are three or fewer, this essential principle is lacking. Now, to explain: although it is difficult for four persons to harmonize, if they can indeed do so, they are then called a *saṃgha*.
For example, if there is one person, he acts according to his own will; if there are two, they act together...

If there is opposition within a single location, although there is opposition, it is not difficult to reconcile them. If there are three people, resulting in two factions with one side sharing the same view, this is also not difficult.
If there are four people, with two on each side, and they form mutual cliques to support one another, it is difficult for their hearts to be harmonized;
only when harmony can be achieved here does the function of the Saṃgha truly come into being. Furthermore, if one person initiates the matter, and two...

Regarding the number of persons required for a formal legal procedure (*karmavācanā*): first, it must be definitively resolved that four are necessary to constitute a *saṃgha* for such purposes. Furthermore, it is explained that this is the natural law (*dharmatā*) requiring four;

one need not debate the underlying reason, just as in the case of a forest or an army, how could one possibly distinguish the reason? As for the subsequent requirement of five persons, the old tradition states:

[the roles are] the proposer (*jñapti*), the proponent (*anujñā*), the respondent (*anuśrāvaka*), the respondent who follows the motion (*anuśrāvakānuvartaka*), and the respondent who follows the invitation (*anuśrāvakānuvartakānuvartaka*). If there were only four, the appointment for the formal disciplinary action would not be established; therefore, five are required.

Only then does it constitute the use for the Saṃgha. If that were so, then in cases such as receiving a formal authorization (*jñapti*) for a period of days, or being separated from one's robes for six years, would there also need to be five people?

Should these be collected by a group of five? Answer: Receiving [the robe] is done individually; it is not possible for all five to receive the authorization for the period of days simultaneously. Therefore, it is not [the same].

If that were so, when the *kaṭhina* robe is for the sake of the community, should it not be a Saṃgha of five? Answer: There are those who obtain the benefit and those who do not; therefore, it is also [not the same].
This is not of the same category. Now, regarding those who perform the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination): first, they are distinct from the *saṃgha*;

second, the five [members] for the *ādeśana* (requesting time) and so forth all perform the *pravāraṇā*, yet they differ from the *guṇavastra* (robe of merit). Therefore, these are the five-member *saṃgha*. Question: Is it because they must be appointed for the purpose of governance that five are required?

Is it precisely for appointment and governance that these five are used? Answer: Appointment and governance are performed by a four-member *saṃgha*. Question: When, then, is the five-member *saṃgha* employed? Answer: [As stated above.]

This is precisely what constitutes the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination). The reason for this is that its original purpose is to bring forth faults (*āpatti*). If there are only four persons, the appointment is not accomplished, nor is the formal act of censure (*codanā*) established;

since the essential meaning would thus be deficient, five persons are required from beginning to end for the *pravāraṇā* and the censure to be fully accomplished. This specifically refers to the time when the formal motion (*jñapti*) has been concluded and the *pravāraṇā* is being received;
it is at this stage that these five persons function. Because [the sūtra] speaks only of clarifying the three types of non-faults and the time of suspension (*pratiṣedha*), we know this.

This specifically refers to the time of the *pravāraṇā* (invitation for criticism). It is intended for use by a community (*saṃgha*) of five monks. Now, let us explain: in principle, it is indeed for the sake of the *pravāraṇā*, yet the regulation requires that there be five members.

This is because at the time of performing the *pravāraṇā*, one must first employ the formal motion (*jñapti*) to assemble the assembly, and then each individual must express their sentiments before the five virtuous ones (*pañca-guṇa*). As the traditional explanation states: "If there are only four, it is not valid."

Regarding the "difference in governance," the meaning is not so. This is because the formal governance (*sāmīcī*) is subsumed within the four-member Saṃgha; whereas in border regions, five members are permitted as a concession relative to the central lands.

Furthermore, it is explained that a five-member Saṃgha is also established by the nature of things (*dharmatā*), because the procedures for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) and the invitation for criticism (*pravāraṇā*) are prescribed as constant practices.

As for the mention of "ten members," the Buddha knew that for those [in border regions], the causal conditions for the subtle meaning were weak; thus, apart from the strong external condition of a group of ten, [the practice would not otherwise arise].

Because the undertaking of the precepts is for the sake of such benefit, the minimum number is restricted to ten; since ten persons can accomplish the ritual, it is called a "monastic assembly of ten.
As for twenty persons, this is because the offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* is the most serious among those that can be expiated through confession.

Since one wishes to eliminate it and rescue oneself from this difficult situation, unless there is a powerful external condition, there is no way to extinguish the karma. Therefore, the rule was established that twenty persons are required to remove the offense; hence it is named the "assembly of twenty."

The Sangha of persons. Furthermore, these four types of Sangha are divided into two categories by way of their status: the first two are established by the nature of things (*dharmatā*), while the latter two follow human sentiment.

Regarding the two established by the nature of things: the group of four constitutes the *pravāraṇā* (invitation) ceremony to prevent future transgressions; the group of five constitutes the *jīṛṇapravāraṇā* (invitation for the aged) to eliminate offenses already committed.

Regarding the two following human sentiment: the group of ten is for receiving [the precepts], giving rise to manifold virtues; the group of twenty is for confession, extinguishing past faults. This is the classification of their functions.
General Discussion. Separated, they form four distinct categories.

Second Gate: Question—Since these have already been discussed generally in terms of both stages and entities, and the four types of Saṃgha have been established, it is not yet known whether these four encompass the entirety of the Saṃgha.

Answer—Since the establishment of the Saṃgha was conducted generally regarding both stages and entities, it is clear that these four categories also include [the Saṃgha] completely and exhaustively. Thus it is said.
Question: It is not yet known how to repent for a grave *sthūlātyaya* (thou-lan). To which category of sangha does it belong? Answer:

Although other schools state that all grave *sthūlātyayas* bordering on a *pārājika* (ai-yi) must be repented before the entire sangha, according to this Vinaya, it is subsumed under a sangha of only four persons. Thus the text says: "The 'great assembly' refers to four or more.

Furthermore, in this passage, the number four is used as a functional requirement; it merely excludes the three specific cases [of formal acts] and does not distinguish the *sthūlātyaya* from the act of repentance itself.
It is clearly known that the *jñapti-karman* (formal motion) for the *pārivāsika* (probationary period) is subsumed under the fourfold assembly (*caturvarga*).

If this is so, why is it that in the twenty-fourth fascicle of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, when there is an immeasurable number of bhikṣu-saṃghas, their true enumeration is resolved without separately manifesting the specific application?

Therefore, one knows that these four types exhaust the inclusion of the Saṃgha. Although this passage does not explicitly mention "immeasurable," the meaning also extends to include them; thus the text says: "The Saṃgha of twenty persons is one..."
All *karmas* should be performed; how much more so those exceeding twenty? This refers to the meaning of "immeasurable. Question:

If a community of four monks is required, is it restricted solely to four, or may there be more? Is the same true for the other three types of assemblies? Answer: Generally speaking, all four positions apply.
A small number is not for the use of the Saṃgha; therefore the text says: "With four people or twenty-one people, it is neither Dharma nor Vinaya.

The same applies to the other three [smaller numbers]. When there are many, it is accomplished; therefore the text says: "With twenty people as the Saṃgha, all *karmans* should be performed," let alone with more than twenty.
If one asks what the matter is: even if there are fifty people, or even up to a hundred thousand, one simply excludes [the deficient ones].
Regarding the *pravāraṇā* and other such acts, those who uphold the remaining dharmas are all comprised within groups of four persons. Thus the text says:

"As for the Saṃgha of four persons, with the exception of the *pravāraṇā*, receiving the precepts, and the removal of offenses (*āpatti-vyutthāna*), all other legal formalities (*karmavācanā*) in accordance with the Dharma should be performed. One should understand that for groups of five persons and so forth, the principle is applied by analogy.

Question: Why is it not stated that a *saṃgha* consists of twenty persons, except for [the acts of] receiving [confession] and the *pravāraṇā*? Answer: The higher [categories] encompass the lower, allowing them to be used extensively.
The lower do not distinguish the higher; they are excluded in relation to one another. Thus, the four-person [saṃgha] has a broad application because its essence constitutes a *saṃgha*.
The remaining three, being restricted by specific matters, become progressively narrower in sequence.
The Third Gate. Regarding the question of why there are four distinctions among the monastics who can uphold [the precepts], while the dharmas to be upheld are only three:

although this may be so when considering the relationship between the subject (the upholder) and the object (the dharma), from the perspective of establishing the underlying principle, the meaning does not correspond to the substance.

A general discussion of those who exercise authority (*adhikāra*) comprises three categories: the individual, the plurality of monks, and the Saṃgha. The individual exercises authority through mental recitation (*manasikāra*);

the plurality of monks exercises authority through face-to-face consultation (*saṃmukha-vinaya*); and the Saṃgha exercises authority through formal ritual action (*karmavācanā*). These three stages of *karma* are all exercised by the Saṃgha. Regarding the essence of the Saṃgha, there are four types;

these were established fundamentally according to the nature of things (*dharmatā*) and subsequently based on conventional circumstances, rather than being dependent on the specific act being performed. As for the three dharmas that constitute the object of the act, they pertain to the actual matter at hand.

Regarding the establishment [of formal procedures], there are three grades of matters—superior, middling, and inferior. In response to these three types of matters, three kinds of *karmavācanā* (formal acts) are established.

For example, the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*, the *Pravāraṇā*, the two [procedures] performed together, or the sharing of alms bowls (*pātra*), etc., are either practices regularly enjoined by the rules, or matters that are not cumbersome and for which consensus is not difficult to achieve.
Because they can be accomplished through a single announcement (*jñapti*), they are established as the "single-announcement *karmavācanā*" (*jñaptikarman*). As it is said:

Regarding the *pārivāsika* (one who has received the day) and the *nissīva* (one who is separated from his robe): for six years and four months, the matter becomes somewhat more serious, and while the conditions for reconciliation are next most difficult, one must first submit a formal announcement (*jñapti*) to apply for a single *karmavācana*.
Only after weighing whether it is appropriate can the matter be successfully resolved; this is designated as a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*.

This applies to cases such as receiving the precepts, the confession of a *śeṣa* offense, or when one treats a person by offering counsel; these matters are of the highest grade, and since the conditions for reconciliation are difficult to meet, a formal announcement is required to express [the intent].
It can only be accomplished by declaring three *karmavācanās*; thus, it is established as the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations).

If that is so, since matters such as *smṛti-vinaya* (verdict based on recollection) involve three grades of gravity, why are all of them treated with the same *jñapti-caturtha-karman*? Answer: If these matters were subdivided in detail, they would amount to nine categories.
However, these [specific cases], such as *smṛti-vinaya*, are all classified as the highest grade; for this reason, they are uniformly addressed by means of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*.
The Fourth Gate. First, regarding the presiding authority (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*), there are three major positions; these are further divided into six.

Within the context of the Saṃgha, these positions are categorized as four, or perhaps eight, depending on the division of the multitude. They are then condensed into three positions, which expand into eleven:

namely, four [positions] with two types of multitudes, and five [positions] with three types of multitudes, with one person following the first two. Thus, there are four positions within the Saṃgha. Therefore...
This constitutes eleven [categories]. As for their essence, one and many are restricted to the two assemblies of four and five [monks] respectively.

The reason for this is that it is established as a general rule of practice to be performed [by these assemblies]. The ten and twenty [members] are established according to specific circumstances; they must be presided over exclusively by a *saṃgha*, and the two lower [assemblies] have no application here.
Next, regarding the discussion of the *dharma*: since the initial capacity to preside [over the ritual] consists of three major positions, there are likewise three types of *dharma*. Namely:

Regarding the mental recitation (*manasikāra*) and the face-to-face (*pratyakṣa*) methods of *śamatha*, there are both general and specific applications among them. To discuss the specific cases first:
for instance, when confessing a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense) within the assembly of the precept seat (*śīlāsana*), this is restricted to one person presiding over the rite.

Second, there are those restricted to being performed before a large group, such as the formal acceptance of robes and bowls, the assignment of pure gifts (*viśuddha-dāna*), the confession of a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (offense requiring suspension), or the minor offenses of *pātayantika*, *pratideśanīya*, and *sthūlatyaya*. Third...

The "sentence" (*pada*) refers to formal acts (*kamma*) performed by the Saṅgha, such as the delimitation of boundaries, the separation of robes, the six-year rule, the *sativinaya*, the *amūḷhavinaya*, and the determination of the place of an offense.

Next, regarding those acts that apply universally, they pertain to formal acts performed by all three groups [of the Saṅgha]. Examples include the recitation of the *Pātimokkha* and the *Pavāraṇā*, as well as the two types of distribution of robes.

When there are many [monks], one acts in their presence; when there are few, one acts in their absence. As for the single person who performs a mental act of relinquishment (*cetanā*) regarding a *nissaggiya-pācittiya* offense, this takes the three [categories] as its object; there is no case where it does not.

People maintain a mind of renunciation. Furthermore, according to the rules for the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat), one person is required; although many may act as four or five, this applies both to the community (*saṃgha*) and to individuals.

Now, this specifically clarifies the *saṃgha*, not the many and so forth. Question: As it is said regarding the *pravāraṇā* (invitation) and other rites, they are performed throughout the three periods [of the rainy season].
What are their distinct characteristics? Why do you speak here exclusively of the *saṃgha*? Answer: There are many distinct characteristics; I shall briefly indicate five of them. First:

There are five distinctions: first, the number of those who hold the procedure; second, the difference in the application of the ritual methods; third, the distinction between universal and restricted scope regarding the location; fourth, the difference between those with desire and those without desire;

and fifth, the variation in the size of the separate assembly—referring to the three categories of "should come," "two," and "one" as separate groups. Because these differences exist, the term *saṃgha* (the community) is used specifically and restrictively to clarify the assembly.
Regarding what is upheld by the *bhikṣuṇīs*, it is explained according to the [rules for] *bhikṣus*.

Next, the text will be interpreted; therein are four sections: first, the announcement of the four numbers; second, the enumeration of the four names; third, the superior and inferior [categories]; fourth, [the specific rules].

This section demonstrates the limits of application. Fourth, "If it should be fewer," clarifies the meaning of insufficiency. Within this, there are two parts: first, an explanation based on the four;
second, the substitution of five and so forth. The first part further has two sections: first, directly explaining that a ritual act is not accomplished if the number is insufficient;

second, using the twenty-three types of persons, such as nuns, to complete the count of four. Although nuns possess full ordination, they are of a different class and thus do not suffice. The following three [sections]...

Those who have not yet received full ordination; those for whom the *saṃgha* cannot perform the formal acts (*dharmakarma*); the thirteen types of persons with impediments (*antarāyika-dharma*), who do not possess full precepts;

the three types of persons who have been suspended (*utkṣiptaka*)—because the disciplinary procedures against them are grave; and those who should be expelled (*pravāsanīya*) because their essence is impure.

When such individuals complete the quorum of four, the formal act is not accomplished, just as in the previous case regarding the minimum limit. This section is abbreviated and does not explain it in detail.
This completes the meaning. If one were to translate this as "sufficient," there would have to be two aspects: first, a virtuous bhikṣu who is the opposite of the twenty-two [cases];

second, even speaking to bystanders to reverse what was previously done. Alternatively, it may simply be intended here to exclude what is insufficient, rather than explicitly clarifying what is sufficient.

Therefore, this passage is omitted. Question: Among the four types of "fulfillment" (*pūrṇa*) mentioned previously, there are twenty-eight [factors], including the five such as *parivāsa* (probation) and so forth;

why are these not included here? The old commentary states: "This [category] refers to those who are insufficient while seated in the assembly. Since the five, beginning with *parivāsa*, fulfill the quorum upon their arrival, they are not mentioned.

If that is so, then if one's body is present in the assembly, one immediately constitutes a formal reprimand (*codanā-pūrṇa*). Why, then, are those [five] included there [in the previous list]? Answer:
This is intended to clarify that a "remote" (*dūre*) censure does not constitute a valid censure. If that were the case, it would fail to demonstrate that a "remote" [censure] is invalid;

therefore, the commentary states: "This mentions four types of Saṃghas and so forth. Consequently, this is included within the category of being "one person short. Since the preceding section did not mention the four types of Saṃghas and so forth, against what would one distinguish "being short"?
The reason for this is that this section specifically explains the meaning of "not counting as a quorum. Why is it not counted? Because it is deficient.

[The list is] complete. Where is there a deficiency? It is because of the separate dwelling in the *ṛddhipāda* (bases of psychic power) that it is deficient; however, it merely states "one is missing," concealing the other names, and thus only twenty-three individuals are listed.

The preceding text explains both the censure (*nigarhaṇa*) and the completeness (*pūrṇatva*). If one says there are fewer people, this may apply in contrast to the full number, but it does not accord with the meaning of "censure.
This is precisely a case of having fewer people; how could the censure fail to be established simply because there are fewer? It is like the four [cases].
Whether there are three people or two, they should likewise be rebuked individually; therefore, one cannot omit even a single person from that group.

Since there is no one left to include, the separate residences (*pṛthag-vāsa*) and so forth are not included, despite the extensive listing of twenty-eight cases. The current explanation does not grasp this essence; logically, they should be present, and their absence is merely an abbreviation.
Alternatively, it may be explained that because those [cases] correspond to the "full" (*paripūrṇa*) rebuke, they must be listed in their entirety, just as in the third phrase.
The fourth phrase is "complete and appropriate for censure. These are listed in full by way of contrast with the opposite cases.

This clarifies the case of being "insufficient," which serves as the opposite of being "sufficient. Since there is no case of being "sufficient" to serve as its opposite, how could it be comparable to "complete censure"?
Thus, we know that "complete censure" and "insufficient counting" differ in meaning; there is no need to labor over comparing or deciding between them.
Next, regarding the six or seven [types of] "non-correspondence" (asamyoga), first explain their meaning through a fivefold analysis: first, enumerating the numbers and explaining the names;
second, distinguishing their characteristics of non-correspondence; third, determining whether their names and essences are complete; fourth, clarifying their general and specific aspects;
and fifth, determining whether they exhaustively encompass all instances of non-correspondence.

Regarding the first gate: it does not arise from deluded sentiments, for such matters are infinite. Now, following their manifestation through conditions, I shall briefly distinguish seven types of "non-dharma" (*adharma*).
First, that which is neither *dharma* nor *vinaya*. Second, non-dharma with a separate assembly. Third, non-dharma with a harmonious assembly. Fourth, *dharma* with a separate assembly.

Fifth, *dharma*-like with a separate assembly. Sixth, *dharma*-like with a harmonious assembly. Seventh, when one’s censure is not stopped and they act without a standard or essential rule; these are called [the seven non-dharmas].
It is illegal (*adharma*). It cannot extinguish evil or give rise to good; it is not the Vinaya. The remainder is called "explanation" (*vyākhyāna*), which can be understood according to the text.

Within this, there are three parts. The first consists of nineteen clauses, beginning with a motion (*jñapti*) followed by a formal act (*karmavācanā*).

There is. "Resolution" (kṣānti) refers to the seven [procedures] beginning with censure, as well as the place of offense. Originally intended for the purpose of disciplining individuals, once they have been disciplined, resolution is permitted.

Furthermore, there should likewise be resolution for the expulsion of a śrāmaṇera. When monks and nuns receive the precepts, and when the six dharmas permit relinquishment—this method of relinquishment is itself its resolution.
Among the remaining *jñapti-caturtha* (four-part) procedures, there is no such resolution. Within the *jñapti-dvitīya* (two-part) procedures, there are eighteen dharmas, namely:

Regarding the thirteen [procedures] such as the *sīmā-bandha* (boundary-binding), as well as the *kula-śikṣā-dattaka* (instruction for families), *unmatta-kaṭhina* (for the insane), *pātra-nikubjana* (turning the bowl upside down), *an-abhivādana* (not paying respects), *śikṣā-pratyākhyāna* (renouncing the training), and *pratyākhyāna-sammuti* (consent for renunciation)—with the exception of these, there is no formal resolution (*sammuti*).
Among the *jñapti-mātra* (single motion) procedures, there is only the renunciation of the *kāṭhina* robe.

Furthermore, if one considers the renunciation of the precepts (*śīla*), how could it be restricted solely to the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (four-part formal act)? Within this context, regarding those applicable to both nuns and monks, there are four additional *jñapti-mātra* procedures, as well as two *jñapti* procedures concerning the identity of physical form and dharma.

Furthermore, there are procedures for relinquishing (*prahāṇa*). Regarding all other *jñapti* (formal announcements), there is no [explicit] rule for their dissolution (*visarga*). According to ancient exegesis: if one accepts [an act] without a conscious intention (*acittaka*), it must be dissolved;

if one accepts it with a conscious intention (*sacittaka*), then dissolution is unnecessary. Now, examining this interpretation, it does not fully capture the essential intent. To investigate its true meaning: do all [acts] equally permit dissolution?

Take, for example, the *tarjanīya* (reprimand) and so forth, as well as the *tatsvabhāva-āpatti-sthāna* (the place of the offense). Are these accepted without conscious intention, such that they require [dissolution]? Or...

The formal act of "releasing" (visarga) may be established. For instance, regarding the rule of permanent banishment (*nigarhaṇīya-karman*), who would wish to take charge of it? The two *jñapti* (formal announcements) of Chanda and the various admonitions are likewise [subject to release].

Among those acts that involve a mental intention to take charge—such as the practice of the alms-bowl, the acceptance of the three [robes], the six-year period for being separated from one’s robe, the acceptance of the [special] days, the staff, the bag, and the separate residence (*parivāsa*)—it is acceptable that these do not require release.

However, how can this apply to the virtuous robe (*guṇa-cīvara*) and the ordination (*upasampadā*), both of which possess formal procedures for relinquishing them? Next, we shall consider this in terms of location.
The details should be understood according to the established rules.

Next, regarding the eleventh [offense], "driving out one who should not be driven out": if it concerns one who is to be permanently expelled (*pārājika*), driving them out constitutes "driving out"; if it concerns one who is not to be permanently expelled, it does not.

Because one who is expelled is not truly expelled, the text answers that they may be either expelled or not expelled. This is because the substance of the [previous] thirteen types of persons is cited again as being fit for expulsion;
thus, their expulsion constitutes a valid expulsion. Aside from these thirteen, all other persons are unfit for expulsion; therefore, their expulsion does not constitute a valid expulsion.
"Chasing" does not constitute "chasing. The explanation of the meaning is presented through four gates; by analogy, it may be understood. The foregoing concludes the *Campa* section of the law.

Next, the *Kṣepaka-khandhaka* (The Chapter on Rebuke) is explained. Within the assembly, there are seven types of persons who are by nature devoid of shame and remorse; they know only how to trouble the Saṃgha and do not protect the communal laws.

Since their transgressions have already become manifest, yet they persist in their conduct and refuse to establish themselves in discipline, they must be subjected to the Saṃgha’s censure so that they may be brought to compliance.
It is harmonious and compliant. Now, this *khandhaka* generally governs seven types of persons; although other names may be mentioned, they all converge upon a single difficulty.

Because it primarily censures those who repeatedly commit offenses—a behavior people are prone to—it is named after its initial application, hence it is called "Censure. These seven rules are not one.
Collected together in one place, it is called a *khandhaka*. Before praising and explaining the text, ten categories are first established: first, clarifying what should be treated;
second, whether the treatment is exhaustive; third, the intent behind establishing the seven [categories], and the sequence of the four [types of] light and heavy [offenses].

The fifth concerns the difference between being separated from or remaining united with [the group]; the sixth concerns whether the quorum is complete or incomplete; the seventh concerns conformity to presence or absence; the eighth concerns the sequence of resolving and repenting;
the ninth concerns the distinction between admonishing and not admonishing; and the tenth concerns the individual interpretation according to the text.
