whether the request or the bestowal is long or short, it is also as previously stated. All subsequent *karmavācanā* procedures for the distribution and possession [of requisites] are likewise so.

Within this, there should be seven or five methods of practice; however, to avoid excessive textual complexity, they are all deferred and clarified below in the section on the method of concealment (*paryuṣita-dharma*). The practice during the six-night period is also...

Thus it is. Next, on the day of the formal act (*jñapti*), one speaks directly of the repeated offense, but does not mention whether it was concealed or not; this is omitted from the text for brevity. Next is the procedure for the six-night penance (*ṣaḍrātra*).
When clarifying the rules of transformation, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Sengqi lü), fascicle 26, states that one should ask:

"Has the separate residence (*parivāsa*) been completed? Is the monastery not empty? Has the separate residence been performed? Are there no original offenses or intermediate offenses? Does one not share a single room with other bhikṣus?"
"Does one remain obstructed? When visiting bhikṣus arrive, was there a formal announcement (*jñapti*) regarding the assembly at the proper time or the improper time?

Having thus investigated according to the Dharma, he is further instructed to establish a mind with the intention of committing an offense that constitutes an obstruction. Once this has been done, the *karmavācanā* is performed for him. Next follows the interrogation for the removal of the offense (*āpattivyutthāna*).
The six-night penance (*ṣaḍrātra*) is not to be conducted as before. When the rite for the removal of the offense is completed, he should be addressed: 'Virtuous son...'"

Listen. You have been cleared of the offense according to the Dharma through one motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-trikarman*). The Saṃgha is in harmony, and a full assembly of twenty members has gathered.

The Saṃgha has performed the *karman* for you; you should be prudent and must not commit such an offense again. The subsequent section on "not concealing" follows the same explanation and should be understood accordingly.
The brief text above is now concluded.

Next, the following section provides a detailed analysis of the treatment for *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses. This text is divided into two parts. First, the method for treating concealment, which expands upon the initial discussion of "concealment" (*paticchādana*).

Second, beginning with the passage "At that time, there was a bhikṣu who committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and did not conceal it," this section explains those who have not concealed their offenses and have not yet been treated, expanding upon the preceding and succeeding discussions of non-concealment.
Within the first part, the treatment of concealment, there are ten major sections. The first concerns multiple offenses.

First, regarding the method for obtaining the *dhamma* (legal status) when the length of time is appropriate for the performance of the rite: at this second stage, there is a bhikkhu who commits two *saṅghādisesa* offenses;
the text below the seven phrases concerns multiple offenses and the obtaining of the *dhamma* through separation or combination, which is illegal.

At the third stage, there is a bhikkhu who commits a *saṅghādisesa* offense and conceals it for two months; the text below the seven phrases concerns a single offense and the obtaining of the *dhamma* through separation.
This is contrary to the Dharma. In the fourth period, there were bhikṣus who committed two *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses;

regarding the differences in time and conditions, the rules for treating old and new offenses are applied. In the fifth period, there were bhikṣus practicing *parivāsa* who committed a grave offense again during that interval;

regarding the re-offense during that time, the rules for treating old and new offenses are applied. In the sixth period, there were bhikṣus who committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and knew the number of days.

7. Regarding the method of treatment for repeated offenses committed through the combined performance of different types [of transgressions]: "If the Saṃgha performs the *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment) for one in an improper manner... 8.
Regarding the method of distinguishing between concealment and non-concealment by comparing person to person: "At that time, there was a separate residence... 9.

Regarding the case where a bhikṣu commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense but considers it a *pārājika*: "...at that time, there was a bhikṣu who committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, yet he claimed it was a *pārājika*..."

The first six sections provide a general explanation of the characteristics of "conscious" and "unconscious" concealment. From the tenth section, "Differences in Time and Residence," onwards, the text specifically distinguishes the methods for treating those who have concealed their offenses, noting that these methods vary in length.
If one were to categorize and explain the text in this manner, this *Khandhaka* would be divided into two parts: a brief and an extensive version.

Alternatively, based on whether a specific treatment for concealment applies or not, it could be divided into four parts. According to the length of the textual passages, it is further divided into thirteen sections. Within these...
The first of the middle [section] and the thirtieth text—these eleven texts briefly and extensively treat those who are obscured (*nivṛta*).

The second and the thirteenth—these two texts briefly and extensively treat those who are unobscured (*anivṛta*). Now, in contrast to the ten texts within the extensive [section], one must perform a fivefold analysis:
first, distinguishing between the obscured and the unobscured; second, clarifying the ruined and the unruined; third, discerning...
I. Whether it is accomplished or not; II. The fourth [section] on the scope of the *abhijñā*; III. The fifth [section] explaining the text. Regarding the first gate, there are two positions:

namely, the second, third, and fourth, as well as the eighth and ninth, which distinguish between concealment and non-concealment, and the methods for remediation and rescue. As for the remaining five texts, they do not discuss concealment or non-concealment.

The first, fifth, and sixth are simply the presentation of the general and specific medicines. The seventh exclusively distinguishes between what is correct and what is incorrect. The tenth discusses the prolongation of the remedy.
[The section on] "Briefly" next clarifies "Destruction. This stage also consists of two parts: four, five, six, seven, and four texts, which distinguish [the stages] by means of destruction;
the upper three and the lower three clarify the "Non-destructible Dharma" (*akṣayadharma*). Next, it clarifies "Accomplishment. This stage also consists of two parts:

two, three, four, seven, eight, nine, six, and four texts, which clarify accomplishment and non-accomplishment. The remaining four texts directly analyze the established dharmas (*prajñaptidharma*); within these texts, accomplishment is not raised.

Regarding the characteristics of non-establishment: next, concerning the universal versus the restricted. Although the seventh, ninth, and tenth [sections] exist, these three—specifically the seventh, ninth, and tenth—are universal in their application to the remaining seven.
As extensively explained in the text of the seventh section, they are "as-it-is" (yathābhūta) and "not-as-it-is" (na-yathābhūta).

This [section] universally subsumes all instances of being as-it-is and not-as-it-is, because other passages merely explain the establishment of the dharma and do not distinguish the specific forms of being as-it-is and not-as-it-is; or, although they may exclude or conceal, they remain restricted.
This matter is incorrect; the present "as it is" (yathābhūta) is likewise not so. It fully encompasses the four types of manifestation.
The ninth section clarifies the characteristics of concealment (*āvṛti*) and non-concealment, thereby explaining the meaning of all concealment and non-concealment.

While the preceding sections established the Dharma by stating that one should treat concealment according to the day of its occurrence, without fixed duration, the present tenth section clarifies the length of concealment. This is because the treatment of concealment does not exceed its duration, whether long or short.
Know that this brief explanation also applies to the remaining texts; all others may be understood by themselves and do not require one another.

Next, the text is explained. First, the initial passage is interpreted. This section contains three dharmas, while within the "concealment" (*paticchādana*) section there are four, as previously clarified.

However, regarding these offenses, they differ from the preceding text because the offenses are numerous and the days of concealment are unequal. Because of these differences, he reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha...

Now, following the principle of taking the short to conform to the long, this is combined with the method for concealing for ten nights (*daśarātra-parivāsa*). In the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, chapter twenty-three:

if one commits one *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, or even many, and conceals it for one night, or even for many nights, and the Saṃgha grants the probation (*parivāsa*), they shall grant the probation according to the number of days of the longest period of concealment;
subsequently, the purification of the offense (*ābṛti*) occurs after six nights, as may be seen in the text.

It is known. Regarding this, there must be transformation through a fourfold analysis: first, the determination of the offense and its category; second, clarifying whether concealment and so forth are present;
third, whether these factors are separate or combined; and fourth, the established ritual procedures. As for the first section, the text simply states:
Regarding the many remaining offenses, one ultimately cannot determine whether these categories are identical or different.

In reality, these ten offenses may consist of two, three, four, or even up to ten types, designated according to the specific circumstances. Since the texts do not definitively establish the identity or difference of these categories, the legal framework for the offenses is also established based on these ten offenses.
Although these ten offenses serve as the legal framework, they may encounter various conditions depending on the situation.
The term "all" (*sarva*) is also used according to the specific circumstances; one must not cling to the literal text and thereby restrict the mind regarding the performance of the rite.
As for the second section, the text cites cases where the number of days of concealment is unequal, which are to be treated according to the longest period—up to ten days.

Furthermore, because subsequent instances may involve fewer days while preceding ones involve more, it is said that there may be an offense even if one has concealed [the transgression] for only one night, up to ten nights. In principle, however, this refers to concealing for ten [nights].
Regarding "night": because one has previously committed an offense, ten nights elapse; for the second [offense], nine nights elapse, and so on, up to the tenth offense.

To conceal for one night constitutes a case where the initial period was long and the subsequent period is short; this is explained as the "treatment for the initial long period. Alternatively, it may refer to the interruption by the day of the offense:

for example, having committed one *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and concealed it for one night, after confessing it after many days have passed, one subsequently commits another *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and conceals it for two nights;
after confessing that as well after many days have passed, one again commits another *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and conceals it for three nights, and so on, continuing for many days.
The day has passed. Furthermore, one commits another *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and conceals it for ten nights. This is described as being "short first and long afterward.

Since the subsequent period of concealment is ten nights, the matter is settled accordingly; the duration of the penalty follows the specific circumstance. Alternatively, it may be that ten offenses are concealed for ten nights.
Regarding the third category: these cases may be equal or unequal. If there is a combination or separation, those that are unequal—in this text—are treated collectively as ten nights.
Parivāsa (probation) is the means for treating short durations; if one has accumulated days and extended the period, one may still be separated from the community.

Completing fifty-five nights of parivāsa is the means for treating long durations. Thus, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Sengqi lü), fascicle 25, states: "Regarding separate concealment (*pṛthag-paticchādana*):

on the first day of the month, one commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and recognizes it as such, yet with a mind of concealment, one does not disclose it to others. On the second day, one commits another offense and recognizes it as such..."
If one commits an offense and, with a mind of concealment (*praticchādana-citta*), does not confess it to a teacher (*śāstṛ*) until ten days have passed;
or if one knows it is an offense but, with a mind of concealment, does not confess these ten offenses to another;

or if one conceals each subsequent offense for one night, two nights, three nights, and so on, up to the first offense being concealed for ten nights—one should be granted the ten types of *parivāsa* (probation) and the other three disciplinary methods (*dharmas*).
One may also transform a single *parivāsa* (probation) and the other two dharmas [of *mānāpya* and *āvarhaṇa*].

If one says there are ten *parivāsa*s and so forth, this constitutes a single offense with a single dharma of attainment, which is treated for a long duration over successive days. If one says there is one *parivāsa* and so forth, this constitutes many offenses with a single dharma of attainment, which is treated for a short duration by combining the days.
This latter interpretation is precisely what applies to the present text; it also applies to the subsequent section on concealment (*channa*).
There are cases of both transgression and concealment. That text contains four permutations: there may be transgression but not concealment;
there may be concealment but not transgression; there may be both transgression and concealment; and there may be neither transgression nor concealment. Regarding "transgression but not concealment":
if a bhikṣu commits ten *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses and conceals all of them for ten nights, the Saṃgha shall grant him one hundred nights [of penance].
Regarding the *parivāsa* (probation). A bhikṣu says, "Venerable sir, I am weak and ill; I am unable to undergo it. I shall briefly perform the *pārivāsika*.
One should not speak thus. When one has obtained the *karmavācanā* for a hundred nights, it may be combined with ten nights of *parivāsa*.

Or, when nights are combined but the offenses are not, such as when a bhikṣu commits ten *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses and conceals them all for ten nights, the Saṃgha may combine and grant ten nights of *parivāsa*.
[The monk] remains. The bhikṣu says, "Venerable sir, I am ashamed. I wish to undergo the *parivāsa* (probation) in full.

He should be told, "It is permitted," provided that both [conditions] coincide. If a bhikṣu commits ten *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses and conceals them for ten nights, the Saṃgha should grant him a *parivāsa* of ten nights.
If the cases are not concurrent, then separate *parivāsa* *karmans* should be performed for each. Only this.

Regarding "equal" and "not simultaneous," there is no separation or combination; this text refers for now to the case of inequality, and the practitioner should understand it accordingly. As for the fourth section:

the text specifies that for a violation of many *śeṣa* (residual) offenses through the recitation of dharmas and mantras, or for concealing one [offense], one must undergo penance for two nights, up to ten nights.

If the officiant performs the rite, they must necessarily record the specific names and their similarities or differences; if following the length of the days of concealment, they are subsumed accordingly.

If one merely adheres to the letter and recites it, the ritual procedure (*vidhi*) will not be accomplished. Furthermore, at the time of the formal announcement (*jñapti*), it is necessary to present a detailed report;
if one were to stop arbitrarily, such a principle would be untenable.
Next, the second passage concerns the many offenses and the attainment of the dharma. This passage consists of seven sentences, which are divided into two parts.

The first part contains four sentences that establish the essential nature of the dharma; these are what clarify its identity. The second part begins with the Buddha’s words, “You all,” and comprises the final three sentences;

these do not establish the dharma but rather cite faults to manifest what is correct. Within the former section, there are again two divisions. The first consists of three sentences where, although the dharma is accomplished, the terminology is ambiguous.

It does not arise from the ear. The following three "flying" sections consist of nine phrases. Next, there is one phrase that constitutes the non-genuine Dharma. Finally, the teaching is explained by the ear.

Regarding the phrase "it does not arise," it is not a subsequent phrase. Among the first three, I shall first explain the initial phrase. This initial phrase contains five parts; the first clarifies the transgression.

2. Regarding the two remaining offenses (śeṣa-āpatti) where both are concealed: this refers to having committed them and failing to disclose either. 3. Regarding the case where one remembers and one does not:

when one wishes to perform the legal procedure (dharma-karma) and request concealment from the Saṃgha, one becomes terrified in the presence of the assembly and consequently fails to remember one of the offenses.

Alternatively, at the moment of making the request, one thinks it refers to only one offense. 4. Regarding that bhikṣu’s confession according to what he remembers: he requests [concealment] in accordance with what he recalls.
Regarding the attainment of the *parivāsa* (probation) rule: while that bhikṣu was practicing the *parivāsa*, he only recalled [the offense] when it was time for the downward movement.

Second, the Buddha said: "In accordance with what he recalls, grant him the *parivāsa*. This statement does not mean "he does not recall" or "he does not descend," nor does it mean "he does not fly up. Why is this so?

If one were to say that when he requested [the probation], he recalled one [offense] but did not recall another, that would constitute a direct instruction (*śruti*). However, it is stated that he does not fail to recall and does not fail to ascend, because the text does not say otherwise.

Regarding the time of requesting [confession]: if one states directly, "I remember one [offense] and do not remember another," and subsequently remembers it, the Buddha stated that the subsequent memory constitutes *paticchādana* (concealment).

Because of this ambiguity, a visiting monk (*āgantuka*) who has committed an offense and remembers one while not remembering another might also request *paticchādana* for both. Therefore, would [the second offense] arise?

Although the initial scriptural passage (*pāṭha*) is thus, the explanation of its meaning consists of five sections: first, determining the similarities and differences of the categories; second, the memory...
It is neither long nor short. Third, one recollects whether it was many or few; fourth, one obtains the weight and number of the dharmas; fifth, one clarifies the recollection by way of time.
Regarding the first gate: the text directly states that two *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses were committed, yet it does not ultimately determine the similarities and differences between these two types.

From the perspective of principle, there may be one kind of offense with two transgressions, or two kinds of offenses with two transgressions; even when the offenses are of many kinds, it is the same.
In all cases, they are designated according to the names of their preceding categories and types. One must not cling to the literal text and restrict them to only two transgressions.
Regarding the second section: the text simply states that one remembers some things and does not remember others; according to what is remembered, the Saṃgha requests the *paryuṣitaparivāsa*.

While he is undergoing this concealment, he continues to remember [the offenses]; therefore, the Buddha permitted that the *parivāsa* (concealment) be granted in accordance with the number of days the offense was concealed. Thus, the *parivāsa-karman* is bestowed.

The duration of the concealment is not fixed; in principle, these two offenses may be concealed for equal periods—both long or both short—or they may be concealed for unequal periods, such as the former being short and the latter long, or the former being long and the latter short. One must simply conceal them according to when they are remembered;
they cannot be treated by a single uniform standard. As for the third section, the text provisionally takes two offenses as the rule. If...

There is no impediment to explaining [the numbers] three, four, five, and so forth in detail. That is to say: one may recollect two, three, or four [factors] but not one; or one may recollect one but not two, three, four, and so forth;
or one may recollect two, three, or four, yet not recollect those same two, three, or four.

Such irregular interweavings are all permissible provided they correspond [to the context]. However, when enumerating the factors of transformation (*nirmāṇa-dharma*), they must be stated exhaustively; one must not adhere rigidly to the literal text and remain restricted by it.

The second is the rule for the Dharma. Regarding the fourth section: although cases such as "remembering" or "not remembering" may involve many offenses, the text establishes the rule based solely on two attainments.
Alternatively, depending on whether there are three, four, five, or more offenses, the rule is applied repeatedly. This is indeed as stated in the response to the text.
To cite two cases as the rule for the method is logically unobjectionable; however, when performing the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*), one must likewise enumerate them all in full.

Since the second offense is obtained in succession and does not obstruct the prior attainment of the third, fourth, and so forth, why should it not be permitted? As for the fifth point: the text concerns the recollection [of offenses] during the period of concealment (*parivāsa*).
The Buddha permitted that, upon subsequent recollection of a second offense, one should be granted the *karmavācanā* for concealment. This is precisely...
There is the separate acquisition of concealment (*paryuṣitaka*), the joint practice of concealment, the joint practice for six nights, and the joint practice of rehabilitation (*ābṛhaṇa*).

After the subsequent night, if one remembers [the offense] while the period of concealment is being practiced, it is also permitted to grant the formal act of concealment (*paryuṣita-karman*) according to that memory; this is the "separate acquisition" and "separate practice of concealment.
One then practices the joint six nights and the joint rehabilitation. Subsequently, if one should remember during the course of those six nights, one should say:
Six nights. Setting aside for the moment what was remembered subsequently and the concealment itself, this constitutes a separate acquisition and a separate practice of concealment;

one separately acquires six nights and practices them together, and through practicing them together, one is cleared of the offense (*āpatti-vyutthāna*). Next, if one remembers after the six nights have concluded, it should be understood according to the above.

Next, if one remembers after the clearing of the offense has concluded, that constitutes concealment, continuing until the clearing of the offense—all of which is distinct. Within the text, regarding the time of practicing concealment:
This briefly cites one instance to illustrate the Dharma. *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, Chapter 26. Regarding the "original offense" (*mūlāpatti*):

A bhikṣu, having concealed [an offense] and already requested a period of *parivāsa*, later says, "Venerable sir, I have further offenses involving *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. When asked, "Are these original offenses or intermediate offenses? he replies, "These are original offenses.
Later, when asked whether they were concealed or not, he replies, "They were concealed. [The teacher] says to him, "Venerable sir, previously..."
Regarding the one who has undergone *parivāsa*: having already practiced according to the Dharma, if he now confesses his concealment (*chādana*), he must again request *parivāsa*.
This constitutes two offenses combined for which he undergoes *parivāsa*, followed by *mānāpya*, and finally *ābhāṣya* together.
This is called "requesting separately but undergoing *parivāsa*, *mānāpya*, and *ābhāṣya* together. The subsequent phrase describes the procedure.

When half [of the period] has passed, it is later stated that there remains another half of the fundamental offense (*mūlāpatti*). The procedure for concealing it is the same as described above, whether done collectively or individually.

When the subsequent phrase regarding the completion of the *parivāsa* (probation) is reached, it is later stated that a fundamental offense exists; the questions and answers are the same as before. One should say to the one who was previously undergoing *parivāsa*:

"You have already performed it according to the Dharma; why do you now conceal it? He should then request to undergo it once more. This is called "requesting separately and performing separately" (*pṛthag-yācanā-pṛthak-caraṇa*) *parivāsa*.
The junior [monk] undergoes the *mānatva* penance together with the *ābhāṣaṇa*. In the subsequent phrase, having requested the six-night penance, he later states that he has committed an offense;

the questions and answers are the same as before. This is called "obtaining separately, practicing separately, and dwelling separately. Having requested separately, they practice the *mānatva* together and perform the *ābhāṣaṇa* together.

In the subsequent phrase, after having practiced the six nights down to the halfway point, he intentionally states that he has committed an offense; the questions and answers are provided according to the rule.

The common and specific [procedures] are as previously explained. In the next section, the practice of the six-night penance is completed; the questions and answers, as well as the legal procedures, are also clarified as before.
In the subsequent section, up until the completion of the absolution from offense (*āpatti-vyutthāna*), it is stated that there is an offense. One should say: "First, the *parivāsa* and *mānatva*."
"Āpattipariśuddhi (expiation). Since you have already performed [the penance] according to the Dharma, why do you now conceal it? You should request [the rite] again.
This is called "requesting separately and performing separately" regarding *parivāsa*, *mānatva*, and *āpattipariśuddhi*. After requesting *parivāsa* separately, if one says, "I have two offenses:
one concealed and one unconcealed," they should be told: "Regarding the unconcealed offense, rely on [the previous procedure]; regarding the concealed offense, request *parivāsa* again."

[He] practices. Whether in common or separately, etc., up to the expiation of the offense (*āpatti-vyutthāna*), it is the same as before. Next, having requested the *parivāsa* (probation), he says there are three offenses:

one concealed, one unconcealed, and one suspected. He should be told: "As for that which was unconcealed, and that which is suspected, you should resolve them; as for that which was concealed, request the *parivāsa* again.
Whether in common or separately, etc., up to the expiation of the offense, it is the same as the separate [procedure]. That refers to seven periods of time.

This serves to clarify the distinctions between separation and union, as well as commonality and particularity. The present text contains five periods in total; employing those seven periods involves no error.

What has been discussed above follows my recollection; since the categories of consciousness regarding doubt are similar to this one case, I shall not laboriously detail them all. Next, within the text of the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*:
Since it states that one "requests concealment" (*parivāsa*), and at that time one confesses one offense and conceals one offense, it is clearly understood that there is only one person involved;

it cannot be the case that there are two. Since the second person has already confessed one offense and requested concealment from the Saṃgha, it is clearly understood that both [offenses] were originally concealed.

This text exists because there is the expression "requesting concealment," which refers to the confession made in the presence of others (*sammukhā-vinaya*); thus, no fault arises regarding the subsequent offenses. Furthermore, for this reason...
Regarding the concealment of offenses by the mind, the text states: "A sense of shame arises, and one recalls [the offense] above," and so forth.

When the mind is deluded, one does not speak of shame. In this regard, it must also be analyzed through five gates; the explanation is no different from what preceded, and thus cannot be described in detail here.
Within this, all five pairs are fully present, as they are all explained in terms of concealment (*paticchādana*). Among these, there are four types of clarity (*vijjā*).

Next, the failure to establish the three propositions is explained. First, the distinction between remembering and not remembering is clarified; this section consists of five parts. The first demonstrates the commission of two *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses while in a state of delusion and the request for the formal procedure (*dharmakarma*).
The second concerns the Saṃgha granting that offender a period of concealment (*paryuṣitaparivāsa*), wherein both the Saṃgha and the offender share a mistaken view and together grant the concealment.
Third, regarding the section "When he was performing the *parivāsa*," it describes how visiting *tripiṭaka*-holders arrived and questioned him after being informed of the situation.

Fourth, regarding the section "The resident bhikṣu replied," it details the manner in which he answered concerning the ritual procedure for performing the *parivāsa*. Fifth, regarding the section "That visiting bhikṣu said," [it continues the narrative].

The regulation concerning the concealment of offenses not yet confessed is presented here to demonstrate the true Dharma for the Saṃgha. In the initial passage, it states that both offenses are concealed;

this is explained from the perspective of the underlying intention (*citta*), because on the very day the offense was committed, one formed the intent to hide it. Therefore, it is said that "both are concealed. As for the statement that "one remembers one and does not remember the other," this is explained according to the principle (*yukti*):

it means that once the offense has been committed, there may be instances of either forgetting or not forgetting. Even though the offense is not disclosed, both cases equally involve the lapse of a night (*rātri*).

However, that which is remembered constitutes concealment (*paticchādana*), whereas that which is not remembered does not. Therefore, it is said that one remembers one offense and does not remember another. That bhikṣu clings to the literal phrasing;
although both remembering and not remembering are alike in being requested from the Saṃgha, what is meant by "clinging to the phrasing"? The answer is:

based on the preceding text, the Buddha permitted that the second [offense] be subject to the *saṃvaraṇa-karman* (the formal act of concealment) according to how it was remembered. In the preceding text, it was "remembered."
First one does not remember, then one remembers the second; the Buddha permitted the *praticchādana-karman* (act of concealment) to be granted accordingly.
Now, I likewise do not remember the first and remember the second; since this is no different from the previous case, why may I not request both at once?

Because of such erroneous adherence, both are said to request it from the *saṃgha*. Next, the *saṃgha* collectively holds the same erroneous view and grants the method of concealment to both. Next, there are two questions; first, the question:

Regarding the offense: therefore it is asked, "What has this bhikṣu committed? This question contains two points: namely, what offense was committed, and whether the concealment was established or not.

Next, regarding his conduct: therefore it is asked, "For what reason did he practice concealment? This question contains three points: namely, the request for alms, the act of concealment itself, and the basis of the text;
thus, both questions may also be understood as applicable. Next, the answer first responds to the initial question, and subsequently addresses both [the remaining points].

Regarding the statement "The Saṃgha requests [the confession] below," this answers the second question. Next, the prohibition of non-formation is presented in three parts: first, the prohibition of non-formation; second, the interrogation "Why is this so?";
and third, the explanation beginning with "That bhikṣu... and so forth. Within the explanation, there are again three sections. First, the regulation establishes what is right and what is wrong:

if one remembers, it constitutes concealment (*paticchādana*); if one does not remember, it is not concealment. Because it is not concealment, the legal act (*dharma*) is not formed. Second, the conclusion of the Saṃgha.
[The section on] offenses. Next, the True Dharma is shown. Although the explanation of the text is thus, its meaning still consists of five parts:

first, the similarities and differences between the two types of determination; second, whether the recollection is long or short; third, whether the recollection is many or few; fourth, the frequency of attaining the dharma;

and fifth, clarifying the recollection according to time. Regarding the first gate: although the words of the Sage provisionally employ the terminology of the dharma regarding the two offenses, they do not definitively establish two types [of determination].
Regarding similarity and difference: according to the actual principle, one may plant one or two offenses, or plant two or three offenses;
these may be designated individually according to the thirteen matters. One must not cling to the literal text and limit [the offenses] to only two.

In the text of the second section, it simply says that for those who remember, the concealment is wholesome, and for those who do not remember, the concealment is unwholesome; ultimately, it does not definitively establish whether this remembrance is long-lasting or not.

[The previous case was] short. However, according to the actual principle, each [case] applies to both long and short durations. Whichever [duration] one conceals, it all constitutes an unrighteous act (*adharma*).
Regarding the beginning of the third section, which concerns two offenses in contrast to the prior accomplishment: speaking according to the principle, it applies to three, four, five, and so forth.
For example, as if one remembers one [offense] but does not remember two, three, or four; or one remembers two, three, or four but does not remember one; or one remembers two or three.
Regarding the four [kinds of] formal acts (*jñapti-caturtha*), it is entirely incorrect not to recollect the second or third [recitations].

One must not adhere to the literal text by restricting the rule to the second [recitation] alone. In the text of the fourth section, whether one recollects them or not, it is stated that the Saṃgha requests [the act];

this is established as invalid based on obtaining the formal act through a single repetition. If one only recollects the second [recitation] after the formal act has already been obtained, and then grants the act, it likewise constitutes an invalidity. How could this be...?
One may obtain the Dharma all at once. The Buddha established the rules regarding what is permissible and what is not. If one bestows [the precepts] sequentially, it does not constitute an offense.

However, provided that two, three, four, or more [people] receive them together, it is permissible; this refers to the opposite of the previous case, such as when offenses are incurred through repeated actions as described in the middle section.

As for the fifth gate: according to the text, at the time of requesting [ordination], it is a shared attainment of the Dharma; alternatively, it may be that after having requested, one attains the Dharma individually. This is also [permissible].
This establishes its invalidity. Just as it is when the offense arises at the time of begging, so it is for the following six times.

However, if one follows the text such that there is a joint begging and a joint obtaining, both are not accomplished. Likewise, if one conceals [the offense] by increasing or decreasing the legal procedure (*dharma*), it is also invalid.

If, later, one remembers and begs separately and obtains separately, then for one who did not remember later, it is not accomplished of itself; for one who remembered previously, it is accomplished of itself. Next, regarding doubt and lack of doubt:
Section on the Gate of Knowing and Not Knowing: This should be understood according to the previous [explanation]; it cannot be described in detail here.
Next, regarding the third text, "Obtaining Many Dharmas from a Single Offense," there are seven phrases within the text. Within these seven phrases, there are two sections.

The first consists of four phrases concerning the fundamental completion of concealment after two months, which is what is meant by "manifesting this. The second section begins with "The Buddha said" and below, concerning the root...
One month covered; one month not covered. This is what is meant by "revealing the non-. The preceding text has two parts:

the first three statements concern the supervision of the lower three non-[factors], while the fourth concerns the ear-instruction not being produced from below. Regarding the characteristics of the initial text, this should be understood according to the previous [explanation].

Within the text, for the time being, the method is based on two months; as for the three equalities and the category of years, they are established without distinction. This is the explanation herein.

Regarding the meaning, it likewise requires five gates. The Dharma and Precepts are the reverse of the former; I shall not describe them at length. However, when many offenses are incurred, they are distinguished by their combination or separation.
Next, the two gates of Doubt and Non-recognition are also the same as the preceding positions. Furthermore, these three must first involve not remembering, doubting, or not recognizing [the offense].
After one month, one remembers and no longer doubts or recognizes it. One month thereafter, while practicing accordingly, one remembers and so forth—only then does it begin [to be reckoned].

Regarding "not recollecting the preceding" and so forth, the subsequent doubts concerning the ear should be understood by analogy. Next, the three negations are raised, which likewise follow the previous positions. They are not established because they have already been explained;
thus, they should also be interpreted through the five gates, as their meaning does not differ from what preceded.
Next, the four textual passages explain the distinctions according to time; there are three parts within these texts. First, the double concealment and double manifestation of concealment.

Second, the single concealment and single manifestation of concealment. Third, clarifying the continuity of these two. Within the first section on double concealment, there are only four propositions.

Regarding the preceding and succeeding categories of the path: their essence is that of a *bhikṣu* who conceals [an offense] and does not confess it, thereby becoming subject to concealment. One must undergo treatment for this;

once the period of probation (*parivāsa*) is completed, since one is no longer a *bhikṣu*, there is no confession, and as the method of concealment no longer applies, there is no concealment and thus no need for treatment.

The explanation of the text is clear. Question: Is there only these four cases here, or can more be established later? Answer: According to the text, there are only four; the others are not clarified. Furthermore, it may also be said...
According to the following section, there should be five pairs in total. Each of these five pairs consists of four lines, forming twenty statements.

Furthermore, within each of these five sets of four lines, the first line is identical while the subsequent three lines differ. Specifically, there are five instances where the first line is the same for both the preceding and succeeding paths;

five instances where the second line is the same for the preceding but different for the succeeding path; and five instances where the second line is different for the preceding but the same for the succeeding path. [The third and fourth lines follow this pattern respectively.]

Fourth, there is difference in both the preceding and the succeeding. Because there is difference, multiple cases can be established. This constitutes being concealed when it is consistently the same, rather than being concealed when it is consistently different.

The reason for this is as follows: regarding memory and non-memory, these are explained within the context of concealment; however, present forgetfulness is not concealment, so how could it be the same as disclosure?
Regarding doubt and non-doubt, these were distinguished within the context of memory; because of the presence of hesitation, [concealment] is not established.

Concealment (*paticchādana*) is not the same as forgetfulness; it certainly cannot be equated with mere non-recollection. Regarding "knowing" and "not knowing," this is distinguished within the context of doubt:

because one does not know [the offense], concealment is not established. Since this is not due to indecision, how could it be equated with doubt? Regarding "having requested" and "not having requested," this is clarified within the context of recognition:

because one has formally requested [forgiveness] from the Saṃgha, concealment is not established. Since this is neither delusion nor error, how could it be equated with non-recognition? These are the twenty [points].
The phrase "this is the practice of concealment" refers to the four subsequent periods mentioned previously; all examples are like this.
Within these, the first twenty phrases involve two offenses, while the following eighty phrases require three offenses and a single object for the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*).

Since there are one hundred phrases, the same applies to the seven subsequent conditions, each having its own set of one hundred. Question: Why does it mention only "two offenses" and not "three," "four," or "concealment" and so forth?

Answer: For the time being, let us take two offenses as the basis for the rule; even more would not be an obstacle. However, since the methods of treatment do not differ, they will not be mentioned separately.
Next, we clarify the cases of single concealment and single confession. Based on the eight types of differences in resolution, there are one hundred sentences in total.

First, regarding the differences in the path of concealment, there are five stages: first, prior to concealment; second, while practicing concealment; third, having completed the practice of concealment; fourth...
When practicing for six nights, five or six nights having been completed, there are twenty instances each, totaling one hundred.

Regarding the first twenty cases where the practice was previously equalized: these twenty are divided into five pairs. First, based on the categories of concealment and non-concealment, four permutations (catuṣkoṭi) are formed.

The characteristics of these should be understood through the sequential explanation of their respective remedies. Question: Since the initial offense was already concealed, what is the nature of the subsequent concealment that is established? Answer: It is explained by means of...

Because the conditions have changed, one must again confess. Since one concealed [the offense] and did not confess it, it constitutes *paticchādana* (concealment). Whether it was confessed before a single person (*paṭimokkha*) or before the Saṃgha, if it is subsequently concealed, it becomes concealment.
As previously stated regarding the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), although the offense was confessed, at the time of the subsequent recitation, one must again confess that concealment;

if one conceals it and does not confess the concealment, one incurs the fault of silence (*tuṇhī-sāvadya*). In this text, for the sake of brevity, the rule is established based on the case of concealing one offense while not concealing another.
Alternatively, if one [of the three] is covered and two are not, the method of transformation for the third and so forth is no different; there is no further distinction to be made.

Next follows the gate of "recollection and non-recollection," the gate of "doubt and non-doubt," the gate of "cognition and non-cognition," and the gate of "begging and non-begging. If these four were identical to the preceding text, they would not be fully cited here;
however, to explain their meaning in relation to this, two gates must be established: first, the definitive classification of combinations and separations; second, the five...
The first [section] is not the same as the first gate. Question: For what reason are two sets of four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) established for the disclosure and concealment [of offenses]?

That is to say, regarding the root [offense] and the time of requesting [forgiveness], there are three cases—recollection, doubt, and lack of awareness—which each consist of only one set of four propositions;

these concern only the root [offense] and whether it was remembered or not, yet they do not include the time of requesting [forgiveness] and whether it was remembered or not. Answer: The four pairs, beginning with concealment and so forth, are all explained with reference to the root [offense].

Regarding the "requesting at the time of concealment": this refers to defining the timing by means of the rules for one's own conduct (*pratimokṣa*). These four pairs are collectively included within the rules of conduct;

thus, each of the four pairs consists of eight [subdivisions], forming thirty-two phrases. Now, taking the disclosure (*āviṣkaraṇa*) and concealment (*pracchādana*) as counterparts to the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*), they constitute the "counter-rituals.
Because these rituals differ, they are divided into two pairs based on the fundamental request regarding the timing, and further categorized according to recollection (*smṛti*).
The remaining three cases do not involve formal procedures (*karmavācanā*). Since they do not involve formal procedures, there are no distinct characteristics;

they truly possess the fundamental [offense] itself, and there is no separate time for requesting [the lifting of the concealment]. Why is this so? It is because, as soon as the offense has been committed, there is already concealment. Regarding the disclosure of concealment:

this refers to whether the fundamental concealment was concealed or not at the time of requesting it from the Saṃgha. If there is subsequent concealment and disclosure after that time, then that is the very time of the request.
Regarding "concealment" (*paticchādana*) and "non-concealment": there is this sense that one may obtain two pairs of distinctions, such as memory and so forth;

however, for the other three [offenses], this distinction does not exist. Therefore, there is only the fundamental offense and no "time of begging" (*yācanakāla*). Another interpretation holds that it refers to a case where, since the initial commission of the offense, there has been no prior concealment;

now, when begging from the Saṃgha, there is either concealment or non-concealment. For this reason, it is called "concealment or non-concealment at the time of begging. If there was prior concealment, then now, upon begging, [the matter] is returned.
"Hidden. This "hidden" refers to that which was concealed at the time of begging for it. Because it is known through the mind alone, it is distinguished as two pairs.
Since recollection and so forth involve delusion of the three minds, they are not divided into two. Regarding the five differences at the beginning of the second section: Question:

What is the distinguishing characteristic between the fifth case—begging for concealment while concealing and giving rise to concealment—and the first four cases, where one confesses and conceals? Why are they divided?

There are two pairs. There are two interpretations for this. First, they are divided into two pairs because the times differ: the first four lines concern whether one conceals or does not conceal [the offense] at the original time;
the fifth set of four lines concerns whether one conceals or does not conceal it at the time of begging.

If they are thus divided into two pairs based on the difference in time, then while it may be acceptable regarding the time of begging, how can it be so regarding the time of traveling? For instance, during the course of travel, there can be no begging; since there is none, [how could there be concealment?]
Question: Since begging [for forgiveness] occurs only once for each concealment, there should then be only sixteen [offenses]. Why are there twenty? Answer:
Regarding the timing of the "practice" (caraṇa) and so forth, the clarification of whether one begs or does not beg is explained differently based on new offenses; thus, they are not uniform.

If one discusses only the old offenses without considering new ones, the meaning becomes restricted and the inclusion of the Dharma is incomplete. This is done to provide a basis for the five [categories].
At that time, because the matters were distinguished, there was also the question of whether one may request [the *pārivāsika* status] during the period of probation (*caryā*) and so forth.

Second, because they differ in that they are not methods for concealing the offense (*chādana*), those who first confess (*vivaśana*) do so by confessing before three objects [of refuge]. The fifth [case], the time for requesting, is restricted to requesting the dharma from the Saṃgha.

Because of these differences, they are divided into two pairs. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that the first four lines refer to those who have previously undergone concealment; [this is] hypothetical...

When begging [for food], there may be cases where it is covered or not covered; however, these are identical to the first case and cannot be divided into two. This combines with the fifth and fourth cases.

Since they have never previously been covered, one begs immediately after the offense has been committed. At the time of begging, there may be cases where it is covered or not covered; because this differs from the first case, the fifth case is collected [separately].

Having already understood that the first five characteristics differ and are not the same, there is no need for the monastic texts to laboriously compare and resolve them. From here on, the various...
Regarding these stages, they must all be explained through two gates. Since the explanations of their meanings are identical, there is no need for further elaboration.
The preceding twenty phrases prior to the practice are now concluded. Following this, there are eighty phrases concerning the four periods; these shall be analyzed by means of two gates.
The first [section] is the classification of the three parts; the second is the classification of the old and the new.

In the first gate, the preceding twenty items concern persons who have not yet received [the formal act], meaning that for both offenses, the legal act has not been performed. Now, with these ten items, persons who have already been subjected to disciplinary action are concerned, wherein there is the acquisition of the legal act.

Upon arriving, the acquisition of the legal act must necessarily be performed through three offenses. If it were performed through two offenses, all four permutations would be obstructed, as follows: [The text continues with the specific permutations regarding the performance of legal acts based on the number of offenses.]
Regarding the four permutations of concealment (*paticchādana*) and non-concealment: in the first permutation, one conceals one offense while not concealing another.

If, after having left the monastic order (*pravrajyā*), one later returns and conceals both offenses, both are subject to disciplinary treatment (*daṇḍa*). This clarifies that for one who does not practice concealment, once an offense has been treated, the prior offense is no longer treated.

Nor is one who practices concealment (*paryavasthāna*). It is clearly understood that once a single offense has been committed and the practice of the Dharma has been attained, one is called a practitioner of concealment.
Subsequently, there must be two further offenses: one concealed and one confessed. Therefore, three offenses are required; two offenses would constitute an obstruction.

This being the case for this phrase, it is the same for the remaining phrases. However, the ancient masters say: "If two offenses are treated as the first three phrases, they obstruct the second and fourth."
Regarding the second phrase: one conceals one offense and incurs one [new] offense. After returning from having left the monastic life (*pravrajyā*), one incurs one offense.

If one concealed it previously and also conceals it now, both the prior and subsequent instances are treated according to the rules. This clarifies that for one who practices concealment, there is one offense incurred previously and one also incurred subsequently;

since neither the prior nor the subsequent instance is treated, this refers to the offense being committed. Because there is no sense of concealment, it is identical to treating the practitioner as the one who incurs the offense. One conceals one.

Regarding the preceding [case]: because both the earlier and later [acts] are concealed as one, it is said there are "two offenses. If one conceals [the act], this constitutes the fourth phrase; the attainment [of the offense] may be explained in the same way. This interpretation is incorrect.
For example, with respect to the two gates of concealment and requesting [expiation], the guest [monk]—by means of not concealing and by requesting—is the very one who commits the offense.
If one does not remember, suspects, or does not recognize [the act], none of these constitute concealment. How could one possibly conceal at a time when one does not remember, suspect, or recognize?
Since these are precisely the offenses being practiced, one knows that this meaning is provisional and has not yet reached the full realization of the six, eight, ten, or animal precepts.
If there were two practices, they would both obstruct the statement "having finished"; against what, then, could "finished" be distinguished? Therefore, all of them constitute obstructions.

Regarding the "old and new" in the second section: the four periods mentioned below concern those who commit a transgression again; these are all discussed in terms of the new offense (*navāpatti*) and do not rely on the old one.

This is for the purpose of clarifying whether the new offense constitutes concealment (*praticchādana*) or does not constitute concealment, and whether it requires disciplinary treatment (*daṇḍa*) or does not require it. Within the ritual procedures (*dharmakriyā*):

One commits a new offense and it becomes concealed. The reason for this is that although one may have performed the *dharmas* (legal procedures) while deprived of thirty-five matters, if there was a mind of concealment, it is no different;
thus, the concealment remains a concealment. This concludes the first section on the differences in conditions. The following seven categories are similar.

Next, the explanation of the two continuities (*anubandha*) is summarized in four periods, forming five propositions; there should originally be six, but because the "original day" (*mūlatithi*) is included within them, there are only five.
Among these, the first and the fourth are "renewal of practice" (*pratisaṃdhāna*); the remaining three are "reconnection" (*pratisaṃdhi*).

That is to say, when one who has already left the monastic life returns and must again undergo a formal ritual procedure, it is called "reconnection. When one continues the preceding practice without requiring a formal ritual procedure, it is called "renewal of practice."
There are five conditions for each of the eight [factors], totaling forty propositions.

Next, the fifth section concerns repeated offenses according to time; this section explains the procedure for the four periods regarding the method of practice. First, it is addressed in relation to a single offense and a person who has attained the status of a practitioner.

This is distinguished within the practice of concealment (*paticchādana*). However, the monk practicing concealment is subject to six forms of discipline (*sappaṭikamma*); this is established within the category of non-concealment.

There are three types of persons: first, one who conceals while knowing the number of days; second, one who conceals while not knowing the number of days; third, one who conceals while both knowing and not knowing the number of days.
These three fundamental cases concern the formal procedure for the practice of *parivāsa* (probation). At that time, there was one who practiced *parivāsa*.

The bhikṣu clearly understands that the meaning applies to three types of persons. Below these three heads, there are nine items for each; within the first set of nine, there are three groups of three. Regarding the first group of three:
first, when one has committed a grave offense (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*), knowing the number of days it was concealed, one performs four types of formal acts (*karmas*):

(1) granting the *parivāsa* for the new offense together with the concealment; (2) granting the *mūlāpakarṣa* for the old offense; (3) granting the six-night penance (*ṣaḍrātra-mānāpya*) for both combined; (4) [granting the reintegration] for both combined.

[The first] is the expiation for the offense. Second, a double offense committed unknowingly, concealed for an unknown number of days; third, a triple offense committed knowingly, concealed for an unknown number of days—each of these four cases is as described above.

These constitute the twelve permutations for the first three types of persons, which are fully enumerated in the text; the remaining ones are omitted. Next, for the three types of persons who commit a double offense without concealment, there are nine permutations of *karmavācanā*:

first, knowing the number [of days] and not concealing it; [the others follow]. *Note: The original text appears to be a technical manual on monastic disciplinary procedures (*vinaya*). The "twelve permutations" refer to the various combinations of offenses (single, double, triple), the awareness of the offense, and the duration of concealment.*

The threefold *karmavācanā* refers to those who have newly committed an offense and do not conceal it; they are immediately granted the *pārivāsika* (probation) for the original offense, followed by six nights of *mānāpya* and the formal restoration from the offense (*āvarhaṇa*).

Second, there are those who do not know the number [of offenses] and do not conceal them; third, those who know the number but do not know the number, and do not conceal them—each of these three cases is as described above.

Next, regarding the three positions of repeated offenses, whether concealed or unconcealed, there are twelve procedures, explained as in the first three cases. These constitute thirty-three cases in total.
Regarding the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual acts): based on the first nine [cases], they constitute the formal rule; the remaining two sets of nine should be understood by analogy.

These twenty-seven persons comprise ninety-nine rounds of *karmavācanā*. If both old and new offenses are to be addressed through the formal rule, there are only eighty-one—namely, excluding the eighteen instances of concealment for newly committed offenses.
Thus far, this has been based on one offense resulting in one acquisition of the formal rule; if other [factors] are considered...
Third, regarding the acquisition of the dharma: when the stages and vehicles are combined, they constitute four positions and twenty-seven persons.

Just as it is with the commencement of an offense during the period of concealment (*praticchādana*), so too is it with the commission of a new offense during the subsequent three periods. In the text, once the concealment is concluded, it is the same as before;
next, during the three periods, one simply takes up the practice of *mānatva*, for which one should say, "it is also thus," because within the practice of *mānatva* one commits an offense again.
Therefore, having cited the commission of an offense, the phrase "without concealing" is stated. Subsequently, the four periods for the emergence of the locus of the offense are presented;

these do not merely restrict the position, nor is the offense limited to each stage individually. Since each stage involves twenty-seven instances of repeated offenses, they fully include the disciplinary methods such as *pārājika* and so forth, without opening [the possibility] for other times.

However, regarding these four periods, when calculated according to the rules for old and new offenses, they are separately assigned within two categories of conduct, each possessing nine [subdivisions].
The nineteenth *karmavācanā* comprises eight categories in total, containing seven hundred and ninety-two formal procedures (*dharma*).
Within the two concluding sections, as these do not involve the violation of the rules, twenty-seven cases of the *mūlāpakarṣa* (removal from the day of offense) are excluded;
each of these contains seventy-two *karmavācanās*. These eight categories together comprise five hundred and seventy-six formal procedures. In total, there are four... [the text ends].
There are one hundred and thirty-two individuals, totaling one thousand three hundred and sixty-eight instances of *karmavācanā*.

This, however, is based on a single instance of repeated offense; if it concerns a second, third, or subsequent repetition, the calculation should be understood as doubling accordingly. Thus, the text below states:

"When practicing the *praticchādana* (concealment) penance, the same applies to a second repetition committed during that interval. The preceding discussion regarding repeated offenses has been explained with reference to concealment.

If it concerns the *pratisaṃharaṇīya-karman* (act of reconciliation) and so forth, the remaining three procedures are explained in the same manner as above. This is clarified by way of the fundamental [procedures]; therefore, there is no mention of "begging" (*yācanā*).

Next, the sixth section concerns the combined performance of different types; within this text, there are four dharmas, namely: concealment (*chādana*), the *mūla-parivāsa* (fundamental probation), the *mānāpya* (probation), and the *āvarhaṇa* (expiation).

The first three are explained in detail, while the last one is mentioned briefly. Regarding the first, the dharma of concealment, the text has four sections as previously stated. As for the term "concealment" (*chādana*):

"Concealing" means having the intention to hide one's transgression; "not concealing" refers to the practice of disclosure (*pratideśanā*). Regarding "equal or unequal concealment," this is discussed in terms of the length of the days of concealment.
As for the "single name," it is the same as *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. As for the "many types," there are thirteen distinctions.

Regarding "intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and non-intrinsic nature," the old translation stating that "ten are intrinsic and three are prohibitions (*pratikṣepa*)" is incorrect; these are precisely the *śeṣa* (residual) offenses to be confessed. How could they be otherwise?

Regarding the refutation of the nature [of the offense], I shall now explain it. If one examines this according to the meaning of the first position, then the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is itself the nature (*svabhāva*).

If it functions as a causal condition for the transgression, it fully constitutes the nature of a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. As for the explanation that "if it is an offense, it does not constitute the nature of a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*," this is incorrect.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "those who abide in distinctness" refers to the old [view] that there are four types [of offenses] because their constituent elements (*dhātu*) differ, this is also not the case; for how could there ever be a time for confession?
The *saṃghāvaśeṣa* [offenses] have now been definitively established regarding their initial categories of transgression. Now, to explain:

if one examines by means of the fifth method, those who conceal [the offense] practice the *pārivāsika* stage, while those who do not conceal it practice the *mānāpya*. Therefore, it is said that they "dwell separately. Question:

If the difference in practice arises from the nature being non-intrinsic (*asvabhāva*) and having been previously possessed, as well as from the difference in the dwelling of the offense, then how is it that the time of the offense and...?

The two phrases "performing the recitation" and "the method for requesting from the Saṃgha" constitute the distinction regarding what has already occurred; it is not appropriate to request this [method] from the Saṃgha.
For example, regarding the terms "concealed" and "unconcealed," even if one is unconcealed, it is likewise not appropriate to request concealment from the Saṃgha.

Since the text mentions "unconcealed," we know that the words regarding the formal procedure (*dharma*) are provisionally set forth in the text and must therefore be fully enumerated. As for the actual performance of the rite:
One must record the offenses according to the specific facts. However, this enumeration of thirteen items is intended to demonstrate the intensity of the mind of revulsion;

by listing them all, they may all be extinguished. From the perspective of principle, it is not strictly necessary to possess all of them; whether few or many are present, all can be expiated through confession.

Next, the Buddha generally indicates the method, stating that one should act "according to the days of concealment. Subsequently, one should request [forgiveness] from the Saṃgha, and one must not recite the words exactly as they appear in the text.

One must also record their names, the types [of offenses], and the length of time they have been concealed. Next, they should request the ritual from the Saṃgha; the subsequent procedures are likewise the same.

Next, the two instances of "original-day" (*mūlāha*) are combined into one because they are identical. Next, the "six-night removal of guilt" (*ṣaḍrātra-āpattivyutthāna*) can be understood through this.

Regarding these, there is a detailed analysis of the three categories of "double destruction": first, the quantity of the double destruction; second, clarifying it by way of time; and third, correlating it with the persons involved.

[The Master] Distinguished: This first section clarifies the method for re-administering the *pārivāsika* (probation) for a transgression committed after the initial offense. Since this matter was not clarified in the preceding texts, [the question arises:

if one were to again violate the rules while undergoing the *mūlāpakarṣa* (reversion to the beginning), how should it be remedied? The Buddha said: "If one violates them again, one must once more undergo the *mūlāpakarṣa*;

this is not the same as the case of a *śikṣādattaka* (one given the training) who commits a repeated offense and is subject to *pravāsanīya* (expulsion). Question: Why is a third repetition of the violation not mentioned? Answer: Because the first [repetition] is already a violation.

Regarding the offense, it is permitted to grant the *bunbi* (the original date). However, if one commits a second violation, it is feared that it may not be appropriate to grant it; therefore, the present text clarifies the case of a second violation.

Since the second [violation] follows the same principle as the three grades [of concealment], and because the nature of a repeated violation does not differ, the text does not provide a full enumeration.

To clarify this in terms of time, let us first consider a repeated violation within the period of concealment (*pācittiya*); since it is thus for concealment, the same applies to the three subsequent periods.
The previous instances of the destruction of the Dharma were all explained in terms of four periods. Now, the meaning of the second cycle of destruction should likewise be so.
Furthermore, according to the text: if the second [offense] occurs during the two periods of practice, there are two methods for treating the original offense;
if the second [offense] occurs at the conclusion of the two periods, there is only a method for treating and rescuing the new transgression, and thus no "original" offense remains.
The method for calculating the days [of concealment] is based on not violating the rule regarding the two limits. Regarding the third section, which distinguishes [the cases] by person:

although the text mentions the rule concerning the days since one first learned of the offense, it does so specifically in reference to a single individual who conceals their knowledge. If one were to follow the logic of the *Vinayavibhaṅga*, there should further be three other categories:
those who know the number of days but do not conceal it, those who know the number and do conceal it, and those who do not know the number. Furthermore, there is the case of not knowing [the number].

The number is three. Furthermore, there are those who do not know the number as the first three, and those who know the number but do not know the number as the first three; these combined make nine persons.

The former interpretation further multiplies these nine persons by the three fundamental heads to produce twenty-seven, and again multiplies these twenty-seven by the four stages of attaining the Dharma to produce forty-eight. This is all incorrect, for they are of different types.
[The text] should be combined for practice. How could one further multiply the three *yathābhūta* (as-it-is) states and four stages in sequence?
Rather, these nine persons at this time should be distinguished according to the four periods; thus, four times nine makes thirty-six. Question:

Why is it that here, following the *yathābhūta*, the text does not state that by multiplying the persons, nine are formed, and no more can be obtained? Answer: Because the six *yathābhūta* states are cited in this text, and since the six have already arisen...

There are nine [categories]. How could these constitute a plurality? Furthermore, since these nine are fundamentally various types combined for practice, they are enumerated horizontally as one and nine;
thus, when written down, there is nothing remaining.
Next, regarding the seventh section on the administration of medicine according to the non-[standard] method, its text likewise cites various types combined for practice; therein are two parts.

The first case is raised to show that [the offense] must be abandoned; the second is for those of middling and inferior capacity, to demonstrate that it must be cultivated. In the preceding text, regarding repeated offenses, there are no more than two categories:
those who know the number of days and those who do not, as well as those who conceal and those who do not.

Now, by combining the knowledge of the number of days with the various permutations of concealment and so forth, there are nine types of persons. The first three take the knowledge of the number of days as the primary factor and proceed through the permutations of concealment.

[The following applies to] the first person, who has three types of "non-legal" (*adharma*) cases: first, the three factors are all non-legal; second, there are three instances of concealment (*paticchādana*), namely:

the original concealment, the first subsequent offense of concealment, and the second subsequent offense of concealment. Although there are these three, they collectively constitute concealment that is non-legal.

Third, concealment and the six-night penance (*ṣaḍrātra*) are like the non-legal case of the formal rehabilitation from guilt (*āpattivyutthāna*). Question: It is stated only that it is "not legal," but it is not known [what this means].

Question: Why is this "non-affliction" (anivṛta) not the same as the other categories? Answer: It is not so, yet it does not depart from the four types of manifest presence (sammukhībhāva). This is because these four types encompass a broad range of phenomena (dharma). Question:

Within the category of "non-affliction," why is there no "obscured" (nivṛta), and why do the lower two [categories] not correspond to one another? Answer: The latter non-affliction does not supersede the former correspondence.

If there were no subsequent [offenses], there would necessarily be no preceding ones; this is because each subsequent offense is formulated by citing the preceding one. Question: Why must the preceding offenses be cited when confessing the subsequent offenses? Answer:

It is because these three categories of offenses together constitute a single process of purification (*pratideśanā*). The first two are the preliminary stages (*upāya*), while the confession of the offense is the fundamental stage (*mūla*).
The same applies to the three non-offenses for each of the second and third individuals. This constitutes the nine propositions for the three individuals in the first stage.

It is not yet finished. Next, taking "not knowing the number" as the head for three persons, there are nine non-cases (*viparyāsa*). Next, taking "knowing the number" and "not knowing the number" as the heads for three persons, there are nine non-cases;
all are exactly as above. Next, within the "as-it-is" (*yathābhūta*), one reverses the non-cases to explain them.
If one considers phrase against phrase, one phrase corresponds to one phrase, up to twenty-seven phrases corresponding to twenty-seven phrases. If...
By means of the "as-it-is" (yathāvat), one overturns the "not-as-it-is" (ayathāvat). Specifically, one "as-it-is" overturns three "not-as-it-is.

Because the six-night period for expiating offenses through concealment (*channa-ṣaḍrātra*) is combined into a single "as-it-is," this constitutes nine "as-it-is" which overturn twenty-seven "not-as-it-is."
Next, the eighth section distinguishes concealment (*paticchādana*) with respect to persons. The preceding sections have not yet distinguished this in relation to specific individuals.
Among these four propositions, the first posits that both parties incur the offense of concealment. Regarding "one who sees another bhikṣu and then conceals it":

this refers to one who hides [the fault] out of shame before seeing a pure (*pariśuddha*) bhikṣu. In this first proposition, both parties incur concealment. In the following three propositions, only one party incurs it.

First, it is not established as a concealment (*paticchādana*). However, regarding whether one remembers or does not remember within the context of concealment: it is clarified that for one person, the memory persists through the night and thus constitutes concealment;
for another person, who forgets on the very same day, although they do not confess, it does not constitute concealment because there is no intention to hide [the offense].

Next, within the context of remembering, one distinguishes between being doubtful and being certain. Next, within the context of being certain, one clarifies the distinction between knowing and not knowing. This "knowing" and "not knowing" is precisely...
Regarding "known" or "unknown": this is to distinguish it from the fundamental concealment (*mūlāpatti*).

Since there is no occasion for begging [for food], the nine subsequent texts apply equally to both what was previously known and what was unknown. In principle, this should also be clarified by corresponding it with recollection (*smṛti*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*), but for the sake of brevity, the text is concise.
Have you ever known [this] before? As for the previous statement that "not knowing does not constitute concealment," one might ask:
what is the characteristic of "not knowing"? Therefore, it clarifies that "not knowing" is merely another name for deluded thought (*misaṃjñā*).

Herein, the offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (formal meeting) refers to the six remaining [offenses] when viewed in relation to the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* category; there should be only six. This is because the five lower offenses share the same class of characteristics; thus, they are mentioned collectively.

This constitutes six [offenses]. The six cases involve the destruction of the *pārājika* (defeat). Regarding the fundamental offense, one must not commit a *pārājika*; it is excluded. Initially, there are thirty-six *pārājikas*. Question:
If one commits these offenses, yet the mind does not correspond to the object, and since there is no concealment (*praticchādana*) to be treated, how can one incur [the offense]?

Answer: Because the mind did not correspond to the object, there was no intentional transgression to be treated; however, because there was a heart of concealment, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) in all cases. As for the previous mention of "knowing," it refers to concealment.
This constitutes concealment (*paticchādana*). Since it is not known what its characteristic of knowing (*jānana-lakkhaṇa*) is, the characteristic of concealment as known is explained next;

this also applies to the subsequent explanations, thus forming six propositions. The sequence for administering the medicine is as follows: first the preliminary means (*upāya*), and so on down to the "evil speech" (*pāpaka-vāda*);
the same logic applies to these categories.
