Next, the tenth section clarifies the duration of concealment (*paryuṣita*) regarding both long and short periods. This is determined by the length of time since the concealment began. This section is divided into two parts:

A detailed exposition of the ritual procedures for the practice of concealment is collected in one place and termed a *khaṇḍaka*. Furthermore, if named according to its subsequent designation, it should be called the *mānatva-khaṇḍaka*;

Third, the Buddha stated that he permits the practice of the *mānatva* penance, specifically the procedure for practicing it for six nights.
The first section contains two sets of sixteen phrases; the first set of sixteen phrases clarifies that these four types of persons may not officiate as legal authorities for one another.

"If that bhikṣu relinquishes his separate residence (*parivāsa*) and goes to another place, he should request [it] from the Sangha there; the Sangha shall have him undergo the separate residence once again."

"Not informing" here means not having previously informed those within the monastery who are walking slowly, as distinguished from those passing through quickly—referring to a monk from outside who passes through this boundary. These are not the formal procedures of the Saṃgha; the pure dharmas (*śukladharma*) are as follows. However, regarding these eight matters, even if one commits them all on a single day, one loses only one night, not all eight.

for if one fails to obtain the harmonious consent of the senior, middle, and junior monks, it will result in schism and strife, leaving one without allies or support, as occurred in Kauśāmbī. The subsequent three texts may be understood accordingly.

Next, regarding the text on the faculties (*indriya*), there are two sections. The first consists of six sets of one and six, which provide a general explanation according to the dharmas: that is to say, the first, third, and fifth [sets] do not constitute [the offense] because they lack the faculty;

the second, fourth, and sixth [sets] constitute a prohibition because the faculty is present. Next, there are two sets of six, which provide a specific explanation in relation to the objects (*vastu*).

That is to say, it can be known whether there is a remainder or no remainder. Next, the time-periods can be understood. Next, regarding the treatment of the offense that conceals the actual transgression:

within this section, there are two parts. First is the treatment of the offense of concealing [the fault] through slander. This passage consists of four sections: first, examining whether the three karmas of the concealer are pure or impure;
second, from "preventing the bhikṣu who recites the precepts" onwards, examining the matter to reveal the truth; third, from "one should ask" onwards...
Examining whether the root [offense] exists or not: fourth, the prohibition against the *bhikṣu* reciting the *Poṣadha*, which is the formal treatment for the offense of slandering;

next, if one prohibits the recitation of the *Poṣadha*, this is the treatment for the actual offense that was prohibited. Next follows the method for withdrawing the prohibition, the text of which has two parts.

First, the text regarding withdrawing [the prohibition] due to illness has three phrases. Second, from "at a different time or place" onwards, it concerns the universal withdrawal of the *Poṣadha* recitation; herein is the text.

Second. First, in order to avoid malicious monks and fearing that there might be matters that would disrupt the assembly, one performs the *poṣadha* (recitation of the precepts) every day according to the text.

Next, if one cannot proceed further down, one performs two postponements (*dvipratikṣepa*). This is done so as to coincide with the *pravāraṇā* (invitation for criticism). There are no three postponements. The preceding section on the methods of prohibition is concluded.
*The Record Elucidating the Fundamental Tenets of the Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, Scroll Nine, Part One;
*The Record Elucidating the Fundamental Tenets of the Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, Scroll Nine, Part Two.

Next, the section on the Schism of the Saṃgha (*Bhikṣu-saṃghabheda-khandhaka*) is explained: practicing the six points of harmonious respect, upholding the Dharma without contradiction, and purifying communal affairs through shared practice.
This is the meaning of *saṃgha*. Now, by using false teachings to alter the truth, the assembly is divided into different tracks and separate ritual practices are performed;

thus, harmony is not achieved, which is why it is called "breaking the *saṃgha*. To extensively manifest the characteristics of this breaking, they are gathered in one place and designated as a *khandhaka*.

The main text is divided into three parts: first, clarifying the breaking [of the *saṃgha*] and the division of the *saṃgha* into different sects; second, from "At that time, Śāriputra... onwards, the two lands...
[The section on] Schism in the Sangha. Third: At that time, he [Devadatta], having departed from that [Sangha], broke the ritual procedures (*vidhi*) based on this inquiry.

The preceding text has three parts: first, clarifying Devadatta’s schism in the Sangha; second, from "At that time, many... onwards, citing the incident and informing the Buddha; third, from "The Buddha said...

onwards, reprimanding him to manifest his transgression. The former [section] has two parts: first, breaking the method of practice; second, breaking the method of the assembly. The former is the breaking of the practice.
The Dharma also has two [aspects]. First, those without wisdom took the voting sticks (*śalākā*). This text was recited once, and there were further five hundred and ten practitioners;
in the thirty-seventh sutra, the assembly recited it three times. During the first recitation, only four companions took the voting sticks;
during the second recitation, two hundred and fifty took them; and during the third recitation, another two hundred and fifty took them. Thus, from beginning to end...

The chant was repeated three times; in total, there were five hundred [monks]. At that time, Ānanda and others—wise men who did not accept existence through transformation—beheld this event and could not bear it.
Therefore, they cast off their *kāṣāya* robes. Sixty others saw them do so and followed suit, all performing this same rite.

Next is the breaking of the *saṃgha* (the monastic community). Within this *saṃgha*, there are those who carry out its formal procedures (*karmas*). Thus, having faith and being fully endowed [with the necessary qualities], one breaks the perfect integrity of the True Dharma.
Regarding this, the meaning of "breaking the *saṃgha*" is explained through a threefold analysis: first, the explanation of the name; second, the identification of its essential nature (*svabhāva*).
The third section consists of various gates. First, the explanation of the name is as before.

Second, regarding the definition of its essence (*svabhāva*): it is that which destroys [the notion of] subject and object. If one asks what the essence of this destroyer is, it has deceptive speech as its nature;

that is to say, it consists of both the co-emergent manifest (*vijñapti*) and unmanifest (*avijñapti*) [karma]. Therefore, among the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), it is included within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), and among the bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*), it is subsumed under sound (*śabda*) and the mental-object base (*dharma-āyatana*).

[This is] because there are two [factors]. Question: Since the schism of the Saṃgha also involves bodily action (*kāyakarman*), preparatory thought (*prayoga-cetanā*), and other vocal actions (*vākkarman*), why is it said that its nature consists solely of concealed and deceptive speech?
Answer: At all times—from the preparatory stage through the completion—this concealed and deceptive speech has the power to cause the Saṃgha to be split;
other actions do not. Therefore, they are not mentioned. As for the essential nature of that which is split, see the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, chapter eighteen.
It is said: The schism of the Saṃgha has as its essence the nature of non-concordance; it is non-obscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*); it is dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta*);

among the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), it is included within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*); and within the bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*), it is included within the base of mental objects (*dharma-āyatana*) and the element of mental objects (*dharma-dhātu*). Question: What constitutes the essence of this nature of non-concordance?

Answer: Its essence is non-possession (*aprāpti*). If that is so, there are two types of schism in the Saṃgha, namely: the schism of the Wheel of Dharma (*dharma-cakra*) and the schism of ritual action (*karma*). It is not yet known [which is meant here].
These two are identical in that both types of breaking [the Saṃgha] have non-attainment (*aprāpti*) as their essence. However, this non-attainment differs according to what it refers to:
if it concerns the Dharma-wheel Saṃgha, it takes the non-attainment of the *principle upādhyāya*; if it concerns the ritual-karma Saṃgha, it takes the non-attainment of the *factual upādhyāya*.
Although it is a non-attainment belonging to the Saṃgha, the reference point is thus distinct.
Next, there are eight sections: first, determining the refutation of the object; second, explaining the refutation of the means of cognition;
third, clarifying the refutation of identity and difference; fourth, determining the locus of the refutation; fifth, explaining the first two [sections]; sixth, the ultimate expedient means;
seventh, contrasting with the *Prakaraṇābhidharma* to clarify the sequence of priority; eighth, the time and place of abandoning the precepts and entering hell.
The first gate refutes the object. There are two such objects: first, the schism of the Saṃgha; second, the schism of the wheel (*cakra*). Regarding the schism of the Saṃgha:

it requires that within a single boundary (*sīmā*), the Saṃgha be divided into two factions, such that they simultaneously perform legal acts (*dharmakarma*) and are unable to reach mutual consensus. Regarding the schism of the wheel:
They repeatedly use these five dharmas to entice and deceive newly initiated, ignorant persons, causing them to falsely accept the four new reliances of a Buddha.
Therefore, the aforementioned text says: "I now teach these five dharmas to the bhikṣus; this is sufficient to inspire faith and joy. The text further states: "He addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
'Devadatta today wishes to establish four new noble lineages. Furthermore, the sixth fascicle of the *Abhidharma-kośa-bhāṣya* asks: "What is the schism of the Saṃgha?"
It is not that the wheel is destroyed; rather, within a single realm, each group performs the *poṣadha* separately.

How is it that the wheel is destroyed but the Saṃgha is not? The Noble Eightfold Path is called the "wheel. When one abandons the Noble Eightfold Path and teaches other paths instead, this is called the destruction of the wheel, not the destruction of the Saṃgha.
In the treatise, these two phrases are analyzed; the remaining two phrases should be understood by analogy. For this reason, there are both the Saṃgha and the wheel.

[This is] distinct. Next, the possession of understanding is explained. This is explained in terms of the destruction of the wheel of practice (*caryā-cakra*). There are three general types of understanding.

First, it must be a *mahā-bhikṣu* and not someone from another assembly who lacks such understanding. Therefore, the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "One who can cause a schism in the Saṃgha must be a *mahā-bhikṣu*; it is certainly not one who is a householder."
[They saw] only those who practice correctly, not those who practice incorrectly; those who abide in pure precepts, not those who violate them.

Thus, they specifically sought a great bhikṣu to stand as a counterpart to the Buddha, rather than one who was a householder or the like, because such a person’s physical body lacks majestic power (*prabhāva*).
This is inferred from seeing those who practice correctly, for their evil intentions and inclinations are extremely firm and deep; they are not [those who practice] incorrectly.
The practitioner, because they simultaneously harbor both [the pure and the impure] within the profound and pure category, remains in pure precepts;

for one who possesses pure precepts is said to be able to inspire awe in others, whereas one who violates the precepts is said to lack majesty. These two [types of practitioners] oppose the three admonitions of the Saṃgha.

When he violates the remaining precepts after the extensive teachings have been established, it is considered a transgression from the outset; the offense is identical to the second [category]. Thus, the *Jianlun* (Treatise on Views), fascicle 12, states:
"Because he did not relinquish [the view] despite the three-fold admonition of the Saṃgha, he commits the three grave offenses that corrupt the mind—namely, insanity and so forth.
Next, there are fourteen distinct conditions: first, one must give rise to the intention to cause a schism. Therefore, in the preceding text, this was established as a consequence.
Not being permitted to eat separately from the assembly, he then gave rise to this thought: "Never before have I eaten apart from the śramaṇa Gautama; this is the food of a newcomer.
I would now rather break that monastic wheel (saṃgha-cakra). Later, he again gave rise to a desire for fame, hence saying: 'After my body has perished, I may obtain renown.
Second, because his skin was not yet peeled off, he gave rise to a dwelling [of thought]: regarding right precepts and views..."

Because it must be broken by two "flaying-knives" (*carma-śastra*) before they can even arise; as for what are called the "two flaying-knives," they refer to the possession of both ethical discipline (*śīla*) and right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*).

Those who possess the precepts say that these five dharmas constitute the Path. Those who hold views deny that the Eightfold Noble Path is the Path. The third [case] is neither the first nor the last; thus the treatise says:
"The first refers to when the World-Honored One had not long since turned the Wheel of Dharma; the last refers to when the Sugata was about to enter Parinirvāṇa.
During these two periods, the Saṃgha was of one flavor. The fourth is not after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa; thus the treatise says: "There is no true Great [Saṃgha]."
The Master [states]: Because they are adversaries, the fifth [condition] requires that this continent (Jambudvīpa) be involved; thus the treatise says:

"Only among the people of Jambudvīpa, when there are at least nine, or later more than this, can the Wheel of Dharma be broken, and not in other continents, because there is no Buddha there. Wherever there is a World-Honored One, only then can there be a rival teacher.
The sixth [condition] is that it must be in a different location within this continent; thus the treatise says: "It must be broken in a different place, and not..."

Regarding the "Great Gathering" (Mahāsaṃnipāta): because the Tathāgatas cannot be easily provoked or intimidated, it is said that their majestic and solemn demeanor is such that no one can prevail against them.

However, as for those in different locations, this refers to the formation and dissolution of the *saṃgha*. Since the first pair of supreme disciples had already been established by the seventh [chapter], the treatise states:

"When the first pair of supreme disciples for śamatha and vipaśyanā had not yet been established, it was the natural law (*dharmatā*) that they would quickly reunite. The eighth [chapter] is not [the case].
Because the boundary has not yet been established, the treatise states: "At the time when the boundary has not been established, there is no single boundary that can be divided into two factions.

Regarding the ninth member of the quorum, it must be complete; thus the treatise states: "It requires eight bhikṣus to be divided into two assemblies. To constitute a schism, one must have a faction capable of causing the split;
therefore, because the ninth person is required, the minimum number for the assembly is nine. The text below states: "In each of these two assemblies, there are four [bhikṣus]."

If a person, through excessive conduct, causes a schism in the Saṃgha by casting voting tickets (*śalākā*) and performing the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*), and Upāli maintains [the position], this is called one who causes a schism.

This refers to the "theory of the abandoned leader" (*pradhāna-bhūta-vāda*); because there are four companions, [there must be] four on each side. If it is the "theory of the concurrent leaders," there must still be nine;

for the tenth is a worldling (*pṛthagjana*) who causes the schism, meaning that according to the standard of the schism, a worldling cannot cause a schism among the Noble Ones (*ārya*), because all Noble Ones...
Because they have realized the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Some say that even those who have attained patience (*kṣānti*) cannot be refuted.

In the preceding passage, the Elder Bhikṣu feared that [the audience] would not accept it because there are eleven types of divergent views and divergent patiences. Therefore, the treatise states: "It is required that the Saṃgha to be split accepts a teacher other than the Buddha;
accepting one other than the Buddha, they claim there is another noble path (*āryamārga*). This can obstruct the wheel of the noble path and destroy the harmony of the Saṃgha. (12) Thus it concludes.

The two dharmas for regulating the community: the communal dharma refers to the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) and the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*). The individual practice dharma refers to the four reliances and the eightfold right path.

Thirteen types of illegal voting-slips are accepted by the foolish. Fourteen involve the performance of communal dharmas while conducting the *poṣadha* separately. These two conditions below constitute a breach.
Regarding the two dharmas for regulating the community, the beginning and end encompass both the general and the specific; when these are complete, a schism is formed. Thus says the treatise.
It is said: This is not a treatise that destroys the Dharma. All Buddhas must rely upon it, for such matters exist due to past karma.

Among various interpretations, as long as there is fault, none constitute a "destruction" [of the Saṃgha]. The characteristics of deficiency can be understood by contrast with this *hetuvidyā* (logic).

Regarding the destruction of the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) of the Saṃgha, the characteristics of a complete interpretation are generally threefold, being largely the same as following the precepts (*śīla*). There are five specific conditions: first, there must be...
The intention must be to cause a schism in the mind and to destroy the harmony of the Sangha. There is no offense if the mind is indolent or neutral.

Second, one must not perform legal acts (*dharmakarma*) while within the boundary (*sīmā*) but outside the designated area for such acts. Third, the number of the assembly must be complete, requiring at least four members in each of the two opposing groups;
thus, separate factions perform the legal act within a single boundary. Fourth, it must be during the time of the Buddha’s Dharma, provided that the Dharma remains extant.
At that time, there is the sense of "breaking. After the Dharma has vanished, a "break" cannot be established.

When two groups—the "this side" and the "that side"—perform *karmavācanā* simultaneously and both fail, this is called "schism in the Saṃgha" (*saṃghabheda*). If it occurs in only one location within the teaching, it is merely a separate assembly (*pṛthaggaṇa*).
Therefore, the third fascicle of the *Abhidharmahṛdaya* states: "If, within the boundary of a single residence, two divisions of the Saṃgha each perform [the ritual] separately..."
Regarding the *poṣadha* *karmavācanā*: one should know that this constitutes a schism in the Saṃgha. Only when both parties jointly uphold the formal act (*dharma*) can it be called a "schism.
Why, then, does the preceding text state that if one calls out [the offender] only after having seen, heard, suspected, or sought [evidence], and yet fails to do so, saying, "He has fled;
he has vanished; I wish to cause him to be destroyed," and then performs the *karmavācanā*, it does not constitute the offense of *sthūlātyaya*? To explain this: such a case is considered evil.
This is a mental offense; it is not the transgression of causing a schism in the Saṃgha.

Next, regarding the similarities and differences: there are ten points that explain these distinct variations. First, concerning the timing: [this refers to] the schism of the Wheel of Dharma (dharmacakra-bheda).
Regarding the breaking of the *saṃgha* through formal ritual (*karmabhedaka*): it occurs exclusively during the Buddha’s lifetime, for after his *parinirvāṇa*, such an event does not exist.
It exists both in the present and the future, as it does not depend upon the Buddha and thus applies at all times. Second, regarding the breaking of the wheel (*cakrabheda*) in terms of location:

it occurs only in Jambudvīpa and not in other regions, because the Buddha did not teach the Dharma in other regions. Since the Buddha did not teach there, with whom could he compete in conversion? For this reason, [it is restricted].
He endures [the status of] a teacher distinct from the Buddha; he endures teachings distinct from those of the Buddha. Furthermore, desiring to split the Saṃgha, he calls himself a Buddha.

He has no Great Teacher, and there is no one who places their trust in him. He splits the *karmavācanā* Saṃgha throughout the three continents, excluding the northern continent because it is a difficult land.

Third, regarding the breaking of the wheel by person: the breaking of the *dharmacakra* is restricted to *bhikṣus* who follow the path of views (*dṛṣṭicarita*), and does not include *bhikṣuṇīs* or those who follow the path of desire (*tṛṣṇācarita*).

The breaking of the *karmasaṃgha* includes *bhikṣuṇīs* and those who follow the path of desire, yet still excludes other classes of persons. Fourth, regarding the breaking of the wheel and the *saṃgha* by ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) versus noble ones (*ārya*):

the breaking of the *dharmacakra* involves only ordinary beings and not noble ones, because those who have realized the Dharma cannot commit the act of schism. As for the breaking of the *karmasaṃgha*, [it likewise applies only to ordinary beings].

The *ma-seng* (breaking the Saṃgha) applies to both ordinary beings and noble ones (*ārya*), because within the affairs of the world, even a noble one may fall into delusion and thus break [the harmony]. Fifth, regarding the number of persons required for the breaking of the wheel:
from five to nine people, the breaking is accomplished. This breaking of the True Dharma also involves the Three Jewels:

one person constitutes the Buddha, four people constitute the Saṃgha, and only when there are at least five people does the capacity to break [the Saṃgha] come into being. Within those who are broken, there must likewise be five people; one person...
This refers to the Buddha. A *saṃgha* is constituted by four persons; since one speaks of "breaking the *saṃgha*," it is necessary to clarify the Buddha [as the object].

Breaking the *karmavācanā* (ritual) *saṃgha* requires only eight persons, meaning that both sides perform four separate ritual acts. Sixth, regarding the breaking of the wheel [of Dharma] based on the principal:

it necessarily requires one person to act as the Buddha, because the Tathāgata is the master of the wheel of Dharma. Breaking the *karmavācanā* *saṃgha* involves members of the same class breaking one another; it does not require [the presence of a Buddha].
A provisional Buddha acts as the master of the Wheel of Dharma. Seventh, regarding the breaking of the wheel through practice, it requires five kinds of ritual procedures (*karmavācanā*).

First, the five dharmas are proclaimed; this is the Path, after which one begins to wield them. As for breaking the *karmavācanā* through the performance of rituals, it is not merely a matter of performing the ritual procedures; it must be done in accordance with reality.

Second, the two assemblies uphold the Dharma to achieve schism. Eighth, regarding the schism of the wheel based on the boundary (*sīmā*): the schismatic must be within the boundary, because performing the *karmavācanā* outside the boundary does not constitute a schism against those who are to be split;
such a person may be anywhere within or outside the boundary, and even throughout the trichiliocosm, they cannot maintain the Wheel of Dharma.
To break a *karmadharma-saṃgha*, it is essential that both assemblies be within the same boundary at the same time and perform the *karmavācanā* ritual together. Ninth, regarding...

The "Wheel-breaker" (cakrabheda) refers to one who violates principle and thereby destroys the correct [Dharma] with various seeds; because the damage to its meaning is broad and manifold, such an offense incurs a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense) and constitutes a *ānantarya* (immediate retribution).

Regarding the breaking of the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual), within the matter itself there is a contradiction: to break the correct with the correct is a light *sthūlātyaya* and not an *ānantarya*. Tenth, regarding the breaking of the Wheel in terms of karmic retribution: the karma is so heavy that it lasts for one eon (*kalpa*) in the Avīci hell;
the *karmavācanā* is explained as being lighter, while other hells do not last for a full eon.
Next, regarding the location: according to this text, although five hundred were transformed at the royal city, this was merely a skillful means;
it was only when they were later brought to Mount Gayāśīrṣa and the *karmavācanā* was performed by himself that the process reached its ultimate completion. The *Mahāsāṃghika* [Vinaya] is likewise.
The preceding text further states: "All [acts] prior to being admonished, such as the intent to destroy, and so forth, up to the stubborn refusal to relinquish all grave offenses.

Furthermore, within the passage concerning the name of Mount Gayaśīrṣa, there is an error; it should instead be called Mount Gajaśīrṣa (translated here as "Elephant Head," because the summit of the mountain resembles an elephant's head).
This mountain is located three or four *li* to the north of Vulture Peak (*Gṛdhrakūṭa*) and lies within the same boundary. [The deity... heaven...
Śūra did not respond. As for the claim that the Master resided there and broke the textual tradition regarding the "Ga" (伽) clan—this is because the Sanskrit sounds are similar;
it is merely due to an error on the part of the translator. However, that place actually has both "Ga" and mountains. This mountain is the Vulture Peak Mountain (Gṛdhrakūṭa-parvata).
To the northeast, at a distance of over one hundred and fifty *li*, they do not belong to the same boundary (*sīmā*); how, then, could they constitute a schism in the Saṃgha?
Furthermore, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: When Devadatta was about to cause a schism, the Buddha established Ānanda and summoned him three times during a single day.

Calculating that the distance was three or four *li* for each round trip, one return would be seven *li*. Over three rounds, this would total twenty-one *li*. If [the distance were] one hundred and fifty...

The remaining distance is three hundred and three *li* for one round trip, totaling over nine hundred *li*. Since Ānanda did not possess supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), he would have had to travel on foot;
without half a day, how could he have completed three rounds? Based on this calculation, it is clear that Keśa is of the Gauḍa lineage.
Regarding the first two [categories]: if one discusses the heinous crimes (ānantarya), there is no taking of the first [offense], because these crimes oppose principle and violate the teachings.
As stated above, there was a non-Buddhist who intentionally killed his parents and came seeking ordination.
The Buddha said, "One who has killed their parents can derive no benefit whatsoever within my Dharma; they must be expelled.

Regarding the *sthūlātyaya* offense of violating the precepts, this constitutes a *pārājika* (defeat) from the very beginning. Since he had not yet committed the offense prior to that point, although it occurred later, it is still considered a *pārājika* from the moment it was incurred.
The offense is the same as the second [saṃghāvaśeṣa]. Why is this so? Because he has already been previously admonished, and now, having violated that admonition, he causes a schism;

therefore, it is the second [offense], not because there was already a prior act of schism. Question: Since Devadatta’s schism of the Saṃgha is the second [offense] for violating an admonition, should the saṃghāvaśeṣa also be the second?
Answer: Schism is the objective matter resulting from the admonition; it is now [classified as such] because of the violation.

Because the offense of schism (*saṃghabheda*) is committed through the act of breaking [the Saṃgha]. When the second admonition is broken, one is admonished for the schism itself; one is not admonished for the refusal of that admonition.
Therefore, because of that refusal of the admonition, the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense should include the initial [act of breaking].
Next, regarding the culmination of the preparatory effort (*upāya*): this present *sthūlātyaya* offense of schism is the culmination, not the preparatory effort.
This is because Devadatta originally desired fame and profit, intending to usurp the Buddha’s position, destroy the Saṃgha, and sever the Dharma;

now that he has succeeded in breaking the Saṃgha and returned to preach his own views, that which he intended has been accomplished. His thoughts are fully satisfied, and there is no further progress to be made. Therefore, it is the culmination.
This is the ultimate [conclusion]. Question: Since the schism of the Saṃgha is already ultimate, why is it not given the name of a *pārājika* (defeat)? The ancient masters explain:

If the substance [of the offense] has no remaining meaning [to be applied], the principle should indeed be so. However, because the matter of the schism is singular, it is intended for the purpose of reciting the formal rules of the *Prātimokṣa*.
If the name *stūlā* (sthūla) were applied to these three [offenses], it would simply be called *stūlā*. Because they are not considered identical matters, the name *stūlā* is not applied to them.

The present regulation regarding *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense) incorporates both light and heavy degrees; this is for the sake of convenience in establishing the principle that applies to all three persons. For example, because one is the primary perpetrator, one incurs a *pārājika* (defeat); whereas others who are not the primary perpetrators incur only a *sthūlātyaya*.
Regarding the four companions, there is a *sthūlātyaya* before the assembly (*parṣad-sthūlātyaya*), and a *sthūlātyaya* through face-to-face confession (*mukha-sākṣin*) among five hundred.

Lan: My current interpretation is not so. It is simply because the task to be accomplished has been achieved that one attains the ultimate [result], yet this does not constitute a violation of the ultimate limit of the teaching;

therefore, no *pārājika* offense is incurred. Furthermore, the four grave rules (*catur-śrāmaṇeraka*) were established for those who violate the ultimate limit of the teaching; since the schism of the Saṃgha is not included among these four, one incurs only the offense of *sthūlātyaya*.
Thus, the reason why the schism of the Saṃgha violates the teaching but is not an ultimate transgression is that, if judged by the gravity of the matter, it is not [as severe as the others].

One should incur a *ānantarya* offense. Since one has already committed an *ānantarya*, the matter is grave. Because the matter is grave, it should be designated by the name of a *pārājika*. This is as with the other three types of killing;

both principle (*nyāya*) and teaching (*śāsana*) reach their ultimate point here. Regarding the breaking of the Saṃgha, one incurs the fault of an *ānantarya*; because one acts in violation of principle to the utmost degree, the damage to the objective reality (*vastu*) is not considered grave.
Therefore, it does not bear the name of a *pārājika*. Question: Since the five hundred [monks] were broken by another, why do they incur a *sthūlātyaya*? Answer:

It is expected that this will be refuted by others; one should not commit a *sthūlātyaya* offense, for [the schismatic] endures the view that the Teacher is different from the Buddha and accepts false teachings. Thus, the *Nyāyānusāra*, fascicle 43, states:
"In order to split the Saṃgha, [the schismatic] must endure that the Teacher is different from the Buddha and endure that there is another Noble Path distinct from the teaching of the Buddha."

Next, regarding the sequence of shedding blood and causing a schism in the Saṃgha: according to this Vinaya, as well as the *Pañcavargika* and the *Daśabhāṇaka*, one first initiates the preliminary effort (*prayoga*) for a schism, followed by shedding the blood, and subsequently initiates the effort again until its completion.

If that is so, since the shedding of blood occurs first and the schism later, how can the *Daśabhāṇaka* state that "nine pure persons can cause a schism"? Furthermore, [how does this accord with] the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya*?

Third, it is said: other immediate karmas (*ānantarya-karma*) cannot subsequently cause a schism in the Saṃgha. Regarding the interpretation that although other schools have the term "pure" (*viśuddha*), this text does not obstruct it;

one must not use the texts of other schools to hinder this interpretation of the meaning. Furthermore, according to another interpretation, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that because he did not commit a *pārājika* offense.
This is called "purity. The reason we know this is that the text itself speaks of nine purities; it first mentions the shedding of blood and subsequently the schism of the Saṃgha.

It is clear from this that, according to this basis, no *pārājika* offense has been committed, which is why it is called "purity. Furthermore, in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, within the section on the questions and answers concerning the ritual for schism, it initially states there are nine purities.
Since the bhikṣus who hold the same view did not originally determine the sequence of these events, there is no error in this.
If it were not so, it would contradict the text itself. Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 119, states:

"If one first commits another immediate transgression (*ānantarya-karma*), one will subsequently be unable to cause a schism in the Saṃgha. If one first causes a schism in the Saṃgha, one will subsequently be able to commit other immediate transgressions;
all those subsequently committed are brought about by the predominant power of the schism, and thus they collectively induce an immediate retribution."
Regarding the results within the hells, the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* (Zàxīn) takes this as its basis for discussion; therefore, it says "the other immediate [offenses]," and so forth.

Furthermore, this does not necessarily determine their chronological order; it simply excludes those who have destroyed the Saṅgha. It requires that one be of noble lineage, upright, or possessed of learning and eloquence, because such a person establishes themselves as a Great Teacher (*mahāśāstṛ*).
One who violates the precepts is not a predominant factor. If one relies on the *Jñānaprasthāna* and the *Śaiśunāga* school, [it is] first...
That blood flowed after the schism of the Saṃgha does not contradict the meaning [of the scriptures]. Therefore, we know that the seventeenth fascicle of the *Śāstra* states:
"After Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana had taught the Dharma and converted beings, the Saṃgha was reunited. At that time, Devadatta conceived a malicious intent and pushed a mountain to crush the Buddha.
The Vajrapāṇi, with his vajra-pestle, struck it from afar; the rock shattered and splinters flew toward him, wounding [him]."
The Buddha’s foot was struck by a finger. The bhikṣuṇī Padmāvatī rebuked him, whereupon he struck her with his fist. The bhikṣuṇī immediately bled from the eyes and died;
thus he committed three ānantarya sins. The same occurred with the Naiyāyika; these cannot be recorded in detail.
Regarding the subsequent account of renouncing the precepts and entering prison, this text merely states: "He was immediately seized with terror and arose;
blood flowed profusely from his face," yet it ultimately does not discuss the matter of renouncing the precepts and entering prison. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, fascicle 25, states:
"At that time, Svāgata kicked Devadatta with his toe and reviled him, saying, 'The Śākya has risen! Then Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana used other expedient means..."

He requested the bhikṣus to depart. Devadatta, startled, rose up and reviled them, saying: "These bhikṣus of evil desire—how is it that they who initially had kind intentions have suddenly conceived such malice?
By means of a stratagem, they are taking my bhikṣus away! He was seized with great terror, and copious blood flowed from his nostrils;
he immediately fell alive into the Great Avīci Hell. This clarifies his entry into hell; it does not matter whether he had renounced [the world] or not.
Regarding the *Vinaya-vibhaṅga* (Ten Recitations), section thirty-seven, which clarifies the occasion for renouncing the precepts, it does not mention entering prison. Thus, the text states:

"At that time, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana transformed five hundred bhikṣus and led them toward the Buddha’s dwelling. At that time, the Sūtra Hall of Devadatta was empty and devoid of the great assembly;
there were only four companions. Then, Kāḷodāyin kicked Devadatta with his feet to wake him."
"Devadatta, Śāriputra, and Maudgalyāyana are using pleasant speech to win over the assembly and take your followers away. Upon waking, Devadatta saw that the lecture hall was empty;
he fell from his couch in a state of confusion and distress. Then his four companions sprinkled him with cold water, and he regained consciousness, thinking to himself:
"I am of the Śākya clan, Gautama. A Great Man cannot be bent down. O monks, listen to my words:
previously there was the Dharma of the heterodox teacher Devadatta, which had become obscured and remained unclarified. I shall now cause it to arise. Listen clearly as you abide within this Dharma;
you should know that from this day forward, I no longer belong to the śramaṇa Gautama. As he spoke these words, immediately—
This is called "abandoning the precepts. It is clearly explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. [The case] even extends to the beating to death of the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā.
He befriended the heretic Pūraṇa Kāśyapa and others; his mind was severed from all roots of goodness, and he lacked shame and remorse—this is the moment of abandoning the precepts.
Later, he smeared a potent poison onto his fingernails, intending to injure the Buddha while paying him homage. Before he could depart, he was intercepted by the King.
Within the city of Śrāvastī, the earth spontaneously split open. A fire chariot came to meet him, and he was born alive into hell.
Next, the commentary explains the text, recounting these prior events in detail to the Buddha.

Next, the second section consists of the reprimand of the text, which has two parts. First, he reprimands his actions in contrast to the preceding events; thus it says, "Foolish man, you have split the Saṃgha.
Second, there are eight points below that demonstrate the gravity of his karma and the difficulty of salvation. Within this, there are two sub-sections:

first, clarifying that the karma of the causal factors is grave and difficult to save from; second, from "If I were to see... onwards, explaining the reason why he cannot be saved. The preceding text has three parts.
This refers to the enumeration and the conclusion. First, the general enumeration is clarified: these eight are not the true path to liberation; therefore, they are not the True Dharma.
To be emotionally attached to these eight factors is called "entanglement. They act as the eight causes of delusion, which, when summarized, are described as obscuring and veiling.

Furthermore, they eliminate the causes for the arising of cultivation; thus, it is said that they "extinguish the virtuous mind. Devadatta has now brought his commission of evil karma to fulfillment. Therefore...
It is said that they proceed toward non-ways and manifest the place where retribution is received; thus they reside in *niraya*.

Speaking of it as "one *kalpa*" makes it clear that the location is grave and reveals the timing of the reception of selection (*vibhaṅga*). To call it "one *kalpa*" indicates there is no method of accumulation; it is named "incurable.

Next, the listing of the eight [factors] reverses the text of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, which lists them as gain, loss, fame, disrepute, praise, blame, suffering, and pleasure. Although these names here—

There is a slight difference in terminology, but the meaning ultimately does not vary. Regarding gain and loss in relation to giving: to praise one's virtues beyond their measure is called "fame" (yaśas);
to disparage them when they do not merit it is called "infamy" (ayaśas). To honor with a disciplined mind is called "reverence" (gaurava);

to be indolent and to find fault is called "lack of reverence. These constitute praise and censure. To be oppressed by adverse conditions is called an "evil friend" (akalyāṇamitra); to rejoice [in such things]...

To allow one's mind to become accustomed to evil is called "taking pleasure in evil friends. This constitutes a pair of opposites: suffering and pleasure. The subsequent conclusion may be understood accordingly. Next, the explanation of the reason for this consists of three parts:

the principle (*dharma*), the analogy (*upamā*), and their synthesis (*yoga*). Within the section on the principle, the contrast between the inverse and the conformative reveals that while goodness is fully realized, evil is brought to completion;
thus, one falls into *niraya* for an eon without rescue. The subsequent analogy and its synthesis may be understood accordingly.

Next, the second section on the text for harmonizing with the Saṃgha. First, the actual clarification of harmonization; second, from "That bhikṣu saw... onwards, raising the matter to reveal past events and showing that ancient precedents accord with the present.
The preceding text is divided into four parts. First, sitting according to the Dharma while falsely assuming the position as prescribed in the text, according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.
When Devadatta saw that Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana had arrived, he immediately dispatched Kāḷodāyin to take the place of Maudgalyāyana and Śāriputra.
Second, at that time, Deva descended as a manifestation of the Tathāgata. Third, Śāriputra descended to transform the assembly and lead them back to the Right Path.
Fourth, Śāriputra descended and lost the assembly, falling into distress. The meaning of these textual passages is clear. Next, the events are cited.
The first part of the ancient text has three sections. First, it cites the past events concerning Śāriputra’s refutation [of the Dharma] to contrast them with the present refutation;

by means of this, it clarifies that although the five hundred [monks] did not lose their prior precepts, they merely committed a *sthūlātyaya* offense through repentance, and because this was not a formal obstacle, they were able to attain the fruit.
Second, from "Maudgalyāyana said" onwards, it cites the past model of the Dharma to contrast it with the present model of the Dharma. Third, at that time, the various bhikṣus...
The Buddha has six instances of turning his back on past acts of ingratitude, which correspond to the present act of ingratitude. In the past, he destroyed [the Dharma] through evil teachings;

in the present, there is this destruction—this is the second [point]. Next, the ritual procedure for breaking the Saṃgha is explained in two parts: first, the ritual procedure for the breaking; second, the retribution for the fruit of breaking the harmony.
The initial text is divided into two parts: first the question, then the answer. Within the question, there are three points.
First, it asks what kind of dharma Devadatta practiced to sever the Buddha’s wheel of Dharma and split the Saṃgha into two factions; thus it says, "How does one break the Saṃgha?

Second, it asks regarding the number of people required to maintain the formal act (*dharmakarma*) and destroy harmony so that the act of breaking the Saṃgha is accomplished; thus it says, "How many must be kept [in the assembly] for it to be called 'breaking the Saṃgha'? Third, it asks...
Regarding those who are ultimately capable of destroying the wheel [of the Dharma], it is not known who is able to accomplish this;

therefore, it is asked, "Who breaks the harmonious Saṃgha? Next, the answer consists of two parts: first, the individual explanation of the question, and second, the joint answer to the following two points.

Within the former, there are again two sections: first, the destruction of the dharma of correct practice by means of the five *bhavas*; among these five, the first three are similar speech (*sādharmya-vāk*) and the latter two are false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*). The explanation is as above.

Next is the performance of an illegal *karmavācanā*. This refers to performing a formal act (*sabhāva-karma*) by adding, subtracting, or altering it during the midst of a legitimate assembly, thereby breaking the legal procedures of the Sangha.
The reason for this is that the Buddha taught two types of practice for the bhikṣus:

first, individual practice, which refers to the four reliances and the eightfold right path—the conduct of training and the track for generating practice; second, communal practice, which refers to the formal acts (*karmavācanā*) and the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*).

The protocols for abiding in the Dharma accomplish the benefit of the multitude. Now Devadatta has disrupted the harmony of the Saṃgha and likewise challenges the Tathāgata by establishing two kinds of dharmas:
first, he establishes five dharmas, thereby subverting the Buddha’s four reliances and the eightfold noble path;

second, he employs illegal *karmavācanā* (formal acts), thereby subverting the correct laws of the community. If a bhikṣu believes in, accepts, and practices these, it is called "breaking the integrity of the correct [Saṃgha]."
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Sengqi lü), fascicle seven, states:

"Regarding the preface to the precepts, the four *pārājikas*, and so forth up to the seven methods for settling disputes and the conforming rules (*anuvartaka-dharma*), that which was not previously established is now established, and that which was already established is now relaxed. This extends even to the rules for householders, those who have left the home life, and those who practice together—namely, the ninefold scriptures (*navāṅga-śāsana*).
Within these ninefold scriptures, one may further transform them through different phrases, different characters, different flavors, and different meanings."
Each [version] has different phrasing and speaks in a disordered manner. One recites and upholds the teaching oneself and claims that one causes others to uphold it.

Next, he answers the two questions below. Regarding "number," it refers to reaching eight persons; regarding "persons," it refers to bhikṣus and not bhikṣuṇīs. Alternatively, it may be that four persons are those capable of causing a schism. The text is divided into two parts.
First, it clarifies that if the number is deficient, the schism is not accomplished. The text states: "A single bhikṣu cannot cause a schism. The meaning is...
This means that a single nun and so forth could effect a schism; therefore, it must further be stated that it is "not by a nun and so forth.

Since it is not by a nun and so forth, the implication is that each side consists of only one person capable of causing a schism; therefore, it must further be stated that "neither side consisting of only one person can effect a schism.

It is not merely that one person is insufficient; even two or three on either side are likewise insufficient. Next, regarding the number required to cause a schism: both sides of the two assemblies must [each consist of...]
There are four people. Because they are companions who invalidate the presiding master, the minimum number is eight.
Next, the retributive fruit is questioned. The text is divided into three parts: first, the question and answer regarding the karmic retribution for causing a schism in the Saṃgha;

second, the question and answer regarding the karmic retribution for reconciling the Saṃgha—these two are as stated in the text; third, Upāli’s six [questions], which further analyze and distinguish all cases.
Regarding the meaning of whether one who causes a schism in the Saṃgha falls [into hell] or does not fall: herein, first the question is posed and then the answer is given.

Within the question, it is asked whether all those who cause a schism in the Saṃgha necessarily fall for one kalpa, or if there are also those who do not pass through a kalpa. Next, the answer has two parts: first, a general response stating that they do not necessarily complete a full kalpa;
second, a specific analysis of those who do pass through a kalpa without being lightened [of their offense]. Herein, based on factors such as the Dharma and non-Dharma, there are in total...
There are nine pairs. Within these nine pairs, one takes each entity as "not the Dharma" (*adharma*) and so forth, forming twelve propositions (*pada*) for each;
by refuting the "Dharma" and so forth in turn, one causes them to be extinguished. With twelve propositions for each of the nine pairs, they total one hundred and eight propositions.

These are formulated upon the entities as "not the Dharma" because they accord with the correct cessation of existence. However, within the turn of "the Dharma" and so forth, nothing further can be obtained.
12. If the substance of the *dharma* and so forth is uniform, yet one performs the breaking [of the Saṃgha] through non-*dharma* and so forth, this constitutes reconciling the Saṃgha;

therefore, it is not mentioned here. Furthermore, if the first phrase regarding the *dharma* and so forth were stated in reverse, its existence could be established, and there would have to be thirteen [categories].

Thus, the preceding text states: "One who dwells in the matter of breaking the Saṃgha dwells in eighteen dharmas. Moreover, there is no increase in the two texts; they cite the eighteen dharmas in reverse order.

To claim that what is established as existing [is otherwise] is to increase the four offenses after the Buddha; to say one has committed an offense when there is none, or that there is no offense when one has committed one;

to call light what is heavy, and heavy what is light—this is called "breaking the harmony of the Saṃgha. Following this principle, one should act accordingly; do not trouble yourself with further elaborations.
Furthermore, although these texts exist, one must not act [accordingly]. These cases simply rely on inverted explanations to establish existence, thereby arguing for the breaking of the Saṃgha.

The principle is not so. Now, one who causes a schism in the Saṃgha must necessarily possess that which is to be destroyed—the True Dharma—and possess that which acts as the destroyer. As for what the True Dharma is that is to be destroyed:
it may be granted that the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*) can be subverted by false teaching; however, it is not understood what constitutes the "Dharma" that acts as the destroyer.

Since there is no one capable of refuting this, I shall not labor further. Furthermore, as this text currently proceeds by taking "non-dharma" (*adharma*) as its basis, I shall now likewise provide a single comprehensive explanation based on "non-dharma" and so forth.
Within the pairings of the bonds, the first pairing is explained first. This first pairing consists of three positions and four propositions.

Within the first set of four propositions, the first three positions involve a subject who falls within a single eon, while the final position involves a subject who does not follow a single eon. The first proposition is: one with a perception of non-Dharma breaks [the bond] by speaking with a perception of non-Dharma.
The second proposition is: one with a perception of non-Dharma breaks [the bond] by speaking with a perception of Dharma. The third proposition is: one with a perception of Dharma breaks...

This refers to speaking with the perception that it is not the Dharma. The fourth phrase refers to speaking with the perception that it is the Dharma while intending to destroy the Dharma. First, I shall explain the initial phrase, which contains seven parts:
first, "if a bhikṣu" identifies the subject who is capable of destroying [the Saṃgha]; second, "arises" indicates the presence of cessation; third, the text states "what is not the Dharma."
This refers to the five types of formal acts (*dharmas*). Because one clings to these formal acts as being the true path of renunciation, it is said that "one firmly maintains the dharma.
Regarding this "dharma": it refers to the time when one is engaged in the act of schism; it clarifies that the wheel [of harmony] has been broken.

As for the phrase "knowing through the ear that it is not the dharma" (*adharma-saṃjñin*), it means that during the preparatory stage (*prayoga*), one knows through the ear that it is not the dharma, and thus speaks of it as "not the dharma."
Regarding those who profess [such views]: while ostensibly practicing transformation, they nevertheless discern right from wrong. How could the four types of false speech possess the Dharma?

Yet, by clinging to the five types of existence as having the Dharma, they claim it can accord with ultimate truth; thus they call it "the Dharma. Furthermore, clinging to the existence of phenomena, they claim these have the power to extinguish evil, calling them "Vinaya.

Desiring to win the faith of others, they falsely attribute these to the Buddha’s own words, calling them "the Buddha's Teaching. Fifth, there is a contradiction between mind and mouth. As for the mind...
To see something as wrong yet claim with one's mouth that it is right; because what is spoken by the mouth contradicts what is seen by the mind, this is called "divergent views" (異見).

To mentally tolerate something as being right or wrong yet claim with one's mouth that it is right; because what is spoken by the mouth contradicts what is tolerated by the mind, this is called "divergent tolerances" (異忍). These six constitute the practice of destroying [the true] matters.
By means of breaking the assembly and performing the *śalākā* (voting sticks) procedure, one may also directly clarify the point of attaining the ultimate state by presiding over the assembly.
Within this context, regarding the statement on the *ajñapti-karman* (formal act of motion), it is contained within the six phrases. As for the seventh, "binding [the offense] for one *kalpa*":

the second phrase refers to speaking with the perception of non-Dharma while having the perception of Dharma; because the preceding preparatory mind knew it was indeed Dharma, it is called "non-Dharma."

The perception is destroyed. As for the time of speaking, it is entirely not [based on] what is true; therefore, it is called "speaking with the perception of dharma. In this context, there are only six phrases of offense.
There is no "different view" (anyathādṛṣṭi) or "different acceptance" (anyathākṣānti). In relation to the preliminary mind, one should speak of "different view";

in relation to the mind at the time of subsequent speaking, it is termed "not different view. If one says "different view," it does not encompass "not different view. If one says "not different view," [it encompasses both].

The subsequent [passage] does not include the divergent views, because the preceding and succeeding minds differ. There is no offense in the text; the explanation of the text can be understood accordingly.

Next, the third phrase explains that the perception of "Dharma" (*dharmasaṃjñā*) destroys the perception of "non-Dharma. This is precisely because the preceding mind was deluded regarding conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*);

therefore, it is called "the destruction of the perception of Dharma. When the subsequent mind speaks, it knows this to be a phenomenon; therefore, it is called "speaking with the perception of non-Dharma. The text does not...
This differs from what preceded; therefore, it is said, "it is also thus. Question: Regarding these two phrases, "mutual" and "not," if one perceives them simultaneously, the offense should be minor.

Why then does one fall for an entire kalpa? Answer: Although one might calculate that mutual delusion should be perceived simultaneously, because the damage inflicted is excessive, it does not depend on the state of the mind [at that moment].
It is like the precept against sexual misconduct: even if the perception of the time is incorrect, the offense remains grave. If that is so, then if—

Regarding the restriction that excessive speech constitutes an offense against the objective realm (*ālambana*): one might argue that the fourth [category] should also incur a retribution of one *kalpa*. The answer is:

because the mind throughout the beginning and end of the fourth phrase is entirely [in error], and since there is no mutual understanding of what is non-existent, it does not fall into a full *kalpa*. By this principle, if one commits sexual misconduct while being deluded from beginning to end, and there is no mutual awareness of the act, it likewise is not ultimate [in its gravity].
Next, regarding the fourth phrase, which speaks of the "perception of phenomena" (*dharmasaṃjñā*) destroying the "perception of phenomena": it is precisely for this reason [that it is so designated].

The preceding mind was deluded regarding conditioned phenomena as being real; therefore, it is said that "the perception of dharmas is destroyed. The subsequent mind, at the time of speaking, is likewise deluded regarding them as being real;

therefore, it is said that "the perception of dharmas speaks. There are seven phrases in the text, and their interpretation is the same as before; however, this concerns verbal expression, which does not contradict the mental vision.

It is called "non-differentiated view" (*ananyathā-dṛṣṭi*). Furthermore, because it does not contradict what is settled in the mind, it is called "non-differentiated patience" (*ananyathā-kṣānti*). Since the emotional transgressions are light and gradual, one does not fall [into the hells] for a full kalpa.
Next, regarding the second set of four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), the text states: "The four propositions concerning doubt and non-doubt are likewise. This should logically not be [the case].
The first phrase is "non-doubt regarding the perception of the Dharma" (dharma-saṃjñā), which refutes non-doubt regarding what is not the Dharma.

The second phrase is "doubt regarding the perception of the Dharma," which refutes the perception of what is not the Dharma while discussing doubt regarding the Dharma. The third phrase is "doubt regarding the Dharma," which refutes non-doubt regarding what is not the Dharma while discussing the Dharma.
The fourth phrase is "doubt regarding the Dharma," which refutes doubt regarding the Dharma while discussing the Dharma. The composition and explanation of these characteristics are as before.
There is no difference; it likewise falls under the first three propositions, while the fourth proposition does not fall [under them].

Next, the third set of four propositions is formulated. The text states: "The four propositions regarding the perception of what is non-Dharma and doubt are also like this. The ancient masters explain:

"One places doubt upon the perception of what is non-Dharma, and one places non-doubt upon the perception of what is Dharma. Thus, in the first proposition, the doubt regarding what is non-Dharma is refuted."

The first case concerns speaking with doubt regarding what is not the Dharma (*adharma*). Because one doubts both [the Dharma and the non-Dharma] and lacks the simultaneous perception that it is not the Dharma, one does not fall for a single *kalpa*.
The second case differs in that one speaks while doubting what is not the Dharma but not doubting the destruction of the Dharma.

Since one harbors doubt toward what is not the Dharma yet lacks the simultaneous perception that it is not the Dharma, the mental transgression is slight and gradual; thus, one does not fall for a single *kalpa*. The third case involves not doubting the Dharma but destroying doubt regarding what is not the Dharma.

It is said that they are distinct. These also do not fall into a single *kalpa*. Regarding the fourth phrase, the lack of doubt concerning the Dharma and the lack of doubt concerning the destruction of the Dharma are said to be distinct.
Therefore, the text states: "The four phrases regarding the thought of non-Dharma and doubt are likewise. Question:
This third set of four phrases does not collectively fall into a single *kalpa*, which differs from the two preceding sets of four phrases. For what reason does the text say "likewise"?

This is so. In principle, it should be the same as the previous two positions regarding falling and not falling; only then would it accord with the phrasing in the text, which also speaks in this way.

Because it does not accord with the text, it must be further explained. Since doubt applies to both locations and is not restricted to one side, while the doubt was previously placed upon the "Dharma" (dharma) in the second tetralemma, it must now be placed upon the "non-Dharma" (adharma) in the third tetralemma. The first phrase is non-...
Regarding the Dharma, there is no doubt as to its refutation; regarding what is not the Dharma, there is no doubt as to its exposition. The second phrase concerns what is not the Dharma:

there is no doubt as to its refutation, yet there is doubt as to its exposition. The third phrase concerns what is not the Dharma: there is doubt as to its refutation, yet there is no doubt as to its exposition. The fourth phrase concerns what is not the Dharma: there is doubt as to its refutation.

This is the exposition on doubt regarding what is not the Dharma (*adharma*). Thus the text says: "The four permutations regarding the perception of what is not the Dharma and doubt are also like this.

That is to say, the four permutations are formed by contrasting the perception of what is not the Dharma with doubt regarding what is not the Dharma. In this context, that which is not doubted is precisely the perception. If one explains it in this way...

The first three phrases follow [the previous pattern], while the fourth phrase does not fall [into that category]; therefore, it is said, "it is also thus. Regarding these three positions and four phrases, when explained in contrast:
the initial phrase of each is the same, while the three subsequent phrases of each differ. Furthermore, among those three subsequent sets, the first two have the same three subsequent phrases.
The mind takes non-dharmas as its object; in this respect, they are entirely the same. Because there is no doubt regarding the perception (*saṃjñā*), they are called "different yet one in essence.

However, the three [perceptions] below this take dharmas as their objects and are all different: the former is the perception of dharma, while the latter is the doubt regarding dharma. In the subsequent stage, the objects of the three below are exclusively non-dharmas.
On one side it is identical to the previous two positions because there is no doubt; on the other side it is entirely different from all other positions because doubt arises.
This concludes the first pair of twelve propositions. It should be understood that the following eight pairs are the same as above. The section on the method of schism in the Sangha is now concluded.
● Next is the Dharma for Settling Disputes (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*). When two parties are at odds and both sides are in conflict, it is called a "dispute" (*adhikaraṇa*).
There are four types of disputes, which differ in their arguments; all four are eliminated by means of seven medicinal remedies, and this is termed "settling disputes.

Because the extensive exposition of these methods for settling is collected in one place, it is called a *khandhaka* (or *grantha*). The text is divided into three parts. The first concerns the seven *vinayas* that are capable of removing [disputes].
The Medicine. Second, at that time, the World-Honored One [proceeds] below to clarify the illnesses to be eliminated by the four types of disputes.

Since both medicine and illness exist, if they were not clarified in relation to one another, then the medicine would lack the efficacy to eradicate [the illness], and the illness would lack the sense of being cured.
Therefore, third, from "If a single bhikṣu... onwards, it extensively clarifies the ritual procedure for the correspondence between medicine and illness. Among these three [sections]:
First, the medicine that can eliminate [the afflictions] will be clarified. To explain this meaning, it is analyzed through three gates: first, the explanation of the name;
second, the determination of its essence; and third, the various classifications.

Regarding the explanation of the names: first, the individual names of the seven types, such as "in the presence of" (*sammukha*), shall be explained; next, the general term *vinaya* shall be interpreted.

Now, within the explanation of the individual name "in the presence of," there are five kinds and three kinds. As for the five kinds, they are: the Dharma, the *vinaya*, the person, the Saṃgha, and the boundary (*sīmā*).
As for the three kinds, they are: the Dharma, the *vinaya*, and the person. If one wishes to explain the collective meaning of these five and three categories, one should...

It is said that the three and the five methods for settling disputes are, in essence, all "present" (pratyutpanna) and do not belong to the past or future; thus, they are collectively termed "manifest before one" (pratyakṣa).

To explain them individually: that which possesses a fixed rule is called *dharma*; because it can pacify disputes, it is called *vinaya*. Those who initiate disputes are called "persons" (*pudgala*), while those who uphold the Dharma are the "Saṃgha.
The Saṃgha, relying on its place of assembly, encompasses the boundaries (*sīmā*). Since three [categories] are subsumed within the five, there is no need for a separate explanation.

[The section on] *Amūḍha* (Not Insane). Next, regarding *Smṛti* (Recollection): when a person of pure conduct is slandered and a foul reputation spreads abroad, and they are accused by others amidst further disputes, the assembly knows that this person is actually pure.
To establish that they have not committed an offense, a formal act (*karmavācanā*) is performed; because their purity is known through recollection, it is called *smṛti*.
Next, regarding *Amūḍha*: although one may have committed an offense due to a mental affliction, if they are now cured and do not commit it again, yet [others] suddenly raise the matter...

Regarding past transgressions, disputes arise because [the offender] fears being accused. The Saṃgha, knowing that this person has come for the purpose of the *karmavācanā* and does not commit an offense, performs the *karmavācanā* to certify their purity.
Because they have come for the purpose of the "not-insane" (*amūḷha*) procedure and do not commit an offense, it is called "not-insane. Next, regarding "confession by oneself":

originally, the arising of disputes is due to clinging to whether an offense is light or heavy and failing to understand the characteristics of the offense, which leads to further confusion. Now, having obtained the opportunity for self-accusation, one recognizes the reality of the offense.
Since the root [of the dispute] has been understood, the contention is eliminated; therefore, it is called "one's own statement" (*pratijñā*). Next is "the majority decision" (*yadbhūyasikīya*):

originally, this arose from a debate over doctrine where the principles were being contested. When a particular individual was present before the assembly, the dispute could not be settled. Thus, a regulation was established requiring everyone to assemble, to deliberate with a sincere mind, and to cast voting sticks (*śalākā*).

By means of the sticks, the wrong is eliminated; since the majority expresses their speech through the sticks, it is called "the majority decision. Next is "the place of offense" (*tassapāpiyasikīya*): this...
When a person commits an offense and is brought forward by another, they may act with duplicity—agreeing at first only to contradict later—thereby giving rise to disputes.

The Saṃgha applies its formal procedures (*karmavācanā*) to carefully examine their previous statements and reprimand them for the point of transgression, imposing a heavy penalty; hence it is called "the place of the offense" (*āpattisthāna*). Next, regarding "covering like grass" (*tṛṇaprastāraka*):

when the Saṃgha’s evaluation of an offense is discordant and the dispute becomes tumultuous, and since the parties have already cleared themselves of mutual blame, the matter is difficult to investigate thoroughly. Therefore, the Sage permitted this [method].
Listen. Without mentioning names or categories, one simply offers an apology, like covering mud with grass; therefore, it is called "grass-covering the ground" (*tṛṇapraticchādana*).
These seven types [of settling disputes] encompass the teachings to eliminate transgressions; where there is no longer any contention, it is termed *vinaya*.
Next, to distinguish the essence: one must presently identify the essence through five aspects. There are two different sections for explaining these five essences:

first, the formal determination of the essence; second, the clarification of existence and non-existence. Regarding the first section, "the factors" refers to establishing the settled points of dispute based upon the sacred teachings.

This is not a principle of harmonious progress. Therefore, the text says: "One should speak well, teach with words that are in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and as taught by the Buddha.
It further asks: "What is meant by 'the Dharma being present before one'?

It refers to upholding the Dharma that extinguishes disputes—that is, upholding the methods capable of resolving contentious matters. As for the term "Vinaya," it refers to the principles of resolution derived from the Noble Teachings. [It] exhorts...
One should accept the patience that brings an end to disputes. Therefore, the text says: "This is the Dharma, this is the Vinaya, this is the teaching of the Buddha;
you should accept this as such. It further asks: "What is the manifestation of the Vinaya?

This refers to the Vinaya that is upheld to settle disputes—that is, the principle of being able to pacify and endure [the conflict]. As for the term "person," it refers to those who initiate the dispute as well as those who...
Regarding "extinction" (*nirodha*): it refers to face-to-face questioning and answering; this is what is called a "person" (*pudgala*). Therefore, the scriptural text says:

"If one bhikṣu is in the presence of another bhikṣu. Furthermore, it asks: "What is meant by 'a person being present'? The meaning is that the subject and the object are reversed; this means that the capacity [to act] and the content [of the action] are designated as the "person.

If one designates the "person" from the perspective of the objective [action], it refers specifically to one who initiates a dispute. Alternatively, it may be understood according to the subjective [capacity].
"Renowned person" refers to one who has received the confession. "Saṃgha" refers to the time when disputes are being settled;

it means that all members assemble in harmony to perform the formal legal acts (*dharmakarma*), thereby deciding what is right and wrong. Therefore, the text asks: "What is meant by 'the Saṃgha being present'?

It means that those who should have come together for the *karmavācanā* (formal motion) have assembled in one place, and as for those who should be censured, they are not censured in their presence. This is what is meant.
Regarding the *dhātu* (boundary): it refers to the communal assembly and distribution within the *saṃgha*, that is, the locus upon which the *saṃgha* relies for its formal acts (*karmavācanā*).
Therefore, the text asks: "What is the manifestation of the boundary? It is that which establishes restrictions through *karma* within the boundary.

The preceding analysis has followed the order of exposition; however, according to the order of practice, one should say: "The *dharma* and *vinaya* of the *saṃgha* regarding the boundary. This refers to...
The five types [of legal acts] reveal their essential nature; when one discusses their three essential bodies, they do not depart from these five.

However, among the three [remaining types], it should be known that the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) is absent, and for this reason they are not considered the Saṃgha. Furthermore, they do not require a formal boundary (*sīmā*). Nevertheless, regarding the other three, the method follows the rules of speech (*vākya-dharma*), and the Vinaya is likewise.

Because the "person" (*pudgala*) in these cases encompasses both the agent and the object, they differ from the [first] five. Among the five, however, the person is solely the object of the action, whereas the method encompasses both speech and the ritual act.

The same applies to the *karmavācanā* and the *vinaya*. Next, regarding the explanation of existence and non-existence, we shall again examine whether the essential natures (*svabhāva*) of these five exist or not.

The ancient masters have many interpretations. One explanation states: "The other four possess an essential nature, whereas the *vinaya* lacks an essential nature; for the *vinaya* is cessation (*nirodha*)."

Since cessation (nirodha) is non-existent, how could it possess a substantial entity (bhāva)? Furthermore, another interpretation holds that although there are five names, there are only four entities:
namely, the individual (pudgala), the Saṃgha, and the two categories of dharma and vinaya. These three have distinct names and entities; however, for dharma and vinaya, there is no separate entity.

Rather, based on their functional utility, the universal application [of rules] is termed *dharmakaraṇīya* (the performance of dharma), and the universal application [of methods] for settling disputes is termed *vinayakaraṇīya* (the performance of vinaya). Moreover, another interpretation holds that vinaya has no separate entity, as its function is based upon [dharma].
The four dharmas constitute its essence. These [other] interpretations are all unreasonable. If this *vinaya* truly had no essence, that point might be granted;

however, since this *vinaya* actually possesses a distinct essence, it is known that [those interpretations] are not so. That is to say, the fact that one is exhorted to accept [the dharma] and to cease disputes through the dharma and other means constitutes its very essence.
Therefore, the text asks: "What is the presence of *vinaya*? It refers to the *vinaya* that is upheld...
The *Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya* states that this refers to the extinction of disputes. Furthermore, the twenty-third fascicle of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* asks:

"What is meant by 'the presence of the Vinaya' (*vinayapratyakṣa*)? By what dharma, by what discipline (*vinaya*), and by what teaching of the Buddha should a dispute be extinguished so that it is indeed extinguished?
This is called the presence of the Vinaya. Question: If there is a dharma at a time when the Vinaya does not yet exist, and when there is a Vinaya it is already no longer a [mere] dharma, then...
They do not arise simultaneously. How, then, can it be said that five are present? Answer: Because they all exist in the present through their continuity, it is said that five are present.

Furthermore, another interpretation is that for the sake of confronting those who initiate disputes, each one is made manifest; therefore, it is said that five are present. Question: What is the purpose of these five being present?

It also applies to the Saṃgha. Why is it that the name "Saṃgha" is used for one [type] but not for the other? Answer: Because the former is capable of presiding over legal procedures (*dharmakarma*), while the latter is subject to the decisions of others;
since these differ, their designations are also distinct. Question: Among the three [types of persons], the object of action also applies to the Saṃgha.

Why, then, is the name also applied to the person and not established in reference to the Saṃgha? Answer: If categorized according to number, the designation "Saṃgha" should be established. However, because [the person] does not preside over [the procedure], [it is designated as a person].

The Dharma dictates that such a person should be taken into custody. Furthermore, they are granted the title of "monk" (saṃgha), yet there is fear that this may lead to the indiscriminate exercise of legal authority.

For this reason, the deluded monks speak of the title being received by the person. Next, regarding "recollection": although Dharmatāpa was truly pure, he was slandered by others. Because the slander had a basis, the accusers clung to that basis to raise the charge.

Those who could raise the charge clung to the basis, fearing it might be deemed a crime of slander; those who could be raised as charges relied on their own purity, fearing the Saṃgha would treat them indiscriminately. It was for this reason [that the rule was established].

Holding to their own sentiments, they consequently give rise to contention. Now, regarding those who practice *smṛti* (recollection): the proponent of the recollection asserts that the basis for the accusation is not false;
the one being subjected to the recollection is truly pure. Furthermore, in the case where the Saṃgha practices mutual recollection, there is no disagreement between the two parties:

the one who brings forth the recollection holds that the root of the charge is not false, and the one being subjected to the recollection is truly pure. Moreover, "those who may be subject to recollection" refers to—
