Regarding the object of this gift, it may be anyone from a bhikṣu down to a śrāmaṇerī. If one follows this text for the recollection, it is not otherwise; rather, one should act according to where one knows the food is to be consumed."

Recite this once. Whether eating from the regular monastic provisions, or constantly begging for alms, or accepting an invitation, or eating on one's own, if there is an intention to attend two invitations, one must relinquish the prior invitation to another person before going to the latter; this is the current method for such substitution.
Only then will one be free from fault. If one is entirely unaware of where food is being provided, one should simply perform a general recollection, saying:

"Today I recollect that I have not turned my back on the invitation to eat. Third, one recollects the precepts one has received oneself, noting the time, day, and number of years—specifically the year, month, and shadow-time (the hour)—and stating whether the summer retreat has been entered or not according to its duration.
Fourth, one recollects the robes and bowl, as well as one's requisites for sustenance.
"Are they complete? If there is a deficiency in the robes or bowl, mention whichever is lacking. For other items that are incomplete, one should intend to provide them at the proper time.
If there is no deficiency, simply state: "The three robes and bowl are complete. Regarding the remaining extra robes, medicine, and bowls, one should know whether they have been mentioned or not;
if they exist, one should intend to mention them at the proper time. If they do not exist, one should say: "There are no extra robes, etc. This is the fifth determination.

Since the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is shared with the community, it is said that mindfulness (*smṛti*) does not follow the communal meal. Regarding the sixth mindfulness—whether one knows if there is illness—if there is illness, one should say, "I am ill;
I shall treat it. If there is no illness, one should say, "I am not ill. One should practice the Path in reliance upon the community.

At that time, people did not understand this, so the reciter chanted it universally; it was not a question, but rather an instruction to state the two mindfullnesses three times. All else is as before.
One explanation is as follows: If one merely recollects and knows the first recitation (*ekavācika*), that is sufficient. This second recollection involves relinquishing the food to another;
for oneself, it does not constitute a formal act (*karmavācanā*) unless it is performed three times. Because of this attachment, the single recitation and the triple recitation differ.

Next, the five sections of text clarify what should and should not be done. Within this, there are three parts. First, the section on the *karmavācanā* (formal act) regarding the management of the monks’ quarters;
the details of this passage are clear. Second, from the phrase "At that time, the bhikṣus... onwards, it clarifies the various items required for the quarters.

For elderly or infirm bhikṣus who are unable to go out to listen to the teachings, [the text explains] how to arrange urinals and chamberpots within the quarters so that they do not cause inconvenience.
The text: Regarding the practice of picking up lice and discarding them according to the Dharma, it is fully explained as set forth in the text.

In the twenty-sixth fascicle of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, when the bhikṣus picked up lice and returned them to their clothes after having removed them from the rooms, the Buddha said, "Pick them up and place them outside the rooms.

When the bhikṣus, during the rainy season, placed them in water, the Buddha said, "One should pick them up and place them inside worn-out rags, breathing upon them with a mind of compassion. Third: At that time, the World-Honored One... [as follows].
It clarifies that Anāthapiṇḍada offered his garden as a gift, as well as various miscellaneous points regarding what is appropriate and inappropriate.

Within the text, it is permitted to construct a fire-hearth. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* (26) states: "Not knowing with what materials to make it, the Buddha said: 'I permit the use of copper, iron, clay, or stone to make it.
It is permitted for the Saṃgha, the four quarters of the Saṃgha, or individuals to possess one. Furthermore, it is permitted to construct a large hearth on the ground."
Next are the six sections of text, which clarify what constitutes a valid gift and what does not. Within this section, there are two parts: first, citing the circumstances to address the Buddha;

second, from "At that time, the World-Honored One" onwards, distinguishing and determining what is valid and what is not. The preceding text concerns only a lay devotee of faithful heart who built a dwelling and offered it to the Sangha.
The person who receives [the gift] must be pure. If that person is pure, there is no fault for which they may be censured; if one then transfers it to give [to another], this is called "unlawful.
If the person is impure, there is a fault for which they may be censured; if one then transfers it further to give [to another], this is not called "unlawful."

For this reason, the World-Honored One sent [the messenger] again to investigate and inquire. Only after knowing whether [the recipient] was pure or impure could he determine whether [the act] was permissible or not. This response is like that of a human being; one must examine their purity or impurity.
In the *Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya*, regarding the single rule concerning non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), it is established that this is contrary to the Dharma.

The subsequent determination of the text has two parts: first, the establishment of the topical outline (*śarīra*); second, the explanation according to the outline. Within the explanation, there are three sections each: namely, the citation, the explanation, and the conclusion. This is not [the case for other rules].
In the *Dharmaviniścaya*, there are five categories: first, a single person; second, many people; third, the Saṃgha; fourth, those of one's own school;

and fifth, those of other schools. If, according to the text, one gives to a single person and then transfers that gift to many people and so forth, there are four permutations for each of the [ten] heads, totaling twenty permutations. If explained according to the meaning, after giving to a single person, subsequently...
Giving to one person and so forth constitutes five phrases. In this manner, by mutual combination, twenty-five phrases are formed. As stated in the middle [section], it is the same for the following.

Next, the seventh [section] clarifies what should and should not be done regarding the property of the Saṃgha. There are three parts in this text: first, raising an objection and reporting it to the Buddha; second, the World-Honored One...
The Venerable One states here below that, in general, monastic property should not be divided, should not be taken into personal possession, and should not be bought or sold;

furthermore, it does not belong to the Sangha as a collective, nor can it be divided by one individual from among many. To take it into personal possession or to buy or sell it constitutes the offense of *sthūlātyaya*. Question:

With reference to what meaning is this *sthūlātyaya* established? If it is said that this refers to the original intention of employing such a method to obstruct the Sangha’s enjoyment [of the property], then it is for this reason that the offense is established.

Regarding *sthūlātyaya*: if one originally intends to steal or cause damage, and the value reaches the required amount for a grave offense (*guru-apatti*), it is not appropriate to incur only *sthūlātyaya*.

If one adheres to this literal wording—that stealing constitutes *sthūlātyaya*—it would contradict the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, chapter twenty-two, where the Buddha stated that it is improper to give monastic fruit to a layperson;
one who commits such an act incurs *duṣkṛta*. How could one who steals monastic property to give to another receive only a *duṣkṛta* offense? Therefore, we know [the original text’s meaning].
Furthermore, one incurs the fault of an improper transgression. Additionally, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Sengqi lü), fascicle 27, states: The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, the fields belonging to the Saṃgha must not be lent to others, nor may they be used privately.
Even if the entire Saṃgha is assembled, they must still not be lent, sold, or used privately. If the assembled Saṃgha lends them or sells them..."
If I were to use it myself, I would incur a *vinaya*-offense (*viniya-āpatti*). This also establishes that one must not steal or damage [an object] in an improper place.

In that text, regarding the theft of monastic property (*saṃghika-vastu*), the offense is formally established as a *pārājika*. Thirdly, below the section on "What are the four? there is a further detailed analysis of the characteristics of what should and should not be [stolen].
This can be understood from the text.

Next, the eighth [section] clarifies whether or not one should be appointed as a superintendent of works (*karmadāna*). This section is divided into two parts: first, the granting of a room to the superintendent;

second, from "there are five qualities" onwards, which concerns whether one is suitable based on their virtues. Regarding the former, if construction is carried out upon monastic land, it does not follow...
Regarding the monastic rule (*saṃghadharma*): one should be told to return the land; there is no further justification for it, as one has taken the *saṃgha*'s land into one's own possession.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "When a bhikṣu builds a house on *saṃgha* land, the elder (*sthavira*) arrives and assigns rooms in sequence.

This bhikṣu does not inform the other bhikṣus and reports the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha says: 'This is a *duṣkṛta* offense. If it is not done in this manner, one should take grass and wood and go elsewhere to build."
This text states that the maximum duration for a person managing construction to reside in a dwelling is three months (Vinaya-vibhaṅga, Pañcavargika, Chapter 25).

While the manager was truly resentful, saying, "I have worked hard at this management, yet instead of obtaining a peaceful residence [for myself], [this is what happens]," he informed the Buddha of this matter.
The Buddha said, "I permit the manager to dwell as long as he wishes. The bhikṣus then granted him [the right to stay] indefinitely. They informed the Buddha of this, and the Buddha—
It is said that one should restore their merit. As for the quantity, it may be as much as possible; permission is granted to remain for up to twelve years.

One should perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation) to grant it. Next, regarding the text on the requirements of virtue, there are two parts. First, clarifying those who should and should not be appointed. Below the section on "five dharmas," its benefits and harms are clarified.
Those who fully possess the five virtues should be appointed. In total, there are eleven matters: first, distributing rice gruel; second, dividing small portions.
1. Food; 2. *khādaniya* (hard food); 3. *khādanīya* (soft food); 4. Lodgings; 5. Bathing robes; 6. Dividing robes; 7. Robes to be taken; 8.
Robes to be given; 9. Appointing a monk as a messenger; 10. Appointing a *śrāmaṇera* as a messenger. Among these, this refers to the appointment based on possessing the requisite qualities.

Regarding the person responsible for distributing the upper robes, a selection is made from among those who distribute the upper robes. According to this *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, there are formal ritual procedures (*karmavācanā*) for such appointments.
Furthermore, that same text, at section thirty-four, states: "In the monastery, there is no bhikṣu who knows the proper time to announce it;
there is no one to strike the ghaṇṭā, nor anyone to sweep, supervise, or plaster the lecture hall and the dining area; and there is no one to arrange the beds in succession."
[The monks] sat down. There was no one to purify the fruits and vegetables. "No one" refers to when, during a meal, although water is being served, people engage in distracted chatter;
or when there is no one to snap their fingers [to signal silence]. They reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said: "A *naivāsika* (resident) should be established.

One who possesses five qualities should be appointed through a formal motion (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*): namely, one who does not follow favoritism, hatred, fear, or delusion, and who knows what is pure and what is impure. Thus, he was appointed by a formal motion.
Furthermore, the preceding text states: "Wherever there are virtuous and eminent monks, a bhikṣu should not be made to serve as their attendant.
Next, regarding "loss and gain," this explains the meaning of the aforementioned requirement to possess virtue. The section on the rules for dwellings is hereby concluded.
● Next, the *Kṣudraka-vastu* (Miscellaneous Section) is explained. The conditions for supporting the Path are immeasurable; it is impossible to list each one by name according to its specific matter.
Therefore, they are collected together and termed "Miscellaneous" (*kṣudraka*). Because various conditions are gathered extensively and reside in a single location, it is called a *vastu* (section).
Within this, there are two parts: first, a broad demonstration of what is appropriate and inappropriate among the various miscellaneous matters; second, at that time, the World-Honored One...

The Venerable One, while at Kauśāmbī, separately clarifies the rules for the observance of the precepts for both the Great and Small Vehicles. In the preceding text, the methods of cultivation were presented without a specific sequential order;
now, according to the matters clarified therein, they are divided into five parts. First, the rules concerning the alms-bowl (*pātra*).
Second, from "At that time, the bhikṣus... onwards, various requisites are explained. Third, from "At that time, the World-Honored One was in Rājagṛha... onwards, [the rules] are restated.
[Section] on the Alms Bowl. Fourth: At that time, the World-Honored One was in Rājagṛha; the following clarifies the bowl as it is not [permitted].
Fifth: At that time, the World-Honored One... [the following] clarifies various matters. Regarding the first passage: a *kāla-pātra* is a black-colored bowl;
a *śara-pātra* is a red-colored bowl. Regarding the second passage: one should not trim the nails so that they are shaped like a half-moon, nor...
The hair on the head should be very short, like a single grain of barley, and should be trimmed; it does not mean that one may leave it at the length of a single grain of barley.

When a bhikṣu does not know how long his hair has grown and should shave it, the Buddha said: "The maximum length is two finger-breadths. If one shaves once every two months, this is the period for the maximum length.
The *Mātṛkā Sūtra*, fascicle three, states: "The reason for shaving the hair is to eliminate the mind of arrogance and self-reliance."
Therefore, if the hair is long, one must not use scissors to trim it; rather, one should remove it using a razor.

The third section consists of five parts: first, the prohibition against manifesting supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) at will; second, the account of how various non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) requested the Buddha’s supernormal power after he established a regulation;
third, the account of the lay devotees (*dānapati*) among the non-Buddhists in the city of Rājagṛha.
[They] gave rise to faith and were subdued. Fourth, at that time, the various non-Buddhists [below] gathered their followers extensively; the King and the local ruler [also joined].

Fifth, at that time, the World-Honored One looked toward the east [below], extensively manifesting supernatural transformations. This was established as a rule similar to the previous one. Regarding the first passage, Maudgalyāyana said:
"I have never, while still a layperson, previously manifested supernatural powers. This means he had never manifested them for his own sake before. If...
One should manifest [a form] whenever it is necessary for the benefit of others; thus, if upholding the precepts regarding householders is beneficial, one should manifest accordingly.

The *Pinjue gongde lun* states: "Pindolabharadvāja was greatly apprehensive regarding the Buddha's teachings. To subdue the heterodox teachers—since the six masters all possessed supernatural powers—he exerted himself with unwavering devotion and then manifested his own supernatural power to take up a bowl.
This does not mention expulsion (*pravāsanā*); other texts state that he was indeed expelled and was not permitted to enter parinirvāṇa.
[The section on] the bowl. Residing in Jambudvīpa has already been explained above. The next four textual passages are clear in their meaning.
Regarding the fourth textual passage, the rules for the bowl: when washing the bowl, one should not wash it while standing. If the grease does not come off, one should use soap powder (*śāṭhī*).
Whether it be salt-earth, ash, cow dung, or mud, as well as other methods for protecting livestock and so forth, they are fully detailed in the text.
The fifth section extensively explains miscellaneous methods; the ritual for preparing the water-strainer (*parisrāvaṇa*) is as described in the text, including its shape and dimensions.
If one uses a water-strainer bottle and fears that fine insects will escape, it is permitted to place a sand-sack inside. One must not discard the sand and insects onto dry land;
they should be returned to the water. If traveling without a water-sack for even half a yojana, one should strain the water using a corner of the *saṃghāṭī*.
The twenty-sixth [section] of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*: There were two bhikṣus traveling together on a road who did not have water-strainers.
Becoming thirsty and wishing to drink water, they saw that there were insects in it. One bhikṣu drank; the other bhikṣu did not drink and died.

The bhikṣu who had drunk the water went to the place where the Buddha was and reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said, "That bhikṣu possessed a sense of shame and was thus able to maintain [the precept]."
One dies [in violation] of the precepts. From now on, traveling without a water-strainer is not permitted. One who violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.

The rest is explained as here. *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*, fascicle six: Without a water-strainer, one must not travel a long distance—except when river water is clear, except when spring water is pure, and except within half a *yojana*.
If one travels within half a *yojana*, provided that monasteries are situated in close succession, there is no offense even if one does not carry a strainer.

Next, lighting the lamp is as described in the text. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, there are thirty-five [rules]. When extinguishing a lamp within a meditation hall, one must not extinguish it in ninety ways;
rather, one should say, "Venerable sirs, I wish to extinguish the lamp," and then cover it with one's hand while proclaiming, "The lamp is about to be extinguished."

When a lamp is about to go out, one must not attempt to extinguish it by blowing with the mouth, fanning it with the hand, or fanning it with a cloth. One should rather [use] a leather fan; if the wick is scorched, there is an offense of *duṣkṛta*.
When lighting it, one must not exceed ninety [blows]. When entering the room to light the lamps, one should announce: "Venerable sirs, the lamps are about to be lit."
When Dīpaṃkara was about to enter [the order], he was not permitted to do so because his discourse as an outsider was intermingled with the Buddha’s sūtras. The Buddha said:

"I permit you to recite and study the Buddha’s sūtras according to the local customs, dialects, and understandings of the country. (The *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, 26th Khandhaka). There were two brothers who were brahmins;
they had studied the *Chāndas* scriptures and later left the household life to join the True Dharma. They heard that the various bhikṣus were reciting the sūtras incorrectly.

They reproached them, saying: "Venerable sirs, you have been ordained for a long time, yet you do not understand the speech of men and women—whether it be a single word or many words, present or past expressions, future expressions, long or short vowels, or light or heavy accents—and yet you recite the Buddha’s scriptures in such a manner."

The bhikṣus heard this and felt ashamed. Two bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, who said: "I permit you to recite and read according to the local dialects of the country, provided that you do not deviate from or lose the Buddha’s intended meaning.
It is not permitted to render the Buddha’s words into the language of secular texts. One who violates this commits a sthūlātyaya offense."
Next are the various miscellaneous practices, as fully explained in the texts.
Next, regarding Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, they were permitted by the Buddha to build stūpas for their parinirvāṇa;

however, as the Buddha’s two most excellent disciples could not bear to see the Buddha [pass away], they entered parinirvāṇa before him, both having attained it earlier. Thus, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 191, explains "the worthy ones" (*bhadanta*).
It was previously stated: "By the nature of things (dharmatā). This means that such is the nature of phenomena; it is immutable and cannot be questioned as to why it is so.
This demonstrates that for all Buddhas and their two noble disciples, it is the natural law that they must first enter parinirvāṇa; this principle is without exception.

There is an analogy: just as a Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin) who wishes to follow the Dharma must have his brave generals lead the way before he reaches a territory, so too does the Dharma of the One of Ten Powers (daśabala) precede the Wheel-Turning King’s Dharma until the realm of the Nirvana without remainder (anupadhiśeṣa-dhātu) is reached.
It was also permitted for the disciples of the brave generals of the vanguard to lead the way according to the Dharma. (Section 26 of the Five-Part Vinaya).

The Buddha said there are four kinds of persons for whom a stūpa should be erected: noble disciples (*ārya-śrāvaka*), pratyekabuddhas, wheel-turning sage kings (*cakravartin*), and ordinary bhikṣus who possess virtue and renown.
In the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, it is likewise permitted to erect a stūpa; that text is in section 27.
It is said: If there is a monk of virtue and renown who is a Vinaya-holder, a Dharma-preacher, or a steward, one should say to that elder:
"This person maintains the precepts with excellence and has made many offerings to the Saṃgha; he has labored in his administrative duties and should be granted land for the construction of a stūpa.
Once these words have been spoken, one should build a stūpa for him. It should be made as a stūpa for a Śrāvaka; one must not see the stūpa first and the World-Honored One afterwards. One should...
Now, one should first see the World-Honored One and afterwards see the stūpa. It must not be located where many people travel; it should be in a secluded place.
It must not be in the walking path (*caṅkrama*) of the bhikṣus. If one erects a stūpa for a śrāvaka in a place where many people travel, it constitutes a *vinayātikrama* offense.

Question: For what reason is the construction of stūpas permitted? Answer: There are three reasons: first, to manifest the excellence of the person [who attained realization]; second, to inspire faith in others.

Third is for repaying kindness. Again, he asked, "I do not yet know what this term 'tā' (塔) signifies. [The Master] explained: "Tā is a Sanskrit sound (*stūpa*). Those who transmit it have not been precise;
some call it *tā*, some *tāpó* (塔婆), some *yōupó* (鍮婆), and some *dǒupó* (兜婆). Some even privately alter it as *sīyōu* (私鍮) to deceive others, or as *sǒudǒupō* (藪斗波).
However, the correct Sanskrit pronunciation is *sùdǔbō* (窣堵波), which here is translated as 'Exalted and Victorious' (*kūṭāgāra*). This refers to the *fútú* (浮圖). Regarding its offerings:

Regarding the maintenance of the stūpa: the food for the bhikṣus and others is as described in the text. Next, regarding the construction of a Buddha-stūpa: it was built because of [the Buddha’s] hair; this is a present-day stūpa.

Regarding the offerings to the stūpa and the food for the stūpa, these should be consumed by the laborers. Next, it clarifies that the merit of constructing a stūpa is profound, as well as the opening of a bathhouse.

Next is the *pātra-nyāsa* (the ritual of overturning the bowl). This section contains two parts: first, the performance of the rite; second, its dissolution. Within the performance, there are four sub-sections. First, instructing the recipient to practice the act of slander.
Second, at that time, Upāli could not be held accountable. Third, from "informing the bhikṣus" onwards, it clearly explains the performance of the rite.
Within this [third part], there are three sections: first, regarding the five dharmas, it says "returning one's own robe"; second, regarding the ten dharmas, it says "returning."
Regarding the offense: third, one should thus perform the formal rite of lowering [the bowl]; fourth, one causes a messenger to announce it according to the text (as in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* 31).
The lay follower Dharmapriya, because he understood the meaning, questioned the bhikṣus regarding those points whose meaning he did not understand;

they treated him with contempt. The Buddha said: "Perform for him the *pātra-nyubja* (turning-over of the bowl) through a *jñapti-caturtha-karman*. The Buddha sent a bhikṣu to inquire about the meaning of salt. No.
Having understood his arrogance, [the Buddha] asked another bhikṣu who was deeply learned in names and meanings. The Buddha said, "This one is an ordinary person;

within my Dharma, he has not yet attained the flavor of the Dharma. He then said, "The previous bhikṣu is an arhat, yet you were conceited and failed to distinguish between the true and the false, performing what is unbeneficial for a long night regarding this Dharma.
Having heard the Buddha’s words in advance, he repented and begged for release from his offense.

The Buddha stated that one is released by means of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations). Next, he permitted the dispatching of fire for cremation. Next was the *karman* for the staff and the water-bag.
In other Vinayas, there is likewise no formula for requesting [permission].
Next follows the analysis of the three stages of resolving through silence and harmonization: first, clarifying the meaning of silence; second, following the text.

Explanation. Regarding the third point, determining whether [the assembly] has achieved its purpose: first, to clarify the underlying intent. In general, when undertaking communal dharmas, the minds of all must be in accord;
one must alternately examine right and wrong and carefully discern gain and loss. Now that a discrepancy has been observed, it is logically necessary to reprimand those [at fault].

However, when wishing to reprimand, one must first advance oneself [in virtue]. If one’s words do not reflect upon things and one lacks virtuous companions later on, then even if one sees what is wrong, one should simply...
One should remain silent and patient; this is why the text says so. Śāriputra saw the community of monks performing an illegal *karmavācanā*, yet no one agreed with him.
He wished to remain indifferent and let it proceed, but the Buddha said, "I permit you to remain indifferent. Furthermore, the *Mātṛkā-sūtra* states in its second instruction:

"If the bhikṣus assemble to perform a formal act (*dharmakarma*) that is not in accordance with the Dharma, and there is someone among the assembly who sees that the monks' performance of the rite is invalid—"
If there are three, four, or five companions, one may admonish them; however, if one is alone, there is no need for admonition. Why is this?

Because the power of a great assembly is vast, and they might expel [the offender], which would be of no benefit to the Dharma and would only cause mutual distress. For this reason, [one should not admonish alone].

One should remain silent and say nothing. If those who receive [the teachings] are capable of discerning things, and later have virtuous companions who see what is contrary to the Dharma, they must immediately reprimand and settle the matter.
Therefore, the text below states: The Buddha told Ānanda, "Āniruddha, when will he be able to extinguish this pure matter?
Is it not the affair of you, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana? Next, I shall explain the text according to its sequence. However, now...
The five positions of the *vyañjana* (phoneme) are divided into two: the first ten are silent, and the subsequent five are harmonious; this is the distinction between silence and non-silence.

If categorized by contrast with the *tathā* (thusness) and *atathā* (not thus), they are likewise divided into two: the first five are not according to the Dharma (*adharma*), and the latter five are according to the Dharma (*dharma*).
Now, based on the preceding explanation of the meaning, regarding the first two sets: the first five are non-Dharmic (adharma), while the subsequent five are Dharmic (dharma).

This distinction between the non-Dharmic and the Dharmic is made in terms of the mind (*citta*). The reason for this is that within the first five, although the objects (*viṣaya*) may be either right or wrong, they are all termed "non-Dharmic" because of the difference in the mind.
In the first case, if it were a Dharmic *karma*, it ought to be performed in harmony; however, because the mind is not [in accord], it is so designated.
The same applies here; it is called "unlawful" (*adharma*). In the second case, since one has obtained a companion who agrees with one's view, one ought to admonish and reprove them;
likewise, remaining silent cannot be called lawful. In the third case, if one sees even a minor offense, it should be addressed briefly provided there are no obstacles.

Although the formal act (*karma*) may be validly accomplished, the Saṃgha commits a *duṣkṛta* offense. One must also reprove the offender for having seen [the fault]; because one fails to reprove them, it is called "unlawful. Alternatively, it may be...

Regarding the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*, when a *karmadāna* (preparer) sees another commit a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*) identical to one’s own, since there is no grave matter involved, it is not permissible to rebuke them;
thus, this is called "seeing a minor offense. The fourth phrase refers to when, during the performance of a formal act (*karmavācanā*), one sees that there is a separate assembly (*bhinna-saṃgha*).

Whether [the assembly] is exposed or secluded, within arm's reach or separated by a barrier, if one remains silent and does not rebuke it, this is termed "unlawful" (*adharmika*). The fifth phrase is as explained in the section on the invitation ceremony (*pravāraṇā*).

When it is time for the boundary (sīmā) to be invoked, one must be present at the site of the precept field (śīla-maṇḍala). If one knows there are monks present alone and remains silent without informing the assembly, taking matters into one's own hands, this is called "unlawful" (adharma).
Next, regarding the five ways of observing the objective sphere, there is likewise right and wrong: if one acts in accordance with the mind’s requirement for silence, it is "lawful" (dharma).

Regarding the first phrase: when one sees another commit an unrighteous act, it is proper to reprove and admonish them; yet, even if one’s words do not penetrate the object [of the fault], it constitutes a formal act (*yathādharma*). Regarding the second phrase:
although one’s words may penetrate the object, because one lacks virtuous companions, remaining silent and failing to reprove is likewise a formal act. Regarding the third phrase:

when seeing one who has committed a grave offense (*guru-apatti*), if one remains silent—even though reproving would have been effective in averting harm within the assembly—it is also a formal act. This applies to both the fourth and fifth cases as well.

The categories of the phrases may be understood from what precedes. Regarding the next five points that should be in concord: the first phrase refers to a legal matter (*dharmakaraṇīya*) that accords with principle;

it is called "in accordance with the Dharma" (*yathādharma*), and because speech is uttered to exhort its accomplishment, it is termed "concordant" (*saṃghaṭita*). The second phrase refers to those who remain silent and acquiesce;

because the matter is in accordance with the Dharma and their minds agree with the action being performed, [it is concordant]. The third phrase refers to those whose physical forms, though obstructed, express their inner intentions through outward signs. The fourth phrase... [text fragmentary]
Although one’s own mind does not discern right from wrong, because it has been heard from a trustworthy person, there is also concord.

Regarding the fifth phrase, during the time when the first four phrases assemble the community, there is concord; this fifth [phrase] refers to one who previously, while within the assembly, acquiesced to what the Saṃgha was doing, thereby expressing their agreement in advance, and thus constitutes concord.
Among these five, the third is concord of intention (*citta-sāmagrī*), while the remaining four are concord of body (*kāya-sāmagrī*).
The minds are in harmony. Furthermore, the first four [factors] are those that should come who have come; the second five are those that should be censured who are not censured;
the third is the granting of consent (*chanda*) by one who should grant it. These five accord with the teaching and conform to reason, and are therefore "harmony.
Regarding the subsequent "non-formation" (*asiddhi*): among the first five, the first three and the fifth are established, because their minds do not agree.

If it were otherwise than the Dharma, the fourth would not be established as being neither mind nor object. Among the next five, the first three are not established, while the latter two are established;
for the mind should be understood as "in accordance with the Dharma" (*yathādharma*). The subsequent miscellaneous points follow the text and cannot be described in full detail.
In Sanskrit it is called *vidadgī* (in the Tang language, "chewing on a tooth-stick").

Next, the *Mahā- and Kṣudra-vinaya-śīla-skandha* is explained. This section exhorts practice by citing the fruits of the Dharma; it likewise serves as a support for the maintenance of the precepts. Within this, there are two parts:

first, the origin story (*nidāna*) concerning the accomplishment of the practice of few desires through the observance of the precepts; second, from the passage beginning "At that time, the Buddha... onwards, the causal conditions.

Furthermore, regarding the dharmas of the virtue of observing the precepts, both great and small, there are five sections in the preceding text: first, the causes and conditions for losing one’s position;

second, from "At that time, the elephant-keeper" onwards, the explicit clarification of losing one’s position; third, from "He instructed the king’s son" onwards, being bound and then released, followed by raising the tally-sticks (*mukha-śalākā*) to deliberate;
fourth, from "At that time, King Udayana approached" onwards, inviting [the Buddha] according to the Dharma and arising [to receive him], yet not accepting the elephant or the gold.

Regarding impure things: in the fifth [section], returning to the monastery, he laid out the matter in succession and informed the Buddha; in response to this instruction, the four [monks] refused to accept elephants, gold, and other such items.
This immediately explains all impure objects. There are eight kinds of impurity, which are extensively censured in various texts.
If one wishes to provide an explanation, it shall be analyzed through three sections: first, enumerating the items and explaining their names; second, what should and should not be possessed;
third, the gravity of the offenses incurred by possessing them. Regarding the first section, the enumeration: first, fields, houses, and groves; second, planting roots and sprouts;
third, hoarding rice, millet, salt, and seeking profit therefrom; fourth, male and female slaves and other people; fifth, raising livestock.
1. Herds of livestock; 2. Sixfold layers of silver coins and treasures; 3. Large beds carved from ivory, gold, and silver, together with cotton mattresses and woolen rugs; 4.

All copper and iron cauldrons and pots—excluding those ten types of vessels not fit for keeping livestock, which are not subject to this restriction; 5. [The remaining items]; 6. [The remaining items]; 7. [The remaining items]; 8. [The remaining items].

If one keeps these eight, they increase a person’s greed and defile their pure mind; therefore, they are called "impure. Although there are variations in quantity between the higher and lower ranks, [they are all considered impure].

[This is] the text. However, it is not the case that [the rules] are insufficient due to being sequential or disordered. Next, regarding the prohibition: among the primary objects, the excessive accumulation of fields and profits is forbidden for individuals;
yet, within one's own dwelling, there is the principle of permission for a certain share. If one were to extensively possess gardens and houses, the Holy One’s regulation does not permit it;
however, a single small room sufficient for one's basic needs is permitted. If one considers the Sangha as a whole, all [of these]...
It is permitted. This is so that the great assembly may be provided for while individuals remain free from greed.

Thus, in the twenty-sixth [section] of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, it is recorded that when various bhikṣus possessed fields, houses, and shops, the laypeople criticized and rebuked them, saying: "We possess fields, houses, and shops because we have the burden of wives and children."
"The various bhikṣus are also like this; how are they different from me? The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha. The Buddha said, "None of these are permitted to be kept.
One who violates this incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense. There were some laypeople who offered fields, houses, and shops to the Saṃgha.
The bhikṣus dared to accept them, whereupon [others] criticized and rebuked them, saying, "These bhikṣus are unworthy of receiving offerings. They reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha...
It is said that the monks shall authorize the *karmadāna* (steward) to oversee this.

Although this is for the sake of the Saṃgha, according to the *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra*, those who are permanent residents of the Saṃgha must number five or more in order to receive [the offerings]. Regarding the second type of object, because it would be excessive if given to individuals, it is not permitted;
however, as there is no burden upon the Saṃgha, it is therefore authorized. As for the third category of objects, if they belong to the noble Saṃgha, all are to be calculated [as such].
Among others, there are those who listen and those who do not. As for those who do listen, it is not as clearly explained above.
Regarding the fourth and fifth [types of] impurity, if one is not ill, all are prohibited; however, if one is old or ill, they are permitted and there is no offense.
Thus, in the third fascicle of the *Mātṛkā-sūtra*, the Venerable Piṅgiyānī was held in high esteem by the people of the kingdom, and he sometimes used a net.
Regarding giving: whether one gives elephants, horses, camels, or carriages, or constructs even a small temple as a gift—Buddha permits the acceptance of all such offerings.
This text also permits riding in a palanquin, provided that a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure attendant) pulls it. Furthermore, the fifth fascicle of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states:
"From now on, we permit the bhikṣus to keep gardeners; if they manage the property donated to the Saṅgha, [the monks may accept] everything."

It is permissible. However, when making a statement regarding giving, one must use pure speech (*viśuddha-vāk*). Thus, the *Samantapāsādikā* (15) states: "If someone gives a gift, the monks' slaves may not accept it.
If he says 'pure person' (*kappiya-kāraka*) or 'attendant' (*parikammakara*), they may accept it. If he gives a cow, it may not be accepted;
however, if he says he is giving the five flavors such as milk and curd, it may be accepted. It is the same for all other livestock."

Sixth, regarding gold, silver, and money: there is no exception for others, whether they are ill or not, as these are all prohibited. This is because their value is great; they increase greed, obstruct cultivation, and cause one to neglect one's duties.

However, within the context of supporting the Path, it is necessary to perform the ritual of purification (*śuddhi-dharma*) and entrust them to a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person who makes things permissible).

By doing so, one may personally avoid transgression. One must always maintain the mental attitude that these are objects purified for the sake of the deceased. As for other matters, they should be understood as previously clarified. If we discuss...

The entire assembly of monks may all obtain the two types of items [bedding and seats] in quantities of seven or eight; there is no distinction between those who are ill and those who are not, nor any question of whether they are permitted or prohibited.

These include cotton mattresses, woolen rugs, and carpets measuring three or five cubits, which may be accepted through the ritual of pure-gift (*śuddhadeya*) and kept. Furthermore, the sixteen types of grazing grounds are also permitted without fault.
All other items are improper, namely: ivory, gold, silver, carved and inlaid large beds, as well as copper, iron, and similar materials used for large cauldrons and pots.
If one considers the perspective of the Sangha, all [monastics] may obtain them. Next, regarding the gravity of the offenses, there are two types: the seven and the non-seven.

Although they increase greed, because they serve as essential requisites for the Path, there is the method of "pure giving" (*viśuddha-dāna*). If they are impure, the fault is grave; it violates the teaching and constitutes a *thullaccaya* offense.

As for the remainder, since they are not essential, the rule of pure giving is not prescribed. Since there is no transgression against purity, possessing them incurs only a minor offense (*dukkaṭa*). Next, the distinction between the Great and Small Vehicles is clarified.

Regarding the Dharma of Preceptual Practice (*śīla-caryā*), there are two parts within the Chinese text: first, the direct designation of the names; second, from "The Tathāgata" onwards, the formal exposition of the practice itself. As for the designation of names:
a *śrāmaṇera* is called "small" because his received body of precepts is incomplete; a *bhikṣu* is called "great" because he possesses the human form and his received body of precepts is complete.
Next is the exposition of the practice. This major section is divided into three parts; the first is the formal exposition of the "Great."

Regarding the practice of the minor dharmas: once this practice is completed, because concentration (*samādhi*) arises from ethical discipline (*śīla*), the second section—beginning with "furthermore, one personally sees that [defilements] below have not yet been severed"—clarifies the cultivation of the practice of concentration.

Once the cultivation of concentration is perfected, because wisdom (*prajñā*) is realized through concentration, the third section—beginning with "he attains a concentrated mind that is pure, free from bonds and burdens"—explains the realization of the five supreme powers and the three types of higher knowledge (*abhijñā*).
The preceding text consists of two parts; the first part clarifies [the preliminary stages].
The ten titles of the Teacher and the three wheels constitute the object for generating faith. Second, regarding the layperson and their titles, this clarifies those who have attained faith;

concerning the renunciant entering the Way, the initial section on the ten titles and three wheels has already been analyzed above. Next, regarding the text on the renunciant entering the Way, there are two parts:
first, it clarifies the minor rules of discipline for śrāmaṇeras; second, from "In conduct, one knows the proper time" onwards, it clarifies [the path].
The *Bhikṣu-mahāśīla-dharma* has two preceding sections. First, it clarifies how a person who has attained faith conceives the thought of renouncing the household life.
Second, from the passage beginning "At another time," it describes the practice of renunciation according to that thought. The first section contains three parts:
first, the Sūtra presents one who has conceived faith and seeks renunciation; second, from the passage beginning "With faith and joy," it presents the matters one should loathe; third...

I shall now briefly manifest what they delight in. Regarding the passage beginning with "The son of a householder named Cūḍapanthaka and others," it is intended to clarify that these individuals, upon hearing the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma, received and upheld it with utmost sincerity, and their minds did not regress; therefore, it says, "They heard the True Dharma."
He then gave rise to faith and delight. Having gained faith and delight, he realized that living as a householder is like being besieged by a prison;
like a jail, it allows for no liberation. Therefore he said, "I am now in a household," and so forth. Since there is something to be weary of, there must be something to rejoice in;

nothing surpasses leaving the home life to cultivate the Way as that which is to be rejoiced in. Therefore he said, "I would rather now... and so forth. As stated in the *Sūtra Attained by Śāriputra*:
Now, as for those who have left the household life: they abandon their parents’ home of birth and death and enter into the Dharma-gate.

Therein they receive the subtle and wondrous [teachings] that cause the Dharma-body to grow; they produce the wealth of merit and nourish the life of wisdom. Next follows the account of the acts of leaving the household, which is divided into two parts:
first, the similarity in outward form; second, from "with the bhikṣus" onwards, the similarity in the Dharma. Within the former section, there are three parts: first, the abandonment of...
That which is loathed is not present at the moment a thought arises; therefore, it is said that "at another time," one abandons wealth, relatives, and things bound to the home.

To now completely cast them off and turn away from them is called "renunciation. Second, shaving the beard and hair and so forth is the practice of what is desired. Third, he and his subordinate [disciples] establish a commonality of the Dharma.
Next, the commonality of the Dharma should include the Three Refuges and the reception of the precepts; their absence in the text is due to abbreviation.
This directly clarifies the practice of following [the precepts]. There are two aspects to this practice: first, the presentation of the essential nature of the ten precepts;

second, the practice of distancing oneself from reproach, beginning with the clause "not taking wives or concubines. In the initial precept of the preceding text, it says, "Those who share the same precepts as the bhikṣus," which reveals what is prohibited here.
The phrase "sharing the same non-killing as the bhikṣus" cites the fruit of the practice, such as the power of renunciation and so forth. This is it.
The antidote is abstention. Loving-kindness is the wholesome root of non-hatred. A sense of shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*) constitute the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*).

Theft and sexual misconduct are treated in the same manner. Within false speech, there is no [separate] antidote; rather, it is through the complete possession of both [shame and dread of blame] that one is freed from the three [vices] beginning with the tongue (slander, harsh speech, and idle chatter), thereby fulfilling the precept of non-falsehood.

This does not mean that the sevenfold śrāmaṇera precepts are fully established [merely by this]. Next, regarding "not looking at" and so forth, the remaining six [precepts] are mentioned together. Next, "distancing."
The practice of detachment can be understood.
Next, the great dharma of upholding the precepts is explained. This section contains two parts: first, citing specific matters to prohibit and prevent transgressions;
second, providing instructions within those matters to initiate practice and cultivate goodness. The former part further consists of two sections: first, describing the ritual conduct.
This causes one to accord with the Dharma of the Path. Second, as for the others who are different from the rest, they practice in vain and do not accord with the Dharma.

The preceding text has three parts. First, it describes practicing that which accords with the Dharma of the Path; when one's actions are compliant and free from entanglements, this is called "the proper time" (*kāla*).

To act in a manner dissimilar to this, characterized by wandering and distraction, is called "improper time" (*akāla*). Next, it concerns knowing contentment regarding clothing and food. Clothing and food are the conditions for sustaining the Path; regarding these conditions—
In this regard, one must necessarily know contentment. This means sustaining the body by returning to the belly; neither increasing nor diminishing [one's needs].

To diminish it harms the physical form, while to increase it leads to affliction. Therefore, it is said: "take only what is sufficient. Next, as for the phrase "the Dharma has come to you," it concerns the deportment of advancing.

Thus it says: "robes and bowl follow of their own accord," and so forth. Next, regarding those who differ from the followers of heterodox paths, such as other śramaṇas—this refers to the śramaṇas of external paths (tīrthikas). This...

Being unable to exert themselves in diligent practice, they know only how to eat their fill, thereby wasting the offerings of the faithful. Seventeen matters are enumerated in total to reveal these faults so that they may be abandoned.

Next, the cultivation of practice is explained; within this section, there are five parts. First is the practice of guarding the gates of the sense-faculties. Second is "That [practice] exists as follows..."

This is the noble restraint of the lower grade, which is the practice of internal austerity and frugality. The third bhikṣu possesses such noble restraint of the lower grade, which is the practice of diligence and awakening.
The fourth bhikṣu possesses such noble restraint of the lower grade, which is the practice of single-mindedness without error.
The fifth bhikṣu possesses such noble restraint of the lower grade, which is the practice of severing all hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*). It is by these that one knows they exist. These are the five.

Wenji: This is because each preceding phrase introduces the subsequent one. The ancient masters established these five phrases solely because they constitute the conduct of the noble ones (*ārya-caryā*);
thus, they are the great method of upholding the precepts for the noble ones. Now, this interpretation is incorrect.

How could it be that when the World-Honored One taught this practice, he did so only for the noble ones and not for the assembly of ordinary beings? Furthermore, after the noble ones have realized the principle, they constantly exert themselves on their own behalf.

Is it not redundant to respond to each matter with such detailed instruction? Furthermore, if this refers to noble ones (*ārya*), how can it be said that one should "cultivate the foundations of mindfulness" (*smṛtyupasthāna*)?

Moreover, among noble ones, what is their stage? Is it only those who are beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), or does it also include all stages of those still in training (*śaikṣa*)? If it is not exclusively noble ones, how can the text state:

"By cultivating and accumulating noble ethical discipline, one attains the noble faculties (*indriya*) and so forth"? If this is an exhortation to cultivate the noble [path], [how do you explain the contradiction]?
Morality (*śīla*) is not itself the noble one (*ārya*). As stated in the aforementioned "Turning the Dharma": "How could these Four Noble Truths themselves be the noble ones?

First, regarding the initial passage which exhorts the protection of the sense faculties, this refers to the morality of the faculties (*indriya-śīla*). This section contains two parts; first, a general and broad presentation of the noble ones.
[The section on] Precepts. Second, it clarifies that although one perceives forms, [the following] explains them in distinction according to the sense faculties.

Regarding the initial passage, "In this matter," it refers to the matter of the sense faculty and its object. "Cultivating and accumulating noble precepts" means that exerting oneself to abandon what is improper is called "cultivating and accumulating.

To cite the essence of what is cultivated is called "noble precepts. These precepts are not themselves noble, yet they are practiced by the noble ones; because they encourage one to act like a noble one, they are so named.
Noble precepts: because one’s conduct arises untainted and is free from craving for superior status, it is said that “internally there is no attachment.

Because one has abandoned faults and perfected one’s practice, awakening occurs with spontaneous ease; thus it is said that “the mind is peaceful and happy. Next, regarding the clarification of the faculties (*indriya*), there are two parts:

first, a detailed explanation according to the individual faculties; second, a general explanation based on their mutual dependence, beginning with the phrase "In this way... The preceding text addresses the eye through four propositions.

First, regarding the sense faculty (indriya) confronting its object: it is said that although the eye is a form (rūpa), this explains how, within that general context, the faculty remains undisturbed with respect to that particular object.
Second, regarding the sense faculty being undistracted: although one views the objective field of forms, one does not grasp at their signs (nimitta).

That is to say, one does not grasp at them as being agreeable or disagreeable, beautiful or ugly, nor does one allow the mind to give rise to defiled attachment toward those forms. Thus, by guarding the doors of the senses, one remains undisturbed. Therefore...
It is said: "The faculty of the eye is firm and abides in tranquility. This explains the general [practice] of cultivating and accumulating noble ethical discipline (*ārya-śīla*).

Third, by eliminating and distancing oneself from evil conduct and its conditions, the mind does not give rise to dualistic thoughts; thus, it is neither greedy toward what is favorable nor distressed by what is adverse.

Therefore, it is said: "Being without covetous desire, one is free from sorrow and affliction. Since the root is guarded, the causes for existence (*bhava*) are forever severed; hence, it is said: "Not..."

[This refers to] the outflowing of various evil and unwholesome dharmas. This explains the general [meaning]. Being internally without attachment constitutes the fourth point, which establishes the essence of practice.

Because one is able to distance oneself from conditions and bring practice to fulfillment, it is said that one "firmly maintains the category of precepts. Because this practice is established, it is called "skillfully guarding the faculty of the eye.
This explains the general [meaning]. Since the mind is peaceful and blissful, and as has been extensively explained regarding the eye, the same applies to the remaining faculties.

The same applies to the *anvaya-nirdeśa* (explanation by analogy). Therefore it says, "The ear and so forth are also thus. Next, regarding the dependence on light (*āloka-pratīkṣā*), the text contains three sections:

namely, the dharma, the simile, and the application (*yoga*). Within the dharma section, the sixfold dependence on the bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana-pratīkṣā*) refers to the triad of faculty, object, and consciousness, which arise through conjunction and depend upon one another for their production.

Thus it says, "within the sixfold dependence on the bases. According to the similes and the application, two [phrases] concerning "well-trained" (*suśikṣita*) are missing here; they should be stated as follows:

One should skillfully train in guarding and maintaining, skillfully train in subduing, and skillfully train in ceasing. Furthermore, one "skillful training" may be applied to each of the two subsequent phrases.
Moreover, ancient masters have correlated these three phrases with the three trainings, stating: guarding and maintaining is ethical discipline (*śīla*);

subduing is wisdom (*prajñā*); and ceasing is meditative concentration (*samādhi*). This interpretation is incorrect, as it contradicts the structural outline of the text. My current explanation is as follows: guarding...

"Upholding" refers to the arising of antidotes, such as mindfulness and wisdom, for the purpose of protection and removal [of afflictions]. "Taming" reveals the essence of its practice: the body and speech become pliant and harmonious.
"Cessation" means that through the perfection of practice, one is freed from faults. Regarding the subsequent metaphors: the level ground and intersecting roads represent the objects (*viṣaya*);

the elephants, horses, and so forth being yoked represent the faculties (*indriya*); and the three phrases beginning with "well-trained" represent consciousness (*vijñāna*). Alternatively, these may be paired and correlated individually with the verses on the Dharma.

[The text] understands this. Next, within the section on the practice of internal provisions (*adhyātmika-sambhāra-pratipatti*), it first restates the accomplishment of the preceding practice; hence it says, "He possesses such [qualities] as these.

Next, it clarifies the essence of the second practice, which consists of two parts: first, an explanation in terms of the Dharma (*dharma-deśanā*); second, the presentation of two analogies followed by their respective applications.

The preceding text consists of three parts. First, a general presentation of the rules for eating. Second, from "nor craving for flavors" onwards, it concerns the cultivation of contemplation to prevent wrongdoing.
Third, from "taking what is sufficient for the body" onwards, it teaches the purpose of eating. Regarding the first, the rules for eating: in all instances of eating, one must know moderation.
Therefore, the aforementioned text says: "Eat with the thought of filling the belly; eat in accordance with this. One must cultivate two practices.
First is the reckoning of merit and the returning of virtue. This means that a single grain of rice is equivalent to a hundredfold labor.

If one’s body lacks pure precepts—or even if one does not maintain them for a set period—then the fruit for the donor will be meager, and the recipient will fall because of that gift. Therefore, the text below states:

"It would be better to swallow a hot iron ball than to receive food offered with faith from a body that has broken the precepts. Furthermore, this applies even if one is fully endowed with the precepts.
If one does not contemplate diligence and so forth, it likewise constitutes falling into the error of receiving alms. Thus, the *Mātṛkā-sūtra*, fascicle two, states:

"If a bhikṣu neither practices dhyāna nor recites the sūtras, nor attends to the affairs of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, yet accepts the offerings of others, he falls into the error of receiving alms.

If one possesses the three types of action (trikarma) when accepting alms, there is no fault. If one previously lacked these three types of action and knows that there is no one to whom they can be transferred or given, then one may accept."

There are two types of giving, both of which fall under the category of "giving. If, after receiving a gift, the recipient maintains mindfulness and reflects upon the donor, the recipient attains great benefit.

Therefore, the *Ratnarāśi Sūtra* states: "If there is a bhikṣu who, having received gifts such as robes, alms bowls, or medicinal decoctions, enters the *anāvartika-samādhi*, he causes that donor to obtain irreversible merit and irreversible karmic retribution."
Kāśyapa, it is as if all the great oceans within the trichiliocosm could be exhausted, yet the merit and reward obtained by this donor cannot be exhausted.
Second, regarding the arising of the mind [of generosity], the *Ratnarāśi Sūtra* states:
When about to eat, one should reflect in this way: "Within this body of mine there are eighty thousand families of worms;
when these worms receive this food, they shall all be at peace and happy. I now nourish these worms with food, so that when I attain *bodhi*, I may nourish them with the Dharma.

Furthermore, one should cultivate the perception of excrement, urine, and so forth, as well as recite verses and the like—this should be understood. Next, regarding the prevention of what is improper (*asat*): there is no such thing as the improper.
Regarding these four: therefore, the *Vyākhyāyukti* states, "All other phrases and sentences should be understood according to the extensive path. The *Tattvajñāna-ṭīkā* explains:

as clarified in the Vinaya regarding the manner in which renunciants receive food, they first observe and then eat; that is, they are free from the four types of observation. First, freedom from playful indulgence:

this refers to being attached to the taste of flavors and seeking gratification by following one's whims. Second, freedom from intoxication through food: [this means] that body and mind are healthy and one does not harbor [attachment].
Third, it is free from [enhancing] complexion; that is to say, food makes the body’s luster fresh and clean. Fourth, it is free from adorning the body;

having eaten, it causes the body’s color and strength to further increase. Because it is free from these four matters, it is said that one "should know" [it]. The present text likewise does not crave flavors.
This is the departure from the fault of attachment to play and pleasure. Sustaining the body is the departure from the fault of intoxication by food.

Furthermore, not speaking of "communication" or "sustenance," yet remaining free from arrogance, is the departure from the fault of [excessive] facial expression. Arrogance is the departure from the fault of adorning the body.
These two—arrogance and the flow toward it—may also be grouped as a pair. The former prohibits the craving for flavors and the nourishment of the body.
Next, one must not give rise to arrogance or conceit. Furthermore, according to the *Mātṛgrāma-sūtra*, at the time of eating the main meal, one should not give rise to anger;
as it is with anger, so it is with the other precepts. Next, regarding the purpose for which one eats, there are two purposes: first, to facilitate spiritual practice.

Second, it causes the body to be at ease. Regarding the "eating" mentioned in the preceding text: it is for the sake of cultivating morality, concentration, and wisdom; therefore, it is said that one attains the cultivation of pure conduct. Next, concerning causing the body to be at ease:
this body in the desire realm subsists by depending on edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*); if one does not eat, it will immediately disintegrate and perish.
Even when eating this food, do not abandon the two analogies; keep these two analogies in mind, for they can eliminate two kinds of suffering:
first, they eliminate past suffering; second, they eliminate new suffering. Therefore, it is said that there is neither increase nor decrease. Thus, the *Śāriputrābhidharma* (Vol. 12) asks:
"How does one sever past sensations and prevent the arising of new sensations? If hunger is the condition, hunger can produce painful sensations in both body and mind.
This is called "old feeling. What is meant by "new feeling"? If one eats in excess, then due to that excess, there arises in body and mind painful feeling; this is called "new feeling.
Since both overeating and under-eating result in faults, it is logical that one should eat with moderation and restraint.
For those who possess strength, this enables them to sustain the body; for those who have no other concerns, it eliminates suffering and affliction. By means of this, the body does not deteriorate.

The continuity of the life-span is dispersed; this is called "peaceful bliss" (*anala*). Next, the metaphorical passage is explained. The first metaphor illustrates the bringing of peace and bliss to the body.
This passage consists of four phrases: (1) men and women represent the monastics and practitioners; (2) the body suffering from sores represents the hunger and thirst of the monastics;
(3) applying medicine represents the nourishment provided by food; and (4) the healing of the sores represents the removal of hunger and thirst. This concludes the application of the metaphor.

This may be understood. Next is the metaphor for attaining the cultivation of pure conduct; its text also consists of four parts. First, "for example, a person returns" is a metaphor for the monastics.
Second, "anointing a cart with oil" is a metaphor for the provisions received as food. Third, "for the sake of wealth and goods" is a metaphor for that which is prayed for. Fourth, "desiring to...

and so forth, is a metaphor for reaching the fruit of the Way, entering from the state of an ordinary person into sainthood, and attaining this liberation. The correspondence between the metaphors and their meanings may be understood accordingly.

Next, the practice of awakening is explained. The text first reiterates the establishment of the preceding two practices. Then, from the section beginning "In the first watch of the night," it reveals the essence of the third practice.
This section is divided into two parts: first, a general indication of the time for exerting cultivation, which briefly omits the "exhaustion of the day" and the "middle watch";

second, from the section beginning "If [one falls] at the exhaustion of the day," it indicates the occasions of decline and the principles for exerting cultivation, as can be understood from the text itself.

Next is the practice of non-confused mind. The text first restates the accomplishment of the previous three practices. From "Always thus" (*sadā evam*) onwards, it presents the essence of the fourth practice.
This section has two parts. First, it opens with two chapters: (1) whether moving or still, one always maintains mindfulness; this is the gate of single-mindedness (*ekacitta*).
(2) One cultivates the contemplation of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) in accordance with the Dharma; this is the absence of confusion in mindfulness.

The Section on Dispelling Confusion. The second part is the chapter on the basis for explanation. First, the subsequent section on mindfulness without confusion is explained; this consists of an introduction, an explanation, and a conclusion.

Within the explanation, there is first a general interpretation of the meaning, followed by a detailed analysis through two gates. First is the explanation of the names; second is the determination of the essential nature (*svabhāva*).

Regarding the explanation of the names: first, the general name "foundations of mindfulness" (*smṛtyupasthāna*) is explained. There are four, namely: body, sensation, mind, and phenomena. For what reason are these four called [foundations of mindfulness]?

They are the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). If mindfulness takes the four [objects] as its basis, they are called the four foundations of mindfulness. Furthermore, it is explained that these four foundations of mindfulness have wisdom (*prajñā*) as their intrinsic nature;
because of the power of mindfulness, wisdom operates upon its objects, and thus they are called "foundations of mindfulness. Alternatively, it is explained with respect to the objects of focus.
First, one gathers and maintains through mindfulness; subsequently, one observes with wisdom to sever the afflictions.

This is like a farmer who first grasps the weeds and other plants with his hand, and later uses his right hand to hold a sickle and cut them. It is the same in this case; therefore, it is called "mindfulness-establishment" (*smṛtyupasthāna*). To explain the specific names:

because mindfulness establishes itself by taking the body as its object, it is called "mindfulness-establishment of the body. This continues up to taking phenomena (*dharma*) as its object, which is called "mindfulness-establishment of phenomena."

Next, the essential nature [of the foundations of mindfulness] is presented. Each of these four foundations of mindfulness has three aspects: namely, the distinction between their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), their dissociation (*vippayutta*), and their object (*ālambana*).
Therefore, while the Vinaya texts speak directly of the foundations of mindfulness without distinguishing these differences, according to the actual principle, each must possess these three aspects.

Among them, the foundation of mindfulness as intrinsic nature has wisdom (*prajñā*) as its essence. The foundation of mindfulness as dissociation has everything coexistent with wisdom, excluding wisdom itself, as its essence. The foundation of mindfulness as object...

The foundation of mindfulness through objects (*ālambana-smṛtyupasthāna*) has as its essence all phenomena that are the objects of wisdom. Next, the text below provides the explanation. First, regarding the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāya-smṛtyupasthāna*), there are three ways of contemplating the body:

contemplating one's own body, another's body, and both one's own and another's body combined. One contemplates the thirty-six impure substances within the internal body, which constantly flow from the nine orifices;
these are truly loathsome and wearying, and though one seeks purity therein, it cannot be found. This is because there are five kinds of impurity.
This is explained in detail as set forth in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. When this contemplation is perfected through the exertion of the mind, it is called "diligence without slackening.
Because right observation manifests before one such that there is never again any notion of purity, it is called "mindfulness without confusion.

When this contemplation is accomplished, it not only eliminates greed but also dispels other afflictions; hence the terms "subduing" and so forth. Although the internal impurity is thus contemplated, one may still fear...
Because it defiles the bodies of others, one next contemplates that others and oneself are no different, being equally impure.

Furthermore, fearing that greed for the object may not be eliminated, one next contemplates impurity by combining the internal and external. Since this is the case for one practice, the same applies to the remaining three;

thus it is said: "Feeling, mind, and dharmas are also like this. Next is the explanation of the "single-mind" gate, which consists of the dharma, the analogy, and their synthesis; the textual structure is easily understood.

Next, the abandonment of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) is explained. First, the prior accomplishment of the four practices is restated; next, the fifth practice is introduced as the basis for delighting in staying below.

This section contains two parts: first, showing the place where one exerts oneself in cultivation; second, returning from alms-gathering to the dwelling place below to abandon the hindrances. Within this, there are again two parts:
the first concerns the skillful means for abandoning the hindrances, such as sitting in the cross-legged posture (*paryaṅka-bandha*), which has been explained previously.

The second section, "Having Abandoned," below, clearly explains the abandonment of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*). This consists of three parts: the teaching (*dharma*), the analogy, and the synthesis. Within the teaching, there is a twofold analysis of the five hindrances.
First is the explanation of their names; second is the determination of their essential nature (*svabhāva*). Regarding the first gate, the explanation of names, the number five is first established:

(1) sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*), (2) ill-will (*vyāpāda*), (3) torpor and drowsiness (*styānamiddha*), (4) restlessness and regret (*auddhatyakaukṛtya*), and (5) the hindrance of doubt (*vicikitsā-nīvaraṇa*). First, the term "sensual desire" is explained.
These are the specific names. To crave and pursue is the meaning of *rāga* (desire). To feel hatred and resentment toward sentient beings is the meaning of *pratigha* (anger).
For the body and mind to be sluggish and stagnant is the meaning of *styāna* (torpor). To cause the mind to become dull and withdrawn is the meaning of *middha* (sleep).

For the body and mind to be restless and agitated is the meaning of *auddhatya* (restlessness). To cause the mind to dwell upon regret is the meaning of *kaukṛtya* (remorse); this very *kaukṛtya* is termed "regret" (*vipratisāra*). This is because...
*Au-dārya* (remorse) is the nature of the mind’s regret. That which causes the mind to be agitated and hesitant is its meaning as "doubt. Next, the general names are explained:
*nīvaraṇa* (hindrance) has the sense of "obstructing" or "covering," meaning it obstructs the Noble Path and the roots of goodness that serve as the preparation for the Noble Path;

therefore, it is called a hindrance (*nīvaraṇa*). *Paryavasthāna* (envelopment) means to cover over all conditioned virtues, preventing them from arising; therefore, it is called an envelopment (*paryavasthāna*). Next...
Regarding the identification of their essential nature: these five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) collectively take the thirty afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm as their intrinsic nature.

Specifically, sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*), ill-will (*vyāpāda*), torpor (*styāna*), sleep (*middha*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), and remorse (*kaukṛtya*) each pertain to all five categories (*pañca-varga*) of the desire realm; thus, five times five makes twenty-five.

Remorse is abandoned only through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), while doubt (*vicikitsā*) is abandoned only through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*). These five, added to the preceding [twenty-five], total thirty. Next...
The following explains the text. By taking material objects as the object of focus, one cultivates the practice of the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) until it is perfected;

thus, being free from defilement, one is not bound by craving. Therefore, it is said that "the practice which remedies stinginess and greed is severed. Because this [remedy] does not share the same substance (*ekasvabhāva*) as that which is to be remedied, it is said that "the mind does not coexist with it.

The remaining characteristics are easily understood. However, within the hindrance of torpor and drowsiness (*styāna-middha-nīvaraṇa*), only "sleep" (*middha*) is mentioned; although torpor (*styāna*) should also be present, it is absent from the text.
This is a brief [explanation]. *Tiao* (restlessness) corresponds to *auddhatya* (excitement), and *kui* (remorse) corresponds to *kaukṛtya* (regret). Next, there are five further metaphors.

The first metaphor illustrates how a practitioner under the influence of the hindrance of greed is driven by greed and lacks autonomy; in meaning, this is like a slave to greed. The practitioner who possesses the sense of autonomy is like a master.
By practicing contemplation to sever greed, one is no longer enslaved by it; in meaning, this is like being born into a noble lineage.
At ease. Having become a servant to that [state], he reflects to himself: "After emerging from the contemplation, the words of Ānanda were followed by a second analogy:

the mind of anger obstructs one's wholesome wealth like a creditor. Furthermore, just as there might be a person who is a practitioner of contemplation, in order to turn away from anger, they take up the property of others and exert themselves in practicing the path;
thus it is said, 'they go about conducting their livelihood. When the contemplation is perfected—"

Because aversion increases, it is said that one can obtain interest and profit. Properly severing the goodness of anger is called "returning the principal. Once this is completed, it is not merely the severance of anger;
one also attains self-composure. Therefore, it is said: "Thereafter, there is equanimity," and so forth. As for "he himself reflects" and so on, Ānanda is as before.

Next, the three similes regarding the manifestation of torpor and sleep cause a person to become dazed, sluggish, and obscured. Therefore, it is said: "It is like a person who has long been ill and grows weary of it."

One cultivates the path and is able to sever lethargy and drowsiness; therefore it is said that one recovers from illness. The flavor of meditative concentration nourishes the spirit, and the inner mind experiences joy, like food being digested.
Once the food is digested, it necessarily provides sustenance; therefore it is said that the body possesses physical strength.

The subsequent stages may be understood accordingly. Regarding the fourth analogy: because there are obstacles of restlessness and remorse, the cultivation of insight is not accomplished; therefore it is said, "It is like a person..."
Having been long confined in the prison, he exerted himself with diligent effort and was able to sever restlessness and remorse;

thus it is said that he has escaped from prison, and his self-congratulation may be known. Next, regarding the fifth analogy: the practitioner diligently cultivates the three trainings, and thus it is said that he possesses abundant wealth and treasures.

Birth and death have no limit, and thus they are called a vast wilderness. Having severed all doubts, they are completely exhausted, and thus it is said that he does not encounter bandits or robbers. He has reached a definitive understanding of the Dharma.

One is not invaded by doubt; therefore, it is said that one passes through [the stage] in peace and security. One rejoices in oneself as described in the text. The subsequent sections can be understood accordingly.

Next, regarding the cultivation of the practice of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the text for the first dhyāna consists of four parts: first, the removal of obstacles to concentration; second, the discernment of the factors for attaining concentration, including the application of the formal teaching with its analogies;
